Here, I made an analogy of this whole situation for you:
What they've basically done is told people about a wonderful mansion they were planning on building for everybody; it would have a waterfall, and monkey butlers, and regular butlers too. If you want to get in on this; drop us some money! You can watch the work come along!
Except, it turns out, they basically have about two walls, and maybe a bit of tarp stretched over a corner or something. Not exactly inspiring stuff; so uh, they're having trouble getting any more people interested in it.
Time to cut it there, they figured, we've made some money on this; let's wrap this up before we invest any more money into it. It turns out they were only planning on building a mansion. Planning! Obviously what we meant by that and what you thought were different things. Our apologies.
But no worries! You have full use of the two walls and tarp. We never got around to adding plumbing, though, or electricity. Also, there's this hobo who keeps trying to shiv people. Finally, uh, the site is contaminated by deadly radon gas, (interesting, because there isn't even a basement) and some of you may have progressive pulmonary fibrosis.
We'll leave a few nails and boards around, if someone wants to improve on things, though. Also, the president of the company is just as bummed about this as you guys are, except not really, because he's got a bit more money out of this deal!
Bottom line: This company has made some good games in the past, but not recently. Early access might work with small studios, but when you've got 60 plus people to support, it doesn't seem as financially viable... Especially when you repay the investors with the early access sales, before the game's even released!
I accept this risk for early access games, but this is the first time I came across a situation quite like this one. I was treating DF by the reputation they had built long ago, not by what they are now. Double Fine? More like Doesn't Finish! or, uh, Don't Fund, or whatever. Boo this company! Boooo!

Rogue Trooper is a bit of a flawed gem. Although it's a few years old now, its' graphics are still fairly good by today's standards. The music, though used sparingly, is above average when present but the story line is nothing particularly special. You are a futuristic clone agent sent to destroy the faction controlling Nu Earth. The games' mulligan is that your comrades can be kept alive in some fashion by pulling the chip located in the back of the skull, where they can continue to narrate your progress through the game. The third person perspective, normally something I do not care for in shooters, actually works fairly well, although the aim assist is so good that veteran players may find the game too easy. Unfortunately the Steam Overlay must be disabled to run this game, and widescreen, though supported, is only available up to 1280x1200 resolutions. None of Rogue Troopers minor flaws detract from the overall experience however, and this game is a fairly good buy.

This game is really different to anything I've seen. In a world where games are mostly violent shooters, or cute and cuddly games, or games with little variation churned out by huge companies, Papers Please is a breath of fresh air. In the beginning you want to obey the game, don't let in that woman, even if it will unlock a secret. Don't follow the order, even if doing it right gets you the best ending. Even trying to not care about your virtual family, who are never seen or named, only known as OK, COLD, SICK, HUNGRY, is not seen as a good thing to do. I must not accept these bribes, they could mess up my track record! My family can go without food tonight. After a while, your heart softens. This guy seems cool, and it's just a silly citation, I'll let him in. My son desperately wants this expensive birthday present. I'll buy it. My niece needs to be adopted. She can some, it's fine. By the end, you should either have a good ending, and the game does offer some replay with the different endings (20 + achievements and collectable tokens). There's only one thing left to say about this game.

This game is absolutely gorgeous. The music, dialogue and visuals meshed seamlessly and beautifully together to deliver a rich and heartbreaking story from beginning to end. I also found the gameplay to be pretty delightful. The combination of turn-based and real-time was great fun, and made me feel like I could keep up, in spite of me usually not being very good at mastering combat controls. The weapons were super customizeable (like Bastion, but next-level), which made it feel like I was totally responsible for every combat success I won, and the little tidbits of story you picked up along the way as the story progress painted a fantastic picture of Cloudbank and the infiltration of the process. Overall playing this game was a great experience and I highly recommend playing... but maybe keep a box of tissues nearby, Supergiant really knows how to yank the ol' heartstrings.

So, you want an old school RPG adventure ? This is it ! Legend Of Grimrock starts you off with 4 prisoners, in a mountain, consisting of 13 levels. These levels are filled with puzzles, evil creatures, traps and more and, obviously, it gets increasingly difficult along the way.
However, the difficulty is a bit random at times. Near the end it took me literally minutes to take down one enemy, even though I had some proper spells and weapons. There are moments where you will be overwhelmed by quite a few enemies. Remember to save often, and try not to lose any of your party members before you reached the end of a level. I had to finish a level with just one rogue and it took me 3-4x longer than it should've.
The game can be finished in about 10-12 hours (in-game time) but in reality it should take you about twice as long.
You will die several times, and some puzzles require thinking, experimenting or just plain luck.
But despite the difficulty, I did have a great time with it !

CONS:
- Moves can be buffered meaning if you spam a button Warren will continue to attack for a while as you buffered an input, this can get frustrating if you spam the attack button too much during a fight.

PROS:

overall I would highly reccomend this game to anyone who enjoys the soulslike formula but I don't feel it is as friendly as dark souls is for a newbie to the genre, in my opinion it requires some of the transferable skills from games like dark souls demon souls and bloodborne as basic combat with normal enemies is more challenging than in other similar games

Pros:
- A return to Dark Souls 1-type of exploration. Relies less on connected smaller areas like Dark Souls 2 and 3 but instead you have a very large enviroment to explore in which you unlock shortcuts to make traversing it quicker as you go. I very much prefer this style, so it is a big plus.
- Enjoyable and meaty melee combat. I daresay it is even better than Dark Souls in some regards, especially when it comes to the bigger and heavier stuff which feel properly impactful and while still slow they flow a lot better than the Greatweapons of Dark Souls.
- Controls perfectly fine with mouse and keyboard. We all know how notoriously bad the Dark Souls-series is on this point, but The Surge definitely pulls it off flawlessly.
- Runs perfectly fine, even on my gaming laptop which is in the middle-ground between "Minimum" and "Recommended" specs.
- POISE! PRAISE THE SUN! The type of exo-skeleton rig you are wearing has stat akin to Poise in Dark Souls, only it actually matters - a lot! When you are wearing the lighter and more agile rigs, you are often sent flying into the air if you are unfortunate enough to get hit by an enemy with a heavy weapon. Wearing the beefiest rigs will not only reduce the damage taken, but keep your feet firmly planted on the ground!
Cons:
- No character creation whatsoever. Now this could be excused if the main character was written in such a way that his set of characteristics were central to the plot, but not as much. There is one spoilerific characteristic he has at the start of the game, but that could easily be given to anyone else. The role he plays could be filled by a myriad of different people.
- No online component whatsoever. Whether you loved it or hated it, the multiplayer aspect is a huge part of the Soulslike-experience and it is definitely noticable in it's absence.
- Retains the dumbest gimmick from Lords of The Fallen: You won't get the "proper" boss weapon unless you defeat the boss while meeting a specific condition. There is no way to know what that condition is in-game as you are fighting them,  forcing you to either spoil the game for yourself by Googling all the bosses and what to do or to miss out on the good version of their weapon. While there is NG+ to let you fight them again, the bosses can't be re-fought in your current NG.
Overall I'd still recommend the game because I feel the positives heavily, heaaavily outweights the negatives.

I played the early prototype of this game that I got with HumbleBundle's Amnesia Fortnight bundle, I liked it the concept but it was clearly in very early stages. Sadly, what we have now is not very different, even though the graphics have been improved.
DoubleFine was looking to cash in on games like Prison Architect. They even said as much themselves. They got investors involved (and successfully paid them off with the huge volume of Steam customers) and then when it wasn't as hot as they wanted, they cut development, did some more sales to lure in a few more suckers and then pulled the plug. In that order.
Most of the people who hadn't bought it yet were waiting for beta or full release, but DoubleFine wanted to make all their money up front. Their business model for this title depended on it, and it is a flawed and presumptuous business model that screws over the consumer.
"Obviously, spending more money than we were making isn’t something we can afford to do forever." - Tim Schafer
Considering that in traditional gave development the developer puts in all the work up front, making the investment in themselves to deliver a great product. In this case, we, the consumer took all the risk. And they took none, while never intended to deliver a full game if it wasn't a pre-release hit with a cult following. Does this sound like a sane sustainable business plan to you? Well, if it does, then congratulations your name is Tim. And Tim, we can't afford to keep spending money on products that never materialize.
I own Prison Architect and its a much more complete game, I recommend getting that instead. It lacks the character and personality of DF-9 and the setting and style is radically different, but its clear that they share the same underlying concept.

After playing for, lets see... about 9 hours, I think I have a understanding of what this game has to offer. It kinda makes me sad... too see all that potential wasted, because of mind-boggling decicions in game functions (I will list some of these below) and despicably predatory business model via micro transaction. However, with all that being said I still can understand anyone that gives this game a "thumb up" because it very much "feels" like a quality mmorpg. Here are pros and cons the way I see it.
Pros:
- Graphicly the game looks pretty nice. Not eye-poppingly good, yes but in its own cartoony way very pleasing.
- Skill/Passive tree is reasonably interesting and the skills look good.
- You get 4 stats per level that you can allocate to strenght, stamina, intelligence, dexterity or luck, which adds to diversity. Im a fan of that.

Cons:
- ... but the fact that you can affect the UI very little is a huge turn off
- No W,A,S,D movement in a game that claims to be a high speed action mmorpg??
- You can not target enemies in any other way than by clicking them individually... no TAB targeting.
- I mentioned the micro-transactions, right? Prepare your wallet if you want to 1) travel quickly between areas, and receive more xp gold 2) have more inventory space... the starting inventory space is no where near enough and the only way to get more space is to buy it with real cash! 3) Maximise your effectiveness in battle since some of those cash shop cloths give you stats.. (I hate when games do this) 4) just buy any potions or anything from cash shop! Why bother spending in game gold on potions since you can just buy them from Cash shop? lol
- The game offers nothing new in terms of innovations...
- I didnt find any way to que up for instances or dungeons or anything..? Yet the game frequently gives you quests that require 4 players in the team/higher level... talk about frustrating.
Now you may be thinking why did I say that I can understand those that give this game a thumb up?... yes, the game is very generic and offers very little new for a mmorpg vet, and yes, it has a lot of micro-transaction barriers but if you dont mind micro-transaction and you prefer click movement/targeting you may like this game! Then again there are better mmorpgs out there.
Im going to have to go with "not recommended". Good try for your first (?) mmorpg Katauri Interactive... try harder next time (and please little less micro-transactions? please)

So I rarely do serious reviews, but I do love this game enough to want a good review to be seen.
First things first; this game is NOT pay to win, in ANY way.
Everything in the game, yes, EVERYTHING, can be purchased with gold. If somoene buys an item with real money, they can sell it for in game gold, and people frequently do.  This is one of the best systems of any free to play ive ever seen.  If you dont feel like spending 5$ to get a "real money" item, just wait til someone else buys it and sells it.  You can just get enough in game gold to buy it off them when you want!
I could continue, going on and on about the game in paragraph form, but ill simply list the Pros and Cons.
PROS:
- Fantastic Music
- Responsive/noncomplicated UI
- Veried Environments and Enemies
- Varied Missions and mission rewards
- Tons of weapons, hats, shirts, pants, shoes, etc; all with unique stats
- Gear Upgrading system. (Find a reall nice piece of gear? Upgrade it and make it better!)
- Lack of Pay-to-Win Elements
- Devs are active! They do announcements in game, as well as work on updates, and help players who are having issues.
- Fantastic community. If youre a new player, 99% of the community will answer any question you have and try to help you along the way!
----------------------------
CONS:
- Occasional bugs, but nothing major
- Bag size is relatively small to start with (this can be expanded at any time)
- Some Quests have you running across large portions of the map, and you move slowly at first (better gear can fix this "problem")
- Game is still in Beta. (This will obviously change, leading up to the full release)
----------------------------

*I decided to revamp this review since the game has been moved to Unreal Engine.
Version: Alpha 0.1.3
Please note that i haven't play Minecraft before (although i have seen some screenshots). I doubt that it'll make any difference with the review though.
Voxelized is a sandbox game about destroying blocks. The looks are similar to Minecraft, as it is claimed to be the said game's clone.
The game has a similar look to the old Minecraft game, with more details and lighting in it. If you have played the game before it moved to Unreal Engine, the models and the lighting is better than the previous one.
There is only one music playing (and one sfx whwhich is quite relaxing and can make you sleep, especially when you are super tired.
The game will start in full screen and you can't change it. The cursor runs very slow to me before i change all of the options in the setting to low. However, the game asks for a firewall permission when i run it for the first time. I don't know if it's because of the Unreal Engine or the game but you can completely skip it because the game will run with the popup on.
There are some improvements in the game compared to the previous version (before it moved to Unreal Engine). First, there is a HP bar, which will be reduced when you fall from a high place. You'll be automatically moved to the main menu when you run out of HP and there is no way to fill your HP bar.
The controls has been revamped, which makes all of the previous control to be useless, except the wasd button. However, just like how it used to be, the controls aren't mentioned anywhere.
There is an inventory which can be accessed with E button. You can use the inventory to switch the items from the inventory slot to the hotkey slot (which is 1-9) and vice versa. However, although there are a lot of items which can be picked and used, all of them will do the same thing, which is "smashing the blocks" into cubes which can be picked up (and can be used to "smash other terrains").
The feature to build blocks in the previous version is completely gone, although you can have some blocks in the inventory (which is supposed to for that purpose).
The last thing i want to say is that the world loads faster after it switched to Unreal Engine.
Pros:
- A big world to do some exploring
Cons:
- All items do the same action
- The HP feature needs some tinkering (do something with it aside from "death by fall" mechanic)

The Surge is Deck 13's second attempt to make a Souls-style game, and their second failure. It's clear that the developers tried to copy the key elements of the souls games, and also that they completely misunderstood how to execute any of those elements.
The first thing most people think of when they think of the Souls games is the difficulty, and, while it's certainly true that they're difficult games, it's a means to an end. The difficulty in the Souls games is there, not for the sake of making a hard game, but to give the player a sense of accomplishment whenever they make progress. When you beat a Souls boss for the first time, or find a bonfire in a new area, you feel a big sense of relief and accomplishment. You think "oh man, I did it!" The Souls games also have pretty solid, smooth difficulty curves that make that sense of accomplishment a consistent thing, without ever pushing the player TOO hard. That's not true in The Surge.
The difficulty in The Surge is more accurately described as a series of increasingly steep cliffs, rather than a smooth incline. Within any given area, the difficulty rarely changes outside of a few encounters here or there (basically whenever you have to fight multiple enemies at once), but jumping from one area to the next is ALWAYS a big difficulty spike, and it very quickly (as in, by the third area), got to the point that the game stopped being fun, and that sense of accomplishment disappeared and was replaced with the ever present thought of "what garbage are they going to throw at me next?" Not only was that the case, but Deck 13 seems to have misunderstood how the Souls games even create challenges in the first place. It's incredibly rare that there will be a difficult encounter in the souls games simply because the enemies have big numbers (health and damage). The vast, vast majority of the time, it's a matter of figuring out the enemy's moveset in Souls, but in The Surge the later game enemies are made difficult not by having interesting, challenging to counter attacks, but simply by having large health bars and 1-2 shotting the player regardless of loadout.
Speaking of encounter design, that's another major draw to the Souls games. Specifically, the boss designs are largely fantastic, but the majority of normal enemies are also fine to great. Incredibly rarely will there be a fight that's simply bad, and lacks any redeeming qualities though they do exist (*cough*BedofChaos*cough*). Nearly every fight in the Souls games is at least tolerable, with a few HUGE standouts in each game that are a joy to fight every single time. This is also not true in The Surge (there's a trend here).
There wasn't a single enemy I enjoyed fighting in The Surge. Not one. Normal enemies ranged from minor nuissances to walking dumpster fires I did everything in my power to avoid. The "best" enemies were the ones that fought most like the player, and the worst were the ones that played by entirely separate rules, but none of them were good. They were either too simple and mindless to fight and as a result were simply boring, or they were jam-packed with obnoxious attacks that, while not necessarily difficult to deal with, were very frustrating for bad reasons. I don't mean to imply that bosses are any better, of course. Every boss was incredibly easy relative to the area they were in (barring the first boss, of course, since the first area is basically a tutorial), and none of them were fun to fight. Even the two humanoid bosses, which should have been the best fights in the game, were simply not fun as a result of the devs not knowing how to make a difficult, interesting humanoid enemy. Rather than those fights being straight fights against another human, following similar rules and using similar tools (like the best fights in the Souls games), they're basically bulkier normal enemies that go away for a bit so you can fight a giant, easy enemy instead for a while.
I'd say that the third major draw to the Souls games is their replayability. There's a good variety of weapons and builds in the Souls games, such that you can play through each multiple times, while getting a different experience each run through. In The Surge, however, there's a whopping 5 weapon types, with no variation in moveset in any given type, and there's no build variety because there are no dedicated builds of any sort in The Surge. Rather than getting a point to invest in a stat of your choice on level up, levelling in The Surge just increases your "Core Capacity" which basically functions as equip burden. Your health doesn't increase, your damage doesn't increase, nothing besides "core capacity" increases on a level up. Naturally, you'd assume that Deck 13 included a wide variety of interesting effects on gear so that you can still get an amount of variety that way, and you'd be wrong. Gear has minor percentage changes on some stats (like a 5% attack speed increase, or a -10% dodge stamina cost) that is hardly noticable, and the Implants that function as  something similar to rings offer equally uninteresting changes to your character. Implants can either be boring passive stat increases (the only way to increase your max HP, Stamina and Energy), or equally boring consumables (healing items and damage buffs). The Surge doesn't even have the benefit of a long critical path with lots of side content like Nioh (the only non-Fromsoft game to successfully execute on the Souls formula), as I finished it in almost exactly 11 hours and there's basically no side content to speak of beyond backtracking to open some locked chests from early areas.
The Surge tried to copy the Souls games, and that's a bold effort in its own right. The Souls games set an incredibly high bar for their own sub-genre of ARPG, but The Surge falls so incredibly short that it can't even see the bar it's trying to meet. I would just recommend playing the Souls games instead, or, if you have a PS4, Bloodborne and Nioh.

Five hours of gameplay.
TLDR - Combat feels very solid. I love the heavy industrial theme.
Been spending most of the time exploring a very well crafted, and what feels like a very huge industrial facility. There are many, many shortcuts that you'll discover that loop around back all over the place. You'll be fighting crazed exosuit employees, industrial machines/robots that feel like they do belong in their environment.
For equipment, the player will be using what feels like industrial tools as weapons, drones that support you in combat, installing hardware onto your exosuit that give you buffs (+HP, extra healing, +damage, +energy gain, blah blah blah).
Weapons and armor are obtained mosly from chopping limbs off of enemies that are carrying it. See that guy with giant hammer? Go cut his arm off and take it. Oh that worker gal has some fancy looking armor, go chop her head off and take her fancy hat. Because that is what's important, hats.
The combat is fast and has a decent amount of challenge to it that has felt very fair thus far. Different weapons have their own movesets. Different armor give different trade offs, less stamina consumption for dodging but less armor and stability, etc.
During combat you will be building up suit energy, which can be used for dismembering enemy limbs, injections that grant buffs, or using your drones abilities. Energy gained during combat will slowly start to drain as you exit combat. So it provides another layer of resource management during combat to use extra abilities to aid you.
Medbays act as a hub area for a location. You'll spend your time here upgrading your equipment and possibly interacting with some other characters stuck inside the facility.
Something I thought was interesting is that leveling up your character only increases your maximum exosuit power and unlocks additional upgrade slots for injections. Your suit power is used to determine how much equipment you can equip on your exosuit. Armor and injections require a certain amount of suit power in order to install on your suit. Your suit power is also used as a way to gate content. Some doors and devices can only be activated if you meet the requried amount of power to activate said device. So backtracking to unlock that door that requries 75 power from the beginning of the game is definitely a thing.
So if you're interested in applying for a job at Creo, I'd recommend it. It might be slightly painful though, but just think of all the vacation time you'll get every month.
And no, there isnt any character customization or gender options.

You ever watch How It's Made, and stay awake long enough to see those huge factories making stuff like cakes or lightbulbs? Hundreds of machines, all interconnected, conveyor belts snaking too and fro between them, devices performing task after task, all working in harmony to spit out the insane number of cakes needed to satisfy the regional demand on a daily basis...
That's factorio. Only you cant make cake... yet.
Sure it's simple enough on the surface. I build a machine here, to take item X, and turn it into item Y. Then I take Item Y, combine it with item Z, make item Q out of that mixture, which gets mixed with items C through F to create item B, which in turn gets used to build a solar panel, for a rocket you're building and launching into space. Definitely not cakes.
It's a game about complexity, automation, and solving problems. This is not a game for everyone, and even those who like it usually shut it down in a moment of crushing depression after overcoming the first few hours with the game. But if you stick with it, keep working out the problems, and get your factory running smoothly, I can almost garauntee you'll be hooked.
This game is rewarding in a way i havent seen in a long time, partly because it doesnt hold your hand at all. Everything in your factory is where you put it, set up the way you set it up, and it lives or dies by your decisions. But let me tell you, when you power up a factory block for the first time, and see it smoothly working, doing exactly what it should, the way you want it, it feels damn good.
...until you realise your iron output is woefully sub par and your new production branch is starving out the rest of your factory. But that's just another problem to overcome.
TL;DR, It's a solid game for those looking for a real time sink. Stable branch is very stable. Bugs are very rare and I've personally never experienced a crash, even with 50+ mods running in the background. Not much end game, but just getting ot that point will take multiple hours. Would reccomend.
Only you know how your factory works, where it starts, where it ends, how to configure it, how to manage it and .... how to make it even better although being close to perfect.

Transistor is truly one of a kind.  Let me start with artistic style, and original music.  The art was amazing in my opinion, and truly made me captivated.  It has its unique style, that makes one say "That's Transistor."  What's great is you get these backdoors throughout the game, and it is an oasis for Red and Blue.  As you do challenges, you unlock more music.  You can play that music, and then have Red hum to the different tunes.  It's an artistic wonder to have that many original tracks with a voice track in a single game.
Second, is battle system.  I havven't played anything like it, and I've played a crap ton of games.  It is both real time and turn based action.  You can battle a fight completely with real time, completely with turn based, or a mixture of both.  I typically used a mixture of both.  You gain these chips or programs, I forget the word it has been a while, that gives Blue various abilities.  You can then use these abilities as passives, or as an "upgrade" to others.  Basically, the sheer variety of your loadout is astounding.  I would say the game doesn't promote experimenting that much, because enemies don't spawn like other games.  It is a pretty linear game, albeit an enjoyable one.  But with a press of a button, you can go from real time to turn based.  It's really really cool.
The story.  The story is vastly profound.  All one has to do is look at this game's forums and look at the constant analyzation of the story.  It's one of those stories that if you want to get the full grasp of it, you are going to have to play the game multiple times.  If you are a gamer that likes to over play a game many times, as I have known some personally, then this is a great game for you.  I personally play a game, beat it, then move on to beat the next game.  I personally did not understand the entire story, as I had to go to the forums to understand it some more.  But I will say, even with the various theories as to what the story is trying to convey, it is a true piece of art as there is no right or wrong answer.  You take away from art what you will, and only you.
If there was a museum for video games, I would put it in there.  It's that good.
It's okay.

What a fun little game this is! It is a very lightweight game which offers a surprising amount of dungeon crawling enjoyment! I think it's beauty lies in it's simplicity - it's basically just a 2D grid environment with 3D perspective graphics. Your party of 4 adventurers take up one tile and can only move one tile at a time either north, south, east or west. Combat is basically hack n slash but there is quite a bit of timing involved and strategy with how you use your 2 'front row' characters who can melee directly as opposed to the 2 'back row' characters who can either use ranged attacks/magic or perks to do melee attacks from afar. But sometimes you might find yourself cornered where monsters surround you and take big bites out of your typically soft back row guys.
There are alot of interesting puzzles some of which can drive you mad trying to figure them out! I really also like how food plays into the game (your guys need to eat!) and how items are very scarce.
Absolutely a gem of a game! A refreshing break from the generic genres nowadays.

The game itself had so much promise, and due to the mismanagement of the dev team and lack of experience with the Early access model they have essentially decided to early realease the main 1.0 without many of the features promised. For people who are interested in puzzle RPGs this one is elegant and original. Each turn you select a monster and kill all the contiguous monsters. The damage you take is based on the creature type, but not how many you kill. Your reward is based on the number you kill. This drives you to select large groups - but the special abilities on the monsters and that you have often make simply finding the largest group a bad strategy.
There are lots of items giving special abiilities and characters. The monster abilities make each one feel different, not just bigger numbers.

This is a group Match 3 game.  The goal is to get as far as possible within the tower.  Matching is a delicate balance between gaining and losing life.  Choose wisely.
Every group you match costs life hearts (some creatures can leave health items as well).  The indicator shows how many hearts the group matching will cost you as well as how many gold coins it will gain you.  Gold coins is how you level up to the next level and replish all of your hearts.  Also, going through a door will replenish some small amout of hearts.  There are also food items that can replenish some health.  When you reach zero health you die!  Balance between short term (losing hearts) and long term (gaining gold to level up and replenish all hearts).  Choose wisely.
You need to find the key to advance to the next level (and replenish mosters for better matching choices).  Keys can also open chests.  The keys are hidden amongst the monsters and only a match with that monster reveals the key.  You don't know when you will find those precious keys.  Choose wisely.
Still, there's more...  you can find items that help.  Gain three extra hearts when moving through a door.  Match diagonally instead of in groups (turn it on or off).  Boomerang that kills one monster with a 70% chance of returning.  Only four slots and many possible items.  You might need to hold off of that chest item just to escape to the next level.  Maybe you really need that chest item right now as it could heal you to full health.  Choose wisely.
Yet even more... monsters have special abilities that will determine the best way to match them (or avoid them).  When passing through a door, one of the monster types at random is removed from the board, and more difficult monsters fill the match grid back up.  Balance between which monsters to match and when.  Choose ... well, you get it.
This is not a blind matching game.  Every match counts.

I really enjoy this game, except for a few bugs which make it feel unfinished and prevent me from recommending it. Otherwise, it's a fun puzzle game. There is a lot of variety in the items you might find, the characters you can play and the enemies you face. The different characters, items and enemies all make different strategies more or less viable. Combined with the flexible difficulty system, there is a lot of room for replayability.
You have to find a balance between fighting and climbing. The early game is a lot easier than the late game, so it's easy to get overconfident and fight yourself into a dead end. This was frustrating for a while until I got a better handle on the balance.
The bugs I mentioned:
1. The gold meter doesn't work when hovering over money bags or pots.
2. The gold meter is often incorrect after leveling up (shows mostly full when it should be empty).
3. The difficulty scoring isn't balanced. You can get a higher score by cranking up the difficulty and dying on the first level than by beating the game on normal mode.
4. There are a few minor misspellings ("ennemies" instead of "enemies", and so on).
5. Some items don't actually do what they say, or don't do anything at all. (sandals, life ring)
6. Sometimes the final boss disappears and the game can't be completed.

The Last Warlock is one of those indie games where the small publisher was able to realize a unique and interesting vision.
There's a lot of variety in how you can play.  Early in single-player, I was trying to keep and equip a reasonable front and back line of summons:  I would keep two zombies (and later, wraiths) around with beat-em-up sticks and shields (and later, scythes, for those undead bonuses) and then have two trolls on the back line hucking rocks and any shurikens I made with leftover steel.  Later, as mobility become more and more important, I started instead summoning a flying mount and pimping out my own archery skills.  Once I found the materials for a bow, I would fly around on my griffin strafing land-bound opponents and then resurrecting them as .
The levels are entertainingly designed and always different enough that no one strategy feels like it's inherently better than the others.  Flying mounted archers are very strong, but the fact that you have to craft or plunder ranged weapons balances them out a bit, and I suspect mounts are less OP in multiplayer where the enemy can focus them down.  You always have multiple objectives and limited time to complete them (kill the enemy warlocks, get all the gems).
Verdict:  A hidden gem!  Incidentally, you're going to be looking for a lot of those!

Veredict: So far, I really like The Surge.

It's pretty straightforward. You are an inspector at a checkpoint for a country with an oppressive government, where you barely manage to get by, and your job is obviously to inspect the documents given (or sometimes, not given) by people who wish to enter the country. If their documents are good, you let em through. If not, you turn them away or detain them depending on their papers (forgery = detain), and if you make a mistake, you are punished by losing your MONIES! If you fail keep your MONIES (credits), you and your whole family will likely die horrible deaths. As you play, more variables and things you must check for pop up, leaving you somewhat paranoid about letting people through (or at least for me, every time I used the green approval stamp I was just waiting to see what I overlooked). It's a very fun game, and the story is pretty great (there are multiple endings depending on what you do, and some pretty sweet token-achievement-things you can get by making some choices). This is another plain ol 'good' game that deserves much praise. If you haven't gotten it yet, I really do recommend that you do so.

Transistor's highlights include a highly flexible and customizable combat system, a gorgeous blend of 2d and 3d graphics, and an interesting mechanic where your narrator is also your companion and weapon.  The combat system is a hybrid of a 2d isometric action game and a turn based strategy game.  The story itself is intriguing, however it never manages to reach the heights of interest that appear to be hiding right behind the narrative.  The story leaves too much unsaid and doesn't give you enough information about the world you are in.
There are numerous challenge zones that require you to defeat enemies in specific ways that help show the depth of the combat, and there are about 15 special limiters you can equip to make combat more difficult... and rewarding.  The new game plus, though nowhere near as interesting narratively as this stuido's last game, Bastion, allows you to continue to develop and improve your abilities, and fight tougher enemies.
I highly recommend this game for its combat and art alone.  The soundtrack is also worth the price of admission.

-The voice acting is absolutely superb. From what I understand they used actors who were actually members of the nationalities they were speaking as. This game is an example of how bad the Early Access model can be. The plan of the developer, Double Fine, was to fund the development from the start with the sales of the (prototype of the) game, reduce drastically their initial investment, and hope that their good name and promises on how they imagined the final game were enough to attract customers. The 'experiment' failed completely because most people interested in the game were holding their purchase to see how the developers were updating the game. It became a self-fulfilling prophecy of failure, in which due to the lack of sales the developers were not able to assign more efforts to the game and, at the same time, exactly that slow development was the reason behind the low amount of sales.
To come to an end to this grotesque scenario, Double Fine decided to stop the development and release the game as it is currently. The game is still in its bare bones and the experience is lacking in many areas, but they will create a tutorial, tools to create mods, and hope for a nonexistent community to continue its development.
About me: I've been a big fan of Double Fine games during the last years. I loved Psychonauts and Monkey Island, funded the Kickstarter of Broken Age and enjoyed other games like Costume Quest, Stacking or The Cave. This is the first dissapointment. It has destroyed the trust that I had in DF and, in the future, I will behave with them as if they are an unknown dev without credentials. I will investigate with caution about their games before buying or I will simply ignore them. Also, I won't buy any Early Access games and advice others to do the same.

This game is just fantastic. You can really feel how much love went into this. It is a mix up of different genres, working out together in an absolutly brilliant way. I already had bought the game on iPad and decided to aquire it again on PC. The PC-version is even better, as controls with mouse an keybord are a tad more fluent.
The Game is turn-based and about defeating the opponent's Warlock. Each warlock can cast spells, which either work directy ("fireball") or summon creatures that fight for you. Each creature has it's own characteristics, strengh and weaknesses. There are chests with power-ups to discover, secrets, weapons to use and items to craft. The envoirment ist distructable and can be included in your strategy. You gain items to "level-up" different characteristics, that suit your gameplay best. Just awesome !
The interactive Tutorial explains the concepts very good, there is a single-player campain and online multiplayer. Multiplayer is just so much fun, unfortunatly there aren't many players, as the game is (totally unjustified if you ask me) still not very known.
It ist so much fun to let your own creativity play in this game. For me the best game of 2015!
Update 6th of June: As you can see, the dev is really behind this and still droping updates and additional content for free. You can't do nothing wrong, buy it for 6€!!
Deutsch:
Dieses Spiel ist einfach fantastisch, Man sieht wieviel Liebe der Entwickler da hineingesteckt hat. Es ist ein Misch-Masch zwischen verschiedenen bereits bekannten Konzepten, das einfach funktioniert und viel Spaß macht. Ich hatte mir das Spiel bereits auf dem iPad geholt, und da es mir so gut gefallen hatte, habe ich es mir nochmal erworben. Die PC-Umsetzung ist genauso, wenn nicht noch besser, da die Bedienung mit Mouse und Tastatur einfacher ist.
Es geht im Prinzip darum, den gegnerischen Hexenmeister (Warlock) zu besiegen. Jeder Warlock kann Zaubersprüche wirken, die entweder direkt wirken ("Feuerkugel"), oder Monster heraufbeschwören, die für einen Kämpfen. Jedes Monster hat seine eigenen Fähigkeiten, Stärken und Schwächen. Es gibt Waffen zum Ausrüsten und Gegenstände zum "Craften", Geheimnisse zu entdecken. Die Umgebung ist zerstörbar, was man nutzen kann und man kann seinen Charakter "aufleveln" wie es zu einem passt. Alles wird rundenbasiert ausgespielt.
Das interaktive Tutorial erklärt einem gut die Steurung und Prinzipien, eine Einzelspieler-Kampanie ist vorhanden und auch online-Mulitplayer. Multplayer macht einfach so viel Spaß, nur leider gibt es nicht so viele Gegener, da dass Spiel leider (zu unrecht meiner Meinung nach) unbekannt geblieben ist.
Es macht sehr viel Spaß die eigene Kreativität spielen zu lassen und dieses Spiel zu entdecken. Meiner Meinung nach das beste Spiel 2015

Hi, this is the first time I have written a review and I feel 'The Surge' earns it. (ye, it's short and sweet)
Combat:  A new unique dodging system and the option to slice limbs to secure weapons and hit weak spots really makes it fun.
UI: Clean and crisp, i can't see anyone having any trouble.
Story: Not the greatest but certainly not the worst (13 hours in). I'm not much of a story guy so I feel slightly biased on this section. The only part I would mention is that you are limited to the one character and there isn't an initial character creation screen.
Loot/Weapons/Armour: While there many not be an initial creation screen, there certainly is a wide variety of weapons and armour to choose from as long as you slice your enemies limbs and collect the schematics. Oh and you can also receive special loot for killing bosses in a special way - no idea about this yet but im sure some of you people will find it out and let me know so i can look at it and then never attempt it.
Audio: I have come very close to releasing many chocolate hostages playing this game and I wouldn't change it for the world. It's intense, atmospheric and makes you wonder what is behind every corner. Ultimately, this is my favourite part of The Surge.
If you're a die hard dark souls fan this may not live up to your expectations but then again what will. But, if you're looking for a solid follow up to LOTF and a game similar to Souls then I definitely recommend it. I have enjoyed 13+ hours of bliss and I can't wait to get back on tomorrow.

If you're a fan of the Souls series at all this game is such an easy recommend, the combat is right up there and even better in some aspects.
The envirnoment and enemy variety is a little lacking compared to the game that inspired it.
The repetitive envirnoment gets a little annoying as you progress because everything sort of starts to look the same, and when you have to seriously backtrack and find specific doors you can now open it's hard to find because everything looks the same.
It's one of the two major faults in the game, the second being how the difficulty is managed. Individual enemies are tough enough but as you progress into the game, they make it harder simply by putting more enemies at you at once. Not a fun or compelling way to increase the difficulty. The first half of the game is really superb though and the pacing feels really good.
If you're a newcomer to this "genre" I wouldn't personally start with The Surge unless the setting somehow is just that appealing to you. There's better more fully fleshed game to be found in the latest iteration of the Souls series, with that said I have high hopes and expectations that Deck13 can make this into a flourising franchise that will eventually steer right in regards to level and enemy design.
I'm not a numbers person, so I will just give this game a rating of recommended, especially if you can find it a little cheaper than the price on steam.

For a game that is seen as "Dark Souls style" it does things rather differently.
The combat is far more hack and slash, and you will be using combos and finishers to win fights. Targeting specific points on the body will return different rewards, if you want leg parts attack the leg, see a weapon you want? go for the arms etc. with the ability to target body parts you will be making quick decisions and going for the weak spots.
Level design is very miuch set in the same roots as Dark Souls, as you open shortcuts and snake around the environment with no set path. on initial thoughts this game does feel more layered with multiple levels within the same area.
Trash mobs are far tougher and can often put you down in 2-3 hits. swinging wildly may work at times, but this will be your end against mobs who are faster than you. strategy is needed for each fight, switch up playstyle depending who/where and how many enemies you are fighting.
Tech trash are your new souls, obviously these are dropped on your inevitable death. Slight difference here though is that you have to reclaim them within 2mins and 30 seconds, failure to reach them in time means they are lost. It means there is a frantic rush to get them back, instead of the Dark Souls calm approach of slow and steady.
Overall a great game if you want a Dark Souls game but dont want Dark Souls.

Been a fan of the Souls games since Demon's Souls launched in 2009. Somewhat ike Demon's, there was no hype. It looked ugly and "clunky," seemingly destined for faliure but gained a strong following through word of mouth thanks to its punishing and addictive gameplay. While The Surge never reaches the heights of the games it was inspired by - it's still a really good game.
I feel that any flak the devs get for the game being a Souls "rip-off," need to recall how genres like "Metroidvania," were born. Because of the genre SotN/Metroid spawned, we now have a ton of quality games to choose from that are too numerous to list. With that said and to avoid TL;DR, the pros and cons.
Pros:
-Great performance, graphics and a game that just WORKS - no crap console ports here.
-Customization system is deep and addictive. Be a nimble killing machine, hulking beast and anything in between.
-Gameplay and controls are the OPPOSITE of "clunky." Tight combat with a modest selection of weapons that feel different and combos to learn.
-Crazy awesome shortcuts to unlock.
-Streamlined and easy to grasp crafting.
-This may be a con for others but the difficulty is brutal. I haven't been this challenged and owned since Demon's Souls and in some ways is more hardcore than the hardest sections of any Soulsborne game.
-Non-intrusive story or hand holding.
Cons:
-The medical bay's excruciating country-lite song on loop. Seriously, you're going to be spending a lot of time here upgrading/crafting/customizing/retreating to restore health and you're forced to have this on loop. Finally turned the music slider to 0 permanently.
-Environments lack variety which is a shame.
If you're a fan of the Souls games, keep an open mind and you'll be pleasantly surprised.

Deck13 has built on the successes and mistakes of Lords of the Fallen and have created something that is unique while also familiar in the Soulsborne ARPG genre. It shows that they have listened to the feedback from their previous game, and as a result crafted an epic sci-fi setting with outstanding level design and addictive combat systems and mechanics.
In addition to the combat systems, The Surge rewards players with different gear and implants to hone their playstyle. Something which is dearly needed during the progression throughout the levels and to overcome the unique and increasingly difficult boss encounters.
The Surge is flawed but between severing body parts for upgrades and makeshift hydraulic weapons, The Surge offers a satisfying take on the extremely difficult Soulsborne ARPGs.
A worthy challenger to the genre.

One of my all time favorite games among my all time favorite games. Factorio starts simple and gets as complex as you want it to be. There is no other game that delivers like this one does. Every morning cup of coffee is that much better in front of Factorio. I'd pay for this game again.
Factorio makes life better.

You ever watch How It's Made, and stay awake long enough to see those huge factories making stuff like cakes or lightbulbs? Hundreds of machines, all interconnected, conveyor belts snaking too and fro between them, devices performing task after task, all working in harmony to spit out the insane number of cakes needed to satisfy the regional demand on a daily basis...
That's factorio. Only you cant make cake... yet.
Sure it's simple enough on the surface. I build a machine here, to take item X, and turn it into item Y. Then I take Item Y, combine it with item Z, make item Q out of that mixture, which gets mixed with items C through F to create item B, which in turn gets used to build a solar panel, for a rocket you're building and launching into space. Definitely not cakes.
It's a game about complexity, automation, and solving problems. This is not a game for everyone, and even those who like it usually shut it down in a moment of crushing depression after overcoming the first few hours with the game. But if you stick with it, keep working out the problems, and get your factory running smoothly, I can almost garauntee you'll be hooked.
This game is rewarding in a way i havent seen in a long time, partly because it doesnt hold your hand at all. Everything in your factory is where you put it, set up the way you set it up, and it lives or dies by your decisions. But let me tell you, when you power up a factory block for the first time, and see it smoothly working, doing exactly what it should, the way you want it, it feels damn good.
...until you realise your iron output is woefully sub par and your new production branch is starving out the rest of your factory. But that's just another problem to overcome.
TL;DR, It's a solid game for those looking for a real time sink. Stable branch is very stable. Bugs are very rare and I've personally never experienced a crash, even with 50+ mods running in the background. Not much end game, but just getting ot that point will take multiple hours. Would reccomend.
Only you know how your factory works, where it starts, where it ends, how to configure it, how to manage it and .... how to make it even better although being close to perfect.

Gameplay felt slow, tab-targetting combat system was personally a turn off for me, story was uninteresting with too much dialogue, and questing felt black and white with fetch quests, go to Point A-B here and there.
Then he told me to hold on and judge the game after I played several dungeons, because that's when the game really started to pick up. How right he was. I originally wanted to write a full paragraphed review but there was just too many things about this game that did things oddly satisfyingly in comparison to other MMORPGs, which I ended up believing it definitely deserves it's subscription based system
Here's a list of... tidbits about the game, with a bit of my opinions in there. I'll call them "Concerns for new players".
- Combat can be tedious at lower levels because you start with only a handful of skills
- Class catagorizes under the Holy Trinity, Tank, Healer and DPS.
- Each base classes get upgrades called Jobs at level 30.
- You can always change classes at any point during the game. You won't have the need to ever make a new character because of this.
- Character customization can be limited, but you can tell how much Square Enix loves their variation in hairstyles above any other customization options.
- You can do the quest that enables you to call your very flamboyant hairstylist to change your hairdo and make-up.
- If hairdo and make-up isn't enough, you can recustomize your character completely with an item called Fantasia. Free on the first month you subscribed. 10 USD per in the Mogstation store.
- If EVEN recustomizing your character was not enough already (like me), at level 50, you have access to Glamour. If you happen to like a look of a certain gear but wish to keep your strong gear, you may do so with this system. Dye-ing is also possible, although limited to one base color of that gear. All this is very accessible to every player once unlockable, and is not locked behind a pay wall. You can even glamour something as miniscule as your earrings and necklaces. Absolutely insane!
- Story (and combat) starts slow and uninteresting with too much dialogue at low levels, but really picks up at 20's to 35. Do note level 35 is the highest level you can reach in the trial version before they encourage you to buy the game.
- Dungeons provide a completely different experience compared to persistant world. I strongly recommend attempting to play a few before finalizing your thoughts of the game
- There are PLENTY of instanced content. No two are the same. Mechanics vary in all of them, while several bosses from several dungeons can be boiled down to tank & spank, they're still a blast. Some dungeons like Aurum Vale for example are notorious to players due to it's structure, despite it still being just another dungeon.
- Leveling experience is really good. There is no shortage of EXP handouts. There are dungeons (4-man and 8-man), guildhests (mini dungeons), Trials (mini dungeons that focuses on a single main boss), Raids (24-man), quests (main and side), FATES (dynamic timed map quests), class hunting logs, NPC Guild hunting logs, weekly challenges, and more. You never feel the need to grind out your EXP on random mobs.
- Fast Travel system is functionable for the most part (Looking at you Waking Sands). You activate waypoints in several areas of a map to access them, then at any time you can always teleport back to them for a small fee. You can also set "home waypoints" to teleport to incase you get incapacitated.
- You get a free mount at roughly level 20. All mounts run at the same speed. Flying (accessible in Heavensward expansion) however sets you faster than ground travel.
- There are pets/minions in the game. Pets fight along side several classes, while minions follow you around for aesthetic purposes.
- FFXIV is the only MMORPG I noticed that made effort on communication across language barriers. There are many sets of premade chat phrases that can be used that will automatically translate into other people's default system language set. Ex: You picked "Hello" in the list of phrases, but in a French player's system it would say "Salut". No, no cusses.
- Guilds are called Free Companies (FC). If you don't want to join one but still keep in touch with several people in a group without having to whisper them, you can make little group chats in game called Linkshells. Very useful.
- There is housing in this game. You can pick among small, medium, and large housing, according to my friend. I personally haven't had enough gil (in-game currency) to try them out myself. Once you buy one, you are advised to visit it within 40 days every time you leave, otherwise you will be evicted to allow other players a chance to purchase a place.
- While your main classes you use to get through the game are called the Discples of War, you also have access to Disciples of the Hand. These are your crafting classes in the game. During your downtime from killing you can always settle down for the peaceful life of carpenting, goldsmithing, blacksmithing, and you can even go grow some plants for you peace lovers (and more, of course). I personally don't think the peace lover life suits me so I have not tried any of these yet.
- Gold Saucer is present in this game. It's your Las Vegas zone to play several minigames (like those test your strength with a hammer, Triple Triad for FF8 fans, plenty more) to gain special currencies to buy special rewards.
- I never ran into any bugs in this game. But to be frank, I don't generally keep my eye open for these things but I really haven't seen anything in the game that made me say "maybe if I restart the game it'll be fixed".
- I cannot commend Square Enix enough for the options menu in this game. They have so many options for everything. From simple graphics settings, camera settings, very good HUD settings menu, turning off special tracks for specific mounts, to small things like Helmet hiding, visor adjustments, and even idle animation timer. Absolutely Insane. Plentiful to customize to optimize your overall experience.
- You can mark targets, and mark locations on the map for party members to see. Very nice implmentation to simplify communication.
- Just like all other Final Fantasy games, FFXIV doesn't hold back on their soundtrack. If it wasn't a sin to AFK during a Trial Boss battle just to listen to music, I would do it all the time.
- There is PvP in this game. 1v1 Duel, 4v4 Ranked, 8v8 "Training" Match (that same friend said this plays like the Battlegrounds in World of Warcraft), and 24v24v24 (3 Main NPC Guilds vs each other in a large map in a capture-the-point ordeal). Doing PvP gives you it's own sets of rewards as well (PvP armor for instance that can be used even in PvE!)
Overall though, with so many things to achieve in this game... I did not know I've spent already 170 hours (and counting), and I've generally just played 2 classes, and neither have reached level cap yet. The game is a blast for me. A breath of fresh air compared to other MMORPGs nowadays. The playerbase is good and steady, with the Stormblood expansion just around the corner from the date of this review, this is going to explode, so much more than it already does.
Edit: Playerbase exploded, even in the server in Asia I'm in (small playerbase in comparison to other servers). At some point I couldn't even start my own main quest instance which led me back to the main menu and not be able to log back in, although the following half-an-hour after that I continued questing with no problems. I still think Square Enix will go out of their way to properly optimize it in the next few days due to it's official release date on the 20th June, 2017 so I'm not worried.

I love this game!! It's so fríken awesome! Reminds me of one of my favorite video series, Firefly. One gets loans to buy ships to deliver goods or carry passengers, or one can get a warship and protect merchants then make enough money to pay off their ships and get rich and get loans to get even more massive ships to get filthy rich. It's singleplay so one doesn't have to deal with dults and children, but the story and npc interaction is so well done that I don't feel like I'm missing out on a lifelike experience.
The gameplay is relistic to some extents but some of the more annoying "realism" stuff that games do nowadays like having to sell back stuff for a price lower than one bought it for by accident 5 seconds ago have been left out so its not stressful like that. To elaborate, one sells and buys merchandise at the value the planet currently has for something. So if they buy and sell the same thing on the same day there's no loss or gain but if they leave the planet to another planet where the value for that item is different they will have to buy/sell at the value this other planet has set so one can gain or lose money on transactions that way but its based on ones own forsight and planning instead of some random bull.
Another thing that is so well done is the autosave, so that even dying isn't stressful. It's also easy to learn and control, and while the default hotkeys are a bit inconvenient one can change them quickly and easily at any time. The save organization is also very cool. There are 2 lists in the save/load screen one for pilots and one for saves for that pilot (and a third screen with information on that save), so that in the second list one only sees the saves for the pilot ones has selected in the first list. Just remember that if you want to delete a save to click the Remove button under the second screen with the individual saves listed not the Delete button underneath the screen that lists the pilots, because that one will delete all of the saves for that pilot if one chooses to accept on the warning popup after pressing Delete.

This game. Endless Sky. It's Amazing. I wan't more. I had seen it in my reccomended games feed a while ago and had ignored it for some time until one day I decided I was bored enough to try it. I was NOT let down. Everything about this game is beautiful from the spritework to the storyline. It's a wonderful universe where you start out as a young kid on one of the poorest planets in the Galaxy who finally worked up the guts to get a Loan to get off of his homeworld. It's hard at first but it eases up after the first few months. Before you know it YEARS have passed and you've been riding the space lanes to planets whose names you've only heard of in movies. It's a story of Triumph, of rising from ruin into greatness. An endless rush until one day someone launches a terrorist attack with a Nuclear Bomb. A forbidden and taboo weapon of mass destruction. The people of the republic are awe-struck and looking for someone to blame, and that group is the Free Worlds, but YOU know better, and you head to the free worlds and get ambushed by Katja. If you play it cool she asks a favor of you and that sets you on the path of establishing a long lasting galactic peace. Together you work together to prove that the Free Worlds is not responsible for the attack, and root out those who are. She takes you to Ijs, pronounced Eyes who's a master at reading planets. Together you work to bring justice to the people of the republic, but it's too late. The republic attakcs and you're forced into action. You join up with the free worlds and take the fight to the republic in self defense. Eventually you clear your names, but not before bringing to an end the biggest threat mankind has ever known. This game is a BEAUTIFUL ADVENTURE and at in that last moment on winter, when Ijs and Katja wished me fairwell. I cried Knowing I'd never see them again. That my time Serving the Free Worlds was truely over. This game moved me to tears and that's hard for a game to do. This is a Masterpiece. I'd pay for this and the devs are kind enough to not only provide it for free, but expand upon it and maintain it for free. For that I am Thankful, for this has been an adventure that I will never forget. My only problem, is that their isn't more, that I won't be able to see Ijs, Katya, or Alondo again, or even the Admiral of the Oathkeepers. Friends that I have spent YEARS working with to bring peace and prosperity to the Galaxy. My only request is that the Devs not only finish the storyline but continue it after they finish implementing the others. Continue all of them. I would pay for the chance to work with Ijs, Katya, and Alondo again. I WOULD PAY MONEY TO SEE IJS, KATJA, and ALONDO again. They're friends, and I miss them.
To anyone out there that's sitting on the fence, or thinks that they may not like the game: GET IT, it is a BEAUTIFUL ADVENTURE, a BEAUTIFUL STORY, and you wont regret it.
TLDR: GET IT, it is a BEAUTIFUL ADVENTURE, a BEAUTIFUL STORY, and you wont regret it.

Pro's:
- Satisfies the desire for an old-school grind MMORPG.
- Many skills and combos, great for PVE and PVP.

Con's:

I've watched ~20 hours of gameplay from early access streamers and I've seen 3/5 bosses, and 5 enemy types in the first three areas. The third and the first area are also nearly identical. The game itself feels souls-like. The combat can go from realistic to ridiculous in one attack. You have dashing attacks that superman punch 30 feet away, and you have normal attacks which feel heavy and damaging. The quickstep/dodge also feels out of place in this setting.
The ability to lock on to specific body parts also removes the ability to target swap, having you lock off and re lock on a new target(since writing this review, I have found out you can target swap. The method is weird, but it's possible); which in some scenarios is quite annoying and leaves you at a disadvantage. It has platforming elements, but all are likely to use your humongous jump that doesnt even seem feasable in the exoskeleton you just moments early put a broken battery into to power on.
This game tries very hard to improve upon Lords of the Fallens failure, and it does just that. It falls short of something spectacular, but its a solid game worth playing. It IS NOT worth the $65 CAD price, however. Wait for a 50% off sale, if you want to purchase. Im gonna go get my refund and wait for Nier Automata to go on sale.

Legend of Grimrock is my favorite indie release this year. Many compare it to Dungeon Master, but I find it equally reminiscent of old pen and paper RPGs, requiring equal parts wit and might to survive. As you traverse the dungeon, you’ll encounter floors with deadly traps, vicious enemies, numerous puzzles and secrets. The puzzles are satisfying and require truly clever solutions in many cases. Similarly, combat requires guile and agility, and you must constantly be on the move, exploit enemies’ weaknesses where ever possible and avoid being cornered at all costs. One of the game’s few negative aspects is the absolute lack of any instruction (even the tutorial fails to explain game mechanics in any detail) and would perhaps benefit from a “show, don’t tell” approach. All in all, Grimrock provides a great amount of content at a price that’s quite reasonable. I’ve already logged about 50 hours and still haven’t uncovered all the secrets.

Wow, this game actually deserves the title of Indie of the Year or even more. Legend of Grimrock is a return to the roots of the RPG genre. It has modern graphics, but the gameplay is really old school. It's not as dynamic as most modern RPGs (not to mention action RPGs), yet it may sometimes require good reflexes. The game is well ballanced in terms of difficulty, the fights in most cases require tactical approach so the party selection is important, but not crucial (this means you can create a team of the most bizarre characters you can imagine and still finish the game). Some puzzles are hard, but not overly mind-bending. The game offers an option to play without the automap and I totally recommend it. It lengthens the playthrough and makes the player empathise more with his/her wards. So gather all the food you can and explore Mount Grimrock to its very industrial bottom!

Who wouldn´t want to eradicate humanity from time to time?
If you say "Yes, here! Me!" then you should probably get some help.. or this game.. maybe both.
Either way, Plague Inc: Evolved is a simple game, where you can evolve your virus/bacteria etc. from a harmless flu to a pandemic mass killer.
While the base game is very easy but fun, Plague Inc. has so many different scenarios, as well as different Plagues from mind controlling worms, zombies, intelligent apes and so on, that you can destroy humanity again and again and have different playthroughs. Beside the bigger changes the ways you customize your sickness offers great replayability.
Last but not least the workshop provides hundred fan made plagues for your pleasure and humanitys demise. Furthermore a multiplayer mode is in the making and the developer is very actively improving the game time and time again.
Conclusio: Even if you know the game from it´s mobile beginnings the PC version is worth it´s money, with a broad array of possibilities and challenges to casually destroy humanity in a relaxing evening session.

As an early access game, DF9 was decent. There was definable progress. I'll admit it, it was fun. There were bugs, and early access gripes, but the EA rule I use is that "As long I can visualize this being finished, done, and fun, I can consider spending money on it." DF9 met those criteria. However, as the game has moved abruptly to a "release", and with the complete stoppage of new features, Double Fine has fallen far, far short of even approaching their planned development milestones. Further, the lack of believable rationales, detailed explanations, or even breakdowns about why this came about mean that I can't in good faith recommend that you purchase this game, or any future titles from Double Fine productions until some form of publically disclosed management shakeup takes place.
They reportedly raised approximately half a million dollars to develop this game. They then stopped development, citing financial reasons. They do not appear to have then offered any breakdown of where said money went. They are now confused, as people are angry and asking "WHERE DID THAT MONEY GO!?" The statements I have reviewed do not appear to show that this logical connectoin has been made.
The final nail in the coffin was a "AWESOME DEV PROCESS GREAT JOB" timeline that was issued as a "We're sorry we took your money, but don't pay attention to the archived feature lists we pumped for months about what we were going to do, instead read this sleek graphic that shows what we DID do! JUST DONT COMPARE THE TWO!" Their conduct in this and other products leads me to the following unfortunate conclusion regarding Double Fine Productions:
They simply are not a worthwhile investment for your consumer dollars. This is not the first time this endgame has come about for one of their product. That is not to say Double Fine is an intrinsically bad company, or that they cannot make good games. But I simply cannot justify spending money on early access titles from them now or in the future.
At this point, Double Fine serves as an argument for Valve to more or less micro-audit game development companies, even basic indie ones, for management practices. Whether that is feasible or a correct response is a different matter, but Double Fine's performance definitely elicits that reaction. That or open up a "Developer Review" page to trash talk developers (This would also be a bad idea, but it is my inclination in response).
A more reasonable option would be for Valve to construct a form of "Warning Stick" that it can publically shake at developers who mis-behave in such a fashion. A "We're reviewing their sales agreement" or "We're considering yanking their priviledge to post on early access" type of statement, to remind developers that Early Access is not a kickstarter equivalent, but is rather an opportunity to generate interest and feedback on your products.

I tried, I really did. It sold me on "Dwarf Fortress in space," and the initial round of bugs were survivable (even if my station did frequently end up knee-deep in my citizens' corpses). But now we're going straight to release with a whole lot of bugs unfixed and features unimplemented, and that isn't what I paid for this game for. Wish I could get my money back on this one.

Do not buy. Incomplete game that has been abandoned.
Loved it when I first got it, and was loving the updates (though slow) that were coming in for this game. But now the company has pulled the plug leaving the game far from what they had promised. Double Fine was a developer that I thought I could trust because they had made good games before. I really trusted them, and they let me down big time. I am extremely disappointed with the whole thing, and will not be second guessing everything they put out for a long time coming.

What a joke that they cite not enough initial support as the main cause of abandonment. If you ask me, the outrageously high Early Access price ($25+) was in and of itself the primary deterrent for shoppers. I've learned my lesson now, and don't intend on purchasing any more Early Access games, and certainly never any other DoubleFine products, again unless they offer some kind of partial refund. This game is practically unplayable on a Mac; there are just far too many graphics glitches and various bugs. In the right hands, this could have been a "game-changer," but now it's nothing more than an utter waste of money. If it keeps dropping in price and hits the $1 marker, then MAYBE consider buying it... Maybe.

I have tried on two occasions now to get into this. Done by the creators of Bastion, which I loved, I was hoping for a similar experience here.
It is, to a degree, similar to Bastion, in that the artwork and isometric gameplay are shared concepts, as is the notion of a silent protagonist and a narrator. That's about where the similarities end, I think.
The gameplay is (IMHO) worse. The pseudo-turn-based combat makes every battle take up much more time, even if they're somewhat easier. And there's a lot of combat, so you'll be doing this a lot.
The narrator won't shut up. He tells you about every little thought that crosses his mind, and he's constantly babbling about something. He frequently tells me every thing he wants me to do, and he's a bit of an♥♥♥♥♥if I don't do it. If I were the protagonist, I'd be throwing that damn talking sword over a cliff and going about my life in peaceful silence. Maybe the main character loves to hear people prattle on about flatbread pizza and tell her how great she is and tell her every little thing that she needs to do - I dunno.
It's also not (yet) entirely clear to me what the motivation of the main character is. It's quite possible this will be explained if I play further, but I don't know if I can stomach hours more of turn-based combat.
On the upside, the artwork and soundtrack are, like Bastion, excellent.
If you can tolerate the turn-based combat and babbling sword, then you'll probably enjoy this. So far, it's not my cup of tea. Not recommended.

More of the same as the previous Hexcells games; if you have played those than this is less a natural progression and more of just filling the same niche.  Which doesn't mean it is bad by any means!  Rather it is just a significantlly expanded collection of logic puzzles without any real alteration in figuring them out.  That having been said, there is a LOT here.  The Level progression seems a bit more erratic than previous ones - some of the puzzles in Chapter 6 are easier than previous puzzles you encounter - but that isn't too much of a drawback in the grand scheme.  I've barely tapped into the "random" puzzle generator (reputed to be 1,000,000 puzzles at your reach) and that is really where the meat of the title is; be aware that the Level campaign of Hexcells Infinite took significantly less time for me to complete than Hexcells Plus (roughly half the time!).  If you don't plan to play the random levels that may be something to keep in mind, but I would still wholeheartedly recommend the game regardless.
On Mac the game ran extremely smooth with no hiccups, freezes, or CTD.  The only problem is when using a Mac Magic Mouse sometimes right clicks were wrongly interpreted as left clicks, ruining perfect level runs (I'm looking at you 6-5!!!!).  If you are a perfectionist and using a Magic Mouse ... use caution or you can ruin 30+ minutes of effort in an instant.  It should also be noted that perfect runs don't have to be perfect: you can actually make a wrong move or two and still get credit as acing the level on some of them.
The latest installment of Hexcells and this game series just keeps getting better (and harder).  Looking forward to another sequal.

Enjoyed this game a lot! Gives a minesweeper kind of feel, which adds in more puzzle enhancements as you progress through the levels. Starts off very basic so that you get a feel for the game, and then you look up and all you want to do is perfect all the levels. So the games goes, there are a few blocks with numbers on the board and you have to puzzle out whether the block is another number or a blue block. The block has 6 sides (obviously) and the number says how many blue block are touching it. As the game progresses, it adds {} around a number to say the blue blocks are sequential, or -- around a number to say they are split. It then goes father to say that there are so may in this line by putting the number on the outside of that row or column. The easy feature which helps a lot for bigger puzzles is that you can click on the outside number and it draws a line through that row or column to see which ones.
All in all lots of fun and challenging at the same time. Gets more challenging as the game goes on. Expansion on the origional Hexcells. The intimate mode and challenge to get achievement is very repeatitive...

But still is a decent game and deserve your attention.
The random seeded puzzles are not as challenging as the main 'story' puzzles but are still brilliant. You can now never run out of Hexcells which is brilliant.
