After playing 108 minutes of "Papers Please". I must say, this game is really intriguing.
NOTE: Yes my hours should be longer. But in reality, this game doesn't have much else to offer other than what I will put in this review.
You are a immigration inspector for the country of Arstotzka. And it is your duty to uphold your civil duties to the nation and helping your family making ends meet. And yes, what you saw on the store page is legit. It's that simple of game. But really layed on political themes. And those themes are handled well. Over the course of the game, you see this dystopian world unfold through your actions. Which can have a serious impact to you or your family. So be aware.
Now your probably thinking. "Surely being a immigration inspector is easy in this game?" Yeah no. Over the course of the game, while you are given tools to aid you. There will be 'events' that might switch things up a bit. Making that pre-determined pattern that was once seemless. Now gone, because of "event". This game isn't going to hand you the victory so easily. You will have to pay very close attention to every bit of detail that the immigrant has given you. Or what the minstry has told you. Even IF you think that you got everything down. Do another check again. Because the smallest detail could really put you in a bad spot.
Lastly the game has an Endless mode.
For it's simple nature. The game really does an excellent job at not being too silly, But rather being semi-realistic. While this game might not offer much. It's a neat little game to pass the time. I recommend it.

The ending I got seemed to be a comment about how sometimes you just can't be close to someone the way you used to, which is a fine message. Sometimes you can't do anything about it and just drift apart. But it felt like the character didn't try, or we weren't given the right choices.

Yeah, The Surge is amazing.
Whenever I play a game that takes inspiration from so many different games, be it in the form of copying gameplay mechanics, or making blanket references to them, I always think to myself, "What is this game's identity? Is this just an amalgamation of so many different previously established ideas? If yes, am I even playing an original game? When does this game become its own game?" The Surge takes inspiration from many games that I can see so far, some such include: Deus Ex (really apparent), Deus Ex: HR, Metal Gear Solid, and of course, Dark Souls.
And given all these influences, do I think The Surge is an original game? Is it its own entity? Yeah, for sure!
Concentrating your attacks on certain body parts is an awesome mechanic. With intense and engaging enemy encounters, introducing a mechanic wherein you can focus your attacks on weaker or stronger body parts was a great idea! Scrolling the mouse wheel and using the right thumbstick (I've played with both) is so quick when locked on, getting to enemy weakpoints is quick and effective. And with an equipment system that heavily relies on the materials you forcibly and viscerally remove from enemies, an added challenge is introduced when your desired body part is stronger for that particular enemy. And all that, is merely a small portion of the combat mechanics.
I have encountered five different weapon types. Each has its own advantages over others, be it speed, impact on it, and energy production (a tertiary stat which determines when you can use certain skills or finishing moves). But most importantly of all, each weapon type has unique movesets. There are so many freaking movesets. If there's one, singular, part of Dark Souls I am so glad The Surge has absorbed, it's the freaking movesets. You have 2 forms of attack: Horizontal swings, and Vertical Swings. The former is the light attack variant, and the latter, the heavy attack variant. Chaining attacks begets different combos, different moves, and different stagger potentials. My personal favorite is the Light-Heavy-Heavy on this particular 1-Handed weapon I had been using. It was pretty damn effective, but I a noticed that sometimes, the moves were different. For some reason, my character was wielding the weapon with both hands and doing a much wider attack, with a significantly bigger weak spot (of mine) revealing itself. I wondered to myself, "What key am I hitting to make these attacks happen?" because I'd keep getting abused for that huge weakpoint.
Then I realized it. The 1-Handed weapons are held in the right hand. Because of that, I had naturally been rotating around enemies so that they were to my right, closer to my weapon. But every single time my character was using that different moveset, it was because my target was to the
With this 1-Handed weapon, if I was targetting an enemy's right hand, and the enemy was to my left, a whole new moveset was being introduced! Bigger, wider attacks were being performed, since the weapon was being brandished across to the left of my body, with my right hand. And with that imbalance, stagger potential became greater. But it was an entirely new moveset! It was soooo insane.
So I test it out with a different weapon type, that is also held in only the right hand. And the very same thing, a whole new moveset.
I god damn ♥♥♥♥ing love all the god damn ♥♥♥♥ing movesets this game has. There is soooooo much combat variety, it blows my ♥♥♥♥ing mind! Seriously man, they hit it out of the park on that front.
And with all these great things, I have to mention the negatives I've experienced. Enemies seem to react to sound better than vision. Sneaking up on an enemy is tough, but if you flash a light in their line of sight, they won't react at all.
Some enemies are just dumb, standing perfectly still and stabbing the air with their weapons. Most of these enemies have weak legs, so I guess it makes sense in the continuity of the game, but they just feel weak. Once engaged, they'll start dealing some heavy hits, but until then, you can just chain them. The first boss (yo this is a legit spoiler)
, which is eeeeeeh. BUT, beating a boss is so rewarding. From the music that plays throughout, to the every satisfying rumble and explosion from being defeated, and that nice little jingle that plays as a little icon pops up telling you, "hey, you did it c:"
All in all, The Surge has blown me away. And I'm like, my worst enemy when it comes to games, 'cause I'll over-analyze eeeeeverything and ruin them for myself. And that's just after the first area. I'm excited to see what more this game has in store.

Hexcells Infinite is a fun little game that will make you feel smart... for a while. Like all the best puzzle games, its rules are simple but their applications can be fiendishly difficult.
I love the mental gymnastics I have to do while I'm playing. "If this is a blue cell, then this column has five blue cells, which means there's only room for one more, which means that black 4 is forced to use two cells from the neighbouring column, which gives that nearby black 1 too many blue cells... therefore (going back to the start) this can't be a blue cell, so it must be black instead." Proof by contradiction. At some point the proof gets too complicated for me to keep in my head so I have to resort to pen and paper, but that's fun too.
I wish the game contained a tool to mark "candidate" cells à la Minesweeper, and it would be great to be able to toggle the advanced rules for the randomly generated levels (I find the "number inside blue cell" mechanic makes the game really slow), but those are only minor complaints. Recommended.

Painfully logical and wonderfully simple (yet woefully complex), Hexcells Infinite builds beautifully on the solid foundation of its predecessors. I cannot recommend this enough for the strategic logic buffs and Sudoku gamers out there.

The final chapter, this game uses the knowledge gained in the previous two games to throw some extremely hard puzzles at the player. These puzzles can be quite the head-scratchers, but again can be solved without any guessing being necessary.
The procedurally generated levels are a nice addition, but they lack the hand-crafted finesse and difficulty of the main levels and tend to have a few main types of layout. This makes them great for passing a few minutes (2-7 minutes depending on complexity and skill level), but they don't come anywhere near the difficulty of the hand-crafted levels.
A very delightul puzzle.

Very soothing and absorbing to play.
Hexcells makes it easy to block out the rest of the world for a few minutes while focusing completely on the logic of a puzzle, without distracting noises, animations, or time limits demanding attention - exactly what I want most from a puzzle game.
The standard levels do a good job of teaching and exercising the mechanics, and the infinite generated levels mean that the game is never exhausted. Doing a puzzle or two makes a good break to reset your brain when you're stressed.

It's not as flashy as some 3D games, but it's beautiful. It isn't as loud as other games, but it's sensational. It's not as verbose as other story-focused games, yet it's very emotional, and managed to tell a story through your actions. Who knew that taking on the role of an immigration inspector could be so nerve-wracking, yet so rewarding at the same time. You just spend your time behind the desk; you approve or deny visas, and wish that at the end of the day, you've got enough money to feed your family some bread.
With your role as an inspector, you get to choose the fate of the immigrants and the country. People desperately want to get inside, and they'll do absolutely anything for an approval. Sometimes, more extreme solutions come into the minds of people, and they'll just climb over the border to be shot by guards. If you fail your duties, the country temporarily goes into a state of disarray, and employs tighter security measures which makes your job harder. A harder job means more papers. More papers means more time observing discrepancies. More time observing discrepancies means that the immigration line moves slower - and a slow line doesn't pay the bills. Don't be surprised if, by the end of the day, your family died of hunger just because you didn't work harder for the country.
It's very interesting to see how something so minimal, could be so powerful. The player works a mere desk job, yet becomes judge and protector of this fictional country. You connect entrants with their loved ones; you give immigrants better lives; you give people a new start - all with a single stamp. It's storytelling at one of its finest moments, and Papers, Please showed what the medium is truly capable of.
And there you have it.

Pros

Play this if...

I have tried on two occasions now to get into this. Done by the creators of Bastion, which I loved, I was hoping for a similar experience here.
It is, to a degree, similar to Bastion, in that the artwork and isometric gameplay are shared concepts, as is the notion of a silent protagonist and a narrator. That's about where the similarities end, I think.
The gameplay is (IMHO) worse. The pseudo-turn-based combat makes every battle take up much more time, even if they're somewhat easier. And there's a lot of combat, so you'll be doing this a lot.
The narrator won't shut up. He tells you about every little thought that crosses his mind, and he's constantly babbling about something. He frequently tells me every thing he wants me to do, and he's a bit of an♥♥♥♥♥if I don't do it. If I were the protagonist, I'd be throwing that damn talking sword over a cliff and going about my life in peaceful silence. Maybe the main character loves to hear people prattle on about flatbread pizza and tell her how great she is and tell her every little thing that she needs to do - I dunno.
It's also not (yet) entirely clear to me what the motivation of the main character is. It's quite possible this will be explained if I play further, but I don't know if I can stomach hours more of turn-based combat.
On the upside, the artwork and soundtrack are, like Bastion, excellent.
If you can tolerate the turn-based combat and babbling sword, then you'll probably enjoy this. So far, it's not my cup of tea. Not recommended.

Really refreshing approach to rpg gameplay mechanics and surrounding set/plot. Visually greatly rendered, haunting cyberpunk atmosphere, which follows storyline and changes gradually accordingly, with beautiful cuts and inserts as transitions between main plot developments. Storyline, narrative and characters very well developed, keeping you busy and immersed.
There's limited set of enemies, which can be felt a bit repetitive in fights. There's only one weapon (named Transistor) of choice, but it can be programmed to broad range of ability combinations. Just remaping weapon abilities will totally transform same battle into new experience, changing overall strategy and tactics. Fights can go in realtime and in sort of better known Fallout VATS mode. Red, protagonist under your control, have stong bond with Transistor which have ability to siphon personalities (souls?), thus possessing powers of persons it absorbed from. This is how new abilities can be added and combined later to chains. Like in it's predecessor Bastion, Transistor have limiters, to make game more challenging if you willing to do so.
Soundtrack is just perfect and tightly connected to story. Also, it can be directly affected with, seemingly useless, HUM action. This slight touch works surprisingly well, deepens atmosphere and creates additional layer of aural experience.
Look everywhere, try everything and be rewarded with many subtle hidden mechanics and easter eggs lurking to be discovered. F.e. unorthodox MMO approach seen in Dark Souls - though game itself is singleplayer, you still can actually see other players as ghosts passing by or humming their songs.

The default mode of changing mini-games every few seconds was not well received by the group. Fortunately, we found the option to allow a mini-game to finish before moving on the next one. Most mini-games last less than a minute anyway.
We also changed the game mode to arena, which was more about being the last player standing than collecting the most coins. We generally figured out the modes by their name, but additional descriptions for each mode would have been helpful.
We found the mini-games to be generally fun. However, with ghost players running around and the sudden game change when there is a winner, we weren't always clear as to who actually won a particular mini-game. We would like to see some celebration, indication, and/or focus on the player who won a particular mini-game.
Overall we thought it was okay, but it didn't grab us and we only played two rounds (so far). We will probably try it again though. I would give it a mixed review if there were such an option. I am going to give Marooners a hesitant thumb up for now. Hopefully another expansion or update will improve some aspects from the game.

EDIT: So I decided to go more in depth for this game, as I felt I wasn't being fair.
Yes, this game still deserves this negetive rating. Why? let's find out...
At first glance this game is an expanded version of one of those Top-down space ship arcade games, only with more of a Permenant feel.
Upon second glance you notice that this game starts with bad controls, YES, these are re-mappable, but I can't help but feel that the person who made this just put a bot into auto mapping the worst controls on the planet, TAB for shoot? Yep. Arrow keys? Yep. But this isn't really making this game bad, I thought I might just point that out so you know to look at the "Prefrences" menu before making your first pilot.
The controls are floaty and unresponsive, as they should be. You're lugging around a 50-10000(ish) Ton hunk of metal around in zero-G, so why wouldn't it be? my main problem is the lack of mouse control support, this is a personal nitpick, but combat would really benefit from mouse controls.
The combat is horrible, it's basically jabbing eachother with your laser beams until one of you goes below 50% health (I'll get to that later), I didn't play long enough to get to the fleet controls, but I imagine that it's basically a swarm of little flying swords jabbing at your foe until it explodes, though I may be wrong. Using projectiles isn't much better because they just fly past your target.
One interesting mechanic is that if your ship goes below 50% health, it gets disabled and you can't do anything. "Interesting" you say, and you'd be right, until it, Y'know, actually happens. It basically becomes a Real-time SOS simulator at that point "Hey, you, help me" "Okay." "I can't help you because some pirate disabled me too." "Help me" "Okay..."
One more thing that I will mention is not a mechanic, I'm pretty sure it's a bug. One time I was following a merchant to see if they despawn or if they stay persistant, and I was helping them by fending off pirates. and then out of nowhere this massive merchant freighter just comes around a blasts me with like, 20 lasers killing my sparrow instantly. I had done nothing against the law in that playthrough, and I also didn't attack anybody but pirates. And if you're wondering, the ship had blue on it, it wasn't a pirate.
Overall, I wouldn't recommend this game, but I do find it somewhat impressive that one person made this. And I could definatly see myself giving this another try if the developer(s) added mouse controls. Wether or not that's possible is unknown, as I don't program games. But if it is, please consider adding it.

Fantastic, simply wonderful. I have long been nostalgic for a revamp of Escape Velocity and was thrilled to find a free EV clone, but Endless Sky is so much more. Endless Sky fine tunes the formula, with a level of polish and attention to detail that elevates the title to something entirely its own. Case in point, the chart/mapping system allows you to precalculate trade route profits relative to your current location by simply opening the map and clicking on systems...and before you get nostalgic for the old pen and paper way of doing things, you actually *need* this extra aid -- the bank always wants its due! There is so much more to this game, having played all of 30 minutes, I feel like I've played it for years and will continue to play it for even longer. Seriously, if you were ever a fan of Escape Velocity or Escape Velocity Nova, damnit, you need to play this game.

This game is a unpolished diamond to say the least, I love the gameplay elements and variety of ships it provides me with.
General Impressions:
The gameplay at the start is fairly repetitive. However, once you get the better ships, the game turns 180 degrees from "I am just a merchant, pirates please don't kill me." to "I am going to murder every single one of you and sell your ship."
The game itself lacks a tutorial, which does not help in new players getting in the game. You also cannot use the LMB as your "Shoot" button, which annoys me, keybindings can be found on the main menu at the "Preferences" button, but a tutorial will be more fitting to the game. If you think that first mission is a tutorial. GTFO. That guy only tells you where to go and how to jump(I think). For further game information on how to play, you need to read the merchant hails in the bottom of the screen. You also need to pay off a mortgage from the bank which will probably take you 3-4 hours of constant freighting around and finding transport and mass trransport missions.
The Campaign: (Spoilers)
The campaign is short and sweet, kicking it off with an sudden attack on the Republic shipyard with a nuke. (Yes, a literal nuke) You then spiral into a storyline where you side with the Free Worlds on reconaissance missions. Later on after said missions, plus a few transport and escort missions here and there, you will be offered to join the Free Worlds, where you get paid money! After this part, you will be asked to fight in the war against the Republic as they have taken a nearby star system. By this time, you should have a fleet of 3-4 ships, or it will be hard to complete the missions the Free Worlds give you. After a lot of fighting and infiltrating, you will discover the Syndicate is behind all of it and you will attack them instead which will make you in turn discover Aliens. You will fight the aliens which have advancd techlogy which you will aqcuire. You will then fight Syndicate Extremists who will launch nukes at you, which you need to evade with a cloaking device. Once that is over, you get marked as a hero and you will return to your normal life.
Late Game:
In the late game, it is pretty much discovering and expeditions, there is not much to do. Get Bactrians and get a jump drive, find the Hai, Wanderer and Korath murder them or buy their technology and kill the Quarg, get their technology and conquer the galaxy. That is literally the aim of the game after the campaign as it gets really repetitive after that. Still. Killing pirates and merchants are still a fun way to test your fleet's strength. If you want more of a challenge, try and go kill the Drak
Final Thoughts and Conclusion:
Generally a fun game to play after you get past early game, repetitive after campaign.
Improvements can be made by extending the campaign a little bit and adding in more variety of enemies and objectives to do after the campaign, like interactions with the Free Worlds and the Republic Senate. Or maybe missions to explore and see new things in the game. It needs some polishing, but it has the potential to become a good game.
To the players, get some addons and mods to make the game more interesting. There are like Star Wars mods in the game and ships are being made by a lot of people. Check Reddit for more addons and ships, Unfortunately there are no Star Destroyers. Developers, if you are reading this, make the Star Destroyer a thing, or maybe you can do other things on planets instead of just a click menu. Thanks for you efforts on developing and updating the game.

There are lots of improvement to its predecessor, but there are some things which were actually done better in the first game.
The graphics, city building and combat are improved. However, the campaign is a far cry from the one in the first game. The original AoW had 2 branching campaigns, each with 3 different endings. Player's character was fully customizable, leveled-up and learned new skills as you progressed through the campaign. You could transfer research, artifacts, heroes and units between campaign maps. Not only is the AoW2's campaign completely linear, but you lose all your research, heroes and artifacts after 2 or 3 maps (depending on wether you play the optional maps or not). And player's character is always Merlin, who can't be customized, can't level-up/improve and (usually) can't fight at all. Leaders are little more than mobile defense objectives that are supposed to sit in a heavily fortified city (preferably one with a Wizard Tower, so they can actually support your heroes in the field).
While the game itself is not bad, it's kinda rendered "obsolete" with the release of "Age of wonders: Shadow Magic", which is, basically, AoW2's stand-alone expansion. Shadow Magic adds new races, units, buildings and spells, a new campaign, and - most importantly - a random map generator.
In short, the game was good when it came out, but now it's better to just get "Age of Wonders: Shadow Magic" (or "Age of Wonders 3") instead.
It's not a Master of Magic but this is the closest one I ever saw.

I wish Heroes IV and Age of Wonders II had a love child. What a brilliant strategy/RPG could that be. Heroes IV had atrocious combat and really weird ideas about which races and units should be present. Age of Wonders II has fantastic combat and units that make sense both lore-wise and ability-wise. Yet Age of Wonders II feels somewhat lacking compared to the sheer richness of RPG capabilities of Heroes IV. Heroes IV had a map editor that on its own redeemed every terrible decision made in the game.
What Age of Wonders II does right, in my opinion?
- Every race as an element of lore is a race as an element of gameplay. In Heroes III and IV dwarves, halfling, elves, and others, where frequently jumbled together in one city type. In AoW they are fleshed out as their own playable races, with unique units.
- Every unit has a list of features, including even which terrain they can traverse without penalties. Which means a flying unit, such as an efreet, can actually fly over a mountain range on the global map. Which potentially allows for some crazy multiplayer tactics, but I haven't played multiplayer and don't know how balanced it is.
- I like the concepts of a wizard, of a Wizard's Tower, of necessity of learning spells and skills.
- You can actually build your own cities.
So if you're into fantasy strategy games, give this old-school goodie a try. For a fairly old game, the mechanics are straightforward and easy to learn, and I haven't encountered any bugs. Although the campaign AI is quite apathetic, so that might make the game not challenging enough.

I recommend this because, at the end of the day, i dont regret buying it, and i dont wish i could refund it (which in all seriousness is what matters) BUT I cant just leave it at that.
The Surge is in all intents and purposes, much what Lords of the Fallen was (these devs previous game), which was a reasonably competent, but otherwise unremarkable Souslike fanfic. What i mean by that, is that its a game that clearly looks at what a soulslike does, where its complexities lie, and where its charm comes from.... before completely failing to recreate it in its same fashion.
Make no mistake, its not a terrible game. But if it cost anymore, this review would change to a thumbs down mighty quick.
Combat- 7/10: While its by all means a functional combat system with complexity and a risk/reward system, it ends up being pretty shallow when taken at the end of the day. Some points are thus:
-Some weapons are clearly better suited for most situations than others.
-This game is another example of why Poise was such an important thing in Souls. (a stat which would calculate how much impact it would take to stagger you. The way of balacing the huge weight increase of heavy armor)
-It has a lot of different additions, like being able to high dodge and low dodge, block, do different combos and such, but at the end of the day you dont really use the more complex additions... pretty much at all. As a matter of fact the game completely fails to mention you CAN do combos which drastically alter the way the attacks come out (as far as i saw, anyway). So while there is all this fancy stuff, it tends to fall by the wayside when you can be just as effective from simply slapping and stepping back.
-Drones are useful additions, but barely more than a small extra attack and/or a means of pulling an enemy from a distance. Melee drone is helpful for a bit of crowd control, but so far ive found a simple bit of cat and mouse is just as effective...
Map- 8/10:
The map is pretty standard fare. Twisty windy side-paths up-paths down-paths, ladders, holes, secrets, destructibles, shortcuts, etc etc. It does it reasonably well, but theres a few too many dead ends with no value, and a bit much twistiness for it to be a superly competent map design. Half the time i spent trying to work out where the hell i was, in order to find a shortcut to open, simply because the corridors were so damn similar to each other.
Does the job, nothing special.
Graphics- 9/10: Aint nothing too bad. Aint nothing too great. Reasonably detailed, and doesnt lack in a bit of asthetics. Doesnt feel that unique though. Spacey scifi standard corridors for the most part. Does the job, and well, but nothing to write home about.
Characters- 7/10: In all seriousness, the characters in this feel like they play very little actual role. Possibly at one point they were more in depth, but in the end most of them seem to exist more as a person to help and then ask "whats going on" to, before becoming another npc for little more than fetch quests or minor (but useful) rewards. Protagonist bland. Just like LOTF, no real reason for one gender or the other, and extra effort is the only real excuse for not having a choice.
Possibly better off to have just had a faceless Protagonist. He basically is faceless 99% of the time anyway.
Technicals- 7/10: Performance is quite good, despite an odd bit of dip here and there (or so it feels. 970, 16gb ram and 4690k, running on SSD), the load times are fine, no serious graphical oddities or artifacts, and the bare minimum of crashes or stalls, bugs or lockups.
HOWEVER. the hitboxes in this game... are barely passable. Easily the games worst aspect. A number of times youll be hit by attacks youre 100% didnt land according to the models, and other times attacks will land before they should seem to.
Its not a deal breaker, as with a bit of extra caution you can pretty much work around it. But it certainly takes you out of the moment when an attack lands you think shouldnt have. Some people might think this insignificant, but these sort of games (Soulslikes) are all about punishing your mistakes. If your only mistake is assuming the models mean anything, then thats not your fault at all.
Overall- 7.5/10.
Not a bad experience to sink some time into, and for the price you could do far worse (as i recently discovered, thinking "Hey, Homefront:TR cant be THAT bad, and its on special!"), but... you could do far better too. Honestly, id put LOTF above this, but barely. Competent Soulslikes that dont really encourage a second playthrough.

Bastion was fast-paced and fun, and time flew when I was playing it. But I found myself only able to play Transistor for about an hour without getting sick of it--it ended up being a bit of a labor to finish the story.
The artwork was beautiful, the music was great too, and the story was interesting and creative. I enjoyed the cutscenes and reading about the corresponding character for each function. I find it extremely difficult to describe this title in the fondest of ways... Words like "elegant" and "prestigious" come to mind when I think about it, but I feel like those terms undermine the perfect interpretation of my experience with this game. I need a choice word; something grander to express what Super Giant's magnificent masterpiece of art, sound and code is... I can't exalt this title enough, and I feel the best idiom I can use would be "nirvana" to explain the preeminence of Transistor. A gorgeously styled game with a sonic collection that rivals those found in mainstream music mediums of yester-year and today. The gameplay mechanics are phenomenal. During my initial playthrough, I would unlock new abilities that could be used and arranged in numerous ways via the game's UI system. Cleverly designed, abilities could be assigned to an active slot, enhance slot or a passive slot, which gave each power a different effect depending on which slot you choose. This adds to a replay ability factor, along with a new game plus feature, which extends the experience to over thirty hours or so. Seasoned RPG gamers will enjoy the mixing and matching formula of the slots, trying to find that ideal build for every battle sequence in the game. Speaking of battles, they can be handled in two ways: real time or turn based. The latter offers the most flexibility because you can carefully plot your moves on the field to maximize your potential damage output, taking advantage of enemy weaknesses. It took me a bit to get use to, but once I got the hang of the mechanics, battles seemed less daunting. There's even an area in the game where you can freely practice battle techniques without fear of penalties. Super Giant Games took an approach to story telling similar to another title the team produced; Bastion. A narrator pretty much forecasts the plot in a way that might not appeal to the masses, but is fitting to the narrative in my humble opinion. Without spoiling too much, let just say that the relationship between the protagonist and the master of ceremony is a vital aspect of the story. The art and music are things to behold and cherish. Alluring cut scenes look like paintings that come to life, filled with vibrant color schemes and sharply drawn characters. The music is "soulful" in a techno-futuristic sort of way, and adds to the experience ten fold in my opinion. Both exceed in enhancing the game to heights I've never seen before in the medium. A lot of titles have tried to fuse these two genres, but not like the way Transistor does. In closing, I'd like to invite everyone to give the game a try. It's an experience that will have many of you re-thinking the argument of whether "games are works of art" or not.
If you only play one video game, let it be Transistor.

This game is a sideways scrolling game where you need to avoid the obstacles, zap the larger fish and solve the puzzles. This is a fish in the ocean, but could as well be a spaceship shooting astroids.
The game is a mixture of figuring out the puzzle and do the right steering. The puzzle-part is fine, the steeering-part is awful. Even though you have figured out the puzzle you have to try again and again by trail and error to get the timing just right. That is very frustrating and will make you leave the game very soon.
The graphic is gothic/grey style and look beautiful. The stability of the game is solid. The sound and music is fine.
Bad stuff:
To much trail and error, timing and reflexes. Its very frustrating. You often have to do it over and over maybe 20 times
To much loading time when you die
Not able to put a puzzle on hold and try the next
Good stuff:
Nice graphics, gothic/grey style
Fine puzzles
Nice menues
Stable game, no crashes
Improvement suggestions:
Reduce loading time when you die
Reduce the trail and error
Conclusion:
The game have a nice graphic touch and stability, nicely layed out menues, and fine puzzles. But the steering is just bad. Not so much the mouse and keyboard, but the timing, the luck, and the endless trail and error, and then the loading times. I almost left at the first puzzle and thats sad because I just love puzzles and can sit for an hour to figure out a single puzzle. But to figure out a puzzle and to hit the right key at just the right moment are two different things. I like the puzzle part, not the action part.
If you like trail and error, this is the game for you.

Have you ever played a game with a lot of instadeath obstacles like Super Meat Boy? Imagine if you had to wait 10 seconds each time you died in those games . Granted this game is not really a platformer but it is formatted around trying to beat the same section over and over .
Akuatica is a mixture of puzzle solving and reflex battles. Regardless of how smart you are, it won't prevents you from constantly dying. There is a 4-second loop after you die followed by another 5-second cutscene. Checkpoints are not always in optimal spots so let us just say it takes 15 seconds to respawn in-game where you will die over 300 times.This game would probably be okayish but the wait time between deaths and checkpoint locations just kill the game completely. If you Developer is reading this review , just remove wait time between deaths and maybe you can salvage this game.
To be fair controls are not awful but you will get caught off guard with some of the interactable mechanics. Hitboxes on some of the obstacles are not very friendly and you will likely progress by trial and error. I think Akuatica makes a wrong impression by making you believe that this is a brain game. In fact, it is actually a rather difficult reflex game that happens to have puzzles while you dodging a load of crap on the screen.
"Challenges that cannot be overcome with sheer force alone. I must use my wits ."  taken from the Trailer.
2 Minutes into the game you are using water bubbles to fight a boat. It was not hard to figure out this puzzle since there was nothing else on the screen. I just refused to try that solution for about 20 minutes because there was no logic behind it. Some of the puzzles would be interesting if you were not waiting 10 seconds between deaths. Most of the sections still require moving timings so solution to the puzzle by itself does not get you through.
The only upside here is that game seems to be pretty long . I am not very far into the game but the enjoyment value ranges from decent to god awful. I guess the unfair frustration raises a challenge for the player which is not a compliment but perhaps worth mentioning. Some of us play the terrible games for the difficulty believe it or not.
The game is presented well but not enough to forgive gameplay problems. Music and level design are acceptable but not remarkable. Some places are more interesting than other.
The time it takes to respawn and try again is counter productive to the format of this game. Easy fix Developers!  Even if you know the solutions to the puzzles you still have to get though many instadeath areas where good reflexes are not substituted for luck. As a result, the hard difficulty of this game is not balanced by rewarding gameplay. On paper the game isn't horrible but it is a lot more frustrating than it should be.

Whoa! Nostalgia! What we have here is a 2012 blend of the old classics, Stonekeep, Eye of The Beholder and of course, the legendary Dungeon Master by FTL.
It's a 3D viewable game, played in the step-forward, back, left and right mentality. The story? Your 4-man party has been thrown into a prison-style keep called Grimrock.
Can you survive?
Yes - that's it.
Surely that's a problem?
No. Not at all.
In the current climate of RPG genres where back-stories, multi-layer character development and seemingly endless dialogue all vie for supremacy, LoG is wonderfully absent of all this 'clutter'. You're in a hole - get on with it.
Newcomers to RPGs may instantly be put off by its appearance - but that's only skin-deep. Veterans of the Amiga/Atari ST days will immediately feel at home with this and end up just spending '10 minutes more' on it. Simple, honest, fun. A brilliant first-step for those people who might think RPGs are usually quite daunting.
Certainly recommended. 8.5

Legend of Grimrock is an amazing game (and would be even without the considerable nostalgia factor), with an incredibly smooth presentation that blows many big budget productions out of water and well-polished gameplay. Admittedly, there are some minor problems here or there, but I'm guessing those will be fixed in the sequel. (There is going to be a sequel, right? Because it HAS TO.)

Old-school dungeon-crawlers have been making a comeback the last few years, and this doesn't disappoint.  Grimrock takes players and tosses them into a labyrinthian underground rife with puzzles and secrets to conquer, while roaming monsters are happy to startle you from the dark corners and shadowy distance.  With no music playing in the background, you are thrown into a place with heavy atmosphere: small sounds tickle the ears while monsters are heard shuffling about, and faint whispers make you wonder if you're actually alone down here..or if you're going mad from the oppressive isolation.  With a team of four, three job classes to choose from, and a variety of builds to utilize, the game is quite balanced and rewards those with quick reflexes as battles are done in real-time.  Those who stay alert and take in details with scrutiny will be rewarded as well, as buttons hidden in stone can be easily missed.  Be patient, cautious, and cunning..and you may find freedom from the dark.

Had trouble getting this to work on Windows 10 at first, but that was fixed by running it in Compatibility mode and going to my Nvidia graphics card settings and using "Add program" to add the Age of wonders II exe from the Steam folder.
This is an old game and the graphics and interface and general game design are clunky and difficult to use till you learn how. Once you do though the campaign is pretty fun, if hard at first.
Unlike in Age of Wonders III , where heroes can become strong but never wildly overpowered, Age of Wonders II heroes can get to level 30 even in the first mission, and along with items from quests, become killing machines.
However the campaign is really a series of 3 mission mini-campaigns for each shere of magic (fire , air etc). When you finish one of them you are back to square one with no items and no high level heroes - but you get to level up new heroes, and it ensures the first mission of each sphere is always a challenge.
There are no random maps available in Age of Wonders II , but there are a lot of campaigns missions (tutorial, 6 lots of 3 magic sphere missions and a final mission) plus some one off scenarios.
The game is very different from Age of Wonders III in some ways - your wizard lord can't gain experience , only get items , spells or skills. Only your heroes can level. And after the early stages of a mission your Wizard may end up just sitting in a city with a Wizard tower , which immediately means that anywhere your heroes are, your wizard can now cast spells.
For the second and third missions of each mini-campaign your wizard may get some armour and items that make him more capable of fighting in a battle, but in the first he will be mostly just supporting with spells.
The quests are also very different, based on shrines you can build to different spirits (order, war, magic and nature) Order and War hate each other, as do magic and nature. Please one too much and the other may send annoying raiders to attack your buildings - but rarely enough to be more than annoying.
I enjoy this game quite a bit , but at first found doing anything in it quite annoying. There is no list of all units you can find a unit from the way there is in Age of Wonders III and it's not as balanced.
The differences from Age of Wonders III make it interesting though - and OP heroes can be quite fun.

I recommend this because, at the end of the day, i dont regret buying it, and i dont wish i could refund it (which in all seriousness is what matters) BUT I cant just leave it at that.
The Surge is in all intents and purposes, much what Lords of the Fallen was (these devs previous game), which was a reasonably competent, but otherwise unremarkable Souslike fanfic. What i mean by that, is that its a game that clearly looks at what a soulslike does, where its complexities lie, and where its charm comes from.... before completely failing to recreate it in its same fashion.
Make no mistake, its not a terrible game. But if it cost anymore, this review would change to a thumbs down mighty quick.
Combat- 7/10: While its by all means a functional combat system with complexity and a risk/reward system, it ends up being pretty shallow when taken at the end of the day. Some points are thus:
-Some weapons are clearly better suited for most situations than others.
-This game is another example of why Poise was such an important thing in Souls. (a stat which would calculate how much impact it would take to stagger you. The way of balacing the huge weight increase of heavy armor)
-It has a lot of different additions, like being able to high dodge and low dodge, block, do different combos and such, but at the end of the day you dont really use the more complex additions... pretty much at all. As a matter of fact the game completely fails to mention you CAN do combos which drastically alter the way the attacks come out (as far as i saw, anyway). So while there is all this fancy stuff, it tends to fall by the wayside when you can be just as effective from simply slapping and stepping back.
-Drones are useful additions, but barely more than a small extra attack and/or a means of pulling an enemy from a distance. Melee drone is helpful for a bit of crowd control, but so far ive found a simple bit of cat and mouse is just as effective...
Map- 8/10:
The map is pretty standard fare. Twisty windy side-paths up-paths down-paths, ladders, holes, secrets, destructibles, shortcuts, etc etc. It does it reasonably well, but theres a few too many dead ends with no value, and a bit much twistiness for it to be a superly competent map design. Half the time i spent trying to work out where the hell i was, in order to find a shortcut to open, simply because the corridors were so damn similar to each other.
Does the job, nothing special.
Graphics- 9/10: Aint nothing too bad. Aint nothing too great. Reasonably detailed, and doesnt lack in a bit of asthetics. Doesnt feel that unique though. Spacey scifi standard corridors for the most part. Does the job, and well, but nothing to write home about.
Characters- 7/10: In all seriousness, the characters in this feel like they play very little actual role. Possibly at one point they were more in depth, but in the end most of them seem to exist more as a person to help and then ask "whats going on" to, before becoming another npc for little more than fetch quests or minor (but useful) rewards. Protagonist bland. Just like LOTF, no real reason for one gender or the other, and extra effort is the only real excuse for not having a choice.
Possibly better off to have just had a faceless Protagonist. He basically is faceless 99% of the time anyway.
Technicals- 7/10: Performance is quite good, despite an odd bit of dip here and there (or so it feels. 970, 16gb ram and 4690k, running on SSD), the load times are fine, no serious graphical oddities or artifacts, and the bare minimum of crashes or stalls, bugs or lockups.
HOWEVER. the hitboxes in this game... are barely passable. Easily the games worst aspect. A number of times youll be hit by attacks youre 100% didnt land according to the models, and other times attacks will land before they should seem to.
Its not a deal breaker, as with a bit of extra caution you can pretty much work around it. But it certainly takes you out of the moment when an attack lands you think shouldnt have. Some people might think this insignificant, but these sort of games (Soulslikes) are all about punishing your mistakes. If your only mistake is assuming the models mean anything, then thats not your fault at all.
Overall- 7.5/10.
Not a bad experience to sink some time into, and for the price you could do far worse (as i recently discovered, thinking "Hey, Homefront:TR cant be THAT bad, and its on special!"), but... you could do far better too. Honestly, id put LOTF above this, but barely. Competent Soulslikes that dont really encourage a second playthrough.
(Review made of my own experiences, make of them what you will.)

Do not buy this game. Although the release is technically 1.06, this is actually a facade to disguise the fact that Double Fine added a tutorial and some bugfixes following the release of Alpha 6D. There was never a beta, so the already content-sparce game was never very well optimized or balanced, which becomes extremely clear after a playthrough or two. The artstyle is very interesting and arguably beautiful, reminding me of wonderful games like Bastion, but a pretty paintjob doesn't mask the unfinished nature of the Spacebae DF-9. If you like the look and concept of this game, a group of settlers colonizing  a scifi environment, I reccomed a look at Rimworld by Tynan Sylvester. It is very similar, but obviously has a lot more work put into it. In the interest of full disclosure, I do not have a financial interest in either of these games. The modders with which Double Fine entrusted the game played it and then realized that Rimworld is a (subjectively) better game, which is why I can not find a single mod for DF-9 and the modding community for Rimworld is thriving. Transistor is a fun experience, with a beautiful art style, great soundtrack, and an interesting real-time/turn-based combat system that allows you to tailor your method of attack according to your playstyle.
The main story for Transistor sports a rather short playtime that never overstays its welcome, but comes with optional modifiers and an NG+ mode to enhance difficulty, and add replayability.
Definitely a buy if you're looking for a good time.

Overall Transistor is a really captivating game and is easily one of my current favourites.
The music in Transistor is beautiful, and really sets the mood throughout the game. The visuals were lovely, and the game has really nice character designs. Storyline and narration may be one of my favourite aspects of the game, and the ending broke me (it came quite unexpectedly but was a really touching).
Gameplay is unique as you can choose to strategically plan your moves or dive headfirst into battle, depending on your preferred play style, but i found both to be enjoyable (though i stuck to planning more). Game was also a good length and has replay value (Recursion).
It is also extremely customisable, as you are able to try all sorts of different combinations with the skills, and the results are often stunning, experimentation with different combinations was really interesting.
I would say this is one of the games you should pick up when its on sale bc it's worth the money :)

The soundtrack was amazing; the gameplay was engaging; the story made enough sense to be engaging yet was enigmatic enough to leave me wanting more.  A really fun, visually beautiful game to play.

If someone told you there is a game whose aesthetic seamlessly combines art nouveau, art deco, noir and cyberpunk, would you believe them? Because that is exactly what Transistor is - a game which perfectly embodies the flamboyant artistic styles of the first half of the 20th century and skilfully applies them to what seems to be a virtual world inhabited by AIs. It is the sort of world that immediately draws you in by its beauty and never fully lets you go. The city of Cloudbank where the game takes place seems to be hand crafted down to the tiniest detail and no two locations are alike. This is how world-building is supposed to look.
Gameplay-wise, the game definitely features a learning curve and initially that aspect might detract a little from your ability to fully enjoy the world, but once you learn the ropes - you'll be in for one amazing experience.
I didn't think that Supergiant Games could outdo themselves, but that is exactly what they did with Transistor.

pros -
- gorgeous soundtrack and visuals
- narration > bastion's narration, in my opinion
- emotionally stirring, thought-provoking story with roots in science fiction
- solid length, and the nature of the game's story-telling makes it to where replaying at least once is still enjoyable
- turn-based, strategy-based almost MOBA-esque combat is really fresh and fun, and can be infuriatingly difficult
- seriously one of the beautiful all around games i've ever played
cons -
- the story is not presented in the most cohesive way (deliberately) so i can see why someone may not fully understand the breadth of what is actually happening
- that's literally it

(Descriptive without spoilers)
Transistor is a tactical game that is rich in atmosphere that combines stylized visuals with just the right selection of music to match it. Red, Transistor's silent protagonist (except for her occasional beautiful, eerie singing) is a minimal figure who is dropped almost immediately into the action.
Combat in Transistor consists of real time segments which are broken up by Red's "Turn()" ability, which freezes time and allows her to make a series of rapid moves in succession. Afterwards, she must evade enemies until her Turn() ability is ready again. During a Turn(), the music becomes an ethereal, airy version of the same combat music that plays during real time. The combination of slow tactical play (turns) and frantic evasion is perfectly balanced so that one never gets bored with the pacing.
You acquire abilites over the course of the game to use in combat. Every ability can be either used directly, attached to another ability to give it a bonus, or attach it to Red herself to provide a passive bonus. For example, one ability pulls enemies to Red. Linked to another ability, it instead causes that ability to create a vacuum that pulls enemies toward it. Linked to Red, it increases her item pickup radius. Discovering interactions of this sort is a main part of the fun in Transistor.
+ Atmosphere, music and art are appealingly stylistic. Looks great on 4k and sounds great on a good system.
+ "Show not tell" style of storytelling reveals backstory over time without awkward exposition.
+ Ability system provides variety and many strategic options to explore
+ Fast/Slow combat system is fun
+ Sufficiently challenging
- When you start to lose in combat, you temporarily lose access to abilities one by one, which will seriously annoy some players, and can make a battle unwinnable.
- Red is so minimal that she can hardly be said to have a personality.
- Railroading. There are no decisions to make about which paths to take. There is only forward to the next encounter, except optional breaks to do challenges. One popular reviewer claimed "most" of his time in the game was spent exploring. This isn't possible, because other than a couple of small side-areas and easter eggs, there's nothing to explore.*
- The only real decision is what ability to select on level up, but that feels more like lost opportunities since you are choosing between two things and you don't know what either *really* does. The proper way to do this would be to let the player experiment with each power before requiring an irreversible choice between them.
- Some environmental interactions are clearly just padding. Have Red stare at what you can already see, for example.
- The game is quite short. While this preserves the freshness of the style, it does mean it's over while you still want more.
* I would level a charge of dishonesty at this reviewer if I thought it would have an effect.

Hexcells Infinite is probably the absolute puzzle game in the Hexcells series (
,
). It feels like a new version of the previous two with new levels and a random generator for even more levels. Since this feels like a refresh of the series I will copy/paste elements from my review of the previous two and build upon them.
Hexcells is a fairly simple game, much of it employing a combination of mechanics from minesweeper and nonograms (Picross) on a non standard 2D grid. It is a logic game were rules of the levels are defined by numbered brackets (minesweeper style) that give information on whether nearby brackets are false or true. This is sometimes mixed in with column markers that do the same, but for a column (picross style). To deepen the gameplay a bit more, you are sometimes also presented with special rules beside the numbers which frankly, in my humble opinion, make minesweeper look like a joke.
The base levels start easy enough but the difficulty curve steeps beyond what was comfortable in the first game yet stays bellow the hellish fires of Hexcells Plus. This time round we are presented with a random level generator which definitely extends the game but sadly does not escape the dredge facing all random generated content. Even though Hexcells level are simple, they always feel like it is you against the designer. Where the designer tried fooling you with level symmetry, hiding some emotion in the puzzles. In contrast, random generated levels feel cold and somewhat uninviting. It's not a dealbreaker by any means but I would have opted for community designed level sharing instead.
As with previous games, It kept me coming back. Infinite is challenging and fun. Cheap and as long as you'd like it to be. Took me 13 hours to get 100% achievements but I have 999,999,940 levels to go.

It's easy to see why this game was overlooked; underneath the cool setting, kung fu fighting and decent graphics it's just an inferior GTA pretender.  I don't mean that because it's a crime centered sandbox, I mean that because it takes all of its cues from GTA but does them worse.
Almost none of the characters are interesting.  They're introduced and killed at the drop of a hat.  You do about 2-3 missions and watch a couple of cutscenes and you're expected to care for these lifeless gangster stereotypes.
The story is disjointed.  You go from some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ apartment to a rich flat in a matter of missions, but you're still apparently working for some guy who operates out of his mom's kitchen.  The game even tries its hand at some laughable attempts at romance.  It just throws romance missions at you that grant bonuses, and then those female characters disappear utterly and are never heard from again.  It's like they chucked in unfinished storylines.
Gun combat is boring.  It's not as frequent as hand to hand, which is fine since that's the only fun part of the game, but it's all also very easy and unengaging.  Car combat is a JOKE.  If you shoot a single tire a car will suddenly go FLYING into the air.  It's fun the first few times but it's just absurd.  You get chased by 40 enemy bad guys in motorcycles and cars and you blow them all up by shooting out the tires and watching all of them spring up into the air like something out of Bollywood.
There's no real clear cut antagonist.  It just switches from some bad guy who ♥♥♥♥ed your sister, to some generic gang that is at war with your triad because... reasons... and then it switches back to the first bad guy's boss.
The main character was interesting and I was hoping the whole conflict between Wei being more of a cop or falling back into the gangster lifestyle was going to go some where.  Maybe the triad and cop bars actually affect the story?   But, spoiler alert, it doesn't.
The game just ends with a string of cutscenes, like they ran out of budget to add additional missions and they just skip days until the big bad guy who was behind everything the whole time is arrested.  Some cliched dialogue is exchanged and the game is over.
It's also really short.  The little side features are dull.  The car with the 2 miniguns is awesome and is one of the few things I really had fun with, but really, most of the time I was playing this I was thinking "Man, I wish they did so and so feature like GTA instead." or "Man, this is a cool set up, I wish GTA 4/5's writers were writing this storyline instead."
After the short 12-14 hour main story, including time to do a bunch of side missions and go on rampages, all this game really did for me is make me want to go and play GTA 4 or 5.
There's nothing offensively bad about this game, it's just boring, poorly written, and not really worth the time.

One of the few open world games I finished.
Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition is well worth the purchase.
The main character, Wei Shen, is an undercover cop who returns to Hong Kong to help infiltrate the Sun On Yee Triad organization. As Wei continues proving himself loyal to the Triads, he gets stuck in war between triad factions while remaining undercover and reporting to his superiors, blurring the lines between him being a cop and being a Triad member.
Positives:
+ Combat system: Consists of striking, grappling, and counters. These can be chained into combos and other cool moves as you unlock more of Wei's abilities.
+ The city: It isn't an exact replica of Hong Kong. But having been there a few times, I can say that the game captures the spirit of Hong Kong beautifully.
+ Story: Really intruiging especially as you go deeper into the game.
+ Great characters.
+ Driving: Probably one the best driving experience i had in open world games
+ Tons of clothes.
+ The Zodiac tournament: A Really cool homage to Bruce Lee's Enter the Dragon.
Negatives:

Disclaimer: If you expect me tho recite all detailed info avaialable for this game - again - you came to the wrong place. I'm mainly writing this review to express my own opinion as well as add my weight to the overall review rating. I think this game really doesn't deserve to get buried by the trending effort of people for unjustified bashing of newly released titles for whatever reason they can make up.
Because it's awesome. It's one of those games where literally all elements contribute to one whole, complete and nice picture - beginning at the technical base/underlay, the excessive amount of graphic and gameplay options, the use of state of the art shader techniques combined with well designed gameplay, an interesting introduction to the intriguing setting and an overall very motivating concept for gameplay and character progression. Combine this with exceptional motion-captured animations, innovative design and variance of enemies, gear and weaponry and you get a good understanding what this game is.
For me personally it's one among those very rare titles where all those aspects are combined into a good game, well worth it's money. The performance is flawless, I encountered no bugs so far and the rarely perceived shortcomings in it's basic design are ironically taken directly from what people rightfully claim to be it's role model, the Dark Souls series. If the devs would have shown a bit more courage and dared to step completely out of it's shadow, this game could have even been more. In my personal opinion it's better than any of the Dark Souls, BUT that ultimately boils down to personal preference. On a sidenote, I'm playing with mouse and keyboard and it feels very natural, is well implemented and fully configurable.
It's not perfect, but perfectionists know that this state is not achievable and just an ideal you can struggle for. Deck13 tried very hard and this effort should be commended.

This game is honestly a pleasant surprise. I haven't had this much fun in a while! I picked it up today, and I don't want to put it down. I've read some posts in the discussions forum that bother me, though. The dark areas are particularly engaging. You're never sure what you'll come across when you can barely see, even with your rig lights on. It makes me tense, and I love it. I watched 10 videos on The Surge before deciding to buy it. Worth every cent so far. I want to go into my own review now, because this has been an awesome experience so far.
GRAPHICS: Ooooooh man... this game is pretty in terms of the fidelity. WOW. 10/10
GAMEPLAY: I love the manner in which you obtain gear and materials. VERY awesome, gruesome and satisfying. Accessing the additional functions of your exoskeleton is actually an enjoyable undertaking, gathering enough items and currency to upgrade yourself to the point that you get a new toy to play with. Very well done. My only gripe is the timer on your "corpse" to retrieve your Tech Scrap. That's really not okay. 9/10
COMBAT: Oh man. A welcome change to the standard flow of Souls combat. Targeting specific parts to get gear, or targeting unarmoured sections to deal more damage. Dealing more damage has saved my life multiple times so far, and while it doesn't yield much in the way of mats for me, it is kind of sastisfying to drop multiple enemies in a row before decapitating the last one. Very well done and extremely entertaining. 10/10
MOVEMENT: Doesn't even feel clunky. It's actually very fluid and manageable. The dodging feels strange at first, having played the hell out of Souls games prior to this. However, you eventually get used to it and even find new ways to approach enemies using the dodge system and the slide system. Lots of fun to be had. 10/10
STORY: I don't really have much to go on right now, as I've just started. But I more or less get the gist of it. I'll add a score and change this once I've advanced further.
CUSTOMIZATION: While it lacks a custom character creation system, the way you manage gear on your character is actually pretty cool! A weapon slot, head slot, 2 arm slots, 2 leg slots and a body slot make up the system in which you customize your gear/looks (let's face it, this will become the new FashionFrame in no time). I'm not entirely sure if you can get additional exoskeletons, or if those can even BE changed, but so far, I like what I see. Still, the lack of a custom character denies it a full score. 8/10
REPLAYABILITY: I've come across enough information and even asked the forums about NG+, and I was told it was a thing, allowing you to upgrade further as you advance through each NG+. Automatic awesome. 10/10
SOUNDS: The sounds of your rig as you move, the enemies and their moans/battlecries, the clang of weapons on armour, the ripping and tearing of weapons through flesh and the pulsing of electricity are all very enjoyable to listen to. Even the visceral ripping, tearing and snapping as you dismember bodyparts is completely satisfying. Now, I don't know if there are weapons with additional sounds (Chainsaw swords, welding torches or the like), but for now it gets a great score! Subject to change in the future if I find some REALLY cool stuff with awesome sounds. 9/10
MUSIC: There isn't really any music so far. A lot of ambience and a few "triggered" sounds to tell you that you're going into a dangerous area, but hey. I guess I'll find out when I fight a boss. For now, no score here until I hear some actual music.
OVERALL: 9/10
PROS:
-Great, responsive combat controls
-Dark and gritty futuristic setting
-Plenty of weapon types
-Fast-paced combat
-Execution system
-Dismemberment (HELL YEAH!)
CONS:
-No Multiplayer/Co-Op features
-No character creation (male/female)
-Timer on Tech Scrap drop (not cool)
-No range weapons (I get it, non-military facility, but still... guns man...)
WOULD I RECOMMEND THIS GAME?
Hell yes I would. And that little piece of DLC? Worth it. A great extra with a bit of an assist early on. The noise the implant makes is annoying as hell, but it serves its purpose. At least it's not Navi the fairy... Pick this game up if you can. It's awesome!

Akuatica:
~~~~~~~
I do not know about you but I always love to sit at the beach, look at the beautiful sparkling water and every now and then I wonder…. Is life under water peaceful? Would it be exciting to discover life underneath these beautiful waves? And then I came across Akuatica….! You have to play it to believe what a hard life it is to be a fish!!
Akuatica is an action/adventure/puzzle game where you play a little fish with 5 red streaks on his back who will encounter interesting situations during his journey. The streaks on his back are the health bar of our joyful little fellow and he is armed with electric bolt (It’s true..! a bit like an Eel) to stun or to send your enemies to the abyss.  However, a boost of speed is very important in this game; as you will really quickly find out, it is quite a challenge to destroy your foe. So, sometimes you will need this extra boost to avoid a terrible misfortune…. And you do not want this to happen to our fish! An important point, it will take about 5 seconds to regenerate your electric bolt and your speed boost.
The game has 27 levels to beat and offers 2 types of difficulty, normal and hard (thank god for that, I got stuck on the piranha level for a while). I have been a long time fan of the Men of War series for years and through multiple iterations of the series and I think this one is pretty good, which is amazing when you consider for years the small team developing this game were just a bunch of modders trying to make their dream of a detailed WW1 mod for Men of War come true.
The game, in its state at the time of this review, is fun. The current French and Russian campaigns are very detailed and interesting, spanning the early weeks of 1914 all the way to the final offensives of the war. The mission variety is very good, with the classic Men of War stealth missions, defense missions in all kinds of terrain where you have to frantically patch holes in you lines after devestating artillery, large scale offensives involving hundres of men on the map at a single time, and even unique missions where you forrage for food and supplies while dodging germans to guiding french airmen in their escape from a German prison fortress.
As you play the game you will find yourself naturally evolving to WW1 tactics just as the officers of the time did. Initially you will see yourself using your 16 man squads to fulfill objectives in mass attacks that wreak horrendous casualties (2000 men died in one mission, and only one corner of a building in a town remained standing) but later slowly adapt to infiltration tactics by smaller units.
The game adds a lot of flavor in addition to the obvious unit design changes (which are fantastic and historically accurate). You can tell the developers truly love this era in time, as each mission is fleshed out with neat things like horse drawn artillery and sleds, units that change appearance as the war progresses (pickelhaubes to stalhelms, etc)
My hours don't reflect my true playtime since I have launched it outside of steam more often than I have from the steam client. Over my entire playtime I can honestly say that the only negative points I can honestly point out would be due to the limitations the Men of War engine (sometimes the UI is tough to use in massive battles on the highest difficulty) and some still evolving issues with multiplayer. Fortunately the devs are very attentive and care deeply about their game so I am sure these issues will be fixed. Multiplayer also suffers from a moderately low player count from the US/Europe.
Another flaw is the campaigns are pretty much all purchased separately, which is a tad ridiculous but you can always make your own I suppose.
Overall 7/10, pretty good but could be improved.

For all those calling this P2W you need to quit reviewing F2P games, you have no clue how F2P works. Every MMO F2P game has microtransactions. Someone has to pay for server upkeep and development, in short no F2P MMO will ever be truly free.
The upper hand Royal Quest has over it's competitors is that over 95% of what can be bought with cash can also be sold in the in game market for gold. Collecting gold in game is also very easy for players who do not want to pay any cash into the game. Even the cash shop currency can be sold. So it gives no advantage to any players that prefer to buy cash shop items.
This is actually a great game and THE MOST BALANCED F2P with cash shop items I have ever played and I have played them all, literally. I am sick of the all the♥♥♥♥♥♥poor reviews of games by players who don't have enough knowledge into said game to give it an factual review.
So let's clear up some of these misconceptions already put out there for this particular game:
1. Bag space. Your bag upon starting is split into 5 sections with 14 spaces each, that is 70 slots total. I've played plenty of "F2P" MMORPG's with less.
2. There is no forced PVP Zones. You can choose to follow your open world quests and grind or you can join the sandbox PVP zone for boosted EXP points.
3. EVERYTHING except the market currency can be bought at different NPC's, INCLUDING CASH SHOP ITEMS AND MOUNTS FOR IN GAME CURRENCY! One of the best mounts in the game cannot even be bought, it has to be unlocked with quest items. You don't have to buy these items just from players. Cash shop currency can be bought through the auction house . And they have included a maximum/minimum cap on how much a player can charge for cash shop currency. This is to fight gold farming companies. IN WHICH CASE NO OTHER "F2P" game has ever initiated a limiting system like this and has actually done very well for this game. You won't ever go into town seeing shouts of "Golds 200k=9.00 US @
or some garbage along those lines.
4. You don't have to pay anything to get in as some other review has mentioned.
5. Another reviewer had mentioned getting constantly killed by another player with OP cash shop gear. You cannot buy gear in the cash shop for this game. You cannot buy the ingredients in the cash shop to craft gear. This RPG much like every other RPG is heavily character build based. I haven't purchased **** since I first started playing and was already dropping characters 10 levels higher in the PVP zone in the most basic gear I could pick up. Also in which case PVP zones are limited by levels also so no getting into battles at level 13 with level 47 characters. PVP Zones are level designated & only allow a 10 level difference.

6. Now with the newest update all classes are about balanced in PVP. The crusader for a time there was a tad bit horrible but the new update has fixed that.
7. No kill stealing, no powerleveling. Everyone who hits an enemy will gain their proper share of exp from it. Even if you are not partied with that/those other person/people. However who ever does the most total damage will get the loot. All characters in a party with the exception of PVP zones, since parties can get split up in the zone, must hit the targets to get exp from it. No letting another character stand aside gaining EXP while a higher level character decimates the battlefield. Each person must attack to get their exp share. Again another way to combat gold farms & their services. In the PVP zones however, you will get exp from ally kills no matter where you are and the total end exp when you leave the zone is what you truly get, it is not split up dismally between the party when you leave. What you see is what you  get.
8. All mobs that can aggro will be aggro'd. A system in Royal Quest needed in most MMORPG's to eliminate people's needs for vacuum hacking. If you run past 20 aggro set monsters in Royal Quest you will pull 20 aggro set monsters. At that point it's fight or flight. Which can make for some interesting save-your-***-moments. Had another character try &  run past me pulling roughly 10 monsters, he ended up dying right next to me and in an instant they were set on me.
9. There is no such thing as junk in Royal Quest. Everything you pick up can and will be used for crafting something or commission(repeatable) quests which give Exp/gold/items sometimes all 3 and a few of them give a cash shop item. Even not so great gear can be broken down for crafting materials. Which makes making money in the game so easy. There is always somebody looking for what you have. And as I had mentioned earler more than 95% of cash shop items are sellable in the market. There really is no upper hand for cash users, unless you think that NO bonus stat costume is giving the player at the controls an ego boost...(At this time there are only 4 total pieces of costumes/pets/decorations that give bonus stats, which are horrible compared to the stats you can get from crafting normally).
10. Fair level up system for those of us who work. Your character gains 2x exp points when you are offline resting. The exp amount is dependant on your character level. Fetch, kill and collect quests are pretty fair in ratio at each level. So for collect quests which take the most time you can grind for a little bit, collect the money then buy the necessary collection items in the market/auction house.
It is your standard point & click, press skill button, type of game. Lightweight on processor and graphic usage. For those that prefer WASD movement like myself...as someone else had mentioned, the point and click system absolutely sucks. Because of this, I would compare this game to a cross between point & click ease of Diablo, skill system of Dekaron, and speed of Dragon Nest (When you get into higher levels of course). Some AoE's have a targeting system similiar to that of Wildstar. Camera movement is very Diablo-esque, which can also be annoying sometimes. This game could also use a better guide on how to obtain certain types of currency in game for specific NPC's, and NO, none of this special currency cannot be bought in the cash shop.
HOWEVER, ONE WARNING: This game has been in open beta for over 2 years now(Yeah, I know that is rather ridcilulous.). So be prepared for major changes that could be postive or negative.

If someone told you there is a game whose aesthetic seamlessly combines art nouveau, art deco, noir and cyberpunk, would you believe them? Because that is exactly what Transistor is - a game which perfectly embodies the flamboyant artistic styles of the first half of the 20th century and skilfully applies them to what seems to be a virtual world inhabited by AIs. It is the sort of world that immediately draws you in by its beauty and never fully lets you go. (Descriptive without spoilers)
Transistor is a tactical game that is rich in atmosphere that combines stylized visuals with just the right selection of music to match it. Red, Transistor's silent protagonist (except for her occasional beautiful, eerie singing) is a minimal figure who is dropped almost immediately into the action.
Combat in Transistor consists of real time segments which are broken up by Red's "Turn()" ability, which freezes time and allows her to make a series of rapid moves in succession. Afterwards, she must evade enemies until her Turn() ability is ready again. During a Turn(), the music becomes an ethereal, airy version of the same combat music that plays during real time. The combination of slow tactical play (turns) and frantic evasion is perfectly balanced so that one never gets bored with the pacing.
You acquire abilites over the course of the game to use in combat. Every ability can be either used directly, attached to another ability to give it a bonus, or attach it to Red herself to provide a passive bonus. For example, one ability pulls enemies to Red. Linked to another ability, it instead causes that ability to create a vacuum that pulls enemies toward it. Linked to Red, it increases her item pickup radius. Discovering interactions of this sort is a main part of the fun in Transistor.
+ Atmosphere, music and art are appealingly stylistic. Looks great on 4k and sounds great on a good system.
+ "Show not tell" style of storytelling reveals backstory over time without awkward exposition.
+ Ability system provides variety and many strategic options to explore
+ Fast/Slow combat system is fun
+ Sufficiently challenging
- When you start to lose in combat, you temporarily lose access to abilities one by one, which will seriously annoy some players, and can make a battle unwinnable.
- Red is so minimal that she can hardly be said to have a personality.
- Railroading. There are no decisions to make about which paths to take. There is only forward to the next encounter, except optional breaks to do challenges. One popular reviewer claimed "most" of his time in the game was spent exploring. This isn't possible, because other than a couple of small side-areas and easter eggs, there's nothing to explore.*
- The only real decision is what ability to select on level up, but that feels more like lost opportunities since you are choosing between two things and you don't know what either *really* does. The proper way to do this would be to let the player experiment with each power before requiring an irreversible choice between them.
- Some environmental interactions are clearly just padding. Have Red stare at what you can already see, for example.
