DF9 was a disaster waiting to happen. And now it has done just that.
I was surprised by how "polished" this game looked back when I first played it in one of the first alphas. The graphics and animations looked a lot more "expensive" than in similar games (mostly because they seem to be using 3D for everything while other games just use simple 2D sprites often with barely any animation), even the UI felt a bit overengineered.
At the same time the releases rarely addressed game-breaking bugs (e.g. airlocks being death traps) and frequently added seemingly arbitrary features that didn't really improve the gameplay other than giving players more bugs to worry about. I guess the project could be described as ambitious, but then again the same would be true for games like Prison Architect and Rimworld, both of which have been able to maintain some level of consistent narrative over a large number of releases (without needing to re-release every single version several times to provide hotfixes).
Some reviewers have said DF made the mistake of treating a supposedly indie, crowd-funded project as if it were another big team big publisher triple-A title. I don't think anyone but the DF9 team can answer that, but it seems telling that a game that was already funded with half a million dollars within the first weeks of the open alpha and that was intended to be entirely financed by pre-release purchases/"backers" has managed to drain its entire budget within only six major releases. If the game needs more than this kind of cash just to make it to 1.0-as-intended, maybe DF shouldn't have attempted to follow through with this idea. If you're burning money, either find a potent investor who doesn't care, or cut down your development costs to a level where you can bootstrap the project without making f-you money.
To quote Robot Unicorn Attack: "Your dreams did not come true."

Given that things haven't really come together in six major alpha releases, I wouldn't expect much from the final release. The game had promise, but in my opinion it simply isn't fun.

This game is honestly a pleasant surprise. I haven't had this much fun in a while! I picked it up today, and I don't want to put it down. I've read some posts in the discussions forum that bother me, though. The dark areas are particularly engaging. You're never sure what you'll come across when you can barely see, even with your rig lights on. It makes me tense, and I love it. I watched 10 videos on The Surge before deciding to buy it. Worth every cent so far. I want to go into my own review now, because this has been an awesome experience so far.
GRAPHICS: Ooooooh man... this game is pretty in terms of the fidelity. WOW. 10/10
GAMEPLAY: I love the manner in which you obtain gear and materials. VERY awesome, gruesome and satisfying. Accessing the additional functions of your exoskeleton is actually an enjoyable undertaking, gathering enough items and currency to upgrade yourself to the point that you get a new toy to play with. Very well done. My only gripe is the timer on your "corpse" to retrieve your Tech Scrap. That's really not okay. 9/10
COMBAT: Oh man. A welcome change to the standard flow of Souls combat. Targeting specific parts to get gear, or targeting unarmoured sections to deal more damage. Dealing more damage has saved my life multiple times so far, and while it doesn't yield much in the way of mats for me, it is kind of sastisfying to drop multiple enemies in a row before decapitating the last one. Very well done and extremely entertaining. 10/10
MOVEMENT: Doesn't even feel clunky. It's actually very fluid and manageable. The dodging feels strange at first, having played the hell out of Souls games prior to this. However, you eventually get used to it and even find new ways to approach enemies using the dodge system and the slide system. Lots of fun to be had. 10/10
STORY: I don't really have much to go on right now, as I've just started. But I more or less get the gist of it. I'll add a score and change this once I've advanced further.
CUSTOMIZATION: While it lacks a custom character creation system, the way you manage gear on your character is actually pretty cool! A weapon slot, head slot, 2 arm slots, 2 leg slots and a body slot make up the system in which you customize your gear/looks (let's face it, this will become the new FashionFrame in no time). I'm not entirely sure if you can get additional exoskeletons, or if those can even BE changed, but so far, I like what I see. Still, the lack of a custom character denies it a full score. 8/10
REPLAYABILITY: I've come across enough information and even asked the forums about NG+, and I was told it was a thing, allowing you to upgrade further as you advance through each NG+. Automatic awesome. 10/10
SOUNDS: The sounds of your rig as you move, the enemies and their moans/battlecries, the clang of weapons on armour, the ripping and tearing of weapons through flesh and the pulsing of electricity are all very enjoyable to listen to. Even the visceral ripping, tearing and snapping as you dismember bodyparts is completely satisfying. Now, I don't know if there are weapons with additional sounds (Chainsaw swords, welding torches or the like), but for now it gets a great score! Subject to change in the future if I find some REALLY cool stuff with awesome sounds. 9/10
MUSIC: There isn't really any music so far. A lot of ambience and a few "triggered" sounds to tell you that you're going into a dangerous area, but hey. I guess I'll find out when I fight a boss. For now, no score here until I hear some actual music.
OVERALL: 9/10
PROS:
-Great, responsive combat controls
-Dark and gritty futuristic setting
-Plenty of weapon types
-Fast-paced combat
-Execution system
-Dismemberment (HELL YEAH!)
CONS:
-No Multiplayer/Co-Op features
-No character creation (male/female)
-Timer on Tech Scrap drop (not cool)
-No range weapons (I get it, non-military facility, but still... guns man...)
WOULD I RECOMMEND THIS GAME?

Awesome game!  A throwback to old tile-based dungeon crawler games, this game is real-time, difficult, and bleak.
You control a whole party of 4 adventurers that are forced by their ankle chains to stand on the same square.  There are tons of puzzles as well as tough monster fights.  Secret rooms everywhere!  Your characters need to eat occasionally or they start to recieve negative effects, forcing you to keep moving deeper towards your own doom.
Everything seems well balanced, though it is balanced towards difficulty.  In order to do well in combat, you are expected to perform a ballet dance, attacking the enemies from the side and sidestepping them before they turn to face you.  You will probably end up dying a lot, so save often.  If you want a real challenge, there is an option to turn off the map, forcing you to use graph paper to map out the dungeon as you go.
The game is said to last at least 10 hours, and a level editor and mod support are coming soon.

[DISCLAIMER: The following review was last updated in 2015, the gameplay may have changed since then.]
Do I recommend this game? As it looks now, no. Unless you want to support the developers, which may or may not help them fix the issues I've encountered below. Don't count on it.
This is going to be my first serious review ever made, because it is needed.
First off, let me explain my experience with the Men of War franchise.
I was an ex-modder for Men of War, Men of War Vietnam and Men of War Assault Squad as well as the head of the Men of War Fanclub on
You may know me as craftan99. This is important to note so that you will know how much knowledge I have of how the game engine works and how it's assets is used. I have safely over 1000+ hours on Men of War offline back when It was a retail version. Now, on to the game.
The developers of this game, "The Great War Team", have claimed that the single player is finished. However, this is not the case. There are several localization issues where items and weapons miss names. The writing of the dialogues are awful and usually the voice acting and subtitles don't match to what they're saying and some dialogue is recorded with a very poor microphone. Also, little is explained as how to accomplish certain objectives without much direction as to what is required to do certain objectives. Some times you need certain items and it's a pain if you've somehow don't have that item because you dropped it somewhere. The game is also very lacking in Sound Assets, or maybe lacking isn't the word to use. I'd say that it has poor quality. Some guns sound very off when it comes to some kind of noise feedback that is in the background. Horses galopping is also a great example at terrible sound. This series is known to have bad voice acting as Men of War's developers had the same issue. However, I don't know if "The Great War Team" was even responsible for the voice acting or if they asked for support from the main developers of the franchise. In any case, it needs to be redone completely. There are tons of people who would volounteer without payment. Websites like
let's people try out for voice roles. Why they didn't do this, beats me.
The mission designs aren't the best either, they aren't very consistent and stealth is usually a hard task, but it is possible. However, stealth missions are rather tedious. Speaking of difficulty and missions, I always found the defense missions in the French and Russian campaigns to be extremely easy to complete. I think it's because the waves of enemies where so small that they were easily fended off.
When it comes to balancing, the artillery reload speed need to be longer and the infantry sprint endurance bar needs to be longer. Either that or faster recharges on the bar. Artillery HE rounds could also use some balancing to maybe lower the AoE just a bit, I always found the artillery redicioulously overpowered. Even with realism, balancing is needed to make the experience more fun and engaging. Artillery spam is hardly fun. Tanks are perfectly balanced in my opinion and I don't see much needed in the ways of improving that.
This wasn't much of a review as it is explaining what this game needs to fix. Even if this is in Early Access, these are things that have been overlooked and should be completely redone.
Basically:
* The Campaign is not finished, even if the developers claim it is.
* Awful writing.
* Awfully easy defense missions where the waves are too small.
* Poor sound assets with bad voiceacting.
* Some icons have bad artwork.
* Localization issues.
* Tedious Stealth Missions.
* Balancing Issues.
Suggestions:
* Add realistic color to the mustard gas, yellow.
* Add more types of gas and apply equally realistic color. (White Cross, Green Cross and Blue Cross.)
* Add more unit types to Multiplayer. (Bavarian Infantry, French Chasseurs, Canadian Royal Rifles, White Russian Guard)
* Add Cavalry and the ability to attack with horses.
* Add better and fresher animations for the infantry.
All in all, I've enjoyed the hell out of the game, but I would enjoy it even more if these issues were fixed. I would be so happy if it was.
Thank you for your time.

Transistor follows the story of a mute young woman, Red, in her journey of discovery. Taking place shortly after losing her voice, she discovers a key like object known as the Transistor, which narrates and communicates with Red in an accustomed manor. Together, they explore a world which has been over-run with digital viruses, which plagues the worlds existence itself.
From start up, I was astonished by the beautiful design. color and soundtrack this feature displays, it all fits splendidly together in a blend that can only impress. The game play is phenomenal, sporting a combination of classic mechanic systems, in a mix that I can only describe as Final Fantasy meets Zelda. The narration is a pleasure to listen too and pays homage to their previous game, Bastion, which was equally fantastic.
The game length tends to be on the shorter side, supplying approximately 8 hours of overall game time. Don't be fooled though, once you've seen the ending you're given the option the restart the journey, allowing you to keep all the items and progression from your current file, which lends to some interesting replay ability.
Overall, the game is a breathtaking experience, every aspect of the game works well together in a new and original concept. Supergiant Games, creators of Transistor and Bastion, deserve a congratulations for creating a masterpiece, this game will will certainly stand the test of time as one of the greatest games to hit the market. I rate Transistor a 9/10.

Before I started playing this game I had no idea how to make spaghetti, but now I can do it without even trying. It's actually becoming somewhat of a problem. Speaking of spaghetti it is also a great game to play if you want to forget to eat or drink throughout the day, but maybe that's just me.
There is so much to do in this game once you get past the initial gathering of resources to start building your factory, you will not likely find a moment in the game where there isnt something you can be building or improving. I also found it very interesting to just figure out how everything works on my own, which is easily possible for the most part, though there is some more advanced stuff to learn that you might need outside help for. Your first few factories are more than likely going to be absolutely awful, but once you finally figure out how to make a good one there is such a great feeling of satisfaction.
It is of course still an early access game, but at this point there is more than enough to keep you occupied for a good long while. There is also plenty of interesting stuff to be added in future updates to look forward to, so I guess that also gives a good reason to come back to it every now and then.
In any case, this game is perfectly ideal for any person who highly values efficiency and is suitable for people who like Breen energy and killing the planet alike.

Overall an A+ game. I loved every minute of gameplay and found it to be fun, challenging, interesting, visually beautiful, and with an enthralling story of right vs wrong.
Albeit your choices in the game don't really influence anything that happens in the main story, you will nonetheless be internally debating the actions you must do (both because of the game script and also because of your character's mission). The two-part XP system (Cop XP/Triad XP) does a decent job of making your choices matter in that respect, though.
The fighting style is incredibly well done. Spectacular hand-to-hand combat augmented by handheld weapons (like a fish, yes, you can slap people with a fish) and a variety of guns (which aren't available in every instance), plus fun, interesting, and devastating moves that you can gain by leveling up and finding artifacts in the world.
I have played many GTA-Like games (Saint's Row series, GTA 1, 2, 3, 4, haven't gotten to V yet) and I feel that this perfectly balances the open-world playstyle with an excellent story, while being realistic with gameply aspects like an inventory system, aka there isn't one. You can carry a pistol, but forget about running around with a goddamn rocket launcher under your coat. You will actually have to run from the police if they pull their guns out.
Lastly, Square Enix did a fantastic job of making this game
There's no console control mixups. No one forgot to change this thing or that thing. Every bit is tailor made for PC users. (sole gripe: Driving some of the cars is a PITA without control sticks. gripe over.)
For $30, this is an unreal steal. I got it on sale but would buy again in a heartbeat.

My Dark Horse pick of 2012, Sleeping Dogs is not quite as good as Saints Row 2 but sits right in the same ballpark, with good gameplay across the board and a more focused approach to level design but with more than enough variety to justify the scope of its world, which is easily among the best open worlds to exist. Hong Kong is the best character in this game, but the others aren't so bad either, despite a hokey ending. A few little flaws, but nothing gamebreaking against the moments of gratification the game offers.

I tried so hard to like it, I really did.
I am a huge fan of the Souls games, and I was so excited about The Surge to fill the Souls hole in my heart. Since Dark Souls will be the main comparison here, then I will begin with the first boss fight.
If you die to a boss in Dark Souls, 95% of the time it's your own fault. You screwed up somehow. You didn't dodge at the right time, you miscalculated a hit, you didn't read an incoming attack correctly. In some way, it was your error, and the boss just capitalised on it.
Let's talk about the first Boss in The Surge -
The boss itself was fairly easy to predict, however it's sword and stomp attacks were able to damage me even though I was not in range of them. Sometimes I had dodged under the boss and was behind it when I got hit by it's frontal sword attack. Sometimes when it stomped it's right leg, I was on the outside of it's left leg and would still get damaged. Other times this was not the case, it was random.
I also didn't even know how to kill it.. Until I realised that when I hit it, an orange bar underneath it's health bar would fill up. Once that orange bar was full, the boss would fall to the ground to "Recover", opening it up to attack. This was the only sequence of the fight where you could actually deal damage to the boss.
I died the first two times learning how this worked, so the third time I thought that I had it sussed. Except, this time once the orange bar was filled, it didn't do anything. The boss continued to attack me as if nothing happened. No matter how much more damage I inflicted, it just kept going. I was dodging around, waiting for the sequence to happen, but it never did. I spent hours dying over and over to trying beat this boss, without even actually inflicting any damage TO the boss.. Because the only sequence of the fight that allowed me to damage the boss wouldn't happen.
I turned my PC off, had a few hours break (I was seething), and came back.. Beat him the first time. The sequence magically worked as soon as that orange bar filled up.. And I was able to defeat it.
Wait until they fix the bugs, and wait until it's on sale to buy this - It's truly infuriated being killed so unfairly over and over.

General recommendation.  Well put together, fun to play.
It's a dungeon explorer with a simple story, but the narrative doesn't do much to drive the game (that's fine though, exploring and moving forward and satisfying and motivating enough.) The game is NOT randomly generated so replayability only comes from wanting to try out different party combinations or difficulty settings.  Though, future content (including mod tools?) is promised.  Nice game length for the price too.

I just finished my first playthrough, and well it sort of left me 'dazed and confused'. Mainly because for half of it I did not realize I was either supposed to be a male, or a girl attracted to my (female) best friend. In fact, I went into the game happily oblivous wanting to be suprised-since the descrption on Steam is so incredibly sparce.
Now , I'm used to playing both male and female protagonists; I play lots of visual novels (most by nature tend to be romance dating games), but I go into those knowing that's the genre I'm dealing with, and my gameplay identity so I can immerse myself.  Going in blind to this, while somewhat fun- ultimately left me thrown where I probably didn't enjoy the game as fully as others who interpreted Chapter 1 (and even 2) differently. This was very disappointing as if I had understood it better, I feel like the story-while amusing- might have had a greater impact on me.
Without spoiling, let's just say Chapter 1 could have provided a lot more clues towards the nature of your relationship with Emily so that later Chapters don't feel so awkward.  But all it sets you up for is that you are friends with a girl named Emily, whom you talk about boys and parties with.
I love the chat interface gameplay; having to actually touch a key on your keyboard to have your dialogue choice typed out is genius, fun,  and makes the chat sessions more authentic feeling. I found it interesting how Emily would 'remember' things, although I haven't noticed how this affects gameplay, which is a bit of a disappointment. Perhaps another play through will make that mechanic clearer.
And I will give it another playthrough, as I do want to see exactly in how many different directions Emily and I's story can go. Especially now that I understand more about our relationship. I just really wish I would have understood it better upfront.
Despite the relationship/character confusion and  lackluster ending (probably due to my play style), I would recommend people check this out if they like interactive fiction or choose your path games. It's amusing if nothing else. And I would like to see more from this developer.

PLAYTIME: ~120-130 Hoursd (+ ~20 Hours for download on two computers)
-Positives-
Story: The story is great, especially for an MMO, which don't usually, or at least in my experience, have a good or in depth story. Characters are built up, and the story has multiple arcs and twists which keep it interesting. The story also ties together the main bulk of your actions in the game, meaning everything* (* Basically) has a purpose, or a quest behind it.
Combat: (Dragoon) Traditional tab-targeting combat, but executed in such a way that it feels great. Despite the 2.5 second global ability cooldown, combat never feels sluggish, especially when you get to level 30-50, where you get to string together multiple abilities together, and always have something to watch out for. While it does get visually manic when in an 8 or 24 man raid/dungeon, the game provides you with a multitude of ways to stay on target. Really good combat, with well done animations.
Classes: Wide variety of classes, some which are quite original. I picked Dragoon as my starter class (Lancer->Dragoon), and Have not regretted it. Abilities are unique and (For the most part) all serve a purpose. Armour looks En Fuego.
World/Design: The world of Eorzea has stunned me a few times so far, and I already have some favourite areas. The general design, art and visuals (texutres, graphical quality etc.) is very enganging and encapsulates the player.
-In the Middle-
Subscription: While I accept the neccessity for a subscription to constantly deliver quality content, I also accept that it can become financially taxing. I have renewed my subscription beyond the free trial, and have not regretted it. It is not the most expensive subscription, but it is not the cheapest. This is really up to you, as to whether it is a deal breaker.
Conclusion: A great MMO with a free trial, you've got nothing to lose to if you try this out, and I recommend this highly, as it is one of  the few MMOs that have captivated my attention quite this much.

Just as epic as i remember it.  Bought it on Steam just for memory sake and am loving it.  By far one of my top favorite strategy turn-based games.  Reminds me a lot of Heroscape, but massive proportion.
Pros:
-Massive replay value.
-Several races, each race having their own large set of creatures and spells, pros and cons.
-Map creator.
-You're free to play how you want to play and have your own strategy, regardless of whether or not it actually works.  Parties dont have to have heroes.  And besides the alignment penalty, you are free to mix, match and group any units you want in a party.
-AI is actually intellegent.  Very little foresight but AI characters usually dont make blatantly stupid mistakes.
-"Board-View" zooms in to "Battle-View" when fighting.  It is still turn based and can be manually controlled, auto-pilot, or skipped all together if you're not one for battle strategy (... but then you probably wouldn't be playing this, would you?  But it does make the game faster).
-Turn-based play makes it possible for multiple human players to play with each other on one computer.
Cons:
-Not the greatest graphics but it was made 10+ years ago, so not unexpected.
-If manually played out a single game on a Large board with normal-hard AI opponents can take several weeks of casual play to complete.
-Takes a while to get use to the rules of the game.  Things like; certain flying creatures can't be attacked by ground units, or the fact that allied units and cities of the oposite alignment have a chance of rebelling every turn and becoming enemies.  These types of detailed rules can make the game frustrating if you forget them.
All this said:
This game is easily worth double what they're charging.

Ok, so you remember the old-school first-person dungeon crawlers? It's one of those, and it's excellent.
Oh, wait, you said "no"? Oh, well, let me break it down for you. It's an RPG with light story, grid-based movement, puzzles and exploration a-plenty, and monsters intent on ruining your day at every turn. You know The Elder Scrolls? It's not like that. You don't go on quests, you don't visit towns, you don't save the world. You get one massive dungeon that you and your party of four wander through in a ceaseless battle for survival and escape. The game is hard for the modern gamer. It requires careful planning, strategy, and knowing a few things about RPGs (fire wrecks undead, poison is wasted on spiders, etc.), but every battle is rewarding.
If you want something old (or something new, depending on your gaming history), grab this. It's incredible, and there's the promise of custom dungeons on the horizon, so you'll have plenty more exploring to do in the future. Good luck.

If you ever wanted a sequal to Stonekeep, get this game. If you liked old first-person dungeon crawlers, get this game. If you like solving puzzles and finding secrets but don't really care about combat much, get this game and play it on easy. Great fun!

Robot Soccer, a merge between the Football Minigame in Robot Wars: Extreme Destruction and Rocket League.
Robot Soccer is of a simplistic design, accompanied with simplistic controls. You control a robot with pincers which allow you to catch the ball. You manouver your robot with the WASD keys and can either Chip the ball, causing a higher ball with less power (Right click on mouse.) or do a power shot, causing the ball to go fast and straight (Left click on mouse.)
So far, whilst being new to the game a problem I encountered is the 1v1 matches ppear to be very one sided to new comers like myself, with the matches seemingly very one sided to the AI. A noticeable feature I noticed is the AI are able to knock the ball out from your pincers and out of control whilst persuing behind you, thus sometimes making you lose control over a fairly won goal and missing a shot that is not quite lined up, whereas no matter how much I spam left or right click this never seems to have any effect on the AI as it does with me. This may just be down to my own skill level and not the games fault, however.
Visually, I commend the designers for creating a pitch that refrains from being bland. The incoorperation of various obsticales makes the game play out in a less linear way, testing your ball contol skills and forcing you to sometimes chip the ball over walls and bounce the ball off them. Certain obsticales such as tires are interactive and can be knocked around the pitch to make it much harder to navigate and reach the ball, a very small but lovely touch I enjoyed.
Overall I do enjoy this game on a casual level, and think I would get more fun with friends and more balanced matches. Personally, I don't think this game deserves its price tag it has currently, and think of this more of a £1.75 game, this could just be me being a cheapskate. However, if new content is added I believe this will still be an enjoyable game. I do not regret buying this. However, if Rocket League is on sale I recommend you pick that game up in priority over Robot Soccer, as the experience is much better and there are more people playing Rocket League on the online multiplayer.
I would give Robot Soccer a 6/10. :)

PLAYTIME: ~120-130 Hoursd (+ ~20 Hours for download on two computers)
-Positives-
Story: The story is great, especially for an MMO, which don't usually, or at least in my experience, have a good or in depth story. Characters are built up, and the story has multiple arcs and twists which keep it interesting. The story also ties together the main bulk of your actions in the game, meaning everything* (* Basically) has a purpose, or a quest behind it.
Combat: (Dragoon) Traditional tab-targeting combat, but executed in such a way that it feels great. Despite the 2.5 second global ability cooldown, combat never feels sluggish, especially when you get to level 30-50, where you get to string together multiple abilities together, and always have something to watch out for. While it does get visually manic when in an 8 or 24 man raid/dungeon, the game provides you with a multitude of ways to stay on target. Really good combat, with well done animations.
Classes: Wide variety of classes, some which are quite original. I picked Dragoon as my starter class (Lancer->Dragoon), and Have not regretted it. Abilities are unique and (For the most part) all serve a purpose. Armour looks En Fuego.
World/Design: The world of Eorzea has stunned me a few times so far, and I already have some favourite areas. The general design, art and visuals (texutres, graphical quality etc.) is very enganging and encapsulates the player.
-In the Middle-
Subscription: While I accept the neccessity for a subscription to constantly deliver quality content, I also accept that it can become financially taxing. I have renewed my subscription beyond the free trial, and have not regretted it. It is not the most expensive subscription, but it is not the cheapest. This is really up to you, as to whether it is a deal breaker.
Conclusion: A great MMO with a free trial, you've got nothing to lose to if you try this out, and I recommend this highly, as it is one of  the few MMOs that have captivated my attention quite this much.

Hexcells is, on the most basic level, a more sophisticated version of Minesweeper. You are given a layout of golden hex tiles, possibly with one or more of them already highlighted or flipped. Flipped tiles have numbers on them, and also labels indicating whether or not adjacent tiles which should be highlighted are continuous or non-continuous (or no designator at all). There are also row and column labels which allow you to see how many tiles need to be highlighted in any given row or column.
Each puzzle mixes these up in a unique way to push you to solve it.
Thinking about this game as a more sophisticated version of minesweeper is, I think, fairly ideal, because that is more or less what it is, and the function it serves. It is something to throw away a bit of time on, not sit down and play continuously.
It is about as fun as Minesweeper is, and I’d basically consider it filling that role in your game library.
The sequels get steadily harder, and unfortunately, I'm not 100% sure all the puzzles are solvable without guessing - there were a few points where I got stuck and the only way forward seemed to be taking a guess. That happened on only a small fraction of the puzzles, but I'm not sure if I was simply not good enough, or if they are legitimately ambiguous.
My advice? Pass. It isn’t a bad puzzle game, but it isn’t anything remarkable either. If you did get it as part of a bundle or something, it isn’t a terrible thing to install and just screw around with when you’d mess around with solitaire or minesweeper or whatever, but I wouldn’t go out of my way to buy this.

+ The gameplay is very simple and mainly consists of flipping over tiles to find the correct pattern. Very comparable to Minesweeper as unactivated tiles will have a number which designates how many adjacent tiles connected to it should be flipped. By using this information along with info from other hex squares you are able to begin eliminating / breaking unneeded tiles and finding the correct ones to activate.
+ Nice relaxing ambient background sounds that is very peaceful
+ The game gets quite challenging later on and has plenty of stages to keep you content for hours
- For me personally, this game feels a bit repetitive after a short while once you understand the mechanics. Every level is different and it does try to add a few new mechanics as you progress, but overall it was just a bit too simplistic visually.

Battle of Empires: 1914-1918 (which I will refer to as BoE in this review) is a pleasantly surprising strategy game made in the mold of the Men of War series. In fact, it originally started out as a mod for MoE but has quickly shifted to become its own entity. So fanboys can stop reading, add to cart, and start enjoying - you're already sold because gameplay will be very similar and, in fact uses the same game engine. There will be a few slight differences which can be considered improvements although some nostalgic MoE players may disagree.
As for the rest of you, think World War I combat strategy on a somewhat grand scale. During gameplay players will have a variety of units to command: infantry, artillery, tanks, etc and each have their own individual inventories to allow total customization based on your combat needs. The combat is real-time and the maps are fully interactive. This means that obstacles can be destroyed, used for cover, and manipulated over the course of the battle as well as reflecting the changing landscape of the battlefield due to artillery shells, bombing runs, or even from building make-shift sandbag barricades to be used as cover. The amount of detail put into the units to reflect the time period is admirable and the effort does not go un-noticed. BoE truly feels like a WWI timepiece.
The game is extremely vanilla in its current Early Access state but still very playable. The developers have 5 different campaigns planned for inclusion into the full release version of the game along with additional bonus missions (possibly DLC?). Currently only the French campaign is included but the Russian campaign is almost completed and the others are currently "in progress." There is already an editor included for the purpose of modding so one can expect a lot of extra community content to be added as well.
The game also features both co-op and multiplayer as well and both are already working in basic form but I believe more features will be added before completion. For an Early Access game there is a lot of content and playability available and I experienced no bugs or crashes so there is no need to wait.
There are a few things that I hope to see improved before the final release. The sound and voiceovers are mediocre at best and still leave a lot to be desired. Another issue is with the limitations on squads. While the game consists of large scale combat, it becomes a hindrance moving troops all around the map when you can only control a specific handful at a time. The user interface feels cluttered and unorganized. It gets the job done but overall it just doesn't feel very efficient.
BoE includes a tutorial along with a skirmish mission before actually beginning the campaign in order to familiarize players with the various controls and such. However, at times this tutorial is vague and can be confusing, even more so for a player not familiar with this type of game and a lot of information is stuffed into this small sampling so it can quickly become overwhelming. Hopefully these elements all get ironed out before the game is released as a final product.
While Battle of Empires : 1914-1918 is still an "Early Access" game and the price may seem a bit lofty, there is already a lot of quality gaming content included with a lot more already in development. Plus it has an early stage multiplayer feature and comes with an editor for modding. I recommend RTS fans to grab this game now because the price could easily go up once all of the content is added. The gameplay is solid, the content is of good quality, and this game is just as fun and challenging as Men of War.

: Is this game P2W (Pay to Win)
: The short answer is NO, however, let me go in depth with this...
When you start this game you get 3 days free premium this gives you:
+50% EXPERIENCE AND DROP RATE
PORTAL SKILL (This allows you to save 5 places and teleport to it at any time including Maidens (Rogues/Assassin/Thief get a skill called Secret Lair which allows you to save only one spot but its free!)).
FREE TELEPORTATION BETWEEN MAIDENS (Even without premium it doesn't cost that much)
+10 QUESTS IN QUEST LOG (I have never needed 30 quest slots even at low levels where I had 18 quests at one time, even with dailies (I will go more in depth into the dailies later on).
Pets are utility centric as in they do nothing but pick up drops for you they do require you buy SIlver/Gold Magnet Collars from Cash Shop, they have a durability called Charge, 1 Charge = 1 drop picked up (Pets are not worth the trouble having other than aesthetics you can easily just pick up the drops yourself with spacebar).
Mounts again are utility centric they offer increased movespeed as well as various stat boost such as attack or health, they require Mount Feed from Cash Shop, Crusader/Dark Knight can get Mounts that do not require food for 300G from Ricker in Varlone City he is in the centre square off to the top right and from Ronda in Iris out of the South Gate of Varlone, these Mounts only give movespeed bonus (Mounts are semi useful for all classes as the buffs from them last for 1 hour even if you dismount, only the classes I mentioned can do mounted combat). You can also use Grass Chewing Gum which gives you 20% Runspeed for 15 minutes, you can get it from a daily quest or dropped from monsters (its rare to get a drop), you can also buy it from the Market fairly cheap.
A Mount and a Pet can be bought from an NPC (Head of the Merchant Guild) to the south of city square in Varlone City.
Reales can be bought from Market for 10-14k gold per Reale, 10x Mount Feed is 29 Reales and last for 1 hour each (290-406k for 10 hours of extra buffs, which you totally dont need if you are just PVMing although it would be useful), Silver Collar 2000 Charge is the same 29 Reales. You can get 100x Mount Feed for 269 Reales and Gold Collar 9000 Charge for 99 Reales. This is on the EU Maragorne Server.
You have 14 slots for each type of item they are split into Equipment, Expendables, Loot and Crafting Items. You can store excess/rare items in your Warehouse which has 27 slots available accessible at any Maiden. The 2 Bags that get full fairly quickly are Expendables and Loot but once you learn what you should keep and what should be sold to NPC or put on the Market you won't have too many bag problems.
ALL Equipment in the game can either be bought from NPCs, Crafted, Dropped from Monsters, Found in Dungeons (Marked by a Cross Shaped Grave Stone with Blue particle effects, these are mostly personal so you will not be able to sell them on the Market) or bought from Players via the Market.
Item improvement is done through Alchemists you will know the NPC is an Alchemist because they will have an Alchemical Cauldron next to them which is used to craft recipes. Philosopher Stone Chips are used to upgrade C Class Equipments only, Philosopher Stone Shards are used to upgrade B and A Class Equipments. Ashkalot Cubes can be used to upgrade any item while reducing its cost and protecting it from breaking (there is a daily to get these cubes), Cash Shop items can help in your upgrading but if you start using those before level 40 you are just wasting your money.
Sealing is EXPENSIVE, this allows your equipment to gain extra stats quality of seal is as follows from worst to best Green/Blue/Purple/Orange. Emeralds are used to seal C Class Equipments, Sapphires for B Class Equipments and Morions for A Class Equipments. Crystal Vessels can be obtained through a daily quest, this item can be used to grant you Blood Crystal which can be used to place a new seal on an already sealed item (The current seal will be DELETED and a NEW seal put on). Emerald, Sapphire, Morion and Crystal Vessels can be purchased from Master of Enchantment outside of Academy of Magic Varlone City bottom right of map. Cash Shop items only help to alter the seals already on the equipment or to allow the lowest quality of Blue to be added.
There will be many dailies but the two worth mentioning are Caustic Acid (This nets you 3 Ashkolot Cubes for 50 Caustic Acid) and Green Slime (This nets you 2 Crystal Vessels for 50 Green Slimes), you can take these quests soon after you hit level 20 from the Message Board in Varlone City centre to the bottom right. You can also get a free Emerald along with 2 Potions from Protecting the Vegetable Garden from Pests taken from Connor Barr in Elgore. You can bring up available quests by hitting the M or Q key and clicking the Available Quests tab top right (You will need to bring up the map and click this tab and quest to see where to go for it each time you lose your way).
You will gain resting bonus experience if you are not on your character for more than 8 hours to a max of 20 hours this works on all quests and monsters you gain experience from will be doubled till it is depleted.
Cards are rare drops from monsters which can be given to Bella for Insignia's of Distinction or sold on the Market. Various items can be bought from Sella for Insignia's of Distinction including PREMIUM TIME as well as a few things that can be bought in Cash Shop which includes Decorations that give +5% Health. They are both located in centre court of Varlone City to the northwest. You can also gain Insignia's of Distinction by PVPing in PVM/PVP areas Rewards are given monthly and you must be in the top 20 PVPers.
Most loots are used for crafting, C Class Equipments are 100%, B Class 80% and A Class 60%. Flax is important in crafting you find this randomly by digging up plants. Ores are also found scattered around areas and as you progress through the game you will find the higher quality ores, digging ores also gets you Anthricite. Elum is obtained through Equipment that you put in the Splitter, the higher level the Equipment the more Elum you will get, Red Elum comes from Weapons, Blue Elum comes from Clothing (Armor, Headgear etc), Green Elum comes from Accessories (Rings, Amulets etc). So keep those Equipment drops! if you plan on crafting (Crafting gets you personal gear with slots, the same as Dungeons). WARNING keep all Gem drops if you do plan on crafting as they drop rarely and are used in recipes at high levels. Some Crafting Recipes can be bought from NPCs inside of PVM/PVP areas, they require you gather Elenium nodes which will give you Alchemical Runes with which to buy the Recipes. Recipes also drop from monsters. You can find all the machines necessary for crafting/splitting at the east side of Varlone City, SPECIAL NOTE the Elenium Converter requires Alchemical Runes to change 1 material to another.
Pushing A on your keyboard brings up a Menu with Battleground, Arena and Store (in the Center, Blue button), You can join Arena 5 times a day to earn Blood Tokens which in turn can be used to buy from the Arena Store to improve your prowess vs other players, there is also a Mount and Pet as well as various potions.
To conclude the game is beautiful the music is great and I enjoy playing it for free.

Not to mention that it's easy to get other copies for your friends. The addition of online play is also a welcome function in the game.
In short, if you're hesitant on getting a party game, Marooners won't change your mind. But if you have friends and want something fast and easy to play, then this is the game for you."

"But I wanna get to level 60 right away."
It's not happening. All of the game content is locked behind the main story. I attacked this task fresh, trying to level up as fast as possible, but the Story quests pummeled me into submission. The thing is, the story has so many great moments.
A tip however. Don't be fooled by the ARR 1-50 quests. They really get bogged down by all the mundane MMO tripe. Past that, it's smooth sailing and you're basically watching a Square Enix movie for about 100 hours or so.
It's at that point the game becomes quite excellent. You really start to feel involved, connected to the characters, and immersed in the fantastic world of Eorzea... Until you get booted back into a town square with 10 red mages rotating on horses, made to wait 30 minutes in the Duty Finder as a DPS, and get thrust into an instance with some random teenagers hopped up on Adderall.
Anyhow, it took me about 200 hours or so of gametime, guildless, soloing, and messing around on the side to get to the end of Heavensward. The story forces you to do instances with other people, so if you want max speed, pick a tank; It will save you a lot of time waiting for dungeons.

I haven't gotten very far yet but I'm impressed. Some quick observations:
- not a console port
- no FPS cap
- 21:9 support
- tons of configuration options for gameplay, graphics, etc.
- pretty good graphics
- runs great even at 4K with max settings; no stuttering, etc.
- doesn't support SLI yet
With regard to gameplay, it's basically a soulslike in a sci-fi setting. Nothing particularly ground-breaking in that respect but from what I've experienced so far I'd say it's pretty solid and fun and worth a shot if you like these kind of games.
The combat feels good and there are some interesting mechanics around how you can focus on attacking certain parts of the enemies (arm, leg, etc.) in order to recover individual components to build up your own rig. It seems like there will be a lot of flexibility in how you configure your character since you have the suit components you can recover in addition to various kinds of implants that you find that give you things like healing abilities or environmental cues or other effects.
There's a story here, perhaps more than you'd see in something like Dark Souls, but so far it's still fairly minimal and I don't feel like it gets in the way or anything like that. You can skip the videos and dialogue options and just get on with the combat and exploring the world after a very brief intro segment just long enough to explain (to some extent) how your character ends up in the condition they are in once things get going for real.
It's a pretty good little puzzle game.  My only problem is that there doesn't seem to be a penalty for making mistakes.

I initially recommended this game but 15 hours in my opinion has changed.  This game is attempting to be a sci-fi Dark Souls sort of experience.
The combat system at first was very satisfying.  The first two levels are very well done and every fight I had felt fair.  Level design throughout is really cool with unlocking different shortcuts and seeing how everything interconnects.  I enjoyed the sound design with the music being very foreboding and atmospheric.  Overall I really enjoy the theme and my main drive in the game was wanting to learn more about the world and story.
I eventually had to give up though.  Enemies in later levels are just broken, and they really point out the flaws in the combat system.  Blocking is useless, as MANY attacks simply go through your block and there's no way to tell which attacks will do this.  Using hit-and-run tactics with your dodge is the only way to make some progress with the later enemies which is not only extremely boring, it still doesn't work half the time because the enemies behave so inconsistently with their ability to be staggered and how often they stagger you and two-shot you before you can react.
The combat, which is the most important part of the game, totally breaks down about 10-15 hours in.  You'll suddenly be dying every minute or two and it will not feel fair.
Character progression is super basic, and your armor choice barely seems to matter, as even with heavy armor you can be one-shot by certain enemies.  Maybe I misunderstood something but it appears that leveling up does not increase your stats at all unless you equip certain implants, and even those implants have limits on how much they can boost your stats based on level.  I wanted to try and grind to get more powerful to maybe offset the broken enemies but it didn't seem to make a difference.
I'm super bummed out because I really wanted to like this game and see where it went, but it's just too boring and frustrating in the later levels.  Hopefully some of this can be addressed in a balance patch and I can return to the game, as there is a great game hidden under an ugly outer layer here.

So too early for full review, will update once I've complated the game.
Pros:
+ Combat, fast paced, feels more in line with modern souls titles, a massive improvement over Lords of the Fallen
+ Have to dismember enemy parts to collect resources and weapons, see a enemy using a cool weapon? chop his arm off and take it!
+ Level design, nicely layed out areas with interconnecting pathways and many shortcuts.
+ Multiplier, the longer you go between refilling your healing the more scrap (souls) you get in return, nice risk/reward.
+ Weapon choice, game gives you a decent amount of weaponry to collect early on, decent amount of choice.
+ No stats such as strength, Int, or dex, so no requirements on weapons, find something cool? use it straight away. (read neutral points)
Neutral:
- Weapon proficiency, the more you use a weapon type the better you get with them thus increasing the scaling amount of damage for weapons of that type, pretty cool. Downside is if you don;t level a weapon type because you haven;t found any you like but then you find something new and cool you may need to grind a bit to bring that proficiency up to make the weapon on par.
- No stat builds may make repeat runs feel samey, can't say atm.
- You have a overall level, which is your power core, this affects your overall power capacity which is taken up by armour and implants, heavy armour takes up more and so do more powerful implants. i.e +20 health may be 2 capacity whereas +40 would be 4 (not accurate numbers)
Negatives:
- Upgrading weapons and armour can take a lot of salvage,with the difficulty of enemies in terms of just their damage and health (general mobs have a lot more health than souls ones) grinding for upgrades may feel needed by players who are struggling.
- The tougher enemies can make progressing feel a little slow.
- Lack of stat points may be seen as a negative by some, but would recommend trying before judging.
Performance and technical side:
Running @1440p on a 5820k, GTX 1070, 16GB DDR4 with the game installed on a 7200RPM HDD
+Performance, the game defaulted to max settings, seems to run around 60-100fps depending on the location and what's happening
+Unlocked frame rate, something souls hasn't managed to achieve even on their 5th game in the series.
+Graphics, the general world and zones look impressive, nice lighting too
+Sound seems good, no problems but also nothing of note like an amaxing soundtrack
+Load times, travelled from one area to the next and it took around 1 second.
- Textures some of these, especially on character models can look a bit too low res close up.

I think the other 13,5k reviews say stuff better than I can, so I'll just highlight a couple of points.
this is NOT turn based. no matter how many "turn based" tags this game has. there is a mechanic called turn(), that makes you stop time to plan out your next move, but it's not like you must attack using this mechanic, or that enemies use the mechanic to their advantage.

I spent quite some time in the game, and although I have my preferred setups, I have screwed around with functions, and I've found loads of interesting tidbits. try jaunt() and get() for a safer getaway. try void() and crash() to save time. try jaunt(), purge() and crash() to ANNIHILATE EVERYTHING.
and it's not like you are completely overpowering enemies top to bottom. in the early game, you will be faced with a number of enemies, and your job is to pick them apart, while in the end game it's more choosing when to attack and striking priority targets.

I'm making this review to show people wanting to play the experience that someone who spend over 5-10 hours before making a  review has had. Most of the negative reviews are telling you things that are true about this game. Yes bag slots are low and you have to pay to get more, there are cash shop mounts, and there are items in the cash shop that give you SMALL bonuses especially campared to the cards in the game, which are found when killing mobs or a few unique kinds from the cash shop. (which aren't very useful endgame) What these people failed to mention is that this is a FREE game. Free games always have to make someway of making profit and profit = cash shop. But by far it is not P2W, you can buy your own premium currency fairly cheap with your own gold that you earned ingame. And the cash shop items aren't even that expensive if you do decide to pay.  For example, a crystal key, which opens a chest that can give you a majority of things only costs 99 Royal Reales, which is less than 5$. As someone who opened 2 of these chests I got a mount that would have cost me 20$ and a 7-day premium scroll. Also on the PvP dungeon side of things, yes you are killed, yes you are camped when you enter one. But what reviewers have failed to tell you is that it WARNS you before entering saying YOU CAN GET KILLED. This is a PvPvE game if you don't like PvP quit or go somewhere there isn't PvP. As of now there are things we still don't know about the game, but I  have had a lot of fun playing it and it does have some interesting content that I have not seen in many MMOs, such as war and the card system. War is when 1 guild declares war on another, no matter where you are (discluding towns) the enemy guild can kill you. This is very fun especially if you enjoy PvP. And cards are very rare drops that each mob has that can give you special bonuses, some are good and some are bad. You can equip these cards in equipment with card slots. So please, if you are thinking of playing this game, take advice from someone who has played way longer than many of the negative reviewers. Just give it a try yourself, who knows it might be your new favorite game.

Do you miss the dungeon-crawling of yore? Ever wished you could play games like Dungeon Master or Eye of the Beholder with modern design? Then Legend of Grimrock is the game for you!
In Grimrock you form a party of four people and explore a vast dungeon. The movement is tile-based and in real-time. You move with the keyboard and all other actions are done with the mouse, like in the classic dungeon crawlers. The overall game is pretty challenging and the combat at times is tough as nails when you fight against multiple enemies. The riddles and puzzles are very well designed (apart from 1-2) and will probably have you scratch your head quite a bit. There are no NPCs to talk with, no towns to sell your loot or anything like that - it's just your party and a dark, scary dungeon (although the game does have a story!). There will be an editor available eventually, allowing people to create and share their own dungeons! Give it a look, it's great!

TL:DR
The Room is better than The Room Two. They are nice puzzle games with beautiful graphics and worth your money (1,69 for 5 chapters).
I started out playing The Room. It has nice puzzles. It had 5 chapters, which was acceptable, because the game was worth 1,69 on Steam Sale. I loved the graphics and the sophistication of the puzzles. It really gave me moments where I scratched my head and thought: "Well that's done, now what? Let me look around for some clues." The briljant graphics gave a relaxed atmosphere to work on the puzzles. The beautiful graphics also ensured that some compartments would stay hidden and made you look for clues or anomalies. I have a feeling that The Room has a lot more potential and that there are a lot more possibilities for harder puzzles.
The Room Two on the other hand has different priorities. I don't think the developers where aiming on the puzzles, rather on the storyline and the mystery behind the Null element. Two things that give me that impression: the graphics, which are less compared to The Room, and the sophistication of the puzzles. A lot of times when you unlock some part of the puzzle in The Room Two, the camera just pins you to the place where you should put the accuired piece. I find that very linear and straightforward.
So definetly a good game, with a lot of potential. The developers should go back to The Room and take that as a basis and concentrate on more sophisticated puzzles with more layers. With more divers pieces, one creates difficult puzzles, because it all seems random and chaotic. It could also eliminate the linearity of some puzzles.
So 10/10 for The Room

I bought into the Early Access alpha version of this game because at the time I looked forward to the initial concept of the game as advertised and had faith in Double Fine, developers notorious for several well-received cult classics including Psychonauts and Brutal Legend (controversial but in my opinion a very underrated game), to complete it on-schedule and more or less in a finished form of the advertised concept.
It seems apparent, that with the sudden push from 0.6 Alpha to 1.0 Release, that this will not be the case. From my experience, the game as-is is interesting but very buggy and sorely lacking in features. The base-building is somewhat simplistic, which, while partially due to the visual format of the game, is not enough to keep me interested in it. The AI for both friendly and enemy NPCs is very glitchy, hard to control and frankly suicidal at times. The user interface is clunky, incomplete and apparently designed for touchscreen support at the expense of UI size. The game has fullscreen support bugs, occasionally crashes without warning and lacks a tutorial.
Resource management is laughably simplistic, relying simply on the presence of basic station necessities (walls, furniture, life support, matter refineries, etc.) and NPCs in enough of a quantity to satisfy some invisible mysterious ratio (with the exception of oxygen/life support-based crew capacity, this is prominently displayed on the user interface, a very good thing).
The long-term gameplay suffers when you take into account that there's a very finite amount of natural resources (called matter in-game) with which to build infrastructure and feed NPCs, which means you generally have to rely on proper choice of starting location in order to ultimately dictate how long you'll be able to keep your base going and how much harassment from raiders you'll get. In my opinion there's something wrong with the game when raider attacks are a promising sign of long-term survival after a certain point.
If derelicts are part of your chosen starting location, then, yes, ostensibly I could see you breaking them down for matter for self-preservation, perhaps indefinitely, but I have yet to succeed at this, either due to a lack of experience or simply because it takes too long, I don't actually know personally because it's completely up to the AI-controlled crew NPCs to do this after the order's given.
NPC deaths (which happen often, due to only security officers being capable of self-defense if I recall correctly, and hardly capable at that) affect nearly the entire crew's morale directly and drastically and how useful they are in performing their tasks. This is apparently impossible to remedy (again, I may be mistaken).
Even beyond these problems there's just not all that much to do, just survive as long as possible and assign new/current NPCs to station tasks and watch them utterly fail to perform them. Or starve to death because they can't find their way to the cantina because they're depressed and oversleeping. Or open up an interior door into a hallway with an oxygen leak and asphyxiate. Or catch themselves on fire and avoid several nearby, conveniently placed fire extinguishers, relying on other NPCs to actually see that their compadres are on a painful path from the psych ward to the burn ward and put them out. This all creates a bit of a death spiral for the NPCs, which is an interesting but infuriating and uncontrollable part of Dwarf Fortress, a game which Spacebase: DF-9's apparently inspired by.
To Double Fine's benefit, survival was one of the game's main selling points. Sadly, in its current state and potential state when released in 1.0, this may be impossible, or indeed, utterly futile and pointless to attempt from the outset.
Hopefully the game will improve once "mod support" is implemented, but it shouldn't take mod support for basic implementation of features and bugfixes to occur.
It seems like the general consensus is that the game has been abandoned. I'd disagree with that verdict and give the developers the benefit of the doubt if it weren't so d**n obvious.
Double Fine, you know better than this. "Big Ambitions, Broken Dreams" indeed.

text: What to say about this game? It's an evolved minesweeper experience, to put in a few words, if you take out the guessing bits and add more logic. It's very easy to learn. Huge plus: Nearly unlimited new levels through seeds = nearly unlimited gameplay possibilities. Higly recommended.

I have played many puzzle games. The hexcells series is simply, in my humble opinion, the very best. It avoids the pitfall of so many similar games: trial and errror. While interesting games like Lyme, Quell, Kami, Unium, etc. are asking you to think ahead, sure, but mostly to try, end up in a dead end, try something else, get stuck, try again, etc.  this is not the case here. The only real way to play for me is to accept no error. In any case, there is never a reason to guess or play the probabilities. There is always a solution and it's always certain.
Clever, just challenging enough without being frustrating, but also soothing. This last opus is even infinite...

If you think "sudoku is fun, but I'd rather try something new", this is a great diversion.  Building up the core concepts and leaps of logic necessary to tackle the end game, level by level, you slowly grow quicker and more efficient at making the deductions and planning your assault on this "mindsweeper on crack".
First you'll pore over seemingly impossible puzzles, wondering how you could possibly make headway.  Then...  You'll see something.  You'll realize a single hexagon has to be blue or clear.  You'll realize this forces its neighbor to be one or the other.  You'll ponder the region, column, or row.  Slowly the puzzle will take shape and bow to your superior intellect.  Eureka...  Satisfaction.  The hexlord reigns.
This game will test your patience, and it's delayed gratification.  Self-select whether this is your cup of tea.
Nitpicks: I wish there had been more end-game content, as the "infinite" mode is a fair step down from the level 5/6 puzzles.

Review: "Hexcells: Infinite"
9/10
Hexcells: Infinite is the third and final installment in the Hexcells trilogy.  I would highly reccomend this game regardless of whether or not you've played the prior two.  Like the previous two, it begins quite simply and progresses in difficulty and complexity through the introduction of more and more complex elements.  What sets this game apart from the past two is twofold.  The first is the difficulty ramps up much more quickly and to a much greater degree.  The second is the ability to randomly generate puzzles, which are solveable and add a near infinite replayability factor.
If you like puzzle games, this is the best one you're going to get on steam.

Fun game. Runs well and a good selection of graphics options to increase/decrease. Full controller support and mouse/keyboard, though I find controller seems a better choice for this type of game but that's just preference. Story so far is "meh".  Voice acting is good enough though not amazing. Nothing wrong with either, but the main draw I find is the fun combat, which can be difficult. Enemies hit hard, and if you don't pay attention you can die easily at which point it pulls from games similiar to Dark Souls, where you respawn back at Operations, a small base with facilities to upgrade gear and weapons. Upon death you lose all scrap you were carrying (used for upgrading gear), but if you manage to get back to where you died without dying again you can pick it back up. And you can "bank" the scrap at the base to store it, but doing so resets a multiplier you accumalate by killing enemies which rewards more scrap per kill at the cost of losing it if you die.
While the levels seem mostly linear, there are side paths that reward items and unlock shortcuts back to the base to make things quicker if you die. Enemies respawn as well (except bosses), so you always have access to more scrap and materials as needed.
The neatest feature incorporated in combat is severing body parts via finishing moves, which results in that part (arm, body, leg, head) possibly dropping the schematic/weapon for use in crafting parts for your ExoSuit. To sever parts you just have to damage it enough while locked on to it (you can swap the lock-on to each part), and then press the button mapped to "Finishing move". At which point you get a nice little execution animation that sometimes adds a slow-mo effect to the kill cam. You can toggle the frequency of said effects in options menu.
So far, I'm thoroughly enjoying the game and will report any additional thoughts I may have as I progress.

Pros>
+ It uses the Souls system with some -quality of life- changes (you can store "souls" you can't use yet).
+ You can kill enemies quickly by hitting unarmored parts or taking more time hitting armored parts that drop loot.
+ The setting is very well done with great attention to detail, especially in the gear.
+ Like in Demon Souls, you don't have a map and you should activate shortcuts.
+ There's lot of upgrades and you can also create your own equipment. Each gear part and weapon can be upgraded four levels.
+ Much, much better than Lords of the Fallen. Levels are bigger than that game and it feels a lot less generic.
Cons>
- Voice acting. The main character looks like a 50 y/o badass and sounds like a young adult reading a script.
- When you interact with panels and switches the character floats to the correct position. Not a big deal, though.
The game doesn't have multiplayer. As someone who don't want to be bothered by humans while I play, it's a plus for me. If you like the PvP from the Souls games count it as a con. Also, as it's single player you can pause the game. It's a godsend for someone like me with a 4 y/o son.
I'm playing the game with a controller so I can't speak about mouse/kb support. It feels great with a controller, though, and as there's no aiming, I recommend a controller to play it.

Transistor is probably a fine game on its own, but it's very hard not to compare it to Bastion, one of my favorite action RPGs. Transistor is more verbose but nonetheless says less about its world and characters. Where Bastion made some motivations explicit and left others to the imagination, Transistor just left me scratching my head. Some of the plot twists and introduced characters seem abrubt or incomplete, making me wonder if parts of the game were cut or rushed.
Aesthetically, the game starts out gorgeous and then devolves into geometric monochrome which isn't ugly but didn't wow me like the first few levels did. That's in keeping with the game's plot and themes, but it's still regrettable. The music is still great.
The gameplay is still an action RPG with mix-and-match moves and perks to match your play style. The modular way you build your abilities and the power to drop temporarily into a turn-based mode keep the gameplay fresh as you advance. The game felt a little short; right as I felt the game was starting to enter the cool design space of end-game fights, the encounters all switched style and then I was at the final boss, who was disappointing and required entirely different strategies from the rest of the game. The ending was annoying and left way too many questions open.
TL;DR (re)play Bastion instead.

Transistor has one of the most unique combat systems of any game I've played. It is both a combination of real time action combined with turned based strategy. What makes this interesting is that you can activate turned based combat at any time, but it comes at a big cost. After you execute a "turn", it is put on a cooldown where most (or all) of your abilities become unavailable for a short time. This makes you very vulnerable to the enemy and creates a very interesting risk/reward type combat system. Do you fight in realtime and suffer from slow attack swings? Or do you take a "turn" getting off those attacks for free, but suffer a large and vulnerable downtime?
Additionally, any ability can be "equipped" to any other ability to modify how it works. Your fast bolt attack can be "equipped" to another attack to make it shoot faster for instance. This gives so many unique combinations of attacks that it's quite overwhelming at first. This dynamic setting of attacks is really rewarding as it feels like your attacks are unique to you. And it allows for a vast amount of different playstyles which keeps combat fresh. You can switch from a heavy hitting melee to a long range mage to a stealthy backstabbing rogue.
But that's not all Transistor has to offer. The backgrounds are beautiful, the voice acting is great, the atmosphere is amazing, the artstyle is sublime, and the story really brings it all together. The mystery of it all keeps you craving for more to make it a true beautiful work of art.

Definitely worth the $15. If you've played this game on iOS or Android, skip this paragraph. Plague Inc is a world-ending virus simulator. It started out on iPhone a few years ago and was a huge success. It consistently topped app charts, had a number of really cool free updates, and it just gives you so much to do. The CDC even liked it enough to meet with the app creator and discuss how to make it more realistic! In this game, you control a plague (bacteria, virus, fungus, man-made plague, brain worm, and more...there's a lot to choose from). You choose where the virus begins, and you watch as it spreads across the world. You control what vectors the virus uses, how the virus defends itself against temperature and medicine, and what symptoms the virus produces (oh, and I'm just going to use "virus" as shorthand for "plague" just because I'm more used to typing "virus"). There's a lot of strategy involved, whether you try to create a nearly invisible virus that, when detected, it will be too late or if you try to create a virus that becomes scarier and scarier as it spreads and just overwhelms cure efforts. The game has been balanced to really support both options. As you infect people, new countries, and kill people, you gain DNA points that you use to alter your virus. The scarier that your virus is, the more you're rewarded with points, but the more that every scientist in the world focuses on curing you. Don't worry, however - the game does a great job of explaining everything to you. Whereas a game like Pandemic can be really intimidating with all of these different medical terms (even one for runny nose - are you kidding me?), Plague Inc prefers to use the common words for symptoms. You're not overloaded with choices (but there are enough for you) and the impact each DNA change has is clearly shown (such as infectivity, lethality, and how scary it appears to the world).
For those who have played it on mobile, not much has really changed. Each plague is unlocked after beating the previous one, there's the world map, unlockable gene bonuses, etc. However, it doesn't really look too polished as of yet. The UI feels outdated and inexplicably cheap. I almost feel like I'm playing a flash game in my browser. The UI is mostly functional, but has a lot of empty space. It also has some elements that are just for show rather than solving a purpose. For example, a bar graph to the right of the country status indicator (the main bar on the UI) has different colored bars that don't represent anything and don't move. I don't know why they're there. It's still early access, so that may change. Also, every country has a picture of it (mostly just showing people and buildings, maybe a landmark). The pictures look like cheap CGI (god knows why - there's no shortage of real pictures of locations), but there are maybe 10 - or less - pictures used for every country in the world. I don't mean that, say, Sudan cycles through 10 pictures. I mean that Sudan, and "West Africa," "East Africa," and "South Africa" (along with most of the rest of the continent) all have the same picture. Cheap CGI with nothing moving. At first I thought it was a neat touch, but that kind of shallowness stands in contrast to how fleshed out the rest of the game is.
On the upside, each plague type has its own 3D image that reacts as you upgrade it. It doesn't change as dramatically as the neurax worm on mobile, but it will stretch out and rebound a bit when you upgrade it and wince when you devolve a feature. I think that's pretty neat, and it doesn't feel as cheap. The DNA upgrade menu is definitely an improvement. Also, the world status menu has been solidified and now has all of the important info on one screen. That's a huge improvement.
Also, this game has Steam workshop integration, meaning that people are submitting their own plague types. I saw one for a Hank Hill virus earlier today. It looks like people are going to have a lot of fun creating and customizing their own plagues, and I think that's great!
In summation, it's the same as the mobile game, but with a new UI (with its ups and downs) and steam workshop support.

This is more of a mortgage & commerce simulator than anything. I spent most of my time trying to pay off ship mortgage and crew salaries. In order to do this, you either buy goods low and sell high, do various transport jobs, or attack pirates and taking any items or ships they have. Not as fun as I hoped.
There is no tutorial. I had to look at key bindings just to figure out what to do. The mouse is not used in battle much at all so battles feel clunky. Much was not explained in detail. The outfitter interface is annoying because the info is not in a static part of the screen. This makes comparing items tedious. Actual ship details took a while to figure out; the interface is not very intuitive. Even after 20 hours I still found much of the game annoying.
Passage of time was not explained. Mortgage payments are made on a daily basis. Every jump to a system, and landing on a planet, take a day each. I almost went broke because I jumped 5 times without realizing most of my savings were spent. Re-landing back on the planet to check one more job or item will cost you.
You cant take direct control of your other ships. No repair function either. If a pirate disables your main ship but doesnt kill you, you are stuck and need to reload your last game. No way to transfer your captain to another ship. Combat, interface, and even trying to go into hyperspace is clunky.
Battles are lackluster. Ship movement reminds me of 1980’s Asteriods; lots of sliding. No zoom on that screen either. Keyboard controls suck. No patrol option, and no way to tell fleet to move somewhere other than to you.
The game gets better, but I spent way too much time trying to manage money instead of any real action. Space combat feels incredibly boring. Maybe having mouse support would help a tiny bit. Also, my time played is incorrect for some reason. Should I recommend it just because it is free? I found the game more about commerce than combat; its interesting, but wasn't my thing.

I've been playing MMOs since something like 2008, and FFXIV is by far the best MMO I've ever played. I tend to stray from subscription based games, but now that I have the means to play them, I feel the game is well worth it. Everything is obtainable for free in the game save for optional items that don't have anything to do with your stats and are just that, optional. But that's the difference between "free to play" and sub-based games.
As for the gameplay it feels really unique and I love the way the classes work. I love the ability to level all the classes on one character and borrow certain skills from other classes. Non-combat gameplay is just as fun and rewarding. The immersion the story provides could be better but is still something I can wholly get myself into.
I would write much more if I was up for it, but overall this game is one I recommend to everyone with the means to play it. There's a lot of negative reviews about the installation and not the game itself, which I tend to find unfair unless it's a huge enough problem. However, with the free trial, these negative reviews feel kaput and again, unfair, since you don't need to buy the game anymore to see how it runs on your computer. You can play the game up to level 35 (on every class, mind you) and if you can't even run it, then what's the point of reviewing a game? (Which is partly why I wanted to add another positive review.) In short, read the terms of installation more thoroughly. I made the same mistake about buying the wrong license for the wrong platform but that was because I didn't read. If it's a hardware error, it's not the game's fault that your computer/connection can't keep up.
