Battle of Empires is a fantastic RTS game.  Plain and simple.  On top of that, it features the horrific weaponry and tactics of WW1 which in my opinion is one of the most underutilized settings in gaming right now.  In so many RTS games, if you have the skill, it can feel like your units posess almost super human ability as a result of your control over them.
In Battle of Empires you will have to make choices, and your men WILL DIE because of them.  Sure that artillery strike might turn the tide of the battle you're in, but this game will force you to click on a soldier and order him to a position where he can mark the target with smoke.  Most of the time you know it's a position he won't make it back from.
What makes it so fun to me in the end is how badly you end up wanting your men to survive.  At the end of a battle I never look at how many enemy casualties I was able to inflict, but how many of my own I was able to save.
My favorite part of the game though is the stories that emerge from just the pre-designed campaign battles.  When you finish a battle and the dust settles and you look over your surviving units, think about where each man started and what he accomplished.  If you keep your forces organized, you can watch some pretty incredible things happen.
I feel like i'm not even talking about a game anymore, which is what makes this one fantastic.
Well worth your time :)

Plague Inc: Evolved is like the Pandemic flash games that many people love. My love of that kind of gameplay ultimately made me buy this. However, Plague Inc: Evolved AKA PIE from here on out is so much better in terms of the options available. You control your disease in all aspects. All the changes to transmission, abilities, symptoms, etc will affect how the disease is spread from person to person, city to country, continent to continent. Watching the news feed isn’t completely necessary, but it will at times give you hints on what you may need to do to further increase infection in the world’s populace, and provide some comedy from recent happenings (goat simulator reference, etc).
Like Pandemic, there are countries that are harder to infect, and due to the similarities, I always fear Madagascar. Though in this game, I sit a little more on edge when it comes to Greenland. This game is satisfying if you’re looking to waste some time, or you just really like a challenging strategy world killing game. You’ve got to pop bubbles to get DNA (which is like currency) to advance you’re disease. First thing you’ll think is, this is a crappy mobile game…you’d be right in a way because PIE started on the mobile market. Due to its popularity however, it has been brought to the master race. Also due to rising popularity, Dawn of the Planet of the Apes creators (I believe it was the creators, maybe producers) recently enough asked Ndemic, James being the creator, for a promotion of sorts. We got the Simian Flu. It makes for amazingly fun gameplay.
Other options include making your own scenarios and events, which is amazing as well if you really want to customize your gameplay to your taste; It’s not everyone’s favorite thing to do, but it’s there if you love to really make the game yours in a sense.  Overall, Ndemic is always looking for new ideas to further the game and they listen to their fans, so you really do have a say in the early access game. It’s already a great game as it sits. If you’ve not gotten it yet, you’re jumping straight in to the great features that the game didn’t have when I first bought it, which makes this game very appealing and very fun.  So if you’re seeking a world destroying game by biological warfare, come let the evil scientist in you free.

You lost far too many hours playing Minesweeper back in the day - and want that all over again.
Not a bad game (but could be more fiendish). Imagine if Minesweeper met Nonograms and had hexagonal babies... then you're close.
Pure deductive logic. The solutions are unique and reasonably tricky, but fair. There's no trick questions or guessing. If you're used to Japanese deductive puzzles (like Kakuro or Ken Ken) then ignore the previous 2 iterations and jump straight to this one.
Unfortunately the 'infinite' puzzles are a bit inconsistent. Many lack much of a challenge, meaning you can kinda mindlessly click through them, akin to Minesweeper: relaxing but not overly taxing. Whether that's a bad thing ultimately depends on what you're looking for. If you want something quite gentle, this'll tick it perfectly. If not... how much are 36 puzzles worth to you?
If you want to up the ante and hit a
fiendish puzzler; a game called 'Patterna' has surfaced on Greenlight (funnily enough, inspired by Hexcells!) - A demo is freely available, so I'd recommend giving it a peek:

First Impressions of the game: The color choice and aesthetic is great, many colors, nice feel to the game, though often very bland in areas that are heavily paved (like the main city). The aesthetic shines the most in field areas with a bit of blending between one zone and the next.
The second thing I notice, is that the Camera is locked in this psuedo-isometric position, which allows full rotation, but limiting tilt. you can look almost straight down at your character if you wish, or at a slight angle, but you are incapable of looking parallel to the ground, let alone being able to see any trace of sky. (Probably to lessen the system-demand for rendering, and the need for a skybox)
The third thing I notice is the obvious Premium service. The game practically screams P2W. I honestly wouldn't mind if there were some benefits to paying players, but what ruined it was the constant self-advertising. The fact that you'd have a Premium / VIP tab right above the hotbar that remains there forever, alongside tabs that would remind you of unspent skill points or stat points. It's also a nuisance to see that little blue 'Premium' tab at the center of your screen as you try to pay attention to skill cool downs and potion counts.
The game spends quite a bit of effort reminding you that you 'could' be enjoying the game better if you paid for it.
Next on the list is the combat, which is a bit dull. It's your standard auto-attack, use skills when ready, repeat on the next bad guy. What's interesting though, are the passive skills (Talents) that somewhat modify the properties of previously obtained Active skills, though quite a bit of advancement is required.
After your first class advancement, you gain this Rift-style 3-option talent tree, in which you can specialize, or become a jack of all trades. Specializing yields you a powerful (or less-than-powerful) active skill at the end of one of the three trees for your class. But frankly, the three-tree system is nothing close to the way Rift handles it, and feels like a dumbed down 'my-first-RPG' experience.
The game itself lacks depth from the beginning, and the overall pacing is slow, the quests are un-engaging, and are your standard 'go kill me some wolves for their pelts' ordeal. Occasionally you will get some quests that mess with the props in the environment, or sends you on an errand run across NPCs, concluding in an encounter with an instance (or psuedo-instance)
Here's another drawback that really bothered me. The fact that what I had assumed what were instanced dungeons, are actually open to other players. Caves, Underground Libraries, Sewers, were all loaded with players with the same quest, therefor your target monster or drop would also be hunted by several other people, making your 25 Slime kill quest last longer than it really should. My only experience with a true instance were the randomly spawning 'entrances' that whisked you away to an extremely linear and un-engaging mini-dungeon, or one of the Boss Dungeons that I fought with a party of four.
Though with that drawback, there is also a certain benefit: The Community. The early-game community is pretty large, everywhere you go you are guarenteed a sighting of another player probably doing the same thing as you, hunting Monsters. Not just one, but many players, all hunting monsters, all having a bit of fun. That's nice. Having lots of players around is nice, which makes this experience slightly more enjoyable. Sort of like you and your friends going to a really really bad theme park, somehow with your friends you were able to squeeze some fun out of it, despite the actual place itself being an uninteresting experience.
There are also a few somewhat innovative features: Like castles that could be fought over for guild dominance (though I haven't experienced this feature myself) as well as competitive 'deathmatch dungeons' were you can grind for loot and exclusives materials only if you can survive the onslought of players doing the same thing. (essentially an open PVP dungeon that only allows you to keep your loot if you can escape). Even a raid boss would wonder into town to face the innumerable number of players turning in their quests, leading to a 15-20 player assault on the big ol' boss guy.
---
In the end the game is colorful and full of life, but also in turn, is uninteresting, even annoying, when alone amongst crowds of other people, all competing for a limited supply of Monsters. The game has it's moments when partied up, and certain aspects are enjoyable, with a few speckles of innovation. But overall, the game feels like an RPG experience lacking in depth, but not lacking in it's P2W ego. It's a game worth trying out to see if it fits you, but also is a game worth completely ignoring if you're a hardcore MMO'er looking for deep an immersive RPG experience.
Not Recommended, but try it anyway.

I have really mixed feelings about this game. The gameplay was enjoyable and it was extremely pretty, with a nice soundtrack. I don't regret buying it. On the other hand, I found the story aspect both disappointing (especially the ending) and at times annoying. I wish there was an "eh' option on reviews, but I'll just choose yes, because I wouldn't ANTI-reccomend it? I just also wouldn't rave about it to my friends. But, unable to choose between the two, I'll go with the nice option.
Spoilers ahead.
I'm a bit of an odd duck in that the story aspect of games tends to be what I go for the most and so a story I'm unhappy with is a big minus for me. For this one, I couldn't really get much of a sense of the characters or connect with them. The most characterized is the guy who lives in Red's sword, who is super into her and never shuts up. He seems nice enough, but it's really unclear whether Red even knew him before he sacrificed himself to become a sword?? If she didn't, their whole epic romance deal is even more unbelievable than it already is. Like I said, sword guy seems nice, but it takes a lot of skill to make a romance work when it's just one dude talking and the game didn't really pull it off.
The ending is what disappointed me most- basically, Red commits suicide so she can live in the virtual realm of the sword with sword guy. Like, I fought through this entire game to save and rebuild this town, and now I'm just screwing off to live in a sword. Something I did not at all need to do, because I could have just kept hanging out with him as a sword. Like, we wouldn't be able to make out but I could have taken the sword on little dates. Sit him across from me at restraunts and give him a little sword tuxedo.
Yeah, blablabla epic romance. Romanticizing suicide is always uncomfortable, but it's doubly weird when like, previously in the game two of the villains (heavily implied to be gay lovers) commit suicide and Sword Guy calls them cowards and the little fight narration even marks them as cowards, which was kinda eeesh to begin with. But then the proagonist does it and it's framed as awesome and romantic. So it's only cowardly if you're not the main character I guess? Or if you're doing it for heterosexual reasons? (That's mostly sarcastic, but then again, 3/4s of our villains ARE implied to be gay, in addition to the dudes, we've got a murderous implied-lesbian stalker). Basically, game needs to decide whether it wants to insult or glorify suicidal decisions, you can't have both.
The plot itself was a bit confusing to follow, despite being pretty standard, and aside from sword guy, we mostly know people through their character profiles. I couldn't really connect with anyone, so while it was fun game to play, it's not one I can get invested in. If you don't need to be invested in your games and are okay with going on a whole journey only for the protag to just kill herself, go for it, it's a fine game. But if either of those are red flags for you, don't do it.

'Paper please!' is a testiment to the capabilities of indie developers out there. Never mind the likes of games such as Bastion, Binding of Isaac, Undertale, Prison Architect and This War of Mine. Each with a point where they stood out the most. From the philosophical Talos Principle to the beautiful Transistor to the fantastic Dust: An Elysian Tail, one aspect all of these games had in common in comparison to 'Paper please!' is that they are all more complex games by design. And yet, 'Paper please!' wowed the world with this simple but effectively complex system of border duty (how they could think to make such a mundane and boring job a fun gameplay concept is anyone's guess). I believe the game is intentionally designed to be rather dull with a sense of oppressiveness to flex its storytelling capabilities (more on that below). Truly, an oxymoron in the sense that it is truly simplistically complex.
What surprised me even more was the curious story occuring around subtly. From seemingly framed criminals to helpless refugees with forged documents to a man wanting to immigrate to stay with his family to people wanting to enter the country for its revolutionary medical scene but lack the appropriate paperwork because it was lost/taken away, all these points to real and serious moral dilemmas that resonates with people in reality. Factor in the fact that you have a family to care for and a duty to serve your country, would you make the "morally right" decision all the time at the cost of your loved ones well-being and risk endangering your country or would you just stick to the system and make your choice based on what you are told/taught to do? What is the "right amount" of balance between making these kind of choices?
You aren't wrong for following rules and regulations after all. And you could also argue against say, allowing a man in without proper paperwork because he could be a criminal or that by allowing him in without proper procedure is to condemn him to further hardship since if he was ever caught he would have to bear consquences. But it is exactly this sort of balancing between rationality and morality that makes us human, that we can have sympathy and empathy for peopl but also to question the extent and how much sacrifice we are willing to take before we sacrifice our conscience in order to get by? The narrative and design of the game reminds me very much of amazing pieces of literature and movies such as
,
,
,
by EL Doctorow,
by Fyodor Dostoyevsky,
by William Shakespear and
by William Poundstone just to name a few.
Be warned though, this game is not for everyone. I can understand why people would find the gameplay boring at first sight or genuinely boring. Without a doubt the best puzzle game available on steam right now.
Hexcells Infinite is just that: infinite.
I did the math. It would take a player about 1,141 and half years (with a 6 minute per puzzle average) to exhaust every available puzzle, and that's assuming that they never eat, sleep, or take any breaks. If you were to buy just one installment of the Hexcells franchise, it would be a mistake not to get this one. It simply has the greatest value per dollar spent. (roughly 228 years of gameplay per dollar if you were wondering, and that's not even when it's on sale.)
Numbers aside, this game is an absolute masterpiece. From the minimal sound effects to the tranquil soundtrack, the sound design is spot on and keeps the player engaged. The gameplay is heavily influenced by japanese logic games and minesweeper, but it still manages to feel completely original and unique. More importantly, the concept is easy to learn and it only takes a few minutes for a new player to get used to the gameplay and environment.
And that's not even the best part - the best part is that it NEVER feels impossible to solve. More often than not, when a player makes a mistake, they immediately realize what they did wrong. Even if you feel like you're stuck, there's always that one number you missed that tells you where to look. This game is like a great magician, in the sense that a great magician leaves nothing to chance despite how wildly impossible their act may seem. If you love puzzle games, Hexcells Infinite is a must for your Steam library.
I give this game a 9.8/10.
Not a perfect score for the following reasons:
- Highlighting an external grid number underneath another highlighted external grid number works OKAY, but I'm sure there are better options than white on white lines.
- You can make any number of mistakes on the infinite puzzles without facing any sort of penalty. Maybe I'm just being nitpicky at this point, but it just seems like a loose end in an otherwise flawless game. They could at least have it set up in a way where the puzzle doesn't count as completed if you make 3 or more mistakes.
Suggestions:
- Themes! I'm talking unlockable themes, different hex colors, player-created backgrounds, custom cursors, and so on. This game would certainly benefit from workshop access and, dare I say, skins. It'd be nice to have a change in scenery after playing with the same background and color scheme for hours.

Also, numbers can be shown on the outside of the grid and show a different symbol with the number to tell you how the tiles you need to mark are laid out.

*This review will cover all three Hexcells games (Hexcells, Hexcells Plus & Hexcells Infinite) as they are very similar.*
Hexcells Infinite is a 2d puzzle game similar in nature to Minesweeper that involves hexagons. Using clues given by previously discovered tiles, more and more of the puzzle is shown and finally completed once all tiles are revealed. This series goes beyond your normal Minesweeper in the fact that clues will often involve more then the directly adjacent tiles  i.e. columns, diagonals, non-continuous, continuous only, double spaces, etc... If you get Infinite, it boasts an infinite puzzle generator that was some estimated 999,999,999 random puzzles to try so, good luck with that. All and all, a really great game if you enjoy the Minesweeper style but also want a bit of originality as well.
Minesweeper is better...

Hexcells Infinite is the third and last game in series, with new 36 mind boggling levels which will keep you preoccupied for quite a while. No new mechanics are added compared to previous games, if you played them you know what to expect but that is not necessary in order to enjoy this one.
It is Minesweeper-like game where your goal is to decipher the pattern and mark the blue cells by gradually eliminating empty ones. They contain numbers which show how many blue cells are adjacent to them. New rules are introduced which add to game complexity, such as number of cells in columns, clusters of cells that must be separated from each other or adjacent to one another and blue cells with numbers which show how many of them are located in a 2 hex radius. I completed the game in slightly less than 8 hours. Much of it were spent in staring at the screen in order to find which cells to eliminate. Ending levels are really big and spotting sometimes obvious solution can be quite tricky.
The biggest change is introduction of an Infinite mode, you can play as many random generated levels as you want. Your brain cells will be happy, your free time surely will not.
Easily worth the money, just throw on some netflix and hexcell.

As far as gameplay goes, there are no new mechanics from the other games in the series, but I consider that a good thing. The core gameplay was fun, so I'm glad that it wasn't changed. This is much more of a visual novel than the previous Unhack. Lots of story occasionally interrupted by short, relatively easy puzzles, much the same as one of Invert Mouse's other productions: Bermuda. Unlike both Bermuda and Unhack 1, I am disappointed to say that Unhack 2 contains no voice acting. Even so, it was quite the emotional rollercoaster all the way through.
The story of this game is vastly improved compared to Invert Mouse's other titles that I have played thus far. It's no secret that there's a plot twist very early in the story; but I will say that said twist is cleverly hidden by a red herring. You'll think you see it coming, but trust me, you don't.
Unhack 2 introduces us to a brand new cast of characters, and also gives us a bittersweet reunion with the cast of Unhack 1 (sans Motherworm, she's as dead as dead gets). Slight spoilers, but unfortunately if there is ever an Unhack 3, we probably won't be seeing Weedy and Debug outside of flashbacks and/or clones; so if you grew attached to these characters, be prepared to shed a few manly tears. Just warning my fellow softies out there.
The villain of this game is significantly better written than the antagonists of Unhack 1, and gave me a legitimate "oh crap" feeling every time she showed up. If you needed evidence that Invert Mouse's writing has improved, this is Exhibit A.
Overall, a very good VISUAL NOVEL, but don't go into this expecting riveting gameplay.

What a ride! The first Unhack was inexperienced and rough around the edges, but Unhack 2 improved all the best parts tenfold. The cast expanded, the plot matured, and the art is so crisp and fresh in every shot. The only real con is that the story's on the short side, but it still kept me interested all the way through. Definitely a fantastic product!

Unhack 2 is the sequel to the puzzle/VN hybrid to InvertMouse's first Unhack. While it still contains puzzles, they are much less of a focus this time around. So much less, that you can skip the puzzles entirely, but they are pretty fun, so I wouldn't recommend doing so.
The art of this game has drastically improved over Unhack 1. I'm not saying the art of the original isn't up to par (Hybridmink did a very good job), but I feel Rosuuri's art fits more with the style of U2, which leans towards a more traditional VN. Also, the composer of Unhack 1 is back again, so if you liked the music of the first game, you'll definitely be in for a treat.
Story is really interesting in how it deals with the concept of sentient AI. I can tell InvertMouse put a lot of research into this topic while creating the game. Like I said before, you really do need to play Unhack 1 to get the most out of this game (it's $5 incl. its DLC and takes less than 2 hours to complete). In this sequel, the Creator returns with a brand new AI companion to battle a mysterious new evil and her clones
. If there's one thing that stands out above the rest, it's definitely the character developments. Although they might be sentient AI, you can't help but grow attached to and root for them
. There's also a  lot of philsophical development and moral questioning, which ties in to the brilliant story and really gets you thinking about the future of AI in real life.
Despite all of this story focus, Unhack 2 is still a little on the short side (though I might argue that it's the perfect length for a kinetic VN). I cleared it in around 3-4 hours without many breaks.
I recommend getting the Complete Edition bundle. It includes both games, artbooks, and the soundtrack of U2 (you can get the soundtrack of the prequel for free separately).

I liked the first game for combining a fun puzzle mechanic with visual novel-style narrative, delivering a very short but very enjoyable experience,Unhack 2 however throws gameplay out of the window fully embracing the Visual Novel aspect (Gameplay sections still exist, but you can actually skip them) and I think this was a good decision.
What we are left with is a heartwarming story about Artificial Intelligence, family, the relationship between humanity and technology, transhumanism and the morality of creating living feeling beings just to treat them no other than a toaster.
Now, one question one might ask is "Do I have to play the first game to get this?"
My answer would be yes and no.
While the game does a good enough job of giving you a "Previously on Unhack" it is definitely a good idea to play through the first one before going for this one.
I usually only play through games one of two ways, either I play through the game in little bite sized chunks over a few weeks or even months or I sit through it in one go because the story is basically taking me hostage.
Unhacked 2 was one of the latter examples.
I personally was leaking fluid from my eyes by the end, I cannot recommend this more.

This game is great! It is a spiritual sequel to the old game Dungeon Master from the 80s, but with modern graphics and updates like better AI and an automap. If you like dungeon crawls, get it. You wont be disappointed.
Its a dungeon crawl like Eye of the Beholder. Graphics are very nice with the traditional square tunnels and chains hanging on the walls, moss ect. Theres alos the occasioanl cool statue or art on the walls as well. Step, turn, strafe and so forth. The puzzles ramp up in difficulty nicely. They are the typical find keys, secret buttons, pull levers in order, run quickly, and so forth. But defintely not stale. Theres also some interesting and unique ones too.  Combat is heavily reliant on the step dance just to survive, a feature I'm not too thrilled about. Unless youre a minmaxer, going toe to toe with an enemy of the appropriate level (on Normal) is not recommended.
Youre going to be freezing the enemy and/or dancing all over the place if you want to stay alive. The enemies hit hard. I would say that this is the games major flaw, as I'm way more of a fan of toe to toe melee than swinging and running all over the place till the enemy dies. Its too bad cuz the AI is nice for a square based dungeon crawler. The enemies will actually try and sneak up on you.
DMs levelling system was better too. In LoG, theres 4 races and 3 classes. Minotaur, human, lizardman, and insectoid, and mage, rogue and fighter. Once you pick, you're that class. Fighters cant learn magic, and mages cant fight (or seem to do much of anything). And you get XP, just like typical RPGs.
Contrast that with DMs "practice a skill and level in that class" style and it just seems...lesser. Also, the game really lends itself to specialization. Pick 1 weapon, 1 magic school. Jack of all trading as far as class skills seems to really hurt in the late game.
The sounds and music are nice, typically dungeon-y without being too intrusive. There really isnt too much of a plot in the main game, but thats not why you're here. You're here for the awesome exploration, wondering whats around the corner and seeing if your condemned prisoners will ever win their freedom.
All in all a great game and definitely worth picking up for any dungeon/RPG fan. Theres a custom dungeon I have, not sure if I d/led it or it was installed in a patch. Its really great. Uses the same assets, but theres a lot added. For instance, theres way more story. Your character actually speaks to his/her self and when you find more party members, you can chat with them. And you only design one char, picking from the 4 races, but also 4 classes, each with 4 subclasses all slightly different.

I have completed the game, here is my review. In short I felt the game started off really well, and got let down by some bad game design decisons as it went on. To be slightly more specific, the emphasis on normal enemies, and hilariously long runs between the 'bonfire' and where you wanted to be.
It's hard to either recommend or not recommend this game. Rather than give a list of pros and cons, I'm going to say what's good about it, and then say how they managed to take that good thing, and ♥♥♥♥ it up.
1. The game is heavily inspired by dark souls. I consider this a good thing, as the dark souls formula is a good one to follow. If you don't like dark souls, you will not like this - in fact, you will HATE this. Move on now, this game is not worth your time. For the people still here who like Dark Souls, this game is a shadow of dark souls - I don't think you will get the same satisfaction you get out of playing dark souls.
2. The combat system is a pretty cool idea. You can select and target body parts, and those body parts can be armoured or unarmoured. You might think, "that sounds cool, does that mean that you get to strategically target different part of an depending on where it may be weak?". Well, not really, it's pretty much always the best idea to go for the head - armoured or unarmoured (at least, this is what I found to be most effective). There are two enemies in the game that I can recall where it's beneficial to cut off a tail of some sort but I really think they could have taken this idea further. So what is this body targeting system for you may ask? Grinding materials to make gear. Yes, they took this concept, and made it primarily into a grind mechanic. Cutting off different body parts gives you different items, which you need to make gear. This isn't terrible, but it's a shame that they took such a cool idea and turned it into a grind mechanic where I thought it would be cool to need to enemies in certain ways (the game does this to some extent, but for me, this should have been the focus).
3. The game is really, really hard. I would say it's probably harder than dark souls - albeit maybe a bit shorter. I think this would be a good thing, except, in my opinion, it creates challenge in the wrong ways. Unlike dark souls which has several bonfires sprinkled through an area, this game has a handful of areas with just one 'bonfire' that you unlock various shortcuts to. The paths from where you are to where you need to be become insanely long, with scores of normal enemies in between. And the normal enemies become LUDICROUSLY strong towards the end game. There is a need to go back and grind a little bit for items because it got to a point where enemies would one shot me with hilariously quick and cheap attacks with hyperarmour. This really becomes the focal point of my criticism with this game. I can look over everything else, but the strength of the normal enemies combined with the ridiculously long paths that you need to take creates a massive challenge which I didn't find very fun. Dark Souls takes the approach of creating challenge through difficult bosses that are varied and interesting to fight, while this game chooses to create challenge through long corridors of the same ridiculously hard enemies over and over again. To be honest, the only reason I kept playing this game was to overcome the challenge just to say I beat it, I stopped playing for fun.
4. This is sci-fi dark souls. Cool idea right? Except this games idea of the aesthetic is factory after factory after factory. The first level in this game really draws you in. By the second level, I just wanted out because I found the aesthetic to be almost unbearably boring, with the same enemies over and over. The enemy variety, and art variety are desperately lacking.
5. The boss fights are fun. I really enjoyed learning the different boss fights and they were very challenging and when you finally beat it, you really had to earn it. So what's bad about that? Well, in a 20-25 hour campaign there are only (if you don't want to know how many bosses there are, don't look at the spoiler)
. And yes, they were really fun, and the body targetting system kind of shined here (although it felt clunky at times, especially on the last boss) but there were so few that it felt like a bit of a let down.
6. The exploration in this game looked kind of cool. There's a few gates you can only access when you reach a certain level which creates incentive to backtrack - I like that. I think I would have appreciated a fast travel between the 'bonfires' in this game since there's only a few of them, and navigating the game can be a pain with such a large amount of ludicrously strong normal enemies.
In conclusion, we have a good idea for a game, that is bogged down by creating challenge in the wrong ways. We just didn't need corridors with dozens of enemies that can each one shot you. Tone down the normal enemies, create more interesting set piece encounters, maybe put more focus on elite enemies that despawn after one kill or something. I love hard games, and I did get satisfaction from completing this game due to it's difficulty, I just found that difficulty was created in the wrong way. Finally, the art style absolutely needs more variation along with the enemies, which need to be designed to take advantage of the body targeting system. If you want a challenge, and you want to get this game purely for the challenge - this is the game for you. If you don't like grinding, factory art style, challenge, Dark Souls - stay clear.

Summary:
Grimrock is a first person (first party in this case) dungeon crawl.  If you've ever heard/played a game called Stonekeep (late 1990s), you'll enjoy this game too.  Well designed, immersive, and an absolutely beautiful sound track.  Some skill is required to be a magic caster / use magic in your party, but if you get good at it, you really feel you've earned the title "mage."
Overall Score:  Worth Getting (Niche game)  -- ( 79/100)
Gameplay:  (56/60 points)
Mechanics (35/35 points) – rules/physics/noticeable glitches
I have never encountered any bugs while playing Grimrock.  The rules of the world fit very well with the challenges you face and you never feel like the game is cheating.
Controls (8/10 points) – ease of operation / button dynamics
Controls are very basic, left, right, back, forward, casting is difficult, but in a good way where you feel really good when you successfully cast a spell.  My only beef with the controls was inventory managment.  Trying to maintain 4 peoples inventory was very cumbersome at times.
Difficulty ( 5/5 points) – how hard is it to progress & does this difficulty work for or against the player
The game trains you as you go.  The first few levels are about learning how things work.  It's a good build up and by later in the game, it's about exploration, adapting and facing challenges that force you to use everything you've learned up to that point.
Immersion ( 4/5 points) –  very subjective:  Being drawn into the game
The environments are realistic enough and the sounds and music will make you forget about everything around you.  The desire to save as often as possible and searching for secrets areas and having to look up a few solutions was the only thing that broke immersion for me.
Fun ( 3/5 points)– very subjective: other enjoyment factors
VERY fun, but not so fun that I actually finished the game.  It was still excellent though, I've gotten further into this game than most.
Content:  (20/35 points)
Story (13/15 points) – Does it exist, coherent, presentation of, and does it enhance game play?
The opening was excellent, there's little scraps of papers and books that tell you more of the story thorugh the ponderings of a former "inmate."  Also every level of the game tells a different story and as you move further in, the very walls and status hint at darker things that have gone into the formation of Grimrock.  I can't say that the story is deep, but it is enjoyable.
Characters (5/10 points) – Interesting, well developed, work with gameplay and story
The characters are fairly standard fare for your Dungeons and Dragons -esque setting, but the manual had some great backstory on each.  It doesn't play into the game, but was good flavor text.
“S.S.D.D.” value (2/10 points) – abilities, roles, tools, NPCs, and general world setting uniqueness
Very typical for a dungeon crawl.

Gamer Parent Factors:  (3/5 GOLDEN points)

Plague Inc: Evolved is like the Pandemic flash games that many people love. My love of that kind of gameplay ultimately made me buy this. However, Plague Inc: Evolved AKA PIE from here on out is so much better in terms of the options available. You control your disease in all aspects. All the changes to transmission, abilities, symptoms, etc will affect how the disease is spread from person to person, city to country, continent to continent. Watching the news feed isn’t completely necessary, but it will at times give you hints on what you may need to do to further increase infection in the world’s populace, and provide some comedy from recent happenings (goat simulator reference, etc).
Like Pandemic, there are countries that are harder to infect, and due to the similarities, I always fear Madagascar. Though in this game, I sit a little more on edge when it comes to Greenland. If you’ve not gotten it yet, you’re jumping straight in to the great features that the game didn’t have when I first bought it, which makes this game very appealing and very fun.  So if you’re seeking a world destroying game by biological warfare, come let the evil scientist in you free.

I'm a huge fan of the Dark Souls series and this sub-genre in general, so I'm fairly qualified to talk (at length) about the pros and cons of The Surge.  You can check out a much more in-depth video review of the game on my channel (i'll drop a link to it at the conclusion of this written review).
The Surge DOES do a good job of making you feel great while you play.  Attacks are meaty, weighty and have good impact.  Just like in any Souls game, you lock on to enemies and play the 'cat and mouse' chess game with them.  Normal enemies are VERY hard, and The Surge focuses almost exlusively on them - boss battles are few and far between.   You can focus armored or non-armored areas, the latter of which giving you access to finishing moves to lop off that armor and take it for yourself as a schematic.  The game is
when you do this, and the gameplay loop that results is fairly unique (albeit...black and white) - focus yellow areas if you want gear, and focus blue areas if you want to live and progress easier.
This game is very, very hard...for both good and bad reasons.  Every enemy can kill you in a few hits, and it's more intense on a moment-to-moment level than let's say Dark Souls.  In addition, the maze like level design feels cramped, which makes the gameplay more intense because there are usually very little places to get comfortable and fight in line of sight of other parts of the screen (to see if other enemies are about to jump you).  Bosses are challenging, fun and fair...just like in Dark Souls.  They are hard but not super hard, usually requiring multiple attemps...I just wish there were more of them.   They are all beatable, because the game has prepared you well given how hard the regular enemies are.  With that said,

Great lightning effects, VERY GOOD PERFORMANCE (never dropped below 60 fps), a unique setting (however, one that the story does a poor job of enhancing and developing), really great animations and execution animations, and one of the best options menus in gaming (everything is explained very well, in detail - and fully customizable).
: The Surge is basically...a SCI-FI Dark Souls.  However, levels are VERY small, and interconnected through a main hub.  This results in a more interconnected experience, at the cost of environmental diversity.  Every environment screams 'I'm a Factory' and has a lot of repeat art assets and textures.  I grew very tired of the levels by the end of the game.  Also, a lack of WOW moments (Borreal Valley in DS3, Dragon Aerie in DS2) - the scale at which the game exists is very small, dense and compact.  The levels feel like mazes...for better or worse.
: There is no character creator (which is fine)...it allows the main lead to speak and have good development in a rich story.  The problem is...the story takes a back seat and is quickly shoved under the rug.  Warren himself (your character) is boring, terribly voice acted and very one-dimensional.  He doesn't question much, nor show very much emotion.  It defeats the purpose of having a pre-defined lead in the end, because he doesn't get developed.  Other NPC's are bland as well, and the voice acting is cringe-worthly.
: I don't like how The Surge focuses so heavily on trash mobs.  They are the meat of the game, in addition to navigating said maze levels finding 'switches' or 'consoles' to open new areas or unlock a door leading to the next boss.  It gets VERY tiresome grinding trash mobs over, and over, and over...and because they are so hard...it feels very sluggish going through The Surge sometimes.  Some people will like that...I did not.
No FOV slider (not required, but would have been nice given how cramped the game is), too few bosses, a weapon progression system that promotes you to stick to a single weapon class (thwarts experimentation - find a new awesome 2 handed staff but you've been duel wielding +3 weapons all game?  Don't even equip it.), and really sub-par music.
:  If you're desperately looking for
of the same Souls goodness - it's just...barely...worth a buy.  If you're
to Souls-Like games - start with Demon/Dark Souls.  If you're looking for
...I have to say wait for a sale and pick it up around $35.

Factorio is a game that keeps you hours for hours, stuck on your keyboard with it's fascinating gameplay. Factorio was first released on their website
and was later added to the steam platform.
The story of Factorio is kept very simple:
Your expedition into space fatally failed in mid and you've crashed into the nearest planet beside you. The Planet you've just bumped into, provides all the natural resources like (wood; stone; copper; iron; coal etc.) where your primary objective is, to rebuild a Spaceship to get out of this place and head back to earth..
But how are you able to build a spaceship in the middle of nowhere??
That's right!     Because thats what the game is all about! You have to build factories. For an example:
You chop down several trees and make an axe.  With the axe you have managed it to dig up some stone out of the rock that was just laying there, or maybe you've found yourself right next to a rock field. With the stone you found, you build a furnace to melt stuff and be able to smelt that rock for a pickaxe to dig up different resources like iron to make a drill and a transport lane to store that resources in the wood chests you've just made and so on..
And maybe after a bunch of hours that suddenly have pasted so quick since your beginning, you came up with an entire infrastructure and a great supply of coal and iron and all the goodies that are straight directed to your basement supply that may has even a research laboratory to come up with new stuff to build, like an oil drill or a train station.
And on top of all this great and endless strategic build and research abilities, it comes up with an INFINITE map to all 4 directions!!
Now..      building factories and researching in the science labor may not be the only thing you should care about, because you're NOT alone!
I don't want to spoil anything that is not shown in the trailer, but when you watch their opening trailer, it is obvious that the drastically destruction of "their" planet and habitats, not affect them to shake hands with you..     In other words,
THEY HATE IT..      and when you think, those are just a normal humanity, i have to prove you WRONG!!     Those are alien predators, that are about to tear down each and every building, you've invested so much time in to get it work, so...
To close this review i have to say, that this game has a highly extendable addiction that'll keep you HOURS in front of that screen!
As a final tip:    try to research in military defenses as soon as you can to protect your buildings in the further future..

Highly recommended. Endless Sky is a 2D space trading and fleet-building game set 1000 years in the future. I've played a few free games but the quality and level of detail here is amazing. Every planet and base that you can land on (and there are many, many of these) has a unique desription that really adds to the depth of the game universe. In my first couple of hours I'd paid off the extortionate bank loan, bought a few freighters and shuttles, switched my flagship for a light warship and then accidentally jumped into the middle of a massive capital ship battle where all of my ships were destroyed or disabled in seconds. Fortunately, the game autosaves when you leave a planet so it doesn't take long to get back up and running.
The trade system reminds me of some of my favourite parts of games like Freelancer where you have to pick out exactly where you are going to break your journey and make the most profit in one round trip. So far, it seems that the safest way to make money is through cargo and passenger missions whilst filling your remaining hold space with whatever you can sell for a quick buck on the way. You can also loot ships and sell the gear but I'm not particularly good at the combat side of things yet.
At the very least, you should give this a go. It's free! What have you got to lose?

Things I liked about the game:
1: It was exceptionally easy to run. Even with my POS pc with terrible graphics cards, I could still run the game at its highest setting with almost 0 lag. Im serious. It was insane.
2: The missions were varied. Like the previous game, you have action levels, and stealth levels, sniper levels, run and gun levels, the whole deal.
3: Captain price.
4: The weapons all felt very fluent and natural. Although technically the guns were all extremely similar, they all felt like they had different weight, and had different sounds and firing pattern.
5: Togglable controls. Probably not surprising for many, but if you have a half functional mouse like I do, being able to change the button locations is a goddamn lifesaver.
6: Smart AI. Im not going to sit here and pretent like it was totally flawless, but the AI in this game was definetly smarter and more natural than the last game.
Things I didnt like about the game:
1: The story was total♥♥♥♥♥ The entire game you are lead to believe that you are going to kill one big, bad guy, and at the last minute they change the antagonist and make you fight him instead. (the fighting was still cool though)
2: Some of the environments felt incredibly fake. In one part of the game, you fight in a suburban US neighborhood. It is so sunny, bright, flawless, and colorful that it doesnt even feel like it belongs in the game. it feels like a goddamn roblox map (Yes, I just said that)
3: The Mulitplayer is very fun, yet incredibly unfair. If you get a certain amount of kills, you can call in things like airstrikes, or fly helicopters or shoot off of jets. It sounds fun, until you realize that you have basically no defense from said attacks. If a few guys on the opposite team gets one of the air-attack rewards, i'd just leave the server. You wont get a chance to leave spawn. The game is over.
4: Some of the mechanics have changed. The biggest one for me is the bullet penetration. In COD 4, you could shoot through any wall like goddamn tissue paper, but in this game, you have no idea what you can shoot through, and what you cant! it is totally luck. Sometimes it shoots through, sometimes it doesnt. It works when it feels like it.
Little things i didnt like:
-------------------------------------
1: The knife no longer stabs, it just swipes. In COD 4, you got to see the knife get stuck right into your enemy, and it was satisfying as hell. Now, you just get to see the swipe, the little bit of blood, and that's it. Why they removed the animation, i dont know, but it was cool as hell
2: Some of the attachments dont make sense. Like why would a thermal scope make my gun have a goddamn heart attack? With sniper rifles in this game, you get HUGE amounts of sway. With acog scopes, you dont. Makes sense, right? So why would a thermal scope, which looks to be the same weight and size as an acog, bounce all over the goddamn place. I literally have no explaination for that.
OVERALL RATING:
7.8/10

Marooners is currently in an early access state but it seems like it's nearing full release. Everything plays really well (I think I encountered two bugs in my entire time of playing) and there is a nice amount of content (I am unsure if they plan to add more). In game there is also a handy banner telling you when the next update is due so you’re constantly aware of when to check back for new things and can know the developers are actively working on it.
Marooners is an objective based party game that consists of many different minigames all with their own goals. Instead of choosing each minigame one by one though you'll find a unique twist to Marooners in which the game will switch between mini games randomly whilst you’re playing, saving where everyone was in that stage and reverting back to that randomly without warning.
There are many different minigames from ones where you’ll be running from a giant boulder whilst dodging objects to games where you’ll have to dig down as far and fast as you can avoiding unbreakable blocks on your way. In every game you’ll be competing against at least one opponent and you can play with five other people at any one time. Each minigame is unique and insanely fun!
You can find powerups in game such as a magnet to draw coins towards you, bombs to throw at your opponents and a speed boost for a few seconds all adding a minor advantage to your gameplay. They are dropped randomly in play so everyone has an equal chance to grab one...if they’re quick enough.
Throughout each minigame you’ll find yourself picking up coins and at the end all the coins are tallied up, the winner is whoever has collected the most across all of the minigames so even if you win the most minigames you still might just lose if someone else played it smarter. If you win a minigame though you have a chance to grab a trophy for 25 points meaning you are more likely to win if you are the sole survivor of each one!!!
To avoid repetitiveness in gameplay around half of the minigames are included in each rotation and they are completely randomized so it doesn’t feel like you’re ever playing the same two games twice.
After each full game is completed everyone who was playing will unlock a new cosmetic weapon or character for use in future plays. As I mentioned all the items and characters you can play as are superficial only and add no stat bonus or otherwise to your gameplay. I think this keeps things fair whilst still allowing you a great amount of customization. It also makes it easier for you to switch players or weapons without feeling like you are being penalized for liking one more than another.
The graphics are really nice with a cartoony feel yet they don’t feel childish. Everything is vibrant without being too in your face. The soundtrack is pretty much what you’d expect from a party game but with a semi-tribal theme to it. Both work well in the game and give it that perfect party theme without feeling serious.
--- Great party minigames.
--- Online and Local play.
--- Ability to play Local and Online at the same time (up to 4 local and filled with online).
--- Up to 6 players (4 local + 2 online or up to 6 online).
--- 2 players per keyboard (optional).
--- Choice of characters & weapons to choose from (superficial only).
--- Cosmetic unlocks after each game for everyone, win or lose.
--- A few more mini-games wouldn’t hurt.
--- Not many players online at once currently.
--- No multipack on sale!!!!
--- When it’s just two players it feels like the minigames switch too fast.
--- No choice on how many minigames are included in each play.
Marooners is in early access still but seems very close to it’s full release. There are multiple minigames to keep you and your pals busy and the unique twist on the usual style of party games is great. Though there are not many players right now for online play if you have friends with the game or can play locally then Marooners is a great purchase. With active devs who listen to community feedback I can see this game reaching it’s full potential and being worth every cent.

I can't say I totally understood Transistor's story, but its gameplay offered a nice variety of challenges. Similar to Bastion, you'll likely find a set of weapons that combine well and you very much enjoy sticking with - and quite a lot of coding has been put in to let every single function also be turned into a "support" for another ability. However, the gameplay wavers between fast action and careful planning.
As with Bastion, soundtrack and voice work are the best you can get; The titular Transistor is almost always given the perfect amount of dialog, with small vocal skips to make his Morgan Freeman-esque voice more conversational and relatable. "Watch ou-...!! Oh. You got it."
Unlike Bastion, reflexes alone won't win you a fight. Half your time will be spent in a planning phase that is sorely needed to avoid getting hit while dealing attacks. Planning is done both before and during fights, as there are LOTS of options for function combos.
At time of writing, Supergiant has already shown E3 trailers for their next game, so stay tuned to them!

My general impression thus far is positive. Having played a lot of MoW, AS1 and AS2 over the past 2 years or so I can say quite honestly that if you've enjoyed any of these games you can be quite certain that this game is worth the investment.
Some things which I hope developers will spend time in improving however:
- The game could be improved substantially in mirroring AS2's interface. It may seem a trivial point but icons above the heads of vehicles, weapons teams, squads and individual soldiers is invaluable in locating and directing them. In several games while defending in Frontline precious seconds have been lost spent trying to find my howitzer/trench gun/machinegun because they are not as well marked or clearly visible as in AS2. I expect this problem will be rectified soon enough as such icons are intuitively lacking to players of past MoW games.
- The camera moves far too quickly. I expect this can be solved in fiddling with the settings but it's far too jerky and sensitive in default. Micromanaging units can be tricky enough without having the screen dart about owing to one's cursor inadvertently coming into close proximity to the edges of the screen.
- I do not understand why the select and move button are both the left mouse key, as was the case in MoW1. It's wrong. I really, really do not like it. The left button should be for selecting and the right for moving.
- The multiplayer maps need more cover and undulating terrain. They feel rather sparse at the moment, lacking even shell holes or craters to aid the advance of men. Quite often infantry are utterly at the mercy of artillery owing to a distinct lack of cover to shelter behind or hide in. I find myself having to spam infantry in the hopes that only a few will survive long enough to acheive what I wish of them. I do however appreciate the developers are trying to reflect the reality of combat in no man's land, I just wish however it could be done a little more sympathetically to those trying to preserve the lives of their men!
That's all I can think of at the moment.

I bought this game alongside Assault Squad 2. Before that I played mostly CoH and the Great 1918 mod for it. I also played a few of Condemned Heroes not long ago. When I bought the two games I was expecting to play more of Battle of Empires, which I did at first, but I instead enjoy Assault Squad 2 more. It may not be fair to compare the two, but in some cases I will.
First of, it is nice to see a world war 1 game. There are not many games that do this theme. I think the French singleplayer does a good job of portraying the war. The missions I played I liked better than Condemned Heroes. However I feel that the multiplayer has a identity problem. It seems without direction. I do not know if it is geared towards competive play or authenticity. Assault Squad 2 strives for competive play, and so we see units of various time periods and even experimental units in the case of Japan. I personally do not like this, but do understand it.
I feel that Battle of Empires fells short on competive play. It seems more casual with the focus on frontlines - assault zones have been added however. Thus I would expect more focus on authenticity. This is personal, but I am not so keen on the mixing around of time periods. Experimental vehicles can especially ruin any authenticity. The Great War 1918 mod did a far better job, it combines historical accuracy and gameplay much better. Compared to Men of War however, Company of Heroes gameplay is something I rather not go back to. When it comes to more realistic gameplay, and so more authentic gameplay, Men of War is much better.
To who do I recommend this? If you would like to play World War One singleplayer, this game is a good choice. It now has a French campaign, but additional campaigns - British, German and Russian - will be added. It is also a good choice if you want to play online in a World War One setting. For competive play I wouldn't recommend this. If you are looking for an (more) authentic Great War mod you might be a bit dissapointed. The Great War 1918 mod does a much better job at that. In Battle of Empires defense, it is more difficult to portray the whole war than a period of it. And Battle of Empires has Russians, will have Italians in some way and of course picklehaube - which the Great War 1918 mod does not have.
We must consider however that Battle of Empires is still in development. Overall it is a decent game. I did enjoy the multiplayer games that I played and I did not experience any bugs.
Keep it up Battle of Empires team!

Unhack 2 comes a few years after the original game and Destruction (both of which you should play before this, since those stories are a huge part of this one). The passage of time not only shows in the story, but in how the game was developed as well. It's a much bigger, more ambitious story than the earlier games.
Gameplay during the unhacking sequences has also changed. It's much more puzzle-focused, rather than requiring fast reflexes like the other games in the series. Enemies only move when you do, so planning your moves is the key to success this time around. Honestly, I prefer the earlier style of unhacking, but that doesn't make the new system bad by any stretch of the imagination.
Most of the game is pure story, told in a visual novel style. The unhacking sequences break up the various chapters. These levels themselves are smaller, but the more involved puzzles create challenge and add a respectable amount of time to the game as a whole. While bigger than the earlier Unhack games, it's not a long game, and can easily be played from start to finish in one afternoon.
The characters were interesting, and the story kept me guessing what would happen next. It was more complex than I expected, so that was a pleasant surprise. I won't go into any detail on that to avoid spoilers, but this game kept me interested from beginning to end.
If you've played the other games, you'll probably be surprised by the changes in style and gameplay, but you'll probably also be as hooked as I was. It won't be quite what you might have expected, but it's still a world worth returning to. Welcome back, dear unhacker.

A surprisingly good sci-fi visual novel about AI companions, Unhack 2 weaves a complex story that touches on social/philosophical issues regarding the nature of artificial intelligence and their relationship with humans, while at the same time having heartfelt moments and memorable characters. That's an impressive feat for a VN that is only about 5 hours long.
If you do give Unhack 2 a try, I highly recommend going through Unhack 1 first as it will give you a good amount of background and character development.

This second title of the Unhack series from InvertMouse now feature a different male protagonist who was thought to be The Creator from Smash Security. With the Motherworm and the source of the 5K Worm destroyed along with The Creator's former AI companions Perfect Weedy and Debug-squared four years ago, the protagonist was shocked to find an army of AI clones resembling Weedy to appear together with a mysterious masked AI launching simultaneous attacks throughout in cyberspace and in the actual living world. As the protagonist attempts to investigate the source of these hacking and actual attacks on him, the protagonist will attempt to hack across multiple different security and firewall systems in the form of 10 puzzle minigames which involve moving a circular icon across a maze to an exit without being destroyed by various environmental hazards and uncover the truth about himself, experience love with an AI and make a sacrifice.
The puzzle minigames are now turn-based with environmental hazards moving after the player has made a move and can be skipped with no missed dialogue or achievements, there is now a gallery to show all unlocked CGs and the game now allows quicksaves, manual saving at any point in the game and the take screenshot button on Steam to work. Soundtracks are good and overall game presentation is also nicely done. Recommended when at sale or in bundle discount as it takes less than 10 hours to finish/skip all puzzle minigames and read through the entire visual novel.

There are things you should understand if you come across an InvertMouse visual novel, its emotional, its very emotional but not very long. IM is quickly becoming a masterclass when it comes to the short visual novel format and this is a perfect reflection of that.
Unhack 2 deals with the very apparent problems that come with AI, in the society we live in this sort of thing is going to quickly be coming into focus, AI isnt perfect because its bad by humans, its in a way a reflection of those humans, their successes their problems, their hopes and dreams and how this can all lead to ones world crashing down or becoming their greatest successes, a story for the people behind the programs that you use, the unsung heroes per say, it is a story about greed and benevolence.
Music for the most part is great however there is one song at the start which seems to have been sampled badly and i could here a bit of noise which wasnt very nice but for the most part it was surprisingly good.
Sadly there was no voice acting in this sequel however with the noticable increase in characters I can understand why.
Artwork is as always outstanding even giving some of the top tier visual novels and artists a run for their money.
Length depends on you, I read extremely fast now so I blew through it in just over 3 hours but several people were well into the 4 hour mark while reading.
The puzzles serve their purpose, im indifferent about them, they work and are a bit complex towards the end.
So to conclude what can I say, InvertMouse delivers again so if you remotely like visual novels then this should definately be on your list of things to read but do yourself a favour and read the first one while you are at it, it may not have the level of polish that this game has but it doesnt take long to finish and can provide better emotional ties to everything.

While I can understand the concerns of others that this is simply a "Play to win" game, I quite disagree with the concept that this ruins the game experience.
After playing the game for almost a week, I believe see that paying certainly does have its benefits, boosting your way to the higher levels and buying more powerful weapons. But by simply playing the game as well, you can have fun whilst levelling up with friends and tackling monsters together. This is rewarding in itself and is much more entertaining than paying to reach higher levels. Finding weapons on the ground and trading them with friends, rather than buying them for extortionate prices at a user-based shop, is a truly wonderful experience that teaches the player to be generous and tactful with their items, rather than spending real-world money and buying the highest level sword you can.
Obviously this game can be played a lot easier if you splash the cash and buy your way to level 50, but where’s the fun in that? Get on, get stuck in and battle your way to it. Then you can truly say you’ve accomplished something, without paying half your life’s savings.
While the fanbase can be small and in-game prices are a little bias in their amounts, we must remember that this is simply an open-beta and things will be changed and fixed in the future. For that reason, I recommend this game to any budding young MMO player, or an experienced try-hard just looking for something fun to divulge your time to.

Release Date: October 8, 2014 [Original Release Date: August 14, 2012]
Developed by: United Front Games
Published by: Square Enix
In Sleeping Dogs, you play as Wei Shen, an undercover cop for the HKPD. He is sent by Officer Pendrew to infiltrate and take down one of the major Chinese Triads known as the Sun on Yee. However, this is a just a simple premise for what happens in the story. The story does get much more interesting in my opinion. I want to avoid major spoilers but the game's story kicks off very fast and it is very engaging. At the end, you do feel a sense of closure and everything makes sense. Overall, the story is brilliant and one of the main reasons you should buy this game even without the excellent gameplay. There is one caveat though. For me, the story is short. Playing through the whole campaign clocked me at exactly 12.3 hours. Although, there is a wealth of extra content which I will get into in a future section.
Like in the story, Sleeping Dog excels in the gameplay aspect. It features a martial combat system similar to that from the Batman Arkham franchise. Sleeping Dogs gives a way to refresh that formula. It adds a lot of combos which have amazing animations and a new environmental attack which lets you grab people and throw then into something which is part of the environment. Some are mild such as throwing a thug into a trash can or a phone booth, but others can be quite gory such as smashing one's head into a moving fan or a saw onto a table. Unlike Batman Arkham, the game features a unique grab system which can be really fun with the different new combos you can learn. Gunplay is good and plays just like your average third person shooter. However every time you vault over a table with a gun the game goes into a slow motion mode like Max Payne which makes the gunplay new and fun. It never gets old. Missions are mostly different except for the cop missions which usually have you tailing or busting drug dealers. All of the story missions are amazing and none ever feel the same with the melee system. The game is set in Hong Kong and this makes a nice change from the seemingly dull San Andreas of GTA to the neon and vibrant Hong Kong of Sleeping Dogs. Cinematics are also produced really well with having many great animations. Sadly NPC animations seem stiff in normal gameplay.
Sleeping Dogs provides a wealth of DLC added already into this definitive version of this game. United Front took a smart move and spread the content throughout the game making it seem like it always there and not DLC. I would say at max that the expansions and extra content in the definitive version give a couple more hours of playtime. For the average person, it would probably be around twenty hours. The PC port is very well optimized. At near max settings, I can play the game at a good 45-60 fps with a 50 fps average. Anyone playing should keep AA at FXAA (the normal) and not max it out. It is a framerate killer even for a GTX 1060. I was very surprised to be able to run the game at 30 fps low much less than 50 fps at high settings.
Sleeping Dogs is an action blockbuster in the form of a video game.The game is well worth it on a sale. It is probably good at the base price of $30 but it is a complete steal at $7.49 on the Winter Sale at time of posting this review. (December 28, 2016) The story can feel short to some only clocking 12.3 hours for me and 15.5 hours on
. I feel that Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition is well worth the price to me with the large amounts of extra content the game has and the spectacular campaign. I give it a solid
P.S. Just as a quick note, the game does not have trading cards. It does have achievements.

10/10 Masterpiece of a martial arts game. No cryptic combos to master like Streetfighter, or Mortal combat, which makes♥♥♥♥♥kicking a lot more fun. The fighting is often compared to Batman Arkhem games, but they seem like they are in slow motion compared to this game. This game is like being in a Bruce Lee , or Jackie Chan movie. You really kick♥♥♥♥♥if you practice. There is quite a bit of skill involved, the moves are not hard to remember, like most fighting games. (Go back into the martial arts school after you retrieve statues, and you can practice. It will show you how to basically beat every character type in the game.)
Driving motorcycles is just like in the old martial arts movies. If you pop-a-wheelie, before you hit certain cars head on you will do a massive jump. If you get good you can do this to evade cops by jumping your bike on top of overpasses, and bridges, so you can get away.
Game was re-published in 2014, so you can run it on a crappy little Alienware Alpha i3 like I have. The Graphics are on par with GTA 5, and even better in some aspects. This game should run on any system built after 2012, with a decent GFX card.
I played the original without the DLC that this version has, and it was about half as much content as this package. It is good they do not sell the original because now the islands and things around the  map are populated, and they make sense  why they are even there.
Main game comes with 2 completely different modules.  One Zombie module which is a cross between the main game, and sort of silly like the Saints Row series of games. The other is the year of the Snake which is a bunch of cop missions which would not really fit well in the main game. . If you win each of them you get a little prize in the main game.
The Zodiac fight on the other hand is in the main game. The original game lacked a good ending as far as winning all the martial arts matches. The Zodiac tournament on the other hand seems like it is the finnish.
There are a lot of police Missions compared to the original game. I think it was originallyy a DLC. You also get cop gear like cars, and new outfits that give you fighting perks, Armor, Guns, and other goodies. Some of the cop cars have shotguns in the trunk too, so if you unlock the unlock cop car trunk, you can always have a pump shotgun when cruizing the streets.
THere is a yellow clothes store in the main market now where you can get other outfits that give you guns, fighting buffs, armor, and even a sword. The guns and other toys cant be used in main missions, but for drug busts they are really fun.
Thre is also a "Super car" DLC that is prety fun. At the end of the mission you get to keep the car. This also was originally a DLC.
Tips:
There are a lot of martial arts tournaments around the city. THe one by the warehouse is the biggest payout, but it also is really hard until you get some good moves. last round is like 7 Big guys, 5 guys you have to grapple, and 10 guys that you can pretty much just box. Be sure to practice the tournaments a lot, and then the missions and drug busts wil be really easy for you.
* This one is a no-bainer, but be sure you get all of the jade statues, so you get all of the moves.
* Max out your Triad, Police, and Face as fast as you can. Be as brutal as you possibly can to get Triad points while fighting. Drive safe, and you will get a good cop score. Your Face will build when you win matches, and help people on sub missions. Face is really importent when fighting.
* Zodiac tournament has a stage with 3 gear wheels you can shove guys into. You do not have to do this more than 1 or 2 times. Focus on the 2 big guys, and after you kill them, the others can be killed in 1-2 moves each. (practice at the tournaments, you get some really neat combos that are not taught in the school)
* Buy complete outfits with guns and grenade launchers for the sewer, or water entrance drug busts. They will be really easy that way.
* Get a boat and check the entire island shoreline, you will find atleast 12 shrines, and power up 2 times. Not to mention lots of red envelopes and blue boxes with goodies in them.
* Explore the building rooftops. There are a lot of goodies up there.

In the good old days of games, companies would invest money into developing a game. Sometimes these investments wouldn't pay off and the game would be unceremoniously cancelled. I've got a real soft spot for InvertMouse's VN's; they get so many things right in terms of the stuff that counts; good characterisation, plotting and pacing that the shallower areas (like the superfluous mini-games and occasional recycled graphical elements) don't really register.
The big shift from Unhack 1 is that this game is a full fledged VN (as opposed the the light-arcade hybrid of the original). There are still a series of 'hacking' minigames which equate to moving a box around a grid avoiding obstacles; these are all skippable without penalty, and you might as well since they don't really serve a purpose except to slow down the story momentarily.
The story itself zips along, introducing new characters with a lot of charm as well as revisiting much of the original game's cast; it steers clear of outright fanservice but I'd still strongly recommend a playthrough of the original first, if only to establish context. The story is linear and there's no opportunity to branch the narrative, but this isn't the kind of tale which would really benefit from such a mechanic; you're here to take a ride with the protagonist (love him or hate him) not to dictate events.
The biggest loss is the lack of voice acting; which doesn't hinder the story, but still left me a little sad since the VAs from Unhack 1 did such an amazing job bringing their characters to life. On the plus side however there's a lot more 'story' this time around which can only be a good thing; I got through the whole game in a little over 4 hours without ever pushing myself and enjoyed the entire trip; well worth a read.

Well what do we have here?
A Visual Novel Style Game with hacking Gameplay that has Virtual AI Characters who guides you along the Way in your Path as "Unhacker" and furthermore interacts with you on some funny and ridiculous Ways.
Damn count me in!!!
That is what I thought when I played  Unhack 1.
So is Unhack 2 a worthy sequel to Unhack 1?
Of course it is and I love it!!!
But there are some things that has gotten lost along the way, that I really liked in the first part.
For example the Gameplay.
The Gameplay in the first part was really something, not because it was especially challenging or anything along these lines. No! It was good because it fitted in the game perfectly and the Story developed during its Gameplay. This is something I really liked about Unhack 1.
But as it is, the Gameplay of Unhack 2 is not really worth mentioning, its more of an decorative accessory than anything else. That was kind of a bummer to me.
The lacking Voice Acting was also something that dissapointed me, especially then the prequel has it.
But I understand that Indie Studios might not have always the most strechable Budgets around the Game Industry.
Still I seek to hear the tired Voice of Miss Debug again, one day!
But even with all my complaints I really love Unhack 2! Why you ask?
Because it is a damn good Visual Novel with uniqe and interesting Characters and a Story with lots of Variety in it.
The Character Development in this one is amazing, the World Building is creative and Immersive.
That, as we all might know, is really hard to do in a Sci-fi World with Virtual Reallity in it and most of its Characters AIs.
Of course you will not get the depth of a Visual Novel with 100+ hours reading time here.
(Well even so there might be some VNs with 100+ reading Time out there that dont have the depth of this game)
But for the Content that is in the Game, it is really a damn fine piece of work.
It certainly is worth the money and worth the time you spent with it.
I know I enjoyed it!

Now Art & Music, the artwork is above your standard anime, in my opinion it's great. From listening I guess there are 20 tracks more or less in this game, they are okay to good. So no worrying, about tracks becoming repetitive while reading.
Following we have gameplay, in unhacked 2 it takes a second seat. You get to do those unhacking, "mini-puzzles," each chapter I feel is quite simple compared to the
first game. You are also given the option to skip (I don't 100% remember if it was in unhack 1), so if you came here for a plain visual novel, cheers to you.  However, it is an
improvement to see, as not everyone wants to do mini-puzzles.
In conclusion/summary, unhack 2 has an increased story to the original, great art, many background tracks, and some bonus mini-puzzles. So I can proudly say I can recommend it :3

Marooners is a Multiplayer game, which can be played either online with random people or if you have a friend you can play on the same keyboard. There isn't much to this game at the moment, as it's still in early access, so take that into consideration when reading this review.
This game is pretty much a bunch of party minigames mashed together to create a somewhat confusing and irritating the first few times you play through this. The mechanic of this game is rather unique for it's simplicity, but starting off with this it may seem a rather confusing jumble of minigames together. But after playing it a few times you start to understand what each minigame has to offer and what you actually have to do in order to win that minigame. The mechanic of this game works as follows, you are placed into a random minigame and off you go. You have about 25-30 seconds to try to get as many points on that minigame as you can until it goes to another minigame and you repeat the process. You will recycle through a few minigames, and be put back into the first minigame of where you where when you finished your first 30 seconds of the minigame. For the time being, the game lacks the amount of minigames that are avaialble but hopefully they will add more in future updates. The keyboard controls for local multiplayer aren't exactly the best, it was hard to play with another friend as it was rather cramped and hard to control. Needs the optition to change keyboard controls.
+ Unique mechanic
+ Local & Online Co-op
+ Full controller support
- Few minigames
- No optition to change keyboard controls
- At the moment no Achievements or Trading cards
For the time being, Marooners is a alright game, with a very unique and interesting mechanic. Although there isn't many minigames, the game does offer Local & Online multiplayer, along with full controller support. I feel like this game will be great in future updates, and when it eventually gets out of the Early Access stage.

The game, unfortunately, needs more work than this to reach its full potential.
That being said its still a reasonable game.
