Summary:
Grimrock is a first person (first party in this case) dungeon crawl.  If you've ever heard/played a game called Stonekeep (late 1990s), you'll enjoy this game too.  Well designed, immersive, and an absolutely beautiful sound track.  Some skill is required to be a magic caster / use magic in your party, but if you get good at it, you really feel you've earned the title "mage."
Overall Score:  Worth Getting (Niche game)  -- ( 79/100)
Gameplay:  (56/60 points)
Mechanics (35/35 points) – rules/physics/noticeable glitches
I have never encountered any bugs while playing Grimrock.  The rules of the world fit very well with the challenges you face and you never feel like the game is cheating.
Controls (8/10 points) – ease of operation / button dynamics
Controls are very basic, left, right, back, forward, casting is difficult, but in a good way where you feel really good when you successfully cast a spell.  My only beef with the controls was inventory managment.  Trying to maintain 4 peoples inventory was very cumbersome at times.
Difficulty ( 5/5 points) – how hard is it to progress & does this difficulty work for or against the player
The game trains you as you go.  The first few levels are about learning how things work.  It's a good build up and by later in the game, it's about exploration, adapting and facing challenges that force you to use everything you've learned up to that point.
Immersion ( 4/5 points) –  very subjective:  Being drawn into the game
The environments are realistic enough and the sounds and music will make you forget about everything around you.  The desire to save as often as possible and searching for secrets areas and having to look up a few solutions was the only thing that broke immersion for me.
Fun ( 3/5 points)– very subjective: other enjoyment factors
VERY fun, but not so fun that I actually finished the game.  It was still excellent though, I've gotten further into this game than most.
Content:  (20/35 points)
Story (13/15 points) – Does it exist, coherent, presentation of, and does it enhance game play?
The opening was excellent, there's little scraps of papers and books that tell you more of the story thorugh the ponderings of a former "inmate."  Also every level of the game tells a different story and as you move further in, the very walls and status hint at darker things that have gone into the formation of Grimrock.  I can't say that the story is deep, but it is enjoyable.
Characters (5/10 points) – Interesting, well developed, work with gameplay and story
The characters are fairly standard fare for your Dungeons and Dragons -esque setting, but the manual had some great backstory on each.  It doesn't play into the game, but was good flavor text.
“S.S.D.D.” value (2/10 points) – abilities, roles, tools, NPCs, and general world setting uniqueness
Very typical for a dungeon crawl.

Gamer Parent Factors:  (3/5 GOLDEN points)
- (WIN) Ability to save / pause and come back later to pick it up right away again
- (WIN) Ability to progress during short gameplay sessions (30 mins – 1.5 hours)
- (WIN) Replay value and game length not related to required repetitive grinding to increase stats
-  (NO)  Ability to play game with spouse or offspring
-  (NO)  Availability on multiple platforms

The purpose of GamerDad Game reviews is to evaluate ‘aged’ games that have been on the market long enough to experience a substantial price drop from their original industry standard price.
Reviewing games towards the end of their life cycle will offer an updated consumer valuation of the game based on if known issues have been fixed since release, value of optional DLC (Downloadable Content made available after initial game release) to gameplay, and if the entertainment return on investment is worth the new price point.

Third game of the Hexcell series, a puzzle game similiar to minesweeper but, but without the need to guess as every puzzle can be logically solved. It uses the same formula as the previous two aside from the fact that there is the infinite puzzle option in which a random puzzle is generated giving the game more longivity than previous version.

I bought the game because it sounded interesting and I'm a lot more willing to buy games now that I can refund if I don't like it. I tried it out and thought it was great, played it for a little bit, then went to bed. The next day, I look at steam and am surprised to see it says "You have played 100 minutes"
I was genuinely stunned - those 100 minutes flew by so damn fast, I swear I thought I had only played for like 15-20 minutes.
If you like logic based puzzle games with clear rules, this is a must have.  Think minesweeper but set up such that you NEVER have to guess. You can always figure out the solution without guessing in any way, like sudoku. Sure, you CAN guess then just remember what the answer was, restart, and pretend like you figured it out with no mistakes, but the way you SHOULD play this game is to never ever click anything unless you are 100% certain you're right. It's much more entertaining and satisfying this way.
Additionally, it's all broken up into fairly small, bite-sized levels, so you can spend just 10 minutes playing while waiting for something and still get through a level or two. Of course you can also do what I did and spend almost two hours playing without even realizing time is passing by...

Release Date: October 8, 2014 [Original Release Date: August 14, 2012]
Developed by: United Front Games
Published by: Square Enix
In Sleeping Dogs, you play as Wei Shen, an undercover cop for the HKPD. He is sent by Officer Pendrew to infiltrate and take down one of the major Chinese Triads known as the Sun on Yee. However, this is a just a simple premise for what happens in the story. The story does get much more interesting in my opinion. I want to avoid major spoilers but the game's story kicks off very fast and it is very engaging. At the end, you do feel a sense of closure and everything makes sense. Overall, the story is brilliant and one of the main reasons you should buy this game even without the excellent gameplay. There is one caveat though. For me, the story is short. Playing through the whole campaign clocked me at exactly 12.3 hours. Although, there is a wealth of extra content which I will get into in a future section.
Like in the story, Sleeping Dog excels in the gameplay aspect. It features a martial combat system similar to that from the Batman Arkham franchise. Sleeping Dogs gives a way to refresh that formula. It adds a lot of combos which have amazing animations and a new environmental attack which lets you grab people and throw then into something which is part of the environment. Some are mild such as throwing a thug into a trash can or a phone booth, but others can be quite gory such as smashing one's head into a moving fan or a saw onto a table. Unlike Batman Arkham, the game features a unique grab system which can be really fun with the different new combos you can learn. Gunplay is good and plays just like your average third person shooter. However every time you vault over a table with a gun the game goes into a slow motion mode like Max Payne which makes the gunplay new and fun. It never gets old. Missions are mostly different except for the cop missions which usually have you tailing or busting drug dealers. All of the story missions are amazing and none ever feel the same with the melee system. The game is set in Hong Kong and this makes a nice change from the seemingly dull San Andreas of GTA to the neon and vibrant Hong Kong of Sleeping Dogs. Cinematics are also produced really well with having many great animations. Sadly NPC animations seem stiff in normal gameplay.
Sleeping Dogs provides a wealth of DLC added already into this definitive version of this game. United Front took a smart move and spread the content throughout the game making it seem like it always there and not DLC. I would say at max that the expansions and extra content in the definitive version give a couple more hours of playtime. For the average person, it would probably be around twenty hours. The PC port is very well optimized. At near max settings, I can play the game at a good 45-60 fps with a 50 fps average. Anyone playing should keep AA at FXAA (the normal) and not max it out. It is a framerate killer even for a GTX 1060. I was very surprised to be able to run the game at 30 fps low much less than 50 fps at high settings.
Sleeping Dogs is an action blockbuster in the form of a video game.The game is well worth it on a sale. It is probably good at the base price of $30 but it is a complete steal at $7.49 on the Winter Sale at time of posting this review. (December 28, 2016) The story can feel short to some only clocking 12.3 hours for me and 15.5 hours on
. I feel that Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition is well worth the price to me with the large amounts of extra content the game has and the spectacular campaign. I give it a solid
P.S. Just as a quick note, the game does not have trading cards. It does have achievements.

10/10 Masterpiece of a martial arts game. No cryptic combos to master like Streetfighter, or Mortal combat, which makes♥♥♥♥♥kicking a lot more fun. The fighting is often compared to Batman Arkhem games, but they seem like they are in slow motion compared to this game. This game is like being in a Bruce Lee , or Jackie Chan movie. You really kick♥♥♥♥♥if you practice. There is quite a bit of skill involved, the moves are not hard to remember, like most fighting games. (Go back into the martial arts school after you retrieve statues, and you can practice. It will show you how to basically beat every character type in the game.)
Driving motorcycles is just like in the old martial arts movies. If you pop-a-wheelie, before you hit certain cars head on you will do a massive jump. If you get good you can do this to evade cops by jumping your bike on top of overpasses, and bridges, so you can get away.
Game was re-published in 2014, so you can run it on a crappy little Alienware Alpha i3 like I have. The Graphics are on par with GTA 5, and even better in some aspects. This game should run on any system built after 2012, with a decent GFX card.
I played the original without the DLC that this version has, and it was about half as much content as this package. It is good they do not sell the original because now the islands and things around the  map are populated, and they make sense  why they are even there.
Main game comes with 2 completely different modules.  One Zombie module which is a cross between the main game, and sort of silly like the Saints Row series of games. The other is the year of the Snake which is a bunch of cop missions which would not really fit well in the main game. . If you win each of them you get a little prize in the main game.
The Zodiac fight on the other hand is in the main game. The original game lacked a good ending as far as winning all the martial arts matches. The Zodiac tournament on the other hand seems like it is the finnish.
There are a lot of police Missions compared to the original game. I think it was originallyy a DLC. You also get cop gear like cars, and new outfits that give you fighting perks, Armor, Guns, and other goodies. Some of the cop cars have shotguns in the trunk too, so if you unlock the unlock cop car trunk, you can always have a pump shotgun when cruizing the streets.
THere is a yellow clothes store in the main market now where you can get other outfits that give you guns, fighting buffs, armor, and even a sword. The guns and other toys cant be used in main missions, but for drug busts they are really fun.
Thre is also a "Super car" DLC that is prety fun. At the end of the mission you get to keep the car. This also was originally a DLC.
Tips:
There are a lot of martial arts tournaments around the city. THe one by the warehouse is the biggest payout, but it also is really hard until you get some good moves. last round is like 7 Big guys, 5 guys you have to grapple, and 10 guys that you can pretty much just box. Be sure to practice the tournaments a lot, and then the missions and drug busts wil be really easy for you.
* This one is a no-bainer, but be sure you get all of the jade statues, so you get all of the moves.
* Max out your Triad, Police, and Face as fast as you can. Be as brutal as you possibly can to get Triad points while fighting. Drive safe, and you will get a good cop score. Your Face will build when you win matches, and help people on sub missions. Face is really importent when fighting.
* Zodiac tournament has a stage with 3 gear wheels you can shove guys into. You do not have to do this more than 1 or 2 times. Focus on the 2 big guys, and after you kill them, the others can be killed in 1-2 moves each. (practice at the tournaments, you get some really neat combos that are not taught in the school)
* Buy complete outfits with guns and grenade launchers for the sewer, or water entrance drug busts. They will be really easy that way.
* Get a boat and check the entire island shoreline, you will find atleast 12 shrines, and power up 2 times. Not to mention lots of red envelopes and blue boxes with goodies in them.
* Explore the building rooftops. There are a lot of goodies up there.

I'm probably going to be lambasted for this, but I honestly don't think that this game deserves as much praise as it's getting. It's a good game; heck, it's a darned good one, but I think people are blowing it a bit out of proportion.
The combat in this game feels very good; think of it as a modernized Fallout (the first two games) meets the active time battle system from Final Fantasy. You can get unique abilities that will cost a certain amount of your meter. What's very cool is that the battle will often incentivize using these abilities in tandem with one another. However, it can also be quite a detriment to the system. I recall basically breaking the game when I got one particular ability. I just kept using the same strategy over and over, and I won every match without a hitch. Even at the final battle, this became the dominant strategy for me. The fights became very repetitive as a result of this.
The story itself is presented like that of Dark Souls or the recent DOOM. Nothing is really put in your face, but there is plenty of backstory and information in the people from whom your abilities spawned. A couple of things, however, like Red's muteness, are never truly explored. It's a bit bothersome, but nothing too bad. The voice acting is all right. I like the voice for Red, but I cannot take the Transistor's voice seriously, especially having heard his voice in a light-hearted manner in Bastion.
7/10 I think that the game is very good, but it suffers from style-over-substance syndrome. I wish Supergiant all the best.

Game: Call of Duty®: Modern Warfare 2
Hours(Currently): 50
Rating: 6.5/10
My Thoughts:
Welcome to my Second Game Review this year thus far. First I'd like to say, I'm only going to be reviewing games that I have close too Fourty - Fifty Hours within the game. This will be my final review until I began pouring more hours into several games. Let us begin, So this game seems to get alot of hate on PC. While I wouldn't say this game is the perfect Image of a Call of Duty PC Game; It definitely isn't awful. There are alot more flaws with the Game then Pros in my opinion, but none of these are very common which is Why I still give it an above Half Rating. Lets begin with some Pros that the game offers. First, This is the most Popular Call of Duty I can think about, You Ask your friend what is there most played Call of Duty; Modern Warfare 2 is most likely in there top three. It Has a very good reputation on console. The Campaign is amazing if you've never played it, The Ending is considered by some the best FPS Ending ever created. Although I differ to agree, but for sure It has one of the biggest Plot twists I've ever experienced. Just playing that and Completing the mission, Then seeing this Plot Twist through me for a spin. I Was in Awe! The Bonus mission at the end of the Campaign isn't the greatest in my opinion, Compared to Modern Warfare the Original; Though it is only a Bonus mission. The Spec Ops are 10/10 in My Opinion, it isn't Zombies from the Treyarch Series with Detailed Story and Developing Characters but it's very Action Packed. Imagine playing Multiple Missions from a 007 Game. That's how it feels everytime you load up with your friends. The Multiplayer is the best I've ever seen in a Call of Duty game. There is a very great balance in maps, Meaning there isn't more awful maps then Amazing remakable quality maps. The Guns aren't the best when coming to balanced but better then *Cough* AW *Cough* The Camos are the best in my opinion, and the Kill Streaks(NUKE NUKE NUKE) Is such a huge gamechanger. When they talk about adding to the newer games they should look at what Modern Warfare 2 accomplished. Something so simple like a Killstreak ending the game, Yet So Powerful and Effective. There are Flaws to the game though, Campaign: The Campaign has some visual glitches at time but are expected for the time period, and the Bonus mission glitches alot while loading and sometimes crashes the game for me which never happened on the console version. Spec Ops: While I still think Spec-Ops is so fantastic, The only real major flaw I can see that happens very often and is game breaking(Which they should fix) is that The FPS Drops frequently, I mean F R E Q U E N T L Y. Finally Multiplayer: While the Gameplay itself isn't that bad and has aged very well, There is one problem that really has ruined the experience, The hackers... While it's expected in every single game, It isn't too frequent as in Aimboting and GodMode in a older game like this, What is more present is Level Hacking. Now I know, "It's just a level" But when your grinding and you enter a Boost lobby it's awful. You can't reset without going through alot of trouble to delete files, And you take the risk of being Vac-Banned(Yes you can still get Vacced, Happens Often) Which really can ruin the experience, I mean without the grind there isn't much to do within in the game besides grind for a nuke or two. What else is there after you unlocked everything? In Conclusion I very deeply love Modern Warfare 2 But because of the Frequent FPS Spikes, and Boosting Lobbies scattered all over the Multiplayer, I'm giving it a Rating of 6.5/10. Although I do recommend Purchasing if your a True fan of the Call of Duty Series.

I will be taking a different approach with this Review. I apologize for this wall of text that most likely contains informations you do not care about. Feels free to read only the last paragraph for some kind of "tl;dr".
I believe Final Fantasy XIV released when I started to solidify into TERA, when I started doing things with my guild and formed my awesome static party. Ever since then, I've been haunted by Final Fantasy XIV and I tried my hardest to ignore the fact I really wanted to play it. It wasn't until recently that I started looking into details for this game. I simply brought it up to my friend as a joke and after that, he kept insisting on trying the game, despite knowing he just doesn't have any time for MMOs anymore because of work and life. So I finally decided to try the game, with that friend.
Despite having spent so much money and time on Blade and Soul in the past 2 months, I haven't played it since then. Blade and Soul was meant to be my final MMORPG, I was trying to solidify into it. I had found a really nice guild and a few friends, I had a lot of laughs on voice chat with everyone. I even spent money to enjoy myself better so I don't just quit randomly. I will say though, it wasn't a completely waste. It might actually have been the best thing for me to play Blade and Soul before Final Fantasy XIV. Blade and Soul has taught me to simply enjoy the game and think less about completing every possible dailies everyday and forcing myself to grind. Just enjoy the content I am currently able to do and slowly move forward whenever I can/want to progress. I will be able to apply this to Final Fantasy XIV. I always stressed myself hard to learn everything at once so I can start grinding earlier, for every single MMOs I've played in the past 10+ years.
Yeah, the friend I started playing with doesn't really play, I expected that. However, an old friend noticed that I was playing this game and asked me about it. That's when I learned that this game had Cross-Platform Multiplayer. He was able to join me through his Playstation 4. It's been years I wanted to play another MMO with him, but he never had a good computer and that computer could barely even run AIKA to begin with.
A concern of mine when playing a MMORPG is that you have to make a different character each time you want to learn more about another class. Achievements and unique items are usually tied to a single character, thus making you work even more if you care about having those on multiple characters. Well, in Final Fantasy XIV, you can learn and level up every single classes on one character and quickly swap between any of them at anytime while out of combat. While, yes, you still have to level up each classes seperately, you atleast keep your achievements progress and other things that could be character bound, such as event exclusive items and costumes, on the same character.
Crafting is usually boring in most MMORPGs and not worth doing at all until end game. Final Fantasy XIV has a slightly different take on crafting. You have Disciple of Land classes(Botanist, Miner, Fisher) and Disciple of Hand classes(Carpenter, Smithing, Alchemy, etc). They are actual classes. They level up and learn skills like Disciple of War and Magic(fighting classes). While there isn't that much more in crafting than other games, I feel that crafting in Final Fantasy XIV is a lot more rewarding and fun to do. I feel good going around gathering all the items I need in order to craft whatever items I meant to craft. Also, there's none of that boring "change character, gather a few materials, change back, then you realise you forgot to transfer the material, you go back to your second character, desposit the item, change back to your main, pick it up, etc.."
The combat does feel awkward at first if you're expecting this game to be more like other Action MMORPGs that has been released in the past few years. Using a "regular skill"(Weapon Skill/Spells) puts all your regular skills on a global cooldown of 2.5 seconds(default). Caster skills have enormous cast times as well. But as you level up, you will learn certain Abilities(uses seperate cooldowns) to fill certain gaps in your skill rotation. It's just like any other MMORPGs, you level up and the game becomes slightly more fluid as you get new gears and skills.
If you're not feeling dungeons or questing, no problem. There is the Gold Saucer, which has in-depth mini games. There is Triple Triad(a card game), Chocobo Racing(racing using a racing-specific chocobo) and Lord of Verminions(mini RTS using minions). Each of these games grants MGPs, as well as other activities called GATEs in the Gold Saucer map(spawns at xx:15 and xx:45).
There is also an Housing system in this game, though I can't tell you anything about it as I haven't looked at that system yet.
With the release of Stormblood, they cut off "Cross Class" skills, but made it a lot more simpler by adding "Role Actions". Classes and Jobs within a specific role shares unique abilities. However, you can only bring 5 out of the 10 at a single time. Gatherers and Crafters can still share skills between themselves. This encourages you to level up all Crafters to atleast 15, where you learn the class' specific skill that can be shared with everyone to increase your overall efficiency while crafting.
The graphics are fairly decent. The soundtracks are pretty good too. The story, while not the most interesting thing there is, has a couple of hype points, but the closure of A Realm Reborn does a very good job building hype for Heavensward story. The main thing about the story in this game is that you must complete all Main Scenario Quests from A Realm Reborn in order to access Heavensward contents. So either way, even if you're enjoying the story, there will be points in time where you will be thinking "this is boring" or "this is taking too long". Also, at 50, you can unlock the Glamour system, which is obviously the most important part of the game. However, it is not a fun system to play with, but it is something that lets you reskin your gears. Nothing is perfect after all.
In the end, I kind of wish I had started playing earlier in time. The game has a lot of contents to explore and enjoy. One of my favorite thing in this game is that you can have all classes on a single character. That alone boost my enjoyment level through the roof. I'm enjoying gathering and crafting in this game, while I don't in other game. While combat may be a little bit slower than an action MMORPG, it gives you more time to think and less time to panic, which mean less stress, while having just as much fun as you would get from an action MMORPG. If fighting isn't your strongest point in your current mood, go visit the Gold Saucer and relax there with a few mini games. I personally like Chocobo Racing the most. The graphics aren't half bad either, as well as the story, though lenghty. Despite being released 4 years ago, the overall quality of this game is still very high compared to some other newer MMORPGs, and it even supports Cross-Platform Multiplayer! The game also features a Free-Trial, which lets you play up to level 35 on every classes for free. Give it a try.

Humans are fidgety by nature. We like to push buttons, turn keys, click things, snap things, and so on. A few game developers have cottoned to this and put extra effort into making their interfaces particularly satisfying to click on, Blizzard chief among them. It took a surprising amount of time for someone to make a game about clicking really satisfying buttons but it finally happened, and this is it. The Room may claim to be a puzzle game but honestly that’s secondary to how utterly enthralling it is just to move the puzzle pieces around.
A mysterious invitation has brought you to an even more mysterious house, containing a most mysterious safe in the attic. Finding a letter and a strange eyepiece, you are bidden to open the box and plumb the secrets within. There’s no one combination or key that will open it, though. This vessel is encrusted with hidden compartments, levers, dials, and keyholes which you will have to puzzle through to crack it open. And that’s just the tutorial, leading to smaller yet more complex boxes within. Along the way you’ll uncover notes detailing the history of the container and the circumstances of your benefactor, all leading to a climactic revelation.
That’s all well and good but what this really is is the world’s most elaborate fidget cube. Each of the game’s five chapters challenges you to break the seals on a particular puzzle box, each teeming with parts to press, slide, rotate, align, or unfold. These mechanisms are manipulated by clicking and dragging (a decent approximation of the game’s original touch controls on mobile) to turn keys, slide out drawers, or rotate dials. What makes this game so delectable though is the incredible detail with which these components are designed. Moving parts are animated with exacting care, allowing you to count every notch on a dial or track the movements of panels as secret compartments slide open. The sound effects in particular are spectacular, capturing every metallic click and latch catch and clockwork whir and creaking board.
The immersion here is stunning, achieved by focusing on the key elements and ignoring everything else. The titular room is mostly dark and featureless for most of the game, with only floodlights to illuminate the object of your fiddling or a table to rest the smaller boxes upon. That draws the totality of your attention on the puzzle itself and the intricate detail with which it is crafted. It helps to remain so focused because some of the puzzles are quite challenging to overcome, especially ones that require combining parts collected from all over the box. Be sure to check every foot the object sits upon and every screw holding the thing together, lest you miss a subtle groove or dial. You get some terribly clever inventory items as well, ones that must be manipulated themselves to fit the situation, along with that strange eyepiece that reveals otherwise invisible features and clues.
There’s really no complaint I can level against The Room aside from it being too short for how delightful it is. You should be able to complete all five chapters within two hours, with no secrets or branching paths to watch out for. The story supports this one well, with creepy overtones paid off in spades by the conclusion. Atmosphere is something this game does incredibly well, from the smallest switch to the ambient whispers of the house. In truth it does everything it sets out to do incredibly well, enough so to make it an instant and unreserved recommendation to anyone. We all like pushing buttons after all, and you will find no finer buttons to push than these, my friend.

I can easily recommend this game if you like brain puzzles. The 36 main puzzles of the game are well made and very challenging, although some of the time you'll just be looking for that one piece of information you missed to progress forward. A lot of the puzzles are huge, and it takes some time to find that one tile you need to swap.
The second part of the game doesn't shine as bright, though; the infinite levels. You input or generate a random string of numbers, and a puzzle is made from that. When you've passed through the crafted levels, you'll likely find these generated levels simplistic and more of a timesink than an actual challenge. It's mostly repetition from what you've learned from the designer's levels, and while there may be some golden nuggets among these numbers, there's an 8-digit string to generate levels from, which is where the "infinite" part comes from. This of course doesn't mean they're bad, they're just not as good as the designed ones.
All in all, I can say that if you like brain training games that challenge your logical side, this one's worth it, and the infinite levels serve nicely as a filler for when you've got nothing better to do.

I would like to preface this review by stating that I only completed Emily is Away twice and honestly generally followed the same formula throughout, as I attempted to choose different options while remaining genuine to what I believe to be my actual personality. I also am a person to become quite easily, strongly attached to others, meaning that my attachment to Emily may have been stronger than the average player's attachment to her.
Emily is Away is likely among the most emotional video games which I have ever played, yet it truly uses so little text in order to portray this. The game length is incredibly short (generally under thirty minutes or so when options are chosen within a short amount of time, which was simply how I naturally progressed through the game), yet, within this small amount of time, I became emotionally destroyed. The game's rather minimalistic dialogue leads to each line simply having such a strong impact upon the player, at least personally. Everything said within the conversations with Emily feels important. Each moment of Emily is Away feels (personally) emotionally investing.
Yet, during my second attempt of Emily is Away, I did feel that many of my dialogue choices were ultimately not important and did not lead to a different outcome. I do believe that at least a portion of my dialogue choices were quite different, which lead me to hope for a much different response in certain situations. This occasionally felt frustrating. Yet, in the end, that may be a portion of the beauty of Emily is Away. Regardless of what you did, regardless of what you could have attempted differently, regardless of whatever you feel may have lead to the situation to ultimately being fortuitous, perhaps it was simply unavoidable.
In general, Emily is Away was an incredible experience. Yet again, I would like to state that I become attached to others very easily, and would like to furthermore state that a majority of my relations to others are text-based as I have few friends, if any, within offline settings, which likely furthered my emotional attachment to Emily. Yet, throughout all of this, I feel that Emily is Away is sufficiently potent to truly immerse the player. I feel that Emily is among the most realistic of characters which I have ever had the pleasure of experiencing within a video game. I rarely write reviews for video games featured on Steam, yet Emily is Away's absolute mastery of character lead me to post my terrible opinions onto Steam.
In short, and if I may be blunt, I highly recommend downloading this product.

This is a fairly simple game, but surprizingly enjoyable!
You start with one of three basic ships. A passenger shuttle, a barge and a fighter.
Your choice here will affect a good first four to six hours of the game.
Shuttle will be your simplest jobs, but it makes money the fastest. You ferry tourists, workers and cargo around the universe and make a quick buck all while paying off your mortgage. The object of this playstyle is to get all the people you can from point A to point B while turning the best profit, and dodging pirates.
Choose a barge and you'll be carrying bulk and rush deliveries of vital supplies throughout. If not taking up jobs, your time is best spent experimenting with trade routes and playing around with prices, selling what to where.
Should you choose arguably the most challenging, the fighter, you'll be pit against pirates. Really annoying space pirates. You start out as a fighter, only taking on other fighters. Once you finally pay off your ship loan and get a better ship, you'll be ready to aid the Navy again pirates and they who call themselves "the free worlds", basically space ISIS.
Allaround, it gets a tad repeditive later on, but funny enough, I never got bored. I always found something to do. I even recorded a lot of my adventures and more dangerous routes and am using it as a base for a novel. Legit.
Eventually you save for bigger and better ships and, one day, may decide to raise a fleet. You can board enemy craft and capture them, should you have the weapons and crew, and everything is just real dandy. Prices fluctuate, you basically run an actual business, and it can all make for a rivetting tale. It's free, so I'd very much suggest picking this up if you have some extra time on your hands.

I've been in love with Sleeping Dogs for the past 2 years since it came out, watching walk throughs of "theRabBrad" play it since I couldn't afford a console nor PC at the time; Now here I am giving a review on this great game!
The synopsis of Sleeping Dogs is that you play as Wei Shen, an Undercover Cop who is investigating One of the most powerful Triads in all of Hong Kong which will eventually lead to unfortunate climaxes to further develop the game's anticipation and action.
First off, the Graphics. Sleeping Dogs in my opinion, still has one of the best graphics even for a 2 year (soon to be three) old video game. Even on "Low" settings it still looks stunning and has a beautiful environment. The atmosphere is VERY live and similar to what it actually is in Hong Kong, it really deserve's the tile of being "The City That Never Sleeps".
Secondly, driving controls. The Driving in Sleeping Dogs is a bit hard for SOME cars, I've drove on some of the A Class cars for some races and missions and I rarely total the car. In Sleeping Dogs your car can get ugly pretty fast after a small little nudge, but I mean, same thing in reality right?
Thirdly, the combat system. The combat is revolved around Kung Fu. All I can say about the combat system is that it's great and very fluid as water. Just learn how to get your counters and combos in and you'll finish the missions easy and maybe without dying once. The combat in this game is a 9 Out 10. The reason why I removed one is because whenever I mash the "E" key to counter hits from enemies it doesn't deflect their hits on me, AT TIMES.
Sleeping Dogs has a great lore and story to really resemble a situation almost similar to a movie directed by Micheal Bay! Action, Drugs, Sex, Explosions, you name it! Think of it as a Hong Kong version of GTA!
Sleeping Dogs overall is a great game that I highly recommend!

Having liked Bullfrog's classics (Dungeon Keeper, Theme Hospital) back in the day, I enjoyed what was released of SpaceBase DF-9 during its early access alpha, and the addition of new features gave me a reason to replay it after every update.
I had a lot of fun with the alpha (when not circumventing the game-breaking bugs), and thought that it was a decent concept which had really good potential. While updates were few and far between, I hoped that the game would eventually evolve into something better and deeper. Both the development scope that they posted on their website, and the hard effort which they put into the design of the game reflected that this is what DoubleFine originally envisioned.
Unfortunately, game development doesn't always go well, and DoubleFine now intend to release a game which when "finished" will be fun to play, but scant on features and not worth it's £19/$30 price tag in my opinion, considering there are deeper games (with a bit more content in them) in the same genre as SpaceBase which aren't priced as high, and that people may get more enjoyment from. This is why I can't recommend people buy it.
SpaceBase will hopefully be playable in version 1.0 after much bug fixing, and I can imagine it being a small and decent strategy game which will be quite fun, but unfortunately won't have a lot to do in it. Maybe if you really enjoy the genre then you'll like the finished version of SpaceBase, but don't expect a lot of bang for your buck - I hope DoubleFine reduces the price before final release.

Because of this, every battle feels fresh, tactical and satisfying. There's also new game+ mode which will further enhances your gameplay experience as you'll get to keep all your powers from the previous playthrough and you'll be facing tough enemies from the start.
The story and voice acting is great and it'll pull you right into the game. Also the soundtrack, it's absolutely breathtaking. The soundtracks alone will immerse you in the game. The visual art style looks great and fits the cyberpunk universe.
Overall, Transistor is a solid game and is a must buy. It's definitely worth the money.

You take control as Red, a songstress who lost her voice in a post apocalyptic world. Automated threats known as the 'Process' run amok and your only way of combatting them, a talking sword called 'Transistor'. With traces of other survivors and a group referred to as 'Camerata', seemingly behind the whole catastrophe. She takes Centre Stage.....

(a) Digital Wonderland-
The way it looks is truly wonderful. No need for all that Mo-Cap dealie (Yes, I get that they're fantastic, realistic and I'm getting sidetracked... David Cage!)
(b) Anti Virus-
Combat against the 'Process' requires ounces of planning and on the spot-reflexes!! The latter not so much, as there is a feature of halting time. Enabling you to trial and error your plan of attack.
(c) One Tough Software-
When you throw in the 'Limiters', recurse through the story upon witnessing The End. (For difficulty chasers) You're in for a real threat; new enemy placements, much more cunning. Apart from that, the 'Sandbox Tests'; Performance, Agency etc, make for pleasant free-will side quests and time consumption.
(d) Soundtrack-
Sets the bar for other video games (perhaps films too) to follow really high. With its Techno beats and infectious rhythm, they are all very much welcomed in our ears. Respect to composer Darren Korb and vocalist, Ashley Barrett (HEART!)
(e) Files Housekeeping-
Tinkering with 'Active', 'Passive' Functions; Although rather restricted. Every different combination transforms each battle into a novel and exciting experience.Not to forget during New Game +, when you can have multiple numbers of the same Functions.... (f) Thoughtful Programming-
Transistor and Red have a solid bond. Writing in the main characters (Camerata included) are memorable. The storyline was out-of-the-box and entertaining.
(g) User Interface-
There are terminals that provide exposition and distractions to the hectic battles. Objects to examine, all the while commentated by none other than Transitor itself.
(i) Recycle Bin-
The negligence of an inventory system removed a huge chunk out of an RPG. (But hey, it works!!)

The Call of Duty Series had a fantastic start with its first game back in 2003.
It did something that no other really game had before, and the experience was intense and really fun. Many think it is the better game in the series, but that could be due to the fact it was the first game/experience of this kind. It was a huge success and the following games also sold really well.
A little later comes modern warfare, which pretty much had the same impact as the first call of duty game, riding on being new and a little different, and also having a good multiplayer.
But was the gameplay that different really, despite the graphical upgrade? I don't really think so. In fact, I think most Call of Duty games are pretty much exactly the same, with just graphical upgrades, plus minor new superficial game mechanics that in the end doesn't change the game that much.
If you consider that most of these games are pretty much the same you have to look at what makes a particular title more interesting than another.
That is, the campaign and the multiplayer.
Firstly, I don't play the multiplayer because it is not my thing. BUT, it could be worth it to mention that the multiplayer is still alive for this game, and thas has to count for something. Back in the day when it was new, it was hailed as the greatest online shooter there was.
For me, the call of Duty games are a "casual" experience that gives you quite a ride. It is an experience that is truly great the first time that is. It is like a movie that you participate in (slightly). Each scene oozes of high production value and clever direction, great music, great action, and great voice acting. The graphics are not the highest but it is utilized so well that it still looks and feels great, and runs quite well on even older machines.
Modern warefare 2 has probably one of the better campaigns, and it probably will affect you even more if you are an American (I'm not). Later titles all have their cool stuff, but since the series doesn't really invent many new ideas there is only so much you can do before the games become quite repetitive and predictable.
Problems:
I mean, these games have never been a challenge. They have never been hard to complete, and there is reason for that.
The problem is that these games are cinematic experiences that really want you to walk down a certain path and do exactly as the devs thought you should do, or the games quickly loses it charms. The first time you do a certain quick time event and/or chase it might be really cool. But if you make a "mistake" and have to do it a few times, it truly sucks. Imagine watching every action scene in a movie 3-5 times in a row. You would hate it. And so the game can never be truly a challenge or it would just be truly frustrating. There are only so many times you are ok with insta-death because you went in the wrong direction.
See, If you want a good, complex shooter with lots of freedom you will not like any of the modern warfare games. Multiplayer might be your thing, but then you have to deal with hacking, stiff competition, and angry 12 years-olds. It is a great experience if you don't have to repeat anything.
I also think these game are way too overpriced, especially the older titles, considering what you get from it. The campaigns are not exactly long in most games either.
But I do think that this is so far the best campaign, and even if other titles have had interesting ideas, they never really managed to nail it like this one. Get this game for a ride, (that might even disturb you a bit) for a heavily scripted roller coaster which will make your blood pump the first time. It is really good at that. But get it on a sale  or you might feel cheated.
Cheers!

This is a testament to the power of games as a medium. It manages to be, all at once, an intellectual stimulation, an escape from reality, and social commentary. It is art, entertainment and work rolled into one. As the player, you are presented with a task that is very much like a lot of paper-pushing jobs out there. Yet here it becomes an intellectual challenge; a test of your mettle and attention. And somehow it is still fun. This is quite an accomplishment in terms of gameplay.
The story, meanwhile, is at once Orwellian and Kafkaesque. It is a kind of social commentary, but not on-the-nose; it is subtle, humourous, nuanced. The recurring characters, with very brief screen time, manage to be interesting and memorable. The Soviet aesthetic is superbly done in terms of design and visuals. The UI can be annoying sometimes, but it's part of its charm and challenge.
Above all, this is a game that is
: its own beast. There are games with similar mechanics, but the aesthetic and the pacing make Papers, Please unique.

Borderlands 2 é um jogo que venho tentando falar há semanas, mas sempre procrastino e acabo indo jogar um pouco mais dele. Resultado? 180 horas de jogo. Isso é mais que o dobro do tempo que levei para terminar a trilogia do Mass Effect (considerando ainda que um playthrough padrão de Borderlands 2 deveria ter entre 30~40 horas).
Enfim, após incontáveis repetições e partidas, tenho finalmente uma opinião formada sobre o jogo.
borderlands2De maneira resumida: diversão sem igual.
Aviso: potenciais spoilers ao longo do post.
Para quem não sabe, Borderlands 2 é uma continuação direta de Borderlands (jura?), um shooter lançado em 2009. Esse shooter ficou relativamente famoso por algumas razões:
– Havia uma progressão de níveis e uma skilltree, como um rpg, da mesma forma que Mass Effect também tem (embora o sistema de Borderlands seja bem mais simplificado);
– O cenário do jogo (por cenário eu falo da história também, não só a parte gráfica) lembrava algo meio velho oeste ou pós-apocalipse, e jogos do tipo estavam em baixa na época do lançamento. O jogo chegou a ser chamado de “space western”, que eu acho bem digno, mesmo não tendo partes no espaço e se passando apenas em um planeta;
– O gameplay era altamente arcade. Era necessário ter certa tática ao invés de ir pra cima dos inimigos na loucura (como os shoot’em up fazem), mas uma vez dominada a mecânica do jogo, a coisa ficava bem frenética;
– Armas geradas aleatoriamente, bem ao estilo de ARPGs típicos, como Diablo ou Torchlight. O ponto máximo que foi citado por diversos sites de jogos era uma shotgun que disparava mísseis;
– Multiplayer absurdamente divertido.
O jogo permitia a escolha entre 4 personagens, cada um com suas características e especialidades, e a partir disso era sair mundo afora fazendo quests e atirando em coisas. Fora isso, ainda havia um certo humor negro no jogo, presente de maneira bem sucinta. Esse foi um dos poucos jogos que mesmo quando cansei dele, continuei jogando simplesmente porque era AWESOME demais pra deixar pra lá.
Borderlands 2 pegou esses conceitos que definiram o título como “imperdível” e ampliou suas proporções (o trailer de lançamento é focado em justamente mostrar isso). Uma coisa que ficou muito clara foi o apelo maior para o humor. Agora os personagens fazem muito mais piadas, são muito mais sarcásticos e as quests são muitos mais sem sentido. A Gearbox se deu ao trabalho de lançar outro trailer apenas para mostrar isso. Tirem suas próprias conclusões:
No trailer já podemos ver os 4 personagens jogáveis em ação. Vale lembrar que foi lançado um quinto personagem na forma de DLC, mas ele não é necessário para aproveitamento geral do jogo, e nem as campanhas extras que TAMBÉM foram lançadas nesse formato. Aqui vou me ater apenas ao jogo livre de impurezas.
Cada um dos personagens segue um estereótipo particular, e se você jogou o primeiro Borderlands vai perceber que há características em comum com os personagens do jogo anterior.
Axton é uma releitura do Roland, que podia colocar um turret para auxiliar durante as batalhas. Apesar das habilidades serem “iguais”, a dinâmica e funcionamento do turret do Axton é bem diferente da que o Roland tinha.
Maya traz de volta em cena a classe Siren, representada pela Lilith no jogo anterior. Na história do jogo, só podem existir 6 sirens ao mesmo tempo no universo, e cada uma delas tem uma habilidade “mágica” específica. Lilith tinha o Phasewalk, que tornava ela invisível e causava dano em área. Maya tem o Phaselock, em que ela prende o inimigo em uma esfera de energia e causa dano.
Salvador representa a classe Gunzerker, enquanto que no jogo anterior tínhamos Brick, o Berserker. A habilidade especial de Brick tinha sido muito criticada, então reformularam algo parecido no segundo jogo, mas melhor aplicável: enquanto Brick ativava a habilidade especial e saia dando socos na galera (que deixavam de causar dano bom em níveis mais altos, se tornando inútil), Salvador empunha duas armas de uma vez enquanto regenera vida e munição.
Zero é, talvez, o mais diferente de todos. No jogo anterior tinha o Mordecai, que podia ser jogado tanto como sniper ou como pistoleiro, e era focado em causar dano acertando críticos. Zero tem esse foco também, mas em menor escala. Ele tem skills voltadas apenas para sniper, e acaba aí sua semelhança com Mordecai, cuja habilidade especial era lançar o Bloodwing, um pet voador que causava dano nos inimigos. A habilidade do Zero é soltar um holograma e ficar invisível, recebendo bônus ao causar dano crítico.
Logo na abertura do jogo (após uma cena terrivelmente engraçada, principalmente por causa da trilha sonora, que ironicamente é adequada para o contexto), podemos ver os personagens utilizando suas habilidades, dando uma vaga ideia de quais são suas aplicações.
Sim, a quest que ele passa é dar um tiro na própria face.
Enfim, você começa o jogo passando por um leve tutorial, que já é conectado com a história, e logo depois parte para a ação e enfrenta seu primeiro boss. A partir daí, a história vai engrenando e o nível de absurdidade das coisas vai aumentando.
O que eu acho interessante falar é que esse jogo TEM uma história. O primeiro Borderlands tinha uma desculpa esfarrapada pra sair metendo bala na cara da galera (você era, basicamente, um caçador de tesouros), mas no segundo jogo foi criado todo um plot centrado ao redor de um vilão que se acha herói. E por mais incrível que pareça, é um♥♥♥♥♥♥personagem bom, todo bem construído, e a dublagem dele é a melhor que já vi em jogos nos últimos tempos. A voz do dublador caiu como uma luva na personalidade dele, e mesmo o cara sendo um vilão totalmente sem escrúpulos que causa raiva em diversas partes do jogo, ele consegue ao mesmo tempo ser carismático e te fazer dar risada. Devia ganhar o prêmio de vilão do ano.
Para dar razão ao novo plot, os quatro personagens do jogo anterior retornaram como npcs, junto a outros personagens que você interagia ocasionalmente. No fim, apesar de tudo isso, o plot ainda é desprezível. Não que seja ruim, mas ninguém joga Borderlands por causa da história. Ela consegue ser envolvente em alguns pontos, mas no geral você tá pouco ligando pra ela, e só vale a pena porque além de ter servido como desculpa para criarem o Handsome Jack, conseguiram transformar a Lilith em uma♥♥♥♥♥♥personagem legal. No entanto, Mordecai é um bêbado que fala termos latinos (wtf?) e Brick é… bom, indiferente como personagem, apesar de importante. Agora o Roland… sinto ódio só de pensar. No primeiro jogo ele era um sujeito todo ♥♥♥♥♥, com falas e voz de negro americano do gueto. Em Borderlands 2 o dublador é outro, e o personagem tem toda uma postura militar séria, que simplesmente quebrou parte do humor de antes. Afinal, nenhum outro personagem gritava “BULLSEYE!” quando acertava um crítico. E agora ele te chama de “soldier” e dá ordens como um militar padrão qualquer.
Mas como eu disse, ninguém joga um jogo desse tipo por causa da história, então dá pra ignorar esses detalhes. O importante é o gameplay, que sofreu uma melhora absurda em relação ao primeiro jogo. A movimentação dos personagens está mais fluida, a animação das armas sendo recarregadas é mais detalhada, e as próprias armas funcionando ganharam detalhes próprios. Todos os poderes dos personagens têm sua utilidade e usos diferentes, dependendo de como você prefere jogar.
No primeiro jogo já existiam marcas diferentes de armas, cada uma com sua característica, mas no geral se dava bem com qualquer uma desde que fossem do mesmo tipo. Por exemplo, uma sniper Jakobs e uma sniper Maliwan tinham pouca diferença de dano, e o fato da Maliwan ser elemental às vezes era melhor. No entanto, Jakobs tinha bônus em dano crítico. Well, after waiting years for the release of this game, I finally had the chance to play it.
It was initially a mod, and now it's... this.
Pros:
- Historical accuracy.
- Well-designed levels
- Combat immersion
- One of the few WW1 games that are actually any good.
- You can charge huge masses of infantry at machine guns and cannons.
- You can also anihilate hundreds of people when the enemy throws a similar charge at YOUR positions.
Cons:
- Well, it's the same old MoW, with all its' flaws. The AI doesn't seem as annoying as in other games based on this engine, but it's still... not stellar.
- For some, the graphics might not be enough, though they are more than sufficient for me.
- You can't give commands to more than 8 infantry units at a time. This problem exists with all of the MoW games, but this is the only one in which you give orders to huge masses of infantry on daily basis. And so, it might be a slight problem at times.
- Minor bugs that will surely be fixed once it's out of Early Access.
If you've been waiting for a WW1 RTS for a long time, as I did, this is a game for you. It's not a polished AAA gem, but it's a good game nevertheless. Especially when you take into consideration that it is the first commercial project of a small studio. If you're somehow new to the genre(and, given that you're reading this, I doubt that), I would  rather recommend chosing one of the more popular, well-acclaimed games in this genre.

In my former review I said that this was one of the best WW1 RTS games. I was wrong. I was overly excited and had my hopes up. Unfortunately now that I've played through and witnessed the greed of the devs as well as the horrid voice acting and bugs, I now cannot recommend this game.
Stuff I said before:
- Yes, this is one of the only WW1 RTS games in 3D. Unfortunately, the GEM engine cannot potray it realistically. However, I know the extents of the GEM engine; they have not tried to do as best as they can. You cant charge trenches with horses, artillery doesn't do enough damage most of the time to kill any enemies and they can just heal almost instantly with bandages. Trying to charge trenches with your soldiers is just boring to watch. First time you are like, cool, my guys are getting mowed down, realistic. Then you realise when they get to the trench, they just stand there and get shot in the head. This is partly do to the GEM engine, but the devs describe the game as super realistic and a RTS set amazingly in WW1. They even are naive enough to release a "season" pass and ♥♥♥♥ over the early accessers, which is a whole different story.
- Game is super realistic. The mechanics are realistic. Helmets fall off, different parts of vehicles break, buildings destroy right, weapons can be picked up, ammo matters, etc etc. That is just the GEM engine, NOTHING that the devs can take credit for. The Men of War devs deserve 100000000 times more credit than these greedy devs.
- Lots of bugs. Yes, end of story. Talk about it more later.
- Cant buy units. This is because I played assualt squad skirmishes before I ever played 2009 Men of War or story mods.
So, here it is, the pros and cons in a longer updated review:
Pros:
+ Has nice models and missions with bugs of course. There is no excuse for this now that its out of early access, but its bearable.
+ Has a nice amount of missions.
+ Has the editor.
Cons:
Everything... kidding.
- Game isn't finished even though its in release.
- Multiplayer is buggy and not balanced.
- Voice acting makes you want to throw up.
- Missions are encrypted in the editor so you cant just mess with a mission and spawn some extra troops for fun. The devs decided their "masterpiece" was worth too much for people to edit. Men of War allowed this and that is called the freedom of the editor.
- Mechanics are buggy and vehicles bug out a lot.
- Graphics are too bloomy even when its in a dark environment.
- Devs decided to take the game out of early access so they could throw out a season pass and a ton of dlcs for a game that is not even finished. Seriously, 7 bucks for a few tank missions easily made in the editor? Low blow. Plus they have pre planned the dlcs and are giving the German and British campaigns in seperate dlcs.
- Devs decided the early access buyers who bought the game not knowing if was going to be finished(which in its current state it still isn't) will not be compensated with the Blazing Guns dlc and instead people who bought it a certain time after release will. The claimed that they promised early access buyers the russian campaign for free and the finished product. The russian campaign is free for everyone, so that is not a valid excuse. The game is still not finished either even though its in release. It wouldn't be a problem if they didn't blatantly give it to the lucky bunch who bought the game in a certain time frame.
- I dont like the fact that they are selling a mod and acting like its their own masterpiece. The price is too high for an unfinished game, and at the current stage the devs think they are popular enough already to release a ton of dlcs and release the game like its finished or 99 percent finished.
After the overwhelming amount of cons and the fact that the devs completely said ♥♥♥♥ you to the community, I will not recommend this game. I recommend you wait for a better RTS for WW1 with an engine designed exactly for that. Not a mod that is being sold.

A brilliant puzzle game! If you play it properly and not just by clicking random cells until you finish it, then it is superb.
In order to get the best out of this game (and in my opinion the only way to play it) you should challenge yourself to not make one single move if you are not 100% sure about it. As many have said before; the puzzles are supposed to be solved without having to guess or be in doubt whether the cells should be blue or not, so do not guess, do not think "hm, maybe this should be blue", "this is probably right" or anything along these lines. If you are not completely sure, then do not click.
Improvements have been made since the last two games. One is that you can save your puzzles and then go back later and finish them (which is what I recommend you to do if you get stuck. Take a break, go do something else and then come back later and you will see new per,c  that you did not see before. It is so easy to get stuck focusing too narrowly on one area or staring blindly on a spot that might already be solved). The other thing is that a random puzzle generator has been added. Although the random puzzles are easy and does not require much effort and thinking they are still addictive! It is very relaxing to solve them and great if you just want to wind down a little bit.
If you are already a fan of minesweeper or sudoku, then you will LOVE this game. Hexcells is the perfect mix between those two.
In conclusion; I cannot recommend this game enough! I loved the first two ones, Hexcells and Hexcells Plus, and now with this one having a random puzzle generator just makes it the ultimate puzzle game.

If you're on the fence about the series or played one of the earlier games and aren't sure if you want to pick up the new one let me sum it up for you: This is the one you want to buy.
Hexcells Infinite, to me at least, is a big improvement on an already fun series. For those not in the know, Hexcells is a puzzle game that's similar to mine sweeper only with 6 sides instead of 4 and an error counts against you but doesn't end the game. Also you never have to guess in Hexcells, there is always sufficient evidence given to correctly select the next move (though you may find yourself pulling out your hair until you find it).
This game has the same clean graphics and soothing atmospheric music as the previous 2 games but does have some improvements. The biggest of which is you now have the ability to save and come back to a puzzle. This is a huge improvement and especially helpful as some of the levels in the base game are larger and more complicated than levels in previous games. You can also now set which mouse buttons you want to use to mark a square as blue or not which is a bonus to us lefties.
Where Hexcells Infinite really shines though is in the Infinite part. In addition to a set of given puzzles you can there's also an infinite mode where a set of 8 numbers (selected randomly, shared with friends or based on the date) will bring you a specific puzzle for you enjoyment. These puzzles tend to be shorter than the 'main' puzzles and are a great way to pass the time or give yourself a quick mental warm up for the day. And yes, you can save you progress on these too!

You'd be forgiven some trepidations about any game that's charted as ... unconventional a course to retail shelves as Sleeping Dogs. It first went into development at United Front Games as "Black Lotus," then transformed to a reboot of Activision's True Crime series. Then, as the mega-publisher let the game slide into the hands of Square-Enix, it lost the legacy branding and was re-redubbed Sleeping Dogs. The ship that emerges from those choppy waters is surprisingly seaworthy, but it's not without a few cracks in the hull. For some, Sleeping Dogs' leaks may be hard to ignore.
Triad gangs took Hong Kong police officer Wei Shen's sister from him, and he's given up everything to take them apart. As Sleeping Dogs picks up his story, Shen's already deep undercover, embedded in a low-level position with the Sun On Yee (a thinly veiled nod to the Sun Yee On, a real-life Triad gang).
Though the Hong Kong setting may be exotic, Shen's story will be familiar to anyone who's ever watched, read, or played a story of an undercover cop. As Shen gets closer to toppling the organization, he's also getting closer to its members, embracing their vicious, glamorous lifestyle until even the player may be left to wonder where, exactly, he stands.
At first, the distinction between cop and criminal is easy to make. Shen has no firearms and so must rely on martial arts (and the occasional tire iron) to bring down members of rival gangs.
You can slam enemy at car's door, or put them at the car's trunk, jump from car to other car, kill people on the street, do kung-fu moves, race, fight club, chock fight bet, and many fun activities.

The soundtrack alone is fantastic outside of this game. Inside the game? The atmosphere and tone of the game is increased ten-fold! Along with the music comes rather stunning visual appeal, especially the backgrounds and with the animation fluidity that instantly hooks you into playing all the way through!
Gameplay itself, it's a mixed view for me. On one hand, the combat is fun to play around with as you pick and choose a plethora of combinations of your functions and passive abilities. Limiters also help to keep you on your toes, and I highly recommend using all 10 (yes, 10!) Limiters on your Recursive playthrough since the game itself can be a walk in the park and quickly fade into boredom without having them in use. My issue with the gameplay is that it starts to become repetitive, as yes, the enemies and the type/amount of enemies do change from area to area, but the problem is how that's pretty much the only thing to do here is fight, fight, and fight some more, in every area! There are terminals to read, function files to read, and an overarching story to follow; however, those elements tend to feel more like background-noise to the constant train of enemies you'll encounter. After completing this game twice, I feel like there's little incentive to play more, as there's never really any alternate avenues to explore beyond choosing some simple options in the terminals that have little effect on the story/game. The replay value really lies in trying out different Function setups and how it stacks up against different types of enemies.
The story featured is interesting at times, and other times feels like a drag, somewhat confusing, and rushed. I will say completing the game is worth it story-wise in order to see what happens between Red and her companion, the Transistor. The story surrounding the setting and the villains fall flat for me. I couldn't quite care for the story going on about the setting because it started out rather lifeless to begin with besides the enemies I had to kill. My only way to grow 'attached' to the setting was through Terminals, but again, this made me feel disjointed from the setting when little went on. Only little glimpses here and there of what kind of place it was, as the Transistor will point out how it used to be rather lively. The villains, or masterminds rather, of the game are largely not part of the journey as you blast through enemy after enemy. In my opinion, there was lost potential to really flesh out the villains. In certain parts of the game, where it should feel like an impactful turn of events, simply doesn't work because the writers never gave such events time to weave into the narrative; it's just there when it happens. The only constant narrative that I was invested in and felt that mattered was the chemistry between Red and the Transistor.
Bottomline, however, is that I still highly recommend this! If nothing else, while the story and story direction could had been way better, Transistor nonetheless offers a satisfying gaming experience with superior soundtracks, songs, fluid (or strategic) combat with a ton of options to mix and match to your preferred style!

The Call of Duty Series had a fantastic start with its first game back in 2003.
It did something that no other really game had before, and the experience was intense and really fun. Many think it is the better game in the series, but that could be due to the fact it was the first game/experience of this kind. It was a huge success and the following games also sold really well.
A little later comes modern warfare, which pretty much had the same impact as the first call of duty game, riding on being new and a little different, and also having a good multiplayer.
But was the gameplay that different really, despite the graphical upgrade? I don't really think so. In fact, I think most Call of Duty games are pretty much exactly the same, with just graphical upgrades, plus minor new superficial game mechanics that in the end doesn't change the game that much.
If you consider that most of these games are pretty much the same you have to look at what makes a particular title more interesting than another.
That is, the campaign and the multiplayer.
Firstly, I don't play the multiplayer because it is not my thing. BUT, it could be worth it to mention that the multiplayer is still alive for this game, and thas has to count for something. Back in the day when it was new, it was hailed as the greatest online shooter there was.
For me, the call of Duty games are a "casual" experience that gives you quite a ride. It is an experience that is truly great the first time that is. It is like a movie that you participate in (slightly). Each scene oozes of high production value and clever direction, great music, great action, and great voice acting. The graphics are not the highest but it is utilized so well that it still looks and feels great, and runs quite well on even older machines.
Modern warefare 2 has probably one of the better campaigns, and it probably will affect you even more if you are an American (I'm not). Later titles all have their cool stuff, but since the series doesn't really invent many new ideas there is only so much you can do before the games become quite repetitive and predictable.
Problems:
I mean, these games have never been a challenge. They have never been hard to complete, and there is reason for that.
The problem is that these games are cinematic experiences that really want you to walk down a certain path and do exactly as the devs thought you should do, or the games quickly loses it charms. The first time you do a certain quick time event and/or chase it might be really cool. But if you make a "mistake" and have to do it a few times, it truly sucks. Imagine watching every action scene in a movie 3-5 times in a row. You would hate it. And so the game can never be truly a challenge or it would just be truly frustrating. There are only so many times you are ok with insta-death because you went in the wrong direction.
See, If you want a good, complex shooter with lots of freedom you will not like any of the modern warfare games. Multiplayer might be your thing, but then you have to deal with hacking, stiff competition, and angry 12 years-olds. It is a great experience if you don't have to repeat anything.
I also think these game are way too overpriced, especially the older titles, considering what you get from it. The campaigns are not exactly long in most games either.
But I do think that this is so far the best campaign, and even if other titles have had interesting ideas, they never really managed to nail it like this one. Get this game for a ride, (that might even disturb you a bit) for a heavily scripted roller coaster which will make your blood pump the first time. It is really good at that. But get it on a sale  or you might feel cheated.
Cheers!

Plague Inc. is disturbingly addictive. Games don't last too long, but the various upgrade trees, virus types, perks, and random events give it a very strong "one more go, and that's it" factor. Some virus types are significantly more fun than others, and there's a few gameplay elements that are more annoying than anything (like how several island countries will close their docks long before the plague gets anywhere near there, adding a frustrating instant loss condition), but overall Plague Inc. is actually pretty fun. This game is not finished, and it has come out that it never will be.  There are a handful of hours that are enjoyable, but not in the way you think.  It seems to be building up to something.  You gather resources and put together a station, and at no time is your progress ever really threatened.  Then, you have everything built up, you've put lasers on the walls and have a small army of security and... nothing ever happens.  There are no truly challenging random events, there are no barriers that you have to work around to build your base, there's never any challenge at all.
And then there's no kind of endgame after this, you can just keep expanding and staring at your stable, boring base (that is in itself neither complex nor complicated, with no tough systems to learn or figure out) for eternity.  And Double Fine has come out and said that this is all that there ever will be.
Don't buy this game.  It's all build-up, no climax.  No challenges.  Even the resource gathering and base/population management isn't difficult because it's too simple and easy.

Hexcells is a puzzle game in which you can use hard logic and intuition to solve the puzzles. If all the numbers put you off, t is less mathematical it appears, focusing more on deciphering patterns. The relaxing sounds are a nice contrast to how hard your brain will work. I thoroughly enjoyed all three and highly recommend them.
The "Infinite" part of this iteration is a game mode which generates levels randomly. None of the random ones I played equalled the hand-craftyed levels, but they were fun nonetheless. They're a little bit like hexcells light.

In a nutshell: Hexcells Infinite is Minesweeper on steroids.
Long story: Just like in Minesweeper, sometimes you’ll have to guess (which may or may not annoy you), but unlike Minesweeper, Hexcells allows you to make as many mistakes as necessary in order to complete a map, and THAT is my major beef with the game, because it detracted a lot from the challenge. That’s right: There is no *significant* reward for completing a map with zero mistakes, and there is no punishment for literally guessing every step of the way and finishing with 20+ mistakes (other than barring your progress through the blocks of preset levels, but unlocking all puzzle groups doesn't really pose much of a challenge, i.e. you can do that even if you finish each map with a few mistakes).
On the bright side, extra points go to sound design, as every correct click results in a soothing, oddly satisfying sound bit; however, there is no volume control in the game, only an ON/OFF switch, which I suppose is aligned with the game’s minimalistic design, but it’s a feature I missed nonetheless.
All in all, the game is reasonably priced, and certainly a step up the challenge of playing Minesweeper. If you’re looking for some casual distraction of the “minesweeping” variety, I’d say go for it.

As a perfectionist, I find short, challenging games to be the best fit for me.
Hexcells Infinite takes the hexagonal challenge to a new level. I found myself spending anywhere from 20 minutes to an hour on some challenges, without getting bored or wanting to give up.
The challenges here are never unfair, but give you great satisfaction when you finally figure out what you were doing wrong. The main focus here is you, your mind, and your way of thinking, helping you evolve your thought processes and think more outside the box as you progress.

Hexcells Infinite, like the other hexcell games, still follows the same gameplay. Basically a mix of minesweeper and sudoku. The game has nice background music like the others and this particular game has an added feature where you can play custom puzzles.
However, where this game fails for me is it’s made the same mistake as hexcells plus. While the original hexcells had a nice difficulty curve, this one's all over the place. I actually enjoyed playing the first hour and I thought they'd redeemed themselves from hexcells plus. I was getting stuck, but still progressing which makes the game fun. But the levels difficulties are all over the place. For example one level introduced a new concept and gave you an incredibly easy puzzle to make sure you understand it. Then just the level after it throws you into this massive puzzle with numbers all over the place and I'm just sitting there thinking, I can't be bothered with this. It becomes more of a grind and loses its fun. I think it would have been nice for the dev to add a mid-level save so you can come back later; some of these levels are massive and will take a long time.
I'm also very disappointed that they added a ? cell. It's so cheap because it forces you to solve the puzzle in only one possible way. It can also be so disheartening; you might spend a solid 5 minutes to find a cell you can make progress on only to uncover it as a ? so you can no longer progress any further down that route.
However, do I think this game is worth buying? Yes! Solely because you can play custom levels. It offers more than the other hexcells games. So, although there are some things wrong with this game I can still say it's worth buying.

Started as a Mage, so I can't really judge in terms of solo difficulty, but every quest up to level 8 at least has you go out, possibly to the opposite side of the current map, kill/loot something, and return back to the starting town again, only to repeat for the next quest. The quest induced yo-yoing is bad enough, but the caves/buildings you are sent to for quests are also shared with the other players, rather than instanced just for you or your party, which can lead to having to struggle against other players in a PvE environment for kills and loot. Admittedly this struggle is pretty standard in MMOs and probably drops off as you level up and the population density declines.
But the breaking point for me was a primary quest to kill a Magical Dragonkin. This quest has you go out into an area teeming with aggressive monsters, and find the one and only magical dragonkin, capable of spawning anywhere in that quarter of the map, and kill it. If someone else kills it before you get there, you have to wait for it to spawn and hope you or your party can get to it first.
That said, I did find the combat itself enjoyable, with the advertised weaknesses present immediately at the start, and all stats being relevant and plainly explained in tooltips. If you're okay with the questing issues and small inventories, you just might enjoy this. But for the average gamer, this feels like a no go.

Legend of Grimrock is a first-person, tile-based dungeon crawler RPG that's filled with puzzles, monsters, traps, and exploration. This gripping game puts you in the shoes of four prisoners as they are forced to traverse through the many layers of the massive Mt. Grimrock in order to reach freedom. Combat is done in real-time and the controls are very simple to get a hang of. The UI is absolutely perfect and makes item management and switching between characters a breeze. The sound is very atmospheric; you can hear footsteps and wing-flapping in the distance, and it'll really keep you on your toes. The visuals in this game are terrific. The monsters are detailed and the lighting system is very impressive. Best of all, modding tools will soon be available to allow users to create their own maps and share them with the world, adding hours and hours of additional gameplay.
Even if you're new to this RPG sub-genre (as I was), Legend of Grimrock is a game worthy of your attention.
