I decided to pay up and try it out.
Well, it was still very broken. Aside from the known bugs that weren't resolved, the new "mood system" introduced some hugely game breaking bugs and it was hard to progress very far at all in the game without having to restart for one reason or another.
I frustratingly put the game down for the weekend, and only played it a few more times until they ironed out some of the more severe mood bugs by 6e-f.
Once those game breakers were (pretty much) out of the way, I was able to successfully establish a base and build it to fair size before wondering the inevitable.. "okay, now what?" of an unfinished sandbox game. The derelict ships provide a little interest, but can sometimes be a pain to deal with. The breaches could be a very fun aspect of the game, but instead balance issues make them either ridiculously easy, or painfully hard with no real explanation as to why one way or another.
This lead me to decide (as I have done with other Early Access titles) to "put the game down" for a bit, and come back later when they have added some more content to make the game more interesting and challenging to play.
It is now two weeks later, and the lead developer has stated that they will be finalizing this game and releasing 1.0 in a month.
This is a woefully unfinished game that is severely lacking in content. While the idea and core features seem real enticing, the truth is there really isn't much at all to do and I dont see the developer adding that much more before actual release.
If you would like a "space base" type game, I would suggest an alternative in Startopia. Yes, it's almost 15 years old, but its funny and entertaining and actually has goals and stuff to do. I guarantee you will get much better gaming enjoyment out of Startopia than this unfinished, yet released product.

I'm re-reviewing this now that I've completed the game once.  I still have a fairly neutral opinion.  It should also be stated that I really wanted to like this game.  I really did.
Story: 4/10
They create a lush, vibrant, interesting world and then tell you nothing significant about it, answer none of the questions raised by the setting, and force you to walk a straight line through it, then backtrack directly across that straight line until the end of the game.  Due to the assumed (again, no answers.) nature of the setting, the story doesn't really feel very compelling at all.
Sound: 9/10
The music is good.  These people know good music.
Visuals: 8/10
What little you get to see of the world and it's inhabitants makes me want there to be a movie or show based around the setting that would actually flesh out the world.  Great artwork with a very futuristic, but also very 1920's New York feel to the aesthetics.
Gameplay: 5/10
The gameplay is either fun, but nothing special, or an absolute misery to deal with.  Enemy balance is way off, and you don't get absolutely essential combat abilities until 3/4 of the way into the game.  Most of the enemy AI is recklessly agressive, faster than the player character, and can take out half your lifebar in the time it takes your turn to come back up.  Add in really claustrophobic battle areas, and the poorly thought out "lose your functions for an arbitrary amount of time if you die" and the combat gets frustrating quick if you're not packing the right functions.  Certain boss fights and a small handful of enemies almost feel like they have an auto-win button if you aren't carrying a very specific build.  They tout having thousands of function combinations for your transistor, but most of them are useless, and not having specific functions on your bar WILL end you mid way through the game, thus creating yet another game with pretty cookie cutter set-ups.  I was almost reconsidering some of my negative opinions of the game, as recursion mode would at least allow you to play through with the skills you should have gotten much earlier in the game, not at the end; but the the last boss fight happens and they let them literally take off half your lifebar before you're even allowed to move.  Maybe you like those sorts of mechanics, where the enemies get to pick and choose when they want to win, but they're nothing but frustrating to me.

I stumbled across this game without any previous knowledge of it, but it was really what I wanted in a game, and I enjoyed it so much.
The visuals were stunning, the story was compelling, and the musical score could induce goosebumps even on the hottest summer day. The narrative organically pulled you along into the world without any sort of exposition or unnatural explanations. It was smooth; the map design left no questions to where you should be, but left room for exploration. Here we are given a powerful female protagonist and a co-hero (he narrates, in a way), and a number of other characters which we can discover, interestingly, by exploring  the game battle mechanics.
As for the gameplay, It is a blend of turn based strategy and RPG style exploration. The learning curve was smooth as well - and the strongest point of the gameplay was being able to tailor it right to user preference. The player can play aggressively, load up thier defence skills, choose tactical maneuvers, all completely valid ways to get through the levels. Even the difficulty is up to you, with the option to stack on "limiters" to make the game more challenging (and you're rewarded for overcoming them).
If I had to point out flaws, I might say that I wouldn't mind a bit MORE free exploration. The game lets you wander a bit, but it's still on a rail. Admittedly, about 3/4th of the way through the main storyline, I felt the story slacken a little bit and drone on just a smidge too much. I also found the difficulty slackened a bit during this point too (of course, I could then just stack on another challenge for myself!). However, even after finishing the game, I still want to go back and try out some new move combinations and skills. There's just so much potential.
All in all, I can't really recommend it enough. I enjoyed every bit and will for sure be diving back in for round two. Check it out.

One of the best single player games I played.
(I know I wrote it several times but meh, I'm what french people call an eternal dissatisfied man, so when I love a game I have to recommend it!)
First, playing in Asia is uncommon enough to be noticed. The environment makes you travel and the moments when you see Honkong by night, with its lights reflected on the wet roads are intense and unforgettable.
In addition, as an eternal dissatisfied player, I often uninstall a game when I feel that I'm not not free of my movements enough. This is what I loved in the game: the Parkour influences in Sleeping Dogs delighted me.
And it's the same for the fights. As a martial arts practicer, I hate when I fight scene isn't realistic. Here, you learn real boxing and kung-fu moves. The weapons are quite rare, which makes you fight your enemies with your bare hands.
But, the thing that spoiled the gameplay is the driving levels. You have to drive a lot for your missions and it's so hard to handle the cars.
The scenario is maybe the best part. It's really simple but effective: you're an undercover cop who must infiltrate a dangerous gang. So you have two personalities and two kinds of opposed missions. Your character will have affection for some members of your gang (no spoil). The only improvement the game could have is a choice system like in Mass Effect to impact your story. But even if you don't really make choices, your character's are always legit and don't really stop your immersion.
Do I recommend it? YEAH, ABSOLUTELY.

I have never played a game like Factorio before. It is so different to any other game I've played, it's hard to compare it. My first impression when friends told me this game is great and I saw some endgame screenshots with "motherboard alike structures", I thought: "How can this even be fun". Some time later I realized,
, so let's give it a try. And I said to myself: "When I'm still playing after like an hour, I will buy it".
I bought it after 30 minutes.
Well, it's a game where you build a factory. Optimize processes and workflows. Fix issues like bottlenecks, build a train network to deliver more materials. etc. etc.
The story is quite simple so far: You crashed on an alien planet with almost nothing and have to find your way to escape from that planet. So the last "task" of the story line is to build and start a rocket. But there is so much more. Most of the time you should set your own targets. Some people do speed runs and getting better and better in it, some building mega and giga factories that are very very big. Some build factories for special purposes.
The game is highly moddable what gives it a very high replayability. Almost everything of the game could be changed. There are already a ton of mods available, some with very high quality and a total conversion alike. Also a lot of mods that just provide QoL.
The performance of the game is very good. It's a 2D sprite based game, with a perspectival topview. In more than 250 hours I rarely found any bugs or glitches. It never crashed so far.
In a nutshell, if you like to automate things, find ways to fill bottlenecks or solve problems: This game is nuts!
I can highly recommend to buy this game, or at least try the demo, if you can identify yourself with some of the gameplay explained above.

I have 250h+ in this game and I still haven't figured out everything in the game.
You start the game with your one guy, you manually mine and bring the ore to your furance, and slowly build machines that mine for you and more furnaces. Then you automate the mining and melting process with the help of inserters. Following that, you start crafting machines, more belts, more inserters, etc and before you know it, you start questioning yourself "well, I am crafting a lot, is there a way to automate it?" To what the game replies "yes, but you have to figure out on your own how to do it."
After hours and hours of figuring out how to automate various systems, I thought the game had not much left to offer, yet I was very wrong. Mods add complexity, quality of life or both if you got used to the systems and are looking for a new challenge. The main mods of today (2017-01-29) are Bob's, Angel's and Yuoki's. They offer so much extra content that you will have many more hours of multiple problems to solve. I have a good 100h into these mods and I have not even scrached the surface of what the mods have to offer.
This game is still in alpha, but it really feels like a finished game. In particular, The game crashed only once, and it was during the 0.13.0 version that
. In that ocasion, I filed the bug in the factorio forums and in the next patch, the issue was fixed. Still, it is important to know that whenever you buy a game in alphayou have to think that you will be happy with the game in its current state. I bought the game when it was version 0.12.X, it is currently 0.14.X and I like the direction the game is taking.
The last point I would make is that this game does not give the feeling of crafting games (namely, minecraft). This game is more about automating and making your life easier. The best way I could summarize it, is with the principle that if you find yourself doing the same task 3 times, you might as well automate it and improve your own experience. If you do not want to automate anything, be my guest, but if you want to just see how YOUR automation solution does everything for YOU, you will have more time for architecture and design.

If you want to just read my original review, scroll down to the bottom.  If you want to know the evolution of my thoughts on this game, read my edits, which have been placed at the top, since they are probably more relevant.  If you want a summary: the game is solid but the marketing is atrocious.
EDIT: 10/24/2015
While I continue to stand by my original rating of the game, as it has solid gameplay and is all around excellent missions, I have to edit my statement on the DLC policy of the developers.  When I had talked of the DLC problem in August, the total cost of the game with all DLC put together was about $40.  Today, the total cost of DLC is over $70.  Although you can still get the whole game by dropping $30 on the Complete Single Player campaign and add the DLC Season Pass for another $15, for a cost of $45 total.  That being said, I would not be surprised if coming down the pipe is another set of DLC that will cost another $15 for a limited set of content.  I am incerasingly worried that the developers are following the Payday 2 development model.  Despite their best efforts to market the game as poorly and arogantly as possible, they have built a rather nice game which I hope survives their best efforts to destroy it.
EDIT: 8/5/2015
As many of you noticed, the company is trying to milk all that is worth out of this game by excessive DLC.  While this is clearly an attempt to rip you off, it is not nearly as bad as you think.  The DLC is only single player campaigns and does not affect multiplayer.  Given that the purpose should not be the single player, you can get away with purchasing the base game and enjoy the multiplayer.  All you lose out on are some glitchy single player missions.  (To be fair, I thought the voice acting and mission scripting was much better than original MoW and I am very much annoyed that as an Alpha buyer I was not given my money's worth for having dropped $15 on the game. That being said, I stand behind my original review of this game.  Terrible sales techniques do not change the solid gameplay.)
Original Review:  From Early Access stage
Sure it is basically Men of War set in the First World War, but it is so much better.  It is asthetically improved and the voice acting is comparatively excellent.  Gameplay is a mix of small unit tactics and massive frontal charges where everyone dies, so you don't have to constantly be bothered by traditional MoW micro management.  Historically accurate references abound throughout the missions and the attention to detail makes this a must for anyone who appreciates the history of the war.  The journal entries give meaning to the campaign missions, so you can enjoy the cast of characters that appear through the missions.  The complexity of the missions really gives the player a sense of how much effort the dev team put into the game.  The player is also made aware of how much this dev team cares about their game.
So in short, its like Men of War but a heck of a lot better because it has a story, it has a dedicated dev team who cares about the quality of the product, and its the First World War.

A lot of times I got citations because “ID/Passport photo wasn’t the same” and crap like that when it was quite difficult to spot any difference! I ended up constantly checking them with the investigate option, and multiple times the game found differences I could just NOT spot by myself. It also doesn't help that the game bugs out at times and tells you that something matches or doesn't match when that's complete horse-sh#t and it looks like it would/wouldn't. Like the ID saying he's 1,55m tall and he seems to be nearly 2m tall, however the game will tell you that there's nothing wrong with those papers. It's hard to trust the game when crap like that keeps happening.
Lastly a third little problem, it’s not a game-breaking bug or anything, but rather an observation: You get paid by who many legit people get through. However, there are days when, I sh#t you not, only one or even no one was qualified to go through, meaning I didn’t get paid ANYTHING. That happened in two days already, and every time it happened I just restarted the day as with no pay, I would be pretty much screwed and forced to get a Game Over.
But besides that, what do you have left? A quite interesting interactive documentary about how sh#t the mid areas of Europe felt during the wars. And even though the countries in the game are fictional, they’re all based on actual countries.
The biggest point the game has running for it has to be the moral choices. It’s up to you who goes through and who doesn’t, and letting the right or wrong people in has consequences.
The audio is also good, fits quite well with the graphics. The main theme is catchy, and the rest of the game usually has ambient sounds with the made-up languages of the characters. Nothing stands out, which is good as it makes everything feel more or less natural.
The graphics, as I’ve said, have a few problems when it comes to the faces, but that being said they fit the game perfectly. Specially the still-images for what happens in special events.
The characters are also surprisingly well written, and could easily pass for real people. From corrupted douchelords to people who only want to survive, from soldiers who are forced to go through this sh#t everyday to jackasses like Jorji who are just lovable in every damn way.
Do I recommend this game? Yeah. It will put your brain to work, looking for what’s actually wrong with all those damn papers, while having a laugh or two with the current, rather sad events. The game also has, for what I know, around 20 or so endings, so that’s a good enough reason to play the game a few times. On a sale, this game is quite worth it for people who look for more casual and relaxing experiences.
TL;DR Edition: Relaxing game about people constantly trying to pass through a frontier with illegal drugs up their #sses. Well written and fun to play, it’s a good pick for any casual player who just wants to have a good time.

Time goes on and life seems to keep getting staler and staler, not many things draw as much attention as they did before. Music, games, or whatever you enjoy the most, don´t have the same enchanting effect anymore, even so, you get to stumble into something amazing once in awhile. And that amazing thing might not be perfect at all but it has something, at least one, that draws you in with such power that you forget every♥♥♥♥♥♥and bad thing that may be happening at the time of your life and just feel that everything is ok, you are in peace and you feel good.
Transistor is one of those amazing things: You get to the credits and boom, you feel at ease with life for some moments. For me, that special thing, the core of the game, was the relationship between the protagonists Red and the Transistor. There is something so haunting about this interaction between the muteness from Red and this "talking sword" Transistor, it feels so unique and by the end of the game you really get to like both of them.
And well, even if my selling point of the game was the relationship between the protagonists, I must say, the game looks gorgeous. It uses this vibrant pallet of colours and everything look so crispy good, pretty much any scene could be screenshotted and saved as a wallpaper, it just looks that good. Also the music is awesome too, a real shame there weren't more vocal tracks but still, I think it´s got a quite good OST, most of them feel really chill, that♥♥♥♥♥♥makes stress fade away; with some of them being a little more energetic. And finally, voice acting is top notch, you just really wanna hear the Transistor talking, for the sake of it.
But, not everything in the game shines. Combat was (The same can be applied to Bastion) somewhat clumsy. I mean, gameplay isn't bad, nor is good. It never gets to feel great or cool, it's more like average. You keep getting weapons and you can try a good arrangement of combinations but even that doesn't help that much with its enjoyment.
So that's it. I can see this game as some kind of hit or miss really because of the gameplay. I mean it has the looks, the music and the characters so, the big question is: How much do you appreciate aesthetics in games? Did you like Child of Light because of the musical score ? Or Dust an Elysian Tail because of the way the game looked? Did you enjoy how Mitzi and Susan interacted in The Cat Lady? If you answered yes, then Transistor might be your game. Just be wary the game is 8-12 hours long, something to keep in mind before pressing that purchase button ;)

Transistor is great.
This game is like Bastion in a few ways: The story is amazing, the characters are unforgettable, the music is hypnotizing, and you'll have an amazing time the whole way through it.
What makes this game better than any other spiritual sequel is that this game dares to try something that isn't what made a bunch of money for the first game. Sure, you can see similarities between the two, but Transistor does things that Bastion does not. The first thing that comes to mind is the combat. Instead of the standard hack-and-slash, Transistor's combat is a mix between a real-time strategy game and LOL. I'm not a huge fan of either of those types of games, but Supergiant melds both genres into something that I really enjoyed.
I'm not a great writer, so I don't know how to segue into this, but another amazing thing about this game is the music. It's  awesome. Most pieces are somewhat slow and solemn, but every now and again there's a more upbeat and happy song too. To top it off, the protagonist hums along with the music if you hold Tab.
I don't know is this is necessary but

I've played Transistor from start to end in a few hours and then replayed a second time in a row. I've just completed it and I'm fresh from the game, so...
Transistor is a beautiful game. Coming here from Bastion, I had high expectations and I can say I've not been disappointed. A darker atmosphere, well-apt to the melanchonic story, an interesting gameplay based on strategy and builds and, more than anything else, a truly marvellous soundtrack subtly intertwined with the plot.
Let's start with the PROs!
- Atmosphere. Really, a 10/10. Beautiful, dark and vivid colours where just a few shades of bright reds and yellows lightened up the mood: Red's hair were truly like a flame in the middle of the screen. The City came out beautiful and well-built and a few almost comic interludes lightened up a bit of the general blues.
- Soundtrack. It was the best thing ever. The songs were a few of the best songs I've ever found in a game, and each one of those wonderful instrumental pieces perfectly enhanced the general feeling while playing.
- Plot. Niceeee plot. Like, a bit overtly tangled and you're left at the end of the game with the feeling that something is missing, but nice plot neverthless. (I've something to say about the ending, but that's going in the CONs.)
- Dynamics. Loved them. It's a strategical based on turns and on your own ability to build and mix your powers, my favourite kind of game, with just enough variety of enemies and sceneries to keep it interesting.
- Easy Mode/Hard Mode. First levels are quite easy; trying the story a second time in Recursion Mode gets the bar a bit higher and you can decide to keep things veeeeery interesting by adding up to ten Limitators. Playing with ten Limitators isn't easy at all, really.
- Levels Up. And you can level up as much as you want - or, at least, that's the feeling I had. I mean, right now I'm at Level 29. That's something I didn't like in Bastion - you could just reach Level 10 and then you simply stopped growing up - and I'm quite happy they decided to change it.
Edit (28/07/16): Nope, it stops at Level 30. Oooops.
CONs.
- No-Face Romeo's Voice in the Background. Wherever you go, wherever you are, the Voice will follow you - and it's not the nice Eastwood-y voice in Bastion, but the voice of someone quite depressed, overtly unhelpful and prone to dramatics and such. I mean, I like a good love story as much as the next gal, but, plese, love, could you just shut up for a moment? I'm trying to play, here.
- Unfortunately Faced Psycho's Voice in the Background at the End of the Game. You get both Romeo and Psycho speaking to you in combo during the last minutes of the game and it's, like, the worse. I badly wanted to mute them someway.
- The Ending. I'm not going to spoiler it, but I played it the first time and I said to myself: "Don't you worry, you're going to replay it and the ending is going to change, it's like Bastion, everything will be all right." Well, everything wasn't all right and now I'm left with the feeling I've missed something.
- The Weight. Like, this game is heavy on my PC and I don't know why. It should be just right for my systems, but it isn't. I was able to play it without big trouble, although.
I'll be replaying Transistor for sure and suggesting it all around to everyone I know. I think I prefer the aesthetics and the plot in Bastion (and That End, that was beautiful, I love Bastion just for its ending), but Transistor's dynamics and soundtracks were my favourites.
It was a nice 9/10.

Hexcells infinite is like nonograms, minesweeper and some special elements all combined to a hex-grid. The game is overally impressive: the saving system works excellently, and the ambient music (even if it is the same all the way) suits very well. The difficulty curve is also balanced.
I particularly appreciate the fact that you can make one mistake in each level without penalties.
The only complainment I have is that after completing the 36 (really well-made) campaign levels, there is hardly any challenge, since the random-generated levels are way too easy compared to the carefully constructed campaign ones. So, a bunch of more levels would be welcome.
9/10

For the uninitiated, Hexcells Infinite is a game where you improve your logic and extend your patience as you purge through cells of impurities by discovering where the “mines” are with the help of numbers. In short, this is the minesweeper of the new generation.
Hexcells Infinite provides enjoyment for both newcomers and veterans alike. Newcomers can enjoy the slow romp of increasing difficulty that teaches you the mechanics of the game. With veterans, they can immediately jump right into the tougher puzzles via Infinite Mode, which gives you difficult random generated puzzles, without concerning themselves with finishing the easier ones (that the newcomers are meant to finish).
Having Hexcells Infinite invalidates the existence of the 2 previous Hexcells games. The previous 2 titles end up only existing as a way of gifting to your friends and supporting the developers. This is absolutely fine because Hexcells Infinite is the next step in its evolution as a game sequel. Everything you need and more is in this definitive sequel.
Ultimately, this is game that is an expertly made for the expert to be. It has evolved in the right direction and should be played & kept by many for generations to come.

The 36 main puzzles are excellent and a pleasure to solve. The randomly generated ones are clearly a notch below, but still very much enjoyable. The ability to exit mid-puzzle and keep your progress saved is probably the only thing this series was missing, and it's here now.
Indispensable for puzzle lovers.

I am someone who has avidly played MMOs for a good 8 years and counting, the best of 5 of those spent on WoW, and FFXIV has the pleasure of being the only MMO to top WoW for me. The story is beautifully written, with loveable and memorable characters, along with a well thought out plot that isn't afraid to take you on a wild ride and has only gotten better since launch. The music is absolutely amazing, and the environments are absolutely beautiful. The gameplay is slower than most MMOs, and provides a very laid back experience, however the game does not let you get lazy, and the late game content provides a sound challenge that most hardcore gamers would welcome. Something that stands out a bit with FFXIV for me is the fact that it integrates raids and dungeons into the main story, in such a way that it teaches you how the game works and prepares you for the endgame. Speaking of which, this game does a wonderful job of slowly introducing you to the game, teaching you how to play so that by 50 you know the ropes, because of which I would recommend it highly for players new to MMOs. The teaching process, combined with the extremely helpful community, creates a warm welcome for any player of the series. There are also myriad things to do, ranging from buying and furnishing your own estate to progressing through massive raids and to just gambling your life away. And, of course, there are mounds and mounds of references to other FF titles across the whole game, and every class gets their own unique lightshow through their abilites. All in all, this game is well worth it's price, and I will fistfight anyone who disagrees. The only potential drawback to me in this game is that being dedicated to it saps a LOT of your time. Once, I made a character that only focused on the main story and it was at least a week before I finished the base game, and that was playing it all day every day.

Early Access Review:
After noticing this the day of release I was grabbed from the start.
WW1 RTS? Actual use of trenches?! (Unheard of in most WW1 games, besides Verdun also check that out too!) TANKS?
So far this game has everything that a WW1 RTS needs. Besides the community, which is steadily growing since release, (say 12 full games last evening), glad to also see the devs responding on discussions and also having a planned roadmap (unlike most early access reviews).
Pros:
Traditional Men of War gamestyle, "If it aint broke dont fix it" is applied very well here. The engine is well built so no major bugs or game breaking glitches found since the engine has been out for a while.
Well detail maps and models, From the rivets on the tanks to the boards in the trenches the game is very well detailed to keep you immersed in the WW1 world. Though I can tell there will be graphical updates in the future.
Still tactical multiplayer, Most of WW1 was mass-infantry charges right after artillery barrages. Which isnt much of a tactic. But with the Men of War engine you have to probe your enemies trenches for weakspots, find out where their arty is before yours (arty is god in WW1), Then when you actually get men into the trenches you have to worry about moving your soldiers through them without getting shot (as much). But still hold true to the WW1 mechanics (still see those glorious infantry charges, and artillery barrages, without losing most of your forces)
Cons:
Lag, still tends to "come up" with a player who tends to have a computer that says "no", first two games were dropped since the client was lost. But that only happened with people 2000+ miles from me (-5 GMT)
First mission is a bloodbath, almost instantly your men get off the train theres a hailfire of artillery and gunfire coming towards your men, prepare your♥♥♥♥♥♥
Editor would be nice! (I can see its coming though so no rush there)
More maps! Maybe add steam workshop support? Community Maps? Potential is great here.
Other than that the game is great and I reccomend any WW1/RTS buff and all friends to get this!

This is my first negative review, ever.
The game itself is actually kind of fun. It's the apparently intentionally confusing pricing in the cash shop and the constant prompts to spend money that warrant the down vote.
Most F2P games I have tried are at least roughly based on the dollar. $10 gets you 1,000 coins, or 900, or 1,100 or something close. Here it is 260 coins for $10. This makes it very confusing to figure out how much anything actually costs.
For example, crystal keys to open chests are 889 coins for a stack of 10 (used to open random high level chests). So how much is that actually? The answer is $33, or $3.30 to open one chest. You must multiply the item cost by 3.8 to get the dollar price (if buying in $10 increments.)
Another example is the item you need to gurantee a combine doesn't fail. They are also over $3. How many ultra-rare reagents you going to see poof before you start buying those?
Inventory slots are 36 cents...per slot and per category (armor and weapons go in one bag, potions in another, etc.) You start with 19 slots in each category, the 20th slot is a "buy" button. This makes it $7.20 to buy 20 bag slots that only hold potions (or only armor, etc.). This wouldn't be too bad if the slots could be used for anything.
When you die you have 2 choices. Run back from town, or pay to res right there. Which would be tolerable, if every town allowed you to bind. I could find no way to bind in the 2nd town at level 11, died and had to run back from the first town. I died because of a level 59 skeleton that came out of nowhere and started one-shotting people.
You can buy a 40% speed mount for (I think) only about $1.60, but that was the only decent deal I could find.
I only played to level 12, but from what I'm reading the grind is very bad at 40+ unless you go premium, which is another $12 a month. And going premium does almost nothing to change the intrusiviness of the cash shop.
I'm not at all against spending money in these games. I do it all the time. But this whole thing would be more reasonable, and not as confusing if you got 1,000 coins for $10. Maybe their pricing is based on the Rubel or something and will be adjusted before release. As it is now, it's very expensive and intrusive.
Bottom line, the game is fun if you have deep pockets.

Surfingers is another game by Forever Entertainment and it is quite similar to their other game Timberman, where you had to chop trees.
As the title already says, this game is about surfing. But you don’t control the surfer himself. Your job is to change the placement of the waves (up and down) to get a good ride and score as many points as you can. You have to bypass different objects like ships, rocks and bones and try not to hit any of these.
But there are not only usual waves to surf on. You can surf in the ocean by day or by night, on snow, in the desert and even in the hell on waves of blood (or maybe lava?). Usually you start surfing in the ocean by day and every once in a while you have to pass a cave with deadly obstacles leading you into a new level and world.
The game offers 26 characters to unlock by getting achievements or by buying them for stars (you get them just by playing the game). Some of them look quite similar to other popular characters. For example there is a super hero looking like Captain America, Timberman, riding a log and there is even Gaben, surfing on a big 100 Dollar bill! And there are some special characters who don’t have to start at the Ocean level. Just take the guy with the snowboard and you begin in the snowy hills, take Aladdin and you start in the desert, the zombie to surf by night or take the reaper, whose starting location is the hell. There are also a number of robots, with nothing special besides showing the number of stars upside down. So if you get bored of water, keep that in mind!
The graphics are very colorful, look very nice and you feel like in a surfing movie. The surf rock music also helps you to get this feeling but as the game offers only one soundtrack this is the only thing you get annoyed of after playing the game some hours without resting.
The gameplay is very easy to understand but hard to master. You have to press 2 buttons, one for bringing the waves up, the other one to bring them down. So you can play with the arrow keys, or pressing W and S or with the help of a gamepad. I even tried to mix it, so I tried to press S with the left hand and Arrow Up with the right but you have to get used to this. And then I called a friend, connected 2 gamepads and the Single Player Mode became a “One-button-Multiplayer”. My job was to press “Down”, his job was to press “Up”, and it was great fun! You know, this brings teamplay to this game and as you always know who messed up it’s great fun to see the reaction and making fun of each other. This way we managed to get the highest score.
Surfingers also offers local and online multiplayer. You play splitscreen and the one getting farther than the others wins. I played a bit with my friend locally (as I couldn’t find anyone online) and we found our invented “Co-op Mode” more fun.
Let’s sum up.
Positive:
+ simple gameplay (2 buttons)
+ many different colorful characters
+ different landscapes
+ cool soundtrack and graphics style
+ very addictive
+ multiplayer
+ controller support
+ achievements and trading cards
+ cheap
Negative:
- couldn’t find anyone in Online Multiplayer
- soundtrack gets annoying after playing some hours
- after a long ride I was dizzy
So all in all I think this is a great game for killing time and definitely fun to play with your friends and have a laugh. And it’s definitely worth the money.

When starting this game, you might think it is a simple and fun change from your average game.
Until you are sixteen hours in and realise that being a virtual border guard has become a way of life, and you know all Arstotzkan immigration laws off the top of your head. It's fun and simple until you realise you know all issuing cities and can tell a genuine dimplomat stamp from a forgery with the corner of your eye.  It's all fun and simple until
Glory to Arstotzka!
The Actual Review:
The game is fun and is very easy to become serious about as it progresses.  It starts off easily enough, making sure passports aren't expired and they are Arstotzkan citizen, but it becomes much deeper very quickly.  I haven't gotten around to playing endless mode, because story is intriguing enough.  When you begin, you want to let the poor immigrants in and help the people who need it, but you will not last long playing like this.  To keep you and your family alive you need to be logical and uncaring, even to your family.  Money is tight as well.  My tip is alternate nights with food and heat, and those without.  Only buy medicine when they are very sick.  However, this game is a commitment, best saved for when you have time and effort to direct towards checking virtual passports.

I would reccomend this game to pretty much everyone. It's almost a genre of it's own.

Transistor is a decent game, and deserves the praise it has recieved, I however don't hink it's deserving of much more than an 8/10. The soundtrack is good, but not memorable (with some exceptions). I think when people say that the OST is memorable, they are referring to the one song that plays during Turn().
The gameplay is good and varied. You won't find yourself using some overpowered move over and over again because no such thing exists. Every attack that is aquired throughout the game has its own strenghts and downfalls, such as being too weak to be able to do anything on its own, but when paired with Load as a passive ability, there are so many more options for different moves. There is a difficulty curve in the game, especially near the end, but most of the time it feels fair. As for the final boss, there's really not much to say about him. IT was an easily won fight. If anything, The Spine boss was far more difficult. And speaking of, when it "comes back", we don't even get to fight it again. Unless I'm missing something?
The art style and palette are easy to look at. Dark and full of shadows, with a contrast of white by the Process, clearly highlighting who the enemy is.
The story is okay It left me grasping for a little more at points, and left a few questions unsatisfactorily answered. As well, the main villains motive/motto seems confusing. Maybe implying that if everything changes, there is nothing else to change, therefore staying the same? But whether it's used as a motto or motive for their actions, it seems lacking. I don't expect a huge backstory to their reasons, however a little more explanation would have suited it well.
TL;DR: Music provides good Ambience, not very emorable, good gameplay and combat, except final boss, easy to look at scenery, encourages exploration, decent story, want a little more from it, minor confusing details

I'll keep it short and simple (for an mmo review)
Good graphics for an MMO despite being a little aged.
Slow building but enjoyable storyline if you don't mind the typical FF theme (duh)
No need for alts unless you genuinely want one. All classes can be played on character, including crafting classes. This is one of the best parts for someone that has trouble making lots of alts. You actually start to remember names and faces you've see before in game.
To build from the above the game has a solid community with a lot of people willing to jump to help new players if they just ask. This is really one of the best parts of the game. You have a few idiots here and there but most people actually like to help newbies because you might see that same character 100 or 1000 hours later and end up in a group with them.
Players and guilds (free companies) can have housing if they have the in game money for it. Lots of customization in this area.
Class (job) diversity is good and new ones are added at a good pace. Before the first expansion released they introduced a new class, then 3 more on top of that shortly after with the first expansion. In less than a year they added four freaking classes. Each was completely unique with it's own story, theme and play style. Stormblood is introducing two more on top if this so finding a class to fit your style is certainly not going to be an issue of lack of variety.
Combat is slightly slower but feels more thoughtful in the sense that you aren't throwing numbers into an ocean of HP on bosses. Most classes don't have a strict rotation that most MMOs suffer from. There is still a basic rotation but many classes have abilities that play roles outside the box of the bland 1234 rotations we get used to in other games. The enemies also don't feel too easy. Even low level enemies will use large AoEs that force you to move and pay attention to your positioning instead of just being mindless fodder. It feels like a happy medium in regard to difficulty.
Wholeheartedly encourage anyone interested to at least give the trial a shot.

Overall this is a great game and I really hope you give it a try if MMOs are your thing!

I have followed BoE since it first appeared on Greenlight, and have been eager to get my hands on a copy. Well, my eagerness has not been dulled since purchasing and playing this early access ww1 game.
The gameplay is the typical MoW style, with objectives to be completed in order to progress. The  models and overall graphics are well suited to the era - and should look quite amazing with the rtm version. No performance issues running on a Windows 8.1 laptop (..mine has 4GBRAM /500GB HDD/Intel HD &Radeon 3670m 2GB (Hybrid) graphics with the settings all maxxed out).
There are many types of units and equipment included in the "ea" release. So far I've played with the Infantry, Artillery, Mounted rifles, a British tank (and yes, they make excellent target practice for the Germans), support troops (ran a telephone line! ...and threw smoke to call in arty). All seems to be well represented and functional.
Missions and factions are limited right now, but more content will be added over time.
There is a passable tutorial, which is good enough to get you started - and a fairly challenging but enjoyable first mission. There are 8 missions, I think, in the current campaign.
The ambient sounds are good, although the gun fire does sound a bit "wrong". The voice overs are definately wrong - but funny at the same time. I feel I'm in command of a rag tag company :P
There are ingame options to select, although I could not get the music to go lower than the tutorial captains voice - so he was hard to hear.
Overall, straight off the digital shelf - this is an awesome effort by the developers  in bringing a ww1 rts to life. It's definately worth adding to the list.. and if you are wondering, it's similar to the CoH mod: The Great War 1918, and of course if you own CoH and/or the Men of War series you know what to expect gameplay and graphics wise.
No crashes or glitches have been encountered - after 1.4 hours of gameplay.

Having played around 3.5 hours now - I have had one crash, after playing a MP match and was in the lobby chatting away. ALT+TAB'd out and when I went to ALT+TAB back in, the game threw an exception. Not a show stopper tho. Just relaunched the game.
Had a few 2v1/2v2/3v3 multiplayer matches - and all I can say is "wow" . The mp is epic! And very true to the murderous "advance with rifle" ww1, strategies.
It has to be played to be experienced...
Having alot of fun in the single player campaign - I have progressed to the 3rd mission (Night before the offensive). It's a stealth mission which brings in quite an interesting element to the game. I've been playing mostly multiplayer - and really enjoying it. I do struggle with the limited squad selection ability, but it does mean a bit more micromanagement - hopefully this gets improved and greater troop numbers are made available to the player. 3v3 is still epic tho!
"The tides may turn, only after many souls have fallen."
So far, this is the best ground level WWI RTS around.

Got this in a bundle. Feels like some mobile port. You pretty much just move your tile of water up or down to match the next tile, all while your character moves faster and the tiles get smaller, and then when you fail, you start over.

There's nothing wrong with the concept, but it's unsatisfying.
You control the terrain instead of your surfer, which is fine. But the gameplay ends there. You collect stars, but they don't serve the game. The collisions are a little wonky.
A couple pieces of extra mechanics could have made it better. I understand wrecking into a higher piece of terrain, but why can't you drop from a wave? A cool down so you couldn't do it consecutively would have made it more interesting. If you get a star combo, the character could jump a wave you missed once per combo (to incentivize going for them). And no way to save progression. Making sure you'll be very familiar with the aesthetic of the first part of the first level and nothing else.
It could have been good, but it isn't. Even for only a few bucks.

A lukewarm audio "choose your own adventure" book featuring Hank, King Arthur, a time machine, and the holy grail.
This game is the sort of thing that English teachers think students find fun - and that's exactly who I'd recommend this to. If you know someone who learns English and is in their third year or upwards, this game can be good because you can read the text and hear it spoken, have it repeated as often as necessary, and have frequent pauses to look up words or ask questions. The dialogue is enunciated clearly and usually written correctly (the only errors I could spot were the words "chavinist" for "chauvinist" and "misoginist" for "misogynist").
If you are looking for a good audio experience, well, the voice acting is stiff, the story is predictable, and it took me a mere half hour because I started reading ahead and skipping the audio (at least that way I didn't suffer from the lack of a save feature). It's good for people who are easily excitable because there won't be any danger of that.

Transistor is a decent game, and deserves the praise it has recieved, I however don't hink it's deserving of much more than an 8/10. The soundtrack is good, but not memorable (with some exceptions). I think when people say that the OST is memorable, they are referring to the one song that plays during Turn().
The gameplay is good and varied. You won't find yourself using some overpowered move over and over again because no such thing exists. Every attack that is aquired throughout the game has its own strenghts and downfalls, such as being too weak to be able to do anything on its own, but when paired with Load as a passive ability, there are so many more options for different moves. There is a difficulty curve in the game, especially near the end, but most of the time it feels fair. As for the final boss, there's really not much to say about him. IT was an easily won fight. If anything, The Spine boss was far more difficult. And speaking of, when it "comes back", we don't even get to fight it again. Unless I'm missing something?
The art style and palette are easy to look at. Dark and full of shadows, with a contrast of white by the Process, clearly highlighting who the enemy is.
The story is okay It left me grasping for a little more at points, and left a few questions unsatisfactorily answered. As well, the main villains motive/motto seems confusing. Maybe implying that if everything changes, there is nothing else to change, therefore staying the same? But whether it's used as a motto or motive for their actions, it seems lacking. I don't expect a huge backstory to their reasons, however a little more explanation would have suited it well.
TL;DR: Music provides good Ambience, not very emorable, good gameplay and combat, except final boss, easy to look at scenery, encourages exploration, decent story, want a little more from it, minor confusing details

So when I just started this game I was actually enjoying the game by quite a bit, you had monsters to kill, nice bright graphics, cheerful music, everything you would expect from this game. However, after playing for about 2 hours, I found out about the inventory space, yes, the dreadful inventory space. You get less than 20 slots per tab, which if you have some RPG gaming experience, would know is not even close to being enough for the later on grinding sprees that you'd need to go on, and if you need more space, guess how? $$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$ Speaking of money, the game is screaming "give me money" as you play, you need $ to buy in game currency to buy cosmetics, which DOES give you stats, and the stats are not exactly tiny (Example: 5% max hp for footprints). Now some of you might argue that you can buy the ingame cash, "Reales" with ingame currency, but when I last checked, 1 REALE is about 14k gold, which is considered A LOT in this game, so if you are planning on buying reales, you might need to spend quite a bit of time. Speaking of grinding, the game also has a "member" system (remember Runescape?), yes, the member advantages are not even close to being as much as Runescape, however, they get 50% increased exp/loot drop rate. All in all, if you are not planning on using money on this game, be prepared to spend money.

I was skeptical. My friend and I have played multiple MMORPGS, and none of them seemed to stick. We'd play for a few months, drag a few friends along, all grow bored, and eventually leave it behind for the next new craze. Oh boy was I absolutely wrong. Not even two months in and we'd found a free company which, to date, has some of the single most amazing people I've ever met in a game. I learned how to better handle the Archer Class, was given gear to help aid me in fighting, developed crucial skills as a Bard, and, despite my still relatively small knowledge about the roll, I am now able to play with a lot more confidence than I would have had I not met them. There are some absolutely hilarious quests in this game, some heart-warming stories, absolutely stunning graphics, and some even more amazingly warm-hearted individuals to guide you. My only advice? This game is a staple for breaking the mold of normal game genres, and my God does it work well! This pixelated stress-fest will definitely leave you on edge and enjoying ever second.
Story:
Nothing too complicated. You're a low-class citizen of the lovely country known as Arstotzka, and while living there you're a "lucky" winner of a raffle. Your prize? Working low hours as border patrol to barely sustain enough cash to take care of your family and health, and possibly make a few bucks on the side. You'll have to decide and manage betweem food and health, and making sure your family isn't dead by the end.
Gameplay:
This is definitely where the game shines. The gameplay is all about understanding what can and cannot go through the border. You'll have to scroll through books and passports to decide if they meet the correct requirements to legally pass, and the pressure is solely on the player. Over time the rules get more strict, and you'll be racing against the clock to make sure you get enough people through (without penalty) to earn some cash. There's a gradual curve, so you shouldn't be too overwhelmed in the beginning, but it can be a real hair-puller by the end when you have dozens of small penalties to find.
Difficulty:
As I just said, there is a curve over the course of each level. It'll start with simple tasks such as which countries can go through and which can't, all with their own special emblems to easily differenciate. But, as time goes on, more rules such as work passes and body searches get implemented, and this is where it gets tricky. Every new day you get two warnings for hiccups while working, but after that you get money deducted, and this can be painfully nitpicky. But, with enough focus and a keen eye, this is a really well done mechanic, even for people like myself who don't like playing games under pressure.
Graphics:
If it isn't already obvious from my profile picture, I *love* pixel art graphics, and this is no exception. The dull colors and gritty look really show the sort of sad side to this game, and it works beautifully well. Every new citizen is different, and even some continuous characters have a familiar look you'll always remember. So, if the look seems interesting to you, you'll enjoy it no problem.
Score: 4.5/5
In short, if you enjoy really simple ideas like this that ramp up over the course of the game, and are willing to pay attention to play it properly, it is an absolute joy that will be hard to put down.

Double Fine dropped the ball on this. They talked up a storm about Spacebase DF-9, and my "Yes" review was based on what they were planning, not what the game currently is. The current games is barebones and not nearly worth $25.
Once modders clean up Double Fine's mess (if they even can), then the game might be worth it.

Since everyone's reviews are solely their views on Double Fine's recent announcement, I'll go ahead and take a look at the game in its current state.
As it is right now, Spacebase DF-9 shouldn't be called anywhere near completed.  I mean, the game works and all but there are a lot of glaring problems with it.  After a few runs through the game, I couldn't help but notice that every space sector you play in has almost zero differences between them.  The astro density determines how much asteroid is in your area to mine from, which is appreciated, but it hardly makes up for everything else.  The threat level has very little difference, as it apparently suggests how often your base gets showered on by meteors and debris, while warpgate proximity indicates how often you get potential new residents passing by.  What is evidently missing is where Raider occurrences would be placed, since they happen fairly regularly.
The Raiders themselves are stupendously overpowered.  The raiding parties vary between one and three Raiders that *will* decimate your population, no matter how well-trained your Security staff is.  The reason for this is because they tank damage like it's nothing while killing a majority (if not all) of your residents in less than five shots each.  The defensive turrets don't offer much by way of defense.  As the camera is locked to only one perspective, you only have the option to face the turrets downward (i.e. towards the bottom of the map) to either the left or right directions.  Seriously, you can't really use them to shoot at the approaching vessels since they have to be *inside* the base.
The base amenities are also a joke as follows:
- Despite having oxygen capacity for X number of people, the second I fill the base to capacity, the oxygen recyclers eventually fail as if I was overbooked (despite each recycler to be working perfectly at roughly 80-85% durability).  This caused my residents to panic and run around, abandoning all jobs and waiting until they either starved to death (because they used up all of the matter in stock) or waited until the next Raider party exterminated them all.
- The bar doesn't offer much, since it's the only thing that works in the Pub zone.  I have seen neither the fridge nor stove used at all so they're essentially useless.
- I set up a Reserch Zone and set a tech to research but my Scientist was busy doing everything else while on duty rather than actually research anything.
Overall, the game pretty much sucks since each playthrough is just the same thing: see how big your base can get before Raiders kill them all.  And given how Double Fine's treating the game now, I'd have to agree with everyone else.  The developers are basically dropping the project and turning the rest of the game's development over to the community after announcing that they're releasing the source code for the scripts and pushing the game out the door with a 1.0 full release version.  Avoid this game and pick up somthing better instead, like the classic StarTopia or even Prison Architect (which I also have). Spacebase DF-9 is simply a waste of time and money.

I was skeptical. My friend and I have played multiple MMORPGS, and none of them seemed to stick. We'd play for a few months, drag a few friends along, all grow bored, and eventually leave it behind for the next new craze. So when the newest one came along (this game specifically) I had my reasons to be weary. Why should I invest getting my hopes up to only lose interest in a matter of weeks? I'd been through this limbo way too many a time, and there was no doubt in my mind that this would again be the case.
Oh boy was I absolutely wrong. Not even two months in and we'd found a free company which, to date, has some of the single most amazing people I've ever met in a game. I learned how to better handle the Archer Class, was given gear to help aid me in fighting, developed crucial skills as a Bard, and, despite my still relatively small knowledge about the roll, I am now able to play with a lot more confidence than I would have had I not met them. There are some absolutely hilarious quests in this game, some heart-warming stories, absolutely stunning graphics, and some even more amazingly warm-hearted individuals to guide you. My only advice? Don't be afraid to be out there. If you wanna say hello, they might not always bite. Rest assured, there is bound to be someone who will take the bait.

The soundtrack is good, but there's no variety. The in-game songs are mostly good. Although this doesn't include the radio tracks. The radio tracks are in a ratio of 20% amazing songs, 5% mediocre songs and 75% awful songs. I know it's mostly taste, but in a fair few cases, the music is just bad.
The combat is really good. When watching reviews by Angry Joe, then you might've heard the opposite. But he's also the type of person to say that the Arkham Freeflow combat is easy because you can win by just countering. But the point isn't to just wait and counter. It'd take you hours to complete a larger fight. That kind of an argument is extremely stupid and frankly just ignorant. The combat flows well, it has a lot of hidden variety and you won't get bored of it for the whole game. That, of course, meaning that you do like that type of combat anyway.
The shooting is powerful. It really has weight behind it and every bullet impact is visible. It's a very simple system still and it's a good thing that shooting isn't too prevalent in the game. Otherwise it'd start showing cracks.
Achievements are not tricky to get. It just requires gametime. Collecting collectibles, achieving medals and so on. They'll take time, it might look a bit daunting, but they're all doable.
Map design is memorable. All areas are very memorable and I can slowly start navigating in that city without the map. But at the same time, the GPS is the worst. I mean, it does it job fairly well, but it doesn't work offroad, when you drive on the other side of the road and it really wants you to follow the rules of the road. It makes sense, but in the end, it isn't fun. This is a Hollywood styled game after all.
Overall
8/10

Best puzzle game of the Hexcell series!
The third version of this game, following Hexcells and Hexcells plus.
Again the basic puzzles are a bit harder than with plus and a LOT harder compared to the first Hexcells.
Where plus gave us additional new rules for the puzzles, this sequel doesn't do that. It only perfects the difficulty of what the previous parts had to offer.
But why the name "infinity"? It comes with a Random Puzzle Generator, offering no less than 100.000.000 puzzles. This is where the true replay value shines. Want to share a certain puzzle with a friend? Just give the puzzle grid number to him and he can load it no problem. You can even save a puzzle midway, Something that is lacking in the standard puzzles.
All in all a very valuable addition to an already great game.
As with the previous two parts, ALL puzzles can be solved by using simple (and sometimes not so simple) logic. You never have to guess to solve something there's always a "if this needs this, then that must be so or so". Highly recommended if you enjoyed the previous parts. If you found 'plus' too hard, the random puzzles are a bit less difficult sitting somewhere between the original and plus.

, is an indie game published in 2013 by Lucas Pope, which sees the player take control of an immigration officer at the border of the fictional country of
, a country based on the slew of authoritarian dictatorships that popped up in Eastern Europe during the Cold War. Set in 1982 after the conclusion of a six-year conflict between Arstotzka and neighboring Kolechia, the player, an immigration officer for Arsotzka, has to decide based on varying rules who is or isn't allowed to enter Arstotzka.
Throughout the game, the player will be faced with tasks largely based around morality: Should this poor old woman be allowed to enter despite her expired passport? Should this refugee be allowed despite his criminal record? Is Cobrastan a real country? The game isn't vague with things and makes it clear the differences presented to the player: Money or Morality? With a family of five (and a sixth possible to adopt) to feed, shelter, and heat, the stakes are much higher and less personal and more interpersonal; it becomes logical to deny the masses illegally trying to enter Arstotzka as long as you're able to keep your family alive.
The rules for who can get into the country tend to change daily in the story mode, and the game makes sure to not keep the player too tired or too familiar with a single rule setup; One day people from the  United Federation will be barred due to a Polio outbreak there, another day they'll be allowed in as long as they bring a certificate that they were vaccinated. The game keeps the player on full alert, and tosses in new mechanics (terrorist attacks and rifles players can use to stop them, armed revolutionary groups willing to sneak through the border to overthrow the regime, etc) to keep the player both on edge and entertained, not allowing itself to fall flat or get boring during the 31 days the game has as its story mode.
In addition to story mode, there exists an endless mode which allows the player to compete against others internationally via Steam in regard to how many people they can get across in a period of time or other factors, such as how quick they can get through people correctly.
The game is a masterpiece in storytelling and narrative, and provides a great deal of stress and emotional impact with the player, along with excellent gameplay which is sure to keep your brain on high alert for a period of time after you finish up. I strongly suggest you buy this game if you enjoy 1984-esque worlds, or if you enjoy puzzle games in general.

I was initially excited for the game. A sim colony game in space. What's not to like? I used to play Startopia (awesome!) and Space Colony (pretty good!) so I was pumped for another game of the kind.
I like that the game does not take itself too seriously. You got funny dialogues, weird aliens, and spacebook. It makes for a comfortable feel too it. The colors are vibrant and the interaction between crew members are kinda funny.
The ability to create your own base and style it the way you want is also very interesting. It makes for a unique base layout each time you make a new game.
And then there are the things that bother me. First, for a base that supposed to feel like home, there's very little items you can put in a room. A potted plant, a monitor, a dresser, a rug, some shelves, and a couple of neon signs are your ONLY decorations. There isn't even any way you can recolor it so you're stuck with the same items in every room.
Second, You can only rotate the camera from north to east facing. That will apply to every item too. It's really frustrating as it limits your design option.
Third, There are still a lot of bugs or unfinished issues (that they might address in the future) No matter what you do at the moment, your base will fail either due to depressed crew members that results into raging and destruction of rooms and equipment or raiders killing everybody even if your security personel had all the upgrades available. Some suggested that you put a decorative object almost every other tile to stave off depression but we shouldn't have to do that. You also had that design issue wherein the item looks like it's floating rather than attached to the wall. Crew members can actually go behind it (i.e. Food replicator, monitor)
Ultimately, I felt like I was ripped off. To put more context, Doublefine did say that they 'might' add more based on the development map that they laid out but with the current and future content (1.0) that will come out, it is wholly unreasonable for the 30$ they are asking. It felt like they just gave up midway through.
The worst thing about this is that since they are giving the community access to the source code, they now wash their hands off it. It is now the responsibility of the community to make the game great. Oh sure, they said they'll be sticking around...for bug fixes.
I knew there were dangers of buying early-access games but I couldn't stop myself. Now I regret it. Don't make the same mistake

I don't know what everyone's problem is that is giving negative reviews. Yes it's pay-to-win and is much like other games, but nowdays, there's just so many mmorpgs, it's hard to find anything unique anymore. Just each games has their own style and variations. And as far as pay-to-win goes, that's what you will get when you play a FREE TO PLAY game... The damn makers of this game have to make money SOME HOW to keep the games going...
Now here's my personal opinions on the game so far:
The graphics are beautiful for this type of game, way more beautiful than I expected.
The things that you can do to upgrade your gear is a nice feature.
So far from the low level maps, I've found these randomly spawned gravestone things that you can click and go into a mini-dungeon (I assume). I've found these quite fun to do because you can get some decent loot from these. I hope there's more in the game!
The characters and customization all look quite nice. The faces look just a little weird on some of the options, but other than that, I really like it. There's a decent amount of options for you're character's looks, more than even some mmorpgs I've played. I'm a sucker for character customization, so I really hope they add more features to this.
I haven't gotten into crafting (if there is), but what I'm seeing looks like it should be interesting as well.
The classes, skills, and stat points when you leveling, all this I really like. There's a unique (to me anyhow) feature for spending your stat points each time you level.
The amount of options you are given in the settings (graphics, sound, chat settings etc...) is very nice as well. Games that give you a lot of settings and customization is always nice.
I do hate the click to move, but from all the mmorpgs/games I've played, I'm use to it by now.
Bag space is annoying, but I just put things in storage I don't keep any time soon, and sell everytime I go into town. So I never really run into many problems with it.
There are pvp zones, I'm not quite sure how it all works, but I look forward to exploring this. From what I've heard though and from what it seems, it doesn't tell you when you are in a pvp zone. Hopefully this stuff will be changed up some.
There is a 10min death penalty. After you die, you're stats are decreased for 10mins, but this can be removed for 500g (which is REALLY easy to get) from the respawn points. So it's not a big deal.
The game has it's ups and downs. To best figure out if YOU like the game, I'd honestly suggest trying it out. Like I was saying earlier though, these negative reviews are kind of BS. Their complaints are stuff you will deal with in almost all free to play games.
Every game is going to have at least 1 thing you don't like, after playing games almost my whole like, and 12 years of it being mmorpgs, I've learned you just work around it and deal with it if you like the game enough. No game is perfect :P

I'm level 20 and about done with this game. This is actually a negative review, only listed as positive so it isn't ignored. I've played MMOs a long time, starting with Maplestory and going to WoW, I also love Final Fantasy games but this one just doesn't do it for me. My connection was smooth the entire time and Square Enix has done a great job with streamlining a lot of traditionally tedious MMO annoyances, especially transportation and combat damage calculations. The controller mapping works fantastically too, making it a true cross platform game.
But the world, quests and characters are so bland. The quests are either a glorified tutorial or run and kill x number of monsters and get x vials of blood from them. The character specialization is non existent, you can be every class and gathering profession as one character and there is a very clear "best" gear for everything. The gear only covers a few generic roles (DPS, Healer, Tank). You don't have tech trees or talents to pick from, the only specialization you get is from choosing a few spells from another class to use. Which is mostly useless except for passive buffs, as your own skills class's skills work better. I like the gathering system but what kills it entirely is you have to switch to the gathering class to even sense nearby ore veins or plants...the locations I've travelled to so far have been pretty uninteresting too which I thought was surprising for a Final Fantasy games. The monsters are great, but unfortunately that's all that's really worth exploring.
As nice and smooth as a lot of the systems in this game are, you don't get to make any choices. You can choose which class to play or which Free Company (guild) to join, but in terms of how you play there character there is a very concrete playstyle and gear set, and the in game HUD queues will walk you through everything. My entire time in combat is starting off with my bleed (3) then alternating between basic attacks 1 and 2, 2 only doing slightly buffed dmg... (I'm a rogue) and so with the quests being as monotonous as they are there isn't much left keeping my playing. What is perfected is the grindfest, if you like to grind and max out everything, this is the game for you. There are hunting logs and gathering logs to fill out. For me having all professions on one character is awful, but it's clear why some would adore this feature.
I'll give it a thumbs up because this won't even get read if it's a thumbs down... but even though I spent $30 on the Heavensward bundle and I'm already done with an entire MMO, in terms of game time I do think I got my moneys worth. And somehow some people do enjoy the in game cities and story... so there has to be some type of people that does enjoy the setting that I find boring, and the actual gameplay itself. I'll say the community is also really friendly, if a bit quiet. I can totally see a shy person finding a FC they loved and then enjoying the game a lot more with other people. I really wished I liked it more, the other reviews have been great and I was really hoping for something that would blow the other MMOs out of the water. But for me now I'm downloading WoW and I'm gonna see if nostalgia has distorted my views
edit : made it to lvl 53 in FFXIV before I finally had to tap out. I stand by all my first impressions, the game has perfected the grind, everything you do is useful, but ultimately you still don't get to make any choices and combat remains incredibly dull. It's a great game for streamers and other casuals that like to zone out while still progressing, but if you want to customize characters or explore a huge diverse world, you're out of luck. And really I'm still amazed how dull the world is. It feels like nothing is alive besides the actual players, the entire world seems like it's at war when the story is that they're rebuilding. I haven't played all the Final Fantasies but hardly any of the interesting things from the series make it in ffxiv. No hypello, shoopuf, or moonglow type landscapes? FFX is my favorite of the series and it literally might be a bigger world than FFXIV, let alone far more diverse and complelling. I just don't undestand why they couldn't take just half the imagination from that one game and point it in here? The characters you choose from are incredibly bland, you choose human, skinny tall human, human with ears and tail, big strong human, demon human, or a child (the lalafell, which really ruins the lore of the game for me, when I'm being trained by a lalafell pugilist...) They come with no racial or gender passives, just a very small stat bonus. Most of the world is green plains, occasional swamps, and some rocks. And I really thought I'd find more creatures.. but everything is just reskinned beginner zone mobs. The raid bosses are the only cool creatures. Transistor is by far the best single-player experience I've had in a while. This game quickly immersed me in its unique world and original story. The soundtrack was stellar, Darren Korb did a wonderful job, not to mention Ashley Barret's vocals. The gameplay was very strategy-based but managed to stay well-paced enough to keep me interested. But what really made the game for me was Logan Cunningham's performance as the Transistor.
The mere fact that the Transistor had a voice and personality was a great choice. Without him, the game would've felt lonely and fairly empty. The dynamic voice lines that made the Transistor react to situations made him feel a lot more real and I eventually fell infatuated with his and Red's relationship. The few other characters were also very well done, and the voice actors for them were all phenomenal.
The gameplay, as said before, was unusual but fun. The "turn" mechanic I had not seen in a game before, but it was very well polished. I found myself trying out functions left and right for new effects which proved very useful, less I go through the entire game with Joust as an Active Function. Many of the fights were simple once I understood the core mechanics, so I added "Limits" in order to challenge myself. I found this to make some specific fights harder, while most stayed the same difficulty.
The art and music added to the feel of the world's dystopian setting. I can't really describe this any better than it would be for you to just watch the trailer or pick up the game. Both are among the best that the video game industry has offered in this decade.
If you are looking for a fairly short game with a lot of replayability, this is definitely the game for you. While not the most challenging game, it's definitely one worth playing through once or twice or five times. Between the breathtaking ambience, stunning performance, and astounding story and gameplay, Transistor is definitely one of my favorite games from the last few years.
