Hexcells is a minimalist puzzle game that I like to think of as a combination of Minesweeper and Sudoku. A comparison that has probably been made elsewhere. Every level is basically the same. You’re presented with a variable number of cells with a number in the top right corner telling you how many blue cells there are in the puzzle. The challenge is figuring out which cells are blue and which are numbers. If you guess incorrectly, it’s counted as a mistake that will affect how many points you get at the end of a level. The numbers on or adjacent to cells are telling you how many blue cells are connected to them. It’s up to the player to figure out the pattern by examining the numbers. In general terms, if there are two unknown cells connected to a cell that has the number “2” on it, they’re both blue cells. There are several different mechanics used to confuse the player and make them logic out the solution. Upon completing a level, you’ll be rewarded with points that are used to unlock additional groups of levels. As such, this does requires you to complete most of the puzzles with a minimal amount of mistakes in order to progress forward.
Hexcells Infinite is the fully fleshed out title. It has Steam cloud, the most challenging puzzles (36 new ones) and a random puzzle generator. It also has the ability to change the mouse buttons. The random number generator has the same pluses and minuses as most randomly generated systems do. It’s a lot of content but the quality of those puzzles will be all over the place compared the developer’s handcrafted ones. Still, there’s a neat level here and there. Additionally, the player is able to save their place in the puzzle and quit the game if they need to. The other two games do not.
Here’s the problem I have with the entire Hexcells series. It’s a pretty good puzzle experience, if you play it how it’s intended to be played. However, I feel that they have a problematic design flaw: all of the puzzles can be cheesily completed. If you’re stuck at a certain sequence, you can just click through the rest of the puzzle making as many mistakes as you like. (I had some puzzles at 50-60 mistakes). What about the points you would get from a near perfect completion? Well, once you nearly finish the puzzle, take a screenshot and then instantly replay the level with your own personal guide. It’s possible to win all three games this way without much effort on your part.
It’s a minimalist game so there really aren’t many settings to change. Since its running on the Unity engine, the Unity launcher menu pops up when you start the game every time. It allows you to change resolutions and turn fullscreen on/off. The graphics quality is set to beautiful and can’t be changed. However, I was able to play this on a basic, five year old laptop running Linux Mint and there was absolutely no trouble running it. Alternative keys can be changed here as well. Hexcells Infinite was the only game of the three that allows you to swap the left and right mouse button functions.
Overall, I think the Hexcells series is a decently executed puzzle idea with plenty of content. I take issue with the lack of anti-cheat but it's not enough to make it an anti-recommendation. (Thanks to a friend for making a case to change my mind on this). It’s a fun logic number puzzle series. And I did play the three games how it was intended too, with a few exceptions. I had quite a bit of fun deducing the my way through the levels and had several “aha!” moments despite it’s more casual nature. Additionally, it maintains a mellow and atmospheric experience that I can appreciate. While there is the less honorable part of myself thinking “you can just easily ‘cheat’ this game and not spend hours on it”, that doesn't disqualify it from being a decent puzzle game. So, if you can avoid cheating yourself, get the Hexcells series. But if you can’t restrain yourself from looking up help on even the slightest bit of challenge, I probably wouldn't get it. Otherwise, that's my thoughts on this series.

A logic puzzle that is like a combination of Minesweeper and Kakuro. Simple design & graphics, fitting music. You have numbered tiles that tell how many adjacent mines there are. And later on there are numbers outside the grid that tell how many mines are in that column and numbers inside mine tiles that tell how many mines are within a two tile radius. You use the information given to get through tiles and eventually uncover the whole area. There are no game overs (so you can continue on despite guessing or making mistakes) but you can do the puzzles without guesswork.
The controls are pretty simple (left click to mark as a mine, right click to reveal). You can also right click on column numbers/mine numbers to hide them. It's not very obvious but you can access the menu/restart the stage by clicking on the word MENU on the top left corner.
I enjoy logic puzzles and these kept me entertained for a several hours (I spent a good amount of time just thinking about the problems and eventually got hints from people on the forums).
The Infinite version finally allows for saves so you can safely take a break during puzzles (which I often did to reset my mind and try again later).
It also introduces randomly generated levels (based on seeds) so you can keep playing after you finish the campaign. However, from my limited experience, the randomly generated levels are usually not as satisfying as the dev-selected campagin levels. The generated levels don't usually require thinking about more than one layer of information at a time and have a good amount of simple cascades. , is an indie game published in 2013 by Lucas Pope, which sees the player take control of an immigration officer at the border of the fictional country of
, a country based on the slew of authoritarian dictatorships that popped up in Eastern Europe during the Cold War. Set in 1982 after the conclusion of a six-year conflict between Arstotzka and neighboring Kolechia, the player, an immigration officer for Arsotzka, has to decide based on varying rules who is or isn't allowed to enter Arstotzka.
Throughout the game, the player will be faced with tasks largely based around morality: Should this poor old woman be allowed to enter despite her expired passport? Should this refugee be allowed despite his criminal record? Is Cobrastan a real country? The game isn't vague with things and makes it clear the differences presented to the player: Money or Morality? With a family of five (and a sixth possible to adopt) to feed, shelter, and heat, the stakes are much higher and less personal and more interpersonal; it becomes logical to deny the masses illegally trying to enter Arstotzka as long as you're able to keep your family alive.
The rules for who can get into the country tend to change daily in the story mode, and the game makes sure to not keep the player too tired or too familiar with a single rule setup; One day people from the  United Federation will be barred due to a Polio outbreak there, another day they'll be allowed in as long as they bring a certificate that they were vaccinated. The game keeps the player on full alert, and tosses in new mechanics (terrorist attacks and rifles players can use to stop them, armed revolutionary groups willing to sneak through the border to overthrow the regime, etc) to keep the player both on edge and entertained, not allowing itself to fall flat or get boring during the 31 days the game has as its story mode.
In addition to story mode, there exists an endless mode which allows the player to compete against others internationally via Steam in regard to how many people they can get across in a period of time or other factors, such as how quick they can get through people correctly.
The game is a masterpiece in storytelling and narrative, and provides a great deal of stress and emotional impact with the player, along with excellent gameplay which is sure to keep your brain on high alert for a period of time after you finish up. I strongly suggest you buy this game if you enjoy 1984-esque worlds, or if you enjoy puzzle games in general.

Papers, Please is fantastic. It combines a charming artstyle, engrossing narrative and a truly unique set of core mechanics for a one-off experience.
You assume the role of a border inspector, and the gameplay revolves around allowing people to pass into a state, denying them, or detaining them. You don't want to know any more than that: the first run through is best done blind, experiencing all the plot twists/quirks as you choose and shape your own adventure. There are twenty endings. The game offers a nice difficulty curve, adding extra documents or rules with each "day" to keep you on your toes. It is never unfair.
The atmosphere, too, is great. The music recalls every Soviet stereotype you can think of, while the art style channels the bleak misery of 20th Century Post-Soviet Europe.
As a broader comment, the game also makes you appreciate/understand to a greater extent the job done by border guards. As a frequent traveller, border guards often seem obtuse or rude: in reality, as this game goes some way to demonstrate, the concentration and vigilance needed is remarkable.
For $10/£7, you cannot go wrong with Papers, Please. If it is in a sale, you have no excuse. Highly recommended.

-DO NOT BUY THE FIGHTER AS YOUR FIRST SHIP: if you do this, you will die a lot until you get used to the gamestyle

-Buy a Mule and a Raven as soon as possible: a small fleet of these is great for quick earning and good defense
-You do not need more than 3 Bactrians at most, as long as you stay in human space
-Shields are more important than anything else, and with good shields, you can just ignore pirates
-Despite what it may seem like the first time you die you DO respawn at the last world you were on
-ALWAYS look for good trade routes, even if it takes time
-NEVER attack a pirate  planet unless you are very sure you can win
That's about it.
Again, really fun game, I highly recommend it.

This is not a review of Spacebase DF-9, this is a review of Double Fine and their recent practices.  Below is an exact quote of post I made in the Spacebase DF-9 forums - (I give myself full permission to use my original post):
"Double Fine has lost all of my faith. There is nobody to blame but myself, and I accept that responsibility, but I am also formally stating that I will not be buying any more Double Fine games. I should have seen the problem during the Broken Age development cycle. Even after fleecing thousands of backers on their Kickstarter project and earning an unprecedented amount of money for a single game development (ie. through Kickstarter, making millions of dollars), they failed to deliver a complete game. That was the first and only sign necessary, and I should have known then.
Then, through their association with The Humble Bundle, they started making numerous other lofty promises - which I did not support based on the fact that they couldn't even finish Broken Age. However, somewhere in between all of that, and before the announcement that Broken Age was going to be released in two parts, I discovered Spacebase DF-9 and I really liked the look of it. Obviously, the folks at Double Fine were giving away keys like candy to every major reviewer and YouTube gamer out there, and the game looked like it would turn into something good. Unfortunately, although the game has evolved over that time since its somewhat buggy beginnings, Spacebase DF-9 still feels unfinished.
In the end, I realize now that I should not have supported Double Fine even though I believed that they were a studio of like-minded game creators and developers who loved games and were passionate about what they do. I was wrong, and spending money on their games is nobody's fault but my own. I do regret it now, but I've also learned from it and I promise never to make the same mistake again. I won't buy any other games made by Double Fine. I have nothing against the individuals at Double Fine, but it's blatantly obvious that Double Fine as a company, a studio, and a publisher, has mismanaged and misappropriated both their time and their money.
To think that Tim Schafer was waving wads of cash around (jokingly) after the first big Kickstarter, leaves me thinking that perhaps it wasn't a joke after all. Perhaps starting projects and then abandoning them, was all part of the plan. Maybe it was naive marketing and projection based on unrealistic sales forecasting. Or maybe it was the millions of dollars that were given, not only through Kickstarter but also The Humble Bundle, and at least a dozen other online gaming portals and retailers (including Steam), by the passionate gamers and hopeful individuals that wanted to see the "small company in a sea of big fish succeed", maybe all of that got to the heads of the people who are behind the decision making at Double Fine. Maybe it's one of those, or maybe it's none of the above.
Either way, Iesson learned. I'm not going to cry about getting my money back, I'm just never going to buy another Double Fine game. There are too many other "small" games studios that thrive under tight budgets and that could actually use the support of enthusiastic fans and customers."

To summarize: Good graphics and details, plenty of Final Fantasy references from the series, Boring most of the story and quests, no build or playstyle build customization, single player "online" in most of the content. For more personal remarks read below.
-------------------------------------------------------------
Plenty of references and music re arrangements from other games of the Final Fantasy Series. This is pretty much the only thing that i really appreciated from the game, having played the previous titles from 1 to 13 and some other chapters like on gba etc.
The maps and locations are confusing and somewhat not very intuitive to navigate, especially if your current objective is on an upper or lower level or in another area compared to your current location. As being said in other comments, plenty of invisible walls and limitations..
The combat system is barely challenging, and the mechanics simple. On certain instances / dungeons people gets♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and tells you to "read a guide" when you get into a boss fight for the first time, as if explaining to simply stay distant to X and avoid Y and use Z in that specific moment is that complicated that it needs to read a freaking guide. What else, do i need to get a FF14 graduation course and read 100 guides one for each boss i'm gonna fight? Which is not even that complicated to figure out in a few attempts?
Dungeons are uninteresting. Once you have it memorized there is one path to follow and the extra rooms are usually skipped. If you ever try to explore that extra room or slow down your pacing chances are you'll have someone in your party complaining and wanting to rush (see community part below).
Not that i would expect it from a Final Fantasy game since it never was its selling point, but there is no character class building or customization. Gear for each tier level comes with fixed stats. You pick a class and it will grow with fixed stats, also have perhaps only one or two ways to play it. Having the "choice" of bonus attribute points  between 6 type of stats is irrelevant, vit goes on tanks (if not maybe some str for late game but still not so relevant), str or dex on physical dps depending on the class, int on mages etc.
Content is locked behind story and side quests. You cannot join someone in a dungeon or a boss fight or an area or some other activity until you ran through the quest that unlocks that point, and which the process of unlocking and completing these quests you usually do it alone. And some of these take lots of time to complete. If you want to play in dungeons with your friends or clan members, well too bad you can't since first you'll have to run your own quests which are for the most part, played solo. It's funny cause some high level players who were like at item level 200 something couldn't join and help me in some "lower level" dungeons since they never did the side quests to unlock them. And some of these quests are quite long (as example Hildibrand quest series).
Most of the quests and story are boring and monotonous. You are one of the "warriors of light", and that's it. It will feel like you are a side character doing biddings for the other npc protagonists such as Alphinaud, Minfilia, Cid and the Scions of the Seventh Dawn. During important scenes you'll just stand there and watch the plot run its course, while your friends fights and gets hurt, the "bad guys" enact a coup of state, kidnap, kills, manipulate and do other generic things that bad guys do. Your character doesn't even talk, he/she will nod at least four times in every cutscene to the other npcs up to the point that it gets ridiculous or grin at max if they get somewhat upset. The story pacing goes like: "run from A to B, speak to this person, now go back to A, then go to C. Rinse and repeat for hundred of times in different areas. We have to save the country from a big danger but first pick up some water from the river and toss it to that person to wake it up. Oh right i'll give you papers to bring to this person then after tending his garden you can resume to fend off dangerous beasts and save the country".
The game is weirdly designed as a mix between a solo style where you play and advance your own quests, for the most time alone, and get cut off from the "online" part as you often are caught in cutscenes and instances which are restricted to single player. The times where you are actually playing with other players are during certain open field bosses or in dungeons / boss fights. For the rest, chances are you'll be playing the rest of the game content on your own, perhaps having some occasional chatting with your clan or friends (FC / Free Company) if you have them. You'll hardly need or be playing with other people for 90% of the content. No, running past another player who is doing their own thing and killing a mob targeted by someone else doesn't count as "playing online".
Sadly the final parts of the main story is where it started to get interesting and intriguing. Not before you run back and forth through uninteresting bland content for at least.. a week, or less if you really spend time and rush the main story.
Community is half decent and half sucks. And once a community starts to show toxicity it will only go downhill with time. As you advance in the game and get into harder dungeons or instances you'll see and deal progressively more with that worse side. There is not much of a point in playing an online game if the "online" part make you not want to play with it, is there? At least in my opinion.
The game has a good attention for detail graphically, but that's it. Most people find it to be a big deal, but not me.
Would i recommend it? No -- the online experience should be what a "FFXIV - Online" should be about, but it didn't feel like that to me.

But don't get me wrong that doesnt make this a bad game.
It is a grind-fest, but for those who like that sort of thing it's perfect. The mobs in the game are balanced well and I found myself needing to heal myself frequently.
It offers a decent variety of classes. (4 base classes, each with 2 advanced classes)
Quests are plentiful and will definitely help you get through the initial 20 levels of the game.
Stats are self allocated leading possibilities of many unique play-styles.
Skills are linear, everyone of the same class will get the same skills. The talent system makes up for it slightly, but it still would be nice to have a "skill-tree" system.
Bag space. It's not that big of a deal, but it is annoying at times and would be better if they gave us double the space.
Although the cash shop isn't that bad, the cash shop definitely saves a lot of time.
If you can get past these hurdles this game can definitely be something worth investing time into.

Transistor is by far the best single-player experience I've had in a while. This game quickly immersed me in its unique world and original story. The soundtrack was stellar, Darren Korb did a wonderful job, not to mention Ashley Barret's vocals. The gameplay was very strategy-based but managed to stay well-paced enough to keep me interested. But what really made the game for me was Logan Cunningham's performance as the Transistor.
The mere fact that the Transistor had a voice and personality was a great choice. Without him, the game would've felt lonely and fairly empty. The dynamic voice lines that made the Transistor react to situations made him feel a lot more real and I eventually fell infatuated with his and Red's relationship. The few other characters were also very well done, and the voice actors for them were all phenomenal.
The gameplay, as said before, was unusual but fun. The "turn" mechanic I had not seen in a game before, but it was very well polished. I found myself trying out functions left and right for new effects which proved very useful, less I go through the entire game with Joust as an Active Function. Many of the fights were simple once I understood the core mechanics, so I added "Limits" in order to challenge myself. I found this to make some specific fights harder, while most stayed the same difficulty.
The art and music added to the feel of the world's dystopian setting. I can't really describe this any better than it would be for you to just watch the trailer or pick up the game. Both are among the best that the video game industry has offered in this decade.
If you are looking for a fairly short game with a lot of replayability, this is definitely the game for you. While not the most challenging game, it's definitely one worth playing through once or twice or five times. Between the breathtaking ambience, stunning performance, and astounding story and gameplay, Transistor is definitely one of my favorite games from the last few years.

Transistor is a great little action RPG by the folks over at Supergiant Games.
What makes transistor great is that the game tells it's story through gameplay, you are barely taken out of te action (only sometimes during scenes where the camera pans over  a next section). For the rest you're always fighting or exploring. You are given the choice to play in real time (sort of as a hack and slash game) or quasi turn based (where you can plan out several attacks, but can't attack until your stamina gauge fills again). You have a lot of freedom in creating combo's to suit your playstyle and you gain more access to the lore of the game by doing so.
Transistor doesn't really rely on cutting edge graphics such as most AAA games, but it takes a much more thought out approach in this regard. The stylized graphics and beautiful artwork together with the amazing soundtrack create a cohesive style that will still look good in a couple of years, while other games will seem dated.
You can beat the game very quickly, however, if you indulge a bit more in the side content and explore a lot of the city you can easily take 7-8 hours for your first playthrough. There is a lot of missable side content and you occasionally have to say goodbye to your favorite combo's in order to gain access to more of the lore. Overall it's a fun game that plays well with kb+m as well as with a controller.

Put on your Sunday clothes, for its a nostalgic review.
Wall-E is and will always be my favourite Disney movie. When I was a kid back in 2008. I remember seeing the movie on my birthday and I remember becoming obsessed over it, so it was only natural that the game would fall into my hands. I got a Wall-E action figure, which still one of my prized possessions today, and I am writing this review with it by my side. I remember at the time I used to hum and sing the Hello, Dolly songs from the movie all of the time. Even though I only knew the segments that were in the movie/game. But as time went on and my young mind moved onto other things, the my disk copies of the movie and this game fell into oblivion. I only just remembered within the last two months that this game existed. I remembered the great and frustrating times I've had with this game on my old Windows XP. And now in December of 2017, as an young adult, I finally returned to this game to write my nostalgic review.
Wall-E the video game is predominately a puzzle solving platformer style game, with some racing style stages and rail shooter mixed in. The game has a similar storyline to that of the movie, but with some divergences. Between each chapter there is a cut scene, which is basically a shortened/simplified version of what happened in the movie. Of course, in these types of games you do inevitably get the, ‘what the hell do i do’ kind of moments. I remember as a kid spending what seem to be constant hours of prostration wondering what I should do, or trying to do that one jump, but in my new play through I didn't have nearly as much problems. But as a kid I never read the instructions, so that explains a lot.
It was and still is always a joy to hear the Hello, Dolly music every time I boot up the game, complete a chapter, and watch the credits, along with the games original soundtrack, which is unique to the game, but the soundtrack is not quite as impressive as I remember it to be. Also I found a quite surprisingly that in the credits of the game, every single musician involved in the making of the original soundtrack is credited in the credits under the instrument that they played. Though in the movie they used the version from the original 1969 Hello, Dolly movie, but in the game they use a reproduction version. A minor issue that I disapprove of.
Surprisingly to my adult self, the game isn't a complete and utter cash grab as I thought it was. A lot of time, effort, and content, has actually been put into the game. The main storyline took me roughly 6 hours to complete with some quite well designed and diverse stages. Heck, Wall-E the video game from 2008 has more content then the latest 2017 EA games.
I also like how the game has some after the credits stages, with Earth being colonised. The stages you saw at the start of the game are now green and lush, but crawling with enemies. There is also such a stage that takes place inside the Axiom as well. All something which I thought was a really nice feature, considering that we only have the ending credits of the movie to guess what happened. But is the video game ending technically cannon?
The game is not incredibly difficult to complete. But it's a kids game, what do you expect?
Unlike other older games on Windows 10 like Rome Total War and Fallout III, Wall-E starts up and runs perfectly well on Windows 10. No fiddling around with game files required. And the game at self is bug free. Only once I had to restart a chapter because of an one off issue with the level design.
Just like in the movie, Wall-E has a cassette player that plays Put on your Sunday Clothes. The cassette player is used to call/attract Reject robots to follow and to complete tasks, which is necessary to complete some chapters. This is definitely a really nice feature, but it would be great if you didn't have to hold Y all the time to play the cassette player
Now on to the negatives.
Wall-E normally costs twenty NZD, which for such an old game is very much overpriced. I got my steam copy for six NZD during the winter sale, which is far more reasonable. So only buy this game when it is on sale.
When you boot up the game for the very first time, a menu will pop up; a menu which is similar to the ones you see when you start up some unity games. At the time I wasn't aware of this, but it was a sort of an installation menu. This is the only menu in the game where you can adjust the resolution of the game. Because this game is made in the pre-wide screen days, unless you adjust the resolution, the game will look kind of stretched on modern screens, but the game was never meant to be graphically stunning anyway. So I think it is a necessary step when playing older games like Wall-E, to adjust the resolution accordingly. But once you press play on that menu you cannot open it up again, and no, you cannot adjust the resolution in the games options. You can only adjust sound and sensitivity in the options menu.
There is only four chapters in the main storyline where you get to play as Eve and all of those chapters are flying/timed races style stages. On none of the regular chapters can you play as Eve. I didn't think this was a problem when I was a kid, but looking back on it as an young adult it kind of is. She as an laser gun in her arm for crying out loud. In the cutscenes she can one shot the police robots. While I'm sitting there trying to deal with all the police robots. Just metres away, Eve is just standing there waiting for me to complete the puzzle and open the door. There is only one stage near the end of the game that is not in a cutscene, where you can see her actively flying around and gunning down enemies. Just something I thought while playing the game.
The Games camera, which is controlled via the mouse, can be really annoying inside tight spaces, especially when enemies at nearby. So the camera can be super annoying sometimes.
But overall, apart from some other minor issues. Wall-E the video game is actually quite a good and enjoyable game, especially if your playing for nostalgia sake. Again, only buy when on sale. I would give Wall-E a seven out of ten and a nostalgic seal of approval.

Note: This review is for both Hexcells, Hexcells Plus and Hexcells Infinite, because they're basically a single game divided in three parts.
The Hexcell games are a series of brilliant crafted puzzles that at first glance may seem like a six-sided minesweeper, but the logic used to solve them is closer to sudoku. As you progress through the levels, you are also introduced to some new mechanics accompained by a tutorial level to make sure that you understand them. Because the puzzles are carefully and wonderfully designed, you never have to guess your next move, but finding it gets hard in the later puzzles. The interface is clean and the sound effects are cool. Hexcells is easy, Hexcells Plus gets harder in the second half and Hexcells Infinite steps back a little at the beginning, but in the end offers the most challenging puzzles. It also comes with a seed-based puzzle generator, adding 999,999,999 additional puzzles (even if they aren't hand crafted, they're still good). My recommendation is that you get and play all three games in order, but if you can only pick one, pick Hexcells Infinite, it's main levels difficulty is nicely spread not to mention the puzzle generator.

Minecraft was a runaway hit, and since then many have tried to copy it. Voxelized is no different. After a rocky start, including 5+ months of no updates (despite a promise of "Beta in 2-3 weeks"), the game has finally started to see some updates. I played some of the game back when it was in "alpha", and I decided to come return to it with it in "beta".  What I found was a revamped game... but it's still not much better.
Voxelized's screen is extremely small, and it doesn't play well at all with the Steam Overlay. The screens you're shown are pretty much Minecraft (including one of the default splashes saying
). The world creation is an extremely stripped down version of Minecraft, and you can crash the game if you make it too large. When you enter the world, you're plopped into the very corner. You can enable flying mode to get above the sky box, or dig down to see the moon/sun as it goes below the world.
While in the alpha version, the most fun I could find was just going for an infinite loop with falling. The beta version provided even more fun - you can use dynamite to flat out break the game. Should you place it too close to the bottom, things start getting buggy. Place it (and explode it) on the very bottom layer? Things really start to break. (I have a video of this in my full article).
Voxelized is looking very promising at being a bad Minecraft. My suggestion is to just play one of those many other Minecraft clones out there (or just Minecraft itself) and just pass on Voxelized.

NOTE: THIS REVIEW IS NOT MY FINAL THOUGHTS OF THE GAME. IF MY OPINION CHANGES DRASTICALLY OR WHENEVER THE GAME IS RELEASED FROM EARLY ACCESS, I WILL REWRITE THIS REVIEW.
Do you or have you ever despised humanity? Do you like video games but you're tired of the same old shoot em ups? Do you want something (fairly) new and unique? Well, my friend, this is the right game for you!
Create a disease from a variety of disease types (which you have to unlock... fun), select special traits for your disease (also unlocked... more fun), select your difficulty, and infect Patient Zero. You then choose some skills to evolve your plague to make it more lethal, easier to infect others, or resist outside forces (i.e. temperature and drugs). Unfortunately the governments of the countries aren't very keen on the idea of you eliminating the human race, so they'll shut borders, airports and harbors and try to cure your disease, so you'll have to race against the clock to infect the world and evolve enough lethal symptoms to kill the world. Rinse and repeat.
The gameplay is fun, there is a bit of strategy on choosing which country to infect, whether you want to be able to infect by air or water first or if you want to invest some points to get bonus infectivity in colder countries. More strategy comes when you get traits for your disease, since they add bonuses to infectivity, extra DNA points, and a couple more nifty abilities. Each disease has some varying traits, like virus evolving frequently, biodisease being so deadly you have to suppress the lethality, nano-virus being built in with a kill switch that you must race against, and there are much more. It's worth it to unlock the diseases, since some of the cooler ones like Neurax Worm (mindcontrol) and Necroa Virus (zombies) are unlocked a bit later and it's always fun to mess around with those. There are also random events that happen that will affect the game, making each experience different.
The display looks nice and it's easy enough to see what's going on. There's a cool little body chart that shows you where in the human body your disease affects. You can see what's going on in all countries, how they're combating your plague, how their cure research is coming along, and if the government is still stable there or if it's falling apart.
There are also scenarios where you mess around with stuff, mostly stuff like little to none plane transmission, a mirror version of Earth where all of the countries characteristics are reversed, a virus that's DNA is damaged, affecting its transmission, and some more. Steam Workshop also makes an appearance, letting you create your own scenario. The communuty for this game is pretty large and I can see multiplayer being popular when the dev releases it.
There are some problems I had with the game, most of them small however. Mostly minor stuff like Portugal being part of Spain, Alaska being part of Canada (to be fair, the dev makes fun of this in an event so I dont care about that :P), Hawaii being nowhere to be seen yet, minor stuff like that. I can see this game becoming a bit repetetive, but it hasn't become that for me yet. One thing I would like to see, though, are different... I guess maps, you'd call them. Stuff like the continental USA with all of the states instead of the whole world, the providences of Canada, a map where the melting of the ice caps has flooded the world, stuff like that. That would make the game more replayable.
Regardless of any criticisms I may have, Plague Inc Evolved is a breath of fresh air with plenty to offer and more to come. 9/10. Never has a game made me hate a country for no good reason like this one has. Goddamn Greenland... Anyway, get this game now. It's worth it even at the full $15 or your regional equivelant. Just know that this is an Early Access game, so the game isn't complete yet. However the dev updates frequently, so it could be coming out of Early Access soon. Either way, though, it's worth getting. So get it. NOW!

Though this game had its development cut short, which was admittedly disappointing, its is still a solid game and one of the better city sims I have played in a while. So please, before judging solely on the fact that development was cut short, hear me out. If you wanna skip the points i will have a final verdict at the end
Pros
1. No preset rooms, you build how you want
2. Dialogue is rather humorous and reading people's thoughts normally gives me a good laugh.
3. The resource management is just right, not too complex, but not too easy either.
4. Since there are no templates you can really make your base yours. If you want the center of your base to be a nice dorm room thats totally doable. If you want to make it a huge club, all up to you!
5. The game keeps you on your toes and often provides great stories such as when one of my engineers went crazy and caught an oxygen recycler on fire and had to be taken down by security!
6. People interact and all have different opinions of each other. They may become best friends or end up knocking each other out!
7. Passing ships will signal you, you may recruit a bunch of aliens waking from their cryo chambers or tell raiders you're gonna kick their butts!
Cons
1. Raiders get a bit overpowered in later stages of the game
2. Morale is hard to regain after it drops and often leads to the end of your base
3. dialogue, while funny is quite limited. You will definitely see the same phrases more than once.
4. This game had insane potential, unfortunately many concept ideas that would have been great will now never be included
Final verdict: While it isnt a perfect game, spacebase possesses a lot of charm and an amazing amount of freedom. If you are a fan of sim games and think this may interest you, at least grab it on sale. Its a great sim game that has many disappointed fans who look at it for what it could have been rather than what it is

If they don’t leave you to figure out the other rooms and the way the spacebase generally functions then you would have played all there is to play of this game in the tutorial. Ultimately the tutorial just seems to highlight the lack of depth to the game.
Spacebase has a rocky history so far, and I feel I really must include a discussion of this so that you can make an informed decision. However, as you will see with the format of my reviews, there are plenty of sections which allow me to consider the game for itself regardless of the surrounding drama.
In the interests of full disclosure: I was an early access purchaser, and yeah, I did get burned with this game. My experience with Spacebase truly set my mind to never buy an early access game ever again, no matter how wonderful it looks and tempting it seems. Nothing is a sure bet, and I will only be spending my money on finished products from now on. I can accept that I took a risk by purchasing an EA game and that it did not pan out in this case, but the end result is still a bad experience with Spacebase and Double Fine by extension. Things did get very dramatic, but I don’t think the company did a very good job of handling things. I’m not going to go on about it, so suffice it to say that I’m not an admirer of Double Fine any more. If you want more information regarding the drama I refer to, please check out TotalBiscuit’s discussion on the subject.
This is a base building game. You build a space station from basic building blocks (floors and walls) and zone different rooms. You fill those rooms with things like oxygen tanks, plants, beds, exercise equipment, tables, food, defence turrets, fire extinguishers, science labs, and matter converters. Mine asteroids to refine into matter, the basic building block/currency of the game in order to build everything else.
There isn’t exactly a tech tree to this game, and there aren’t any crafting recipes (although there is scientific research). It seems to be more about the simulation of how people interact with one another, but there are so many characters that join your base that it’s impossible to really follow many interactions in a very meaningful way. So I end up concentrating on building the base and trying to see just how big I can make it. Once you get a vast crew though, things start lagging up and the bugs start to get obvious. Ultimately you will find that there is an imposed limit on how big a base you can create and keep running not by design, but because (I'm afraid I must repeat) this game wasn't really completed.
I really desperately wish that there was a blueprint function (like in prison architect) so that one could plan their base out before starting construction.
Although you can use the mouse to do everything, there are thankfully plenty of hotkeys. Some of them aren’t as intuitive as I might like, but I got used to them over the course of many hours of play. I found the camera controls to be fairly good, with my most appreciated camera functionality being the ability to pan around. It’s also always a plus to have a simple pause/start button to hit, which is good old spacebar.
I can’t say there is much of a storyline. I think the original intention for the game was to immerse yourself in the lives of the different people on the base and sort of imagine your own story. However, there isn’t sufficient depth and breadth to the rest of the game to allow you to direct any sort of imaginary storyline. It was an interesting concept which didn’t really get developed or thought through well enough.
I really like the sound in this game. The music is quite atmospheric (appropriate to the universe they created) and interesting to listen to. It may get repetitive after a while, but it is more like it fades into the background of your awareness rather than becoming irritating. Meanwhile, the sound effects are pretty much functional, nothing much to warrant remark.
The artwork in this game is really very good. It’s certainly got a specific style to it, however that style is stuck to throughout and that consistency helps to establish a weird and wonderful universe. I really only have good things to say about the graphics, it’s a shame that all this creative work is now trapped in the wrapper of the rest of the game. Alas.

I LOVED this. First of all, I squealed over every new page of 200x-related icons - so much nostalgia. It's free, just play it, hop into the time machine for half an hour.
Looking beyond the "OMAYGAWD teenage me got SO hurt and angsty over EXACTLY THIS"-circlejerk for a moment, I lovelovelove the writing in this game. I very much related to both protagonists and I found it a nice note that the genders could have easily been switched with a few adjustments; it's a game about friendship, empathy, missing chances and, yes, teenage awkwardness in dealing with "the feels". For me personally, the answers I picked often typed out exactly - and I mean word for word - the way I would have formulated them. I don't know what exactly that says about me or the game, but I really liked it.
I also liked the realness of both sides of the experience this managed to capture. That it's not about loser-boy and perfection-girl (or v.v.), but about two HS friends who kinda sorta like each other, but never quite found their way into being together as "more" than friends - and about how there's much more to life than that one relationship, which is good, but also the main reason it never evolves to the next level. Of course it's up to everyone how to interpret the nuances here, but I would urge every player to not get lost too much in recalling the angst; if anything, this shows that we somehow all went through this and this game captures the very specific experience of it happening through IM-ing very nicely. I definitely had a somewhat hurtful, somewhat warming feeling of recalling similar conversations that never really went where you wanted them to go... at least eventually.
Also: Easy achievements for my fellow completionists!

No seriously. I almost feel dirty for having bought this discounted at SGD4 (compared to the original SGD20.. Or whatever it was, can't remember). This is one game that I would be willing to pay full price for and for so many good reasons too. And you know what is the best part about it? This isn't even the sort of game I would ever imagine myself playing... But damn did I play it anyway and damn did I enjoy it. Bloody. Hell. This stands out as exceptionally stellar and I am sure if I had played it on release, it would have been my game of the year hands down.
But enough of that bootlicking. Why is this so good? Well allow me...
The gameplay is a unique blend of turn-based tactical and action RPG. But to me, that is just an interesting tidbit. The real meat here are the many skills available in the game and how they interact with each other. In this game, you can set skills in three particular positions, as an active skill, an upgrade or a passive ability. Due to that, each skill has got three different versions that could be mixed and matched to create your personal style. Wanted to add lifesteal to that super awesome bolt? Bam, you can do it. Wanna create a bomb that can suck everyone in so you don't have to set anything up? Boom, done.
I've went through my first run changing up my skillset so much that by the end of it, though I was essentially using the same skills, they no longer looked the same. Did I also mention that the skills also look a little different when you mix up the matching? Jeez, if more games were to emulate the way skills worked here... Believe me, I'll throw my money at the games company just for them doing that.
It's certainly no Final Fantasy or some next-gen graphics. They went instead for an aesthetic thats undoubtedly based on Bastion I suppose it's fair to say. And mind you, I'm no artist or some art critic, but damn was the whole aesthetic just... Beautiful. It's not just the combat and skill animations either. Really, everything from the backgrounds to the occasional cut-scenes. I don't know what else to say aside from... Well, it's some beautiful♥♥♥♥♥♥right there.
Now music is easier to talk about right? Right? ... I'm no music critic either, but the music in this game was really on point. Fun fact: pressing TAB when out of battle makes your character hum. I didn't care much for it, but then there was one location where the background music was just a thumping beat over some instrumentals. Tried TAB-ing that♥♥♥♥♥♥ IT SYNCS TO THAT BACKGROUND, and suddenly the pure-instrumental background music suddenly has a voice humming to it.
That said, even the background music itself is on point in a lot of the situations, with the appropriate emotion matching the situation.
Finally, one of the aspects I appreciate most about the game was the plot and characters. I've played way too many games and watched too many dramas. Tropes have become quite an annoyance as a result. I admit they are inevitable, and even this game does not avoid several, but it struck me as an exceptionally unique piece of story-telling. This ties in well with the characterization, particularly that of the protagonist's partner, whose relationship was demonstrated by means of their interactions (albeit subtle). I greatly appreciate the fact that they never felt the need to create any exposition to explicitly lay out the relationships. That I feel is a mark of good story-telling and characterization.
The voice-acting also helps. For one, the one person that talks the most in the entire game has a pretty cool voice. Then the other two characters that do talk do a great job at conveying their emotions in appropriate fashion. Might be a small spoiler to mention but some examples below (in spoiler tag). But yeah, great voice acting, I feel.

Heads up: this is the final game in the Hexcells series. If you haven't played any of the previous games, I highly recommend buying the original Hexcells before buying Hexcells infinite. While this game can be played without the previous two games, it's much harder to comprehend the scenarios and best moves without the original game as a guide/starter.
If you've played the previous two games, Hexcells Infinite amps up the difficulty. As a personal analogy, I didn't have much trouble with the first game until somewhere around World 6. On the second game, I started running into trouble about halfway through World 4/beginning of World 5. In Hexcells Infinite, I'm running into blocks around late World 3/early World 4.
The random puzzle generator works as intended; all puzzles that came up for me were all unique solutions. On average, the puzzles seemed reminiscent of Hexcells Plus in their difficulty; I think the main levels in Hexcells Infinite were, on average, harder than the randomly-generated puzzles.
Hexcells Infinite delivers on it's promise and is a satisfying last game of the series. I highly recommend this game and its predecessors to anybody who likes puzzle games.

Throughout my life, and perhaps many other lives that people have had, there's always this one phase related to a movie, TV show, or video game
and you just can't shake it off your mind. WALL-E is the biggest example of a game AND movie like that. And to be completely fair, this game ISN'T shovelware, unlike most IPs based on movies and shows!
WALL-E is a game published by THQ and Developed by  Asobo Studio, and man does it impress me. Whilst the story is a bit rushed in the cutscenes in game and it doesn't exactly match the movie it's based off of, this game is amazing not only for the fact that it's not shovelware, and that it plays extremely well. The real "Flaws" I call in the full review are really just nitpicks.
If you aern't aware, in this game you take control as the two main characters of the movie, WALL-E and EVE. Most of the time you're playing as WALL-E, but there are certain sections that you can play as her aswell. The pacing is pretty dang good, having the action segments and collecting item segments keep you engaged. And truth-be-told, the experience is pretty absorbing. Even though there is very little replay value, it does a good job of keeping you in the whole way through with the secondary objectives other than to go through the WALL-E Story, playing with friends. Overall I really feel the gameplay works, and doesn't feel too gimmicky or bland when playing through the story. One gripe I do have, is the way the secondary objectives work on action maps and sometimes the more confusing collecting item maps. If you miss one thing for those secondary objectives, you can't restart and you have to go back out to the chapter menu first then pick the mission you missed all the crates for. This can take a lot longer, since you actually have to play the level and re-collect everything. Itteration time is not a friend here.
I actually can say I owned this game before it came out on steam, and came out for the PS2/Original XBOX. There is another game for the PS3/XBOX360, and they are completely different. If it ever comes on steam, I might do a review. Since I never really played PS2 for games excluding this one, I can't say for certain if the quality of the graphics are good enough. Although, I do feel the game is capped at 30FPS and the graphical settings are turned down (Minus the fact they are set to 'high') since the PS3 and XBOX360 were out by this time. Even though this is the case, I gotta say, either because a GTX 1060 wasn't even a glimmer in NVIDIA'S eye by the time this was first release, I do like how there are no loading times AT ALL. Either that, or the manditory unskippable cutscenes do a good job of fooling you into not paying attention to load times. Which was a smart move, I gotta say.
One thing that makes me hate this game with a passion
is the fact that every time you die, you always get these super cruel cutscenes showing WALL-E falling into oblivion, looking up at you in the light like a ASPCA PSA, and it really hits me in the feels, man. Zenyatta would not be happy about this.
If you're a fan of the curious little robot trash compactor, I whole-heartedly recommend this game. It may have some small flaws, but it shows how shovelware is beginning to slow down and that good movie games do exist.

NOTE: you MUST set the In-Game Jump key and the Menu-Confirm key to the same button, or else you'll get stuck.
Review:
This game is a really fun 3D Platformer.
It brings a very interesting twist on platforming, as Wall-e, being a robot, can not jump very high.
However, if Wall-e uses a ramp and gains some speed, he can really leap very far.
This adds a lot of dynamic to the game.
The game also has a great variety of stages. There's platforming stages, exploration/collectaphon stages, speeding stages, flying stages, and shooting stages.
And while it starts pretty easy, it does get more difficult later on, as platforming will get more difficult, and enemies will try to prevent you from making progress.
Most of the stages also have collectables for you to find, which consist on BNL crates you can break, and Artificats you can collect. This adds a lot of replay value if you're into those kind of things.
My only complaint is that the later levels get pretty long, and the checkpoints are few and far between. Which means, if you have to quit, you might not have enought time to reach the next checkpoint, and therefor have to leave, erasing some progress.
The "video cutscenes" also don't look very well on modern computers, and the fact that you can't scip them can get annoying. However, the cutscenes made on the game's engine are very well made, and althought they don't give you the feelings you would get from watching the movie, the story is still very well presented. Both the Earth and the Axiom look great, giving you 2 very different enviorment styles - the junk that has piles up on earth, and the cleanness modern coridors of a space ship.
Overall, this game is a very enjopyable experience.
Just remember that this is a 2008 game, and a port of a PS2/PSP game, so expect to see PS2 graphics.
But they still look great.
I really like this game, it was a big part of my childhood, and even to this day I still have a lot of fun playing it. However, I recommend using a controller instead of keyboard.

Wobbly Jungle is a difficult little platformer that is a great way to pass some time. The art style is colourful and simple, and the level design is ensured to keep you on your toes, introducing various new obstacles and enemies that you will need to avoid. A game-pad is definitely recommended for this game, it really gives you a lot more control over your character. There is a good amount (60) of levels, and plenty of action in each and every one of them. You will be forced to negotiate your way past buzzing saw-blades, jump onto moving platforms, make leaps of faith over the unknown, and much more. A very nice little game to keep you entertained, and you easily get your moneys worth!
>Nice art style
>Difficult without being impossible
>Simple mechanics and controls
>A good amount of levels with a decent amount of variety
>Music can get quite repetitive, but cannot be muted
>Occasionally a little buggy when jumping and landing on saw-blades (I managed to encounter a bug at one stage where I became invincible and passed through obstacles)
A neat little game, great to play when you feel like a challenge.

Forget the cute graphics and presentation. Sourena Game Studio’s second game on Steam, Wobbly Jungle, is one of the most difficult precision platformers that I have ever played. And that’s a wonderful thing. The studio based in Iran previously developed Legends of Persia (not to be mistaken with Ubisoft’s Prince of Persia franchise). I have to admit that I was almost going to quit the game without having completed the second level as it wasn’t immediately clear where I had to go after reaching a certain point in the level. Thankfully the skill that was being taught in that level, the double jump, held the answer to my prayer and I was able to continue on and complete the level.
I unfortunately do not have very much to write about the game because of just how difficult the game is. This is a game that I want to dedicate some time to so that I can write a better review. I find the graphical presentation to be more than suitable except when you’re left guessing at what is off screen which resulted in most of my deaths. I would argue that this is unfair but that’s my personal opinion. The music sounds good but unfortunately becomes quite repetitive. This is a little bit of a disappointment because had the soundtrack been more varied it would have been a very good soundtrack. The controls are a little on the floaty side but not to the point where it is a detriment to the game. If you spend enough time with the game they will become comfortable.
Although I haven’t gotten very far into the game as of yet I am definitely leaning on the positive side. There’s just the right amount of charm to keep you engaged with the game thanks to good, not great, production values and factoring the sub-$5 price tag.

+ For a platformer this game has very fine tuned controls, very precise and fluid movements similar to Super Meat Boy
+ Very cute and colorful levels and creatures
+ Upbeat background music (in combination with the level design it made me smile)
+ Slowly introduces new mechanics and challenging enemies
- I would have liked to have seen more variety in the environments, music, and more story elements
- Since you can't zoom out, there are a LOT of jumps that are "leaps of faiths" or in other words you can't see where you are jumping or falling to and this can sometimes lead to deaths / starting the level over if you fall or miss a platform.
Decent game that does not bring anything new to the table and is P2W.

In short, don't support this game if you're not into another very generic MMO rpg that better belongs with it's browser brothern. Thumbs down and I'm uninstalling.

EDITED: My previous negative review stated it would remain negative until Tim Schafer released a statement of apology. He did so, and although it didn't addrerss every issue I had with the way things were handled, it did address a lot of them and was an apology I felt was sincere.
The harshness of my previous review was due to anger seeing an early access game come to a sudden halt (Tim Schafer does address the lack of communication and the lessons learned from this experience. He specifically apologizes for the communication issue which was my main problem. Had there been communication about the state of things before hand, I would not have been upset. I would have been sad, but not angry. So I appreciate the fact that Double Fine realized their mistakes and apologized for them.) -- it was not, and I feel bad for not making this clear in my past review, but anger clouded my communication skills... -- it was not a negative review targeting the quality of the game.
In fact, I really enjoy Spacebase, which is why I became angry. It's a game that from the beginning of early access, was getting things right. Yeah, there was rough patches, but the core of the game and vision was there and I was excited. And whether or not the finished game met all the "features we want in the game" dev list or not was not an issue for me. And my anger was not really aimed at the devs of Spacebase, really. I was angry at Tim Schafer. I'm stating this due to the amount of anger that has been directed at the developers. I think they've done a great job developing the game. Communication was not there. But that was an issue with Double Fine as a whole, not just this one development team.
So, going from a thumbs down to a thumbs up becaue of an apology might seem odd to some people. And that's my fault for not being clear as to why it was getting at thumbs down. It's a good game. As it stands. And I'm sure it will be better when they release the last update. Am I sad that they weren't able to achieve what they wanted to? Yeah. But is the game bad because they weren't able to work on the game actively for a few more years? No. It's a good game.
I'll be curious to see what happens when the community has the ability to create mods and etc and curious to see how if Double Fine keeps an eye on things and maybe works out a way to be there in the form of a helpful guide to the community down the road.
Developers of Spacebase, you made a great game and I'm sorry you were unable to work on it as long as you wanted to. As long as I wanted you to, as well. And thank you, Tim Schafer, for you apology. It wasn't "perfect", but it was an apology I felt was sincere and that's what I needed. And yes, I know that addressing the devs and Tim Schafer in my review is silly (I don't expect them to read this.) It's what I want to include in my review. *shrugs*.

Structure of this review:
The story of this game is rather simple and nothing with the depth of a high tier novel. (I sincerely hope that this game isn't based on one, if it is, I'll immediantly change this part)
Arstotzka ended its war against Kolechia recently. As a result, Grestin, the city you live in, is the border vetween the countries and a lot of people want to immigrate to Arstotzka.
You play a border inspector, to be specific, a passport inspector. It is your duty to check the passports. While playing, you will encounter an organization which wants change the state of the country by revolting against the state. You can either join them (secretly) or be a loyal citizen. But I'll come to that later.
The gameplaymechanics are rather simple:
You are in your small (glorious) booth with a (glorious) mic, a (glorious) book for all the important information you get from the (glorious) government, a paper with what has been said between you and the inspected, (glorious) stamps for accepting or denieal and some other (glorious) improvements which benefit your (glorious) life a lot. They are mainly checks if information is right and hotkeys to spare some time.
But how do you get these upgrades? By buying them! And how do you earn money? By checking trespassers' passports (this hurt my tongue). The more tresspassers' passports you check before your shift is over, the more money you get. But ofc, living in (glorious) Arstotzka costs you money! Heat, food and rent are things you need to take care of. And because you don't live alone, you can't just use 100000 blankets to cover yourself at night. If you think you didn't earn enough money the last day, you
neglect food and heat. The positive sideeffects: You have a bit more money! The negative sideeffects: You, your (glorious) wife, your (glorious) son and your (filthy) mother-in-law are cold. If you let them freeze for longer than 1 day(except the son, he might get sick instantly), they will get sick and eventually die if you don't buy medicine (I'd be ok if it'd only effect the M-I-L.
).
BTW: Certain events will occur from time to time, these usually cost you a bit of your hard-earned money if you consider paying for them. Yes, you dont have to pay for them. But can you live with the consequences...?
Back to actual gameplay!
So after a few days, you will notice that you won't only have to let (glorious) Arstotzkan people pass, but also people from other countries. If certain conditions are met, which the (glorious) government tell you at the beginning of each day by looking into your (glorious) notebook. If all of the conditions are met, you did a great job and the government will be pleased. Overlook one of the conditions and the government will be rather...unpleasent. While they tolerate 2 mistakes per day, you will recieve money penalties after that. And since money is very important, you don't want that to happen.
Conditions quickly said: Starting with a passport only, it continues with additional papers and ends up with seperate paper(s) or passes for different groups of tresspassers. While at first you only need to check for the expiration date, you will start to check for the gender, age, exact numbers of passport, picture and so on. It might seem easy at first, but again: The more time you need the less money you earn. The game won't make it easy for you in the mid to late game. But I bet you were aware of that...right?
But the life of a post-war-border-passport-inspector-of-glorious-Arstotzka-in-east-Grestin is just as exciting as the length of the word I just used! As I already mentioned, there is a organization called
which wants to end the "terrible (glorious) government" of Arstotzka. What your part is in this? They will try to get into the country to do their operations. And which border is the best?
. They will try to persuade you by giving you a few "missions" to do to help them. It's up to you if you will secretly work with them to crush your (glorious) country or stay loyal and be a respected (glorious) member of Arstotzka.
But that isn't the only exciting thing that will happen to you. Sometimes you will talk with a few people, they are either bothered, have a story to tell to which you will have to react as a human being or just plain funny (1234-okok).
Just remember:
Oh, I almost forgot: The graphics of this game are plain simple: pixelated, simple and rather cold coloured.
Graphic-wh***s might be might be instantly uninterested but actually: It's all about the gameplay, right?

Possibly one of the best puzzle games of all time. The hand crafted puzzles offer are a challenge and will no doubt make you think logically. If you just want to finish the game, then it might not take you that long, but I personally believe that the game is meant to be played like a perfectionist. It is far more fun and rewarding to attempt to finish every puzzle without making a single mistake. That will take you a few hours, if not more.
After finishing all of the puzzles, you can then move onto the infinite mode, where there are enough puzzles to last you a lifetime. As one might expect, the puzzles are in no way superior to the hand crafted ones, but they still offer a fantastic challenge and will challenge you in similar ways to the HexCell puzzles you are used to. If you are a fan of puzzles in any form you can possibly think of, there is no doubt in my mind that HexCells Infinite would be a great game to add to your collection.

Firstly, I wanna point out this game's community. Despite being small, the game has a decent community around it.
Let's move into gameplay. The game handles well, and while it depends mostly on RNG(randomization), there is a level of skill and planning involved. If you just jump around, expecting nothing bad will/could happen, you will probably be disappointed. Mostly everything is balanced well, and with every game, it's not perfect.
Next up, story. While the main campaign isn't the most compelling story I've ever seen, it has its merits. Involving the games lore, it holds up pretty well. But, it does feel like there's progression and character development. One thing I wish is that the characters had more to them. As in, being involved in there own sub-plots, for example, a character learning more about their own morals or getting over a dispute with a long time rival.
Dynamics. In the world of video games, the words "dynamics" and "mechanics" are often used interchangeably. Dynamics refers to the part of the game you see, which is born from the mechanics. The dynamic aspects in general are well thought out. Better drives take more fuel, and giving more ways to gain said fuel is a nice addition. Combat feels difficult, but polished and fair. The other races,
have their own strong points, yet also have clear weaknesses, even if you can't, at that moment, exploit them.
There's also a VERY STRONG sense of mystery in the game. The first time through, I was TERRIFIED to go outside the areas I've discovered, as I thought they'd be full of pirates. However, once you step out of your comfort zone, you find that, no matter where you go, there's always risk involved, and taking that risk could lead to great benefits. Or your untimely death. When I first beat the campaign,

I will also admit that the game has its faults. While not entirely a fault,
The game doesn't always make full use of some features. Such as Combat Rating. It's almost entirely pointless until it gets higher up, and even then, it has limited uses. I'll give this game credit though, since it's still in its more developmental stages.
A lovely addition, although complex in nature, would be player-governed systems. Terraforming is mentioned a couple times in the game, and it could be used by the player. This would allow a great many uninhabitable places to be built upon.
Another topic, I only recently considered: the developers. While no dev team can spend 100% of their focus on the player-base, it seems like many bugs get fixed in decent time, here. Not only that, but players can actually contribute to the development of the game. This is definitely an aspect I adore.
Overall, I love this game, and I would definitely recommend it to anyone. If you're able to overlook the graphics, the game plays very well. 9.8/10.

I'm in love with Endless Sky. It is very much a spiritual successor to Escape Velocity. The look and feel are unmistakable. That alone scores it big points with me, since it scratches an itch that hasn't been scratched in a long time.
But it's not a simple clone. Endless Sky preserves the basic design of EV but improves on it in many ways. Fleets are the big one, and ES is way more flexible in that regard. I don't think there's any hard limit to how many ships you can command (money and CPU cycles being the limiting factors), and you are able to fully customize them as you would your own.
And, of course, the game is free and open source. Modding is a cinch and makes it easy for the community to contribute. The developer is also hard at work providing new updates; as of this review, the 0.9.0 beta has been out for a few weeks, and I have to say it is quite impressive.
This bodes well for the game, since right now the one area where it is lacking is content. EV: Nova had 6 extensive story campaigns, whereas ES still has just one. Though far from being a complaint, I am excited to see what is still to come, since what story I've seen so far is impeccably written. The game already has an intriguing backstory in place, scattered about in the flavor text and various hidden side quests and alien races, with plenty of room to grow in future updates.

Endless Sky is kinda like if EV Nova was a bit too fast paced, focused heavily on having a fleet rather than your warship doing the work, and loaded the pirates up with heavy weaponry on basically every pirate ship.
Otherwise it's very similar. Same grind to earn money/reputation, same obscure way to start plot(s), same tendency to sort of abruptly murder the player.
I'll be coming back to the game once the modders get their teeth into it, hopefully adding something like the railguns from EV Nova (my favorite weapon, sadly missing here). For now, I'd say wait til further in development.

A few months ago I likely would have recommended this game. While development was fairly slow, they were making progress and the game was getting better. I was hopeful for the future as the game had, in my opinion, a very solid foundation.
With the news that this game is now only getting one more major patch; I can no longer in good faith recommend it to anybody. This game was initially touted as a 'Sci-Fi Dwarf Fortress," but make no mistake, it offers nowehere near the complexity or longevity, The feature list is incredibly underwhelming for a sim game of it's type, and you will very quickly lose interest in the little this game has to offer. After a few hours you will have experienced absolutely everything. They could have done so much more with the concept, (and planned to,) but nothing in this game will strike you as particularly unique or groundbreaking. The fact of the matter is this game seriously underdeliverd on the features that were going to distinguish it from other games in the genre. You can go back and look at the archived dev plans to get an idea.
Of course, this was always the danger of early access. There's no guarantee that the game you fund will make it to it's fully realized state. If a game becomes unprofitable; they'll ship it in it's current state regardless of planned features. As far as I know, this is the highest profile early access game that has seriously underdelivered. Let it serve you as a warning when buying other early access titles. After this I don't think I'll be putting money behind any more games that have a chance to be released so woefully unfinished.

When I first looked at this game I didn't expect much from it. Looked like a very basic, simple platformer. And whilst it isn't revolutionizing the genre, it certainly did a very good job at offering challenging, long lasting and varying gameplay.
The controls are very basic - move and jump - with the addition of double jumps and wall jumps.
Whilst the game seemed to be quite simple at the first few levels, I soon was faced with a repertory of crazy and challenging
twists - forcing me to act both fast, and cleverly.
The game offers 60 levels, which come with lots of hours of diverse adventure.
The only real problem I encountered whilst ingame, was the camera management - often you don't see where you need to jump and you're just forced to leap and hope for the best.
Thus, the gameplay overall is solid, what is missing are some other things:
The menus are very confusing and lack some features (for instance the ability to manage the volume!), and the game comes
with only one track, which repeats every 3 minutes.
Furthermore, great potential was given up, by leaving out the ability to create own levels and share those.
+High variety in gameplay
+A lot of content
+Challenging
+Simple controls
-Poor menu management
-Soundtrack consists of one track
Alltogether I can praise this game for both its length and challenge and can only recommend it.

When I first looked at this side-scrolling platformer, I've known at once it will be like Mario (Mario with edited levels, to be precise). And I doubted I'll manage to make a quick run with it.
Boy, I was right. The game is quite challenging just from the start, and I really don't know how many hours of pain and rage-quitting it will bring to people, but I'm sure there will be plenty.
I'm still not that deep into to name Wobbly Jungle a rival for the Super Meat Boy... But surely, it is much, so much more killing than any of the Dark Souls, self-proclaimed "hard games".
So. The game is tough and challenging, yet gratifying. I strongly recommend to use a joystick, though, as your keyboard arrows and space button aren't that precise and durable, as the game demanding.
The only noticeable downside of the game (unless you're a sissy which afraid of the real challenge) - is music. Sure, the looped track sounds nice... for a first hour or so. Yet, there are absolutely no means to tune the volume in the game. It really, really lacking such option. Jeez, even the most most basic flash games have a "mute" button at least! I really hope the devs will do something about it, as the frustration is growing with every hour I'm spending on the same level, with the same track - without the possibility to do something about it!
So far I can recommend the game for the little sessions (about 10-30 minutes long) for the players who are fit to break hard platformer games. This little piggy holds much we're all so fond of, from the times of the first Mario game.
My mark 7.1/10.

Hexcells Infinite is the third game of its' series. Previous game: Hexcells and Hexcells Plus.
There isn't much can be said about the game's visuals asides from that they're minimalistic. Pretty much the same thing can be said about the game's audio.
There is no difficulty mode option that's assigned. But each of the puzzles has their own difficult.
Hexcells Infinite basically has same formula as its' predecessors Hexcells and Hexcells Infinite. So the objective remains the same. Which is to figure out which cells to make blue and which cells to make black.
There are total of three slots with six worlds that has thirty-six puzzles to solve. The first world for each of the three slots are automatically unlocked. Completing one world will unlocked the next one. All of these puzzles can be replayed after the first go around. Please do note that the puzzles in the other two slots are the same as the ones in the first slot.
There is a special feature bonus that Hexcell Infinite has. Right beneath the three slots, there's an option for continous gameplay of Hexcells. Henced why the game called Hexcell Infinite. The special feature bonus gameplay can be customized in many different ways that the regular gameplay of Hexcells cannot.

The game itself is a wondeful world of experience but the battle system is fundamentally flawed. Its something big fans like me ignore mostly and Sqenix themselves pretend is a feature not a bug (which in this day and age, for a team as supposedly talented as Sqenix, is frankly embarrasing. If you are familiar with telegraph systems in mmos you can skip a bit, if not, here it is. Telegraphs are sigils on the ground that indicate the direction (and sometimes ferocity and speed) of incoming attacks. Basically you must step out of the telegraph before the attack happens. The telegraphs do not properly discern who is stationary (being a nub), who is edging (healers for instance timing one last heal before moving out the telegraph) and who is even fully outside of the telegraph. You will find yourself (especially if you play other telegraph system games like the funny space one i cant remember) being constantly hit by moves that you were no where near the telegraph for. Its infuriating and it does essentially break the game if you choose to let it. It renders battle utterly preposterous for any serious gamer. Its my assumption based upon what i know that the bug is far too deep in the game engine to fix without recoding the entire battle system and so the bug has become inherent. Again, if you don't mind an entirely innaccurate battle phase or three this wont be a problem. Again, my advice? Don't bother.

Was a very fun and interesting title. However due to its lack of a playerbase and servers, I reccomend holding back on this one.
If you really want to play it and get somewhat of a playable experience, you can host a single player server like this:
1. Go to your Steam directory.
2. Go to steamapps/Minimum/Binaries.
3. Open MinimumLauncher.exe and make sure "Bots Allowed" is checked and set "Server Type" to "Lan". After that, select "Start Server". Feel free to mess around with the options as you please.
4. Wait for the server to fully start up.
5. Then, launch the game or open it if you have already launched it.
6. Select the game mode you have selected from when you created the server and then click on "LAN".
7. In the "IP" section, type in "localhost" or "127.0.0.1" as the IP, then click connect.
8. If you are at a loading screen, congrats! You just hosted a server!
Hopefully someone big in the gaming community will revive this and make it have a bigger playerbase, but for now, hold off on it unless you are extremely interested in the title.
