Gorgeous art, a beautiful soundtrack and compelling characters. Transistor has all of that going for it, but the most important part of this game is the combat.  Thankfully, the combat –a mix of real time with a key turn-base activated ability- is on-par with the presentation.
You will get 16 different abilities (called "functions" here) during your gameplay. You can use each of them on 3 different ways: as an active power, as a passive skill or as buffs for others. Mixing and matching gives different results, which makes it entertaining and the game forces you to do it by taking one active function away (temporarily!!) each time your health bar goes down.
The enemies' AI is competent and they pose a challenge once you use limiters, passives that give you more XP but make the opposition stronger.
Even with an award-winning presentation, the core of the experience falls on the shoulders of the combat. And the combat is fun, challenging and engaging.
Believe the hype.

Definitely a 'Yes' review here.
There are two spiritual successors to Escape Velocity that I know of.  NAEV and Endless Sky.  NAEV has some people doing a great job (also a great game), but with much slower development.  Endless Sky is very polished, very content rich and has a lot of UI features none of this line of games ever had.

I often spend small quantities of money trying out games on steam and didn't even realize until revisiting the store page that this game is FREE.  Holy cats.  I'll need to post a donation to the game devs.
Good things:
1) The turn based boarding mechanic is a wonderful way to add an interest to boarding operations without it consuming much time or interfering with the central feel of the game play of piloting a starship.
2) Good ship progression.  I see some complaints of a slow/humble start.  I did experience that a bit.  The game does reward doing fun things like combat and piracy and tends to discourage focusing too much on trade or missions.  Once you get over the hump you start moving right along.
3) Better shield regen is VERY nice for things like demanding tribute from planets.  In the old EV games, particularly Nova, it reached a point where your shield regen was basically how fast you could kill ships and you spent tons of time kiting and waiting.
4) Kiting is less rewarding.  The ships turn and lose interest and often come at you at different speeds forcing more variety to how battle large fleets.  You're more likely to duck in and out of engagements with heavy ships and pull back to lick your wounds.  Also anti missile prevents waiting out long barrages of missiles.  A good improvement on EV style combat mechanic all around.
Suggestions:
1) Battleships are god tier.  I tried so hard to make a lighter more maneuverable cruiser work, but in the end just wrecked everything with a shield beetle.  Probably hard to tweek the balance at this point, but it'd be fun to be able to get by on being 'dodgy'.  I'll keep trying a bit.  Not ruling it out completely yet.
2) The lock on mechanics aren't great.  It uses a selection of always choosing the closest ship rather than selecting from what you facing or cycling through promising opponents (if re-selecting within only a second or two try a different ship than selected).  So that annoying fighter behind you robs your lock from the ship you actually want to strike.
3) You can lock a target and spin to face it automatically.  I'm less into that.  I'd like to be forced to maneuver and fire with my perhaps my turrets and guns veering towards the target to the degree that each is able.
4) Command points (ala Sword of the Stars) would be AWESOME.  As your notoriety grows or perhaps through some other means gain the ability to command more vessels and otherwise have a sort of fleet limit so that you have to be choosey with your ships used for end game content.  Perhaps a maximum of 6?  I see a lot of posts of people accumulating masses of shield beetles with shield regenerators to keep them alive and then enough weapons quantity to contribute to your killing.  Might be cool to limit that a bit.  Maybe command points are vastly more generous/more efficient for smaller ships as well?  Maybe you can have only one Heavy Cruiser as a command ship and all the others must be lighter?  Might need a good end game medium vessel to compensate that had some survivability.

The game itself is a wondeful world of experience but the battle system is fundamentally flawed. Its something big fans like me ignore mostly and Sqenix themselves pretend is a feature not a bug (which in this day and age, for a team as supposedly talented as Sqenix, is frankly embarrasing. If you are familiar with telegraph systems in mmos you can skip a bit, if not, here it is. Telegraphs are sigils on the ground that indicate the direction (and sometimes ferocity and speed) of incoming attacks. Basically you must step out of the telegraph before the attack happens. The telegraphs do not properly discern who is stationary (being a nub), who is edging (healers for instance timing one last heal before moving out the telegraph) and who is even fully outside of the telegraph. You will find yourself (especially if you play other telegraph system games like the funny space one i cant remember) being constantly hit by moves that you were no where near the telegraph for. Its infuriating and it does essentially break the game if you choose to let it. It renders battle utterly preposterous for any serious gamer. Its my assumption based upon what i know that the bug is far too deep in the game engine to fix without recoding the entire battle system and so the bug has become inherent. Again, if you don't mind an entirely innaccurate battle phase or three this wont be a problem. Again, my advice? Don't bother.

Let me start off my review by stating that I am in no way an avid MMORPG player. The last real MMO I played was Runescape. That was back when installing Battlefield 2, Halo CE, and Gunz at your local library to have LAN sessions with other kids was common. I did resort in Guild Wars 2 for a time but outside of playing with friends I found myself barely engaged with what was going on. And I guess you could count The Secret World but the interface and design mechanics are a bit overwhelming for someone who doesn't know what they're doing.
That's one of the main reasons why I think Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn has currently 6 million active online users. It's not an overwhelming MMORPG. In fact, it's quite the opposite. It's a very laid back and calming experience that will not overwhelm newcomers but at the same time gives hardcore veterans enough of a challenge to really sink their teeth into. It also helps that FFXIV is a labor of love; a project directed at the helm by a gamer for gamers to give us the MMO we should have expected from the first iteration back in 2010. Yoshi P. and his team have done a phenomenal job of rebooting the game and continuing to expand on it. There is a wide variety of things to do. You can play the game following the main story line, or you can just ditch the main story line all together and head down to the casino to spend your days gambling, participating in chocobo racing and breeding stronger chocobos, or capitalize on the player-driven economy by supplying goods and services through leveling up jobs, loot collecting, etc. Hell, you can even do it all on one character if you want to!
This game takes a lot of influence from a copious amount of other successful, and even unsuccessful, MMOs and their mechanics and melds it together flawlessly. You have a job system that allows you to switch roles any time you want, and two jobs can be leveled up to create a different job as well. Each job carries a specific responsibility and unique play style so you don't want to worry about trial and error or looking up guides to find out what abilities mesh well together. The only game changer is that you can add additional abilities from other jobs you have leveled up to provide you added benefits for the main class you're working on. FFXIV also provides a fruitful amount of dungeons and trials (bosses) that are all very unique in both design and mechanics. The game's core fighting mechanics are based on a standard triangular job system meaning that any and all dungeons must be tackled by having one person, the Tank, crowd control all mobs and bosses while healers, well, heal, and DPS (damage per second) classes must kill everything. There are also random open-world events called FATEs which are essentially little quests that pop up around the world for all players to see and participate in and rewards are based upon how much you contribute to the objective or objectives.
Now, all the good doesn't mean there isn't a bit of bad. The biggest blunder that FFXIV has as a whole is the quest system. As I mentioned before: FFXIV is a calm and laid back MMORPG. All of the main story quests and side quests primarily have you going around and simply talking to people. There's of course your standard fanfare of, "go here, kill x, collect y," type of quests, but it's mostly all talking to people. This is because it is a heavily story driven game much like other Final Fantasy games before it. However, that being said, it's only a speckle on an otherwise perfectly chiseled face on marble and if you're someone who is into reading hours and hours of dialogue and are all in for the story than this is the perfect experience for you. To the game's credit the characters you encounter, despite not having any voiceover work 90% of the time, are unique and interesting both in their stories and personalities and there are a lot characters to meet.
The game also has this really bad tendency of being too quiet in general and barebones in its cutscenes. I'm unsure if it's due to the limitations of the engine or because the developers want to keep expanding the game without eating up too much of the hard drive, but the silence of the game is really jarring especially in its cutscenes. There's no ambiance to any of the areas you go to and it's mostly all driven by an absolutely wonderful soundtrack. That being said, it makes the game feel cheap when you're watching a cutscene that's made purely with the in-game engine, no voices, and animations recycled from the emoticons you can use around the game and the only audible sound heard are footsteps when characters move. And when the game decides to have voice acting it's not only bad, but it feels even more awkward since there's still barely any sound going on in the background and the actors sound like they're in a closed recording studio despite characters standing out in the middle of a blizzard. However, the oversights in terms of world building is quickly overshadowed by the beautiful design of game's environments. Every place is absolutely gorgeous to see and it's easy to get lost in.
That's really the only negative point the game has. It's mechanics are damn near perfect, the story, characters, and world are all very well done, and the constant expanding universe through free updates the developers roll out quite frequently really make the game feel like it never truly does end. I've sunk over 500 hours into the title, and I've still yet to see everything. I've only just reached the Heavensward expansion, and they've already added in a bunch of new dungeons and story content that's set after all the events that occur in Heavensward. It's a game of love, passion, and dedication and it truly shows its charm despite it's shortcomings. This is the MMO you have to play. Plain and simple.

Yea I had just beaten Bastion and went to purhase this and to my luck it was on 80% sale or something. To counter that I realized I'd just spent 14 on Bastion 2 days earlier... Kewl.
The game is just as deep as Bastion, if not more. Great graphics and art, nice music (even though I had my radio on in the BG), nice combat and the controls just works wonders. I had zero issues with wonky controls or anything, which was the same case with Bastion. Great and polished work. Do note, that while you might catch some familiarity with Bastion, this game is VERY different and that might put you off at first, but after 3-4 battles, you'll love it.
The game is sadly EXTREMELY short. I picked up on my progress, by looking at how many skills and limits I had, and was surprised, that I was soon to beat the game. It made me a bit sad, but all I can say is that I was very entertained, from start to finish.
The combat is very fun and can be performed in endless ways. If you get tired of your current playstyle, just shift and mix up your skills, to make a new playstyle. Nice and refeshing mechanic. It can however, stand out as overwhelming and confusing to begin with, yet you just have to battle a bit, read a bit of info, that is in the skill's description and you are good to go.
While I really liked Bastion's extra content, such as getting memoirs, weapon tests and wave battles, Transistor offers this through repeated gameplays. You will most likely have to do a second run, in order to get all the extra stuff and steam achievements. Don't worry though, they are actually pretty fun. If you liked Bastion's, then you'll like Transistor's extra stuff. Though I must admit Bastion had alot more.
That being said hurry up and buy, it really is a steal at this price. Other than that if you liked Bastion, or like Games, then you will enjoy this short, but very good and re-playable game.

The game is designed in such a way that rewards you for ingenuity, and encourages you to keep rebuilding, develop your own unique technique and maximize your productivity, to build bigger, faster, and more powerful factories. in my first week or so, ive already ground my way up to 50 hours, and launched my first satellite into space at hour 46. and I haven't let out a sigh of relief at completion like that since Gwyn at the end of dark souls.
Its a long rewarding grind, and really taps into that problem solving sector of your brain, If you like puzzles, unforgiving challenge combined with a massive open world I encourage you to give Factorio a try.
on a final note The demo doesn't include it, but the game does in fact have a sandbox mode.

Honestly the best overall MMO I have ever played. There are other MMO's that do some things better than FF14 but as a whole this blows me away. There are many unique races and classes to choose from that make you feel a part of the gorgeous world(seriously the visuals are stunning). The best way FF14 does this is it's quests. As you move up in lvl the enemies become more complicated and interactive and let me tell you going through dungeons with a party is a treat as you learn and discover how to fight all the unique bosses and their signature moves they throw at you. All in all if you want to play an amazing MMO, FF14 is the one.

Another great addition to the hexcells line! The acceleration of difficulty in the puzzles is not quite as steep as in Hexcells Plus, so you could start with Hexcells Infinite without first playing Hexcells. (I recommended practicing with Hexcells before diving into Hexcells Plus.) This edition comes with a really neat feature to generate puzzles randomly (hence the "infinite"), which provides endless hours of puzzle-solving fun! My only complaint is that the randomly generated puzzles seem to be relatively easy, for the most part, due to a lot of duplicated/unnecessary information provided. I don't know what sort of algorithm the authors use to generate the puzzles, but if the algorithm is flexible enough, it would be nice if the amount of information provided could be customized so that players could choose their difficulty level. Otherwise, Hexcells Infinite is a great puzzler that I'm sure I will be enjoying for a long time to come.

Was recommended and not disappointed. I got the full set Hexcells / Plus / Infinite and this is by far the best value, just because it has the randomly generated puzzles. The generated puzzles aren't near as clever as the hand crafted ones, but the daily puzzle makes it fun. I try to do each puzzle a day, and very casually compete with my BFF.

It's a fun gsme that can really make you think. Only problem I have is it will on occasion devolve into a frustrating guessing game which will lead to restarts. Sometimes there simply is no math to get wrong and you guess and you fail.

The first and most obvious comparison of Hexcells is to Minesweeper, with two extra sides, and that's what you're going to get. Minesweeper is great for killing a few moments, from the basic versions in Windows 2000 and XP to the shiny new ones in 7 and 10. Start menu, "mines", press Enter, and away you go. Even when the hardest difficulty defeats me time and time again, I still find myself looking for it over Solitaire or Hearts.
So why does the "ambient logic" of Hexcells annoy me so much? Well, if you've picked up on how pretentious that quoted phrase sounds, you're riding the same wave of boredom that I am.
To put it plain, this game feels more like a tumor growing on Minesweeper than any real advancement. It's slow, it's overcomplicated, and it's not really about puzzles. It's about processes of elimination, like Sudoku, and with the pressure to complete every stage without error, you will feel discontent when you have to guess what's behind that next orange tile.
Don't kid yourself on this point: if you're looking for any shred of entertainment you'll have to guess. Life is too short to work out every combination and deduce if you're about to ♥♥♥♥ up the tantalizing "Mistakes: 0" in the corner when there's regularly 50+ tiles and 10+ column hints to combine. Math majors aside, I don't know who could find that fun.
But enough of taking potshots at my humorless peers, let's take potshots at the developer instead. This game really is dead-set on monopolizing your time and attention. Minesweeper is a game to be played for a few minutes, preferably with the ability to quickly background it when something more important pops up (e.g., your boss rounds the corner). You're better off playing it on mute anyway; the audio is annoying and the interface is minimalist to a fault. Quick, exit to the stage select screen without touching the mouse (you can't) and without waiting for the pause menu to fully scroll into view (good luck). On OS X, this game disables every normal exit strategy to simply access another window - Cmd+Tab and Mission Control - and for what reason? Both Microsoft and Apple go to great lengths to disallow this behavior because even with the best of intentions, no application is so important as to block access to everything else. Yes, you can exit with Cmd+Q, yes, you can play it in a window by guessing at keyboard shortcuts, but disabling the ability to use my system as I see fit while it is running is really what made me cross over from indifference into irritation. And with gameplay this shallow, that's the strongest emotion this game musters up.

Yea I had just beaten Bastion and went to purhase this and to my luck it was on 80% sale or something. To counter that I realized I'd just spent 14 on Bastion 2 days earlier... Kewl.
The game is just as deep as Bastion, if not more. Great graphics and art, nice music (even though I had my radio on in the BG), nice combat and the controls just works wonders. I had zero issues with wonky controls or anything, which was the same case with Bastion. Great and polished work. Do note, that while you might catch some familiarity with Bastion, this game is VERY different and that might put you off at first, but after 3-4 battles, you'll love it.
The game is sadly EXTREMELY short. I picked up on my progress, by looking at how many skills and limits I had, and was surprised, that I was soon to beat the game. It made me a bit sad, but all I can say is that I was very entertained, from start to finish.
The combat is very fun and can be performed in endless ways. If you get tired of your current playstyle, just shift and mix up your skills, to make a new playstyle. Nice and refeshing mechanic. It can however, stand out as overwhelming and confusing to begin with, yet you just have to battle a bit, read a bit of info, that is in the skill's description and you are good to go.
While I really liked Bastion's extra content, such as getting memoirs, weapon tests and wave battles, Transistor offers this through repeated gameplays. You will most likely have to do a second run, in order to get all the extra stuff and steam achievements. Don't worry though, they are actually pretty fun. If you liked Bastion's, then you'll like Transistor's extra stuff. Though I must admit Bastion had alot more.
That being said hurry up and buy, it really is a steal at this price. Other than that if you liked Bastion, or like Games, then you will enjoy this short, but very good and re-playable game.

This MMO reminds me of those older Asian MMOs that came to NA many many years ago (pre-2007). This game is much more polished however, and I absolutely enjoy the ease and depth the game has to offer. With a weapon upgrading system as well as a card augmenting system and mobs dropping some very rare gear, I highly recommend it.
There is a premium status you can purchase for your account which gives you moderate perks (slight boost in EXP/Drop Rate) but it's not necessary to enjoy the game. There's also your typical MTX shop but it's not blown out of proportion like other games, or at least not from what I've seen anyway.
In one quest you have to play Plants vs Zombies. No joke, I have a screenshot if you're curious.

This game is really fun. I don't understand how people are voting it down because you have to click to move. Like, have you played Diablo/Torchlight? Get over it. Anyway, back to the game:
It's an MMO, so be prepared for a lot of fetch quests. Besides this, it does some pretty unique things.
First of which would be the leveling system. It's typical in the sense that every level you get stat points and sometimes a talent point, but the stat system is really cool. basically, every 10 points put into a specific stat, you get an extra bonus to it, and your 'rank' in that stat increases. So if I put 10 points into stamina, which is the rangers base stat, I'll get +15 to my damage output, on top of the points I put into it. Very unique and I enjoy ranking up stats.
The talent point system is also fairly unique, as they're all passives. There are multiple paths to travel down, which each give your class a unique playstyle. I'm not sure if there's a way to reset these, but I'm sure there is.
This game is NOT pay to win. You can obtain the premium currency by using gold, the in-game currency. Actually, gold is pretty easy to obtain as well, and so are most of the items in the game. It could be a bit of a grind, but that's how most MMOs work anyway, so it's not a big deal.
I really have been enjoying my time with this game. It's fun, it's a good time waster, and it feels like there's been a lot of love and time put into it, in order to make it good. I would recommend it to anyone looking for a fun MMO to play with.

A solid but familiar MMORPG experience. Some people may not like the top-down camera or the click-to-move controls, but I think they work well.
It's a really nice looking game and has a pretty high level of polish for a F2P title, the exploration and questing is pretty standard but does the job.
There are 4 Classes with 2 specializations and each specialization has 3 skill-trees. You get 4 stat-points each level to spend on your main attributes. Combat is fine, it's auto-attack with hot-bar skills.
There are plenty of different zones and each area tends to have a dungeon or two - some of which have open-PvP which again some people may not enjoy, I think it adds to the fun.
Lots of theme-park style questing from hub to hub and from what I've played you level up pretty quickly - though that may change at higher lvls.
I won't comment at this early stage on whether the game is P2W or not, but I may update my review at a later date to clarify on   the cash-shop.
Overall I think it's a good game and I recommend it to people who don't mind a more typical MMORPG.

I'm sort of confused by some of the negative reviews, as I'm finding this to be a pretty decent game that doesn't have many problems.
First, it has a lot of lore and story to it.  It's not just quests like "Kill 10 rats because I stubbed my toe and need toe medicine" - the quests have more detail and story to them than that.  Each quest has been pretty detailed so far with lots of extra tidbits of story and lore you can get out of the NPCs if you select to ask them certain questions.
You also find a lot of NPCs that aren't part of the quest line but that actually have story bits to add if you talk to them.  I find this extra work and detail to help the game to be much more immersive.
The classes are all very different.  If you don't like the way one plays, you really should try the others as they all have their own different way to play and their own feel.  The powers are all different and specific for each class line and greatly change and affect the way you play.  This isn't like some games where the only difference in classes and skills are that they make a different graphic for them but they play the same way.  Here they all really play in specific unique ways.  Even when two classes have traps, one class they are auto traps and the other are traps you manually detonate.  There are a pretty good amount of skills too and they all have purpose and do different things rather than just being damage upgrades that look a little different.
The game plays out just fine and quickly.  Yes, your main attack if you click something is set on default to autoattack (like 99.9% of every MMORPG that exists, so why one would complain about that I don't know - especially since you can toggle it off to manual if you really want) but in most classes that attack is very fast and you're going to be worried about using all your skills all through combat.  You quickly end up using a lot of them.  The only class that plays a little slower to start out is the Warrior, but even they end up with a lot of skills in time too.  If you're into melee and want faster combat, play the Rogue.  The Warrior is meant to actually be a party tank and has a lot of taunts and things instead of the fast pace skills of the other classes.  That isn't to say they are lacking, they have quite a few and you'll see them as you level up more.
The game isn't well known here, so there aren't a lot of people in game right now.  Not only that, but they don't really understand why it's a free game they can't get in (the first week is just for people who buy one of the DLC packs, but they only say that if you go searching elsewhere to find that info and didn't post that here).
I'm not that into PvP, but for people who are they have these nice castles your guild can take over that spawn chests of loot and have other neat little extras in them.
I don't really get their whole "PvPvE" thing - that's just a fancy way to say PvP zones.  Most MMORPG games with PvP also have monsters in the same zones but they just call them PvP zones instead of trying to be fancy with the wording.  I really very much dislike PvP and want to avoid it, so I'll have to see how much it affects my gameplay as I level up.  I hope it's avoidable and not too too bad.  A description at their web site says there are quests in those areas which I never enjoy being forced to go to PvP zones to do quests, especially in game that has so much story and I really am enjoying reading all the quest text.  I'm not really there yet though to see how that's going to affect my play.  It could have a huge negative affect for me and even get me to quit if it's bad enough but I'll just have to wait to get there to see.
The camera angles really aren't that bad.  I think they limited it in order to make the game work better on lesser systems, I'm not sure.  It runs very smooth and pretty though and I don't really see why they can't allow you to pan it so you can see into the distance a little more but you do have some tilt control and it's really not too bad.
The one thing I dislike though and very much want to see change is for us to get the ability to use WASD movement in the game.  A lot of games like this launch with click to move movement only, and it's always the same.  I get sick of clicking so much, it's a pain in the butt after a while.  They really need to change the game to allow keyboard movement controls as well.  I know it doesn't work great for every situation, like if people set the camera to auto movement, but they could always disable it if you have auto camera on or find some other work around.  Too many people are going to want WASD movement controls, maybe they'll listen and put them in game in time though.
So I'm finding a pretty decent game here.  You may want to wait and not chance it, and give it another 4 or 5 days until it's opened for free to everybody, but I for one am very happy with the game as it is and am glad I bought a DLC pack so I could play now.  Even if PvP areas make me quit later (again I still don't know if they will or not, it depends if I can still level and quest around without having to deal with them for the most part) - I still will be happy that I got and played the game.  It's been interesting and fun and is a good example of how to put real story and more meaning into quests.  It also is doing something very right with the skill system all being so different.  Hopefully once it's opened for free a lot of people will find out just how much they like it too.
The video they have here really doesn't show much of the game, you can find videos elsewhere online of people playing the game if you really want to see how it plays though.  They don't take the time to read and go through all the extra text and things in those videos however, so if you're a person who really likes story and lore in your games you won't really see how cool it is until you're able to get in there yourself.

If you grew up in the 16-bit era this is a must have. Let's face it, there are loads and loads of games on Steam right now trying to pull on the nostalgia chords. Loads of pay for roms and emu packages of games you know and love, and tons of indie games developed in the likeness of games you know and love, but what those games can't deliver is what Dorke has in mass quantity; an authentically new SNES experience. This isn't a game like a SNES game. This isn't a SNES game you've beaten countless times. This is an authentic SNES title you never got to play. If it was unplayable it'd still be a wortha few bucks to check out, but given it's actually a decent game it's a gem of an experience. I'd say the closest thing to Dorke and Ymp is when you find a game that never came to your nation online and in your language or at least a fan patch.
So what's the game actually like? It's decent, but nae great. If it did come out during the SNES days it definately wouldn't have excited me as much as it does now. It's slow, and hard, and some things are kind of lost in translation or just all out weird, but it's not horrible. The pair of characters over one PC is pretty neat. It may not be the only game to do something similar, but it is an interesting take and easy to do. You never have to think about which one you're going to use, just what you need to do and the pair takes care of the rest. My favorite thing about the game is the in game animations. There are quite a few animations that remind you not to take the game too seriously despite is being seriously difficult. The cutsenes are long, but I enjoyed them. I'd rather have them than not, though skipping would be nice sometimes.
I'm not sure what Piko did to finish the game. It's clearly another rom+emu package. It's a bit of a hard game and I wasn't so taken with it that I wanted to prove I could beat it without cheats so I took the rom and uploaded it to my Recalbox build to play Dorke and Ymp with fast foward, rewind, shaders, save and load states, etc. I'm not sure why pay-for emulators have less than free ones, but they do and that's the case here. I definately advocate buying the rom to support Piko for bringing it to us, but once you have it play it on your favorite emulator because the one it comes with is bogus.

I was struggling a bit with my opinion on this game.
Right from the start, I was greeted with a choppy music and ugly characters in an overly long cut-scene, that after a while I couldn't care less about and then promptly skipped (well, it's not like anyone plays old-school platformers for their story anyway.) Then I had to wrestle with awkward controls and clunky mechanics, accompanied by ridiculously annoying enemies that drain all your health away before you're able to kill them. I died so many times it's not even funny (THOSE DAMN BEES!)
On the other hand with what I've seen so far, the level design is rather good, although a little bit obstructed by the limited view distance, forcing you sometimes to do a leap of faith. Thankfully, they forgo the classic 1-hit, 3-lives style of difficulty that the old games liked to do, and allowed you to do a lot mistakes by giving you 50 lives from the start and a bigger than normal amount of hit-points, which also helps at the beginning, when you're still getting used to the controls, which can take a while.
It's nowhere near as good as the best of the genre from SNES era, it makes me think of something more akin to Lester the Unlikely. But, after spending a couple of hours in it, I can see myself playing more of it.
It's not a game I would recommend to most people, but if you played a lot of SNES platformers (other than Mario and Megaman,) you'll feel right at home. So if you're looking for that nostalgia fix, this might be perfect for you, despite its faults.

This game is kind of like Dwarf Fortress in space, a little simulator where you design rooms and manage the roster for your space station.  You don't control the citizens directly, but instead you put down work orders, and the citizens will handle it on their own.  You sketch out rooms and order furniture and so on and your citizens place it.
The first few mintues of the game were a lot of fun for me.  You're kicked out of your life support pod drifting in deep space and have to build a little self sustaining environment with an airlock and some life support systems before your citizens run out of air (about 5 mins).  This was an encouraging first glance for me, because it's pretty hard and will probably require a few resets if you don't know what you're doing, and the systems seemed interesting and complex.  Eventually, though, I figured it out and started branching out, putting up a refinery to allow my miners to mine nearby asteroids, using the materials to build a residence and a bar and a garden and a lab and stock it with furniture.
And then the game ended.
I don't mean it dumped me to a "game over" screen or anything, there just wasn't anything left to do.  Once you've got a half dozen rooms down and functioning, which takes maybe an hour, there's nothing else you can do except wait for your science team to sloooooowly research some unnesescary upgrades, or maybe have your security team scrap with some raiders (note that this isn't an RTS, combat in this game is just a matter of setting a point for your security team to defend and maybe they will if they're not on break or hungry or tired or sad).  Sometimes a derelict will show up and you can... well, tear it down, nothing else to do with them really.
If you've ever played Dwarf Fortress, basically imagine that game but with no workshops.  You can make rooms and designate areas and place furniture, but there's no crafting system, no economy, no trade, resources are all boiled down to a single currency which is used to buy everything from walls to furniture.  The game just has no depth at all, and it's competing with some of the most complex and deepest simulations on the market right now.
The devs seem to have responded to this by ramping up the challenge, which makes things a bit frustrating.  Colonies can die from parasites before you get a doctor, waves of raiders can annihilate an underequipped security force, and once things start to fail, it's pretty much a chain reaction to an abandoned base.  Colonists freak out and refuse to do their jobs so vital equipment isn't maintained or repaired so colonists freak out even harder and things just spiral downward.  For example, if the air supply gets low, colonists will freak out rather than do their jobs, so if the area with the life support systems has air problems, you can't ever fix it because whoever goes in there is going to panic instead of fixing the air generator, and the problems get worse.  And this doesn't really do much to fix the problem with the game being short, because once you've got whatever it is you need to counter them, then they're not that big a deal.
The 1.0 update added a lot of nice features, but the game still has serious issues with longevity.  There are still occasional glitches with draw order and some AI issues, but the game works pretty well mostly.  I've only played a bit, but pathing does seem improved and the interface does make things clearer now.
I don't want to sound excessively negative, this isn't the worst game ever.  I had a lot of fun with it.  It's just really short, and the asking price is kind of high.  On sale, for $5, I'd say this is a good deal.  At full price, I don't think it's worth it.  I'd recommend looking at something like Startopia or Space Colony or grabbing something like Gnomoria or Dwarf Fortress if you're not in love with the sci-fi aesthetic.  All of these games are cheaper, deeper, and more fun in the long term than DF-9.

I guess an immediate comparison I made was that the game is kind of like a typical mobile game of the likes of King of Thieves or Clash of Clans etc. and brings it to a Steam port because of the many aspects it takes from those kind of base management games in creating your own "Relik". This isn't necessarily a bad thing, though. "Relik" incorporates four different types of puzzles which you slowly increase in power as you play the game. Like an RPG, you can pick and choose which puzzles you want to focus on improving at any one time. Unlike the aforementioned mobile games, you don't have to wait to upgrade and retinker your coniving little defense.
I thought it was really cool that there aren't any real base setups where you just plop one in you find online and leave until you get your next town hall upgrade or whatever because there are so many stages a person can be at any one time. This being said, there is still opportunity to create a community. Could you consider some community tips and tricks? Probably. Adaptations on your existing base? Yes. Complete copy paste online to your "Relik"? Nope. There's always something to do in upgrading your puzzles. This is probably the most charming thing about the game, being able to create and adapt your own puzzles over time, while similarly wracking your brain around others.
By investing your time in this game, "Relik" pays dividents in return. You get a stronger focus on puzzles than most games: it is the core of the gameplay, which is appealing to some players like me and also a more fluid sense of progression when the game does feel like giving you cards and gold. Essentially the progression curve ends up being enjoyable but stops frequently, which is a bit of a bummer. With some strong development direction, "Relik" could make it there as an established F2P game. It's hard to recommend these kinds of games due to the commitment the nature of this type of game demands from its user for it to be as enjoyable as possible, but in its current state I believe the developer's are working to create the game experience first instead of being a cashgrab. <3

A game like this is very hard to find. Its complexity is within its simplicity, and the fact that the puzzles that you come across are made by other players makes the game greatly influenced by the thought of challenging not only yourself but others as well.
With the main idea of the game is consisting of a puzzle cube, comprised of four puzzles scattered across the six sides, one can't help but wonder how many possibilities and combinations can be created on this cube. The calm, ambient background music and mellow, relaxing sound effects pair incredibly well with the intense competitiveness of solving other player's puzzles. The rewards system is a "choose your fate" found in many games where the player is given the opportunity to pick cards... not the most overused rewards method, but effective nonetheless.
While the majority of gamers are tired of the "pay to win" style many games have, Relik's in-game store merely offers a chance to challenge other players faster, while also supporting a well formed indie game's growth. While it may still be bothersome to see an in-game store, the options are limited to basics. One can finally purchase new customization themes, instead of more lives.
Relik, overall, is a must-try for all looking to test their memory. Future updates may provide us with more content, such as 3D shapes beyond the cube or a greater variety of puzzles, as a few ideas, however this game seems to be at a point where it can support itself strongly against the other puzzle games on the market.

I am a person who grew up playing JRPGs, but I've never been a big fan of some WRPGs or RPGs on PC. In my opinion, sometimes they seem to bog the player down managing trivial details such as repairing armor, managing backpack space, and the narrative falls far behind. I was pleased to see that this game has an interesting campaign and the gameplay does not bog the player down in senseless micromanaging.
Disciples Gold: Sacred Lands is a pretty good, but dated game. I bought this on a steam sale for $0.79, and I think it will yield many great hours of gameplay. The game seems pretty well done as far as the presentation is concerned. The game play took a little bit of figuring out, but I'd say I've pretty well got it now and I've never read the manual. To me, it reminds me a little bit of warcraft when it comes to the overworld and resource management. The fights play out like a simplified version of a turn based game. You do not really control what actions the players take or the order in which they take turns, but you control who they attack or heal, as well as the ability to skip players or run away. So, in some regards, it plays out like a top down Strategy RPG, but instead of the fight actions being represented merely as points of damage, it goes to a separate fight mode where the player has the ability to influence the outcome of fights. Then after the fight is done, it goes back to the overworld.
All in all, I'd recommend the game, especially if you can get it on sale. 79 cents is a steal, and I'll be looking forward to playing more of this game.

conclusion: this game isn't worth your time, there's way better mmorpgs out there.

Yah so you're probably thinking ah yes a new review. Wrong. This is just a random pavlova recipe cos you are probably hungry after surfing the reviews.
Ingredients
4 egg whites (5 if you are using small eggs)
250g pure icing sugar or fine castor sugar, sifted
½ teaspoon white vinegar
1 tablespoon cornflour, sifted
Method
1. Preheat your oven to 200 degrees Celsius.
2. Prepare a baking tray by placing baking paper on it. Put a little melted butter or vegetable oil spray on the tray so that the paper will stay in one place while you are spooning the pavlova mix on to it.
3. Using an electric mixer, beat the egg whites on a medium setting until soft peaks form.
Once soft peaks appear, add the sugar all at once and beat the mixture for a minute or so on full speed. Do not stop the machine to add the sugar. It needs to be a continuous process to trap as much air as possible in the egg whites. You'll see the mixture change texture almost immediately, from loose, soft peaks to a more glossy, meringue-style mixture.
4. Turn the mixer up to high until the mixture thickens and the sugar has completely dissolved. It needs to reach the ribbon stage – when a spoonful of the meringue mixture poured back into the bowl sits on the surface like a ribbon.
5. Slow the machine, add the vinegar and let the beaters make three rotations, then remove the bowl from the mixer.
6. Sprinkle the cornflour over the egg white mixture and, using a clean spatula, gently fold in the cornflour – no more than six folds.
7. Spoon the mix on to the prepared tray and mould it into the shape you want. Kabboord prefers to leave it pretty heaped. Don't mess with the mix too much, though, as you want to get it in the oven quick smart. The other option is to use a preheated and lined tray. Speed is the key here.
8. Place the tray in the middle of the oven and immediately turn the temperature down to 120 degrees Celsius. Don't use the fan.
9. Cook for 80-90 minutes but don't let the pavlova colour. You may see a little sugar syrup seep out of the bottom but the crust should be firm. Inside, it will be soft and marshmallowy.
10. Cool to room temperature and decorate using quark, Meredith goat's curd or mascarpone (cream is boring!) and your favourite toppings, such as chopped summer fruit or passionfruit custard.
Enjoy! (And the game)

Despite being in
(At the time of the review), Relik isn't as complicated as you think.The game, surprisingly, is a lot of fun and pretty addictive as well. You set up your 4 puzzles and play other people's 4 puzzles. It's pretty simplistic and easy to understand for both newcomers and experienced players.
The game involves you trying to solve 4 puzzles in a short amount of time from another player. You also setup your own four puzzles and upgrade them to make them a lot more challenging for players to try out. As I said before, it's very simple and easy to understand, even for person who isn't into puzzle games. This game does require you to use your memory to solve the puzzles much faster and efficently. Anywhom, there's currency that you can use to upgrade your puzzles, clocks for time and themes (which cost gems). Gems, which are the rare-to-get currency, are a bit meh.. It's definetely NOT pay to win, I can definetely say that. But there are customisable themes that you can apply to your cube. They cost around 100 gems and you can only get gems through card drops which have chance of a currency type, that including gems. I know it's just a cosmetic feature, but it's a right now, it's mehh... Overall, gameplay is pretty solid but the minor transactions can put some people off.
For an Indie Game, the visuals are simplistic but they're very good. The default theme is very cool in terms of colours. As I said before, there are themes that change not only the style of the cube but also the interface. Other than that, there's not much I can say. Pretty nice overall.
The music is pretty nice but it's extremely subtle, for me at least. It's relaxing and fitting to the game though. Music isn't one of the major components of the game so you'd probably want to play your own music. the SFX are pretty good and satisfying. It's less subtle than the music but not by much. Besides, there isn't much to talk about in terms of music and SFX.  To put it short, they're a nice but somewhat minor addition.
In the end, Relik is a pretty good
game for those who aren't much into puzzle games. They contain simple puzzles that can be played without too much thinking (on lower skill levels). However, if you really suck at memory games, then this isn't for you to enjoy. Also, the minor non-p2w microtransactions for the themes and other stuff may also seem a turn off to others.
+Simplistic puzzles
+Easy to understand
+Nice Visuals
+Nice SFX and music despite being extremely subtle
-Minor, non Pay-to-Win Microtransactions may turn you off
-Music is very subtle and can be ignored pretty easily.
-Puzzles rely on memory, which may turn people off.

I guess i should update this review now that the game has been released and has been updated to 1.05.
I still play this game, and at the time of the edit to this review, i've invested about 70 hours into countless new games.
The updates have helped a whole lot, but the game still has some playability issues:
Doctors will often ignore corpses, which leads to bad morale, which leads to violence which leads to drastic crew loss.
Raider events are too randomised, and can often lead to base failure in the very early game, or general drastic crew loss.
The added raider mega-fleet event is a good idea in principal, but is vastly over-powered.
Construction crew often take huge detors to the next block to be built when in space, which can lead to a new base failing, or causing unrecoverable crew loss in the very early game.
Even with my reasonable system spec and the relative simplicity of the game, it tends to lag-out far too much.
Generally; Base failure seems to be down to chance rather than skill.
There are mods appearing now, which is great. The community is addressing balence issues and adding reaseatch and similar.
Workshop support is still very much missing, sadly.
Has the potential to be a reasonable casual game, but really isn't worth the full price at all. Perhaps at a quater the price, it woulnd't be so bad.

Asteroids HD:
~~~~~~~~~~~

Space Pilots, are you ready for combat? Well, you’d better to be, as you will engage in battle against your foe in the middle of an Asteroid field. Only the most skilful and fearless pilots will make it out alive!
Asteroids HD is an action / space simulation game. The game has two modes, single player and multiplayer. In the single player mode, you will need to clear all Asteroids to finish the level. Your vessel will be equipped with a laser and a few nuke missiles at the start of your first mission. Each time you hit an Asteroid you will be awarded credits which you can use to purchase upgrades for your spaceship. Depending how big an Asteroid is, it will explode into four smaller ones upon impact. On top of having a lot of these space rocks to destroy, you will also contend with some alien probes! You will see icons floating around, too, and by flying through them you will be able to – Recover health, regenerate your shield and add extra missiles to your ship. Others have a passive effect; pass through the Unlimited Ammo icon and you will be able to send many nukes to the asteroids for a little while.
In the multiplayer mode, you will be able to play a survival, objective and Deathmatch game.
The graphics are good and polished. The controls works well and the gameplay is fun. As the game is on early access, there are a couple of bugs (icons disappear just before going through them) as expected.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Fun gameplay and concept
-	Good graphics
-	Single and multiplayer modes
-	Good number of upgrades for your ship
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Repetitive (single player)
-	No achievements / trading cards
Asteroids HD is graphically well-polished with a fun game play.

Well if so, or even if not so... Welcome to AsteroidsHD!  This is an early access rock and enemy ship blasting game that is worth MANY TIMES it's asking price!  At 99 cents for his early version of this game, the developer shows that his heart is much more about delivering a fun experience then he is trying to make a quick profit!  ..That alone deserves some respect in my book here on Steam, especially considering the sheer amount of rip-off crap that is launched in early access these days here.
Controls are simple and easy, WASD to move through space, and your move your ships direction around, while your mouse buttons give you two different types of blasts to clear enemies and those big space rocks floating around.  A joy to play with very responsive and understandable controls.
You start off in a space void with a few huge rocks, and a single enemy ship who will shoot at you if you don't find him and blast him first!  Thhere is also plenty of different power ups, ship repair, and ammo icons floating around to aid your cause.  Shooting a space rock blasts it into many smaller rocks at high velocity, and damage values are clearly shown as you blast the rocks and baddies making it a satisfying endeavor.
While the first level might seem casual and too easy, just keep clearing out all those space rocks to move on to the next level, and pretty soon you'll be in over your head and having to dodge all kinds of crazy enemies and rocks which multiply each time you pass a level.  Super fun, especially for the price!
Sadly, not enough players have bought this game yet when I reviewed it in early access, but I will buy a copy for my son and have him play some multiplayer games with me and update my score and post some video links when that happens.  ...For now this game scores an impressive 75% from me, with a good chance of only going higher once more players are available for the "Up-To-8-Player Multiplayer action" and as this game continues to get further developed through early access.

There is an initial investment in the game which is not fun -- paying off the mortgage for your first junk-tastic ship. There should be a discount on your first ship to help boost you into the economy rather than being saddled with a big debt to start.
That means there's not much choice to the way you start -- you can't start out as a pirate with any ships you can afford with that loan. The game dynamics force you to haul cargo initially as best I can tell. In fact, the battle component of the game seems largely like an annoying afterthought and avoidance is the only profitable strategy because losing ships is so costly. Thanks to the poor maneuverability of most ships in the game and the way ships almost universally tend to get destroyed as you're boarding them this dynamic is largely useless and you are, again, funnelled into the cargo hauler role.
I liked the trade interface once I realized how to use it with the map. The map interface is actually better as a trade view than the trade interface available after you land.  That said, the trade goods themselves leave something to be desired -- they are named differently but their uses are no different. They only exist so I may exploit the price differences. Moving them between systems does not seem to affect the universe in any way -- just my account. Maybe trade goods could expand planets/stations along the lines of the goods I'm moving. Or maybe I could use some kinds of them to repair my ship, refuel it, or supply emergency reserves in a particularly difficult dogfight.
I liked how the mission system eventually became far more profitable than the trade grind, or it did at least for a while. I like that it seems to oscillate which one is generally more profitable. Missions are fun to stack up and then finish, especially with the time constraints on some of them. The mission interface for escort-then-return missions (pleasure cruises, science expeditions) leaves a lot to be desired. Either it needs to be clearer what you're expected to do by showing you a route to the destination and back or these missions need to be split into two and the second part made optional. Also, they tend to cross the map such that the return per jump is much lower than trading and other missions. Having huge cargo and passenger capacity and stacking the missions is what makes the missions profitable with trade filling in the gaps.
The gradations of hostility are interesting too, and they seem to affect when and especially where other ships tend to attack you. I haven't played the non-cargo-hauler role much yet. So the aggressive fighting and/or diplomacy angle may be there and I've just not seen how it's supposed to work yet.

I'm gonna start by briefly comparing this game to Timberman; if you enjoyed Timberman, you'd probably enjoy this. If you don't know what Timberman is, then continue reading.
Surfingers is a game that is controlled entirely by two buttons: the up and down arrow keys (or the W and S keys for up and down if you don't want to and/or can't use the arrow keys). The object of the game is to prevent your surfing character from crashing by moving the terrain he's on (be it water, snow, etc) up and down to keep his path continuous. You gain a point for each 'section' of terrain your character successfully surfs.
Another thing to note is that the game supports both local and online multiplayer, and also has achievements and trading cards.
Every rose has its thorn, however; My complaints about this game begin with how fast it is; it feels like I'll be punished for even blinking once whenever I get to the snow area (i.e. zone 2), as the game is moving so fast that it's based purely on lightning reflexes (which quite honestly feels faster than the average human reaction time). To prove my point, Zone 1 ends at around 80 points; as of writing this review, only 12.4% of players (according to global achievement stats) have the "Score 100" achievement (meaning they've made it a little bit into the Snow zone), whereas a measly 2.5% of players have scored 200 (presumably beating the Snow zone). To add insult to injury, the highest scoring achievement is "score 500", which a whopping 1.2% of players have achieved. Another thing is, unlike Timberman, Surfingers has an active multiplayer search function rather than a passive one; If you want to play online multiplayer, you're gonna have to wait for a match rather than be notified after each run in singleplayer when a multiplayer lobby is available.
Overall, the game serves as an excellent timekilling game that shouldn't be taken too seriously.

The best, most brain-busting game in the hexcell "trilogy"... at least for the main, "campaign" puzzles. If you're looking for is many hours spent staring at yellow, grey, and blue hexagons, wondering for five straight minutes where the next move is, then this is made for you, but if you're hoping for perpetual puzzling potential, then move along.
Be aware that the problem with the infinite mode is my only complaint. This is still a great game, but since the infinite mode is such a big part of the game that it's in the title, it has to be addressed.
The campaigns through all three games have a good number of memorable puzzles, some of which employ excellent variations in implimenting of the game's hint mechanics, but no such thing can be found in the infinite mode. Infinite puzzles are all bland, unmemorable blobs, and they offer no surprises in how they combine various hints. After playing about 15 infinite puzzles, you can be fairly confident that you have seen everything infinite can offer you in terms of challenge--even if it can challenge you at all. If you've managed to complete the entire campaign honestly, working to understand complex chains of hints, then most infinite puzzles should be trivial to complete.
A trivial puzzle is not a fun puzzle.
So, yes. If you love puzzles, buy this game, but don't expect to be playing it for months and remain entertained.

Troubleshoot review:
Game would not lauch : failure to find fonts.
Just go to the installed folder, go to the 'Exe' folder and look for the 'DISCIPLE.INI' file.
Open it with an editor and edit everything beneath '[Installation]' and '[InstallationClient]'.
Change every path from the default C:\program files (x86) to the path were you installed the game.
Game works like a charm afterwards

The Disciples series has always been one of those I hold close to my heart. I started out playing a demo for Disciples II: Dark Prophecy and fell in love with that game's dark atmosphere, music and gorgeous gothic illustration used for the UI and character portraits. I then saw Disciples: Sacred Lands on a shelf in Circuit City. It seemed so unassuming sitting there among all the more recent titles. And yet it was that game that my eyes were drawn too. I paid the ten dollars for the game and walked out of that store feeling as if I had stumbled upon the holy grail. Now things could have gone differently. I figured I loved Dark Prophecy so the first one had to be good too right?
I got the game home opened up the nice little box the jewel case came in and installed the game. A gorgeous cutscene played and before long I was in the game and having a blast. The core mechanics that made Dark Prophecy such a joy were present here. And while the game wasn't quite as pretty as its successor it still was a gem. A diamond in the rough.
Today when there are so many big budget games that turn out to be disappointments. Its nice to see a classic gem like this find new life through digital distribution. If you are a fan of the Disciples series or Disciples II Dark Prophecy you owe it to yourself to play this game.
Now there may be some issues with getting this game to work on modern PC's. But there seem to be numerous ways of editing the ini file to get it to run properly. I imagine you could also try running the game/steam in compatibility mode.

At first glance, it is not impressive in the least, but this is a very well implemented and insanely addictive game. It's both extremely simple and extremely complex.  It really is what you make of it.  It is a great test to your creativity and problem solving abilities, but in a very fun way.  It's not an annoying puzzle game nor is it a simple, say, city builder.  It's really hard to truly describe this game.  One has to play it to really appreciate what the developers have done here and it's STILL EARLY ACCESS.  It blows my mind.  The more you play it, the more you will enjoy it.  At which point that changes, I have no idea.
There's a reason why this game has an "overwhelmingly positive" review rating with over 15,000 reviews.  It's one of the better games I have played in a long, long time.
Not only are the developers making an absolutely fantastic game, they give you a free demo!  Not only do they give you a free demo, the game itself is only $20!  Not only is the game itself only $20.... THEY MADE IT MODDABLE.  Not only is it moddable... it's EASILY MODDABLE.  Holy... freaking... crap.  You can play it literally however you want to.  Yeah, I only have about 52 hours in on the game, but I'm playing vanilla and I'm still absolutely loving it and about to start another game.
If you like creation.  If you like problem solving.  If you like making something as simple or as insanely complex as you want it to be, I HIGHLY, HIGHLY recommend this game.  It will be the best $20 you've spent on a game in a long time.  I guarantee it.  I can see myself playing this for, at the very least, hundreds of hours, seriously.
I'll be honest, I want to just donate even more money to the developers simply to say a thank you for creating a wonderful game in a time where people are cranking out garbage games left and right for a quick cash grab, especially the A class game developers.  I can tell this game is made from the heart of these developers and from what I've heard, they truly love creating it and the amazing reception it has had.
In my opinion, this game is up there with Minecraft and Terraria, if that tells you anything.

Is Minesweeper a big thing for you? Do you enjoy cracking puzzles using logic? Do you want an endless amount minesweeper inspired logic puzzles that require 0% guessing and 100% pure thought to solve? Well Hexcells Infinite is just the game for you.
Aesthetically the game is very minimalistic, clear and clean. The ambient music and the soothing ethereal piano keys played, when you unravel successive hexes, can be quite relaxing.
The game has a finite amount of hand-crafted puzzles with a decent enough difficulty curve. The earlier levels are pretty easy to grasp and as more elements and guidelines are introduced the puzzles get increasingly harder. The last of the hand-crafted puzzles can be seriously challenging to beat using just your logic and not guessing without making any mistakes. But like I've said each and every one of these can be beaten without guesswork, just need to look at it in the right angle.
After you've completed the hand-crafted there's the infinite puzzle generator. While I've noticed that the levels you get using the generator are usually a lot easier than the last of the manually created levels, so there's not that much challenge there anymore for me, but I still occasionally find myself popping back in to complete a few of them. It's refreshing to warm up your brain's logical thinking with them I suppose.
All in all I have to recommend this title to any puzzle fans and especially to those who love minesweeper (because it's pretty much minesweeper but better). Great value for the price. Even more so if you can get it with a discount.

Hexcells Infinite is the successor to both Hexcells and Hexcells Plus, puzzle games that look rather like Minesweeper. Players are presented with an orange grid comprised to hexagons and it is up to them to determine whether these cells belong to the blue pattern or not (black cells). The black cells not part of the pattern have a number in them to indicate how many blue cells are adjacent to them, thus providing a clue as to how to proceed.
After completing a puzzle the player is awarded blue hexcells based on the amount of mistakes made; these in time accumulate to unlock one of five new areas - allowing you to complete more difficult puzzles. Some areas also introduce new clues and rules to help you, making the puzzles more complex over time.
The biggest addition to this game is the infinite mode, where puzzles are randomly generated so there is always a new puzzle to try out.
Although similar to Minesweeper as mentioned, there is a key difference: there is always a logical next step. You never have to take a gamble so if you feel stuck, take a step back and focus on another area.
Hexcells Infinite is a very simple puzzle game in its visual design. The menu is simple and provides the players with the option of turning the ambient music on or off, selecting which mouse button turns the cells blue or black and selecting one of three save slots. The same can be said for the puzzles themselves; a grid of hexagons on a white backdrop. To me this is good design, as I'm here for the puzzles and that's where the focus clearly lies.
The puzzles themselves are interesting, more difficult than Hexcells but slightly less difficult than Hexcells Plus.
What's more, my biggest problem with both previous titles has been resolved; it is now possible to leave a puzzle mid-game, thereby saving your progress and being able to continue next time where you left it.
However, like previous titles it is still not possible to erase a save slot so starting completely from scratch is not an option if all three slots are in use.
Furthermore, I personally find the infinite mode wanting. The randomly generated puzzles are neither as difficult nor as interesting compared to those made by Matthew Brown, the developer of Hexcells.
That being said, I recommend this title (and both previous ones) wholeheartedly for anyone interested in puzzle games.

This game is ridiculously easy to get into, but it gets some nice difficulty as you progress.
You play as an underpaid, solo border officer whose job it is to be the sole customs officer monitoring immigration to the fictional country of glorious Arstotzka. Each person you successfully let in (following the rules laid out at the beginning of each day) contributes to your salary.
Each day has a new set of rules defining who is /is not allowed in and which documents they need to have to prove eligibility. You have a manual that tells you what to look for, and how to scan for the inconsistencies and deny passage to those who aren't allowed in.
At the end of each day, your earnings are tallied, and you get to see what's left over after certain expenses, and then choose to still have heat or electricity, etc. It really puts the pressure on to try to be successful because every right answer at the border makes it possible to stay living.
Highly recommend for something you can pass the time with, and it's even better to be supporting an indie dev.

Papers please is a memory game, where you need to go through people's passports and other documents. Then you figure out, if you let them through border or not. The game starts with simple rules to remember to check, but difficulty advances over time.  You start to get multiple rules to remember and gameplay can become really hectic.
The game has two modes. The first mode is a story mode. In the story mode you live through events, which of some are scripted and some randomised. You have some choices while story advances.  Occasionally people can come to ask for your help. You can either be rewarded or being penalised for helping them. The story is limited to certain length and has multiple endings depending on choices you make. The other mode is called endless. It's completely randomised. Also time is not limited in this mode. You unlock this mode after playing story.
Overall the game captures really well grim atmosphere of cold war era communistic country.

One of the first things that is apparent with this game is the graphics. They're absolutely stunning, even if you're using the lowest setting because your computer lags too much (which was the case when I played through). Every room and box is intricately and beautifully designed, that simply watching a playthrough of this game done by somebody else would still be a worthwhile experience just for the experience of seeing how much detail went into every puzzle. The puzzles themselves are intuitive but not too easy, just the right level of difficulty for someone who wants to be challenged, but not stumped. For some of the harder puzzles, the hint system works great to give just enough information to make the solution apparent, but not obvious.
However there are a few puzzles which can be frustrating to figure out, but these are few and far between. The story elements are good, not great, and the ending leaves a little to be desired. Another problem I ran in to was one puzzle being unsolvable on the lowest graphics setting, when a vital instrument of one of the boxes was obscured. It took a google search of the walkthrough to realize this and turn up my settings to see the full image of the box. However there wasn't a large effect on the gameplay, it simply seemed to be either a glitch or a small oversight.
With the $5 price tag and the beautiful and intriguing content the game provides, this game is very easy to recommend.

I put off playing this game for far too long. My two best friends insisted I play it, but I just never got around to it....until now. The soundtrack is gorgeous, the gameplay is unique, and I was grossly invested in the storyline as it unfolded. I still haven't completed it, but I'm already hooked. The game is out for $3.99 right now, so go go go!! Go get it!!!

There's a lot I could say about Transistor, but very little I can say without spoiling the story. There are a fair amount of reviewers complaining about the ending, but I think part of that might stem into the fact that many people want HAPPY endings where everything is solved and the world is saved and life goes back to normal. Transistor doesn't give you that, so if you don't like your endings with a bleak touch to them, then you might be disappointed like the aforementioned reviewers.  I, however, enjoyed the ending. It was emotional, touching, and I could understand WHY Red did what she did. To go into more detail would spoil a lot, so I'll stop there.
Endings aside, the game is visually stunning. The atmosphere is captivating, the music is fantastic, and I may have had a little too much fun with the fact that hitting the 'Tab' key makes Red hum along to the background music.
The story is fascinating, and I wish the game had been longer so that we could learn more about the characters and the world they're in.
The game play is smooth and requires a great deal of thinking. You have to be very careful about how you arrange your move sets and the actions you take. The wealth of versatility with the abilities you unlock is also wonderful, as it allows you to get creative with customization. Learning effective combinations of active abilities, support abilities, and passive abilities (and every ability can be used in those three categories) is essential. The restriction with how much you can use at a time forces you to think hard about what abilities to select and what function to give them. As well. every time your health bar hits zero you lose an active ability for the rest of the battle and then some (and when you run out of active abilities, of which you can only have four, it's game over), so you're constantly forced to re-evaluate your set-up.
Another aspect of game play is planning. You have 'turns' in which time slows to a crawl and you can execute a certain amount of moves, and game requires you to be clever in how you use your turns. You also have to 'recharge' before you can use a turn again, which leaves you vulnerable if you aren't careful. Some reviewers have expressed frustration that the combat works like this, but I personally enjoyed the challenge. It requires you to think and strategize rather than just button-mash and run around. If that doesn't appeal to you, then this game is going to get real frustrating, real quick. If you like strategy, though, you'll enjoy it.

A truly amazing puzzle game right here people!
Relik features a very basic engine that allows players to get used to the game very quickly and understand it very quickly, the interface is compact and simple, a bit confusing to navigate at times but other than that it's great. There are two main options on the home screen, Attack and Build. Firstly to the build side, your "Battle Cubical" features 4 legendary defences, Sequence, Runes, Mimic and Maze.
First off to Sequence, you can choose a specifid pattern on a 5x5 game board the Sequence length it altered by the level of that side of the cube. You can upgrade a certain side with the parts to it, (Gold and in this case Sequence Parts). Upgrading the sides of you Battle Cubical will increase your limitations of defence, so from lv1 to lv2 I can increase the length of my sequence defence pattern. With sequence you have to have the pattern touch another part of the pattern, so you can't have a block in 1, 1 and then another in 5, 5 if that makes sence, alothough this is a great feature for begginers, it does get a little boring later on.
Second, Runes. This is by far my most favoured Cube SIde. Basicly, Runes is a game where you have to match up two of the same icon, (E.g. E&E). You can level this up too! Although you can't specifically tell the icons where on the board they can go, you do have the 'shuffle' option which moves the icons all around. Though the one problem I have had with this is that it does always have two icons next to each other; no biggie though!
Thirdly, Mimic. One of the most challanging ones I've had I must say. Mimic os a game where you have to follow the Battle Cubicals owners pattern specifically! One wrong move and it sends you back to square one! Upgrading the Mimic will allow you to increase the length of the mimic pattern, the higher level the pattern is the harder it is for challengers! But remember, you can make yours real challenging, the other players can too!
Finally to the maze side. Maze is a mode where you have to follow a line of (lets call it road) to the objective. You have three sides of the cube at your disposal! The game board is 7x7 on each face, so in reality it's 7x7x3 but let's not have a maths lesson here. You can make a road as long, as bendy and as straight as you want, you can drag one road from face to face without limitations! But don't make it simple, the objective is the finish point! Suclude it as far and make it as complicateed from the start as you can!
Now to the game itself,
Relik features a Level/ Rank reward system. If you defeat your opponents BattleCube fast enough you will get 4 stars, with this comes a reward of anywhere between 10-35 trophies and anywhere between 10-35 gold. The cards can feature many things, Gems for the store, Gold for upgrades and most importantly, Upgrade Parts. The trophies will go towards your rank, 0-199 is Leauge I, 200-399 is Leauge II, 400-799 is League III and so on. The higher up your League the better rewards you get from winning a battle, though at the same time the oponents do gain a harder challenge.
Overall I highly suggest this game to anyone who loves a challenge, puzzle based games or just wants time to relax, there isnt anything wrong with the game at all, and I can't possibly make any suggestions to the devalopers because it's all alredy here. Anyways, good luck with you Battle Cubical!

This game is ridiculously easy to get into, but it gets some nice difficulty as you progress.
You play as an underpaid, solo border officer whose job it is to be the sole customs officer monitoring immigration to the fictional country of glorious Arstotzka. Each person you successfully let in (following the rules laid out at the beginning of each day) contributes to your salary.
Each day has a new set of rules defining who is /is not allowed in and which documents they need to have to prove eligibility. You have a manual that tells you what to look for, and how to scan for the inconsistencies and deny passage to those who aren't allowed in.
At the end of each day, your earnings are tallied, and you get to see what's left over after certain expenses, and then choose to still have heat or electricity, etc. It really puts the pressure on to try to be successful because every right answer at the border makes it possible to stay living.
Highly recommend for something you can pass the time with, and it's even better to be supporting an indie dev.

Occasionally people can come to ask for your help. You can either be rewarded or being penalised for helping them. The story is limited to certain length and has multiple endings depending on choices you make. The other mode is called endless. It's completely randomised. Also time is not limited in this mode. You unlock this mode after playing story.
Overall the game captures really well grim atmosphere of cold war era communistic country.
