You need to infect the entire population of the world, and then kill them. With all kinds of different disease/virus types, gene modifications, and the choice of which symptoms you want your disease to display in its patients.
Different ways the disease can be transmitted, resistances to temperatures and different climates.
I like to think of this as a kind of "total world-destruction solitaire". Take that how you will.
Some of the game is very skill-oriented, where as some times on harder difficulties you may rely on the chance of your disease spreading to other continents and having to re-try several times, if not sever dozens of times. So that's the luck part.
This game is very in-depth strategy that puts you in the role of a vengeful, wrathful evil god (or perhaps scientist, who knows?)
If you ever played the popular flash games Pandemic or Pandemic 2 years ago and enjoyed them, this is your game.
It draws obvious inspiration from those games, but adds even more depth and realism to the strategy involved.
More ways to destroy humanity, more information on how your destruction is coming along, better visuals.
In all ways imaginable it is a beefier, better re-creation of Pandemic into a higher-tech envinronmnt than just flash games would be able to bring you.
Overall, for being in early access, I still feel like I got more than my money's worth. Plus, there's new content being added, constant fixes, and upcoming multiplayer with versus and co-op.

This game is
more fun than you'd expect someone's free-to-pay pet project to be.  Much of what story currently exists is admittedly sparse and largely only in place as a means of pointing you in the direction of your next target but it has some interesting lore and side missions already and the potential for much more.  What's more, the game gets updated relatively frequently.  New ships & new equipment, bug fixes, new features, new worlds, new races to meet -- basically whatever the developer can come up with and find a way to integrate.  Add to that the incredible ease of modding (all you need is wordpad) and the game offers considerable time sink potential.
If you ever played the X Universe games then you've got some idea of what you can expect here.  Basically those but scaled down, easier to run and played from a 2D, top-down perspective.  How you persue your career amongst the stars is pretty much entirely up to you.  Maybe you want to establish a flotilla of trade ships and rake in the credits.  Perhaps you'd like to someday command a fleet of fighters from the bridge of your own cruiser (or even carrier, if you play your cards right and your luck holds out) and make earn a living hunting bounties & bringing law to the lawless pirate sectors.  Or, for that matter, maybe you'd like to assemble that fleet and pillage the core worlds.  You can make a decent living off of piracy once you upgrade from one-man fighter craft and, with a sufficiently fearsome reputation, you can even demand regular tribute from the worlds upon which you prey.  Or maybe you'd just like to pilot your own lone, cozy little shuttle craft -- maybe upgrade to a fancier cruise liner down the road -- and just ferry people & small shipments of goods from world to world and enjoy a simpler experience.
All in all, it's hard to decry a free product for not meeting a minimum standard and yet the developer decided to hold himself to one anyway.  Given the short download time, you won't even be out an afternoon if it fails to grab you.  If it sounds at all like something you could enjoy even just putting an hour or two into here and there then there's really no reason not to grab a copy for yourself.

The devs just bailed on the game, leaving me with mixed feelings. Releasing the source code is kind of nice, and at the same time is quite useless in itself.
This is a game which was "prototyped" in a fortnight. Which meant it was written on a language enabling quick prototyping. In this particular case, Lua, which I don't think is precisely the best programming language to develop a project so ambitious as this one was sold to us as being. What sold me the early alpha back in October 2013 was the vision. If I knew the vision was backed by that, ehm,
technological foundations, well, certainly my scepticism about the whole enterprise would have been higher.
On the other hand, the writing was on the wall for all of us to see. The development team promised monthly major updates and a continuous stream of bug fixes between updates. That development wasn't going quite right for this title was obvious when those updates started to lack regularity, at some point after February 2014, right after the "Amnesia Fortnight".
Indeed, Double Fine seemed to forget about this one, since the fortnight turned out to be a couple months. Since then there have been "major updates", but to be honest, I am not sure that the new features added since May are that interesting, well thought out or functional, as the "backbone" of the game. Which I now reckon hadn't changed much between February 2013 and February 2014.
I'll look forward to the source code release. It will be good to see how things were implemented, and probably will inspire others to take up the concept. It will also, to be blunt, allow to rewrite the f*cking thing using tools actually meant for this kind of job (say Unity and C#, or Unreal/Cry Engines and C++). In that sense, hats off to the devs of Spacebase DF-9 and to Double Fine for putting this into the public domain.
Of course, this last paragraph will only make sense to people like me, who understand and appreciate the real hackers' ethics.
What I don't appreciate
is that this comes out of the blue, without saying a "we're sorry but the early access revenue wasn't enough to support development". Which would have been a very a straight way to approach the community, without giving excuse to people to think that they have been duped. I also see some astroturfing going on: it seems like some community management person is trying very hard to spray a giant smiling emoji on top this. And failures like this one are sad.
So I'd say that Double Fine doesn't deserve a sale of this title unless
If you're just interested in a game that you can play now and you can get value for money, just stay away, and look out for that rewrite I mention above.
DISCLAIMER: if the source code turns out to come out with a very restrictive license, i.e. one that prevents people from doing what I suggest above, then I'll be sure to come back to this review and use very different terms.

It's hard not to compare Transistor to Supergiant's previous game Bastion. Both are very different games with Bastion being more of an action rpg with weapon selections, dodge rolls and items, while Transistor works like a tactical action game with turns, positioning, and kitting out your character.
The game throws you right into the middle of the plot, but catches you up on the central events by the time you reach the first boss. The details are left ambigious and the world itself is kept in the background, the player largely skims the surface because it feels like story is just a vehicle for the gameplay and the interaction between the two main characters. The story becomes stranger and more incohesive as the game world begins falling apart. By the time you get a grasp of the story and the gameplay, you're already at the end of the game.
As for gameplay, I mentioned how it was more of a tactical game. You get a lot of options on your abilities and each one can be an attack, an upgrade to an attack, or a passive ability. As a result, even after the first boss you will have enough options that it can become overwhelming and some of the more ideal tricks - like backstabbing - are not clearly described. Ultimately, you will be using the ability to take a turn as both a crutch and your primary means of dealing damage. Enemies come at you agressively and in large enough numbers that taking turns are crucial for surviving. Losing your life bar isn't the end though, as you will lose one of your attacks for the duration of the battle and it won't be restored until a determined number of checkpoints are visited. At the checkpoint, you still have the ability to change out a 'broken' ability and wait for it to repair.
This game is incredibly short with a great sense of art direction, sound, and an interesting method of gameplay, but it's over in such a short time. I encourage you to try this game, but get it at a discount if possible. I look forward to the next game by Supergiant Games.

Having now spent 30 hours on this game I think the time has come for me to finally write a review for this masterpiece. It truly is a complete masterpiece and I don't think anyone could come up with a better long lasting puzzle idea if they tried. Wheras I find most puzzle games loose there charm after a while of just doing very similar puzzles over and over again I find that hexcells has enough variation to keep it intriguing and fun to play for hours on end!
So hexcells infinite is a follow up to the originals, hexcells and hexcells hexcells plus. They are pretty much identical games with a few differences. I will cover all of the games in this review because I think if your going to play them you should start from the beginning and play all of them. The original hexcells is a very easy concept version of the two later games. I say concept because this is what it felt like at this stage. Its as if he was just testing the water as to whether people enjoyed it. It was very simple and when replaying it, it only took me around 1 hour to complete. But then you go on to hexcells plus. This is a very large step up in difficulty and really does get you thinking. Infinite follows on with this step up in difficulty following around the same level of difficulty.
Well what do you do in hexcells? It's basically an upgraded version of minesweeper. Having the field instead in a hex format makes for much more extensive gameplay. They have extra functions in around the hexes instead of just numbers. You have {} which say that the hexes are connecting each other. - - show that they aren't connecting each other. You have large orbits (Not sure what to call them so that name will do?) which show how many hexes are in a large area. And finally there are numbers above some rows that show how many hexes are in that row. So all of these new elements really make you have to think and utilize all of them together to complete a level without making mistakes.
This newest entry series introduces a new feature called inifnite mode. It is a randomly generated field of hexes that is unique every time. There is said to be 999,999,999 different combinations so good luck getting through them all. I have currently done about 150 puzzles. This is where the real longevity of the game comes from. Although infinite mode isn't quite as challenging as the story puzzles it does make it so you don't have to keep playing the default puzzles over and over. I have found myself playing hours on end on this mode.
There is one thing that makes this truly better than minesweeper. No guessing. Yes you heard that correct. There is no guessing at all in hexcells. The maps and algorithms are specially crafting so you never find yourself uncertain to whether there is hex there or not. This makes the gameplay infinitely more fun and makes it so it doesn't get aggrivating after a while.
So if you are a fan of minesweeper or any puzzle game at that hexcells is definitely for you. You can currently buy the hexcells complete pack for a price of £5.99 which is an absolute steal for the amount of time of gameplay you can get out of it. It is an ideal game to spend 10 minutes or so on now and then whenever you have a moment.
Really this isn't the kind of game I expected I would lose my life to but i'm glad I found it!

You need to infect the entire population of the world, and then kill them. With all kinds of different disease/virus types, gene modifications, and the choice of which symptoms you want your disease to display in its patients.
Different ways the disease can be transmitted, resistances to temperatures and different climates.
I like to think of this as a kind of "total world-destruction solitaire". Take that how you will.
Some of the game is very skill-oriented, where as some times on harder difficulties you may rely on the chance of your disease spreading to other continents and having to re-try several times, if not sever dozens of times. So that's the luck part.
This game is very in-depth strategy that puts you in the role of a vengeful, wrathful evil god (or perhaps scientist, who knows?)
If you ever played the popular flash games Pandemic or Pandemic 2 years ago and enjoyed them, this is your game.
It draws obvious inspiration from those games, but adds even more depth and realism to the strategy involved.
More ways to destroy humanity, more information on how your destruction is coming along, better visuals.
In all ways imaginable it is a beefier, better re-creation of Pandemic into a higher-tech envinronmnt than just flash games would be able to bring you.
Overall, for being in early access, I still feel like I got more than my money's worth. Plus, there's new content being added, constant fixes, and upcoming multiplayer with versus and co-op.
Easily a 10/10
Highly recommended

There is so much I love about this game, and would recommend it to any Final Fantasy fan. Fantastic combat, awesome dungeons, beautiful art style, killer looking battle skills, one of the best crafting systems in any MMO to date... It could have been perfect except for one problem:
The ABYSMAL story quests. Go across the world, talk to person nobody cares about, come back, then go there again, maybe fight five trash mobs, go back, repeat five times and hope you finally get to the next dungeon so you can actually fight and use your awesome combat skills. And guess what? If you want any of the cool new classes or expansion content, you HAVE TO DO IT ALL.
The weird thing is that many of the side quests and class quests are more fun and interesting than the entire main story quest combined. It's tragic that a Final Fantasy with such great characters and lore chooses to ignore that for 90% of the story quest, instead making you do menial tasks for faceless npcs you won't be able to remember if your life depended on it, while trudging back and forth like some kind of mailman.
Despite this tragic waste of potential, I'd still recommend picking it up. The community is great, the gameplay (when it lets you actually get to it) is fantastic. I'll continue dreaming against hope that the Main Story quests get streamlined and sheared to hell, but I suppose it's a testament to the rest of the game's quality that I'm willing to endure it.

This game is ingenious. It actually feels like you are working an increasingly tougher job, and it's really quite stressful. However, in terms of originality, and sheer innovation, it is a brilliant game.
Much like a real job, Papers, Please is best played alongside a friend or two, and it helps to delegate inspection duties within the group. Do this, and you'll have some crazy times managing Arstotzka's border. It is a game full of surprises, and it nails the dystopian, Orwellian atmosphere perfectly. The art style fits well There is a real sense of immersion, right from the start, as you start learning the things you NEED to know, to do your job. And of course, just learning your job is not enough, as things constantly change, making your job harder and less bearable. Again, just like real life!
You'll want to start by learning the game's geography: neighbouring countries, and the major cities within each one. And since everything here is fictional and fantasy, you NEED to pay attention. There are things to learn, and you really need to organise yourself to work effectively. Otherwise you soon find yourself unable to buy medicine for your child, and your mother-in-law won't like you anymore (not sure she ever did, tbh). The game is quite frankly, amazing. It feels like hard work, and it feels just as rewarding...and sometimes just as punishing...
Either way, you'll always have a memorable experience whenever you play this.

Factorio is a survival, Real time strategy, Resource gathering, science fiction, combat, gratifying automation monstrosity that has a top down feel like classic starcraft.
The game concept if you've ever played Minecraft with the technical expansions like Tekkit, or Voltz, gets combined with objectives that border on crazy.
The game is designed in such a way that rewards you for ingenuity, and encourages you to keep rebuilding, develop your own unique technique and maximize your productivity, to build bigger, faster, and more powerful factories. in my first week or so, ive already ground my way up to 50 hours, and launched my first satellite into space at hour 46. and I haven't let out a sigh of relief at completion like that since Gwyn at the end of dark souls.
Its a long rewarding grind, and really taps into that problem solving sector of your brain, If you like puzzles, unforgiving challenge combined with a massive open world I encourage you to give Factorio a try.
on a final note The demo doesn't include it, but the game does in fact have a sandbox mode.
Five minutes in Factorio is about an hour in the real world

You can improve in a great many games, if not all of them, but when you revel in the simplicity as games like duet, and tetris, and super hexagon invariably do, it's a mountainous visceral improvement. You climb through try after try, getting better on the bloodstained blue and red failures that pile on and on.

As the third in the series, it unfortunately doesn't bring much more in terms of mechanics than the previous. The "campaign" is nice as usual, neither worse nor better than the previous. This time, though, they introduced a random generator, so you can play an infinite amount of riddles - hence the title. These do not feel as polished and nice as the campaign puzzles, but it's a nice addition when you've completed all the games in the series.

Hexcells Infinite does it again, marking yet another great entry in the Hexcells series. Just like its predecessors, it features fantastic Minesweeper-like mechanics that are supplemented with different methods of revealing information about the solutions to its well-designed puzzles. It also features that same ambient-style soundtrack that leaves players both relaxed and focused. One small but appreciated addition is the ability to quickly restart puzzles and save progress on the current puzzle. It's especially great for taking a break from those bigger puzzles.
The difficulty here, save for a puzzle or two, felt slightly easier than Hexcells Plus. I'm not sure if this is actually due to the hours of practice I've put into the first two games, but regardless I'd recommend at least playing through the original Hexcells before taking on Infinite.
My reviews of the previous games contained complaints about having a limited replay value and, even as well-crafted as the game's pre-designed puzzles are, this is still an issue. But now the game tries to counter that with its Infinite mode, creating randomly generated puzzles to provide an infinite amount of content.
The only problem with this is that many of the puzzles generated are nowhere near as satisfying to play as the ones included with the game. Few of them approach the challenge and cleverness of these pre-arranged puzzles. Playing the randomly-generated puzzles makes one appreciate the care the designer took to make the pre-built puzzles enjoyable. In spite of this, it's hard to complain: Infinite mode is just icing on the cake and is something that will likely make me keep this game installed for quite a while even though I've mastered all the built-in levels.
The bottom-line is that Hexcells is a brilliant game series and Infinite is, while not the most challenging entry, the best entry yet. It's easy to recommend for anyone who enjoys logic-based puzzles.

Hexcells Infinite adds what the first two games most needed; a level generator. Hexcells and Hexcells Plus each had 36 AMAZING hand-built puzzles of ever-increasing difficulty, but once you completed the puzzles with no more than 1 mistake each, that was it. The game went back on the shelf.
Hexcells Infinite also has 36 well-crafted hand-built puzzles, but once those are done you can keep playing with randomly-generated levels. If you buy only one of the trilogy, get this one.
To the developer(s): There are a couple things I'd still like to see improved.
1 - The randomly generated levels vary widely in difficulty and in how long they take to solve. I like to play Hexcells during a 15-minute break at work, and I'd like to be sure I can solve a puzzle in that time. So I'd like to see some size and difficulty settings when generating levels. It would also be nice to be able to disable some of the mechanics, like line clues and blue cell clues, when generating levels.
2 - Just a small UI annoyance. When you go to the Infinite screen to start a random level, it always has 000000 as its seed. You have to click "use a random seed" and then "start". I almost always want to use a random seed, so just pre-populate it with one and save me a step.
3 - Eventually I'd like to see player-built levels (and even worlds/series of levels) be an option. Random maps are great, but I bet some of your players could come up with really awesome, brain-wrenchingly difficult, beautiful puzzles. Steam has tools (Community Workshop) that make sharing user-created content easy. If this has to be done in a 4th title, then I'll be happily buying another Hexcells game when it's finished.

Great potential for the genre.
You build puzzles that other players try to solve, while also attacking (trying to solve) their puzzles. If you solve the enemy puzzle you get rank points; if they solve your puzzle you lose them. The game features the usual gems/gold currencies that you can buy with real money. You need those to buy more "materials" to craft harder puzzles. You can earn gold by just playing and there are no "energy bars" or anything. You can play as much as you want. At the end of each victory you get some gold. It appears to be at random and not based on performance which is how I wish it actually worked. One thing that happened to me after a while was that I kept getting 0 gold after winning. I'm not sure if there is some kind of a daily limit to gold or what but it could also just be a bug since the game is in early access.
Some things I hope to see in the future:
-Obviously more than the 4 puzzles that the game features atm.
-More puzzles like the maze that are really fun to make on your own. It's my favorite thing about the game.
-Different kinds of difficulty increasing mechanisms. Like visual clutter for example, or a shaky screen. Some other stuff you could spend your currencies on to make your puzzles harder.
-Maybe a replay system for the battle log (where you see if others solved your puzzles or not). It would be cool to see how they failed and what made your puzzle difficult for them. Also some kind of statistics tracker so you can for example see a particular puzzle's solving rate.
There's really so much that can be done to make this game better. This is why I'm recommending it. I truly hope to see it grow.

So I think i've played this game enough to write what I think about it so far. So, being the first person to reach 1000 trophies, I already see a problem. There comes a point in the difficulty curve where nobody will be able to beat anyone else. I see this becoming an issue in a week or so as I feel people will obtain such high levels on their reliks that they won't be able to be beaten. The struggle begins at around level 16. This is when the challenges become so long that it is almost impossible to beat them without using some third party program to track what is happening and copying from there. At the same time, you also are able to pay for the gems to purchase pack openings, and with enough microtransactions, I feel someone could become the #1 player and never be able to be beaten. For example, someone who pays for enough packs to reach level 20 in each puzzle could easily hold the top unless someone uses a recording software to track everything and play it back for themselves.
However, when everything is fair and balanced from levels 1-15, I feel that the game has a nice competitive edge. The competition between players to win trophies and take them from others is the type of nice and friendly competition that I personally enjoy in a game. The mystery of opening up cards and the joy of getting a red or yellow is always nice when you're looking for that typical pack opening feel in a game. Being able to design your puzzle any way you like it and change as often as you like gives this game a lot of potential.
In conclusion, the game is great. I highly recommend you download it if you need a nice relaxing brain exercise. However, the issues with high level and pay-to-win capability are a bit frightening for players. Perhaps a level cap or some form of upgrade system to counter the nearly impossible puzzles would assist in making this a bit more playable at high levels. While I haven't seen any player reach this level yet, the bots that are present when you have no evenly matched players to fight show this as their level progresses. The beginning is very fun and I highly recommend downloading for it, but perhaps the higher levels deserve some form of downgrade or counter.
Thank you for reading! Enjoy the game!

This game is ingenious. It actually feels like you are working an increasingly tougher job, and it's really quite stressful. However, in terms of originality, and sheer innovation, it is a brilliant game.
Much like a real job, Papers, Please is best played alongside a friend or two, and it helps to delegate inspection duties within the group. Do this, and you'll have some crazy times managing Arstotzka's border. It is a game full of surprises, and it nails the dystopian, Orwellian atmosphere perfectly. The art style fits well There is a real sense of immersion, right from the start, as you start learning the things you NEED to know, to do your job. And of course, just learning your job is not enough, as things constantly change, making your job harder and less bearable. Again, just like real life!
You'll want to start by learning the game's geography: neighbouring countries, and the major cities within each one. And since everything here is fictional and fantasy, you NEED to pay attention. There are things to learn, and you really need to organise yourself to work effectively. Otherwise you soon find yourself unable to buy medicine for your child, and your mother-in-law won't like you anymore (not sure she ever did, tbh). The game is quite frankly, amazing. It feels like hard work, and it feels just as rewarding...and sometimes just as punishing...
Either way, you'll always have a memorable experience whenever you play this.

It was a great game, however it has a lot of technical issues and I can't recommend you buy it. The Steam version is the same as the one on GOG, so don't expect that one to be any different. Both are at version 1.1 (the menu will say 1.0, this has always been the case, the patch never changed that number, so ignore it, and ignore all the people in the forum thinking they have to install the patch. That does nothing.)
The game's level design is pretty bad, but otherwise it was a fun FPS that also had decent car combat (and every car had an interior camera view!). It was fun blowing up bad guys into red chunks, and the way your weapon would transform into different versions was very cool. The animation for turning your assault rifle into a buzzsaw or sniper rifle was always entertaining.
Sadly, as I said, the game has a ton of issues currently. I was able to get it running on Windows 10 (though a lot of people in the forum can't get it to run at all. I did nothing special, so I have no idea why others are having issues getting it to launch), however you cannot change the resolution any higher than 1280x1024, the framerate is capped at 30fps, there's no way to increase the extremely small FOV, and if you use one of the fanmade patches to get a higher resolution (I was able to get it to launch at 1920x1080) the game will not run through Steam. Hence why it says I've only put a handful of minutes in the game.
Among other smaller issues is that the mouse will go wonky in some menus, slowing to a stuttering crawl, making it very hard to change keybindings and graphic settings. The soundtrack is screwed up and every single level starts with the same loud song (track02, which you can find under the Bonus Content folder), which plays for about 2 minutes and then stops. It doesn't play any of the other 8 songs this game has, it doesn't loop that one song, it just.. stops.
That one song will begin playing once a cutscene starts, too, so if you haven't turned it off (it's the "CD Audio" setting) then you'll have an impossible time trying to hear any of the characters.
If you don't mind playing with no music, a tiny resolution, mouse issues, and the often crashes, then it's a fun game. The level design is, as I said, kind of awful, and you'll get lost a good bit of the time. But the weapons are fun, the vehicles handle nicely, each one has an interior view, and the characters are pretty goofy and entertaining, especially whoever voiced Bork. Goodness, that voice.
Anyway, I can't recommend it, it's too buggy. Not even for the $0.97 it's currently at. I hope that this game sooner or later gets an official patch to fix at least a handful of the issues I've mentioned, but until then just play something else. You aren't missing too much. This is an entertaining, but altogether forgettable game.

Hexcells Infinite is easily my favorite logic puzzle game at the moment. I strongly recommend it to both casual and hardcore puzzle fans. While I've never played the two previous games, I've also never played a puzzle game that so elegantly turns simplicity into difficulty without any sort of contrived pressures such as time limits or fail states. You'll go from feeling like Aristotle to agonized trying to faultlessly solve later levels.
Some describe it like Minesweeper, but I have no attachment to minesweeper. I never even understood it until a friend explained it to me in my 2nd year of college. You just deduce (and in my experience, with enough thought you'll never need to guess and check) where blue and gray hexes are in a field of uncovered, yellow ones. It's simple, but grows fairly deep as new mechanics are added.
Between the 36 handmade levels and the practically infinite levels, Hexcells Infinite packs more than enough content for me to recommend it at a full price. While it begins easy and ends quite hard, there's no fail state, so you can play as carelessly or cautiously as you wish. It also has some of the best puzzle mechanics for such a simple foundation such that it doesn't need to necessarily increase the number hexes to increase the difficulty of a level. The designers deserve a lot of praise, as the later levels are able to both hide and provide information, cleverly entwining hints and further complexity into one hex. It's casual, for sure, as it doesn't pressure you. I like this, because some of the levels truly frustrate me. If anything, it actively tries to sooth you with its clean and calm ambiance.

I have to admit. I've had fun with this game. The developers have done a very good job providing immersion, so much that I have seen comments from people claiming to be real hunters praising the game.
Pros:
- It has nice graphics taking into account how old it is. Some landscapes are really good.
- Sound. Very well done and especially in not becoming annoying after a time. You really feel like walking in the middle of the woods.
- Working weather system.
- Mechanics do the job. Not perfect, though I know nothing of hunting.
- Big world, though you cannot go seamlessly from one reserve to another, each reserve is big enough for this to be a non-issue.
- Several dozens of animals with different levels of difficulty.
- The game continues to get more content.
- It runs in a potato (I have a potato Intel HD 4000 graphics). Very low RAM and Disk requirements.
Cons:
- Doc. Doc is a supposed mentor. He is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. He's only a NPC (I hope) but he'll put himself in your friends list. There are certain rules in the game, quite dumb (but again, I'm not a hunter, don't even know one). Anyway, breaking these rules, especially the ones about which ammo to use with certain animals, will cause you to lose that particular prize, this only means that it is not going to count towards your score. This ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, Doc, is going to send you a mail each time you broke a rule and remind you. At the beginning especially is annoying, because when you shot your first pig with your starter riffle, you had no clue that that wasn't allowed. Anyway, I ended up hating the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and replying back with some choice words the moron seems not to understand as he didn't reply back (lol).
- As I say before mechanics are not perfect. You shot an animal, it is wounded. You follow its tracks. Suddenly it stops bleeding, stops running and it's simply roaming around, sometimes coming over its own tracks in several directions and you are not able to find it anymore, it takes only for you to examine a different set of tracks and you lose it. Then you have a mail, from Doc of course, telling you that you failed to track an animal that you wounded, and that you made the poor beast suffer, as if it was always so easy.
That's it. Overall a very good game.
However, this is really not a free to play game. It should be more properly labeled as a 3 day demo, after which you need to become a member. I'm really disappointed of how limited your options are if you are not a member. The ingame money (gm$) can only be used for consumables, and you don't earn it just by playing, you need to complete missions that award 100 gm$ each, I currently can only do 3, 300 gm$ that are exactly good for nothing. Some missions even require you, if you are not a member, to buy a license to complete them. For example, my next available mission is basically to track and hunt a grizzly, the license to hunt a grizzly for 1 day, 1800 gm$; I could, however, pay roughly 2 dollars for the 1 month, no, for a 28 days license. Really, couldn't even go a full month without needing to pay again?
You receive 2 guns for free. I got an additional riffle by confirming my email, though it is only a skin. And I have no idea how I ended up with 3 shotguns, which are exactly the same too. So 1 riffle and 1 shotgun for free. They each don't work in all animals, even more, with the most recent update there are 3 species that you cannot hunt at all with those. Suppose you want to play without a membership. You are going to need a third weapon that can only be bought with real money, I would never find a problem with this, if not for the fact that, without membership you need to pay also for the ammo for that additional gun (starter riffle and starter shotgun, you get the ammo for free). You won't be using it always though as free players (guests they call them) can only be hunting 5 species at the time, with 3 fixed and 2 rotating each week. Of the fixed, rabbits and pheasants are worthless in my opinion, some even think the other fixed one, the white tail deer is also worthless, but let's say 3 species a week.
Subscriptions go as cheap as about 3$ in my country, and you receive 7 weapons and lots of stuff, equipment, callers, tents, etc, though you have to pay a whole year in advance. But this puts this game in the range of 40$, that you'll need to renew in a year. And on top you need to pay for anything else not included in the package. Think for example, a dog, that'll be fun to have, then it would 10$ more. Want an additional tent? roughly 6 more dollars.
I understand there is people out there that really love this game and don't see an issue. That's ok, if you have tons of money and this game is really your passion. Totally worth it. I personally believe in paying for good games, but not a fixed subscription.

*edit* since playing after uploading this review, I have had the game crash twice after completing a puzzle cube. stas are uploaded, the game just freezes up. once might have been a strange glitch, but twice is a coincidence. will continue playing and if it happens a third time will update my reveiw again
*edit 2* didn't crash but when i went back i found that the next time i went to play a puzzle i had maxed out the daily gold reward, so yeah thats a thing as well. also found out that the clock item gives you an extra 45 seconds on any one puzzle and can be used only when you are under 5 seconds left (damn bot with a lv 10 mimic puzzle) a sidenote is that even the concentration game and sequencer become challenging at around lv 9/10
The game is a very nice puzzler with a solid amount of room for growth. There could be new puzzle types added in the future, thus making your cube differ from the cubes of others. or alterativly, the puzzles you spend hours on could be copied by everyone else through a simple press of the "Print Screen" button. that is one of the problems i thought of as i was playing the game.
Pros:
+It's free, so you can at least try it without spending a penny
+the puzzles might start out easy, but by level 6 mimic, the patterns really start becoming exponetially more difficult (could also be a con if you don't like puzzles, but if thats true why are you even reading this?)
+there is (as of the 2 days after release) only the 4 types of puzzle: sequence, maze, Concentration, and Mimic ('simon says toy' style of memory game)
+While you need points to upgrade your puzzles, to make others fail at it, which does something??? (I havent yet figured that bit out yet) you can earn them in a random choice card pick which you are presented with after completing a puzzles cube, granted it's not a lot, and the upgrades cost progressivly more each time you upgrade.
+Your puzzles(the ones on the cube that you are trying to make Impossible) aren't just randomly assigned to you (though you do get random ones at the start) you can make your puzzle as difficult or as easy as you see fit
+premium currency is earnable from the post cube card picker, but it is low amounts, and more about getting lucky with your free picks, due to the paid picks costing way more than what you'll ever get in return (at least in league 1)
Cons:
-premium currency, and all that having it entails in a game
-since it is free there are In-game purchases, but they arent thrown in your face immediatly.
-the P2W is gonna be real in this. like literally able to make more difficult puzzles faster real.
-There is a daily limit to the amount of post cube card pickers you can do (resetable by spending premium currency, obviously) this means the f2p community will literally be behind the p2w community thus no leaderboard leaders will be f2p, at least not after the first month or even week of this game being up.
-Puzzles that manage to defeat someone are bound to be copied, and then once they become commonplace, beaten easily, this means that to be competitive, not only do you need to be P2w, but also constantly adapting your maze, sequence, and mimic pattern (the Concentration cards can only be suffled by the game, no human interaction there)

Simon Says x2, Concentration, Maze-- that's the entire game in a nutshell. I imagine that the later levels are much more complex and challenging, but I haven't had fun with mazes, simon says or memory games since I was 8... I'm probably the wrong audience.

It was really hard deciding whether to recommend it or not. Here's why I decided not to (followed by what I like):
At its current state (Alpha 6e) there are a few bugs I consider gamebreaking.
1. When exploring a derelict that for various reasons doesn't refill it's oxygen, citizens will walk around and even go there (!) - like technicians wanting to fix something, botanists if there is a garden, etc - until the oxygen is low at which point they start running around panicked. With no way to add oxygen, they do this until they die, often wiping out most or all of my security crew, along with a couple of other idiots who went there.
2. I can't seem to get them to calm down after throwing a tantrum. Most of the time, they wake up (or when they're released from the brig) and throw another. Rinse and repeat until someone kills them.
3. Technicians are quite useless at their work (which goes for all citizens, really, but it's most noticeable with the technicians). It takes forever to fix something.
4. (Related to 2) It's too damn hard keeping your crew happy. I just can't seem to do it, at all!
Ok, so that's why I would not recommend the game at this point. If these things are fixed in a coming update, however, I would definitely recommend it! Here's why:
I really like the challenge it is to build a base in space. Things like broken or incomplete walls are suddenly a major deal. It's fun with the research letting you get better and I like that there are derelicts appearing that you can explore. *  Citizens fight each other far too early into the base development.
*  Citizens become depressed over anything meaning they don't do their job.
*  Citizens stand about in airlocks meaning people can't come and go.
*  Raiders appear too often in low risk zones.
*  Security teams run off when you are being raided leaving citizens to fight and die.
*  Security just orbit around a derelict when you place a beacon on it.
*  Security don't always go into a derelict attached to your base when the beacon is on it and just stand outside.

I really want to like this game, because it seems to want to have so many elements that I like in games - however it is ultimately so frustrating and hard (not difficult) that I inevitably put it down after a short while.
One of the very basic problems is that the 'dangers' feel too contrived.  One starts playing and within a period of time there will be a 'space debris strike' aimed at your balls.  This doesn't feel like randomness, it feels like designers clutching at introducing adversity.
The other problem is that the AI in the game is suicidal at best.  While building structures they will seal themselves into rooms with no air, or no exits.  They will do stupid things such as ignore danger when someone is shooting at them while building or destroying structures.
Also and finally the game's biggest problem of all is that there is no 'border.'  Enemies enter anywhere on the base by attacking in the faux-3d of the game's world.  This means that there is no safe area, no main gate or wall.  The bigger your base gets, the more likely you are to suffer an attack or air leak where you can't contain it and you'll lose half of your crew to something utterly stupid.
All in all, I keep starting the game but then I quit in disgust and frustration,  I see what they are trying to do, but it just feels very unsatisfying and annoying to me.  I'll try again later and report back with the new builds.

The finale of the Hexcells trilogy, Infinite is more Hexcell-y goodness with the added treat of more procedurally generated puzzles than even the hardest core fan will ever be able to play through. If you liked the first two,  you definitely want this one.
One of the best puzzle games. Finally a level generator is added, but the difficulty of the generated puzzles is not too high comparing to the hand-made ones.

Sequel to
and
, Hexcells Infinite is more of the same in a similar package and with fairly similar ambient musical theme and abstract graphics. This is in no way a bad thing.
Like in the originals, the game mechanics are simple but interesting: you have to find out whether all the hexes within the puzzle are blue or black with rules similar to Mine Sweeper and Hanjies. Baseline is that you can always deduce everything: no guessing is required. Though guessing is not punished either. Nevertheless, you need a near-perfect streak to acquire most achievements.
The mechanics have not changed at all after the originals: black hexes contain a number that states how many hexes around it are blue, and blue ones might contain a number stating how many hexes in a two-hex radius are blue. In addition there are Hanjie-like column-numbers that state how many blue hexes are there in a given line.
All 36 puzzles are new, so the owners of the original ones will be pleased. The difficulty curve is a bit steeper than in the original Hexcells but little less than in Hexcells Plus. In effect, it is great as a stand-alone title requiring no knowledge of the two games from before. For me it took 8 hours to complete all 36 hand-crafted puzzles.
Thankfully, saving within a puzzle has finally been provided! I have to wonder why it wasn't featured in the originals. The other new, much-sought after feature are the random-generated puzzles that add a ridiculous amount of replayability: you provide a random number seed and the level is generated, there being supposedly 2 billion levels. Unfortunately, I found the random levels frankly uninspiring and underwhelming in difficulty when compared to the original puzzles. Curiously, the way the random seed is provided introduces a social feature: you can post the coolest random levels (i.e. their seeds) to public forums for others to try. With so many random levels, there are bound to be some gems in the flock discovered only by trying.
With Hexcells Infinite, I'd wager this kind of puzzle game has pretty much been perfected as a concept. I would certainly welcome there being more of these cleverly crafted and well-designed puzzles. The graphics are as perfect as they can be for an abstract game and the ambient music fits the abstract theme splendidly.
If you already played and enjoyed
and
, this game is a must-buy. Otherwise I'd really recommend either
or Hexcells Infinite for their balanced difficulty curves.

If you had one of the older Microsoft Windows versions, than you might remember the game Minesweeper. You had to find the mines and avoid them by marking them. It worked with some clues, since numbers gave away how many mines are close by.
The Hexcells games are very similar to it, but they are not working in square blocks, they come in hexagon shape and often remind of chemical combinations when you open the next level. These shapes make it sometimes hard to figure out what is going on and in later levels you get extra clues for the lines of hexagons and stuff like that.
playing Hexcells is fun in a kind of weird way. Even if you don't want to make your math homework, you sit down to "calculate" the grids, but it is not that much math anyway, more like drawing lines from dot to dot.
Later versions of Hexcells (Hexcells Plus & Hexcells Ininite) are basically the same thing on harder levels and Infinite includes an Endless-Mode that let's you play levels created by chance. Start with the normal game and get infected, this game is addictive and you should consider buying the complete pack right from start.

From the makers of Bastion, this is another beautifully illustrated isometric third person game.
, this is a very different game than Bastion, which features real-time combat and a series of upgradable weapons as well as unlockable skills and passive modifiers. Transistor, on the other hand, is semi-turn-based (recharging skill bar is used to plan combat turns with real-time in between) combat and features a series of skills that can be combined with each-other to produce different effects. The same skills can be used as active attacks, modifiers for those attacks, or passive buffs. This leads to a huge variety of strategy and a wealth of build options.
This is a short game designed for replayability. It reminds me of a few other games I've played in that way--the first one that comes to mind is Squaresoft's The Bouncer. It's a short, story-driven game with combat gameplay that gets better the second (or third) time through. You continue to level-up, the challenge continues to escalate, and the depth of strategic options becomes more rewarding. Plus, you might notice some things the second time you didn't see the first... or were they there at all?
Gameplay Notes:
Style Notes:
If the words "beautiful game" sound appealing to you, chances are you're going to enjoy this. If that phrase sounds just a little too effeminate, there might be a couple design decisions in this game that rub you the wrong way. This game is from the perspective of a female singer; and while the gameplay itself is all stragegic RPG combat, the presentation is still from that delicate place. There's a button to jump up in the air for no other reason than it's a stylish, graceful thing to do. It's in the name: "flourish". There's another button to make the character pause and hum to the background music. This serves absolutely no functional purpose in terms of defeating the enemy--but it does serve the purpose of engaging the player with the character they are playing, and contributes to the beautiful, somber, haunting atmosphere of the game.
I loved Bastion, but I might actually love Transistor even more. I know it's usually the other way around, but I found the story and style of this game to be really engaging.
9/10 Highly recommended.

Typically games are only for a small niche of players, but Borderlands 2... Oh boy
Do you like RPG games?
Do you like FPS games?
Do you like looting?
Do you like grinding?
Do you like raid bosses?
Do you like co-op games?
If you answered yes to any of these questions, Borderlands 2 is for you... Also if you answered no to any of these questions Borderlands 2 is for you.  What I'm getting at is that in this massive game there's something for everyone.
The level of diversity in playstyles between characters as well as the expansive amount of content will always leave you wanting to play it more.
That being said, before you buy it you should know a few things.
The game WILL get stale after a while if you don't switch characters occationally or play it exclusively single player
The playthroughs WILL get repetitive eventually, but this becomes far less of an issue once you get to the super late game content where it gets fun again.
This game is far better with friends, and I highly reccomend playing with other people.  The difficulty scales well with the number of players you have, but make sure you're about the same level as your peers for the best experiance.
This game is worth it at full price, but I would implore you to wait until a sale (which happens often for Borderlands 2) where the game + most of it's DLC goes for about $8-$12.  For the content you get, that's an absolute bargain, but please note that if you want the full experiance (12 more levels on the level cap plus the OP playthroughs) you need to buy the Digistruct Peak DLC alongside the game.
TL;DR
Is it worth it? Yes, but try to get it on sale with the Digistruct Peak add on

What can I say that has not already been written in various reviews?
I spent, or should I say mis-spent many thousands of hours over the years playing MMOs and other online multiplayer games, because I always believed the only solution to providing a real challenge was a real person playing against you. But little did I know, and after starting to let Factorio become a part of my daily routine, and eventually would I come to realize, there is no better opponent against me than myself.
Thats the beauty of Factorio - it's as elegant as chess, but doesn't limit you in really any way other than your imagination and time - you don't need a player, you literally create your own constraints and obstacles to overcome. No sooner do you discover a new skill, or a better way to build, than you try to take that and mentally puzzle yourself on how you can now use that new knowledge to replace and enhance everything that came before.
I've opened up old factories I made in my first few days and smiled at the quaintness of my designs, marvelled at lessons I learned and have in some cases long forgotten, and been frightened by the sheer number of hours I've sunk into this game over the past year.
And if that wasn't enough, even after having some involvement with developer teams in other games, I've never failed to be impressed with the dedication, passion and engagement with the players and community that the Factorio team share with us.
I'm a curmudgeon in many things in life, and admit that I give credit when its due far too rarely, but I can't help but have massive admiration for everything that Kovarex and the entire team have done to make Factorio the perfection that it is so far! The fact that there's so much still to come (4k hi-res! nuclear age! robotic twinkies!) is just mind-blowing.
One final item that often gets overlooked that I want to call out as a joy is that there is absolutely nothing in this game that represents a grind; something that you see all too often in other progression games - everything you do in Factorio is purposeful. Far too often game makers figured the only way to keep you in the game is to provide an artifical barrier that takes some inordinate time/money sink just to make you stay engaged until a nominal achievement. I've only ever stopped a map because I had a yet even better, more efficient idea in my head that I just had to try again to do the 'next' time, only to find after dozens of hours that once again, I have a new revelation and just need to start that 'one' more map... oh how there's ALWAYS just one more thing to try...
Get this game if you get no other this year. Or don't, if you value your time, because you will easily find yourself submerged in gigafactories that would put Tesla to shame every day once you start. Amazing.

It's an amazingly fun game to pick up and play for hours, but the same issue that plagued the first game still exists in this one.  There are too many 'trial and error' puzzles.  A good example of this very early on would be in level 1-4.  In this, the game teaches the player how a {#} hex works in that the active hexes are consecutive.  The only problem with this is that in the very middle there's a lone {2} hex with 4 blanks on either side and an active hex on the top.  There is no possible way to figure ou from that puzzle, which side the blue hex is supposed to go.  It could go on the left, or it could go on the right.  There's no indication at all on where the active hex is supposed to be.
Like I said before, this game is amazing fun, but there are a lot of these trial and error puzzles that are just impossible to figure out because the puzzle itself doesn't give the player the information they would need to solve it without either chancing it, or cheating.

Not surprisingly, more of the same, but that's a good thing. Still a bunch of clever puzzles based around a hybrid of minesweeper, picross, and similar ideas,. The benefit of them being hand-crafted is that they can pull some neat tricks and have a pretty good difficulty curve, and you both know that there's some sadistic jerk out there responsible for it when you get stuck on one and then get to feel smart when you beat HIM instead of the computer.
What's new is the "Infinite" mode, which randomly generates new puzzles. They're still satisfying to play, but they do show off why the previous two games and the other half of this one have human-made puzzles. The machine-generated ones don't have nearly the intricacy or intentionality that a person can come up with, so even though they do add to the game, they're not quite the same. It is interesting seeing the differences though, and they have their own kind of flavor, but they're generally somewhat easier and a bit...weirder. Still enough fun that I got all the achievements though, but the highlight is the main mode, and if you want more of those puzzles, the previous two games have those (although if you can beat this one, the first game will be very easy, and you really should've started there first).
Edit: I have continued to do randomly-generated puzzles for the two years since originally writing this. Send help.

I got this game on my tablet and it was pretty enjoyable to play. Glad to see they're adding some new things to their PC version. So lemme just recap the good things:
- You can name your disease "Cuddles" or something ironic like that
- You act as the god or scientist on a sattelite, upgrading the abilities, symptoms, and the types of spreading of the disease while watching over the world, making sure your virus spreads by any means necessary
- Any player can play this game pretty easily once you get the basics handed down. If you're just a casual gamer like me then just go to casual mode, or if you like a challenge and realism go to Brutal mode to test your knowledge on how a disease outbreak can destroy the earth (in the game of course :P)
- The game itself doesn't require a good PC to run, I'm running this on my laptop which has a medicore graphics card and it still runs fine with no issues.
- Loads of information on the screen, both based on your disease and world events (news, cure research, activity, etc)
- The disease tree allows the player to add a more personal touch to their disease and it doesn't force you to stick to a certain pattern to win, contradictory to what I just said it all depends on your knowledge on how an epidemic starts. For example: a disease that can only be spreaded through water and hot climates will eventually be cured if the traits are kept that way because the world is smart in this game.
- Diseases in the game have a pretty "realistic" nature. If a disease can be spreaded through kisses and hugs it can do that. Be careful though, humans are realistic too, and will eventually thwart your plants by stopping people from hugging and kissing each other eventually. Plan your diseases carefully and upgrade them to the best of your abilities, or personal taste. Make sure to stop the humans from finding loopholes to your epidemic by finding loopholes in their ways of curing people or at least stopping the spread.
- Controls are pretty straight forward, just point the mouse and click. No need for mulitple key bindings if you don't want too, but that's up to personal preference to dictate whether it's good or not to have a game relying on a cursor most of the time.
Now lemme recap the bad things:
- Trying to attempt this game in real life (by that I mean actually starting a real disease) will get you in big doo doo
- If you can't understand what disease is and how it spreads, as well as basic disease terminology, this game may be difficult for you
- Blindly picking stuff from the tree is bad, I've been there and had my disease stopped on Casual difficulty (the easiest difficulty in the game). Reading IS required for the game since the symptoms and diagrams provide you with hints on what each symptom and trait your next choice have and how they behave.
- Recap: Reading is required. Not too much but you need to at least have a basic understanding of reading and some big words. If you don't like reading, then this game isn't for you.
All in all this game is great! I hope they keep developing more things to add to it. Been a fan ever since the app came out for phones and tablets, still a fan for the PC version :D

Sleeping Dogs is one of those rare games that everybody loves, and every recommend to each other, but somehow no one has ever played it ( as far as you know).
So I picked it up during a sale after it had been sitting on my wish list for a long time, and wow.
I get it now.
Sleeping Dogs is an incredible open world game, unique, lovingly crafted, and expertly written. Does it have its faults? Of course it does, as any game does, but the risks it takes, and the ways it succeeds far outweigh any nitpicking.
Protagonist Wei Shen is an interesting, layered, and complex main character, in a world and surrounded by characters that are just as complex as he is.
The story about Hong-Kong Triads is very well done, and every character has so much personality, that you stay curious about how the story will unfold.
I personally still haven't finished the main storyline because I simply don't want it to end. I treat myself to a story mission every now and then, like a delicious slice of cake on the weekend.
But while the story itself is quite serious, as gangsters usually are, the story does make plenty of room for a bit of humor, and especially nods to Hong Kong action movies.
The combat is unique and fun, the world vibrant and interesting, the characters complex, the story great.
Please play Sleeping Dogs, so you can start recommending it to your friends who will also wait months to actually do so, like you did.

Transistor wins my "Biggest Video Game Purchase Disappointment of 2016" award.
This game was advertised as an ARPG. In practice, it handles poorly in real-time. Regular dodging isn't viable, healing in combat is near nonexistent, and there are few defensive skills. The only feasible way to avoid most incoming damage is Matrix-dodging through pause-and-plan. Most attacks force your character to stand still or root you in place, leaving you unable to dodge. If you were looking for the next Diablo, Torchlight, or Sacred, you aren't going to find it here.
Transistor utterly fails as an RPG. There are no meaningful player choices in the storyline and the game world is completely linear. Most zones actually block you from backtracking.  The entire game railroads your character through a linear path, and the only choices you make are your skillbar and how you handle fights. There are no explorable side areas. Might I suggest the (somewhat derogatory) description "rail-playing game"? The story is confusing, vague, incoherent, and makes no sense in some places. The ending was so bad that I actually hammered on my right mouse button hoping for a Mass Effect 2 style Paragon interrupt.
Leveling and experience is highly arbitrary per fight and made almost no sense either - instead of rewarding the player for each enemy defeated, the experience system is more like a bunch of checkpoints and you level up after clearing a fixed number of checkpoints. The only replay value is the "New Game Plus" option - start a new game and keep your levels and progress. Even worse: after starting a New Game Plus, the game actually lost all my levels and character profile.
The soundtrack was largely disappointing, sometimes bordering on background noise. I have no idea why it was tagged with "Great Soundtrack" - Supergiant's previous game "Bastion" had a much better soundtrack. Plenty of classic games from the mid to late 90's had much better soundtracks that took up 1/10th of the disk space.
Transistor also lacks a proper main menu and I found the UI to be confusing at first and unwieldy after getting used to it. when you start the game, you get dumped to the intro with no clue about what happened. The skillbar UI needs a lot of work - you have to select each skill and choose a slot when the obvious proper solution would have been a drag-and-drop interface.
The general lack of content is mind boggling, especially for 3 GB of storage space on disk. I was able to finish the game in 6 hours (the same day I got it), including figuring out the UI and testing various ability upgrades.
The good:
Most fair negative reviews will find at least something positive. The combat system's time-stop mechanics and the function upgrading are innovative (if you enjoyed the function upgrading, look for Magicmaker - another indie game designed around similar ability-mechanic combining). Most fights were well-balanced (although there were a few  unreasonable ones).
Summary:
Disappointing trainwreck of fail. No idea why Transistor consistently gets 95% positive reviews - if that's what people like, then I have serious concerns about the future of indie games. I got this game on -80% sale ($4) and IMO didn't get my money's worth. Bastion was better in almost every way (and the price is actually lower too).  The $20 base price is ridiculous considering that Skyrim costs the same and has 100-200x more content (not including mods).  If you like games with tactical pause, you're better off with Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Aarklash: Legacy, Dragon Age, or Mass Effect. If you want a regular ARPG, there are tons of those out there.

Ok, so here's the review. I love this game, and it's one of my favorites. I'm going to do a run down of each part of the game.
POSSIBLY LIGHT SPOILERS WARNING
Overview:
Like Supergiant's last game, Bastion, Transistor is an isometric hack-and slasher with a good story and narrator. Story can be a little bit pretentious, but the combat provides a solid core and everything else is either excellent or good enough that I can reccomend this.
Combat:
This is what you'll be doing most of the time. While it starts off relativley simple, it gains depth as you aquire more Functions (your skills) from corpses you find. The main "gimmick" (but it's not really a gimmick) is being able to freeze time and plan what moves you'll use. You can freeze time, jump behind an enemy, and get a backstab with a melee ability. The combat is a bit complex, but you'll get the hang of it. You (eventually) get four active Function slots, each which can be buffed with two more Functions, and on top of that you can have 2 (or possibly 4 but that's hard to do) passive Functions. The only way to get story documents about corpses which gave you functions is to use the functions as an active, equiping another skill with it, and using it as a passive. This encourages trying new things with the combat. There are also things called Limiters, which you unlock over time. Equiping one makes the game harder, and tells you about the enemy it corresponds with. Combat: 8.5/10
Story:
The story is really good if you can figure out what's going on. The characters are mostly given depth through their Functions, because the only characters that talk are three of the villains and your sword. Red, the main character, is a singer who lost her voice because of the villains, which is all I can say without spoiling anything. The sword, getting to talk the most, is the most developed character, but Red is still the favorite of most fans. The story is great, but very confusing without reading some of the community's threads. It regards the cyberpunk city of Cloudbank, where the citizens democratically control what the sky looks like, what the weather is, and what buildings are constructed. (Can't say how without spoilers.) But patterns develop, and the system designed to bring novelty results in nothing changing. This leads to a terrorist orginization of Cloudbank's administrators killing off artists and the people who change the city, and eventually they release an evil called the Process on Cloudbank. The ending of the story is a gut-punch moment. Story: 8/10
Aesthetic:
While the art is great, it's nothing compared tO THE MUSIC IT'S AMAZING. (There are people who bought this game for the soundtrack and still haven't played it.) Aesthetic: 10/10
So if you're looking for a short, replayable story based (slightly pretentious) hack and slasher with the greatest soundtrack of any game ever (seriously), Transistor is the game for you.
Overall: 8.83

Now, the story is quite deep for a seemingly simple game (to be honest I didn't get it all until I checked it online) but I'll give you a spoiler-free, rough idea of what this game is about.
A city called Cloudbank is attacked by the Camerata which is a group of individuals who intend to change the city using Processes which are basically robotic creatures. You play as Red, a female singer who fights these creatures with the Transistor, a weapon that can also speak to you.
Throughout the game, you will receive new abilities called Functions for the Transistor which can be combined differently to produce different effects on your attack and defence. You will be able to change and combine the Functions together at terminals called Access Points to help you fight different foes with different abilities. There are also Sandbox areas for you to test and experiment with the Functions.
Armed with the Transistor, you will fight your way through beautiful locations, unlocking new Functions and facing new enemies. Your talking, sword-like weapon will keep you company and help you make sense of what is happening.

I remember first encountering this game during Amnesia Fortnight 2012, Double Fine's crowdfunded event in which they put out a series of rapid prototypes to test out a bunch of different game ideas.
I'm going to bottom line this for you: the game hasn't evolved significantly beyond what was originally shown off as a rapid development prototype nearly two years ago. Updates are slow and add to the backend with new features that increase complexity, but don't actually add content or meaningful gameplay in any way. Worse, the developers have completely removed the "Future development plans" backlog from their website with no explanation. This is to say nothing of the numerous game breaking bugs and brick-dumb AI which have survived for release after release.
And yet I could deal with all of that if the game were fun to play... but it's not. Games like its inspiration, Dwarf Fortress, are fun because of their emergent gameplay - the stories and situations which unfold around you are completely unique to each playthrough, creating a different experience every time you play. This frankly isn't true in DF-9, at least in its current state. Fire up the game and start on a random map and you'll have built and encountered everything there is to see in around an hour; there's no point in starting a new game since the same story unfolds every time.

First let me say this: I have a very deep love for Dwarf Fortress. I absolutely adore that game so I have bought almost every dwarf fortressesque game on early access.
However, this game: Spacebase DF-9 is not a good game. Why? Several reasons, but most relate to really bad controls. To build stuff or select or anything is really fiddily because it has a hard time registrating where the mouse is pointing on the grid - so you have a really hard game just controlling the damn game. Also the UI is hard to understand sometimes. The citizens all have their own individual "twitter feeds" where they write what the think of your space station, but the problem is that it's hard to understand exactly what their problems are. The game is also very unbalanced so it's hard to get a space base running and the nature of space means that it's important to make sure that you build correctly the first time. More so than in dwarf fortress where you can occasionally correct mistakes or convert rooms. Here your items often take more than 1 space on a grid so you'll find that its harder to convert rooms to other things. Also the rooms needs to be substantially bigger and you cannot put stuff like beds beside walls because they need all of the bed's adjacent squares to be free.
EDIT: It has been a long time since the developers decided to abandon this project. I think I speak for all of us who bought this game when I say that we're all deeply disappointed in them. We all think it's a scam, and that it was not finished like it should have been. They never fixed the interface or the controlling problems. Stay away from this scam if  you  know what's good for you.

This is the third game in a series of addictive puzzlers (Hexcells, Hexcells Plus, Hexcells Infinite), and I would not recommend starting here -- go back and play through the others as the difficulty here is tuned assuming you've already taken the training wheels off.
The overall idea is not that complex; like Minesweeper and Picross, you use partial information to slowly reveal whether a tile is "on" or "off" until you are done.  You never need to guess; the information is always there.  The magic here is in the ways the information is presented (at varying times you will learn how many tiles are on in a given column, row, or diagonal, how many tiles adjactent to a tile are on, how many tiles in a region are on, and whether the tiles that are on are contiguous or not).  Early in the game there is enough information to happily click through and solve the puzzles; late in the game, every bit of information has you trying to figure out how it can combine with existing information to yield one more "yes" or "no."
The end result is incredibly satisfying, a well-earned "perfect" score.
It also has replay value with a random level generator, but the real magic of the game is in the hand-crafted puzzles that force you to collate all the available information until the next logical action pops out.
It's a thing of beauty, and I recommend it to anyone who enjoys logic puzzles.

The best version of Hexcells by far.
The simplest way to describe it is a mix between minesweeper and picross; and it adds even more puzzle elements.  Any fan of those games will certainly appreciate Hexcells.
Infinite keeps all of the mechanics from Plus and adds a random generator so you can essentially never run out of hexcells puzzles to play.  The generated puzzles tend to be more simple than the handmade puzzles but it's better than nothing.  There is also a way to import user made puzzles using a code, so that's great too.
Easily recommended for any fan of logic puzzles.  I really look forward to future creations from Matthew Brown.

Duet is a feat of elegant and minimalistic game design, in the "easy to learn, hard to master" genre.
The entire gameplay revolves - literally - around a single axis. And yet you'll be surprised at the variety of levels. It plays well on keyboard, controller or touchscreen, and runs as smooth as can be.
It's a game you play in small bursts, as these are short levels, but there is also a lot of replay value with perfect runs, achievements, endless mode, daily and nightly challenges etc.
I should get frustrated at some of the later levels which require devilishly precise controls, but yet I don't because of the awesome relaxing soundtrack. Duet is my pick-me-up when I want to chill for 15 minutes.

I just realized that I've never reviewed this awesome game. I don't know what it costs now as I bought my 3 copies a long time ago but this game is worth every cent. If you like micromanagement type stuff you'll, without a doubt, love this game. I know its EA and people get scared of that. I can tell you; you don't do not have to worry about that here. It's a complete game with an insane variety of mods.
You can set it up where you can mine crazy different types of resources and turn them into a cornucopia of different compnents, all to build  a crap-ton of different buildings and facilities that have a vast array of different tasks and functions. Or you can plop down a series of said buildings and have them do it for you while you do some mad-scientist-type♥♥♥♥♥♥on the other side of your complex.
I'm playing with bob's mods right now so it makes the game alot more intricate but the tech tree opens up tons of new stuff to build and when you finally gather all the resistors and rubber bands and duct tape you need to open up new things you feel a great sense of having accomplished something epic. Especially later on, when you get trains or when you can get robotics and have little drones do all your dirty work for you. This effect is made even better in mulyiplayer, although we did have quite a few connection issues, which may have been on my end, we played a long time and had a huge base set up. That aside; it was an excellent experience co-ordinating all the choas of supply chains with a partner. I can only imagine how much fun it would be with more players all doing their own thing and yet working together against a huge alien swarm.
Did I forget to mention that? Its not just the craziest logistics simulator I've ever had the pleasure to lay my gray matter on, it also has alien swarms that tear your stuff up and cause havoc to your smooth running operations. You can turn them off too if you want. Well, make them not attack you first. They'll still attack but you have to go to their nests and provoke them. The dirty smog that rolls from your power plants and machinery sets them off otherwise. You eventually need some of the resources from them so sooner or later you'll end up duking it out but the reprieve from constant attacks can be nice when you first learn the game. Which is the next point I would like to stress...
There is ALOT of stuff in this game. I thought the learning curve was pretty big. I'm not the brightest guy but I can usually figure out what I need to. I've played Kerbal Space Program and spent nights reading articles on rocket science, if that's any indicator. Although I'm pretty sure I spelled cornucopia wrong back there. Maybe not. Anyway, what was I saying? ... Yea, lots of stuff. Add in a few mods and you'll be confused all over again. Personally I love this. Some people probably hate it. If you stick with it though, its truly rewarding.
+++PROS+++
=You can harvest everything and turn it into something else.
=You can play with train sets.
=Alien swarms will tear through your base, build towers to stop them.
=You can deforest the planet with huge tanks spewing smog into a normally peaceful alien homeworld.
=You can do it with friends!
---CONS---
=Sprained pinkie alt+tabbing to read wikis.
=Those alien scum are gonna pay for shooting up my ride.
=Headaches from trying to connect 5 outputs into 4 inputs for 27 hours straight.
=Vehicular manslaughter.

First let me say this: I have a very deep love for Dwarf Fortress. I absolutely adore that game so I have bought almost every dwarf fortressesque game on early access.
However, this game: Spacebase DF-9 is not a good game. Why? Several reasons, but most relate to really bad controls. To build stuff or select or anything is really fiddily because it has a hard time registrating where the mouse is pointing on the grid - so you have a really hard game just controlling the damn game. Also the UI is hard to understand sometimes. The citizens all have their own individual "twitter feeds" where they write what the think of your space station, but the problem is that it's hard to understand exactly what their problems are. The game is also very unbalanced so it's hard to get a space base running and the nature of space means that it's important to make sure that you build correctly the first time. More so than in dwarf fortress where you can occasionally correct mistakes or convert rooms. Here your items often take more than 1 space on a grid so you'll find that its harder to convert rooms to other things. Also the rooms needs to be substantially bigger and you cannot put stuff like beds beside walls because they need all of the bed's adjacent squares to be free.
EDIT: It has been a long time since the developers decided to abandon this project. I think I speak for all of us who bought this game when I say that we're all deeply disappointed in them. We all think it's a scam, and that it was not finished like it should have been. They never fixed the interface or the controlling problems. Stay away from this scam if  you  know what's good for you.

AI would rather sleep then do a job you have assigned them to; AI get's stuck within a structure with no doors or other forms of escape after you ask them to build it.
