I will personaly be continuing to attempt playing this game, but can't recommend it to others that haven't already paid for the alpha.

The set up of this game is really simple; rotate a couple balls so that don't smack into some blocks moving down the screen.  It really does seem like it would be that simple, but it's actually really challenging and addictive.  Every time you collide a ball with a block it'll splash some paint and restart the level.  And you're happy to restart.  And restart.  And, damn it, restart again!  You want to keep playing. You don't want to have your little globes of paint smashed against the blocks, you want to get them to the end, and you're sure you will this time.  Just.  One.  More.  Go...  Eventually you'll notice you're flying through some kind of Jackson Pollock painting!
Simple but effective graphics, music that feel right at home, and a pretty addictive game play.

Duet is a difficult but fair minimal action puzzler in the vein of Super Hexagon and Pivvot.
The pacing of the game is admirable: the difficulty curve ramps up progressively without ever looking like a step function (looking at you, Osmos). There is a story of sorts, too.
Recommended for fans of the above mentioned games.

Judgement:

Preface: At the time of writing, Transistor and it's soundtrack, along with Bastion and it's soundtrack, are available for $10. This is less than half the price of Transistor's full price alone, sans soundtrack. Transistor alone is worth the $20 asking price, but adding in the phenomenal soundtracks of both it and Bastion, as well as Bastion itself, makes this a deal you absolutely shouldn't miss. For the price of a decent lunch, you can have two of the best sounding and looking games that weren't made by CD Projekt Red.
Plus, I'd pay way more to hear Logan Cunningham talk to me any day of the week. Seriously, this guy gives Morgan Freeman a run for his money.
I don't know quite how to articulate into words what Transistor is, or how it accomplishes everything it sets out to do, but there are a couple of things that need to be said about it nonetheless.
First off, this is the single most fitting example of the idea that games are art. From the color pallete, to the painting-like mostly-still cutscenes, everything about this game has some element of beauty to it. I've yet to see another title which so effectively integrates an art style into both the gameplay and narrative of a game. Transistor simply stands alone in this respect.
Secondly, someone needs to explain to me how Darren Korb manages to make such great goddamn music so consistently. He's managed to put out two albums for two separate games, and in that span of something like 50 ish songs, he hasn't produced a single bad track. I may prefer certain songs, but I've yet to hear something from him that didn't at least have some merit to it, which isn't something I can say for any other musician I've listened to.
Also, as a side note, other reviews make mention that the reveiewer couldn't exactly grasp some of the story, which I will grant is a valid complaint. Transistor takes very little effort to explain what's going on at any specific point, and even in the beginning is hesitant to tell you what has happened, and to many that creates a problem. I, personally, kinda enjoyed the fact that I was lost within the narrative. Part of the story to me was being the veritable wrench in the machine. You don't quite need to know how a copier works to break it, and the story of why The Camerata did what they did isn't a neccessary piece of information to Red or the player. At any given point, Red is unaware of the motivations of those she pursues, but that seems like a fitting part of the story. Her motivation is of a personal nature, rather than to save the world, or any other standard video game scripting. That, to me, is why it so excelled, and why the wrapping up of the story was so effective. The point isn't about why any given thing is going on, it's about how people manage to deal with it. This isn't exactly what many others were looking for, though, and if you wanted a sweeping story of espionage and attempted takeovers, then your milage will vary a lot depending on the attention to detail you pay. It's a little fitting, I presume, that two of my favorite things of recent times have embraced similar themes. A show on HBO recently called The Leftovers follows the same ideology of narrative. The real motivating factor isn't to determine why an event occurs, it's to understand how that event has an impact on the people involved. They're both stories inevitably about people, even though they place themselves within the backdrop of much greater forces around them. Anyway, following the unreasonably long expose on the story, I should probably just congratulate anyone who made it to this sentance, and then end the review sooner rather than later.
I'm not going to be able to say much that hasn't already been said by others, but at the end of the day, a game like Transistor doesn't come around very often. It seems a fully realized idea, which is a rarity. Oftentimes, you can tell where the vision behind a game slipped at least a little bit, but every part of Transistor seems like it was deliberately created in this fashion to give the End User this unique and unforgettable experience. Truly a work of art, from start to finish, and I'm not saying that lightly. Hell, just look at some of the screenshots people put up and you'll see for yourself.
Keep it up Supergiant. I've yet to find another developer with such obvious passion and skill for the interactive arts, and as I optimistically awaited Transistor following the release of Bastion, I will now await their next title, Pyre. Here's hoping they go 3/3.

The game´s good and its atmosphere is fantastic, but the puzzles are way too linear.

You spend the entire game focused on one object at a time. You have to figure out all its secrets before you can move on to the next object, and the entire thing is very linear. Thankfully, it's really easy to figure out what you should be concentrating on.
The objects (safes, boxes, etc.) looked lovely, and I really liked the way the goggles, which allowed you to see things you couldn't before, added another dimension to the puzzles. The puzzles were intriguing but not really all that hard, especially since I occasionally made use of the game's hint system. I usually didn't need more than one or two hints to figure out what I was supposed to be trying to do.
The controls were sometimes a little annoying. There was one box I had difficulty opening up because I was looking at the object from the wrong angle. Also, there was one puzzle that drove me to a walkthrough video. It turns out that I'd actually figured it out, but I hadn't slid one of the tiles far enough into its slot to trigger the next part of the game.
The story was paper thin, just enough to tie all the objects and magical symbols together.
I bought this on sale and was happy with what I got. It was a nice few hours of entertainment. True puzzle fiends might wish that the game's puzzles were more difficult, but I enjoyed them. It was fun to see what new thing would open up each time I solved a puzzle, and my overall feelings of frustration and confusion were low.

UPDATE 2:  Just played 1.05, the "release" version of the game.  Some of the bugs I've mentioned have been addressed, but only a few.  Now features a "tutorial" level that is basically just a pre-built base with some lame text overlays telling you to perform a few tasks.  I played the level after the tutorials were complete, and was immediately swamped by a continous stream of raider vessels.  Base went from 12 occupants to just 1, and when I saw that last "Raider breach vessel incoming!" message I just quit the game and un-installed it again.
Pros:
☑  Er.  I wish it were a good game that had potential?  Cuz I would love me a Sim Starbase game.
Cons:
☒  Very buggy user interface.  I commonly had to "trick" the game to build an item by building another and then canceling it before completing it in order to get it to build the second item (which is the item I wanted in the first place).  If items overlap, then it is impossible to click on one or more of the overlapped items.  (Say if you have a claim-territory flag that is overlapped by an oxygen generator.)
☒  Obtuse needs and wants system.  My crew fights and kills each other, and I am never sure why without carefully inspecting each cluttered needs/wants screen for each crew member.
☒  I've lost dozens of crew without even really knowing why.  The notification bar fills up with tons of "XXXX needs medical attention" and "XXXX is dead" messages before I can even react to whatever is putting my crew in danger.
☒  Your first base is going to result in dead astronauts.  So will your second, third, fourth and likely fifth.  Margins are extremely thin at the beginning of the game, so if you screw up in the least (such as build a room too small to hold a refinery, without knowing how big that refinery is) you have to start over.  There is no way to undo or fix a build mistake, so if you make any at the critical first few minutes of the game, then kiss your space-butt goodbye.
☒  Zoning system is clunky and requires you to build a special-purpose room to simply place one item.
☒  Annoying fixed view that cannot be rotated, nor is there a "fade behind" effect when someone or something is behind another object, so it's easy to lose people or things.  This will likely never change either, because while the crew are rendered as 3D models, it's clear the walls and objects are static sprites, and if the devs didn't account for rotating views at this point in the dev cycle, they probably never will.
☒  Overall quite buggy.  UI elements end up becoming corrupt, crew get stuck in rampaging loops and can never be subdued, miners will drop ore in the middle of space during a crisis and never pick it back up, etc.
☒  Feels very unpolished, and like an early WIP.  Expected more progress for this game since the last time I looked at it (about a year ago).

This is the third and definitive entry into the Hexcells series. This game remedies the primary problem with the first two games in that it has a random level generator. Now, unlike the first two games, you have a good degree of replayability when you've finished the main progression. Difficulty in this game is, as far as I remember, at least as hard as Hexcells Plus, so it will be quite a challenge, especially if you attempt to perfect all of the levels. This is the best Hexcells game, so if you just want to buy one, this is the one.

This is a very fun puzzle game, a cross between Minesweeper and Picross/Nonograms. It has great relaxing music and visuals, and the puzzles themselves are designed to be fun and relaxing.
That first paragraph is the one I copy/pasted between all of my Hexcells reviews. Hexcells Infinite continues the trend the others set, but is FAR more polished with more features.
Firstly, along with the standard 36, there's a new puzzle generator using 'seeds'. Seeds is just a random string of numbers used to generate something, in this case a puzzle. You can choose for the Puzzle Generator to either randomly generate a seed for you(and therefore a random/new puzzle), or use the current days date, making it a sort of daily challenge. Either way, you can share the seed with friends and compete to see who does better.
Secondly, there's far more sounds and music tracks to listen to while you play, all of which are wonderful and relaxing.
And lastly, theres some customization options now. For those who have played the other two Hexcells, you know of the mechanic/clue thats a blue cell with a number in it that tells you how many blue cells are in the area, and that you can left click it to make it highlight its 2 cell radius. In Infinite, there's an option to make that highlight flash, or to make it not flash and have a black border. Either way improves visibility in the way you like it. Next is that you can switch which mouse button does what, so instead Left Click for Blue Tiles and Right Click for Black Tiles, you can reverse that so it's Left Click Black, Right Click Blue.
Anyway, if you like Hexcells and Hexcells Plus, then Infinite is a absolutely must have. If you haven't played any, and can only afford one of the Hexcells games, then I recommend this one, as it has the Standard 36 Puzzles, Puzzle Generator, More Music/Sound, better Customization, and just generally better overall. And for those who don't know, each Hexcells has little text tutorials that does wonders for teaching and isn't invasive/hand-holding.
Each new Hexcells DID introduce new mechanics, and while Infinite does explain it properly, I'd say get the Hexcells Complete Pack since it's such a great Puzzle game. But again, if you can only get one of them, get Infinite, I definitely recommend to any Minesweeper/Picross/Nonogram/Puzzle fan.

Very polished game for being in Alpha. Definitely worth the price ($6 as of this writing).

I used to like this game. Post version 6 release, it now totally sucks.
Why?
Specifically the AI doesn't seem capable of managing the new functionality. Also the threat system is totally broken. For some reason in my "extreme low" hostility sector I get constant pirate raids (and I do mean constant. Like... 30 seconds after beating the last one there's another).  Or a meteor impact. The "game" (if one can call it that anymore) has gone from a space colony sim to a constant crisis.
But more fundamentally... the brig system doesn't work right, nor the tantrum system. So first the brig system: enemies can often get "subdued" where they just stand there endlessly until they starve. If you have a brig, you can store them there instead. There doesn't appear to be any reason to do this that I can see. There is no benefit. Its preferable to let enemies starve, especially because sometimes captured enemies lose their "subdued" flag and simply walk out of the brig to shoot up your base again. Seriously... WHAT IS THE POINT? Also... did you guys even test this release?? Its almost entirely unplayable.
Okay so now to the tantrum system. Colonists can get freaked out, wreck the place up, and fight with fellow colonists. Yet for some reason this happens to happy colonists sometimes. I suppose one could say they "just snap" or something but... once again, what is the point of happiness if it doesn't do anything? Bigger problem is after a tantrumed colonist is subdued they lay there and nothing happens. Even if you have doctors on staff, they don't seem to treat the person like... laying there in the hallway injured. It appears that the primary role of doctors is simply corpse disposal, rather than anything doctor-y.
If steam had a numeric rating system, I'd give this 1 of 5 stars. Its really abysmal and should never have been released with the numerous game-breaking bugs. At least it was playable before.

First off, I absolutley love this game to no end. Albiet it is VERY slow starting off, it really starts to grow on you after you've made a few shipments, get just absolutley wrecked brutally and without mercy somewhere close to (if not in) the anal region by space pirates, follow a lot fun little questlines that just add that much more to the game. If you've got the eye for it, you can spot all the funny little puns and references.
The devs in the game are always busy, and they gladly accept help to add on to the game, which would be a great thing for talented people to do because there's only one main faction line so far, and half the entire galaxy hasent even been mapped out yet! There's so much promise here for the makings of an absolutley amazing game, but thats the thing, it already is, I still have trouble finding where exactly all the history begins from now to "present day" in game, i really look forward to seeing it completed.
There have been times in a mission where i had to really just sit there and debate what to do for my next action, because the writing is just that good, could use improvments in some places, but overall is just fantastic. The game goes on day by day which is a neat aspect. events tend to follow a time set in the calendar and i always look forward to what can happen next.
As maybe some suggestions or requests from me, I want more detailed stories that follow longer paths, for example that lovely couple from the Smugglers Den, I thought I'd get a lot more from that and I didn't, but thats just me nitpicking it. I want more ships, species, and ship attachments. More diversity among the fighters, warships and whatnot.
I'd personally like to see a pirate storyline complete with a whole new layer of story and depth. Maybe if you get dangerous enough, some pirate contacts you and sends you to a planet to either meet his boss or become his protige? i dunno, just a cool thought.

the options or rather lack of options is not very good, give us at elast the option to change the sensitivity, that would be great with the horrible camera control, and as for the graphics, i believe that it should remain as it is, perhaps refine the textures to make them seamless.
the idea is decent, the engine is refined, the game sadly is horrible as of yet, but i have hope for this game, perhaps extra help and more time taken to edit the game would do it much better, perhaps even include like a voxel-like creator where users can create their own assets and put them in the environment like beds, bunks, TVs, and a ton more things.

There's a fine line between hypnotic and pretentious.
Duet is the most fun I had with a game in years. It hits the right balance between challenging and relaxing. Visually simple it's still very pleasing to the eye and does give you just enough context beyond the bare gameplay mechanics to keep you engaged. The gameplay keeps evolving from chapter to chapter so you don't get complacent and the soothing soundtrack is almost mesmerizing.
Duet might not be for everyone but I enjoyed it immensely. It made me think about other abstract games in recent years like lovely planet, thomas was alone or older games like Rez or Vib Ribbon that sometimes border on pretentious but are at least attempts at creating a gaming world filled with more than angry football players bouncing around with rocket launchers or angry wrestlers swinging axes at other angry wrestlers with green skin. I think diversity adds spice to entertainment and the odd little indie title wouldn't fly as well without the braindead arm chair general masturbation fantasy, but i would love to conduct an experiment (if I can go off-topic in this review which no one will ever read): ban graphically violent games for two years, not because media violence is harmful to the youth but because it's become so
, and force developers to find new ways to entertain us. Force them to be clever. Wouldn't that be fascinating?

This game feels like it's going to be extremely good.  But right now it's more like a horror game.  The whole time you're playing, you have this horrific, sinking feeling that something is going to happen that makes absolutely no sense, and you'll have to restart (or, more likely, quit).
I've played several times on earlier versions, and I just played 3 games on the latest alpha (6b).  First game, I ran out of minerals before I built my refinery.  Whoops.  Second game my guys finished the building, but then wouldn't enter it, despite everything being apparently in order.  They all died of asphyxiation.  Third game, I got the base up and running, things were looking great, but then meteors came and smashed into my base.  While no walls or floor were visibly damaged, the oxygen dropped to 0% and everyone died.
I can't say the game is just flat out broken, but it sure feels like it.
That being said, the potential is there... they just need to get this out of alpha.  I really wish they hadn't made it early access so darn early.  This latest update does not fix the game enough to warrant being released as early access yet.
I think I'll love this game eventually, but it pains me to say that I think they released this so early in order to fund other projects.
The developers may love this game, deep down.  "But it's not who you are underneath, it's what you do that defines you."
Edit: Is it any surprise that people disliked this negative review, and yet, I feel I hit the nail on the head now that the game has been "released".

/edit I love how I posted this and then they did the 180 on the game like a couple days later. Belief misplaced. I really wish someone would finish this though, it was really fun.

Hexcells is an expertly-crafted mind-bending game of deduction and observation, reminiscent of two great classic puzzle games, Minesweeper and Picross.

The tutorial in World 2-1 explains that a cell with a notation -2- has 2 blue cells around it that are

A puzzle game in the vein of Minesweeper, but more complicated. It’s the best of the Hexcells games, and the random level generator on top of the main game’s levels gives it more gameplay.
4-8 hours (Main game)
7/10
For those not familiar with the Hexcells series, the gameplay is similar to Minesweeper in that you must determine which cells on the board contain blue hexes, and which are vacant. There are various ways the game indicates which cells contain hexes, and which are vacant.
Vacant cells will often contain a number indicating how many adjacent cells contain hexes (though sometimes they merely contain a question mark). Simply left click to mark a cell as containing a blue hex, and right click to mark it vacant (the game will indicate if you’ve made a mistake).
As you progress through the game more ways to determine which cells contain hexes are introduced. Columns (even diagonals) will contain a number indicating how many blue hexes are in that column. Numbers (for both in vacant cells and columns) will sometimes be encased in curly brackets indicating that the hexes are all connected in a line. Numbers may also be surrounded by a hyphen, indicating that not all the blue hexes are in a line (so there’s at least one break).
Blue hexes may even contain a number, indicating how man blue hexes are in a 2 cell radius.
The main new feature to this game compared to past games in the series is its random level generator. So after you’ve completed the 36 levels in the main game, you have the option to keep playing as many randomly generated levels as you please, giving the game more longevity than past iterations.
The difficulty of Infinite is greater than the first game in the series, but notably less than the second. The difficulty curve is much more natural, and lends itself well to players who are new to the series. Depending on if you’ve played the past games or not, Infinite will probably take you about 4-8 hours to complete the main game.
Hexcells Infinite manages to fix one of my main criticisms towards its predecessors, namely that you may now exit a stage mid-way through and save your progress, allowing you to resume playing later.
Unfortunately, the game doesn’t manage to the other main criticism I’ve leveled at the series. That being to introduce something akin to Picross’ overlay feature, allowing you to map out a potential solution before applying it to the board. This would be especially useful in more difficult stages when you must look at how many different cells and numbers interact together to determine which cells contain hexes, and which cells are vacant.
If you’ve never played Hexcells before, this game is a good one to get. The series pack often goes on sale for under $3 if you want to get all the games. If you only want one game in the series, then it’s best to just get Infinite. It has all the features of the prior games, a reasonable difficulty curve, and the level generator should help keep you busy if you want more stages to complete. If you’ve played the first two games then the decision really comes down to if you want more levels or not. However you choose to go, it’s worth giving Hexcells a chance.

I do not claim to be a strategist, but this game seems to be telling me that I'm not good enough for it. Players start the game with their only choices being bacteria or "simian flu", with none of the modifiers being available. I can't win on normal mode, and I like to have enough pride to avoid "easy modes". There is one way to win: kill every last human being on planet earth. Anything short of that, you lose, and gain nothing.
"YOU GET NOTHING! YOU LOSE! GOOD DAY SIR!"
While several tantalizing options such as mind-controlling "Neurax worms" and purpose-built biological weapons are available, I cannot access them because Madagascar, or New Zealand, or Greenland/Iceland close their only ports and ending 99% of human life is still as much of a loss as being eradicated within the first year. Modifiers can improve your plague out of the gate, but because one only unlocks them via winning, this becomes redundant.
Before one of you decides that I'm just a loser, I'll compare this to another game based on difficulty, Dark Souls. Hypothetically, playing Plauge Incorporated would be like playing Dark Souls, but only if you didn't get to choose your class, you HAD to kill every boss, and when you died, you had to start from the beginning. I enjoy roguelikes, but those are USUALLY tests of skill and or getting ♥♥♥♥ed by the RNG. Plague Incorporated is actively attempting to prevent your success like nothing else I know of.
The ideal strategy would be to infect everyone before they noticed and shut down everything, but random events including the "mutations" which give you a random boost to something serve to throw a wrench into your plans every time. "Are you trying to be subtle? How's about your plague now makes people spontaneously combust!" seems to be the norm.
TL:DR  this game isn't enough fun to be worth smashing your head against the wall to unlock the fun.

I just played through the Definitive Edition late this summer - after craving a return to its perfect blend of martial arts/GTA-esque urban world. My previous review of the original still holds true: a wonderfully executed open-world action/driving game - Sleeping Dogs surpasses Grand Theft Auto (IV and earlier) in all but the volume of content. Even with the triple-A writing and voice budgets of the current age of gaming, Sleeping Dogs' writing is still as polished, with equal parts humor and ridiculousness that keep the immersion alive and the Internal Affairs detective fantasy moving. The original title isn't available anymore and that's just fine: the overwhelming DLC was too much and with Definitive Edition it is all integrated. So much of it is cosmetic, but thankfully it doesn't force you to dig through all the old troubles of $0.99 outfit packs to look for the real fun of the Martial Arts island and integrated James Bond car mission expansion packs.
WIthin the normal game, the collectibles are diverse (and not overwhelming), the city environment is tight yet detailed, and the gameplay is fast-if-simple. I have never been a fan of 'combo-moves' in many games but Sleeping Dogs' safely takes advantage of them and rewards the players' mastery without making you dependent on the martial arts moves. The melee combat system is still the standard for games to follow, it is fluid and enjoyable much like The Witcher's swordplay system albeit combos seem easier to achieve here. It is a wonderful model of Hong Kong for an action computer game and I would recommend it to any fan of GTA or melee fighting games.

Pros:
- Galaxy full of unique star systems
- Lots of different ships and equipment; plenty of customization options
- Good story, with some (limited) ability to choose your own path
- Missions system has been improved; making money is a lot less grindy-feeling, and there are lots of ways to do it
Cons:
- Many planets just don't have anything of value; you'll visit the ones with extensive outfitters or shipyards a lot, but most of the others are pretty much just gas stations.
- The progression as you get better and better ships is somewhat linear; some ships just outclass the others, even within the same class. Outfits are quite a bit more diverse and balanced, but once you start getting alien tech, a lot of human stuff ends up being thrown out.
- Only one storyline is currently available, but a total of at least three are planned.
- The one storyline that is available and the other scripted quests are easy to miss unless you visit the spaceport at the right planet after the right events have occured. The tutorial quest does mention that you should check out the spaceports, but it's still a bit of an issue.
Overall, I would definitely recommend playing Endless Sky; it's a fun game, and what shortcomings it does have are to be expected from a game that's still in development. Even in its unfinished state, Endless Sky is entertaining and expansive enough for many hours of gameplay, and I expect only more goodness from this game in the future.

I randomly saw this on the front page of steam, then I saw it was free and was surprised! But moving on to the review and overall experience. But before getting to that, check out the Endless Sky site, it has good info you'll want to know when playing!
easy review:
+A large universe
+Plenty of ships to choose from
+Plenty of shenanagins to get into (mostly fighting, escorting, and trading)
+Definitley effort in describing each planet and lore (there are even holidays and events that happen on certain dates!
+Moddable (right down to credits in a text file if you dont want to spend hours trying to get out of debt, but thats part of the fun! .... unless your a cargo/people carrier?)
+Can be a sandbox if you want. (Not forced to do story missions)
- Sound effects could really use work (beam lasers and thrusters especially)
- Lack of music (but that is what the steam music player is for?)
- Uncommon graphical glitches (for my AMD graphics card at least). Extremely minor, just a flicker of a color (green or blue) for an instant, probably happens about once an hour?
- Start off in massive debt (opening story), interest is very unforgiving. (not necessarily a con, but it makes it a rocky start).
- Combat and flying takes getting used to (it feels awkward to me, as opposed to most other space games, I honestly thought it would feel closer to something like Starfighter: Disputed Galaxy)
- Capturing ships is stupidly costly (Losing a single crewman and you are already paying 1/3 of the ship's worth, by the way, death benefits is calculated using the SHIPS WORTH, which is really really stupid and frusterating.)
Sory of my experience:
You start off taking a loan, a HUGE loan to buy a ship, you get to choose from a passenger ship, a cargo ship, and a combat ship. I personally chose the Sparrow. Named it the "Capt. Jack Sparrow" (the ship type was literally Sparrow) set off on an adventure and doing what seemed like tutorial missions with that guy heading off to retire! (good pay)
Quickly realize I am getting milked dry from the ship mortage interest rate of 0.4% a DAY. Each system warp is a day, every time you land on a planet is a day, You have to make a good bit of profit to get out of debt! Choosing missions that are close and pay enough you get more money than you lose to make the trip (funnily enough escort missions are best for that to me!) Best part about escort missions? Who needs to fight? You can just spin up that hyperdrive with "J" and run like hell! Just watch all the bystanders and the navy mobilize to outright OBLITERATE any pirate who happens to give you a hard time! Ever seen a pirate dumb as bricks chase after you to the Sol system? I'd say you will, but he would be too busy dying within seconds! You wouldn't even get a chance to see his ashes! Tons of laughs for sure.
*much questing happens*
Finally made it out of debt! .... now what? Left directionless I just kept doing escort missions, saved up for a new better interceptor class ship! Bought myself a Beserker, instantly fell in love with it as opposed to my Sparrow!. I dubbed my new ship the S.S. Biscuit.
*Some Escort missions later* Finally done enough to get better scort missions! Now instead of getting 15,000 or 20,000 credits per escort, I now get 60,000! however the ships turn like whales and are average sized freighters.
*To be Continued* The story goes on ...
P.S. They have a "cheat plugin" with tons of credits and all tech (Ships?) in human space. Enjoy.(for you sandbox lovers)

I LOVE THIS GAME! Granted, I'm a ♥♥♥♥in shill for the FF series outside of 13 and onward, but this game really won me back. I tried it a few months ago, got a Lancer to level 27 and dropped it due to lack of interest. Keep in mind that I did not put in any effort regarding learning the game, and just played it to play it. That being said, recently made a new characer on a different server, got Heavensward, and tried a new job (Ninja), and I cannot put the game down. Here are some of my pros.
Pros -
-Game is pretty good looking for being this old. The game is about 7 years old and hasn't aged that much. Character models look great, the animations are nice, and the enviornments are very pretty with some decent textures. This is no black desert, or TERA in terms of visuals, but it's at the very least nice looking, and looks better than WoW's visuals imo.
- Great story, ESPECIALLY in heavensward. It goes from a nice fantasy tale, to some light comedy, and to some pretty dramatic moments. Characters are memorable and you can get pretty attached to them.
-The class/job system is awesome. You don't need multiple characters to play this game in order to experience multiple classes. If you got your starting class past level 15, you can meet a guild of a particular class you want, and join them in order to level that class! This doesn't reset your previous class's levels either, so you're not rerolling a class like you would in other MMOs. The job system works well in that category since you can essentially used a much more powerful version of your major class. I chose ninja, which requires you having a lvl 30 rogue and lvl 15 pugalist. It's a ton of fun to try out these classes!
- Variety in classes for each roll! DPS, healer, and tanks have quite a few choices that don't necessarily have huge factors for which is better or worse. Sure, some may be better at their job than others, but nothing is really "bad" in FFXIV.
- Heavensward content is the most fun! Flying mounts, finding aircurrents, clan hunts, some of the best dungeons, and primals! This is awesome content!
- A wonderful community of players! Man, it's really refreshing to play a game where I'm not getting called slurs 24/7. Granted, I'm sure i'll experience these players eventually, but I've yet to really meet anyone truly toxic in this game, all while doing multiple dungeons and duty roulettes on the reg.
-AWESOME COSMETIC CHOICES! The glamour system in the game is so unique. I guess you'd consider it like transmogging in WoW but without the major restrictions. Juts get a prism for a type of gear, and make it look like whatever gear that class could possibly wear. It's dope, and gives you some unique qualities while playing.
- PRIMALS ARE THE BEST! I love the primal fights. Whether they be in easy, hard, or extreme mode. They're some of the most fun I've ever had when raiding and fighting a boss. Mechanically, some can be a pain, but they're worth the pain.
- OST is insane! It's got such a wide range of music! I was honestly shocked when I experienced shiva's theme in her primal fight. It's some of the best ff music to date in my book.
Now onto some cons.
- SUBSCRIPTION BASED GAME. Yes, this is clearly a game you cannot play for free. This is only a con because.. well, it's money. To be honest though, I wouldn't really see that as a bad thing since it means the servers and updates get taken well care of, and you don't have to deal with any P2W or ♥♥♥♥♥♥ locked dungeons for mediocre gear.
- Leveling an alt class can feel grindy. Unfortunately, the downside to getting new classes means you kinda have to grind that class out, which can get tedious. Despite this, there are plenty of ways to level grind. FATEs, hunt logs, clan hunts, dungeons, etc.
- Queing for a specific instance might take a while depending on what it is. I noticed this specifically for the primal extreme fights. They'd take forever to instance 30+ mins. Make sure you're questing or grinding a specific character if you have to wait for long ques.
-Heavensward is the best content, but is an expansion, which means you have to pay for it.
-If you're gonna play, I'd suggest waiting till stormblood before really investing in it. Stormblood is bringing both content and massive gameplay changes to ffxiv. So, I'd probably just wait it out until really trying to grind out some levels in this game and going for end game.
Overall, I love ffxiv. I really went off in this post, so I apologize for this essay. I give it a 8/10. It's not perfect, but I didn't expect it to be. It's keeping my attention, so there's that.

This is a must-buy game for fans of logic puzzles. It is similar in concept to Minesweeper, but is played on a hex grid. Gameplay consists of deducing which hexes are empty and which should be marked blue ("mines"). The similarity to Minesweeper ends there, and Hexcells improves on the experience in a couple of very important ways.
First, the levels in Hexcells are hand-crafted, not the randomized grid of Minesweeper. And the level design is flat-out brilliant. You're led through a series of challenges of gradually increasing complexity, at each point figuring out new ways to combine the information you have and make forward progress. In all, the main levels constitute perhaps 6 to 10 hours of gameplay.
This version of the game (Hexcells Infinite) also includes an infinite mode with computer-generated levels. These aren't quite as aesthetically pleasing as the hand-made levels, but they are still very enjoyable. With infinite mode the game has infinite replayability.
The second thing that makes this game so fun is that all of the puzzles -- including the computer-generated ones in infinite mode -- can be solved using pure logical deduction. No guessing is needed, ever! (One could solve levels using trial and error, but that really isn't in the spirit of the game.) The sense of satisfaction here comes from figuring out the logical deductions, the "aha!" moments, that allow you to advance. The levels are brilliantly designed to give you just enough information -- if you're clever enough to piece it together.
Buy all three of the Hexcells games. Each has different puzzles and all are equally rewarding.

Remember the free old Windows game Minesweeper? Remember how fun it was finding those hidden mines, and how you could feel your brain scream "NOOOOOOOOOOO" whenever a mine would pop its stupid head up and kill you? Remember how immensely frustrating it was when it was entirely impossible to solve levels without guessing?
WELL, NO MORE! Hexcells to the rescue.
Hexcells is very similar to Minesweeper in that you have to use various clues and reasoning to find the hidden blue cells on each level, but unlike Minesweeper, Hexcells' soultions can ALWAYS be reasoned, and if you're doing it right you will never have to guess.
The levels start out easy, with simple rules and puzzles, but new tricks are added just regularly enough to fully grasp, and before you know it, you'll find yourself scanning through 15 different criteria to find the 1-in-100 blue cell to start a level off. It's very satisfying.
Speaking of satisfying, the puzzles here never seem overwhelming or too tricky. Take my opinion with a grain of salt (since I have always loved games like this), but the level of difficulty in these puzzles was just perfect, and while some levels did force me to stare at them for a while, the solution was always there somewhere just waiting for me to grab it.
The Hexcells series is really 3 games: Hexcells, Hexcells Plus, and Hexcells Infinite. They each have different puzzles, and they are each worth getting, but Hexcells Infinite is the one to get if you're on a budget. It has the most advanced puzzles, and it includes a random level generator, so you can literally play to your heart's content. All 3 of them will slowly progress you through the mechanics of the game, though, so don't feel like you will be overwhelmed if you jump right into Infinite.
It's worth mentioning that the random levels in Infinite are mere pale shadows compared to the premade levels (they are often quite easy), but for fans that cannot get enough and don't want to go back to the guess-fest Minesweeper, they can be a lot of fun.
I highly recommend this game. If you're a fan of logic-based puzzle games, you can't go wrong with any of these 3 games. The prices are cheap, and the series is rather unique. If the devs could have just tightened up the infinite level generator ever-so-slightly, this game might be the only game I've rated to pass Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons.
Scratch that Minesweeper itch, my friend!

This is the third game in the Hexcells trilogy, and I definitely recommend that you play the first game (Hexcells) and then the second game (Hexcells Plus).  If you don't, jumping into Hexcells Infinite is going to be extremely difficult.
As the final game in the trilogy, these are the puzzles that separate the men from the boys (or the women from the girls).  They are big, they are complex, and they are at times seemingly impossible.  However, every puzzle does have a solution (with no guessing required), you just need to look at more than just the immediately obvious information, and start looking at the bigger picture.
Even if you finish the set puzzles, you now have the option of playing an "infinite" number of generated puzzles.
(Okay, not infinite, but more than enough that you could never possibly play them all in a single lifetime.)
And if that isn't enough, you can also upload user-generated levels (from various parts of the web) and give them a try.
If you've played the first two games in the series, I can't imagine that you wouldn't want to play Hexcells Infinite.
This game, and the whole trilogy, are definitely worth playing.

NEEDS WORK. RECENT CHANGES ARE APPARENTLY GAMEBREAKING. I really wanted to like this game, but mana is apparently unacquirable, which makes ores unacquireable, and I still haven't figured where to find gold. I tried attacking some other stuff once i googled and found that was possible, but got completely clobbered several times. Then I pretty much read that the default game mode is supposed to be competitive instead of a sandbox which is where all the idiocy is coming from. Super not-happy with the gameplay so far.
Then I tried a single map game and realized I couldn't get any mana or ores and gave up.
Then I played a free play game and suddenly my keeper died without warning just when I was starting to have fun like 10 minutes into the game. Why was he even attacked? What the heck is going on? I'm really getting angry with this game.

There is nothing wrong with KeeperRL but it just doesn't do anything better than other, more polished games at this point in time. Right now, I would suggest you look into War for the Overworld if you're looking for a dungeon-building game or RimWorld if you're looking for just a great simulation game period.
Overall, I'm uncertain whether to refund this game or not. On one hand it shows incredible promise, like it could be a game I could really fall in love with. On the other hand it seems to have a long way to go yet and feels like it could just take a long time to get there or even not get there at all, who knows? In that sense a refund seems like the best option and I still could get the game again later on if it ever "gets there".
What would make the difference for me right now when considering a refund would be for this game to actually offer something that I couldn't get anywhere else: massive combat with dozens of units and crazy roguelike spells and mechanics; a challenge mode where you have a small amount of time to finish a single scenario in a couple hours (instead of a full run); having a dozen Keeper classes to choose from, each with a unique playstyle...
Sure, it has roguelike-inspired turn-based combat and a Dwarf Fortress-inspired adventure mode but neither of them are that interesting to me personally and they're not the type of feature that will get me to stick around and wait for this game to become a fully featured title, sadly. If I actually want an adventure mode with turn based combat, I'll just a play a roguelike, which again, does it better than KeeperRL ever could.
Also, when compared to other games like RimWorld or War for the Overworld, KeeperRL seems to have zero Steam Workshop support. Mods are a great way for fans to pick up on the places the developers are lagging behind - especially a lone dev like Michal here... without mods and looking at the current state of the game, it just gives me the impression I will run out of content pretty quickly, even though I haven't actually played that far into the game.
Unfortunately, the way the game is right now, it feels that I can just go elsewhere to get pretty much the same experience but with vastly more polished gameplay and literally hundreds of mod and scenario options from the Steam Workshop if I ever get bored with the base game itself. KeeperRL just isn't there yet.

Perhaps the most fun I’ve had in an open world crime game since first playing Vice city, thoroughly enjoyable with a lot of replay quality however, one reflection for this review I’ve noted a glaring issue with the games concept. While it in no real way impacts on the enjoyment of playing there is an on-going tussle in the background, between gritty realism and silly♥♥♥♥♥fun.
The inception, sitting comfortably in the realism camp is a nice take on the working for the Mafia trope of similar open world games, as an undercover police officer you have to work your way through improving your Street Rep while not getting nicked yourself. The Mechanic of this is quite simple and easy to manipulate on replay to give you all the options available in the game.
This is not an RPG, and while there are progression systems that improve your character and your development in this world, no real decisions are left to the player, instead you step out your characters shoes for the cut scenes and have to deal with the consequences of his actions later on.
The obvious comparison to the GTA series has been prepared for by the developers who have given a few touches to allow a number of things that are possible here and not in say Liberty City, some appear to have been created for the very purpose of distinguishing it from a rockstar game or even one upping them. Some are, however, interesting mechanics that sit well with the setting and style,
At the forefront of what stands this game aside from competitors are its combat which seem more rocksteady than rockstar and benefit from the aforementioned progression systems, additionally once you get the hang of jacking a car at speed it becomes quite an adrenaline rush. The Environmental combat is also fun although as with much of this game once its set out its serious notes and achieved its cool points it seems to get bored and silly quite quickly. (see DLCs)
So what wins out? In the end this is a game that gives what you put into it, you do have the option to participate in the playable narrative, sit back for the cut scenes and enjoy its departed-esk narrative. If, however, you are a completionist, then prepare to be chasing blue ghost bunny men around the night market, yeah.

This game is excellent.
The format is very similar to a GTA game; open-world, story driven, crime themed.
TL;DR Beautiful and authentic scenery, interesting collectibles, great story, interesting characters, good DLC, solid game mechanics.
The world is Hong Kong island, beatifully realised and although not replicated street for street the nuance they've added brings the world to life and really sets the scene. The collectibles that are standard with any open-world game are generally not overly difficult to find or out of the way and genuinely help you in-game if you make the extra effort to find them. This also gives you the perfect opportunity to explore more of the beautiful Hong Kong scenery.
The story (no spoilers) revolves around undercover cop Wei Shen and his dealings with the local Triads. I consider the story of Sleeping Dogs to be the best I have ever seen in any open world game. Because of the Triad/Cop storyline there are additional mechanics within the game that allow you to tailor your skills based on whether you closely follow the rules of the police or are happy to be a mad criminal. (Ultimately it is possible to get all skills, you are not limited to one tree or the other.)
Mechanically Sleeping Dogs has taken some of the best mechanics from games launched around the same time period. The combat system feels similar to that introduced in the Batman Arkham series, the map is easy to use, with features first seen in Saints Row 3, some activities that could easily have simply required a button press instead require a small minigame, which never feels unwelcome. Overall Sleeping Dogs does very little that is new, but what it delivers is the best of previously tried and tested mechanics.
The DLC that comes with the Definitive Edition adds the "Year of the Snake", an entertaining additional story line based after the main game. Less serious though are "Nightmare in North Point" and "The Zodiac Tournament", NiNP being a classic save the world from the undead story, but with a Chinese twist and TZT being a short story driven campaign based on classic kung fu movies. All three packs are very enjoyable and provide an interesting use of the Sleeping Dogs world.
This is honestly one of my favourite games in the last 5 years. I will happily replay this every year or so for a long time yet.
Happy Gaming

Never before have a played a game so emotionally draining and depressing... Yet I mean that in a good way!
Papers, Please is a simulation game in which you play a Border Control Officer in the country of Arstotszka, a country that has recently reopened its borders after a long internal struggle. You encounter various people trying to enter the country, and your primary duty is to admit them or decline them, based on their paper information. If everything is clear, you let them go. If not, then slap a red stamp and send them their way.
And that's when things get a little tricky.
On occasion, you will encounter someone with a story behind them. A woman who lost her papers but her husband went inside ahead of her. A girl desperately trying to evade a man forcing her into a prostitution ring. A cult of anarchists seeking to bring down Arstotska. The list goes on and it's up to you to decide their fates. I'm not gonna lie, after a few choice encounters, I felt like the biggest sack of crap on earth for turning certain people away and letting monsters into the country.
This game can be best described as an experience into figuring out what kind of person you are. Do follow the rules of the nation, or do you let your heart decide? Either way, everyone finds something new each and every time, with multiple endings to boot. My final verdict is an 8/10, a recommended buy just to see what the fuss is about.

I LOVE THIS GAME! Granted, I'm a ♥♥♥♥in shill for the FF series outside of 13 and onward, but this game really won me back. I tried it a few months ago, got a Lancer to level 27 and dropped it due to lack of interest. Keep in mind that I did not put in any effort regarding learning the game, and just played it to play it. That being said, recently made a new characer on a different server, got Heavensward, and tried a new job (Ninja), and I cannot put the game down. Here are some of my pros.
Pros -
-Game is pretty good looking for being this old. The game is about 7 years old and hasn't aged that much. Character models look great, the animations are nice, and the enviornments are very pretty with some decent textures. This is no black desert, or TERA in terms of visuals, but it's at the very least nice looking, and looks better than WoW's visuals imo.
- Great story, ESPECIALLY in heavensward. It goes from a nice fantasy tale, to some light comedy, and to some pretty dramatic moments. Characters are memorable and you can get pretty attached to them.
-The class/job system is awesome. You don't need multiple characters to play this game in order to experience multiple classes. If you got your starting class past level 15, you can meet a guild of a particular class you want, and join them in order to level that class! This doesn't reset your previous class's levels either, so you're not rerolling a class like you would in other MMOs. The job system works well in that category since you can essentially used a much more powerful version of your major class. I chose ninja, which requires you having a lvl 30 rogue and lvl 15 pugalist. It's a ton of fun to try out these classes!
- Variety in classes for each roll! DPS, healer, and tanks have quite a few choices that don't necessarily have huge factors for which is better or worse. Sure, some may be better at their job than others, but nothing is really "bad" in FFXIV.
- Heavensward content is the most fun! Flying mounts, finding aircurrents, clan hunts, some of the best dungeons, and primals! This is awesome content!
- A wonderful community of players! Man, it's really refreshing to play a game where I'm not getting called slurs 24/7. Granted, I'm sure i'll experience these players eventually, but I've yet to really meet anyone truly toxic in this game, all while doing multiple dungeons and duty roulettes on the reg.
-AWESOME COSMETIC CHOICES! The glamour system in the game is so unique. I guess you'd consider it like transmogging in WoW but without the major restrictions. Juts get a prism for a type of gear, and make it look like whatever gear that class could possibly wear. It's dope, and gives you some unique qualities while playing.
- PRIMALS ARE THE BEST! I love the primal fights. Whether they be in easy, hard, or extreme mode. They're some of the most fun I've ever had when raiding and fighting a boss. Mechanically, some can be a pain, but they're worth the pain.
- OST is insane! It's got such a wide range of music! I was honestly shocked when I experienced shiva's theme in her primal fight. It's some of the best ff music to date in my book.
Now onto some cons.
- SUBSCRIPTION BASED GAME. Yes, this is clearly a game you cannot play for free. This is only a con because.. well, it's money. To be honest though, I wouldn't really see that as a bad thing since it means the servers and updates get taken well care of, and you don't have to deal with any P2W or ♥♥♥♥♥♥ locked dungeons for mediocre gear.
- Leveling an alt class can feel grindy. Unfortunately, the downside to getting new classes means you kinda have to grind that class out, which can get tedious. Despite this, there are plenty of ways to level grind. FATEs, hunt logs, clan hunts, dungeons, etc.
- Queing for a specific instance might take a while depending on what it is. I noticed this specifically for the primal extreme fights. They'd take forever to instance 30+ mins. Make sure you're questing or grinding a specific character if you have to wait for long ques.
-Heavensward is the best content, but is an expansion, which means you have to pay for it.
-If you're gonna play, I'd suggest waiting till stormblood before really investing in it. Stormblood is bringing both content and massive gameplay changes to ffxiv. So, I'd probably just wait it out until really trying to grind out some levels in this game and going for end game.
Overall, I love ffxiv. I really went off in this post, so I apologize for this essay. I give it a 8/10. It's not perfect, but I didn't expect it to be. It's keeping my attention, so there's that.

All in all, Transistor is nothing short of a masterpiece. Whether its the stunning visuals, amazing soundtrack, intriguing plot and characters or its unique and fun gameplay, Transistor excells in it all.
Throughout the game you play as the mysterious (like just about everything else in the game) but also very driven Red, whose motives may not be the clearest to people coursing through the story for the first time. You are accompanied by your transistor, a powerful weapon that holds much more than meets the eye (*wink wink*) who does a good deal of narration throughout your journey and even throws in a few jokes here and there.
Upon confronting enemies, Transistor's unique battle format has you plan out your actions in advance- with a limit on how much you can plan at a time. New abilities (functions as they are called) are unlocked throughout the game, and the game encourages you to try them out and alter your strategy every now and then. While the story is just about set, this strategic planning is where most of your in-game freedom will come from, and it's definitely worth making the most of, especially seeing as battles take up a huge part of the game. While some parts of the game are more challenging than others, overall Transistor isn't all that hard so long as you think things through beforehand and plan well. However, it is possible to increase the game's difficulty using what are known as limiters, which like functions are unlocked throughout Transistor.
As fun as the strategizing portion of the game is, the true beauty of this game is most apparent through its visuals. Cloudbank, the high-tech, (post)dystopian city where most of Transistor takes place is absolutely breathtaking. The game knows this too, and every so often puts a stop to all the chaos to have you admire its marvelous cityscapes. This, accompanied by an epic soundtrack and the unceasing mystery of the plot will keep you wanting more. It is of no surprise then that there is an achievement for completing the game more than once.
To conclude, Transistor is for anyone looking for a game that is mysterious, highly artistic, has a great soundtrack and requires strategic thinking. However, most of the game isn't too hard (at least not by default) and be prepared for a lot of battling. 4.4/5

The final entry of the trilogy of Hexcells puzzle games this is the best of the lot - the 36 developer designed levels are better than ever, really getting you thinking of where the next move is and what piece of information you have overlooked each time you get stuck, and the great moment when you finally realize what it is and wondering how you could have missed it all that time.
The main bonus compared to the previous two entries is that after the 36 levels it isn't all over, you can move onto the seeded "random" levels. This obviously gives the game replayability which the designed levels don't really have, however the down side is that the random levels have a tendency to be feel fairly samey after a while, and it rare to find anything really challenging. But still it is a nice option to have and no doubt some relatively fun levels have been picked out by the community by now, so of the three this is definitely the one to get - although I think the entire trilogy goes on sale for a very reasonable price regularly enough, giving the advantage of easing you into the game more progressively, as well as having a bunch more of the excellently designed levels to challenge yourself from the two earlier editions to add to the ones in this edition.

I don't think I've ever experienced a more perfect puzzle game. The premade levels can be very challenging, and the randomized infinite levels are a lovely mix of challenging and zen. There are even user-made levels you can load up.
This is the best of the Hexcells trio, but all three are stunningly good puzzle games.

The Hexcells series (Hexcells, Hexcells Plus and now Hexcells Infinite) has been an incremental polishing of a strong concept. The game base mechanics feel like a mix between Sudoku and the old Microsoft Minesweeper.
One difference should be pointed out, though: Sometimes in Minesweeper, you would end up having to guess, because with the information available to you, there were more than one possible solution. Not so in Hexcells. There's
enough info to get you one step further. You just have to be able to process the information properly. Don't get me wrong - there are times when I've been completely stuck. Some of the later pre-made levels are monstrously tough to do flawlessly. The fact that you
it's all down to you and your abilities though, makes it more of a challenge and less frustrating.
The ways the information about the board is communicated to you, has been one of the primary points of evolution in the series. To my mind, the developer has been extraordinarily clever in devising new ways give you hints. If you haven't played the earlier games, the major difference for you as a player, is that the boards are much more varied in this version, simply due to the developer having more tools available to play with. The earlier games are good, but this version truly shines.
This latest iteration is called Infinite for a reason, though. He has finally been able to make a level generator, which only needs an 8-digit seed to produce a board. That means if you really want to, there are 100,000,000 boards to play. It's not really infinite, but for all intents and purposes, it might as well be. One of the fun things about this level generator, is that it gives you the possibility to challenge other players to complete the same boards as you do. All you have to do is tell them the seed for that board.
In short, if you're a fan of abstract, number-type puzzles, this game should keep you occupied for quite some time.

Minesweeper meets picross, with minesweeper's pick up and play replay value through randomized puzzles, and picross's criss-crossing clues that ensure you're always provided enough information to complete the puzzle without mistakes or guessing. It's also got a nice feature that lets you extend guides to indicate which cells are covered by which clues, and to grey out clues you're done with.
That description should be enough to instantly decide whether you'd enjoy this game or not. A simple, chill timekiller.

Hexcells Infinite is a final entry in a trilogy of minesweeper-genre puzzles. Or stand-alone expansion pack, whatever you want to call it. And it comes packing 36 more levels and, guess what, even more level.
This game is pretty much stands for Hexcells fans who just want more and more, because more is more fun. And enjoyable not only for fans.
The formula didn't change. Neither did any art or soundtrack. As players will still have to solve field full of hexes, clearing and tagging the "mines" based on information provided and revealed in these non-randomized puzzles, making your brain go hot. Or rather making your eyes twitch around, trying to find what you missed. While listening to ambient something that is nothingess that is supposed to be sound and soundtrack.
What it gives is 36 more levels. And they are as real deal as in Hexcells Plus, tutorials taking little time before sending you to solve many challenging puzzles. Maybe even slightly harder, one level takes a lot of "what if blue hexes were there" preplanning.
But well, that's about it, the puzzles challenge isn't as different as between Hexcells and Hexcells Plus and Infinite doesn't introduce not even a single new element this time around.
Oh, and you can also easily cheat, by clicking on everything on the map, then remembering it and redoing the puzzle perfectly. Better resist this and instead do it all fairly, restarting upon a single mistake.
Instead it gives you a whole new mode: Infinite mode!  Which brings out a randomizer into play, finally. And it's still more fair than Minesweepers.
Puzzles there are generated from the certain some-digit number, so it could be shared. You are present with few options, where you can either randomly generate it, or you can generate based on current date (so you would know what some others got to experience same puzzle as you today), or you can paste the number (that you saved because you want to farm achievement on easy puzzle or because friend shared with you) or you can continue the puzzle on which you leaved the game.
Puzzles are always made to be so you can figure them out fairly. And well, there are so much you can randomize and keep it fair, that you find the experience actually quite repetive. You will quickly learn the possible field form. All the methods it uses. Even more annoyingly, it can be overloaded with more than enough information. So this much-awaited feature isn't going to last so long either.
It's still probably the best Hexcells out of pack, having levels as good as in Hexcells Plus plus the bonus randomizer feature. Though you still should get the whole bundle.

If you like "Hexcells" or "Hexcells Plus", you should definitely buy this one.
As you would expect, it has new and challenging puzzles. But it is also an incremental update over the previous games:
- It saves the progress of puzzles, so you can exit the game and resume where you left.
- Has a seeded puzzle generator, so you never run out of puzzles (hence the "infinite" in the name).
- Supports custom levels (you can create your own or find some community created ones).
- and other minor improvements.
PS. the level editor is not integrated. It's called "SixCells" and is created and maintained by the community as an opensource project.
Hexcells started out as an interesting puzzle game, and has slowly gotten harder and harder. The puzzles have increased and increased, and levels of enjoyment has only followed suit.

Perhaps the most fun I’ve had in an open world crime game since first playing Vice city, thoroughly enjoyable with a lot of replay quality however, one reflection for this review I’ve noted a glaring issue with the games concept. While it in no real way impacts on the enjoyment of playing there is an on-going tussle in the background, between gritty realism and silly♥♥♥♥♥fun.
The inception, sitting comfortably in the realism camp is a nice take on the working for the Mafia trope of similar open world games, as an undercover police officer you have to work your way through improving your Street Rep while not getting nicked yourself. The Mechanic of this is quite simple and easy to manipulate on replay to give you all the options available in the game.
This is not an RPG, and while there are progression systems that improve your character and your development in this world, no real decisions are left to the player, instead you step out your characters shoes for the cut scenes and have to deal with the consequences of his actions later on.
The obvious comparison to the GTA series has been prepared for by the developers who have given a few touches to allow a number of things that are possible here and not in say Liberty City, some appear to have been created for the very purpose of distinguishing it from a rockstar game or even one upping them. Some are, however, interesting mechanics that sit well with the setting and style,
At the forefront of what stands this game aside from competitors are its combat which seem more rocksteady than rockstar and benefit from the aforementioned progression systems, additionally once you get the hang of jacking a car at speed it becomes quite an adrenaline rush. The Environmental combat is also fun although as with much of this game once its set out its serious notes and achieved its cool points it seems to get bored and silly quite quickly. (see DLCs)
So what wins out? In the end this is a game that gives what you put into it, you do have the option to participate in the playable narrative, sit back for the cut scenes and enjoy its departed-esk narrative. If, however, you are a completionist, then prepare to be chasing blue ghost bunny men around the night market, yeah.

This game is excellent.
The format is very similar to a GTA game; open-world, story driven, crime themed.
TL;DR Beautiful and authentic scenery, interesting collectibles, great story, interesting characters, good DLC, solid game mechanics.
The world is Hong Kong island, beatifully realised and although not replicated street for street the nuance they've added brings the world to life and really sets the scene. The collectibles that are standard with any open-world game are generally not overly difficult to find or out of the way and genuinely help you in-game if you make the extra effort to find them. This also gives you the perfect opportunity to explore more of the beautiful Hong Kong scenery.
The story (no spoilers) revolves around undercover cop Wei Shen and his dealings with the local Triads. I consider the story of Sleeping Dogs to be the best I have ever seen in any open world game. Because of the Triad/Cop storyline there are additional mechanics within the game that allow you to tailor your skills based on whether you closely follow the rules of the police or are happy to be a mad criminal. (Ultimately it is possible to get all skills, you are not limited to one tree or the other.)
Mechanically Sleeping Dogs has taken some of the best mechanics from games launched around the same time period. The combat system feels similar to that introduced in the Batman Arkham series, the map is easy to use, with features first seen in Saints Row 3, some activities that could easily have simply required a button press instead require a small minigame, which never feels unwelcome. Overall Sleeping Dogs does very little that is new, but what it delivers is the best of previously tried and tested mechanics.
The DLC that comes with the Definitive Edition adds the "Year of the Snake", an entertaining additional story line based after the main game. Less serious though are "Nightmare in North Point" and "The Zodiac Tournament", NiNP being a classic save the world from the undead story, but with a Chinese twist and TZT being a short story driven campaign based on classic kung fu movies. All three packs are very enjoyable and provide an interesting use of the Sleeping Dogs world.
This is honestly one of my favourite games in the last 5 years. I will happily replay this every year or so for a long time yet.
Happy Gaming

Never before have a played a game so emotionally draining and depressing... Yet I mean that in a good way!
Papers, Please is a simulation game in which you play a Border Control Officer in the country of Arstotszka, a country that has recently reopened its borders after a long internal struggle. You encounter various people trying to enter the country, and your primary duty is to admit them or decline them, based on their paper information. If everything is clear, you let them go. If not, then slap a red stamp and send them their way.
And that's when things get a little tricky.
On occasion, you will encounter someone with a story behind them. A woman who lost her papers but her husband went inside ahead of her. A girl desperately trying to evade a man forcing her into a prostitution ring. A cult of anarchists seeking to bring down Arstotska. The list goes on and it's up to you to decide their fates. I'm not gonna lie, after a few choice encounters, I felt like the biggest sack of crap on earth for turning certain people away and letting monsters into the country.
This game can be best described as an experience into figuring out what kind of person you are. Do follow the rules of the nation, or do you let your heart decide? Either way, everyone finds something new each and every time, with multiple endings to boot. My final verdict is an 8/10, a recommended buy just to see what the fuss is about.

You know, I actually WAS a fan of Call of Duty. However, the series rooted itself to death quite fast with this “A sequel every year” b#llshit, and specially since they’re so damn f#cking expensive. SERIOUSLY, MW2 AND 3 ARE QUITE OLD AND YET THEY’RE STILL WORTH AROUND 20€ AND 40€ ON STEAM, WHAT THE SH#T. However, is MW2 worth it or not? As usual, I will start with the bad stuff of the game.
First and foremost, the first time I played this game after so many years, I got a bunch of problems and weird issues all in one go. To start with it, the game won’t let you change your preferences before putting a quite important video that explains quite a lot, so you have to either suffer through the video with the smallest and sh#ttiest resolution, or skip it, change the options and figure out how to see it again. That’s f#cking dumb, just let the player change them BEFORE SHOWING ANYTHING, DUDE! Not yet done with that, the first time the game loaded, still with the wrong options, it took quite an insane amount of time to load. I’m not sure AT ALL why that happened but it was weird, thankfully there where no other long loading screens after that.
Another thing that I don’t quite like about the game has to be some gameplay things, specially when they conflict with the forced events. Why the hell are you allowed to carry OVER 1000 BULLETS FOR A RIFLE THAT ONLY HOLDS 30, AND YET YOUR CHARACTER SOMEHOW LOSES ALL AMMO ON A CUTSCENE!? There are also some stealth sections on the game, and at times I was detected in weird ways… Although maybe playing on a high difficulty had something to do with that. The game also pushes multiplayer killstreak unlockables into the story mode and some of those are quite forced into your throat, like them or not. It's not done to death as it was on MW3, but it's still a but wrong.
Lastly, the way the story is handled in these games. Seriously. Just look at it, if you’re American, British, Irish or so you’re pretty much made of iron and you will only die in cutscenes. If you’re from ANYWHERE ELSE, you’ll die by getting tapped with a butter knife on the foot. It would be okay if it wasn’t always Russian people getting butchered over and over, I end up feeling like Call of Duty is actually made by the government in an effort of making every country get extremely racist with them. I mean for f#ck sake, even if one of the villains ends up not being Russian, HIS ONLY OBJECTIVE SEEMS TO BE TO KEEP GETTING RUSSIANS KILLED HORRIBLY. I bet Activision got bribed by the 'Merrican military to make this games this cool to try and get poor idiots to join them.
That crap aside though, what do we have left? A decent FPS with an actually quite exciting singleplayer story.
Seriously, the story mode feels like the classic Hollywood movie, with Bruce Willis playing as the main character, getting shot from everywhere and yet not dying while killing half the planet’s population with grenades. There’s a great emphasis on ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that would be COMPLETELY AND UTTERLY IMPOSSIBLE in real life, but that makes the game quite interesting as you don’t know what will happen next. It's weird as the previous game was more focused on realistic military crap and in this one you go around with A THOUSAND F#CKING ASSAULT RIFLE BULLETS, but it's good enough.
Some of the tools you can end up using are actually quite fun to use. The sentry guns, the missiles, the drones, and even some of the weapons. However, a LOT of the weapons feel the exact same, especially since half of them are rifles quite similar to either the M4 or the AK47, which gets repetitive quite fast. The game also does shotguns no f#cking justice and that pains me as I LOVE SHOTGUNS.
Another part worth mention has to be the music. In certain special parts of the game, such as the snow chase early on, it adds to the kickass factor of the game. Kinda sad though, that most reviews don’t even talk about good soundtracks.
Lastly, the game also adds two other modes, the classic “special challenges” (it’s called special ops or something like that, don’t quite remember now) and the multiplayer. The challenges were fun, although I completely ignored the multiplayer, mainly because if you want a CoD for the multiplayer, you’ll probably do better to buy the newest yearly CoD title, as they usually stay with the same price in Steam as they’re too lazy to change them.
Is it worth purchasing? Yeah. However, the devs won’t change the prices for sh#t, which means you’ll rarely find it at a low price, low enough to be worth purchasing. I recommend leaving it on your wish list if you’re interested on the game, and then checking on it during big sales. If it still doesn’t go too low, maybe look for a used copy for consoles instead, which would probably cost you near to nothing.
TL;DR Edition: Good game about shooting Russians in racist ways. Quite overpriced, wait for sales or buy it for consoles instead. Buy it for the single player, it’s good.

Best MMO on the market right now in my opinion. There's a lot of main story quest which everything is gated behing, however IF you have the patience to get through it and not get caught up in the typical MMO mindset of "must get to endgame as soon as possible" then you'll find a story which (while having many filler quests) is as good as every other Final Fantasy game.
Coming from other MMOs the combat does certainly feel slow at first (and it is) but I advanced, got more skills that were off the global cooldown, and faced bosses with more demanding mechanics, I found that the slower pace definitely didn't hinder the game at all.
A really good feature that I think many people miss out on is how Square Enix treat previous content too. This is probably the biggest problem in a game like WoW. As soon as a new patch,or expansion releases, previous raids and dungeons become almost completely irrelevant. In FFXIV there's systems in place which makes it so that even at end game, all previous dungeons and bosses still provide relevant rewards for the majority of the playerbase, so while you will be repeating the same content often, there's such a large pool of content TO repeat that it stays more interesting for longer than say a raid in WoW does, where you may be sick of it after you have it on farm and have to just repeat it every week, while progressing through the same raid, with the same bosses and the same mechanics, but on a harder difficulty.
It should be added that the zones, music and story in general definitely make for one of, if not THE, most immersive experiences I've had in any MMO in about a decade or so.
Criticisms about the volume of story quests shouldn't be ignored (especially the unnecesarry fetch quests etc, I wont defend them), but I think people who say it's an objectively bad thing are missing the point that it's meant to be a story that you progress through like in a singleplayer game. And it definitely feels more rewarding getting through the story to access the endgame as opposed to just doing random meaningless quests and dungeons like in other MMOs.
Pretty much this game is great, and for people who want a 'traditional' Pay-to-Play MMO that has an insane amount of polish, and a development team who obviously care deeply for the game, I don't think there's anything that comes even close that's currently available.
I think FFXIV has pretty convincingly cemented a spot as one of the best MMOs of the last decade, if not of all time.
