Gameplay-wise, it's a standard action RPG with two very interesting differences: (1) when your "Turn()" bar is full, you get to pause time and plan out a series of moves that will happen at high speed, and (2) you collect power modules that you get to modify with other power modules for a vast range of possible effects.
E.g., the Jaunt() module is normally a short range dash/teleport type move, and Spark() is an attack that throws out several exploding shells.
++ But if you make Spark() a Jaunt() modifier instead, it causes your dash to drop bombs all along its path.
++ Or if you attach Jaunt() to Spark() instead, then your Spark() attack now can be used during your power cooldown period.
Since I enjoy optimizing my power set in creative ways and love tactical games, this was a joy for me to play.

Imagine Hexcells Infinite as a modern version of Minesweeper, only with hexcells, an increased difficulty and well thought out new game mechanisms. The hexcells themselves and the new game mechanisms like indicators, which will reveal, how many blue fields are widespreaded in one straight line or how many have to be in a certain area and in which order (in sequence or detached), are great innovations and can deliver a great and satisfying challenge for your brain, especially in huge levels, where you can easily loose the overview and have to count a lot. Much like the original Hexcells and its sequel, Hexcells Plus, Hexcells Infinite is an updated version of the classic strategy game Minesweeper with a bit of added style: you play with hexagons instead of squares. The board starts with an oddly shaped field made of orange hexagons. Mines are marked by left-clicking a hexagon, turning it blue. Hexagons are revealed by right-clicking, showing the number underneath if you click correctly and shaking the piece and adding a tally mark to your mistake count if you're too hasty in your decisions.
Hexcells Infinite expands upon the original two Hexcells games by giving players an additional thirty-six puzzles to complete that contain familiar gameplay elements for Hexcell veterans. Unlike the original Minesweeper, Hexcells is a much more complex game involving a board marked with various different types of clues that give the player hints about how many mines are in each column or in the surrounding area of the board. Hexcells also includes the dreaded ?, a marking that denotes a hexagon that has an unrevealed amount of mines around it, as well as numbered mines that indicate how many mines are in a two-piece radius surrounding the hexagon. These clues come together to create a thought-provoking experience that provides players with more depth and interaction than the traditional game of Minesweeper.
Of the three Hexcells games, the original Hexcells remains my favorite. Both Hexcells Plus and Hexcells Infinite include a few gameplay elements that I find more frustrating than enjoyable (namely the addition of ? hexagons that make an otherwise well-balanced game irritatingly challenging and often cause the player to have to make risky clicks based off of luck and some logical guesswork). However, if one were to purchase only one Hexcells game, that game would have to be Hexcells Infinite. As the name implies, Hexcells Infinite is the only game in the Hexcells series to include a puzzle generator, opening up endless gameplay and increasing the value of the game ten-fold.
Hexcells Infinite can be seen as an expansion to the original two Hexcells, adding thirty-six new levels for players to complete, or it can be played as a standalone experience, with the basics of the original Hexcells being explained in the earliest levels of Hexcells Infinite. This is the third and final game of the Hexcells series, with the developer not intending to produce more. After completing the set of levels contained in Hexcells Infinite, be sure to check out the original Hexcells games for more hand-created puzzles or continue on playing Hexcells Infinite with some of the randomly generated Hexcells levels.

This title has been in development for a couple of years now, and I have to say, now that I've bought it, I'm a bit surprised by how many things that should be in the game simply aren't.
Here are a few of my complaints from firing up the game and running a few Endless Modes to learn the game trial-by-fire style:
There's a serious lack of intuitiveness to the controls.  For instance, I found no quick way to to double-click or right click to center on a unit.
When you're commanding a combat group, there's no way to scroll the screen to see what's happening on the rest of the map, short of giving up control of that group, scrolling and then taking over the group again.  In the middle of a combat this is really dangerous for your troops, but it's also doubly dangerous to not be able to keep an eye on your Keeper, who seems to have a penchant for getting himself in trouble, no matter how many doors you hide him behind.  In fact, I'm still trying to figure out how he got through a locked door when ants were attacking...
There aren't volume controls for music and sound, only on/off.  That gets damn annoying when you're trying to have a conversation online or off, so you have to mute the game or turn the music off.  (The music itself though is pretty good for an indie title.)
EDIT:  For a couple of days I thought there was no way to alter the turn-based system speed.  Probably because there's little to no key info and no evident key-binding.  Turns out that you can click on the very easy to miss 'Speed' text itself in the bottom left corner to change the speed OR press 1-4 keys to go from Slow to Very Fast.
This really matters because combat itself can be over in a blink before you even see an enemy.   And beware archers firing from off-screen, which is an old pet-peeve of mine.
Factions have the uncanny ability to stalk the Keeper wherever he is.  In one game I was being chased by 3 factions that added on one after the other, until I finally was killed by an archer one turn before I was going to teleport away yet again.  There was no way to hide or wait for reinforcements.  Not a fan of that radar mechanic at all.
Lack of ambient sounds diminishes the feel of the world itself, and I really would like to see a sun/moon icon somewhere in the UI to keep easy track of the days and nights.  Some mobs simply can't travel in the daytime (i.e. zombies).
In addition, technical problems I've read about in other reviews are also hitting me in the Single Map playthroughs.  Severe slow-down that makes my current save almost unplayable.  EDIT:  I seem to have fixed the issue by altering the speed several times using keys 1-4.  Hopefully a better fix will be addressed in a future patch.
I'm not going to recommend this game right now, but I intend to keep playing it in all its various modes (Campaign, etc.) and if I believe after this that it is worth the $15 price tag, I'll give a thumbs up, but as of this very moment I cannot honestly recommend it.

Got this game for 50 cents on sale and enjoyed the hours of puzzling that it provided.
Highlights:
- This game is very beautiful! It also ran at full graphics settings on my computer which I built five years ago.
- The puzzles are all well crafted and creative, and for the most part they seem unique from each other.
- The soundtrack sets the mood well - ethereal and spooky.
- The hint system is there if you get stuck. It'll definitely get you unstuck, but also starts with subtle clues before giving it away.
- The story is creative and keeps the puzzles tied together in a reasonable narrative.
- There's a neat 3D/perspective puzzle that is fun to solve.
Small criticisms:
- The hint system is hit or miss in its applicability. At first I thought it was amazing at knowing when I needed help. Later, though, it gave hints much too early or after I was already on the right track.
- Some hints were literally just telling me what to do next - even the first hints in a series. (More like instructions than hints.)
- Some puzzles which could have had some dead ends didn't have them. If you just keep going, you always get to the end without having to think much. I definitely prefer a little thinking for some of the puzzles at least.
- The perspective puzzle is used a lot. Sometimes it has different twists, but many of them felt like the same puzzle over and over again.
In short, I liked the game. It had a few things I though could have been improved, but it was also delivered a fun couple hours of puzzling. (I do recommend turning off the hints if they start to bug you.)

This is easily one of the most addicting games out there. The premise of the game is simple, yet extremely complex. You've crash landed on an alien world and you need to get off. So how do you escape? You build your way up to a rocket!
Most of the challenge in the game lies in automating everything. You can mine resources, which in turn can be used to build components, which in turn can be used to build more components, etc, etc. But why mine it by hand? Instead, build a mining unit, then create some transport belts to move the mined resources to smelters. Then use robotic arms to move the resources into the smelter and back out as a crafted good. Then use more belts to move them along to crafting stations to make more items. And so on.
Some of the recipes are extremely complex and require a ton of ingredients. You also have to research new technology and unlock new things to get to higher tiers in the game.
If this all sounds easy but time consuming, well there's one more tidbit - aliens. As you build up, you'll create pollution. The native wildlife doesn't like pollution so they will come and attack you. You need to use turrets, armor, tanks, walls, robots, etc, etc, to defend your base.
This is easily one of the best indie games out there. If you're on the fence on this one, don't think, just buy it. You won't regret it.
One last thing - kudos to the devs for selling it for $20 instead of the normal 19.99 garbage. I really like that.

You know, I actually WAS a fan of Call of Duty. However, the series rooted itself to death quite fast with this “A sequel every year” b#llshit, and specially since they’re so damn f#cking expensive. SERIOUSLY, MW2 AND 3 ARE QUITE OLD AND YET THEY’RE STILL WORTH AROUND 20€ AND 40€ ON STEAM, WHAT THE SH#T. However, is MW2 worth it or not? As usual, I will start with the bad stuff of the game.
First and foremost, the first time I played this game after so many years, I got a bunch of problems and weird issues all in one go. That’s f#cking dumb, just let the player change them BEFORE SHOWING ANYTHING, DUDE! Not yet done with that, the first time the game loaded, still with the wrong options, it took quite an insane amount of time to load. Another thing that I don’t quite like about the game has to be some gameplay things, specially when they conflict with the forced events. Why the hell are you allowed to carry OVER 1000 BULLETS FOR A RIFLE THAT ONLY HOLDS 30, AND YET YOUR CHARACTER SOMEHOW LOSES ALL AMMO ON A CUTSCENE!? There are also some stealth sections on the game, and at times I was detected in weird ways… Although maybe playing on a high difficulty had something to do with that. The game also pushes multiplayer killstreak unlockables into the story mode and some of those are quite forced into your throat, like them or not. It's not done to death as it was on MW3, but it's still a but wrong.
Lastly, the way the story is handled in these games. Seriously. Just look at it, if you’re American, British, Irish or so you’re pretty much made of iron and you will only die in cutscenes. If you’re from ANYWHERE ELSE, you’ll die by getting tapped with a butter knife on the foot. It would be okay if it wasn’t always Russian people getting butchered over and over, I end up feeling like Call of Duty is actually made by the government in an effort of making every country get extremely racist with them. I mean for f#ck sake, even if one of the villains ends up not being Russian, HIS ONLY OBJECTIVE SEEMS TO BE TO KEEP GETTING RUSSIANS KILLED HORRIBLY. I bet Activision got bribed by the 'Merrican military to make this games this cool to try and get poor idiots to join them.
That crap aside though, what do we have left? A decent FPS with an actually quite exciting singleplayer story.
Seriously, the story mode feels like the classic Hollywood movie, with Bruce Willis playing as the main character, getting shot from everywhere and yet not dying while killing half the planet’s population with grenades. There’s a great emphasis on ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that would be COMPLETELY AND UTTERLY IMPOSSIBLE in real life, but that makes the game quite interesting as you don’t know what will happen next. Some of the tools you can end up using are actually quite fun to use. The sentry guns, the missiles, the drones, and even some of the weapons. Another part worth mention has to be the music. In certain special parts of the game, such as the snow chase early on, it adds to the kickass factor of the game. Kinda sad though, that most reviews don’t even talk about good soundtracks.
Lastly, the game also adds two other modes, the classic “special challenges” (it’s called special ops or something like that, don’t quite remember now) and the multiplayer. The challenges were fun, although I completely ignored the multiplayer, mainly because if you want a CoD for the multiplayer, you’ll probably do better to buy the newest yearly CoD title, as they usually stay with the same price in Steam as they’re too lazy to change them.
Is it worth purchasing? Yeah. However, the devs won’t change the prices for sh#t, which means you’ll rarely find it at a low price, low enough to be worth purchasing. I recommend leaving it on your wish list if you’re interested on the game, and then checking on it during big sales. If it still doesn’t go too low, maybe look for a used copy for consoles instead, which would probably cost you near to nothing.

I finished this game couple of times with different endings, but it wasn't until latest playthrough that I thought of writing review.
On the surface it's about working as the immigration officer, processing documents of people trying to gain entry to the country of Arstotzka. You analyse documents and people themselves, searching for discrepancies in papers, signs of forgery, contraband or threats to internal security, after each day, allocating earnings to tend to needs of your family.
But that's just a surface for something deeper.
You see, this is a game about evil.
Not the stylish and over the top but ultimately fake moustache twirling kind of evil. That doesn't really exist in real life, apart from some edgy teens who, for the lack of moustache, can't pull "moustache twirling" part anyway. No. This game is about real evil. The sad, scared, ubiquitous and hideous kind of evil that hides behind words like:
"I'm only doing my job."
"That's not my problem."
John Stuart Mill said: "Bad men need nothing more to compass their ends, than that good men should look on and do nothing." which often is misquoted and misattributed to Edmund Burke as "All that is necessary for the triumph of evil is that good men do nothing.".
Papers, Please lets you play either side.
It's easy to be the hero in games designed to have no other option, you can't not be a hero in Mass Effect series, no matter your choices you end up a hero, the only way to fail there, is to die and refuse to reload the save. Here you can be a villain, complicit in the existant evil or you can be a hero working to change, if you are willing to risk not just your life, but also those of your family, but then again, can risking lives of others be the right choice?
When you hear someone misspeak duration of stay, you are allowed to deny them entry without saying a word, or, you can let them correct the mistake. Both are valid choices and there's nothing to stop you from doing either. When you catch the wind of sex-slave trader before police does, you can let him in if his documents are right or you can expose and arrest him, neither choice is wrong within rules of the game. You can mercilessly stick to the rules, or you can sometimes bend them to set right what someone else made wrong. You can reinforce the regime, acting as one of multiple fingers of it's iron fist hoping that other fingers never find reason to crush you, you can work within regime, softening it on that little spot which is your kingdom despite severe risks it carries or you can help topple the regime, if you are willing to risk that your family may pay ultimate price.
As can be seen on screenshots, graphics and sound are made in retro style. In this case it's not just an artistic choice, this convention helps connect theme of the game with certain places and events that happened in real life. Portraits are clear and distinguishable. Sound as well as colour palette work well with the mood of the game.
I can't recall any crash, lag or stuttering. And I don't believe I encountered any bugs.
From technical point of view game appears flawless.
In Papers, Please you won't be the villain dreaded by billions and you won't be the hero remembered by generations, instead you will be the villain, or the hero, of the kind that you meet every day of your real life.
Play this game, it will help you understand real meanings of often touted but rarely understood terms like "good", "evil", "responsibility" or "courage".
Very fun game, reccomend it to everyone.

Critical Annihilation is a fantastic voxel based shoot em up game that puts you in the role of the last human alive on the planet, your mission not just to survive but to annihilate all invading aliens and drive them out of the solar systems one planet at a time. The game mixes RPG aspect such as the leveling systems that unlocks further abilities you may use innately and those that you must call forth at the right time, such as an ac-130 gun ship to rain fire down upon your enemy or a sentry tower to provide cover fire for your well planned escape. You will also gain ability points to spend in such skills as speed, health regeneration, and a number of others that will give you the upper hand you may need in order to succeed as the levels grow harder and harder with every victory. This extremely fast pace game will get your heart racing as you jump and fire in all directions as chaos consumes the screen in a bright and vibrant display of both color and carnage.
Pros:
- Great level design even if at first they seem simple, given the ability to damage the surrounding areas with your weapons allows for an ever changing play through.
-Leveling system is well balanced giving you just enough to allow you an edge without making you to overpower to soon.
-The three difficulties is just right for both beginner and expect alike allowing you to tailor your own experience.
-Replay value is definitely there as you can go back to try your hand at a high score everyone can see or simply go back to get more experience to level up and try and beat that pesky level giving you a hard time.
-Music is amazing and only further adds to the immersion effect
Cons:
-The game is rather short at the moment but given time I have no doubt they will be adding more levels to the game (side note: even though there aren’t a great deal of levels to play, depending on your skill this still may take you a good amount of hours to beat)
In conclusion, a great game definitely worth the price and will only get better as time goes on, I for one can’t wait to see what lies ahead for this game and this company.5 out of 5, one of the best voxel based shoot em up games I’ve played in years. The Winner of the Dragon Games Award.

I got this game a few years ago as part of a Humble Mobile Bundle. Now that I've picked it back up on PC, I can say that I enjoy the additions. As for the game as a whole, it was impressive back then, and it's still impressive now.
In this game you pilot two circles that travel around a ring avoiding boxes that fly down at them. It's kinda hard to describe how it handles, but it's still easy to wrap your head around. The "story mode", if you want to call it that, is based around the stages of grief, starting with Ignorance and working your way to Acceptance, with a new challenge thrown in at every stage. The story itself is told only through the level titles (named after the stages of grief) and a narration that follows you through each stage. It can elicit some feels when it all comes together at the end, but the story isn't that important. What really makes or breaks this game is the gameplay, and after beating the story, the epilogue, and the encore, I can say it's very solid.
If you've played Duet before, you'll probably get back in the saddle pretty quickly. What's new to me is the achievements and the encore stages. My only gripe is the achievements that require you to do the daily challenges a lot. I'm okay with the "not dying" achievements, even if they're a lot harder. It's just one of those challenges to hone your skills and push yourself, which is really the best use of achievements aside from suggesting alternate ways to play.
Also, the soundtrack is like audio syrup. If a difficult game (like this one) has a sweet soundtrack, that soundtrack can be the thing that keeps you from rage-quitting. Luckily, it's free on Bandcamp, so go get it, even if you don't want this game. You'll thank me later.
I recommend trying the demo first. Using that to wrap your head around the movement mechanics will help you decide whether to buy it or not. The ultimate factors deciding whether you'll like the full game are whether you can figure out the mechanics and how easily you can give up in the face of a difficult challenge, both of which you'll figure out by the end of the demo. It's not Super Meat Boy difficult, but it does have teeth. Patience, hand-eye coordination, and a little determination are all you need to have fun with this game.

The bottom line of this review is this: THIS GAME IS NOT EV NOVA. If you want to play EV Nova, GO PLAY EV NOVA - to this day, there is no suitable replacement for the original Escape Velocity games, and although Endless Sky comes close mechanically, it falls short atmospherically. The original EV games still hold up so if you are like me, with a hankering for that old EV feeling, you might as well just go play one of the originals.
[EDIT: I feel like I should just amend my review to say that Sunless Sea is a great modern game which is mechanically (if not thematically) similar to EV Nova and does a great job with atmosphere and writing, just with boats instead of space]
I was dying to play some EV Nova so I thought I'd try this game. It is a very accurate clone of many of the aspects of the Escape Velocity series, right down to the button labels and some ship designs, but somehow it doesn't all come together. Combat in Endless Sky isn't something you engage in, it's just something that seems to -happen- and then you either die or your enemies die. Every time I engaged in combat it felt totally binary, as if nothing i did tactically would alter my chances of win/loss. The game seriously needs to have its combat stats rebalanced to slow things down (esp. in the early game) and allow more drawn-out tactical encounters.
I did very much appreciate some of the improvements to the map/mission/trading interfaces, they make buy-low-sell-high a piece of cake with their profit/loss tracker. BUT, after several hours I actually found this detracted from one of the things I liked about Escape Velocity - the writing. It was so easy to fall into a trading groove that I actually found myself not even glancing at the planet and spaceport descriptions, and I found that after 12 hours I hadn't absorbed any of the flavor of the universe. Every planet became reduced to a set of pricing data. It just turns into a game of how-can-i-make-these-numbers-bigger.
My recommendation to other gamers is that instead of playing this game, you just find a copy of EV and play that. My recommendation to the developer of this game is to find a way to slow combat down and recapture the tension of EV (where did escape pods / hardmode go?).

All in all, Transistor is nothing short of a masterpiece. Whether its the stunning visuals, amazing soundtrack, intriguing plot and characters or its unique and fun gameplay, Transistor excells in it all.
Throughout the game you play as the mysterious (like just about everything else in the game) but also very driven Red, whose motives may not be the clearest to people coursing through the story for the first time. You are accompanied by your transistor, a powerful weapon that holds much more than meets the eye (*wink wink*) who does a good deal of narration throughout your journey and even throws in a few jokes here and there.
Upon confronting enemies, Transistor's unique battle format has you plan out your actions in advance- with a limit on how much you can plan at a time. New abilities (functions as they are called) are unlocked throughout the game, and the game encourages you to try them out and alter your strategy every now and then. While the story is just about set, this strategic planning is where most of your in-game freedom will come from, and it's definitely worth making the most of, especially seeing as battles take up a huge part of the game. While some parts of the game are more challenging than others, overall Transistor isn't all that hard so long as you think things through beforehand and plan well. However, it is possible to increase the game's difficulty using what are known as limiters, which like functions are unlocked throughout Transistor.
As fun as the strategizing portion of the game is, the true beauty of this game is most apparent through its visuals. Cloudbank, the high-tech, (post)dystopian city where most of Transistor takes place is absolutely breathtaking. The game knows this too, and every so often puts a stop to all the chaos to have you admire its marvelous cityscapes. This, accompanied by an epic soundtrack and the unceasing mystery of the plot will keep you wanting more. It is of no surprise then that there is an achievement for completing the game more than once.
To conclude, Transistor is for anyone looking for a game that is mysterious, highly artistic, has a great soundtrack and requires strategic thinking. However, most of the game isn't too hard (at least not by default) and be prepared for a lot of battling. 4.4/5

Hexcells Infinite
$5.49*
Puzzle
20 hours
☺ ☺ ☺ ☺ ☺ (out of 5)
First of all, I would strongly recommend buying the bundle of Hexcells games if you don't already own any of the previous two.
I've had a slightly rocky road towards enjoying the Hexcells series because I've always felt they were too easy and too short. Hexcells Infinite addresses both of those issues, though with varying success. It has to be said that the concept behind Hexcells is fantastic, and my issues with the games truly stem from wanting more, more, more!
As I said in my Hexcells Plus review, you'll get the most enjoyment out of the game if you  are disciplined and refuse to let yourself make a blind guess. Every puzzle is solvable without making a guess, even when you're absolutely convinced that there is no other option but to guess. You'll find (if you post on the forums) that you've inevitably missed some subtle piece of logic which will get you past the hurdle.
This issue was addressed in two ways - later puzzles are harder, and community made puzzles - although I don’t find my appetite for these puzzles sated yet. The later puzzles got quite difficult and took me a significant amount of time to solve, which I enjoyed and appreciated. The community made puzzles are a good way of getting some tricky puzzles to do. Lastly, I have to say that I was disappointed to find that the first few worlds were once again a too easy tutorial, and I wish that the tutorial levels had been put into a separate section of the game so that we could have had 6 full worlds of puzzles to exercise “the little grey cells” to quote Poirot.
Again, this second issue was addressed in two ways - infinite mode, and community made puzzles. Infinite mode generates random puzzles for the user to complete and it certainly satisfies the issue of there not being enough puzzles. However, whilst it delivers quantity, it fails at quality. By quality I mean difficulty, because the randomly generate puzzles are far from difficult. It seems like a great idea with potential, but it could definitely do with some difficulty settings so that you can request hard random puzzles. The community made puzzles offer some harder choices to do, but it will take time for the selection to be built up.
I know this is getting a bit long, but this is an interesting new part of this particular Hexcells game. I will point you to the post that explains it and strongly suggest that you watch the two videos there because they do all the explaining (I originally didn’t bother to watch them and was confused for it). It is very easy to play custom puzzles, you simply copy the puzzle to the clipboard, open Hexcells, and click the option in the bottom right to play a custom puzzle. Making your own puzzles is something I haven’t yet explored. One note is that I’ve learned to mostly avoid any that have custom rules because the logic sometimes seems a bit sketchy leaving you to guess.
**
The concept of this game is wonderful. It adds a few levels of complication than Minesweeper and the solutions are all attainable through pure logic. No guesses are required, if they are sometimes tempting to do, so get in touch with your inner vulcan mind.
Some of those complications I mentioned include:
Very simple - right click and left click. Plus, now featuring a button in-game to flip the button functions! Rejoice! This can also still be changed about in the options dialogue that pops up when opening the game.
Although, by this time I've become entirely accustomed to them and didn't make too many stupid mistakes by hitting the wrong button.
No storyline, doesn't need one.
Relaxing gentle zen echoey noises. Also, when you click a cell you get nice tinkling chime-like noises. I don't know why that makes it more satisfying to click on cells, but it does! It's fun to go back to the really easy puzzles and click through like mad to get a cascade of tinkling noises.
Very crisp, clean, and clear. The numbers are reasonably large. Some puzzles form an interesting overall image or pattern, and overall, the puzzles come across as well designed. There is also an option in-game to make blue cells with numbers have a different outline effect.

WANNA LEARN HOW TO MAKE A PIE? NO WELL TOO BAD
Ingredients: 1/2 cup sugar
1/2 cup packed brown sugar
3 tablespoons all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon ground cinnamon
1/4 teaspoon ground ginger
1/4 teaspoon ground nutmeg
6 to 7 cups thinly sliced peeled tart apples
1 tablespoon lemon juice
Pastry for double-crust pie (9 inches)
1 tablespoon butter
1 large egg white
Additional sugar
Directions: In a small bowl, combine the sugars, flour and spices; set aside. In a large bowl, toss apples with lemon juice. Add sugar mixture; toss to coat.
Line a 9-in. pie plate with bottom crust; trim pastry even with edge. Fill with apple mixture; dot with butter. Roll out remaining pastry to fit top of pie. Place over filling. Trim, seal and flute edges. Cut slits in pastry.
Beat egg white until foamy; brush over pastry.

I finished this game couple of times with different endings, but it wasn't until latest playthrough that I thought of writing review.
On the surface it's about working as the immigration officer, processing documents of people trying to gain entry to the country of Arstotzka. You analyse documents and people themselves, searching for discrepancies in papers, signs of forgery, contraband or threats to internal security, after each day, allocating earnings to tend to needs of your family.
But that's just a surface for something deeper.
You see, this is a game about evil.
Not the stylish and over the top but ultimately fake moustache twirling kind of evil. That doesn't really exist in real life, apart from some edgy teens who, for the lack of moustache, can't pull "moustache twirling" part anyway. No. This game is about real evil. The sad, scared, ubiquitous and hideous kind of evil that hides behind words like:
"I'm only doing my job."
"That's not my problem."
John Stuart Mill said: "Bad men need nothing more to compass their ends, than that good men should look on and do nothing." which often is misquoted and misattributed to Edmund Burke as "All that is necessary for the triumph of evil is that good men do nothing.".
Papers, Please lets you play either side.
It's easy to be the hero in games designed to have no other option, you can't not be a hero in Mass Effect series, no matter your choices you end up a hero, the only way to fail there, is to die and refuse to reload the save. Here you can be a villain, complicit in the existant evil or you can be a hero working to change, if you are willing to risk not just your life, but also those of your family, but then again, can risking lives of others be the right choice?
When you hear someone misspeak duration of stay, you are allowed to deny them entry without saying a word, or, you can let them correct the mistake. Both are valid choices and there's nothing to stop you from doing either. When you catch the wind of sex-slave trader before police does, you can let him in if his documents are right or you can expose and arrest him, neither choice is wrong within rules of the game. You can mercilessly stick to the rules, or you can sometimes bend them to set right what someone else made wrong. You can reinforce the regime, acting as one of multiple fingers of it's iron fist hoping that other fingers never find reason to crush you, you can work within regime, softening it on that little spot which is your kingdom despite severe risks it carries or you can help topple the regime, if you are willing to risk that your family may pay ultimate price.
As can be seen on screenshots, graphics and sound are made in retro style. In this case it's not just an artistic choice, this convention helps connect theme of the game with certain places and events that happened in real life. Portraits are clear and distinguishable. Sound as well as colour palette work well with the mood of the game.
I can't recall any crash, lag or stuttering. And I don't believe I encountered any bugs.
From technical point of view game appears flawless.
In Papers, Please you won't be the villain dreaded by billions and you won't be the hero remembered by generations, instead you will be the villain, or the hero, of the kind that you meet every day of your real life.
Play this game, it will help you understand real meanings of often touted but rarely understood terms like "good", "evil", "responsibility" or "courage".
Very fun game, reccomend it to everyone.

Duet is an interesting little indie game that is simple in design and execution that has a certain magic to it. The entirety of gameplay involves controlling 2 dots, one red and one blue, that spin in a circle while blocks fall from the top of the circle of the screen and you have to dodge them. As the game progresses, the block behavior changes; some come spinning at you, some shake violently side to side and you won't know what position they will be in until it's too late to change your trajectory, and some even go invisible a second after being on screen so it tests your ability to memorize patterns on the fly. After the main story is complete, there are two alternate "stories" to be played, one that has blocks falling at a wonky angle (it's really hard to describe, you just have to see it for yourself) and one that places you at the center of the screen with blocks coming from above and below.
The "story" moved me more than i expected. The different chapters follow the stages of grief, and the narrator is like a psychologist or best friend trying to let you know that everything will be okay. As somebody who has formerly suffered from a rather debilitating depression, this was unexpectedly moving, and quite a welcome idea in this pure of a form.
Altogether I would greatly recommend this game. I got it through a humble bundle that I purchased for other games, and this was a very nice gravy addition that is well worth the full price ($2.39 is an absolute steal!) It's very clearly a small indie game, but still a fun and interesting little game to play for a handful of hours that gives a sense of satisfaction for having completed.
This game is mesmerizing, you'll enter another universe, and when you'll leave it, you'll have a hard time getting used to.

I'm offering up a cautious recommendation here. This game is very promising, while still being far from a complete experience in its current state (Alpha 5d). I bought it on the strength of it being made by Double Fine, who I think have a habit of putting out some really fun games. The recommendation is partially based on their reputation.
As other reviewers have mentioned, the UI is great and the overall aesthetic brings to mind 70s/ 80s SF such as Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy or Dark Star. Having said that, the devs should really set about implementing some goal-based gameplay soon enough. It seems an odd move to put it out in its current state since there's not the level of freedom for it to act simply as a light space survival sim. There isn't really enough depth at the moment for the player to come up with their own objectives beyond not dying for long enough to build a space-pub. In its current state it looks like you can try out all the space- decor and experience the space- mining and space- pirates in a fairly short stretch of time. Basically, I love the content so far and I'd like there to be more.
I really hope there is continued support and funding on this project. There have been a few negative reviews on Steam but most people acknowledge the potential here. I look forward to seeing the updates and in the meantime, I can set about building my Silent Running style interstellar greenhouse.

The bottom line of this review is this: THIS GAME IS NOT EV NOVA. If you want to play EV Nova, GO PLAY EV NOVA - to this day, there is no suitable replacement for the original Escape Velocity games, and although Endless Sky comes close mechanically, it falls short atmospherically. The original EV games still hold up so if you are like me, with a hankering for that old EV feeling, you might as well just go play one of the originals.
[EDIT: I feel like I should just amend my review to say that Sunless Sea is a great modern game which is mechanically (if not thematically) similar to EV Nova and does a great job with atmosphere and writing, just with boats instead of space]
I was dying to play some EV Nova so I thought I'd try this game. It is a very accurate clone of many of the aspects of the Escape Velocity series, right down to the button labels and some ship designs, but somehow it doesn't all come together. Combat in Endless Sky isn't something you engage in, it's just something that seems to -happen- and then you either die or your enemies die. Every time I engaged in combat it felt totally binary, as if nothing i did tactically would alter my chances of win/loss. The game seriously needs to have its combat stats rebalanced to slow things down (esp. in the early game) and allow more drawn-out tactical encounters.
I did very much appreciate some of the improvements to the map/mission/trading interfaces, they make buy-low-sell-high a piece of cake with their profit/loss tracker. BUT, after several hours I actually found this detracted from one of the things I liked about Escape Velocity - the writing. It was so easy to fall into a trading groove that I actually found myself not even glancing at the planet and spaceport descriptions, and I found that after 12 hours I hadn't absorbed any of the flavor of the universe. Every planet became reduced to a set of pricing data. It just turns into a game of how-can-i-make-these-numbers-bigger.
My recommendation to other gamers is that instead of playing this game, you just find a copy of EV and play that. My recommendation to the developer of this game is to find a way to slow combat down and recapture the tension of EV (where did escape pods / hardmode go?).

This game has potential. There is a lot to like here. However there are some fatal flaws for me. Prices seem to be static. So you can easily pick a trade route and keep doing that. Or you could try your hand at combat. Unfortunately combat is boring. You are either way outclassed and have no hope of surviving or there are so many ships that losing is impossible. Disabling a ship to board is very much a crapshoot since the AI won't usually let ships live. Also, every missile ship seems to target you even if you have not fired, are running away and the attacker is under attack by others. A one on one with another ship never happens. So it's easy enough, with some time, to capture ships that accidentally are not killed, but it never feels like your own victory.
Ships are always so filled that there really is very little customization possible. Your starting ship esepcially allows for almost no relevant customization. I've not reached the advanced ships, but all ships are always filled with equipment, and there is very little choice in equipment especially between equivalent options. There is some diversity but it is not unclear between two options which is superior.
Then there is targeting. Easy enough to target, but when you want to board you have to ram the b key in the hope of getting it before the ship is destroyed. At this point you will inevitably discover that b is not board selected ship at all. It is  select disabled ship to board. So in the middle of combat all of a sudden you target a disabled ally whom you then may accidentally shoot and turn everyone against you. You should just dump your weapons, since doing combat alone is pointless anyway, but then what exactly is the game you are playing. If it isn't grind to get money without actually participating in the game then your good. Otherwise, forget about it, this game makes combat tedious and pointless.
-edit-
So, everything I said is true, but I judged too harshly. The game is still in development and it does have a certain appeal.  There is fun to be had exploring a bit and buying a huge fleet and attacking a pirate world is feasible. So this is definitely worth checking out and will probably get better in the future.

Critical Annihilation is a Shoot 'Em Up game, which focuses mainly on killing enemies and destorying the environment around you. The game itself is really well presented and polished up for the current state that it's in (Early Access), the art style of the game is really niceand the current amount of weapons is decent for the time being. It's very addicting to play and is insanely fun. It is worth noting that this game does demand for your computer to be decent, especially when it comes to destorying the enviroment with all of the explosions happening and big craters that are on the ground. If you are having troubles with performance issues of this game, then I suggest you do some changes in the opitions menu to make the game run smoothly.
Critical Annihilation is a fast paced shoot 'em up with some really cool perks, and character progression. The game is strangely addiciting along with all of the enemies that you have to kill. The destructable enviroment of the game really fits well with all of the enemies that will be running at you trying to kill you. Although, when playing through the game, it seems that the game is really demanding for your computer to be decent. With all of the explosions happening when you pla through the game and craters that appear on the ground, make sure your specs of your computer are good enough to run this game decently. There is a rather large selection of weapons available up for use to kill your enemies with. Providing that there is also randomly generated drop system in this current stage of the game, it is really impressive to see that sort of detail be in the game already at this stage of the game that is currently in Early Access.
The decent visuals and art style of this game really fit the type of game the developers made for this game. Most of the stages are very well detailed, with vibrant lighting and colours which really bring this game to life. The games graphics are made out of voxels, but upon doing some research of this game, it was also based upon the voxel engine which allows for the destructable enviroments that happen during the game. The lighting really comes into play when explosions happen throughout, the lighting is really well presented when exlpsions occur and that's when the lighting effect is best shown off.
Generically, the sounds are very nicely done and presented when playing through the game. With the music in the background that really fits the fast paced shooter game, with a kind of dubstep music to it. The sounds of the guns and the enemies are fairly nice, not annoying like some game where they use the same sound effects for each gun.
A very fun and addictive game to play, with some really nice graphics and explosions that occur through the game. Although it demands a bit on your PC, so make sure that your specs or up with the recommened specs. If you are having trouble then tweek some settings to make the game run smooth. Some really nice music to fit the fast paced type of game.

Over The Void fits the psychedelic subgenre even though I simply prefer to call it “abstract”. Steam has a well formed niche for this type of games and the one I’m reviewing today is a platformer. Right off the bat you’re introduced to beautifully crafted and ever shifting structures, while the chromatic and aural diversity set the game apart from most platform games you played in a long time. Sure, it might seem just a pretentious excuse for an arthouse title but Over The Void doesn’t feel forced and even if it’s short, it is definitely worth its asking price and offers Trading Cards as well. Giving this a positive vote because there is no neutral option and I don't think it deserves a negative, despite its flaws.
Gameplay-wise, the premise is fairly straightforward. Each zone has a number of red buttons and a locked exit door. Navigate yourself close enough to the red buttons to activate them (causing them to change color). Once the buttons have all been pressed, the door is unlocked and you can move to the next zone.
Movement is fairly typical: 4 directions + jump (though for some reason the default keys are QZSD?? I had to exit the game to change them). Most of the zones have no floor and if you fall through the bottom you will respawn at the beginning of the stage. You have the ability to place temporary platforms in front of you (or whichever direction the camera is pointing). The standard platforms are green, but you can also place blue platforms which act as a trampoline. Cool idea, but the most efficient way to move around is to point your camera down and keep dropping trampolines directly under your feet until you get where you need to go.
Based on the trailer and the game description, I was expecting something different. Parts of the trailer appear as though the player is flying freely, and the frequent mention of "wandering" suggested that there would be more open exploration. The reality is that each zone is a boxed-in area. If there are no visible walls, moving too far from the play area will count as a fall and you'll respawn. Each area is effectively a solid sculpture. You can climb on the solid forms you find throughout each zone, but they'll also get in your way as you try to bound around on your platforms.
I experienced some problems during my playthrough, and I don't know if they're common. Occasionally I would hear the chirp of success when I reached a button, but when I turned to look directly at the button, I saw that it was still red. Pressing it again changed the color but didn't activate the sound. Additionally, in several levels, I found myself flung downward at great speed and barely caught myself from hitting the bottom. I'm not sure if this was the result of my bumping an object that I couldn't see or if there was a downward current in place with no visual cues (unlikely, since after catching myself I could generally ascend without difficulty). Either way, it was very frustrating.
Ultimately, I think this game is trying to do 2 directly opposing things. It's very closed and linear but bills itself as a wandering experience. It features narrow platforming and falling death as a primary obstacle but wants to be "relaxing" exploration.
I think it would be a good idea for the dev to explore these ideas separately. Make one game with fall danger, linear progression, and precision platforming. Make another game with massive expansive areas (not necessarily unobstructed), free exploration and high mobility. Thinking about stuff like Grow Home (especially in the late game), Antichamber, and Proteus for inspiration here.

Gameplay is simple yet strategic and ranges from pretty easy to quite challenging, but never too easy or hard to make you lose interest, even at the very beginning or end.
Even with all that being said, when I think about this game in the future, the story and relationship it covers is what I'm going to remember.  Absolutely amazing.

I think someone said it best, 'this game is like seeing an extremely beautiful and cute new born baby being dropped on it's head. Even if it gets picked up again you just know there is something going to be wrong with it.'
Yes an incredibally stunning 3rd person shooter game with MOBA elements added, just dropped by both publisher and developer in a most appalling fashion. Regardless of it once having thousands of players a week, today you would be extremely lucky to find 50 a week. What happened? Why did it suffer a sudden catastrophe?
Well for one thing the developer/publisher decided to delete premium content that customers had paid good money for when they made a complete overhaul of the game in one of their updates. Its not a question of wether the publisher had a right to do this as any careful scrutiny of small print will show when it comes to microtransactions that the publisher ALWAYS hold the right to the stuff that you buy. Instead it's more the question was this a wise move on the account of the publisher/developer? And lets just say that the mass exodus from the game has already answered such a question.
The problem is, in my experience, no constant nagging or complaining will ever, ever, ever bring that premium content back to you. Yes you might as well just accept the fact that you are a victim to that small print you earlier ignored. However in reality, gamers never, ever accept this fact and before you know it you have a negative tsunami of bad reviews completely devastating any chance of new ones coming to enjoy the new product for what it is. This negative feedback has seriously taken it's toll on the game and as of now, there are not even any servers being maintained by either publisher or developer. Instead the request has been made that the consumers themselves start to host their own servers for the game so that the hardcore fans of the game can continue to enjoy its content and at the same time save costs for both publisher and developer.
Because of this newly introduced strategy you will hardly ever find a server to join and if you do it will most likely be team death match meaning that the principle other two modes of gameplay are completely ignored and you will hardly ever get to experience it.
First there is Titan mode: Each team has a titan (a massive transformer robot) whose objective is to destroy your enemies walls in order to gain access to their nemesis power plant and destroy it. You can level up your titan by harvesting creeps which are spider like things that crawl along the ground. This mode often required good team strategy and some real challenging head to head combat. Now unfortunately this mode is but an elusive dream.
Horde Mode: 4 players are stacked up against progressively tougher wave spawns of enemies. Only expert players were ever lucky enough to go the hard yards in this mode. This mode required a professional approach all the way.
Team Death match: Its the only mode you will most likely still occassionally find. More often than not you will be pitted against bots and the occassional pro that just can't let the game go. Problem is the pro will be ruthless and you stand very little chance being anything other than fodder. This mode is still enjoyable if you can play it with friends and it is easy to farm bots with and level up quickly so you can unlock the large assortment of guns that the game does have and which is completely free, no microtransaction needed.
Personally this game is practically dead, the only chance of revival is if they were to make it free, but this would off course bring the microtransactions back which everyone hates. Maybe they can make it free for several weekends every year and hopefully spark some interest back into it? Maybe some communication from the publishers and developers and a formal apology will go a long way? Maybe its worth an earnest effort to see if that they can again get some dedicated 24 hr servers running for the game? What are the chances of this game making a comeback and not entering into an early grave? Poetically I think it's chances are quite 'minimum'.

--Revised Review--
So, after getting some other replies commenting that I wasn't giving fair review to the game, I've decided to give  another shot before revising the review. I brewed some coffee, have some nice cookies on plate. Clicked the game, headphones on, play time.
Things that I noticed, is that this game is incredibly logical. Horsemedic (guy who commented) was right, this game is entirely made out of logic, to the point of ridiculousness.
One of the rule, "-#- means that blue numbers of panels are NOT connected", sounds quite simple, but when you think about it, this phrase DID NOT say "ALL blue panels are NOT connected". Which means, there is at least one panel that isn't next to each other, but has no guarantee in -3- as this can have 3 blue panels that are not connected, or have pair that is next each to other and have one separated. While this only make the game confusing, it still is, following the rule of the game.
Further that I played, I noticed that this "hole" of the rule isn't conflicting the game at all. If you get stuck, you can look for other clues. Eventually you'll hit the spot you were stuck on, but with more clues to help out.
I've already said in the last review but the graphic and music are top notch. I like the color use of this game, it's gentle and comfortable to see it for long time. Music is very relaxing, good soothing sound.
I guess, the only complain that I can make at this point is that I wish there were spread sheet of set of rules instead of explaining it beliefly and let you try it out during the gameplay. (which helps too but isn't very clear sometime) As understanding the set of rules become the most crucial part of this game I think developer could have spent a little more time for it. Maybe, on the first Hexcell, it might have been more user friendly. I haven't tried it yet.
As a last note, this is NOT a minesweeper. Who ever said it is, did not think enough through like me. The format is very close to it, I agree, but the minesweeper somtime takes you to a gamble while Hexcell can make "educated guess" to clear without making single mistake.
So let me say it again- this game, is NOT a minesweeper. It is more like a Sudoku. Don't expect be like one; this game has no timer, nor any score system for it. Take your time. Grab coffee or tea. Rewind your brain and take the challenge.
I recommend this game.

This series is criminally overlooked.
If you enjoy games like sudoku, you will find logical puzzles here that work your brain for hours. While a naive comparison, the game plays similarly to a very advanced Minesweeper. By the second act, though, you'll have discovered the futility of that comparison; this game is on an entirely different level and has an elegance in the solutions that random Minesweeper puzzles cannot ever hope to achieve.
A couple of the puzzles stumped me for more than 90 minutes, and my roommate rapidly grew tired of me talking the solution out loud as I moved my mouse around. There's a brilliant simplicity to the gameplay and yet, while playing, one must keep a large amount of logic in their head. It's easy to get overwhelmed by logic in one area of the puzzle while overlooking the simple move forward in another area, and the feeling is intense when you slap your forehead in stupidity on discovering it.
The soundtrack is quite relaxing, and even after working on the same puzzle for an hour it did not grow tiresome. It's really fun when you get on a "roll" of solving the puzzle, too, because you generate little ditties as a reward.
The only negative of Infinite compared to the rest of the series is the randomly-generated puzzles. The developer added these so that he could put a bow on the series and call it done and, while they do indeed fill a gap, you can tell they're a far different experience than the handmade puzzles (don't worry, Infinite has the same number of handmade puzzles as the previous two). Sudoku has this issue, too, and it's just the nature of puzzle generation algorithms. Still, if you're dying for a new puzzle, they might hold you over, otherwise I'd just play them for the achievement.
At any rate, I've found if I step away from a puzzle or play others, I forget a solution, so you could probably revisit the entire series in a few weeks' time and have a whole new game.
The entire Hexcells series contains puzzles that are among the greatest I've ever solved. I highly recommend the entire collection, and also very strongly recommend that you start with Hexcells. It is easier than the other two, this one included, by far. Definitely, though, work up to this one. Absolutely worth your purchase.
For perspective, I am not the greatest logician, and I invested about 13 hours solving this campaign -- for 13 hours of gameplay, this game is a steal.

I've put most of my hours into the non-steam version from Github so, if there are not hundreds of hours on my play count to back up this review, know that there should be.
This is, bar none, the best EV-like project ever made.  The story is long and rich, and as development continues it sounds like they are adding additional branches.  The lore is deep, and you can pick up little bits of history on all sorts of side quests.
Trading is actually fun:  You don't just grind a trade route (though you could), but you can pick up a variety of missions opportunistically, and do trading on the side to fill the extra space in your hold.  Planning routes and trying to bunch-up jobs along that route becomes a fun planning activity.
Ship balance leaves something to be desired.   Once you have the money, there are a couple hulls which are plainly superior to all others.  This is particularly dissapointing as there are some clearly specific roles such as cargo capacity, passenger hauling (or crew hauling, for boarding operations), and various combat roles... but some hulls are just better at *all* of those things at once rather than allowing a stand-out specialized hull in each area.
Even the special (EV throwback) ship is inferior to the 'best' hulls in the game, which you will already have by the time you are able to unlock the special ship.
Ship balance aside, the game is amazing.  Lots to do, plenty to explore, and a little to easy to use as an idle time-filler!

Every now and then you come across a game so unique and elegant that you think to yourself, why isn't this more popular? Duet is a highly simplistic indie game that combines challenging puzzles with an amazing art style. Indie games never cease to break through the boundaries of game innovation and this gem will be sure to give you one hell of a ride.
Duet is a game where you have to control two blobs of colour, red and blue. Imagine if you will, an invisible ring and each blob is put on the ring at a position opposite to the other. You now have control of this 'invisible ring' which you rotate in order to keep each blob from touching any obstacles in the way. Obstacles come down towards you (or if you like to look at it the other way, you are moving towards the obstacles) and your job is to rotate the circle at the right moments, in the right directions to keep your blobs safe. I used an xbox one controller to play this game, however I'm sure a keyboard could work as well.
Playing this game requires good timing and a bit of memory, as the stages don't keep changing. Failure is highlighted by paint splashes on the objects you hit, and reminds you of areas you may have messed up on. I especially loved the fact that the game didn't go to some lengthy cutscene each time you died, instead, it pretty much "rewinded the track", and put you at the beginning.
Early levels were of course simple, and mostly forgiving. The story mode gradually teaches you how to adapt to varies types of obstacles, not by some intrusive tutorial or walkthrough, but by letting the player try over and over until they make it through that particular obstacle. And it is so satisfying, to finally beat a level that required intricate movements and an unbelievable amount of concentration. You'll soon discover that your skills grow rapidly as the levels become longer and harder
...and there may be times you're actually too mentally fatigued to continue. But we both know you'll be back real soon, trying to get that timing just right.
Duet is a beautiful game. The simplistic art style of the foreground objects is complemented so well by the 'dancing background' elements that keep the stage feeling alive and active. In fact, if there was a motion-less background, the game would feel a lot worse to play, but that may be an issue of preference.
Combined with amazing visuals, the music in Duet is really impressive. It has an indescribable melody which varies per level and can go from calming to upbeat in seconds. Regular sounds are well done as well, and fit the style of this game perfectly. At no point was I disappointed by anything I heard, which is quite impressive for such a simple game.
Duet is an awesome game wrapped in a simplistic package. It can go from relaxing to mind-numbingly frustrating in just a few levels and it always keep things fresh. After playing highly competitive or mechanically demanding games, sometimes you just want to find something simple to ease your mind. Duet manages to find the perfect middle ground between these.
10/10 -

Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition is quite the thrill ride! It takes place in Hong Kong, and you take on the role of an undercover cop, Wei Shen. It is tasked to you to infiltrate the Triad gang known as the Sun On Yee (新安義), and become one of their own. Wei Shen starts his way into the gang by means of his childhood friend Jackie Ma, slowly gaining trust and respect along the way.
The game is played in third-person, from behind the main character, though you have free camera movement to look from the front, sides, up, down, etc. There are various play styles along the way, from casual walking and running, to driving cars or motorcycles, to combat moments, parkour chases, driving gunfights, and so on...
The visuals of the game are gorgeous, the city is bright and beautiful, especially when the lights all come on at night. When it rains, which usually is a pretty torrential downpour, is always visually beautiful, everything is wet and shiny. The surface of a simple puddle on the ground reflecting the world around it, it's absolutely stunning. When driving fast in a car or on a bike, the way the world streaks and blurs away in motion is great.
There are clothes shops throughout the city that you can purchase different elements of clothing from shirts, vests, jackets, coats, pants, shorts, shoes, glasses, hats, chains, watches, bracelets, etc. There are also vehicle stores for purchasing cars and motorcycles throughout the city as well. Some clothing and vehicles are unlocked automatically through game progression, but most you will purchase as you make money on jobs and favours (and running over parking meters on the sides of the street with your car, haha).
Many missions are presented to you throughout the game, some are through regular game progression, some you have to find, including small favours from shop owners, random people you meet on the street, fellow gang members, etc. These are optional, but I find that they are often very much worth doing, as you gain money and respect / influence.
Gameplay is fluid, very smooth and natural, running, walking, driving... the parkour requires you to be smooth, you need to time your jumping over objects just right, or else you end up clumsily hopping over something and slowing down, trying to catch your bearings. The combat is sometimes difficult, and not so smooth. You will often have someone attacking you while you are dealing with one guy, and you need to counter their attack. Counters, grapples, and environmental kills are often fun, but have to be done just right (but those can often be quite brutal, yet satisfying).
With the Definitive Edition of the game, you get all the DLC packs that were originally purchased separately from the main game, the key ones being Nightmare at North Point and Year of the Snake stories, which I would recommend doing after you have completed the main story. Year of the Snake pretty much takes you to right after the main game is finished, you're a beat cop investigating a cultist group planting bombs all over the city during the Chinese New Year. Nightmare at North Point takes you into only one area of the city, North Point (obviously) is only one of four areas you will see on your map. It is in this area that supernatural occurrences start taking place, as the undead start to rise by way of their leader Smiley Cat. But you gain some new supernatural abilities as well to deal with them.
Overall, I had an awesome time playing this game. Put in about 70 hours at the time of this review. Main story and the DLCs, completed all missions and favours, and have 100% achievements. It was, as I said, quite a thrill ride, and I loved it. Highly recommended 9.5/10

Over The Void is a platformer that flips the genre upside down. Instead of relying on well performed jumps, you're able to place a platform below you to catch you fall. This allows for levels you've never seen the like of before, with some pretty colors.
That being said, the game is far to easy. There's no limit to how many platforms you can place and one platform is basically a trampoline so you're just left rocketing off trying to get to the buttons as fast as you can, which isn't fast enough. A fun little puzzle game akin to Mine Sweeper. Plus is the follow up game to Hexcells, adding more levels. A final entry to the series called Hexcells Infinite rounds out the series with a random puzzle generator allowing the ability to play forever!
Masterpiece
- 10/10

This series is criminally overlooked.
If you enjoy games like sudoku, you will find logical puzzles here that work your brain for hours. While a naive comparison, the game plays similarly to a very advanced Minesweeper. By the second act, though, you'll have discovered the futility of that comparison; this game is on an entirely different level and has an elegance in the solutions that random Minesweeper puzzles cannot ever hope to achieve.
A couple of the puzzles stumped me for more than 90 minutes, and my roommate rapidly grew tired of me talking the solution out loud as I moved my mouse around. There's a brilliant simplicity to the gameplay and yet, while playing, one must keep a large amount of logic in their head. It's easy to get overwhelmed by logic in one area of the puzzle while overlooking the simple move forward in another area, and the feeling is intense when you slap your forehead in stupidity on discovering it.
The soundtrack is quite relaxing, and even after working on the same puzzle for an hour it did not grow tiresome. It's really fun when you get on a "roll" of solving the puzzle, too, because you generate little ditties as a reward.
The only negative of Infinite compared to the rest of the series is the randomly-generated puzzles. The developer added these so that he could put a bow on the series and call it done and, while they do indeed fill a gap, you can tell they're a far different experience than the handmade puzzles (don't worry, Infinite has the same number of handmade puzzles as the previous two). Sudoku has this issue, too, and it's just the nature of puzzle generation algorithms. Still, if you're dying for a new puzzle, they might hold you over, otherwise I'd just play them for the achievement.
At any rate, I've found if I step away from a puzzle or play others, I forget a solution, so you could probably revisit the entire series in a few weeks' time and have a whole new game.
The entire Hexcells series contains puzzles that are among the greatest I've ever solved. I highly recommend the entire collection, and also very strongly recommend that you start with Hexcells. It is easier than the other two, this one included, by far. Definitely, though, work up to this one. Absolutely worth your purchase.
For perspective, I am not the greatest logician, and I invested about 13 hours solving this campaign -- for 13 hours of gameplay, this game is a steal.

I love the multidirectionality of Hexcells Infinite: solving a single cell can affect three lines of cells, as well as the set of surrounding cells. At first, it felt much like a hexagonal version of Minesweeper. When the lines were added, I was reminded of nonograms / paint-by-numbers puzzles. Then, as the puzzles continued, my mind became so occupied with the intersecting logic that I stopped trying to compare it to other games at all.
The level design is excellent, and the puzzle progression slowly encourages you to learn new solving techniques, with no huge jumps in difficulty. In addition to the handmade puzzles, Hexcells Infinite includes a random puzzle generator to increase your playtime, and add a nice break when you get stuck in the main game.
Hexcells Infinite improves on the previous versions by allowing you to save your progress in every. In spite of that, it may be worth also getting Hexcells Plus for the additional puzzles, and the slightly easier difficulty.

What can be said ?...: Spacebase DF-9.
[ An Early Access Preview ]
*Uninterested exhale/grunt.*
*Leaves to get coffee.*
*Returns, sips coffee.*
*Writes this prologue in a way, that hopefully delivers the feeling of indifference.*
This, is exactly why. You cannot properly review an Early Access game, since most of the games content is not present. It is like Minecraft in Alpha, its a proof of concept with not much context, polish or content.
And thats why, i cannot write a review about it...
What ? Dont look at me like that, when you think about it properly. You'l see exactly what i mean, it would be like reviewing something just based on its trailer.
.
But allright...
Spacebase DF-9 is a game, where you try to build a working Deep Space outpost.
This is only hampered by the AI and its questionable prioritisation. Multiple times, my only technician thought it would be more important to talk to Johny the SpaceSlug than to, lets say, repair the Life Support systems.
And this is one of those games where there is a certain build plan. And deviating from it will just result in failure.
That is, if you can get the builders to do everything in time.
And speaking of "doing stuff on time". That is an ironic statement/joke, that i hope several of you will get. The citizen of your station are complete and utter lazybones.. 'ses.
Most of their life consist of eating food and talking to others. And this they will do even if they have other, more important stuff they need to do. Like maintenance to make sure the station wont disintegrate like a clown car.  Another rather ironic thing to say about this...
So to compress that all:
Spacebase DF-9  is like Minecraft in Alpha, very lacking in content. But the concept is easy to get, now it just needs some care and attention to make it a full game. And for gods sake, repair the AI.

It was fun for a while, until you start noticing the stupidity of the AIs:
- Miners don't use the nearest airlocks and suffocate.
- The techs spend their day getting fat instead of repairing equipment (especially the turrets outside the station).
- Doctors don't always grab the bodies floating in space.
- Everyone runs around panicking when the station loses air instead of suiting up and repairing the hole.
There are also graphical glitches:
- Sometimes phantom fires stay lit in the floor if the crew put the fire out without a fire extinguisher.
- Airlock LED indicators often stay floating in space after the doors are removed.
There are more problems, and the game features don't feel fleshed out enough. I would recommend trying this game later in its life.
Edit: Now that the developers have stopped, well, developing, the game isn't a worthy investment unless you want to cry tears of sadness.

KeeperRL is a lot of fun for an early access title, although it's still a little rough around the edges. It basically plays in two modes, although they play out in the same map and interface.
There is a pausable real-time building mode that plays like Dwarf Fortress/Dungeon Keeper. In this mode, you create your own dungeon. You designate where your imps will dig out tunnels and build rooms, and work towards meeting the requirements to recruit minions.
Then, when you have enough minions to create a squad, you can take direct control of them and switch to roguelike mode. This play in a standard turn based mode like any other roguelike. In this mode you control a single unit, along with your squad of allies that follow you around and act on their own. You can take your minions and raid enemy towns and dungeons.
As long as the final release adds some better documentation and an effective tutorial, and does a balance pass on enemies, this is shaping up to be a really creative blend of roguelike and dungeon building.

The game is a frustrating, perfectionist, puzzle game.
It has no sense of flow or groove, like other games in the genre. One mistake and you're jarringly whipped back to the beginning of the level and forced to replay it while looking at paint splatters of where you died to remind you how much you suck.
It's not a music/rhythm game as the soundtrack, which is actually very good, has nothing to do with the puzzle unfolding before you or story. Each level has a random quote that is supposed to make a "story", but it's completely incoherent and sounds like they just pushed a random button on a Dr. Phil sound board to generate each one.
Each chapter adds some new gimmick "mechanic": invisible blocks, moving blocks, spinning blocks, blocks coming in at a 45-degree angle, etc. None of the new mechanics feel integrated with the music, story, or have any logical sense of progression.
The fact that there is an achievement for watching the credits succintly sums up the "not recommended" rating. If I didn't get this game as part of a Humble Bundle, I would have returned it.
Note: I didn't suffer from the motion sickness that other negative reviews have commented on.

As a port, this game is pretty alright. It has a FPS limit that's capped at 91 and a FOV locked at 65. Both of which can be changed with mods.
Thanks to the introduction of IWNet and the neglect of a seven year-old game, multiplayer is a very lackluster experience. The game uses a peer-to-peer connection and if the host of the lobby leaves (a person that the game chooses at seemingly random), the game will pause and try to find another host. It can be liable to disconnecting the entire lobby. It really doesn't have to be this way on a PC game.
There's automatic matchmaking (also called IWNet), so you can randomly get thrown into a lobby with a hacker or with a bad connection, over and over until IWNet decides to roll you something good. Infinity Ward has been faced with this problem before with their previous iteration, Call of Duty 4. Unable to do much, they simply told their users to play in private lobbies.
Thankfully, VAC is implemented. But, it's useless. Hackers aren't deterred by VAC in the slightest, and thee's no incentive on IW's end to address this problem any longer.
Infinity Ward succeeded in what they wanted to do, they hamstrung the PC port's multiplayer to function similar to a console's, giving us all a baseline experience.
Don't buy the DLC. It's overpriced and none of the few players left have it. If you're going to buy this, then understand that you're playing a decrepit husk.

This is easily one of the most addicting games out there. The premise of the game is simple, yet extremely complex. You've crash landed on an alien world and you need to get off. So how do you escape? You build your way up to a rocket!
Most of the challenge in the game lies in automating everything. You can mine resources, which in turn can be used to build components, which in turn can be used to build more components, etc, etc. But why mine it by hand? Instead, build a mining unit, then create some transport belts to move the mined resources to smelters. Then use robotic arms to move the resources into the smelter and back out as a crafted good. Then use more belts to move them along to crafting stations to make more items. And so on.
Some of the recipes are extremely complex and require a ton of ingredients. You also have to research new technology and unlock new things to get to higher tiers in the game.
If this all sounds easy but time consuming, well there's one more tidbit - aliens. As you build up, you'll create pollution. The native wildlife doesn't like pollution so they will come and attack you. You need to use turrets, armor, tanks, walls, robots, etc, etc, to defend your base.
This is easily one of the best indie games out there. If you're on the fence on this one, don't think, just buy it. You won't regret it.
One last thing - kudos to the devs for selling it for $20 instead of the normal 19.99 garbage. I really like that.

1.0 review update:
I don't recommend this game anymore. The developer decided to quit working on it simply because its alpha release did not net them the money they were hoping to get. Not everyone goes for an alpha release. Some want to see the finished product.
Considering the developer thinks of the 1.0 release as the finished product, let me say that I'm thoroughly disappointed in the product. I would not have bought it in this state.
Instead of complaining about the lack of funds they received for their in-progress game, the developers could have simply hammered on the bugs, made a well-rounded game, and then the 1.0 release could have brought so many more people in. People who would have paid them.
This is yet another example of why Early Access fails; developers pulling the plug on projects because their expectations were impossible to realize.
