I've been a long time RPG player, FF nut, WoW player (Vanilla launch all the way to legion), played FF11 for a few years, and decided to try FF14. I had played off and on for some time. My review is for how the game stands today, which finalizes Heavensward's story leading into Stormblood. (I've completed all MSQs to date).
Graphics: 9/10
I've played a lot of games and seen a lot of different engines used, but this game runs flawlessly and looks outright gorgeous in so many different places. I found myself saying "This is amazing!" quite a few times, during boss fights, or flying through a new zone. This engine is spectacular, and even with a low end machine can enjoy some truly marvelous moments. Animations in this game blow pretty much anything in WoW and FF11 away.
Sound / Music: 8.5/10
I want to rate this higher, really, I do. Let's start with the sound.
For the most part, SFX are very solid. Spells sound on point, and weapon skills are satisfying to execute. I wish there was a bit more of a callback to the older FFs (Summoning sounds from tactics/FF4 for example.), but I haven't had anything that was very odd. Outside of my Machinist yelling everytime they fire a shot. But who wouldn't do that anyways?
Music. There is a love / hate relationship here. Most of the music in the lower level dungeons / Fates is just boring, uninspiring to me. You will hear them again and again. You'll wish there was some form of option to change the music to something you'd like in the game tracks (Perhaps a great idea in the future?). A lot of music is reused a lot in the cutscenes and it can take away a lot in a really critical scene.
Now the good stuff. Primal fights / Trials / Super baddies for the most part, have incredible soundtracks. Check out Alexander Prime's "Rise" theme or Locus on youtube for an example. Shiva's fight gave me goosebumps (Maybe I should have said chills?) the first time I fought her. The music is so uplifting and powerful in all the right moments for these fights, it makes a massive difference in the experience.
Class Design 7.5/10
I play the following jobs: Machinist, White Mage, Astrologist, Scholar, Summoner, and Bard. I've delved a bit with melee and some tanking, but not a lot... But enough to get a glipse of how everything shakes out.
I do feel that a lot of jobs are overburdened with abilities that should be pruned or baked into others, because it seems a bit excessive to have so many buttons. Healers can seem pretty linear for the most part (Tank takes little damage, Cure 1. Tank takes a good amount of damage, Cure 2. Party takes a lot of damage, Medica 2, ect) others can be really complex, such as a Machinist opener to hit a lot of different buttons in sequence, and failing to perform it correctly merits a huge damage loss.
I really do hope they work on remaking Summoner a bit for the expansion, it was the only job that was pretty boring to me. Currently you only have 3 'Egi's and they are really waterdowned versions of a few famous FF primals
I do hope abilities on the whole get smoothed over for Stormblood.
There is certainly a higher learning curve for learning how to do your class very well, as opposed to an easier skillset in WoW.
Story: 9/10
I think there will be some difference of opinion on this, and I'll be the first to admit, in ARR, the story can drag at points. It can be some fetch me quest, or need to visit the other side of the world to talk to a person. There were parts that were fantastic, and others that were very much skippable. That said, coming into Heavensward, it starts really picking up. SE knows one of their best strengths can be story telling, and from HW beginning to end was delightful. There is a sense of urgency when it is called upon, and not every quest is the end of the world beat the bad guy. The characters are very well done, and voice acting is great overall.
That said, there are a LOT of quests. Hundreds, to even get to HW, and a hundreds more to get it all wrapped up to this point in time. I play a good bit, but tend to be a mostly casual player. You'll probably spend months getting through the story. If you are just starting, don't burn yourself out, remember you are going through 7 years of content. Enjoy the story as it unfolds, and if you find it a bit slow at first, just wait.... Trust me.
Content 9 /10
There is a ton to do in this game. Raids, dungeons, daily roulettes, gold saucer, crafting, gathering, fishing, dancing naked in front of a giant crystal, building your own house, airship, collecting mounts/minions, glamours, leveling other jobs, beast tribes, palace of the dead, diadem, main quests, side quests, anima weapon quests, hunts.
It goes on, and on, and on. SE is amazing with content, and every 3 or so months is a major patch introducing more.
My only con for content is PvP.
PvP is a massive joke in this game right now. Balance is all over the place and nothing seems polished.
Things I'm not fond of:
I've stated a lot of pros for the game, but there are things that feel lacking as well.
First and foremost, Level sync. I don't care for this system. If you are level 35 and just get regen for whitemage, which is an amazing and fun ablity for me, but get a daily random into a level 15 dungeon.... I have basically cure 1 and medica (party cure). All those amazing spells I had can't be used at all, and even though im getting some experience, most of the time I tend not to for roulettes (Even if my gear is up to date). My summoner has 3 different set ups because of this. One for really low content, one for level 50 content, and one for 60 content.
Why not just make spells/abilities scale accordingly? I feel you earned them through your process and it is headscratching to have it taken away.
Tanking / Threat: I didn't care much for tanking when I did it. I'm sure others do. It was a rather bland experience for me.
I do wish threat in general was easier to generate for tanks, as it can be severe problem if tanks don't know how in lower levels, get flustered, and quit their tanking job for something else. I've seen this in other MMOs and in vanilla WoW as well. I feel the entire role needs to be smoothed a bit for others to want to tank and have fun with it.
The Game Launcher
This really needs an overhaul yesterday. When you compare Blizzard's launcher to FF14s launcher... It's like Apple's current website vs my Geocities 1996 myspace techno glitter festival website. Seriously. Even PlayOnline for FF11 was miles better.
Verdict and Final Thoughts
I give this game a 8.8 total. The amount of content, job design, primal fights, and exploring this world is a fun time, but be patient, allow yourself to learn, and enjoy the totality of the story, graphics, music, and if you are an old fan of the series, there are a lot of callbacks to the older games. Those moments are utterly delightful. Recommend.

I'm going to review two aspects of this game: The game itself, and the community.
The game itself is pretty great. Not many MMOs keep me hooked as long as this one has. The graphics are pretty nice, the job balance is done well, the storyline (though not my cup of tea) has more depth than most MMO storylines.
My only real complaint (though it's a serious one) about the game is its end game. Once you've leveled everything to 60 (which can take a while), you're basically just going to run daily dungeons for currency to by some of the top tier gear. This currency caps at 450 per week though. Besides that, you can also run a raid and get a drop once per week for another piece of top gear.
After you do both of these things, you may be out of reasons to login for the week. Which is obviously not good.
There are complaints about the PvP in this game. It's very casual and does have its problems, but it's certainly entertaining in my opinion.
Now we get to the second aspect of the game....the community:
The community in this game has been a roller coaster of ups and downs in my experience. Unfortunately more downs than ups.
Outside of the hardcore raiding scene, it's not uncommon at all in my experience to run into that one person (or sometimes multiple people) in a group that have to be carried. And I'm not talking about someone that hasn't quited learned their abilities yet but is obviously trying, I'm talking about someone who demonstrates a willful, obvious, almost proud ignorance. Many times these people simply ignore advice or actually get offended by it.
I've also encountered trolls in dungeons more than once. Everything from someone using cross-class tank skills to intentionally provoke enemies off the tank to annoy them, to people abusing the kick feature in the game to wrongfully remove someone from the group. There are 4 people in a dungeon group, the person who is being voted on cannot vote. The other 3 can, however since the 4th person can't vote, it only takes 2 people to vote Yes (One actually technically since the vote initiator is automatically counted as a Yes) to successfully kick them. This enables all kind of bad behavior from people who queue with a friend. And basically if there's a disagreement, whoever starts the kick first wins.
The server I play on (Balmung) has also had some interesting people. I was once kicked from an FC for talking about insects. The leader's girlfriend was triggered by insects, apparently she has a crippling fear of them (despite playing a game with plenty of large insects in it as enemies). I questioned her, the FC leader lost it and kicked me.
TL;DR: The game is good, the community is not so good in my experience. I'll probably get a lot of hate for saying so, but it's simply my experience, the truth of it. Everywhere else I've said negative things about the community, I've been made out to be the devil, but seeing as this is where reviews go I want this place to be more than just an echo chamber.
Since I can't give this a 5/10, I'll have to vote not recommended since the community of an MMO makes an MMO as much as the game itself does.

My village was allways... special. Special towards the unknown. They burned everything which is not right in their eyes. Imps, Doppleganger, Orcs. It doesn't matter. It's all the same for them. I don't want to end up in a fire where my soul burns for my "sins". So I fled. I decided to hide in the mountains where noone can see me. I also found a few new friends on my journey. They were Imps. My family was allways so wrong. They are just some harmless creatures (If you can stand the smell ofcourse). I told them who I am and why I am not with my kind anymore. For some reason they believed me. A few days later we made it to the foot of the mountain. Till then my "power" grew. The imps weren't friends anymore. They obey me now. There was some nice experiment I made with it. I told one Imp to scratch his arm until I say stop. Sadly I fell asleep because it was allready dark. He scraped with his sharp claws down to his skull and... beyond. It was a huge mess. Maybe that was the point where I changed. Ofcourse not just because of that, but also because of my family. I had to leave or I will die. Now someone else died because of me. Whatsoever we made it to the mountain. For some reason Imps allways have enough equipment with them to dig in dirt or rocks. So I made 'em dig. We build up our own basement, my power grew and grew and it lured more creatures to me. Willing to obey me.
A few months later we found some dwarfs in the deep belly of the mountain. They noticed that we aren't normal anymore. We are, by far, not these creatures that we used to be. Hunter's Legacy is an average to above average action platformer.
The game's basics are what you would expect from the genre. You jump between platforms avoiding obstacles and enemies. You have a sword and arrow attack. Basically you go around the world gathering new abilities that you use to beat the final boss.
At first I found Hunter's Legacy to be a little slow. The first couple of levels don't really do anything highly original. The beginning of the game is perfectly fine but doesn't really grab you since it just feels like every other action platformer.
Then at around the halfway point the game turns the corner. This is mostly because the game starts to add some more original mechanics to the game. I particularly liked the hot/cold mechanic that is featured in one of the worlds/lands. The final level is also really well designed utilizing all the skills and abilities learned throughout the game.
Difficulty wise I would say the early game is pretty easy while the later game is moderately difficult. The bosses are not surprisingly the hardest parts of the game. The rest of the challenge comes from the occasional "cheap" hit where you get hit when you probably shouldn't have due to it being hard to sometimes tell where the collision detection is on various hazards and enemies.
Length wise I would say the game is around 7-9 hours. If you go after all of the bonus/secret levels you might get a couple more hours out of the game.
Basically I would say that Hunter's Legacy is a good action platformer but I have played better games in the genre. If you don't like the genre the game is not going to be for you. If you like the genre though I think you will enjoy the game.

I had previously left a review that personally left me embarrassed by my childishness at what was a monster of my own making. I figure this is my way to attone for it.
Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn is a reboot of the original Final Fantasy XIV after gameplay issues caused the MMO to stagnate and become near unplayable. However with its reboot, with the death of the 1.0 version being a canon happening, players start out as an adventerer in the fictional world of Eorzea a diverse land governed by several city states that are under threat not just by the Garlean Empire threatening to invaid, but by beast tribes summoning their respective gods as Primals beasts that absorb the aether from the land and threaten to do far worse than push back the people. However blessed with the power of the Echo the players strive to fight back these threats and bring Eorzea to a whole.
Starting off you have a few races to choose from and they are purely cosmetic as stat differences mean very little the more you play. Make your character and choose your starting class from one of the many combat classes which not only determines your roles in dungeons but might also be your main class when progressing through the story quests.
The starting classes are:
Marauder a Tank class that goes up to the job of Warrior
Gladiator another Tank that goes up to Paladin
Pugilist a Melee damage dealer that turns into a Monk
Lancer a melee damage dealer that becomes a Dragoon
Archer a ranged physical damage dealer that becomes a Bard
Rogue a melee damage dealer that becomes a Ninja (Only available once you reach Level 10 in any other class)
Conjurer a healer that becomes a White Mage
Thaumaturge a Ranged Magical damage dealer that becomes a Black Mage
and Arcanist a Ranged Magical damage dealer that becomes either Summoner or Scholar.
The fun thing about classes and jobs is that you can be either the class or job at any time once you obtain it. You can also play any class at almost any time you want on one character which is needed to get the jobs because for example to be a White Mage you have to be a level 30 Conjurer with 15 levels in Thaumaturge. This adds a push to getting characters to play the other classes, and believe me I ended up enjoying Thaumaturge so much I nearly leveled it up to a Black Mage before I forced myself to get back on track.
The game is easy to play but challenging to master. Each class has its own strengths and weaknesses. For example DPS classes deal damage with ease but need to avoid taking damage just as much. Tank classes can take hard hits on the chin, but have low damage dealing and might struggle to keep their health up. Healers can outlast the best of them being able to keep their health up, but lack the damage output or defence of the other classes. These differences are vital to the party based gameplay that Final Fantasy is known for especially in dungeons.
The dungeons in Final Fantasy XIV can range from easy, to frustrating, but never boring. After the first dungeon every following one features at least three bosses with interesting mechanics to them. From avoiding attacks to area wide effects that can leave each class with a list of tasks to do each time. I advise playing with a friend who has challenged these dungeons before or at least looking up visual guides to them as certain mechanics can be difficult to learn first time. However these dungeons can get rather complex when you add in more people.
The standard light party in this game is four people typically one tank, one healer, and two DPS. However the max full party is eight people doubling the number of classes needed. This means a lot of co-operation is needed and knowledge of terms such as Main Tank and Off Tank, Rez, and so on will be needed as these are standards in communicating strategy to other players. You may get the odd bad Tank/DPS/Healer, but all in all the party members generally have the same understanding of the game that you have at that point.
In addition to fighting things there are also two non-combat class types: Disciples of the Land, and Disciples of the Hand, or Gatherers and Crafters. As you defeat enemies you'll obtain things like skins, meats, and other such things in addition to gathering through Mining, Botany, and Fishing that you can use as a Carpenter, Blacksmith, Armorer, Goldsmith, Leatherworker, Weaver, Alchemist, and Culinarian. These generally are used for making money or making items you can use in game such as food, potions, or even some equipment.
Social interaction is an inevitability in this game. With MMOs there's bound to be other people playing and as such you'll run into people who may want you to join their party for a bit, or their free company. Free Companies are the guilds in this game. Player owned and operated guilds can be set up for nearly anything such as raids, helping new players, or even roleplaying. Various perks are earned as players in the free company earn points including buffs that affect the whole company such as increased EXP from battles. In addition Free Companies can more easily get the money needed to purchase an estate in one of the many residential areas. For a fee you can buy a plot of land, or an apartment that you can decorate and make your own. The cash needed can be quite a lot but chances are the benefits will really apeal to you if you enjoy a lot of customization and really making spaces your own. You can add guardens, combat dummies, chocobo stables, and much more however it's purely optional. However it's nice to have a place to let your character rest when you're ready to log off.
There are issues with this game of course, it's not perfect as much as I wish it was. The biggest complaint is the subscriptions which requires that you pay money to keep playing the game every month. This is an issue until you realize that they give you the first month free, feature free play events, and give you access to everything you want. Understandable that you don't want to pay for an MMO you might not play more than once a week, however I don't see it as an issue.
Another issue is in the inherent saturation of DPS classes. Queueing for a dungeon could take half an hour if you're lucky where as with Healer and Tanks they arrive and join in the DPS queues that were waiting for so long. Hardly surprising however but as more classes are added with expansions there's a larger number of Tanks and Healing classes available as well.

Now, I know it probably seems a little early for me to leave a review on this game, considering how I`ve only played around 30+ hours, but I feel like I have done enough research on this game to form an honest and factual opinion. So here we go!
Pros
*Square Enix provides impressive support for this game, servers rarely go down at all, and I have yet to encounter big lag issues, even when engaged in massive battles with multiple players and enemies.
*Class system: probably one of the best systems I have seen in an MMO, and trust me, I have played a lot of them. You essentially only need one character. You can switch between classes on the fly, as long as you have the class set with you, and individually level each one up. This completely removes the need for alt-accounts, as you can basically become every single class in the game on one character.
*Healthy playerbase: There are many people playing this game, and it`s not uncommon to find yourself surrounded by hundreds of players in the capital cities.
*Friendly playerbase: The community surrounding this game is shockingly friendly, and open to almost anyone. After playing for only two hours, I was invited to a guild by a complete stranger, and all of my guildmates were extremely helpful, and taught me how the different systems in the game worked. Also, there is almost always at least one or two dudes ready to help you, if you for instance need some teammates for a dungeon.
*Good subscription-based MMO: This game utilizes one of the best subscription-based services I have seen to date. There is so much value and gameplay to get here, and the monthly fee isn`t overly expensive either.
*Story: The story in this game is probably one of the best stories I have ever seen in an MMO. After playing for a while, I found myself looking forward to doing the next quest, only so I could see how the story would unfold. Fair warning though: It does take some time to get into the meat of things, but once you do, you will find yourself captivated by the world and its characters.
*End-game raids: The 24-man raids and events you can do once you hit max level, are quite frankly fantastic. The awe-inspiring bosses, the cool dungeons and locations, the beautiful music and the level of teamwork needed to complete each raid is simply perfect. Final Fantasy XIV has always boasted itself on it`s amazing end-game raids, and I must truly say, it definitely lives up to its promise!
*Beautiful music: Many of the locations in this game have terrific music, and sometimes, I find myself listening to the soundtracks alone whilst doing homework or other tasks. From the soothing vibes of the jungle to the intense music of boss-battles, Square Enix really put some incredibly hard work into the scores in this game.
*Cross-platform play: PC-players can play with players from both the PS3 and PS4 version, and vice versa. A very nice thing if one of your friends happens to own the game on a console instead of a PC.
Cons
*Dungeons and Raids queue time: Sometimes, it can take up to half an hour to get into a dungeon or raid if you are soloing. Especially annoying if your current quest involves completing a dungeon. You basically cannot progress further into the story unless you beat the dungeon first, which can involve sitting through a queue-time of up to 30 minutes or longer (if you don`t have any friends or guildmates to help you).
*Gil (currency) sellers: Now, I know that this is pretty much a common thing in MMO`s these days, but that doesn`t make it any less annoying. If you find yourself in one of the main cities during "rush hour" (when there is the biggest amount of players online), it is not uncommon to see the chat bar filling up with spam messages about selling Gil. This is extremely annoying if you are for instance trying to have a conversation with another player. Your messages get lost in a sea of spam, and you basically have to party up, only to utilize the party-chat so you can actually see what the other person is writing.
*Boring "fetch" or "kill" quests: There are quite a few standard "go here and kill 5 of these", or "bring this item to this NPC" quests littered throughout the game. This is a pretty common thing in MMO`s these days, but still, it`s worth mentioning.
*PvP: Very long PvP queues and few players. Also slightly unbalanced. I don`t really do PvP all that much, so this doesn`t bother me, but if you are one of those people who loves PvP, then this might put you off.
*End-game (yes it`s here too): The end-game in Final Fantasy XIV can be very grindy and tedious at times. You might have to redo the same raid or dungeon multiple times only to get the gear or item you want. Most of the end-game is built up around raids and dungeons, so if that isn`t your thing, then there really isn`t much point in continuing to play after you hit max level, except for maybe to level up alternative classes.
Conclusion
Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn might be one of the best MMO`s I have ever played. It has a great class system, steady support from the developers, awesome end-game raids, a friendly and healthy community, a great story, beautiful music and cross-platform play. I am extremely happy that I decided to start playing this game, and I can`t see myself stopping any time soon!

Of all the MMORPGs out there, Final Fantasy XIV has one of the most in-depth, incredible stories. This is the closest to its roots Final Fantasy has felt in many years, and I highly recommend it. Between character customization and the main story quests, there is plenty of content that non-MMO players can play with little to no need for other players interference. And for those who like the social aspect, there are Free Company's (guilds), lots of dungeons, and an amazing community of players from around the world looking to have fun and make friends. All in all, this is an amazing game, and I recommend it to anyone looking for a golden years Final Fantasy experience.

This game's story was easily one of the best stories I've played through to the very date.  Is this game perfect? No, but it sure is worth a shot. In the game, you are Wei Chen, an undercover cop with a troubled past. Now, in the present, Wei is charged with the task of infiltrating a triad in Hong Kong, the Sun On Yee. It is up to him to do what ever it takes to get them to trust him and for him to take down the Sun On Yee from the inside. The story is one of the greatest parts about this game, it deals with 'stockholm like' stuff and getting overly attached, it also blurs the clear cut line between what is right and wrong. The characters are also memorable and well written.
The gameplay is also another great thing about this game. The game is an open world game where you can drive cars or take taxes to your destinations. Driving around the city is pretty fun and the city is fairly large. Along with the main missions, there are other things to be done, such as go on dates, do favors for people, shop for clothes and food, buy cars, stop drug deals, steal cars, karaoke (Yes, karaoke), and do police cases. There are also collectible items and shires to collect/activate, which reward you (New fighting moves and health upgrades).
The fighting is another key factor in this game in which the creators take pride in. The fighting is similiar to the Batman Arkham series, but is different enough that it isn't copying it. As you go you, you learn more moves, which is extremely helpful at times to take down those annoying thugs. The fighting is martial arts based and can be very satisfying. There's also 'environmental take-downs', which allow you to shove someone into a fish tank, or close a door on someone's face, or even put them in an ice chopper (brutal!). There's also gunplay in this game that isn't really anything new, but is still fun. There is, however; a slow motion mechanic that is pretty cool. The driving isn't also anything that new, but the cars handle well, depending on the car, and it does have some pretty great driving mechanics.
The one problem that I had with the game is that a good majority of the buildings in the game were just shells. It really doesn't affect the gameplay that much, but it is still worth mentioning. Like many open world games, there are radio stations. The music provided in the game is pretty great and adds something special to long drives or even some chase scenes. The missions in the game are very fun, some are similiar but most feel different and are definitely worth the time to play through them (they aren't usually that long). Being that this version is the Definitive Edition, it also comes with the dlc, which adds some more story to do after the campaign. The dlc is definutely worth checking out too.
Overall, I had a blast playing through this and I look forward to coming back to in the near future. I personally got this game on sale, but I'd definitely buy it for its full retail price!

KeeperRL has some serious potential for an indie dungeon management sim. It certainly feels charming like the classic Dungeon Keeper which is borrows from more than a little. The top-down look works well and the simple indie graphics have their charm despite a lack of animations.
Where it shines is your ability to micromanage your dungeon layout and build teams of multiple units and take direct control of them to attack your enemies. Despite finite resources, particularly in the form of gold, granite, and iron, you will rarely feel too rushed and are given ample time each playthrough to develop your dungeon as you see fit, and once you've mustered strong defenses it's really up to you when you decide to set out and conquer.
The biggest downside of the game is the difficulty caps pretty early, despite having your dungeon attacked by enemies that can early on prove to be quite devastating, once you've figured out the basics of dungeon management you will be able to conquer with little problem, and as more enemies are defeated, your job just becomes easier and easier to the point that you could just zerg rush the enemy's base at the end and win with overwhelming force. Having the game come with randomly generated worlds was a nice touch but with the same type of enemies in each, it quickly becomes rather easy to plan a winning strategy.
Do I recommend this game? If you love Dungeon Management, it's definitely worth picking up and it is a lot of fun to figure out, but if you consider yourself a strategy veteran you may find the lack of challenge in the game to be a serious detractor.

Factorio is building blocks for adults.  What once captured our imaginations as children, playing with trains and trucks, has copulated with the stimulating art of engineering and produced (through some dark art) this b@stard child of addiction.  For those of you who have not yet been "reconditioned," let me tell you why Factorio is worth that salty Jackson in your pocket.
What makes a video game "great?"  For some games, it's all about story.  This isn't necessarily a bad thing; there have been many titles in the past that have exploited story and the perspective the player is placed in with respect to it (usually designating the player as the one who controls the protagonist).  Though this type of experience is valuable in it's own right, it is not exclusive to the medium of videogames as it can be achieved through other forms of entertainment (mostly cinema, but even through music - see (for example) Mars Volta
, and other forms as well)
Arguably, most "great/memorable" videogames which do not outright rely on story for their greatness, have some form of "game mechanic" that makes their overall experience not only unique, but compelling and mentally stimulating to the point where their "enjoyability" is not derived from novelty (edging the player forward with difficult levels or monotonous tasks) but from the idea of limitnessless and awe.  Minecraft once was working off of this idea, but was quickly adulterated by the cheesy third-rate "RPG" mechanics which have violated the game's original essence of creativity, survival and exploration and have overshadowed it with a dull grind and an over-complicated system of levels, strange-items that feel as though they do not belong, enchantments, potions, swords and special arrows, and other odd clutter.  Not to digress, but Minecraft lost it's charm which relied on the elemental hierarchy of things we know of in their most basic forms (coal, iron, wood, brick, water, lava) and the use/rearrangement of such elements to create structures and survive in a hostile environment.  The beautiful simplicity of these base elements was quickly lost to the "glistening melons," the "bane of arthropods iron sword," the "blaze rod," ect.  These odd, complex items and their even stranger effects are not AT ALL evocative of human intuition, but instead feel grossly out of place in a world that was supposed to be simplistic.
So what exactly does Factorio's game mechanic do that rekindles this aforementioned limitless and awe that games like Minecraft destroy?  Factorio, at its core, is a game about creating factories which automate the production of intermediate products which are used to create other factories and so on.  The one thing that makes Factorio worthy of that salty Jackson mentioned earlier, is that the player must use their own creativity, intellect and intuition to build and optimize their factory such that it is able to achieve the goal that the player themself creates.  The player has the ongoing understanding that their factory "could be better if X" and resultantly, the will to create a system that is tailored to both efficiency and player preference is exalted without end.  Every player has a unique approach to offer to a certain problem, and seeing those unique approaches shine through in your own factory and work is one of the most rewarding feelings ever.  When a player is rewarded for something they themself thought of, they are no longer constrained by the limitations of the code that made the game; the game takes on a life of it's own, and you'll find this to be both figurative and literal in Factorio.
This game gets to join Undertale with a 10+/10 for me, but for a different reason.  This arbitrary rating system can't fully do it justice.

Having had dumped around 50 sum hours in the first week of owning the game, I think it's fair to say that I enjoy the game; However, it does have it's pros and cons, like any game.
Starting off with the CONS:
*Multiplayer servers often provide very bad connection.
*I'd imagine very frustrating if you don't know what you're doing (Look up Aavak's series: "Factorio Beginner's Guide", it's amazing)
*Crafting times can be very long if you aren't prepared and/or don't think ahead.
PROS:
*A game that can provide an endless amount of entertainment
*Fair-Good graphics
*Procedularly generated world that isn't buggy
**Very cheap for only $20, not $19.99, which I guess I kinda respect. Keeping it real.
*Constant challenges and obstacles to keep you on edge
*A very large amount of automation, logistical work, and killing can be done in very diverse ways.
*As someone who isn't into tech and automation, I was hesitant, but this game makes complicated simple, while still giving experienced users a challenge (mainly due to them challenging themselves to do more)
*There's always MORE to do, as I've said, the game keeps you wanting to do MORE, even though you may not need it.
If you're hesitant, go watch Aavak's series (as listed above). Shen and Aavak really do an amazing job introducing and explaining the game.
Also, there's an achievement for running over trees that's called: "Run Forest, Run!" Thought some might find that amusing, as I did when it popped up awhile back.

What can I say? I'm 40 hours into this game and I like it a lot, but I feel like there's some missed potential here too.  This is yet another gang themed sandbox action game, this time with you playing as an undercover cop in Hong Kong.  Like many games of this type, the missions are pretty repetative and the story is very action movie stock, but after that it's pretty DAMN good.
For one thing, the melee combat is much deeper and more strategic than pretty much any other sandbox game out there. At times the game almost feels more like an open world beat 'em up! You can get really lost in the many ways to fight, with countering being a cirtical skill to master.  At the same time, it never feels overwhelming.  You won't be counting frames or anything as convoluted as a modern fighting game requires.  If anything, the combat errs on the easy side.
But this is where the problems start.  Since it's an open world game, a lot of the other elements feel very shoehorned in to add content.  The street racing is very fidgety and annoying and you can still come in last despite doing a near perfect run of the course.  Side quests are numerous but they all boil down to the same few activities over and over (driving, defending or fighting).
There's a great game underneath all this, and I'm still having fun playing, but I think part of me just really wants it to be Shenmue 3 instead of Grand Theft Auto.

Excellent game. Papers Please isn't the longest or largest game, a single play through wont last more than a couple hours, but it is an entertaining game none the less. The premise is that you have been given the job of a Soviet-era border guard on the Berlin Wall. You must inspect people's passports and other papers and admit or deny them entrance into the country, however, there are enough other activities to keep you entertained.
The pacing is excellent in this game, once you get into it you don't want to stop playing. There is enough continuity and significant player choice to affect how you play the game, and a lot, if not most, of your actions have some sort of consequence. This creates an extremely effective draw to the game, as you feel like you are actually a border inspector.
Artistically, Papers Please is somewhat of a consistant piece of eye candy. The art style plays very well with the music and the setting of the game, and the way they characters talk, act, and interact, you feel very much like you are in a dystopian world.
tl;DR - Get Papers, Please if you like checking expiration dates, refusing visas, occasionally shooting at terrorists, and playing covert politics.

Many people like to argue about how "fun" a game is, whenever they rate it. It is, in my opinion, a foolish concept of game criticism, as the "level of fun" a game has is purely determined by subjectivity.
However, I can definitely say that most people out there wouldn't find Papers, Please fun. And my response to that is... that isn't the point.
I know not everyone on Steam is an adult, but if you grew up with video games, I'd certainly hope your tastes have matured. I have some conversations with 30-year-old men who still can't stop gushing about how great Super Mario Bros. is, even thought it's simply just a fun game, and nothing more. It has nothing to say about humanity, it has no high artistic value, but it is still a fun game.
But fun isn't what makes a game. I love Spec Ops: The Line, and that game made me feel like I had swallowed gravel.
Papers, Please hasn't made me feel like I've swallowed any gravel, but it has made me walk away with a new perspective on the world around me and about how video games, as a whole, can be narrated.
On the surface, Papers, Please is a relatively simple game in concept: you work for a border, check travelers' passes, and either let them enter Arstotzka, or deny then entry depending on their documentation. But it's how the game continues to expand on this gameplay and on its simple story, that things start to get more... interesting, as the game goes on.
The game, as many critics have complained, is indeed monotonous at times. I know checking the details of someone's passport to see if it matches their access pass doesn't appeal to many people, but if you ever wanted to simulate the life of a border inspector, this is a regular thing they would have to do. And it helps settle in that feeling of living in a lifeless country, where the only excitement you get it from the occasional denial of entry.
I get the same satisfaction from playing Papers, Please that I get from my day job: a box office cashier. Sure, my job isn't as detailed as the one in Papers, Please, but after processing hundreds of people to see the same movie over and over and over again, I always get some maniacal joy from telling spoiled families, "Sorry, this showing is sold out." Deep down, I grin menacingly, as I watch the passive mother turn sour, and ask if I'm joking. Like I'd bloody joke about a showing being sold out, you whiny b****.
Dark, intimate feelings aside, Papers, Please also offers a healthy dose of self-reflection on your own morality, by posing a lofty question: what would you do at your job if _____? Think of anything to fill in there, and the game throws it at you. Lovers being separated by the border, vigilantes seeking the murderer of their children, and people physically bribing you to let them in. It constantly makes you wonder where your loyality truly lies. Do you find morality in yourself? Perhaps in altruism? Or is it to the government, who gives you your daily pay, from which your family would not survive?
See, you can't just pass over every person carelessly, or accept every pass, because you'll receive citations. The first two of the day are just warnings, but after three starts pay dock. And you earn money from each person you process, so inspection is key. I've heard some friends complain about how hard the game is, but I only had my pay docked twice. I'm a very thorough inspector.
The design of the game's screens even enforces this feeling of isolation and dull monotony. Every day, you see your nonexistent family, read the paper, and walk to the same screen of work. However, the color palette isn't limited to just grey and brown. There's still some color variation in the people themselves, which is a unique design choice, as a man who appreciates aesthetic design.
I'm sure you can tell I really enjoyed Papers, Please. For a long time, I hailed The Last of Us as the best game of 2013... but now I'm beginning to have second doubts. I certainly wouldn't recommend this to anyone who wants to have "fun" (whatever that is), but I do recommend it to anyone who wants to play something totally new. This is a fine addition to my new favorites list, and I'm giving Papers, Please a well-deserved 10/10.

As one review succinctly put it, KeeperRL is "Dwarf Fortress for sane people." Let me expand on that.
Dwarf Fortress is a game I love to read about. You get such awesome stories from it, like
(one of the more succinct, well-presented ones).
I've always loved reading DF stories. But when I try playing it, even after sinking 20 hours into playing and working through tutorials, I'm still quite baffled by what to do, why things happen, or how to get things done. I've never had a functioning Fortress. I've never been able to figure out how to brew booze (which Dwarves need for life, like water). I think it has something to do with plants I have to grow, but I can't figure out what plants, how to grow them, etc etc.
Enter KeeperRL.
After 20 MINUTES into KeeperRL, I have a (rather haphazard, admittedly)

.
It works. It functions. The game prompted me on the very basics I'd need. If I wanted to deviate from that, it let me; it even lets me turn off those hints... but it didn't assume, from the get-go, that I wasn't a new player. It never assumed that I wanted to spend as much time researching this game as it takes to write a college paper just to be able to play the game on the most basic level.
That's important in such a complex game!
The Dwarf Fortress game cycles like this: Play, Die, Boggle, Google. Repeat.
But KeeperRL cycles in like this instead: Play, Die, LEARN. Repeat.
That makes it, even in this Alpha state, far more enjoyable than the glorious complexity of one of its main inspirations, Dwarf Fortress.
TL;DR, yes, KeeperRL is DF for sane people.

Exactly, precisely what it says on the tin.  Dungeon Keeper + a roguelike.
The DK mechanics are there: you'll be digging out areas and building familiar (for DK players) rooms in them.  You'll summon creatures, and set them about their tasks accordingly.  You'll build traps and doors, mine for iron, gold, and stone (each of which requires a storeroom), and construct equipment for your beasties.  But instead of the realtime 3D of DK and its ilk, you are presented an old-school roguelike UI with the sundry keypresses to boot.
As of AUGUST 23, 2015, the barebones mechanics are there.  All of the rooms work, monsters are summoned correctly, as go about their tasks and level up as you would expect -- even to the point where they will occasionally visit an equipment storeroom to grab any goodies that catch their eye.  The imp AI is especially good in prioritizing tasks you give them.  Grouping up critters and manually controlling them (the only real way to send out a raiding party/army) works fine as well.
Outside of the barebones -- which as I stated before, actually work well, and is the most important feature! -- there's not much to do.  You obstensible goal is to conquer 5 enemy outposts to win the game.  When you attack one of the enemy races, they will occasionally send their forces to attack your dungeon; conquering the race ends that particular threat.  Nonaligned bandits will also show up.  There's a few other "special" events and areas, but the game as it stands right now basically revolves around building the best dungeon you can, then controlling your forces out to overrun the five "good" races.  The building part is pretty fun; the conquering is kind of a chore.  (Of course, it could be said that this repetitive pattern of build-then-zerg is part of DK's DNA, not a failing of KeeperRL).
Should you buy the game now in its state as of this review's writing?  I'd say yes only if you acknowledge you're getting a game that has its core mechanics nicely in place, but not much to do with them.  Of course, you'll also be supporting the game's development into something bigger and better.  If you want a fleshed-out experience with lots of interesting decisions, I'd wait.
One thing that I do want note is that KeeperRL's DK design is nice and streamlined, and follows the original DK2 monster and item variety pretty closely (although it adds individual weapons and items for critters, which is nice).  I was uncomfortable with War for the Overworld's changes and additions to the DK roster, particularly in the way that many things were added simply for the sake of being cool rather than important to the game design.  KeeperRL right now is all meat, no-filler, 4/4 time and I hope the dev keeps it this way.

This game treads the line between puzzle and reflex-based gameplay. The gameplay is entirely skill, so any time you get sent back to the beginning of the level, it's on you. The difficulty ramps up a little bit slowly for my liking, but once you beat Story mode, you have the freedom to play some really tough levels. On the subject of Story mode, it may look a little short the first time you fire up the game. Make no mistake - it is, but that's not what you're here for. All of Story mode is essentially a tutorial for the Epilogue, Challenge mode, Encore mode, and speedrun mode.
As a speedrunner, I feel it necessary to comment a bit more on this game's speedrun mode. In this game, speedrun mode takes you through your choice of Story, Epilogue, or Encore, and you set the pace. You get to adjust what speed you play the game at on the fly. This means you can crank it up to 200% and blast through levels you're comfortable with, and perhaps even drop it down to 100% on levels you'd rather just get out of the way. The timer keeps going if you have to restart a level, after all. I'd like to believe this means no two speedruns will look the same, but I can't say for sure.
The art isn't flashy or mind-blowing, but it is absolutely fitting for what the game is. The music, on the other hand, is excellent in my opinion. It's definitely fitting, and while it's not crazy enough to be distracting, it's still good enough that I'd enjoy listening to it while not playing the game. In fact, getting to hear the next chapter's music felt like as much of a reward as actually getting good enough to beat each chapter.
Overall, I'd recommend this game, especially at a discount. As a side note, if you've played and enjoyed the game 140, I think you'd really enjoy Duet. If you enjoy Duet, you'd probably like 140 too.

I usually don't play games where you have a skill bar of 1-9 and pressing that button and this button. I am more of the black desert online/vindictus "HOLY ♥♥♥♥ DID I JUST STAB THAT GUY 10 TIMES AND SHOVE A SWORD INTO HIS SPINE IN HALF A SECOND" fast pace action MMO guy. BTW Black Desert Online sucks♥♥♥♥♥♥only play it for the PVE. Anyway. When I played this game it was a different experience the combat is a 1-9 bar but the mechanics are interesting dodging attacks by moving out of the way or sometimes getting behind cover to avoid a blast keeps me enticed to the gameplay and it's not just a button mashing fest. The skill animations and effects are gorgeous as well but at the end of my session my eyes have gone blind mainly because I play at full brightness right up my face. The combat is not just the same buttons again and again you have to add some buffs and skill timings for maximum effect nothing is old when it comes to combat. Especially the raids.
The class system is great and encourages you to delve into new professions/classes with an extra EXP bonus to help you level up faster. Being a tank is not just standing there and getting your♥♥♥♥♥♥slapped out of you, you are sometimes responsible for landing stuns or inflicting status effects to help out your party and sometimes the dungeon throws minions in boss fights and it's up to you to make sure those extra mobs don't kill your buddies. I only play as a tank for now since I love what I do.
The crafting is frustrating however but it's very rewarding if you craft a high quality item, it's a little minigame of chance and strategy to achieve the ultimate goal of completing the craft. It's not entirely RNG as you can guarantee a successful craft but the quality will not be High. High QUality is not mandatory but if you want some extra stats or to turn it in for extra EXP it's highly recommended to HQ.
The story is amazing although the voice acting is nothing special (sometimes cringy). It starts off with voice acting but unfortunately it just drops in the last half but some of the bosses you fight actually speak which is quite strange. After that in the new Heavensward expansion it will include much more constant voice acting and a lot of british accents.
The story is one of betrayal, triumph, and friendship and some lighthearted moments. The moogle sections are the most  entertaining in my opinion. There are some moments where you want to strangle an NPC for being an idiot and sometimes for acting like a♥♥♥♥♥♥and that shows alot about how the game immerses you into the story.
The other small mechanics like the screenshot system or the group pose system are amazing and makes the game alot more personal so you can take some amazing photos of your travels or with friends. The raid/dungeon finder is a great system as you can pair up with other people across servers. JP/ENG/Etc. However if you play as anything but a healer or tank prepare for long queue times because tanks are the least played class which is a shame. However if you do play as a tank queue times won't be a problem for you. The duty finder comes with a function called roulette where it finds a raid/dungeon/boss fight at random. So if a max lvl vet applies for the roulette they can be queued into the lowest level dungeon in the game but still get decent exp for it and the completion award is also scaled so it's still rewarding for vets. This roulette systems allows beginner content to still be populated so that beginners are not left alone while everyone else is queued into high level dungeons. Housing in this game can cost a bit for the furniture but the inital cost of buying the host can cost millions so it's suggested that you work hard for gil or join a guild that owns a guildhouse.
The armors and weapons in this game look absolutely amazing and a new expansion is coming around summer time that adds even more items and sometimes the community can design the items so if you love designing and sharing your creations this is a great game to share your ideas with. Right now there is a DPS Gear design contest 1/31/17. The world looks beautiful however the textures are not next gen and some parts can look ugly but this game has been out for a long time so yeah.
Overall I love this game and the gameplay is something that caught me by storm, I look foward to the new content that is being pushed and more adventures with moogles. kupo.

The game uses a somewhat unique system of having you choose a hand of cards. Out of those cards you can pick towers, units, or quick use defenses. This was a unique feature that not many games use currently. You could then upgrade the towers played once you deployed them to preset places.
While the game itself is somewhat enjoyable, the lack of information and lack of options during a map to place towers (your given preset placement options) that most tower defense and building games give is a deal breaker for me.
The further into the game i got the more I realized I was going to keep being limited by the maps forced placements, the RNG that is the ingame booster packs and the fact that I had to grind a few times to ugprade towers through their combining system is what makes me give this game do not recommend.
As for the lack of information. You could see how much damage a unit could do, you could upgrade units and towers to do more damage. What you could NOT do is see how much health was left on a minion going down the lanes. Yes they had a health bar but unless you counted each time a tower shot at them you could not tell how much HP was left on that unit. And when there is 10 units tightly packed sometimes the health bars overlapped or looked like they were merged so it was hard to tell where to bolster defenses.
Audio issues was one of the other deal breakers for me. If multiple of the same sound was played at the same time it would not play them all at once but instead multiply the sound level by however many units shot at once. IE if 5 units fired their gun at the same time you would hear the gunshots at 5x the volume instead of 5 gunshot sounds being heard at once.
Final issue is the fact that you had to spend an ingame currency, that you earned by beating a level without getting hurt, to upgrade your tower cards and unit cards unless you waited out a timer that is ever increasing based on upgrade level. I am told that the newest patch removed the timer and currency putting said timer to 1 second yet I had already spent a good amount and the patch did not refund me after said patch. Meaning I would have to restart my profile in order to recoup what i had spent. Which means playing chance with the ingame RNG of booster packs, match timers and builds etc.

I came to this game after seeing its trailer on a co-optional podcast. I thought, huh, it has been while since I had tried a tower defense game, especially one with some form of meta customisation so I thought I would give it a go. At first? Solid enough, I loved the initial carddraw mechanics and gradual raise in power as you went and combined more and more cards. Every hour you even got an increasingly large card reward with some "legendaries" which certainly helped.
But then I hit it, that wall. Suddenly upon reaching the first survial match I went from getting all 3 stars to getting 1 star. Without getting three stars I had no more gem income, without gem income I couldn't "buy" the card packs. So I was basically farming the survival match getting one new random mech piece (and one random pointless area attack thing). I couldnt reach the gems level, so I couldnt farm cards. The game had slowed down to a crawl in more ways then one however.
=== This section has now been fixed. Though, they should have included an additional way to earn when they removed the hourly rewards===
There is a combination system, which, at first seemed really good. Until you realise that each lvl 1 combine takes 1 min, then each level 2 combine takes 2 mins, and so on. It may not seem like much, but once you have a large number of cards from either booster packs or from the "hourly gifts" these add up. Dramatically. Add in the fact that the actual number of cards and towers is pitifully low- the game is definately a miss.
How could they fix it? For one, remove the combination time- this isn't a f2p mobile game anymore, the main use of gems should be purely pack pulls. Also add a "combine all" button so we can combine our whole inventory in one push. When I started to get cards it became stupidly tedious to combine.
=====
Secondly, the game gets stale rather quickly, I suggest adding new rarities to the towers. Everything else has four rarties but towers has none. They are all "common" and a single (useless) legendary factory that takes far FAR too long to repay itself. If there were different levels of rarity I could stack my favourite kinds of towers and hopefully get lucky with a better form as time goes on. In a similar vein, I would remove the gem reward for 3star, replace it with something else, and make a smaller repetitive gem reward for beating levels. This would open the door to further gem purchases such as metaupgrades and new booster pack varieites that would help the game stay fresher longer.
There are a lot of levels, a lot of broader playtime content, but the game far too quickly runs out of content on the tower front and it becomes more about combining and little more. Which is also the single most annoying part. If there were additional rarties of towers, then the choices would really start to matter. Do I want the legendary gattling tower that is stupidly OP and has a tiny number of upgrade slots right now, or the one that starts a little weaker but can be powered up. You could even add additional upgrades to rarer towers to make them more useful, but that isn't too important. In a similar vain, it would also be cool if max upgrades were not 100% decided based on level of tower- if I have a level 4 tower I may want to invest 4 points into one side of the upgrade tree and not touch the other- however the current system is simply linear and removes choice and even a lot of the value in upgrading cards.
Overall, it has promise. The fact they did remove the timers does make the game more "playable", so I must praise them for that. Who knows, they introduce another patch I may be able to change my review. Props for the change.

Interesting take on tower defense, inspired by Kingdom Rush (in my opinion)!
Developers brought nice arts and animations to put us into steampunk world there rebellion is going on.
Gameplay wise there are some familar features - Heroes (few of them) and less to more powerfull towers (4 types) to be unlocked with game progress. But also there are major additions to overall strategy and in every battle tactics:
- we're allowed to chose wich towers or heroes we want on every location - we pick them as cards to fill a limitied deck. Yes, towers and heroes and other stuff - cards here
- every hero, tower and robot part (see below) are subject to upgrades (simply by stacking cards of same level in separate interface we may craft a higher level card)
- winning round rewards differently depending on how good you performed - additional cards or crystals and crystals are very useful. E.g. to revive hero on the battlefield or remove wait timer on cards crafting. Crystal can also be used as currency in ingame store (no real money microtransactions included) to buy sets of cards.
- survival mode! It is very very praiseworthy mode to vary the game expierence.
- we can defend our base entrance with huge steam-powered robot as our last defence line; and we may upgrade that robot's systems - weapons, armor, power sources
- we can't sell towers that were once placed though
All that provides times more strategies to develope than usual wich is amazing.
Also, there is some sort of passive rewards for a time spent in game - cards with upgrades drops every hour and the longer you play the game the more rare cards you get. It is convinient for a strategy there we usually lose the count to hours, righ?
Back to arts - there are some aminated cut scenes telling us the story behind our rebellion, but so far I just learnt the type of next round boss from these. Judging on a lo-o-ong road through the world map, there are many battles to win before we get to the final of this steampunk story which is exciting for such a humble price!
Interfaces are nice and intuitive, tutorial is in place and it is both short and informative, so you won't be confused to learn how operate the game. Though being mobile port game kept some interface features, like drag'n'drop to operate the cards.
Soundtrack is simple, but pleasant in the way. Interface sounds are OK. Sounds in battle though might me annoying.
On the downside, I see no Steam achievements for the game yet. Also, first few rounds might make you think game is oversimpliefied, but wait for the round 8 and you'll be challenged over-the-top.
Fresh, challenging solid tower defence with good arts for such a moderate price - there is no doubt in my mind to recommend it to everyone who loves good old towerdefence genre.

Should have checked before purchase but it's just a port of mobile game.  I can't recommend it.  Now if you really want to play a mobile tower defence game on PC then then sure go ahead.
Cons:
* Time gated mechanics.  Upgrades and rewards are delayed by real time like in mobile games.  Can skip time delay by spending crystal resource which would typically be the purchased resource on mobile but doesn't seem to be option to purchase here.
* No options other than audio levels and fullscreen or windowed.  Can't change resolution or anything else.
* Tutorial popup windows tend to block actual information on screen preventing you from really understanding what's happening.
* Made for touch screen interface so incredibly simplistic and doesn't understand things like right clicking or other actions that are intuitive on PC for getting information or options.  Lots of drag and drop actions required.
Pros:
* Nice art style
* Seems to be a decent number of cards though haven't played enough to get a feel for how different or useful they all are.
* Quick and easy to jump right into playing
Overall I wouldn't recommend.  It's cheap but it's not really a game that's worth the time to me and I don't like games that disrespect my time by gating mechanics with timers.  I'm also one that doesn't like these mechanics on mobile so if you are OK or even like these mechanics on mobile then you may like the game more.

What can I say? I'm 40 hours into this game and I like it a lot, but I feel like there's some missed potential here too.  This is yet another gang themed sandbox action game, this time with you playing as an undercover cop in Hong Kong.  Like many games of this type, the missions are pretty repetative and the story is very action movie stock, but after that it's pretty DAMN good.
For one thing, the melee combat is much deeper and more strategic than pretty much any other sandbox game out there. At times the game almost feels more like an open world beat 'em up! You can get really lost in the many ways to fight, with countering being a cirtical skill to master.  At the same time, it never feels overwhelming.  You won't be counting frames or anything as convoluted as a modern fighting game requires.  If anything, the combat errs on the easy side.
But this is where the problems start.  Since it's an open world game, a lot of the other elements feel very shoehorned in to add content.  The street racing is very fidgety and annoying and you can still come in last despite doing a near perfect run of the course.  Side quests are numerous but they all boil down to the same few activities over and over (driving, defending or fighting).
There's a great game underneath all this, and I'm still having fun playing, but I think part of me just really wants it to be Shenmue 3 instead of Grand Theft Auto.

I've put a few thousand hours into this game across the Xbox 360, Xbox One, and the PC, so I could be just a wee bit biased.  However...
Borderlands 2 is one of the best FPS games I've played, followed closely by its predecessor, Borderlands.  Many FPS games lack a good measure of depth, and you spend most of your time empting round after round into generic bad guys, aliens, or what have you.  While Borderlands 2 also embraces those traits, it goes above and beyond the typical shooter.
The story and characters, while not milestones in game design and storytelling, are well done and enjoyable.  Some you will love, others you may despise, but in the end they all come together for a great overall experience.  The voice acting shines for the most part, which only helps to elevate these two elements.
The game's RPG elements give some added depth to the gameplay, allowing you to tweak and upgrade your character (and not just your weapons) in a myriad of ways.  Each character has three skill trees from which to pick your extra abilities and strengths.  While there are, as always with this type of game, certain skill combinations that will do better than others, the choice really is yours on how to build your character.  The Game of the Year edition comes with six (6) total characters, each with very unique playstyles, powers and skillsets.  You're sure to find something to your liking!
Loot is diverse and plentiful, spewed forth by a system that will be very familiar to folks who have played the Diablo franchise and similar games.  Loot is randomized and color coded depending on rarity, with the chances of finding two weapons with the same stats and configurations very unlikely.  This doesn't mean that every weapon or piece of equipment you get will be amazing, and poor loot rolls WILL have you pulling your hair out from time to time.
That being said, the game plays extremely well, and though there can be some repitition and boredom at max level, every playthrough is different and unique, and it's always a blast.  Even better with friends!
Best game ever?  Nah.  Still super enjoyable, five years later?  Yep.

Please read my full review at my personal blog:
Exerpts from review:
"Papers, Please is a funny little game in that it is so dedicated to its theme that the game actually does start to feel almost like a real job. You have to click and drag to open up documents, sort through papers, check dates, make sure the document was issued in a valid city, and so on. It's a lot of mundane work, and if you miss any little detail, then you have an omniscient boss who will print out a citation. I quickly came to anticipate the sound of a citation being printed with a Pavlovian anxiety after sending applicants through, even for the ones whose documents I thought I had thoroughly checked. You get two warnings before your omniscient boss starts docking your pay, which keeps constant pressure on you to try to be as close to perfect as possible. Paying for this game is almost like paying for a second job that you, yourself, don't get paid for. And it's kind of a crappy job, at that."
"But even though the job you're simulating is a crappy job, the game isn't crappy by any stretch of the imagination. The mechanics are fairly simple and straightforward. You just click and drag to shift papers around on a desk surface, and click to turn pages. If you notice something in one document that violates a rule or contradicts with another document, you press a button to highlight the two contradictory items and then click another button to question the immigrant about it. You then line the passport underneath an "approve" or "deny" stamp and then drag the documents back to the immigrant to either let them through or send them away. It reminds me of the interrogation segments of L.A. Noire distilled down into an entire game. Except that it manages to avoid the ridiculous tone shifts and somehow manages to create a more natural and engaging process with the possibility of genuine failure."
"You shift from following simple procedures, to following more complicated procedures, to eventually making judgement calls and moral decisions. It's all very smoothly integrated and creates a growing escalation of tension and stakes as you have to balance your own individual budget with the demands of your government, the bribes of a mysterious insurrection organization, and the requests of the people who you are supposedly trying to serve. As you're playing this very simple, small role of checking passports at an immigration checkpoint, an elaborate story of war and political tension slowly reveals itself and escalates around you."
My only complaint is that it could maybe use a better tutorial, as the interface does take a little bit of getting used to. Other than that, this is an outstanding game that I highly recommend.

Do you like resource management type games? Do you like simulation type games? Do you like science fiction? If you answered yes to two of the previous questions you should check out Spacebase DF-9. Even though this is an Early Access Game there is still enough playability and fun in it to occupy hours of your life.
Basically you build a space station or as the name suggests a Spacebase. You do this by laying out rooms and zoning them for specific tasks. At first you'll need an airlock and a life support system so that your virtual Spacebase residents can breath. As you play, you'll discover that you need to expand, and that takes resources. You'll need to build more rooms and different types of zones to make your Spacebase function. Things like refineries, sleeping quarters and pubs. Yes, they have pubs in space.
To add to the gameplay each of your Spacebase residents has his or her special skill set. You need to assign them tasks based on their individual skills or train them in new ones, if you wish. As they get better at their tasks the station starts to hum along nicely. As you progress, you'll discover that the natives get restless and you'll need to attend to their complaints and unhappiness by building new rooms or maybe mixing up their work routine.
All that is enough to keep you busy, but there is more. Every now and again a spaceship will pass by. They can be friendly folk and join your Spacebase or they can be your worst day in space. Sometimes you can weasel your way out of sticky situations but eventually something is going to rain on your Spacebase. You'll need to prepare for that eventuality and defend your Spacebase if you want to hold onto it.
This is an Early Access Game and it’s in Alpha 4b as of this writing. Even so, there is plenty of fun to be had with this game. Double Fine Productions, the developer, is actively releasing updates. They are shooting for updates on a monthly basis and that’s good.
Now I don’t want to mislead you. I’m having a ton of fun with this game, but it is and Early Access Game and it’s still in Alpha. That means it’s not for everyone. The game isn’t finished. It’s not even close to finished. It’s Alpha. Don’t buy this game expecting a polished game. Even if you have Beta tested before, keep in mind that this is pre-beta.
That said, this game promises to be something extremely fun to play. If you want to be in on the ground floor and watch, as well as give feedback, as the game develops then you should definitely pick up a copy of Spacebase DF-9. It’s okay, the waters warm, jump in. You will have fun.

I do not like this game.
Maybe it's a matter of expectation, I expected to find a skill based rhythm game/endless runner puzzle hybrid, what I found was a poorly executed frustration engine.
Visuals: Dull. I don't dislike minimalist styles, and it's not BAD looking, but when you only have two spheres and 3 types of rectangle in your game, I would expect them to look at least a little bit interesting. Not to mention how the constant blur effect makes it surprisingly difficult to see what's going on sometimes, especially with spinning blocks. The visuals are actually detrimental to the gameplay. The pulsing background effects are cool.
Gameplay: Memorize sequences of left and right presses. There is some skill involved, but it's basically just remembering how long to push left or right for various combinations of blocks. It's very unrewarding. It is an interesting rotating concept, but it doesn't deliver. Every time you mess up you have to restart the level. Levels are short and the reset takes only a second so it's not a big deal, but it's not fun. That is how I would describe the gameplay here: not fun.
It has a minimalist narrative which is pretty cool.
Audio: This game actually has a great soundtrack, I really like the background music and when it gets going it starts to tie the game together and make it almost enjoyable. The in game sounds are lackluster. The "narration" is a nice touch.
In short: It's not terrible, not the worst thing you can buy for sure. If you just want to pay £2 to kill half an hour then it's not bad, but I wish it had been so much more. It could have been with just a little bit more time/effort/money.

Not bad for a fiver. Basically a slimmed-down Caesar 3, with the population mangement taken out. Seems to have around 3-4 hours of content in the campaign, but there's a sandbox mode if you just want to sit building cities.
You build houses and then provide goods and amenities to upgrade those houses, producing more tax income and so allowing you to build more stuff. There's an economic chain of production with a dozen or more goods - about as complex as you'd get from a Settlers game, really. Goods can be made for export, or used to support your population's gradual evolution from bottom-tier slave workers to high-end villa dwellers.
One EXTREMELY annoying feature is the fires, which are dealt with by spam-clocking on the burning buildings. Whoever thought this would make a cool feature needs to go and seriously think about their lifestyle choices, because it's just annoying; I get the idea of fires to force you to build a fire brigade, but for God's sake just let them automatically tackle fires rather than introducing this mobile-friendly tap-sim.
All in all, it's pretty good for the price, but since you can probably get Caesar 3 or 4 for a couple of quid more, you're likely better off going for those.

Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn has a spot in my gaming heart. I ventured into Eorzea during its first appearance as patch 1.0. I won't deny how awful the game felt during that time. It felt barren and I truly had no idea what was happening. Square decided to take the game down and guarenteed a promising return - they did so with patch 2.0. The game came back completely revamped with nothing but positive improvements. I returned at the start of patch 2.0 and played for a good six months before I broke off to play..., -sigh- World of Warcraft again. I enjoyed the new changes, the classes had their own unique abilities and the main story kept you interested. I returned once again in 2016 and once more when I purchased the game for my Steam account. This time around I was more unhappy with where my journey in Eorzea ended.
Pros:
- Engaging story to follow and just the right amount of side quests to keep you busy in other zones and other classes to level.
- Easy learning curve - very new player friendly with the active help.
- Always something to do and plenty of classes/jobs to level up.
- One character is all you need to play everything in this game.
- The party finder is one of the best I've utilized in every MMO I've played.
- You get your moneys worth when it comes to the amount of content released per game.
- Being a part of a Free Company (Guild) actually provides useful benefits with buffs/housing.
- Plenty of jobs to level and crafting jobs to keep you going if you ever need to change up from your primary build.
- Fantastic UI customization built in. You can move practically everything, disable what you don't want to see and even change the size. No need for UI addons for this game!
- Some of the best music you can hear in an MMO. I never get tired of hearing Shiva's theme.
Cons:
- Patch downloading - I want to really hit this hard on a personal level, because before patch 3.0 there was never an issue getting the game patched up and running. I know people have said their say on the discussion section on how you can get past this, but I should never have to alter my network settings or download a VPN to get a game patched up.
- Because I used a VPN to get the patch I continue to receive the error i2501 when I try to input any payment to activate a subscription or even buy items from the Mog Station. I've submitted multiple tickets and had three replies now stating my issue has been submitted to someone higher in the customer service chain. To this day I still cannot activate a subscription.
- During dungeons cutscenes occur, and there are times when you just want to get going in a dungeon you will have some new players wanting to view the scenes. I don't hold the new players accountable for wanting to watch these scenes, I just wish they didn't happen before and during the group play. I know in Heavensward they minimized the amount of scenes.
- Because of the amount of jobs you can level up, running old content over countless times becomes tedious and extremely repetitive, I'd suggest not trying to level everything up at once to avoid this. I did it my second time through and I got everything to level 30 and became burnt out.
- Battles do feel slower in regards to the global cooldown of a default 2.5 seconds. Early in the game it will make fights feel longer than they need to be.
- Inventory space needs to be larger. This is a con for now, but it was said when Stormblood arrives we will see an increase for our inventory.
- Converting items into materia. I really dislike the approach to this mechanic, because you need to have a spiritbound with the item before you can even think about turning it into a useful piece of materia. Creating a bond with a piece of equipment just feels weird and pointless. If I happen to obtain a piece of gear I don't need, I'd rather just convert it instantly.
- The approach to sell your items on the market is tedious. You use two retainer NPCs (or more if you bought more with real money) who will hold up to 12 (I believe it is 12) items in the market for you to sell. I think a general auction house such as something on WoW would suffice. Why make something that just lists your items a pain?
There are more pros and cons floating in my mind, but that is just bringing it down to detailed knitpicks. I loved this game a lot, it was just unfortunate how it has ended for me. I wanted to keep playing, but their entire account setup is completely frustrating and more work than it needs to be. However, I will continue to recommend this game as it continues to grow and change. Red Mage job is coming and who wouldn't be excited about that?
