When people get offended by something, one of more common defenses is that the offended party "can't take a joke". What this tends to overlook is that the joke needs to be funny in the first place. Bird Assassin is obviously supposed to be a joke but goes over about as well as taking your vegan roommate to KFC. And lacking that humor, there's not much else to do but mindlessly blast birds until you start to question the choices that got you here.
The setup is that you're a pot-bellied noodle-legged trailer-trash hunter out with your pappy when an ostrich of all ♥♥♥♥ing things caps pappy with a revolver. Mourning over the gushing neck stump, you vow revenge against all birds because I guess it's not just the enormous flightless ones that are psychotic. So begins a ten-level quest to rid the skies of murderous mallards, terrifying turkeys, and deadly doves with an arsenal of quality Wal-mart armaments. And don't worry, he brings all the meat home after each killing spree.
What this amounts to is a simple platformer with a whole lotta shootin' and not a whole lot else. Each of those ten levels has you strolling to the right as flocks of murderbirds flap in to dive-bomb and peck you to oblivion. They come in waves as you advance so real quick you'll learn to creep forward and blast groups at a time. In the meantime you have to hop over bear traps and sticker bushes, sometimes using platforms scattered about, and sometimes snagging coins for more cash and mushrooms to regain health. Most levels just end, but a few have a short chase scene and three have a boss fight. The same one. All three times.
Between levels you can spend your bucks on new weapons, armor, and upgrades like faster shooting and slower enemies. As long as you're not blindly running through levels your upgrades are going to far outstrip your enemies, though. You can have the ultimate weapon, a Terminator 2-style minigun, just after the midpoint of the game. And at that point you're really just shuffling a few steps at a time and sweeping the screen, over and over and over again. It's great if you love mindless slaughter or the sound of bird carcasses slapping the earth, but don't expect any sort of challenge whatsoever.
Actually that's a lie, some of the braindead design choices might challenge you a bit. Bird corpses persist on the ground for quite a few seconds, and when they pile up they can completely obscure ground hazards that do loads of damage. There's also some dodgy detection on the platforms that can get you stuck when trying to hop off or fail to connect when you hop up. And the one boss (repeated three times) only has three attacks that it doesn't even use all of in any given encounter. So I suppose you might not be challenged by difficulty (there are no difficulty levels either), but you may be challenged to care after 20 minutes.
That's not so bad though, because the game only lasts 30 minutes. 30 minutes gets you all ten stages beaten and all upgrades unlocked. There are no extra modes or higher difficulties or anything. You get half an hour of mindlessly shooting birds and that's it. I know sometimes we need a good time-waster between bigger games (that's why I play hidden object games!) but there needs to be a bare minimum of content and care found within. The content definitely isn't here, and I'm sorry but watching a dopey redneck splatter hundreds of birds isn't real funny to me. Maybe it is to you, and maybe 30 minutes of it is enough, but honestly I don't really see how.

I must congratulate Lucas Pope for being able to turn a mundane task into an entertaining experience. Never in my life I would have guessed I'd someday enjoy to examine passports and permits.
However, I am probably one of the few people not able to see a deeper message to this game. Ok yeah, dictatorship sucks, but we all know that. It doesn't really give you another point of view in the matter. Also, I did not feel some sort of conflict. If I deny someone, so what? There's one point in the game where you know that if you deny the woman ahead of you, she will be killed in her country. That's the only time you may feel a dilemma. I never thought I'd say that and I'm really sorry to do so, but the problem here is the graphics. There's just a bunch of pixels in front of me, not displaying any emotion whatsoever. I don't know what's wrong with me since everyone seem to be able to feel empathy toward those characters, but I really didn't care about her. It was a spoiled opportunity to make me infringe the strict rules of my country.
Also, the other side of the dilemma is supposed to be your family. If you don't do well your job, like if you accept someone that you shouldn't, you won't provide enough money to make them survive. This would be great if I felt attachment toward my family. The thing is that the only time you "see" your family is between two days, on a static screen that displays "Mother-in-law", "Uncle", "Wife" and "Son". Yeah, you don't get to see them, and you don't even know their name. So what if "Uncle" die? Will I grieve?
As much as I love minimalism and believe graphics are not what make a game good, this game really would have benefit from better aesthetics. Regarding its emotional impact and its political statements, there is room to improvement.
In the end, I still recommend it because I love it very much as a GAME; sadly, it will not be more than that for me.

I saw this game a few times on my "recommended for you" list on both steam and humblebundle. I watched the original trailer but was not really impressed. (the original trailer shows a completed factory, not how to actually get to that point.) But one day I noticed that it had a 98% positive rating on steam... with human nature making it more likely to take the time to write bad reviews instead of good ones, I wondered how that was even possible. Then after watching a youtube video on a different game, autoplay queued up a factorio "let's play" video that I watched. I was hooked.
Factorio is a base building game. You start with nothing but a hand axe and manually build up to the automated factory you see in the trailer. Of course, the true intent is to build your factory through automation, not by hand. Eventually you will build a rocket which will take you off the planet you crash landed on.
Factorio is deep. Factorio is complex. Factorio will keep you sitting in front of your computer until the early morning hours just to get "5 minutes more." Factorio has a steep learning curve, but it is not un-surmountable. There are plenty of tutorial and let's play videos for it, an online beginners guilde, active forum, and wiki. And best of all, you can ignore all the advice and just build it the way you want to build it.
Now that I own it and have played it, I know why the game has such an overwhelmingly positive review feed back... Factorio is fun, it is engaging, and it is well polished. The only reason why it is still early access is because the devs want to add even more to it before a full release. It is very stable and has a lot of existing content. (including multi-player.)
TL/DR...  Just buy it now.  not convinced? Watch a few videos... play the Demo... then buy it.
UPDATE: 11 months later... Factorio is still a great game. I have over 850 hours playing it now. I still love it. It is still in Early Access, but the devs are still adding more content to the game and enhancing the graphics and UI. Well worth the money you pay for it.

Have you ever wanted to destroy human-kind with a deadly virus? well, now you can!
That cheesy start line aside, Plague Inc: Evolved is by far an addicting game. If you enjoyed the flash game Pandemic then I have no doubt in my mind that you will love this addicting little number. Now, If you're not familiar with the game, you basically choose a disease and plot to infect humanity with various transmissions and abilities.
It takes something so tragic and to be quite frank, utterly horrible disasters and makes it enjoyable to figure out your plagues strength and weaknesses and in effect destroy the world as quickly as possible without being cured. All that being said, it does teach how dangerous and quickly one tiny little bug can spread if gone undetected or if you go for the quick kill route, even dead bodies can be infectious which is where the danger really amplifies.
I hate to drop the educational word as it tends to make games lose their appeal to some, but it really is without you even noticing. Having to tailor make each decision of evolving certain things to make it more lethal, infectious, to be harder to cure or to be hardier in cold environments etc. It gives you a sense of how they work as well as perhaps opening a different pathway for said virus. Given it may not be 100% accurate, it's still a good perception of it.
Within the main game you begin playing as the starter bug; bacteria. The most common thing and the easier one to beat to then unlock more complex virus's, and then in the next selection, extra add on's such as a start game bonus of DNA points and such. You can make it to suit your own play-style once you learn how the game works, which makes it so much more appealing.
Now, from a completely different viewpoint, it can be seen that you're commanding these viruses to in simple, destroy everything. Which in itself is a fun stress reliever.
With the recent update of it being added to Steam Workshop, you are able to make some amazing scenarios as well as download some incredibly done ones from other people, just that expands the game so, so much.
Not to repeat myself, but it does again add onto my constant point of how Steam Greenlight brings out a lot of talent that may generally get overlooked. With most of these games, the active development is incredible, so much work goes into keeping these games updated and bug free, especially this one. Also getting involved in making Christmas events are a nice sign of things to come for catered game modes and what not for different life events, I for one, love that. It gives the game character in the sense that it's basically involved in current events.
To conclude, this is an amazing game that I would recommend wholeheartedly, it's one that keeps on giving and deserves all the support possible.

Spacebase DF-9 is a "Space Station Simulator" from the people at Double Fine. The game starts out on a map screen letting you pick the best spot for your Seed Pod and every pixel has a different variable ranging from, Stellar Density, Warpgate Proximity, Threat Factor and Magnetic Interferance and all change how you game will play out. Once you have your Seed placed you will go into the space base part where you will have 3 crew and 2000 matter (Currency) to start out with, but be warned as your crew only have a limited ammount of time until there oxygen runs out so you have to be quick building a simple foundation and a good amount of oxygen genorators. Now getting more crew is as simple as waiting for a ship to come by but be warned as it could be pirates who will latch onto your ship and try to kill your crew one by one unless you have a good defence, but it could be just people wanting to be crew of your station. Mining is also a main thing that you have to be checking as if you don't mine you will slowly runout of matter and have no more.
Your crew has needs such as; sleep, food and morale if any of these get low it can cause them to do their job slower, sleep longer of worse die so you do have to farm and have food replicaotrs to counter act this. Apart from the pirates being a thret  meteors can also hit the station and kill your crew so you have to be on the ball if you have a large station and have emergancy alert systems in place to get your crew out of danger.
Now This game does look good but on slower machines can be slow so always check for the latest drivers and be sure that you can run this before buying, as for anything.

My first experience with this game involved scrambling to build an airlock and life support structure so my poor crew could breathe that sweet sweet air before asphyxiation ended their greatest adventure.  Sadly I was too late and my workers did not understand the importance of building that suit locker which would allow the air lock to operate properly.  So I watched as my worker scrambled to build the suit locker that would save his life only to be a few seconds too late.  He and the rest of my crew succumbed to the cruelest of fates; I can only hope it was painless.  Armed with new experience and a greater understanding of the fragility of life in space I took another bold step forward and my second base was born.  Things went much better for much longer.  The basics were established with ease and in a very timely fashion.  Mining operations were going smoothly and I was about to establish a pub for recreation and relaxation.  My builder was ordered to remove some interior walls in order to expand a room and it was hoped that he would finish the exterior walls first (you know the ones keeping the cold empty death void that is space outside of my lovely base.)  Alas this was not to be and as the second crew member was pulled into the blackness of both death and the cosmos I knew I had learned another valuable lesson in the fragility of life in space.
With just these few experiences I must say that Spacebase DF-9 has a lot to offer even as an early release.  It is a little rough around the edges and your workers will tend to aggravate you with poor decision making, but stick with it and you will be proud of your accomplishments in time.  Failure and loss is a part of this game so don’t be too frustrated when you need to start over from scratch.  If you enjoy building and management games you should at least give this a shot.

For a free game, this is a pretty interesting time killer. Once you get the hang of the basic controls, you can rack up money fairly quickly.
Tips
-Always buy the local map when you can, it will save you a lot of time.
-Start with the cargo ship, because transporting cargo is a steady way to make money. When you have some extra money, buy the cargo expansion and get an extra 15 slots for cargo, or chip away at the debt at the bank.
-A quick way to gain money is to find missions for cargo that are within 4-5 jumps. Take a look 1-2 jumps ahead to see what item will give you the most profit per unit, fill up on that, and go to that station, then repeat until you reach your destination.
-Cargo transports are like buying low and selling high, but you get the cargo for free, so the profit is WAY higher.
-How I started was with the cargo ship, and when I had about 500k extra, I bought another cargo ship like the one I started with. I got about 3-4 of them, then bought a small fighter to add to the group, they fight automatically.
-Open map with M, select a place to go to, but make sure ALL your ships have enough fuel to make it, you get refills by stopping at a planet.
-Use J to set all your ships to go to that place, they'll keep going until they get to the zone, but once you get there, make sure to hit L, or your ship will drift endlessly until you turn around to stop the momentum, or give it the land command with L.

Just recently decided to change to the steam version so my play time is more like 60+ hours. Been playing this for the past year or so, and from the start was my new favourite MMO, which was previously WoW.
The main thing I like is the ability to change my character's class (Arcanist is my main, well technically Summoner) to another one, just by changing my main weapon. The questing is like any other MMO, can be tedious and repetitive at times, but with other activates like the Manderville Gold Saucer and FATEs, you can waste a couple of enjoyable hours.
The profession system in the game is great and easy to use, once you understand that to change to and use the profession, you will need to equip the needed item in your main hand slot i.e. for Mining you would equipped a pickaxe in your main hand.
Other little things that I have found to be quite well done are the Inventory and Armoury Chest that just helps have a clean inventory (well for me anyway :D). It basically being 2 separate inventory systems one to store junk and resources (I Think armour and weapons will go in here as well if the AC is full), and the Armoury Chest to store character armour and weapons etc...
Just going to end it here as for a game this size there will always be loads to talk about and do, and I'm too lazy to write all that down. Above though are just some of my favourite things that I thought of when writing this up. If you're into MMO's, this is Definitely a MMO I would recommend, and if you are not too sure about subscription games at least try the trial and go from there. An immersive look at the life of a customs agent working for a totalitarian regime, though with only enough content for one look.

Pros: Decision points in the game mesh well with the overarching mechanics to drive home the sensation of being an overworked, underpaid, and overall terrified agent.  Writing has a good mix of humor and humanity.  Multiple endings based on performance and choices.
Cons: The actual gameplay gets stale after a while.  Decision trees do not change unless you follow previously unexplored branches (you'll get the same decision points on the same days).  Most of the memorable moments of the game come from "gotcha" experiences that don't hold nearly as much gravitas after the first playthrough.
Would Recommend To: Gamers looking for a thought provoking or immersive experience who can tolerate some samey gameplay.  People looking for about 2-4 hours of a unique gameplay experience.

Supergiant Games delivers again with Transistor, a beautiful and incredibly well-desinged game with a fantastic combat system, which is an interesting twist on both turn-based combat and action RPG's.
Combat is based around the Transistor, or, more accurately, the abilities that the player applies to the weapon. Abilities can be placed into three categories on the Transistor (active, upgrade and passive), with each ability giving a different attack or applying an effect to said attacks, or the player. The number of abilities that can be applied is limited by Memory, which is upgraded as the player levels up.
Active commands are used as attacks: initializing an active command will apply that command's effec to the environment or the enemies. Certain commands, like Help(), do not directly damage enemies; this command in particular summons two allies to the field, helpful if the player is being swarmed by a large number of enemies. Others, like Crash(), are attacks that have attached effects; Crash() in particular afflicts enemies with the Crashed effect, preventing them from moving and attacking as well as making them more vulnerable to attacks for three to four seconds. If the player's health hits zero, the active command taking up the most memory, a stat affected by applied upgrade commands, will "Overload" and become unusable until the player uses a certain number of save points.
Upgrade commands are commands placed in active command upgrade slots. The player begins with one, then gains more as they level up. These commands do not have direct effect on the field or the enemies: instead, they apply a special effect to the command they are attached to. For example, if Jaunt() is applied to any active command, that command may be used instantly without it's bootup animation, which may take one or two seconds, and can be used while Turn() is still charging; more on that later.
Passive commands are commands placed in passive slots. Like upgrade commands, the player begins with one. These commands effects apply to everything, and they cannot be de-equipped by Overloading, like active or upgrade commands. This is were some commands are at their best, and it is often a difficult choice whether to make a command an upgrade or a passive.
Turn() is Transistor's interesting twist on turn-based combat; it is a default function present from the beginning that allows the player to stop time, plan out a series of movements and attacks, then enact them with a push of a button. While some commands have effects that only act on a target for two or three seconds, Turn() makes this small amount of time irrelevent, allowing players to strike for maximum effectivity and damage. However, once used, Turn() needs up to ten seconds to recharge: while Turn() is recharging, any function without Jaunt() in an upgrade slot will not work, making the enacting of Turn() a necessary risk. This forces a player to strategize and prioritize targets rather than striking out at random.
My personal combination of active commands is Crash(), with Jaunt() applied as an upgrade, Get(), Void() and Cull(). With these four commands utilized in Turn() (Get(), Void(), Void(), Void(), Crash(), Cull()) I can consistently get damage that numbers into the two-thousands. However, with things like the raised difficulty of New Game mode and the added difficulty of Limiters added in, as well as the risk of commands overloading, a player can find themselves constantly shifting and attempting to compensate by completly remixing their commands and styles of play.
Finally, one of the largest reasons for shifting around commands into different positions: every function that you possess... Was once a person. Their stories are still attached and can be unlocked, but each function must spend a certain amount of time in each of the three slots before the story is available for reading. This constantly enocurages the player to return, to change their command deck, in order to find out the stories of these people, and how they came to be a part of the Transistor.
Basically, get this game. You won't regret it.
Cheers!
-Camolot

This is a sale target in my mind. It gets a recommend because it's worth picking up at some point, as the base gameplay has enough of an alteration in the top-down shooter genre to be worth something. The fact that your core can be attacked by yourself and the fact that enemies take you down in one hit, that's a nice change of pace for the genre, and does make it stand out a bit. The animation and art is great, even with characters like PewdiePie making an apperance. But where the game majorly suffers is variety: it's the same thing very, very quickly, and doesn't have the lasting power to keep your entertained over a long haul. The unlocks do small things to help, but enemy and arena variety would have gone a long way to help the game out: and it fails at it. And it doesn't help that the online play is ancient: this is 2016 and you're asking for IP host/join in game, with Steam as your base platform? Not a good move. In the end, I'd wait for a sale regardless, as while I had fun, I can't say that you're going to get your moneys worth at this current price, but eventually, you will.

Now let me say, it dosen't really do THAT much in inovation, but the whole package as a beat 'em up, open-world, chinese crime-thriller with an excellent, well-crafted, atmospheric world creates an excellent game to either loose yourself in or blast through it like any other game.
Either way, it does it's job to appeal to both parties equally, in my opinion, and as long as you like some of the things I mentioned earlier, you're in for a good time.
Graphically the game holds up really well, but that should also kinda be excpected with the Definitive Edition.
The combat is fantastic, just the right amount of weight and control to create an awesome fighting system.
The story is fantastic, brutal, and quite real, at the same time being one of those classic brutal crime-thrillers. Great cast of memorable characters, good dialogue, and a good flow that make you really care and immerse yourself in the situations.
The world is probably my favourite thing about this game. Atmospheric, big, and full of fun stuff to do on the side. Wanna talk immersive worlds? This is one of the best.
Some things I don't like that much:
It is a little, and sometimes, very dated in some areas, but that is mostly small annoyances, and those vary depening on how forgiving you are
Physics can be very clunky sometimes and controls can sometimes get a little tedious.
Free-running is very limited, though it works, it's still pretty rough.
Glitches, but mostly fun ones so that's ok with me.
Still can't recommend this game enough though.

While I can see this game tries something interesting in letting you be an immigration inspector. Denying or accepting the people who wants to come in or through the country, it was a really horrible experience playing it, to the point where I won't finish it.
The good thing is that it tries something different, and the idea of deciding who gets in or out depending on their information is fun. However it is way too punishing, as you live the life of a guy, who suffers an existence worse than slavery. When you are a slave all you do is sleep, eat, and work. Here you get to work and sleep, but can't be sure if you get to eat. So a positive point, I guess, it makes it more understandable why free people in ancient Greece and Rome would sell themselves into slavery. -.- At least then they got to eat in exchange for the work they did.
"You must decide who can enter Arstotzka and who will be turned away or arrested." I had expected that meant you got to decide, and that you would be judged based on what the people might do once in the country. But no. Accompanying you in the booth is an all knowing entity, that can instantly tell if you made a mistake. If the passport had an invalid issuing city, if the names didn't match, if it was expired, if the picture was wrong. Making your existence pointless. If they are able to instantly tell if I denied or accepted the wrong person, why the ♥♥♥♥ have an immigration inspector? Clearly the automated system works perfectly. I refuse to believe that in a low technologically advanced country, that they would be able to instantly know every mistake every single inspector makes.
And because of this all knowing system, it doesn't become about choosing who to let in or out, since you get fined every time you don't follow protocol to the letter, or make a mistake. (Again if they can see every single slip up, what is the point of the job? It is not just a crap job, it is an utterly pointless one.) It becomes about working as fast as possible to check the information, opening up stupid info, and since you get paid based on the number of people you process you often have to gamble if looking something up simply takes too long with the small space you have to work with.
I do think this game could be enjoyable, if the difficulty could be turned down a bit. So all the information you had to sort through could be on the screen at once, and you didn't have to look up or remember the things that were in the rule book about the different countries all the time, or if the time each day was longer, so you could get more people through.
As it is, I would only recommend it to people that want to play games that feel more punishing than difficult. Or those that just want a game that tries something interesting, even if not enjoyable.

...lots of complicated scoring, sudden wins, and characters I don't recognize.
The video is pretty honest. What you see is what you get: authentic reach mahjong, slightly translated, rulebook not included. The game does a good job of letting you know what your options are at any given time. Even if you're only acquainted with the rules, you can just click on tiles until one of the characters (hopefully yours) starts making happy noises. The process is cathartic in a solitaire type of way, but do this enough and maybe you'll even start to figure out what's going on. You do need to win a few times to unlock any new characters beyond the starting four, so it'll be a while before you meet everyone in the game.
The sound design is worth praising. The music is actually pretty good, the tiles make various satisfying clacks, and the voice acting isn't too annoyingly prominent.
There's no story whatsoever, so if you're looking for a visual novel, keep looking. The "translation" is an insult to the word, to be honest. The English that is there doesn't appear to have come from someone fluent, if it came from a person at all. None of the girls' quips are translated, but I can assure you that you aren't missing much.
The graphics are... well, redundant to comment on. The static nature of the game makes those screenshots above pretty representative of the actual game. It does have the option to run at 1080p, that's not always a given with these Japanese doujinsoft. The game is very responsive, there isn't any downtime while playing it on the default (quick) setting. There are a few spots where the game expects you to click and drag (to scroll or look around), which gives the impression it's friendly to touch screens.
So this game has a lot left to be desired, but it's worth your attention if you are interested in 2D girls, Japanese, and (
and) reach mahjong. I give it eight bucks out of fifteen.

Note: This review is about the changes in "Definitive Edition", not about the game itself.
So what is the difference between the original version and definitive edition? Not much, it's just patched original Sleeping Dogs with full DLC and some improvements to the graphic that are either insignificant or unimportant.
I can play the original version at max setting with solid fps, but I have to play this one on medium because the fps are too unstable (FYI, my spec is more or less the same as recommended), I also have a problem with ingame screen resolution, it causes me to have some kind of slightly visible letterbox appears at times, which is annoying because original version didn't have it.
But as I said, the changes to graphic are insignificant. World density is the only improvement that worth mentioning, which makes the world more living by adding more cars, people on streets, NPC variations (less clones),... but this change can be achieved by a free patch, not a patch being sold. Also, still no Steam Cloud, wtf dev? Seriously?
In short, Sleeping Dogs is an amazing game, but this Definitive Edition is a quick cash grab, patched games being sold at high price. Don't buy it if you already owned the original version, it's not worth it.
For people with spec below recommended: Don't buy it because the spec given by the dev is inaccurate, you can play it on low smoothly, but it will look worse and less stable than the original version on medium. It seems the game doesn't use up all the CPU power, but depends mostly on GPU power, which means you need a strong GPU to play this game on high smoothly.

Plague is one of those rare games that you play, you enjoy and have fun with for funs sakes.  You get to be an evil infection, with the freedom to grow and mutate with one goal in mind; Destroy the world!  It's addictive fun, but after hours of playing the game, you eventually find yourself looking back and coming to a harsh reality.  This game depicts the spread of disease, and just how slow, or fast it can get out of control.  It's a harsh reality check to makes you look at the world differently, and glad that real life mutations in bugs is generally a random thing.  But it also puts into context just how quickly our planet can face a real life epidemic with no way of stoping it in time.
Outside of this reality driven horror your mind goes through, the game is engaging, exciting and extremly enjoyable.  In itself, the game has a simple setup when it comes to graphics, as it's basically a map of the world and prooves that gameplay makes the game, not the graphics.  Choose your disease, mutate how you want, start in any country and see how you fair against humanity.  Unlock deadlier diseases, and engage in scenarios, or make your own.  The game has a lot of potential, espeicall with the addition of the scenario creator.  This game can easily bring you hours of enjoyment.

This is one of those simple walking simulators that consist of walking around looking for notes to unveil a story. I'm usually not a fan of this type of game, because most of the times the story is either cryptic/impenetrable or just plain uninteresting. This is NOT the case, though. Fingerbones' story, however simple, is compelling, dark, and shocking. Even though there is margin for different interpretations, the core of the plot is pretty clear, and it doesn't feel cryptic or cheap.
Gameplay-wise, there's only walking around and finding notes. The notes contain bits of the story, as well as hints for passwords which allow you to access different areas and unfold the story further.
A good point is that it's a very short game (around 30 minutes), so if you're looking to spend a few minutes uncovering a dark story, I highly recommend playing this. Reading the discussion session afterwards might help you understand a bit better what happened, and to see other people's "theories".
If you're interested in the story, but doesn't care to actually play the game, you might want to consider watching a "Let's Play" video on YouTube. You won't miss a lot.

While I can see this game tries something interesting in letting you be an immigration inspector. Denying or accepting the people who wants to come in or through the country, it was a really horrible experience playing it, to the point where I won't finish it.
The good thing is that it tries something different, and the idea of deciding who gets in or out depending on their information is fun. However it is way too punishing, as you live the life of a guy, who suffers an existence worse than slavery. When you are a slave all you do is sleep, eat, and work. Here you get to work and sleep, but can't be sure if you get to eat. So a positive point, I guess, it makes it more understandable why free people in ancient Greece and Rome would sell themselves into slavery. -.- At least then they got to eat in exchange for the work they did.
"You must decide who can enter Arstotzka and who will be turned away or arrested." I had expected that meant you got to decide, and that you would be judged based on what the people might do once in the country. But no. Accompanying you in the booth is an all knowing entity, that can instantly tell if you made a mistake. If the passport had an invalid issuing city, if the names didn't match, if it was expired, if the picture was wrong. Making your existence pointless. If they are able to instantly tell if I denied or accepted the wrong person, why the ♥♥♥♥ have an immigration inspector? Clearly the automated system works perfectly. I refuse to believe that in a low technologically advanced country, that they would be able to instantly know every mistake every single inspector makes.
And because of this all knowing system, it doesn't become about choosing who to let in or out, since you get fined every time you don't follow protocol to the letter, or make a mistake. (Again if they can see every single slip up, what is the point of the job? It is not just a crap job, it is an utterly pointless one.) It becomes about working as fast as possible to check the information, opening up stupid info, and since you get paid based on the number of people you process you often have to gamble if looking something up simply takes too long with the small space you have to work with.
I do think this game could be enjoyable, if the difficulty could be turned down a bit. So all the information you had to sort through could be on the screen at once, and you didn't have to look up or remember the things that were in the rule book about the different countries all the time, or if the time each day was longer, so you could get more people through.
As it is, I would only recommend it to people that want to play games that feel more punishing than difficult. Or those that just want a game that tries something interesting, even if not enjoyable.

Transistor, from the makers of Bastion, both games are among my favorites. Transistor and bastion have many similarities, and many differences. While bastions combat is based on weapons, and a couple upgrades for each weapon, in transistor, there is only one weapon, the transistor. Instead, combat is based around skills (functions) to use with the transistor, as well as being able to augment skills by equipping skills onto skills, and providing passive buffs by equipping skills onto yourself, that combined with the turn() function and a lack of environmental clutter made the combat feel a lot more varied and responsive. Unlike bastion, transistor doesn’t have levels with a hub, but rather has you progressing through a world with occasional visits to the ‘Sandbox’. While in Bastion, pretty much all information is centered on The Kid, in Transistor, everything is surrounding Red, but not really centered on her. The story is delivered in a similar, but different manner. Again, like Bastion, Transistor is not a particularly long game, around 8 hours. However, it’s well worth investing yourself into. P.S. gorgeous soundtrack, with or without hum tracks is subjective, personally I like them with humming, but even if you don’t plan on getting it, give the ost a listen.

Ingredients
1 duck (or chicken) breast, fat trimmed
1/2 teaspoon Chinese five-spice powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
1 teaspoon olive oil
1/2 pound whole-wheat pizza dough
3 tablespoons hoisin sauce
1 cup baby spinach, chopped
1/2 cup shredded part-skim mozzarella
1/2 red bell pepper, cored, seeded and diced
4 scallions, thinly sliced
2 tablespoons black sesame seeds
Preparation
Heat oven to 400°F. Sprinkle duck with five-spice powder, salt and pepper. Heat oil in a medium skillet over high heat. Cook duck until browned, 4 to 5 minutes per side. Transfer skillet to oven; bake duck until outside is cooked but inside is rare, 8 to 10 minutes. Cool 4 to 5 minutes. Thinly slice on the diagonal into 8 pieces, then cut each in half. Set aside. Form dough into 8 even balls, then flatten to form 3-inch disks and place on an ungreased baking sheet. Spread hoisin sauce on crusts with a pastry brush. Top with spinach, cheese, bell pepper and duck. Bake until cheese is melted and bubbly, 20 to 25 minutes. Remove and garnish with scallions and sesame seeds.

Originally, I really enjoyed this game.  The controls are straigtforward; there's a lot of freedom and choice; even the writing is good.  The game is also rather difficult and you die a lot.  That, in itself, is not an issue -- I like hard games.
The problem is that there is no penalty for death.  You simply restart from your last autosave... and that effectively removes all tension from the game.  Gameplay is no longer about survival, or getting rich, or being a badass fighter pilot.  It becomes a content treadmill where you grind through endless missions in order to upgrade your fleet... so that you can grind through more missions.
Even worse, death is very random and largely out of your control.  You can jump into a star system and be instantly killed by pirates.  Reload from your last autosave, jump into the same system, and there will be no pirates.  It's not like you made a bad decision (or even a risky decision) the first time; you simply moved forward, and the result was instant death.
I tried playing in my own personal "permadeath" mode, but that didn't work either.  The early-game is all about paying off a mountain of debt, and that gets very boring to replay.  As mentioned above, you die randomly all the time, so any "permadeath" session is going to be very short.
(Also, they're *pirates*, not serial killers.  It makes no sense for them to vaporize me, nor does it make any sense that they'd be so interested in my single, low-budget cargo ship.)
I have a recommendation for the developer: instead of having the pirates kill me, they could disable my ship(s), take everything of value, and leave me to drift in space.  Then, after they leave, I could get a loan, rebuild my fleet, and continue the story.

This is the themepark MMORPG for the Final Fantasy series. Final Fantasy XIV is its own game that isn't like the previous games but will reference many characters, bosses, monsters, areas and much more through its content from previous Final Fantasy games. If you have been a long time Final Fantasy fan you may enjoy playing this game by catching onto all the references, However, if you aren't a long time Final Fantasy fan you will also be alright because FFXIV does a very good job of attracting players who have never played any other of the FF series games or MMORPG before. I'll sum up my thoughts of the game below,
: Game is fun and can be enjoyed by old time FF series fans as well as new FF/MMORPG fans.
+Catgirls.
+Boob physics.
+Raid tiers split into usually 3 tiers
which consists of 4 boss battles/dungeon like encounters.
+Players can
craft anything that isn't current raid tier gear.
+3 Gathering and 8 Crafting Classes
+13 Combat classes with more to added with future expansions.
+Big in game world with more areas to be added with more expansions.
+Amazing Soundtrack.
+Good Storyline.
+Mounts/Flying mounts
+Quick travel to different areas
+Many minigames like Chocobo racing and triple triad
+Instanced dungeons with any players in your Data Center (Like matchmaking you get paired up usually as 1 tank/1 healer/ 2 dps)
+Exciting boss fights with specific mechanics.
+Glamour System - you can make your gear look like anything as long as your current class/job can equip it (i.e a mage can change their boots to different set of mage boots but not tank boots since they cannot equip them.)
+Regular raid difficulty with a Savage mode (Increased difficulty) option once the regular mode is cleared for loot.
+Good emotes, a lot of the emotes in this game are pretty high quality and look natural rather than rigged like in some mmd program by an amateur.
+Tutorial for roles, the game will give the most basic guidelines for what your role should do and reward you with armor and exp boosts for doing the tutorial instances. These can be done around level 15 before you enter your first dungeon.
+Mentor system for new players to get help from veterans with a dedicated chat for tips and guidelines from them.
-REALLY boring start, this game is fun but it does not do a good job of engaging new players into the game early on.
-Everything is segmented into different areas so you will be loading a lot for different zones.
-Textures can be pretty low quality for some armor pieces.
-Some teleport spots are awkward and require moving around somewhat long distances to get to designated quest areas
-Time gated content, you will not in most cases be able to rush to get your best in slot gear right away as there is a weekly cap for the currency/drops needed to trade in to purchase/upgrade certain pieces for gear. It is however easy to do as you can simply do certain duties that will give out a daily award(once a day) for the currency needed to buy those pieces.
I could keep adding more points but that would simply make this review more ridiculously long than it already is and I feel like I got the general idea of the game down for new players to look at. I enjoy this game very much and I would honestly recommend it to my friends. One word of advice I would give new players is to simply play the trial of the game and see how the combat and movement feels for them. The game has a slow start but it definitely picks up once you level up more.

Ah, Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn. What an MMORPG it is. Though, like many MMOs, it may be far from flawless, it still is a lot of fun to play since they ditched the atrocity that was the original FFXIV. Though some people may be sceptic at the idea of a subscription-based MMORPG, I didn't see many other MMOs where a sub fee was actually worth it.
To further convince you to pick up your blade and fight alongside many others, let me show you both the strengths and weaknesses of this AMAZING game.
- - - - - - - - Presentation - - - - - - - -
Be forewarned: You might need a somewhat good computer to run this game at a constant 60 FPS, even on the lowest settings, seeing as it is a Square Enix game and they ALWAYS focus on insanely good graphics.
You rarely come across two areas that feel the same, even within the same raid or dungeon, like e.g. the Crystal Tower gives off a calming vibe at first, before you reach the upper areas where it quickly increases in tension.
Furthermore, there are a lot of different music tracks that very rarely feel out of place and GUARANTEE there will always be at least one track you will love. Also, whenever they DO feel out of place, it still feels fitting due to the situation presented.
- - - - - - - - Gameplay - - - - - - - -
Since FFXIV also has a PS4 support, you can feel free to play with either keyboard and mouse like any other PC MMO, or with a gamepad for the console game feeling. And while some people might think the controls for an MMORPG couldn't work properly with a gamepad, it works WAY better than you may expect, so there's hardly a disadvantage in that.
Actually fighting feels a little slow, but satisfying. Every single job class feels drastically different from one another, even if they fulfill the same role in a group, e.g. the Marauder/Warrior feels very offensive for a tank compared to the far more defensive Gladiator/Paladin.
Also, you don't feel compelled to play through the story multiple times to learn and master each playstyle, since the system in FFXIV allows you to play multiple classes on the same character, not to mention carry over certain skills from one class to another, which gives a very rewarding feel to every single level-up you gain. In fact, FFXIV ARR even rewards playing as a different class than you started off as with a slight EXP boost, just so the level grind will go a tiny bit faster.
Also, whenever you go into a dungeon, you rarely feel overpowered, since the system will lower you down to a certain level/equipment cap if needed so you can run through a dungeon hundreds of times while still maintaining a certain challenge to it.
- - - - - - - - Community - - - - - - - -
The community within the game is way more cooperative and friendly than you would expect from a subscription-based MMORPG, though expect a few disappointed tanks or healers to leave the dungeon prematurely because of low-level content.
Rarely do you find a toxic or salty player, seeing as the majority are helpful and patient towards newcomers, and even if you find one leaving a dungeon prematurely, you can always search for a replacement via the duty finder.
- - - - - - - - End-game - - - - - - - -
With an expansion as popular as Heavensward and soon Stormblood, you would expect the end-game around the old level cap of 50 to be left in the dust, but nope. Even for people without the expansion, there is still a ton of end-game content like raids, crafting, gathering, arena PvP and the procedurally generated dungeon "Palace of the Dead". Furthermore, there are Hard Mode variants of a lot of bosses, like Ifrit, Shiva and Leviathan, so you can push the skills you've learned and honed to their very limits, which, if you aren't prepared, can take quite a bit of time to get down.
Crafting and gathering, while boring in most MMOs, feel like their own skills to be honed, since it isn't just "click button to gain item". Instead, like with the combat classes, you get a lot of skills to put to use and a lot of equipment to boost your chances of success. It even rewards the optimal use of skills by raising a crafted or collected item to High Quality status, which increases the stats or buffs an item or equipment piece gives you.
- - - - - - - - Expansion - - - - - - - -
Heavensward can be accessed after you've completed the main story questline from A Realm Reborn, giving you a HUGE new area to explore ranging from the snowy city-state of Ishgard over the mountains of Dravania up to the floating islands of Abalathia, as well as three new jobs to play with: Dark Knight, Machinist and Astrologian. All three of these jobs start off on level 30, making it much less compelling to give them a try and level them up for end-game use. Every job class gains 5 new skills through level-up from 50 to 60, sometimes helping whatever weaknesses they may have had, sometimes completely switching up the way you play them.
The story of Heavensward is quite a bit more serious in tone, but this little serious tone was admittedly needed with a conflict like that, and it gives the player a few moments to breathe inbetween the fighting, making it much easier for the player to adjust to the shift in tone.
In terms of end-game, the expansion has a lot to offer, ranging from the weekly challenges of Khloe Aliapoh over challenging the sealed primals of the Warring Triad up to the raid line that is the gigantic mechanical behemoth called Alexander, all of which have the potential to reward you with superb rewards like rare items and powerful equipment.
- - - - - - - - Verdict - - - - - - - -
Gameplay: 8.5/10 Some minor nitpicks like the slow fighting system, but still very good
Presentation: 9/10 Gorgeous graphics and amazing soundtrack, as to be expected from a Square Enix game of this scale
Difficulty: varies depending on dungeon/job class/group composition
Final rating: 8.5/10 A must-play for any Final Fantasy fan and/or MMORPG player

At first, I liked Mother Russia Bleeds. It's a fairly basic, cathartic, lovingly-drawn-in-pixel side-scrolling brawler that somehow takes the award from Hotline Miami for "Most Grimy, Violent, ♥♥♥♥ed-Up Game I Have Ever Played." I started out having enough fun with it, but as time went on the game revealed that its entire difficulty curve is composed of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, at least in my book, is gameplay design that allows players to lose health, die, or otherwise fail for reasons beyond their control. The main way Mother Russia Bleeds uses it is with stunlocking: every other enemy can get you in ridiculous long, damaging combos that leave you completely helpless for what seems like minutes, while other enemies hit you or prevent you from completing objectives that only have a window of a second or two where they're doable. You'll race toward an ally you need to quickly heal and keep alive, or a special enemy you have to kill as fast as possible, and some yahoo will jump out of nowhere and pin you down for a veritable eternity as that ally dies or enemy barrels towards you. Every single goddamn level is like this, and the bosses are somehow even worse. They've all got some dumb gimmick that takes forever to do, and none of them have health bars so you have no idea how far you are. The final boss, which has, like, four stages, took me SEVENTY MINUTES to kill, mostly because I kept failing when some pointless rando jumped on me just as I was about to do something important, and then his three friends joined in on the fun. What's more, because I used a health item at any point during that fight, I got the bad ending. ♥♥♥♥in' ♥♥♥♥ you, game.
Adding to this frustration is the checkpoint system. Not how it revives you; that's pretty good and forgiving, and is the only thing that got me through the game at all. It's a noticeably more infrequent towards the end, but that's a comparatively minor issue. No, the problem I have is with how often it saves; that is to say, only at the start of chapters, which are ♥♥♥♥ing far apart. The reason I didn't quit that seventy-minute marathon of a final boss halfway through and, I dunno, break an end table, was that if I did I'd have to redo the entire chapter before that. Another time, the game basically crashed right before a chapter boss, making me restart and losing me a half hour of progress. ♥♥♥♥. THAT. This is one reason why I advocate manual saves: as a backup against technical issues.
I'm certain Mother Russia Bleeds is better in co-op, where you can save your friends from all the stunlocks and hurt bosses way faster. However, in single player, it's just a ♥♥♥♥ing chore, one that I unfortunately cannot recommend. I want to like Mother Russia Bleeds, with its lovingly animated pixel violence and crunchy sound design and commitment to being completely tasteless and edgy, but it keeps getting in the way of its best qualities with its ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. It's a shame more than anything. Waste of a good opportunity.
Also, the dialogue is perfunctory ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and there's a ton of it. You can skip it, but still.

Short version: High concept, low execution. You get what you paid for.
Long version: It is a strong belief of mine that a choice-based game's choices should matter. In this one, they don't. Regardless of the decisions you make or events you choose to make reality, you end at the same point, with roughly the same in between. It gives a pretense of a very interesting concept! Framing two characters through their IMs is certainly a novel and dare I say effective way of showing a player a new kind of interaction. The lens to look through was there, and it was great: the problem was the material you were viewing.
Also, suspension of disbelief may have needed some help. Particularly, as an avid internet denizen since middle school, I know very well that not talking to someone at a different school for two months can kill a friendship through neglect. God knows what an entire year would mean. (Actually, we don't need God to answer this, I can: one less friendship, faded away into the void.) I feel like intermittent conversations would add so much to this game, in both believability and sheer amount of content. Because let's face it; it's short, even for a short game. Maybe I'm just a fast reader, but I know I blazed through it. Most of the gimmicks are icons and the like, anyways.
I feel like this game had a lot of potential, but I can't say it's a good game where it stands. Not worth the hour or so you'd spend playing it.

This game is the yin-yang to any Grand Theft Auto game. Where as, in GTA, you mostly use your guns to fight and melee as a secondary. In this game, that's the complete opposite, but it's oh so fun.
Pros:
-----
-Combat. The combat in this game is some of the most fun combat I've ever played with in a long time. Using Karate to punish all the gangs, who also use karate, and knocking someone out with a kick to the face. Couldn't be more satisfying. The gunplay however is nowhere near as fun, however it does play with a slow-mo mechanic which I kind of like.
-Choose your side. This game has a very interesting way to play. You can level up 2 different 'factions', and your level-ups for them are determined by how often you help one side or the other. It's kind of a play your own way thing, with no actual bearing on the main story, (to my knowledge) but it's pretty fun nontheless.
-Activities. There's an abundance of side activities to do throughout the game, and they're all either miscellaneous or faction-based. Needless to say I haven't done many myself, but the fact that there's so much to do beyond the main game is thrilling.
-Parkour. This one is a little more of a personal opinion, but I absolutely love the parkour in this game. Especially when you're chasing down a bad guy like a thief, or climbing over obstacles/climbing buildings to get a vantage point. This mechanic alone is what makes this game great for fighting and racing.
-Environment. Not that the setting of Hong Kong isn't a beautiful site to behold, but this isn't the point of this Pro. The environment always helps you in this game. Whenever you're in combat, you've obviously got your karate to keep you occupied, but what if that gets too boring? Well, grab them, and smash them into an air duct, or a vending machine, or just slam down a shop barrier on top of them. You can use dozens of these environmental hazards to K.O an enemy in an instant, and is oh so statisfying when you do it.
Cons:
-----
-Camera. Now this one is a big one for me, whether im running and i want to turn around, or im driving, and trying to back up someplace. The camera is constantly against you in this game, and is absolutely horrendous with regards to turning someplace. I've fiddled with a lot of the controls/sensitivity, but it doesn't seem to help. Giving the player good control of their camera is necessary for these kinds of games.
-Gunplay. I referenced this earlier in one of my Pros, but as much as I love the combat in this game, the gunplay is the one part that makes me feel iffy on all of it. First off, the gunplay isn't even that great, it's boiled down to a mediocre gunfight which anyone can win as long as you have cover to slow-mo out of. The controls for the guns are wonky as all hell, considering the crosshair and the precision you need for even the most basic guns is ludicrous. And the variety you get in actual guns is just lame. To my knowledge, the only 2 classes of guns you can get in the game are pistols and SMG's. Nothing more.
-UI. Now this one is a bit iffy for me as well, the UI in this game is OK at best. The mini-map for example seems a bit too small, the icons for getting to places, as well as collectibles aren't as big as they probably should be, the phone menus look like TRACFONE garbage, and there aren't really enough options that allow us to resize this part. As much as I love the rest of this game, the UI isn't a very strong point.
-Lack of Fast Travel. This game is huge, I mean, really huge. Perhaps if I could compare, I'd say *slightly* smaller than GTA IV. That being said, there's no method to fast travel in this game. Overall, a really solid game with a couple irritating misfeatures.
* biggest misfeature of all: the ORANGE and RED bubbles. They're the very *definition* of useless busy-work. The fact that there's a DNA option to pop them automatically is equally ridiculous - using up an entire ability slot to give you points you would have gotten anyways.
* lack of strategic variation. Maybe I've missed something, but the only viable strategy I've found is "keep severity as low as possible, infect everybody, then turn lethal". Once the game starts reacting to your disease's presence, there doesn't seem to be any way to stop the reaction. This seems odd, as I've watched the entire planet shut down land / sea / air travel over a case of the sniffles and stay that way for YEARS.
* use of permanent DNA points for one-shot activities. I get why things like zombie and ape colony movement cost DNA - there needs to be *some* way of rationing the use of those abilities. DNA doesn't seem like a good match, however, since its effects are usually permanent (evolving symptoms, transmissions, etc) versus a one-shot "move some Zombies over there". The pace at which DNA is awarded in the endgame can also make this painful - for instance, watching 200 million zombies starve to death in Russia while there are uninfected adjacent countries, all because you don't have the 4 DNA needed to MOVE the zombies.
None of these issues are hard to fix, so I have high hopes for this game's future.

NOTHING BUT GAMING CULTURE AND KATS!
Never thought I'd say this but there's just something weirdly satisfying about a game where your sole job is to do paperwork. Seriously, that's all you do!
In Papers, Please, you play the part of a lucky proletariat picked from a lottery to work at a newly established checkpoint between Soviet Union era-like satellite states. Your job is simple; prevent anyone with false or out of date paperwork passage in or out of the ficticious country of Arstotzka while letting the right ones in.
It's just a wacky good time, processing the flow of depressingly monotonal proletarians to the oppressive thrum of Soviet era propaganda music. The revolving door of characters you encounter are very human in their motives for crossing the border and includes concerned parents, arms dealers, and a beguiling hobo.
Your perspective is as limited as communication with the world outside the grey colored Berlin style city while juxtaposed color palettes off set the drabness of your surroundings. The sound is simple yet precise and at times, the compulsion to lick your thumb before flipping through another page of procedural nonsense is simply overwhelming.
The process is intuitive and not too precise in the sense that where you stamp or place paperwork is not a set thing, allowing for a kind of freedom that is severely lacking in more cerebral titles such as Papers, Please. As a result, you'll find that your in-game desk quickly becomes a reflection of your very own in terms of organization and tidiness. Expect the random pipe bomb thrown from the grey clad masses to disperse the crowd which will thus bring about more stringent and meticulous scrutiny from your bosses.
Check out Papers, Please if you're looking for a more cerebral challenge and have the desire to feel like another cog in an Eastern Block ghetto.

Transistor, from the makers of Bastion, both games are among my favorites. Transistor and bastion have many similarities, and many differences. While bastions combat is based on weapons, and a couple upgrades for each weapon, in transistor, there is only one weapon, the transistor. Instead, combat is based around skills (functions) to use with the transistor, as well as being able to augment skills by equipping skills onto skills, and providing passive buffs by equipping skills onto yourself, that combined with the turn() function and a lack of environmental clutter made the combat feel a lot more varied and responsive. Unlike bastion, transistor doesn’t have levels with a hub, but rather has you progressing through a world with occasional visits to the ‘Sandbox’. While in Bastion, pretty much all information is centered on The Kid, in Transistor, everything is surrounding Red, but not really centered on her. The story is delivered in a similar, but different manner. Again, like Bastion, Transistor is not a particularly long game, around 8 hours. However, it’s well worth investing yourself into. P.S. gorgeous soundtrack, with or without hum tracks is subjective, personally I like them with humming, but even if you don’t plan on getting it, give the ost a listen.

Decent gameplay. It gets fairly repetitive (especially the sandbox tests). The enemies change enough; different skills and weaknesses and combinations of types, but you can win pretty much any encounter by mitigating damage and waiting for your Turn() to come up. The limitors keep it interesting by ramping up the difficulty to frustrating levels.
Great music. For a mute former singer, you can spend a lot of time at the music player in the sandbox or simply holding Tab to hear Red hum.
Great art. The world backgrounds are very well done and you feel a part of it despite the limited interactivity. The themes and colors certainly do their part in telling the story.
There are a couple inivative moments in the game where you use skills outside of their normal realm; Turn() to be in multiple places at once, an attack to finish off a foe outside of traditional combat; that are one-and-done encounters. It felt like you were learning skills to use later and they were never revisited. A bit strange.
The game tells a good story in a fairly fun and undeniably beautiful environment. You learn more about the people of the world by using the skills in their various slots, making for countless combinations of attacks. And once you've made your way thought it all with your favorites, there's incentive to play through it all again with new access points, tougher opponents, and more story.

This is still an early Alpha version of this game, but even in it's rough state I was hooked. There are some bugs, and you can feel the need for a greater goal beyond building and maintaining your space base.  This game feels like a merging of Sims with the 90s classic Outpost from Sierra Online.

This is an excellent start to what the developers hope to eventually achieve with the game. At the moment you can build your base (including multiple rooms), take on new residents (meaning you'll soon need to expand your base to cope with the extra people), fight off hostile enemies, claim "derelict" bases nearby as an expansion of your main base, and assign each resident to a job, which they progressively get better at.
Eventually, you'll have a well-run base that is looked after by a team of highly trained staff, but to get to that point, you might have to survive a couple of scares near the beginning of the game (a meteor strike which leaves your base on fire when your technicians aren't well-trained to deal with it, or raiders when your security forces aren't trained up, etc).
In the future, the devs want to add depth to the game with a research system, job zoning, and so on. Once those are implemented, the game will really be something. I think there's enough for more than a few hours of enjoyment here already. Definitely recommended.

This is the themepark MMORPG for the Final Fantasy series. Final Fantasy XIV is its own game that isn't like the previous games but will reference many characters, bosses, monsters, areas and much more through its content from previous Final Fantasy games. If you have been a long time Final Fantasy fan you may enjoy playing this game by catching onto all the references, However, if you aren't a long time Final Fantasy fan you will also be alright because FFXIV does a very good job of attracting players who have never played any other of the FF series games or MMORPG before. I'll sum up my thoughts of the game below,
: Game is fun and can be enjoyed by old time FF series fans as well as new FF/MMORPG fans.
+Catgirls.
+Boob physics.
+Raid tiers split into usually 3 tiers
which consists of 4 boss battles/dungeon like encounters.
+Players can
craft anything that isn't current raid tier gear.
+3 Gathering and 8 Crafting Classes
+13 Combat classes with more to added with future expansions.
+Big in game world with more areas to be added with more expansions.
+Amazing Soundtrack.
+Good Storyline.
+Mounts/Flying mounts
+Quick travel to different areas
+Many minigames like Chocobo racing and triple triad
+Instanced dungeons with any players in your Data Center (Like matchmaking you get paired up usually as 1 tank/1 healer/ 2 dps)
+Exciting boss fights with specific mechanics.
+Glamour System - you can make your gear look like anything as long as your current class/job can equip it (i.e a mage can change their boots to different set of mage boots but not tank boots since they cannot equip them.)
+Regular raid difficulty with a Savage mode (Increased difficulty) option once the regular mode is cleared for loot.
+Good emotes, a lot of the emotes in this game are pretty high quality and look natural rather than rigged like in some mmd program by an amateur.
+Tutorial for roles, the game will give the most basic guidelines for what your role should do and reward you with armor and exp boosts for doing the tutorial instances. These can be done around level 15 before you enter your first dungeon.
+Mentor system for new players to get help from veterans with a dedicated chat for tips and guidelines from them.
-REALLY boring start, this game is fun but it does not do a good job of engaging new players into the game early on.
-Everything is segmented into different areas so you will be loading a lot for different zones.
-Textures can be pretty low quality for some armor pieces.
-Some teleport spots are awkward and require moving around somewhat long distances to get to designated quest areas
-Time gated content, you will not in most cases be able to rush to get your best in slot gear right away as there is a weekly cap for the currency/drops needed to trade in to purchase/upgrade certain pieces for gear. It is however easy to do as you can simply do certain duties that will give out a daily award(once a day) for the currency needed to buy those pieces.
I could keep adding more points but that would simply make this review more ridiculously long than it already is and I feel like I got the general idea of the game down for new players to look at. I enjoy this game very much and I would honestly recommend it to my friends. One word of advice I would give new players is to simply play the trial of the game and see how the combat and movement feels for them. The game has a slow start but it definitely picks up once you level up more.

Ah, Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn. What an MMORPG it is. Though, like many MMOs, it may be far from flawless, it still is a lot of fun to play since they ditched the atrocity that was the original FFXIV. Though some people may be sceptic at the idea of a subscription-based MMORPG, I didn't see many other MMOs where a sub fee was actually worth it.
To further convince you to pick up your blade and fight alongside many others, let me show you both the strengths and weaknesses of this AMAZING game.
- - - - - - - - Presentation - - - - - - - -
Be forewarned: You might need a somewhat good computer to run this game at a constant 60 FPS, even on the lowest settings, seeing as it is a Square Enix game and they ALWAYS focus on insanely good graphics.
You rarely come across two areas that feel the same, even within the same raid or dungeon, like e.g. the Crystal Tower gives off a calming vibe at first, before you reach the upper areas where it quickly increases in tension.
Furthermore, there are a lot of different music tracks that very rarely feel out of place and GUARANTEE there will always be at least one track you will love. Also, whenever they DO feel out of place, it still feels fitting due to the situation presented.
- - - - - - - - Gameplay - - - - - - - -
Since FFXIV also has a PS4 support, you can feel free to play with either keyboard and mouse like any other PC MMO, or with a gamepad for the console game feeling. And while some people might think the controls for an MMORPG couldn't work properly with a gamepad, it works WAY better than you may expect, so there's hardly a disadvantage in that.
Actually fighting feels a little slow, but satisfying. Every single job class feels drastically different from one another, even if they fulfill the same role in a group, e.g. the Marauder/Warrior feels very offensive for a tank compared to the far more defensive Gladiator/Paladin.
Also, you don't feel compelled to play through the story multiple times to learn and master each playstyle, since the system in FFXIV allows you to play multiple classes on the same character, not to mention carry over certain skills from one class to another, which gives a very rewarding feel to every single level-up you gain. In fact, FFXIV ARR even rewards playing as a different class than you started off as with a slight EXP boost, just so the level grind will go a tiny bit faster.
Also, whenever you go into a dungeon, you rarely feel overpowered, since the system will lower you down to a certain level/equipment cap if needed so you can run through a dungeon hundreds of times while still maintaining a certain challenge to it.
- - - - - - - - Community - - - - - - - -
The community within the game is way more cooperative and friendly than you would expect from a subscription-based MMORPG, though expect a few disappointed tanks or healers to leave the dungeon prematurely because of low-level content.
Rarely do you find a toxic or salty player, seeing as the majority are helpful and patient towards newcomers, and even if you find one leaving a dungeon prematurely, you can always search for a replacement via the duty finder.
- - - - - - - - End-game - - - - - - - -
With an expansion as popular as Heavensward and soon Stormblood, you would expect the end-game around the old level cap of 50 to be left in the dust, but nope. Even for people without the expansion, there is still a ton of end-game content like raids, crafting, gathering, arena PvP and the procedurally generated dungeon "Palace of the Dead". Furthermore, there are Hard Mode variants of a lot of bosses, like Ifrit, Shiva and Leviathan, so you can push the skills you've learned and honed to their very limits, which, if you aren't prepared, can take quite a bit of time to get down.
Crafting and gathering, while boring in most MMOs, feel like their own skills to be honed, since it isn't just "click button to gain item". Instead, like with the combat classes, you get a lot of skills to put to use and a lot of equipment to boost your chances of success. It even rewards the optimal use of skills by raising a crafted or collected item to High Quality status, which increases the stats or buffs an item or equipment piece gives you.
- - - - - - - - Expansion - - - - - - - -
Heavensward can be accessed after you've completed the main story questline from A Realm Reborn, giving you a HUGE new area to explore ranging from the snowy city-state of Ishgard over the mountains of Dravania up to the floating islands of Abalathia, as well as three new jobs to play with: Dark Knight, Machinist and Astrologian. All three of these jobs start off on level 30, making it much less compelling to give them a try and level them up for end-game use. Every job class gains 5 new skills through level-up from 50 to 60, sometimes helping whatever weaknesses they may have had, sometimes completely switching up the way you play them.
The story of Heavensward is quite a bit more serious in tone, but this little serious tone was admittedly needed with a conflict like that, and it gives the player a few moments to breathe inbetween the fighting, making it much easier for the player to adjust to the shift in tone.
In terms of end-game, the expansion has a lot to offer, ranging from the weekly challenges of Khloe Aliapoh over challenging the sealed primals of the Warring Triad up to the raid line that is the gigantic mechanical behemoth called Alexander, all of which have the potential to reward you with superb rewards like rare items and powerful equipment.
- - - - - - - - Verdict - - - - - - - -
Gameplay: 8.5/10 Some minor nitpicks like the slow fighting system, but still very good
Presentation: 9/10 Gorgeous graphics and amazing soundtrack, as to be expected from a Square Enix game of this scale
Difficulty: varies depending on dungeon/job class/group composition
Final rating: 8.5/10 A must-play for any Final Fantasy fan and/or MMORPG player

This game has some great music. Both from the general background music, to the songs sung[or hummed] by the main character. This couples with the great art of the characters, enemies and backgrounds makes it fun to just wander around, stopping to enjoy the scenery every now and then.
The story attached to all this is good, and you can find out about either by simply playing through the game, or by making different combinations of the modules, and exposing the history of the other people in the city.
The gameplay itself is also very good. It's a hack and slash game, but does require some thought and strategy planning if you want to go through it on a harder difficulty. There are a wide range of attack moves that can be chained together, and level of which you can use the modules to change the way the game works goes very deep.
The system the game uses for planning out attacks works very well, and the game does offer some 'side quests', I guess you could call them, which you can use to help refine and hone your playing skill.
As for replayability, the game offers quite a bit of it. You may not unlock everything the first time around, so it offers what is essentially a 'New Game Plus' mode once complete, to let you play again, but with previous unlocks and harder enemies.
This game has definitely become a favourite of mine.

Easily my favourite MMORPG, FFXIV is a well polished, highly enjoyable experience. The main story, while slow at certain times, is definitely a strong carrier of the FF franchise's name. The endgame raids are fun, well put together, with interesting mechanics and detailed locales. The lore is great, very deep and well thought out, such that nothing feels out of place. And of course the main gameplay for the various classes is engaging and challenging when trying to optimize your output.
With all that being said, there are still a few bad thing.
While the dev team does seem to listen, implementation of new, community requested features can take a long time to come about. A couple things that were asked for at launch are just now showing up years later.
It is a tab-targeting game, which turns some people off. It does it very well though.
Real money trading, although greatly reduced due to newer reporting tools, remains an annoyance on smaller servers.
As with basically any MMO, it can be grindy at times. Endgame content loop sends a fair amount of players I know on hiatus on occasion.
Personally, though, I have found FFXIV more tha na match for other MMOs on the market today.
