Pro 1: The Argument from Non-Cognitivism.
The following syllogism is taken from Magic8000’s debate1:
There are three attributes of existents which concern us particularly, these being:
Primary Attributes - The basic nature a particular thing is composed of. What a thing is, specifically, that it may do particular things or affect those around it in a particular way. The following two types of attributes provided below can only be applied to a thing if they can be related to an existent’s primary attribute and the primary attribute is positively identified
Secondary Attributes - Character traits or abilities a particular thing may enact or possess. examples: being generous, kind, powerful, wise
Relational Attributes – What we associate with the character. For example, in the case of President Obama, the fact that he is the President of the United States is an example of a relational attribute.
B as well as C are dependent upon and must be related to an existent’s A in order to be considered meaningful.
The term “God” lacks a positively identified A.
Because of this, the term “God” holds no justified A, B, or C. (From 2)
However, an attribute-less term (a term lacking A, B, and C) is meaningless.
Therefore, the term “God” is meaningless. (From 3, 4, 5)
Therefore, the god concept is invalid.
When someone says to you, "God exists", how do you normally respond? For most atheists, the answer is simply "prove it." However, this is a bit premature. Before we can get into whether or not God exists, we must first know what a God is. Indeed, many intellectuals have discussed and debated the subject as to what God is throughout history. The fact remains that from its original form, the ANC has stood as one of the most significant threats to the Christian/Theist worldview.
For example, consider the following dialogue2:
Mr. Jones: “An unie exists.”
Mr. White: “Prove it.”
Mr. Jones: “It has rained for three consecutive days—that is my proof.”
If this exchange seems less than satisfactory, much of the blame lies with Mr. White: his demand for proof was premature. Mr. Jones has not specified what an “unie” is; until and unless he does so, “unie” is nothing but a meaningless sound, and Mr. Jones is uttering nonsense. As W. T. Blackstone puts it:
“Until the content of a belief is made clear, the appeal to accept the belief on faithis beside the point, for one would not know what one has accepted. The request forthe meaning of a religious belief is logically prior to the question of accepting that belief on faith or to the question of whether that belief constitutes knowledge.”
Conclusion
Until my opponent specifies what a God is, the god-concept is invalid and “god” is just an utterly meaningless sound.
Pro 2: Incoherence of God’s Attributes
The following argument is tied in nicely with the last. Theists have attempted to provide us with a list of what God is. According to the 1968 National Catholic Almanac, God is3:
[A]lmighty, eternal, holy, immortal, immense, immutable, incomprehensible, ineffable, infinite, invisible, just, loving, merciful, most high, most wise, omnipotent, omniscient, omnipresent, patient, perfect, provident, supreme, true.
As you noticed, these answer the secondary attribute, but fail to answer the primary attribute. Moreover, and more important, the above definition is incoherent. If God is incomprehensible and ineffable, how can the other attributes of God be known if he can neither be understood nor described?
Anything with contradictory attributes cannot exist.
God has contradictory attributes

Games take many twists and turns throughout the preconception and development process, sometimes becoming totally different games. Overwatch used to be a MMORPG named "TITAN", Halo used to be a Mac exclusive RTS strategy game, and Grand Theft Auto used to be some lame nonviolent racing game, leading them to become some of the biggest names in gaming (maybe a bit too early to say that of Overwatch but that's besides the point). Today's subject started off like this. Originally going to be another part of the True Crime series as "True Crime: Hong Kong",  Activision cancelled it and it seemed like it would not see the light of day until Square Enix saved the project by buying it, leading to the game to later be released as Sleeping Dogs. Originally released back in 2012 to decent enough reviews, it was later rereleased in 2014 to open the game up to the new generation of consoles and desperately get some more money as it didn't meet financial quotas. Is the game worth picking up though or not though is the question, and that is what I plan to answer. Let's take a look.
STORY: You are Wei Shen, a man who returns to his native Hong Kong after years of living in the United States to infiltrate the Sun On Yee, an organized crime circuit that is beginning to dominate the streets of Hong Kong, in order to help the local police shut them down. The game essentially follows his climb to the top of the Sun On Yee foodchain, from a footman to the head of the organization. The story is alright if not a bit generic, it keeps you interested enough to keep it going, though I do have so say I am disappointed that the story is kind of linear. It would have been interesting to choose between the Hong Kong Police and the Triads in certain situations, though sadly the game is fairly linear storywise. That isn't a bad thing necessarily, I appreciate what they did and that's good, but don't expect an A+ effort storywise, because it feels a bit dull.
GAMEPLAY: Third person game, mostly fighting with some shooting thrown in. I'd recommend using a gamepad for the game as it's simpler for most of the gameplay in the game. You'll spend most of your time fistfighting, which is essentially a slightly watered down Batman Arkham system. X is attack, Y is counter, B is grab as well as some action buttons, and A is sprint, which is simple enough. Being a watered down Arkham game is not a bad thing, by the way, because it still feels pretty good. The gunplay in this game is also decent enough, even with a controller, which is nice. Driving is decent, though the cars do feel a bit floaty, and freerunning feels pretty good. Overall it handles very well I'd say.
GRAPHICS, PERFORMANCE, AND AI: 60FPS with decent amount of the highest settings on on 1080p. The game looks pretty good and Hong Kong looks and feels pretty realistic as far as I can tell from pictures and travel videos, which is nice, and it's cool to visit a different looking and feeling place than we usually visit in the world of gaming. There was a crash once or twice in the game, which is fine enough if not inconvinient. The AI can be a bit derpy at times, though, as sometimes the civilian drivers stop in the middle of the road and such.
CHARACTERS AND VOICE ACTING: Wei is an alright character, he doesn't make any stupid decisions that make you think "Oh you ♥♥♥♥ing idiot, what's wrong with you?" and at the end of the day I ended up liking him. The rest of the characters are decent as well, and I only ended up hating the one's I was supposed to hate, which is nice. The voice acting is top notch, a decent chunk of voice actors switch between English and Cantonese, which adds to the authenticity of the game. The character animations, on the other hand, look pretty awkward, almost like robots.
SIDE ACTIVITIES: There's a decent amount of missions out there to gain Face, which lets you get specific clothes and cars with each level. It's an interesting enough mechanic, and I don't mind it too much. There are a bunch of miscellanious collectables along the map as well; lock boxes which give you money, health shrines that boost up your health level if you use enough of them, and jade statues that let you learn a new karate move. The last two are pretty useful to get but I just forgot about the lock boxes after a while. There are also street races you can take part in as well as gambling and, get this,♥♥♥♥♥♥fighting. Not that you pervert, with chickens. Overall decent enough, if not barebones.
FINAL THOUGHTS: For a GTA wannabe game, this does a decent enough job to stand itself out. 7.5/10, it's worth picking up on sale if the location interests you or you're in the mood for a decent beat-em-up and you don't care about a kind of generic story.

Another stellar work by Supergiant games. A spiritual successor of sort to their smash hit Bastion, Transistor follows the story of Red and her adventure through the Cloudbank, aided by the mysterious power and sexy voice of the titular Transistor.
GAMEPLAY:
Transistor mixes up the Bastion formula of intense isometric combat with an added, optional 'planning' phase, during which moves and attacks can be preplanned and executed with lightning speed, at the cost of a few seconds of helplessness after execution. Like Bastion(you're gonna see that a lot, don't worry), there are several abilities, attacks, passive bonuses, and difficulty modifiers to choose from. Unlike Bastion, up to four can be equipped at once and each ability and attack has a unique secondary and passive effect, leading to a near-endless variety of loadouts.
Another departure from the norm is how death is handled. Rather than being shunted back to a previous checkpoint, upon death the player loses an attack. Even if the player survives with the remaining three, the lost attack is temporarily disabled and can only be restored after visiting enough save points. This encourages players to not become comfortable with any single loadout and encourages creativity, something not many games these days do.
STORY:
Like Bastion, the story of Transistor is one of ambiguity and successfully straddles the line between giving the player the power and freedom to interpret as they see fit and completely losing a player in confusion. Compared to Bastion, the story is far more linear, as opposed to the hub-world setup of Bastion. In a nutshell, things be happening in the city of Cloudbank and it's up to you and your Cyberpunk-MC Escher Buster sword to play sewage plant worker and sort that♥♥♥♥♥♥out.
Another noteworthy thingy about the story is how well integrated it is into gameplay. Your character, the Transistor weapon, your enemies, your allies, all seamless merge together into an impressive display of...well integration...for lack of a better word.
LOOKS:
GAWWWWgous. I mean, seriously. Wow. I mean it's Supergiant so it's kind of a given, but seriously. Completely or mostly hand drawn levels (at least they look that way. Bugger if I know how someone could 3-D model something like that) are the least impressive thing about the game's looks. And that's saying something. I speak no hyperbole when I say that just about every single moment in the game is screenshot worthy. Many are straight up wallpaper-quality.
GRIPES:
Autosave would have been nice. The game doesn't actually save at save points unless you interact with them, despite there being an animation whenever you approach one. I learned this the hard way during the final level and had to restart the whole thing after I messed up pretty late in.
Also it's kinda short. Clocking in at about 3 hours. Though that's not really a super serious gripe given how cheap the game was when I got it and just how dense those 3 hours are.
VERDICT:
GET()

This is simply one of my favourite ever games ever made ever.
I thought Super Giant's first game Bastion was pretty good, but I wasn't as in love with it as everyone else. Transister functons in much the same way in terms of movement, albeit with a more linearly layed out world.
The combat is where it really shines. You run around in real time battle, trying to avoid enemy attacks while your gauge fills, and at any time you can freeze time and used that gauge to plan out a sequence of attacks in order to for them to stack and do the most damage to as many enemies in a single move.
The attacks are unlocked and switched out like cards, and can be combined to give eachother bonus effects. It's really cool!
The story is nice. Not very detailed. Not anything special really, but like Bastion, the story feels superb because of how it's delivered. Again, it's narrated, but this time by your big glowing sword, which talks to you the whole game.
And of course, Darren Korb returns as composer and Ashley Barrett for vocals in a few killer tracks! Easily the best game soundtrack of its year.
It is a rather short game. If you made some time to sit down and spend a long evening with the game, you could knock it out in one sitting.

If you enjoyed Bastion, this one hones a similar style with a more strategic approach to the gameplay.
The stories are a bit similar, too. Transistor might be somewhat of a  repackage of Bastion.. But not with any small effort. It's like, they took Bastion and carved out most of the guts, ate the bones, too, and then put robots in place.
I enjoyed Bastion, and SuperGiant did an awesome job on the concept of Transistor. The length is just right on a normal difficulty playthrough.
Red, the main protagonist is wonderful to play along with.
Just buy it.

A puzzle game filled with objects so intricate they would make Lara Croft jealous.
The Room isn't a long game.  It can be completed in just a couple of hours or so.  But if you're a fan of puzzle games, it's a fun time.  The constrained nature of the game prevents it from being too frustrating.  You're confined to looking at one particular object at a time, such as a safe or box.  But the detail on each object is stunning, and the mind-bending nature of some of the puzzles makes for a fun time.
And hey, if you get stuck there is a hint system, although I feel like it pops up too fast.  It basically gives you about thirty seconds before it's like "hey, you stuck?"  And when that question mark appears in the upper-left corner you're usually just like "chill bro, just give me a minute...I got this".  The clues themselves aren't too obvious either...more like subtle hints directing you where to look (they might get more blunt if you're really stuck...I didn't use them outside of a couple times).
But don't play this game for the story.  While there is a context for everything, it's very sparse and not too fleshed out.  And the ending of the game is fairly unsatisfying.  It's basically a message that says "good job" and tells you to prepare for more to come.
Overall, it's a budget remaster of a mobile puzzle game.  And for what it is, it's a fun little time.

I really loved this game, but the sheer ballsiness of the developers on this project has caused me to have to flip my thumb downward. Instead of continuing development on this game, a potential gem for simulation games, they're finishing their current tasklist then moving it on to the community to complete the game. I could see this for $5, as a personal project from someone who doesn't necessarily need the money, but not from a renowned developer like Double Fine.
To avoid railing on the devs, who actually did a fine job
, there are quite a few things wrong with the game itself.
Pros
1. The few stylized art pieces of the game, especially the character portraits are really charming.
2. Base development is very interesting and lends a lot to imagination, since the base can be torn down and rebuilt as well. You don't even have to keep oxygen in the rooms. :)
3. The music is pretty catchy.
4. The UI is
clean.
Cons
1. Citizens sleep for an unreasonably long time. A bit over 4 minutes wouldn't be much time IRL, but considering that the game isn't running on real time, it's basically like taking a member of the community into a temporary community. If there's a tiredness stat, there's only one static way to rejuvenate it, and it takes forever. Might as well just skip making beds in the first place.
2. Raiders and other attacks are completely devastating to a young space station. Not necessarily a con, but having to stop working on a base expansion in order to tear down a docked station is a bit discouraging.
2a. You can't tweak any of these settings - meaning that raiders, pirates, parasites, (I don't believe Killbots are there yet), and meteor storms just happen.
3. Personal inventory is hastily implemented. Essentially it's just a clutter simulator now.
4. Space beds take up too much room, making personal bedrooms an undesirable solution. Yes: you wouldn't want to join a space station that doesn't give you a comfortable place to live, but I doubt that's a necessity when you're just trying to keep your people oxygenated.
5. No ability to customize characters or furniture.
6. Spacefrog logs tend to take up a lot of the dev log, but essentially it's just text-based in a personally unused section of the character profile panel.
7. Once your base is maxed out, there are few activities aside from keeping your food chain going, keeping oxygen/energy machines going, and patrolling the base. No hostile interaction, no other space bases to communicate with, no overworld map for shipping minerals back-and-forth, no super-future tech. Just more of the same, with decreasing intrinsic threat.
8. If you don't play by the dev's rules when entering derelicts, they're completely bugged. For example: if you want to enter a derelict by punching a hole in the wall and sucking the raiders out into the vacuum, then the derelict will remain hidden by the fog-of-war. You'd have to rebuild the wall then explore it with a security team (good luck if anyone's sleeping). After that, if you unclaim the rooms then they'll go back into FoW, iirc. There's an oxygen generator on the derelict? Oops, looks like your base's oxygen support counter just incremented and you'll need to unclaim it and quickly destroy it, good luck if anyone's sleeping. Or you'll need to unclaim it and wait for it to destroy itself, or get to it before it can go back under the FoW.
Basically, imagine if the Prison Architect guys quit this time a year or two ago. The game would still be fun and playable, but there would be just such a lack of depth.
This game isn't done. There is an entire host of ideas and game mechanics than can be iimplemented to make this game a true genre piece. Instead, the devs are just going to quit on it to go lurk behind some other title hardcore simulation fans probably won't buy.
Bah.

This game is not for everyone, wish it was but it is not. I could lie but I won't. Fair warning right now, this is the only game I know and known where spawn killing is not frowned on and is actually encouraged and is a must when playing competitively. This game is probably not good for post-millennials. It's not shiny (graphically intense), there is no in-game music (jamming to custom tunes is awesome though), requires you to type alot, (from talking to others to commands) it requires you yourself to play to get better (no dlc/in-game purchases to pay for to make you better), requires you to have fast hand eye coordination (especially if playing competitively), it has a steep learning curve (from the text commands to the games simple yet complex controls - there is a lot to take in and can be frustrating) and is not for the faint of heart (you may get called names via chat or after perfecting your ships controls for weeks, learn when going against a vet in a fight, you barely scratched the surface).
This game is amazing at wasting time and having nothing to show for it. This game is for those who have a deep and passionate competitive drive, from learning controls/ships/strategies/playstyles, doing lots of practice and fighting other players using nothing but 100% player skill vs player skill. (To this day as far as PVP gaming is concerned, this game is by far the BEST) This game is also for you if you have no ZERO competitive drive and just want to hang out with people (public arena's) and attempt to blow stuff up while making new friends or some new enemies. (I do this too mainly when I am inebriated or if there is no competitive matches for me) This game really caters to those seeking some retro, 2D gaming for cheap and are into the whole space/sci-fi genre.
*Free
*Can be habit forming.
*Takes place in space with a nice variety of ships to master. (NOTE: Ships 1 + 2 are most common in competitive play)
*Simple control scheme for most ships.
*Has a steep learning curve despite its simple nature that constantly challenges you, fending off boredom.
*Physics are awesome, especially for its time.
*Offers a variety of maps/zones to keep things fresh. (Trench Wars is the BEST. Sorry Extreme Games/Hockey Zone)
*Easy to mingle with people and make new friends.
*Caters to both people who just want to relax/hangout and those like myself who play competitively.
*Is staffed by dedicated players, you'll always get help and the competitive play is moderated by real people. (Getting help is a simple command you type into the chat. It is: ?Help YourQuestionHere)
*Has deep automated leagues with their own websites that collect your play data from every competitive match you've done. (Ex.


and MORE depending on what your participating in!)
*Squad creation and joining squads. Here is our squad.
(Some people I've met on my squads are closer to me than my own family, they are great. They can also be awful too but it's just part of the nature of them, working with potential strangers/friends for a common goal!)
*People are nice, warm and welcoming to newcomers.
*Much More! Going to stop here.
*Free = Lag Spikes (You WILL experience people not dying when shot at aka “eating” a bullet. It has been this way for me since 01’. It is infrequent, though happens from time to time. A good playstyle will prevent this from being an issue if you prepare that everyone you shoot might not die and have an exit strategy.)
*Can be habit forming. (1200 in 6 months.. I don't even play as much as I did in my teens when I really had no life.. for 16 years..OUCH!)
*Takes place in space with a nice variety of ships to master. (Mastery doesn't happen overnight or even over 3 months.)
*Simple control scheme for most ships. (It is frustrating because it’s so simple yet it becomes very complex when you’re learning playstyles like "sniper", "rusher", "bomber", especially in a competitive environment surrounded by veteran players.)
*Has a steep learning curve despite its simple nature that constantly challenges you, fending off boredom. (This gooes back to being habit forming for those perfectionist few..)
*Commands.. There is a lot to learn and game relies heavily on players using them.
*Hard for newcomers to pick up. (Just creating a ship/profile can be daunting, let alone everything else I touched on.)
This game has some barbed hooks once you get past the first few road blocks to get into it. Once you do though, you'll see why so many of us are still around playing it, 16+ years later. It's free too, for the potential hours of entertainment you'll have it’s a great deal. If you’re on the fence, check it out for yourself.
Thanks for your time.

So I bought Papers, Please on a whim. I didn't really bother looking at the reviews or researching much into the game. It was on sale, I had some extra money to use, I thought it looked vaguely interesting and Steam recommended it to me. For the longest time, I avoided the game. The more I thought about it, the more I regretted buying it.
But then I opened it.
Then I quit for a while because it was slow and boring.
BUT THEN I CAME BACK.
It was a much different experience than what I am used to in games, sitting and analyzing as quickly as you can, so risk losing everything.  I came to feel the path I was taking from cold apathy to the people behind the papers or forgiving sympathy, from the quiet, burning passion of hating the repressive government with all of my being to hating the group who dared destroy the life I was making for myself. The game makes you feel for what is going on around you while also forcing you to analyze at breakneck speed and I love it. After playing for so long, I have all of the issuing cities memorized ((except for a few hiccups)) and I find myself getting faster and faster every playthrough. I find this greatly satisfying, and I love the new procedures because they add a whole new element, even though they can be tedious sometimes, especially when you add the ocassional work pass. The game still manages to lace in well-placed humor, though, even when you're working at a job where you have to deal with miserable people in a desolate place.
Somehow, the way that your choices aren't extrememly consequential is also pleasing, because it shows that, in real life, certain things you do really won't matter in the big picture, but it mattered to someone, and that's what's important.
On to less of my feelings, the game play is smooth, although, at the beginning, it can be frustration to have to use your mouse for everything, but once you get a little further, the booth upgrades work wonders; plus, when you don't have the opportunity to upgrade, it's mostly in the part where you can cast a single glance at the documents and decide their fate. The game isn't very large, either, so it's easy to run on your computer without having to deal with much lag, unless you are severely overloading your computer.
I keep coming back to this game again and again when I want to get away from everything, and I would highly recommend it to anyone.

Mother Russia Bleeds is a phenomenal game, and without a doubt the best purchase I have made all year. Devolver Digital has once again delivered with a blood-splattered, high-octane, kick♥♥♥♥♥pixel game.
The gameplay is tight and responsive, with varying enemy types with different moves, all of which can be countered(Dive-Kick EVERYTHING). Stunlock foes are very annoying at the beginning of the game, but once you learn and master the many moves the game offers, you'll be punching your way to the Kremlin and back. Gameplay revolves around NEKRO, a drug that can either heal you or put you in a rage mode, and has to be regularly refilled of of convulsing corpses. Different strains of Nekro with different abilities can be acquired by reaching wave 10 in arenas, but that is much easier said then done. I have only unlocked one new Nekro strain, but this could also be because I do not play with bots. The game's bosses are also incredibly well done. They are difficult and may take some attempts to figure them out, but it is easy to figure out the bosses, and it is likely that an online guide will never be needed throughout the entire game.
The soundtrack to this game is absolutely incredible.
The only real "problem" I can see with this game is that the game doesn't save, and if you leave in the middle of a level you have to start it over, but that really wasn't an issue for me. Also, I feel like you either like the game or you don't. The gameplay is a turn off for many, but if you still hate the game by the third level, that's what the steam return policy is for, right?

Another stellar work by Supergiant games. A spiritual successor of sort to their smash hit Bastion, Transistor follows the story of Red and her adventure through the Cloudbank, aided by the mysterious power and sexy voice of the titular Transistor.
GAMEPLAY:
Transistor mixes up the Bastion formula of intense isometric combat with an added, optional 'planning' phase, during which moves and attacks can be preplanned and executed with lightning speed, at the cost of a few seconds of helplessness after execution. Like Bastion(you're gonna see that a lot, don't worry), there are several abilities, attacks, passive bonuses, and difficulty modifiers to choose from. Unlike Bastion, up to four can be equipped at once and each ability and attack has a unique secondary and passive effect, leading to a near-endless variety of loadouts.
Another departure from the norm is how death is handled. Rather than being shunted back to a previous checkpoint, upon death the player loses an attack. Even if the player survives with the remaining three, the lost attack is temporarily disabled and can only be restored after visiting enough save points. This encourages players to not become comfortable with any single loadout and encourages creativity, something not many games these days do.
STORY:
Like Bastion, the story of Transistor is one of ambiguity and successfully straddles the line between giving the player the power and freedom to interpret as they see fit and completely losing a player in confusion. Compared to Bastion, the story is far more linear, as opposed to the hub-world setup of Bastion. In a nutshell, things be happening in the city of Cloudbank and it's up to you and your Cyberpunk-MC Escher Buster sword to play sewage plant worker and sort that♥♥♥♥♥♥out.
Another noteworthy thingy about the story is how well integrated it is into gameplay. Your character, the Transistor weapon, your enemies, your allies, all seamless merge together into an impressive display of...well integration...for lack of a better word.
LOOKS:
GAWWWWgous. I mean, seriously. Wow. I mean it's Supergiant so it's kind of a given, but seriously. Completely or mostly hand drawn levels (at least they look that way. Bugger if I know how someone could 3-D model something like that) are the least impressive thing about the game's looks. And that's saying something. I speak no hyperbole when I say that just about every single moment in the game is screenshot worthy. Many are straight up wallpaper-quality.
GRIPES:
Autosave would have been nice. The game doesn't actually save at save points unless you interact with them, despite there being an animation whenever you approach one. I learned this the hard way during the final level and had to restart the whole thing after I messed up pretty late in.
Also it's kinda short. Clocking in at about 3 hours. Though that's not really a super serious gripe given how cheap the game was when I got it and just how dense those 3 hours are.
VERDICT:
GET()

I liked Transistor but I didn't love Transistor. The reasons are difficult to grasp. Its similarities to Bastion run deep yet it differentiates itself more than enough to stand on its own and everything it does it does well. I guess the world just felt a little more sterile, the story not as immediately penetrable and intensely engaging. I didn't feel like the narrator was talking about what I the player was doing like in Bastion. The chemistry between the two main characters is never really established. It feels super one sided. I mean... she can't speak but I guess that's part of the challenge of the design.
It was fairly short at 9hrs and I didn't feel like I was hugely challenging myself though I only stacked 2 limiters up. Its combat was cool but maybe felt a little bit limp compared to Bastion. I liked planning ahead. I like the RPG elements. I just never felt like a badass and never felt everything flow.
The cyberpunk world of Transistor is beautifully realised. The art style is quite a departure from Bastion's lived-in, beat-up wildlands. Transistor is straight-lines and ordered geometry. Restrained and readily coherent colour schemes. Like Bastion's world unfurled in front of you there's still a sense of jazz in Transistor's aesthetics as you explore its Escher-esque spaces.

I thought Super Giant's first game Bastion was pretty good, but I wasn't as in love with it as everyone else. Transister functons in much the same way in terms of movement, albeit with a more linearly layed out world.
The combat is where it really shines. You run around in real time battle, trying to avoid enemy attacks while your gauge fills, and at any time you can freeze time and used that gauge to plan out a sequence of attacks in order to for them to stack and do the most damage to as many enemies in a single move.
The attacks are unlocked and switched out like cards, and can be combined to give eachother bonus effects. It's really cool!
The story is nice. Not very detailed. Not anything special really, but like Bastion, the story feels superb because of how it's delivered. Again, it's narrated, but this time by your big glowing sword, which talks to you the whole game.
And of course, Darren Korb returns as composer and Ashley Barrett for vocals in a few killer tracks! Easily the best game soundtrack of its year.
It is a rather short game. If you made some time to sit down and spend a long evening with the game, you could knock it out in one sitting.

It's certainly

So I bought Papers, Please on a whim. I didn't really bother looking at the reviews or researching much into the game. It was on sale, I had some extra money to use, I thought it looked vaguely interesting and Steam recommended it to me. For the longest time, I avoided the game. The more I thought about it, the more I regretted buying it.
But then I opened it.
Then I quit for a while because it was slow and boring.
BUT THEN I CAME BACK.
It was a much different experience than what I am used to in games, sitting and analyzing as quickly as you can, so risk losing everything.  I came to feel the path I was taking from cold apathy to the people behind the papers or forgiving sympathy, from the quiet, burning passion of hating the repressive government with all of my being to hating the group who dared destroy the life I was making for myself. The game makes you feel for what is going on around you while also forcing you to analyze at breakneck speed and I love it. After playing for so long, I have all of the issuing cities memorized ((except for a few hiccups)) and I find myself getting faster and faster every playthrough. I find this greatly satisfying, and I love the new procedures because they add a whole new element, even though they can be tedious sometimes, especially when you add the ocassional work pass. The game still manages to lace in well-placed humor, though, even when you're working at a job where you have to deal with miserable people in a desolate place.
Somehow, the way that your choices aren't extrememly consequential is also pleasing, because it shows that, in real life, certain things you do really won't matter in the big picture, but it mattered to someone, and that's what's important.
On to less of my feelings, the game play is smooth, although, at the beginning, it can be frustration to have to use your mouse for everything, but once you get a little further, the booth upgrades work wonders; plus, when you don't have the opportunity to upgrade, it's mostly in the part where you can cast a single glance at the documents and decide their fate. The game isn't very large, either, so it's easy to run on your computer without having to deal with much lag, unless you are severely overloading your computer.
I keep coming back to this game again and again when I want to get away from everything, and I would highly recommend it to anyone.

I gotta say, the story is slightly random, the pieces do come together, but there are something that you have to deduce your self, which is why I can't give it a 10/10.
The music, without a doubt, it great and fitting for the game, I liked humming to tacks in the challenge room while I took a break. The art is great, I loved how it ran at around 60fps on my low end laptop, but I still go the full experience with the beautiful effects and cut scenes. I loved how you could combine moves and mix and match to get awesome combinations, I spent our seeing all of them, and each one differs from the other, and have draw backs too, but I'd live to see that sort of style be implemented in more games, where the player can become powerful through trail and error as well as intuition rather than just levels.
Now we get to the slightly sticky part, I liked the story and people seem to adore it, but it sometimes confused me for too long, it took too long to figure out what was going on, and there were missing pieces I was expected to figure out my self. The story felt random at times, definitely not lazy, but it was hazy, the sort of haze you have at the beginning of a hard hitting drama that starts midway through the story, and at the end it feels like you're still at the beginning of that plot, you get some character development from the extra reading, but most the characters are ones you bare no attachment to, I'd like to see more flashbacks and narration of the story. So All in all it's gets a 8/10 from me, I feel like the 9/10 are from the hipsters who thought the hazy story was a great addition that simpleton could never comprehend, but I'm someone who adores story rich games so finding one with a good set up only to be left semi confused is a valid reason for me to rate it slightly lower.

The game is not without flaws. Some skills are unbalanced. Sure, I haven't used all limiters, only three, but I have discovered a good build sometime around mid game and ended all late fights in first attempts without more than few scratches - I know, I could have cranked up the difficulty, but didn't feel like. Last 20-30 minutes of the game were a bit stretched and I hoped the thing resolved quickly. Finally, the game is short: 8 hours to complete is not much.

You enjoyed, not only the gameplay, but the story and experience of Bastion (Supergiant Games' much acclaimed title before this one). I'd recommend checking that one out first if you haven't.
This is an artistic experience more than a game.
I know, I know... what the heck does that even mean...
Transistor's strength lies in the way the story unfolds. The plot (and its twists) are excellent, the characters brilliantly designed and the visuals are outstanding (pretty much what we've come to expect from Supergiant games after Bastion). The combat is clever and good fun... but not ultimately what you keep coming back for.
And therein lies the one downside... the story is a bit short. It's not the fastest game to get into, and by the time you're hooked and going "hey, y'know what... this is getting pretty good" - It's actually drawing to a close. Slight shame, but still 10 very worthwhile hours (There is technically newgame+, but that has less appeal for me)
On the plus-side, at least the enemies also get stronger in NG+, so it's not like Bastion where you replay and just stomp everything flat with super-powered weapons. If you like the combat and challenge, that at least continues to deliver through the second iteration.
The combat itself is refreshingly unique. It's essentially about using Fallout-esque 'planning' time to compile devestating combos - combining strategy to an otherwise innocuous hack-and-slash. Throughout the game you acquire 'functions' which can basically be applied in one of three ways... as a 'move', to provide an added-effect to a move, or to apply a passive bonus. Bear in mind, you can only apply a function once and are limited to how many are in play - so there's a lot of variety to be had. You're encouraged to try out different combos (by unlocking backstory as you do) and the game is thankfully forgiving enough to let you experiment (i.e. there is no single 'correct' combo). It's fun enough but, as mentioned before, only goes so far in keeping the game interesting.
The gem is really the narrator again. Combining authorititive guidance with human touches of humour, emotion and vulnerability; it adds warmth to an otherwise (intentionally) structured, robotic setting. The part where he's spaced out is particularly entertaining (I lost it at "hey... that's not a bike..." and was too busy chuckling to realise I was dangerously low on HP).
If you enjoyed the experience of Bastion (not just the gameplay) - This should be well worth checking out

Community (If we can call it that is mostly pleasant although there is very little reason for any established group of players to invest any time into newer players. With limited duty finders and menu teleporting around the 'world' you cannot blame them). As a player I wanted to try the endgame savage raids but the duty finder was barren (1-3 party finder groups would spawn per week on my server. Serious players are best off getting a static but with the limited oppurtunities for "Savage" raiding and "training" on my server (Moogle) This was not possible during my time in Eorzea. With very little oppurtunities to practice Raids, static groups will most likely reject newer players. (As was the case with me)
I simply cannot recommend this game in the current state that it is in. Players looking to craft and enjoy a "theme park FF experience" will perhaps find much longer term satisfaction in this game than I did.

I had planned to do this review earlier, after having done my due diligence with this game and it's developers,
I can now complete this review.  With the Steam platform, theHunter and it's rightful owner Avalanche Studios
and developing partner, Expansive Worlds, a subsidary of Avalanche, which utilizes their proprietary Avalanche engine, this original game is nothing short of a typical and often seen "pay to win" game.  Yes, Avalanche brought us the "Just Cause" title series, so you expect a great game.  Listed as "free to play", which it is, but it is overly limited.
As many of the previous reviews have "warned" many of users who comes across this title, it is a CLEAR picture
of what the "bottom line" is here.  Yes, you can hunt animals, not all 40 animals, not with all weapons, and not
in all areas, without subscription.  It doesn't stop there.  To successfully reach all achievements, you will
have to spend additional money, outside your normal subscription rate.
While it is not uncommon for gamers to experience the ever-increasing titles of game using this business model,
I decided to watch two live streams from Expansive Worlds to garner a more in-depth of the game and the minds
behind the madness, so to speak.  On September 5, 2017, EW was streaming theHunter: COTW, considering the HYPE as of late, it took "them", the developers, the players, the people behind the madness 10 minutes to get the game on screen.  Shortly after that, it seemed the player didn't know how to play the game.  Just over an hour watching someone learning how to play the game -- I'm serious!
Moreover, while Twitch Chat was active and active viewers posing real questions about the game and not trolling,
the "bottom line" became all-to-clear within minutes.  This only continued on September 7, 2017 in another
just-over-an-hour long stream but this time theHunter: Classic was the game (they forgot to change the Twitch stream title).  Improvements were made with a BETTER player, someone that actually knew the game.  But the voice there, seen in the first stream on 9-5-2017, was the same.  The same British guy who wouldn't answer any Twitch Chat quality questions that the fans want to know.
It was appaling, to say the least.  The game, while it's release was in 2009, it's a decent game.  It's fun and
entertaining.  The world is nice, the play is nice.  However, in the back of my mind, these continous FLOPS from
the Twitch streams coupled with the inability to provide any insight into content or direction the title may be headed
in the future.  The current negativity received from their latest release of theHunter: COTW and it's failure cause
the business model is failing them -- it's just not enough.  Not enough for this user to spend $$$ for something
where the people behind the design, the people in-charge of where's the title is heading, are so inept at simple
things that any game development company should be highly skilled in was more than I could take.
I would not recommend this game to anyone for two reasons:
Deceit by omission
Inept personnel who continue to push a failing business model
Personally, this is clear as night and day -- two companies who had success some years ago, decided to revisit
the drawing board, make some cosmetic changes, and release a remake to garner a new audience because there are
more gamers today than in 2006-2009.  Apparently, old habits are hard to break as this pay-to-win business model
continues to deter many from a decent gaming experience.  But hard to be so critical, after-all they are European!

The launcher fails to download required patches leaving you unable to play the game. It seems the solution to fix this issue is to disable every modern security measure on your computer or install a third party program and maybe, just maybe, one of these "solutions" might work. (Spoiler: They won't.)

Well,
I know the game itself is fun because I've played on PS4 previously.  That being said apparently the problems on PC start after the Square Enix FFXIV launcher start trying to download all the game files that aren't delivered via Steam.
It fails during the download process with "Unable to download patch files" and then it list three sets of numbers which I assume are error codes.  There is no helpful information about the issue from the FFXIV support site.  I've requested support on that site repeatedly and they don't even respond.
What I've found is that their are entire threads all over the web and places like Reddit devoted to this problem.  People have written about various arcane solutions that require all sorts of config changes to the PC in an attempt to get this luancher to successfully download files.
Anyways my point is I am running a very high end gaming PC, I don't have internet problems as the support forums on FFXIV site seem to suggest, and my computer is not the issue.  The fact that every single game I download from Steam downloads at an average of 16.9MBps and installs without problems says a lot about the quality of the product Square Enix has put forth on the PC.  The best speed I've seen that launcher downloading files (until it inevitably fails) is about 8MBps.
What's more is I work in IT professionally and when I am home and not working I'm not going to jump through a bunch of hoops like Square-Enix suggest to try to get their launcher working.  It should just work and if it doesn't they need to patch it.
That being said I can't recommend this game because like me you may buy it and find that you can't even get the launcher to download the rest of the game.  Oh, and the included 30 days of game time start counting once you log in to the launcher and enter the games keys.
You've been warned.

"Now! This is it! Now is the time to choose! Die and be free of pain, or live and fight your sorrow! Now is the time to shape your stories! Your fate is in your hands!" - Auron
MMOs have innovated greatly and has always been the staple of open world traditional fantasy gaming since their conception more than a dozen years ago. All MMOs suffer the catastrophic sympton of the level treadmill and Final Fantasy 14: A Realm Reborn is no exception. What separates a great MMO to a good one is a subjective one, and while FF14 doesn't bring anything new to the table, it does what it does extremely well.
While not the most impressive MMORPG I've ever played, it certainly does grant a plethora amount of content to do. At first, I was afraid that FF14 was simply riding on its brand loyalty and kept my expectations low in case it was just another lackluster and half-hearted mess, but what I found instead, to my surprise, is a high quality MMO with superb art direction and average narrative. You are not limited to a single class or a single craft and are able to freely change between them at your leisure. While you are not granted as much freedom as you are in WoW, FF14 is still a worthy contender that deserves your attention.
I have played dozens upon dozens of MMORPGs over the years, starting from EverQuest II, Maplestory and WoW, to Japanese and Korean MMOs which are not available on this side of the world. Most of them are plagued with toxicity in the community or unfaithful publishers and developers. Fortunately, FF14 seems to have kept these pitfalls to a minimum and for the most part, are quite pleasant. Of course, nobody can really control how the community evolves and it all depends on the server you chose to reside in.
One of the most glaring issues I have found in FF14 so far is the lack of character customization options, which I think is mostly due to the fact that this game is still being supported on old-gen consoles. Many MMORPGs, even pre-2013, are able to support more options and basic sliders. Hopefully this will be improved in the near future. Another issue which personally I don't mind, but some players might, is the lack of evident PvP options and activities. Final Fantasy was always about collaboration and PvE content so I was not too disappointed by this.
Overall, Final Fantasy 14: A Realm Reborn is a solid MMORPG with very little flaws and should be praised for its high production quality. There are no free or paid MMO which is similar in vein, and should you be an MMORPG fan, at least give it a try.
If you are planning to get this game, be aware of which version you buy. If you buy FF14 on steam, you must buy everything else on steam. If you buy it off the official Square Enix site, you must also buy everything else on there. The customer support will not help you if you manage to muck up one or the other.
There are also numerous issues with the patcher itself as well. If I factored the patcher's quality into the score, it would be more like 3/5 or lower because of its glaring issues that needs immediate attention
. If you are getting errors of [30413], [25008], or within the 5.26 - 5.27 patch dates, you must use a VPS to solve it. Once you are past these patches, you may download the game via your normal speed again. I have a decent internet of 30/5 down/up, and it took me about two days to download the entire game due to this issue.

Overall yeah it's old, but it's plenty of fun, it's totally free (not p2w, not sub, not anything, just play for free).  There are no levels, no unleveled playing field based off time played, just experience and knowledge.

Update: As promised, I am updating my review because Minimum is finally playable again!
Minimum is a game that was pretty much left for dead somewhere in 2015. It was progressing steadily enough but then the servers went down indefinitely and the entire community was left with a bad taste in their mouth. Come 2016 however, we had news of a revival and in the last month or two the servers have come back up and there are improved features.
Minimum thrives off high-intensity, action-packed and extremely competitive combat. Whether you choose deathmatch or titan mode, you're sure to have a blast. One thing that makes Minimum stand out from the crowd, is its unique weapon-evolving system. When someone dies, they drop some fragments. Picking those up will automatically add it to your weapon, granting it a more upgraded form and more damage. This is one of the most fun aspects of the game, as you're essentially competing against other players in an effort to not only collect those upgrades, but keep them, because dying will cause you to lose all your weapon upgrades. But that's not all.
Minimum also has a similar armor upgrading system. You have three parts of armor which you can upgrade in a match. Each armor section has different benefits, and once you lock into an armor path, you can't switch it again. For example, if you choose the berzerker chestpiece, you have to continue to upgrade that specific item, and you can't swap it out. However armor pieces can be mixed and matched, so that you can have different chestpieces, boots and helmets. Dying does not cause you to lose these upgrades, so even if the enemy team is somewhat 'stomping', you have an opportunity to shut them down, and beat them with the right upgrades. Each weapon and armor piece has different attributes and abilities, so there's a ton of fun to be had here.
Titan Mode is one of the most fun modes I've played in any game ever. Essentially, each team is fighting to get their titan to the opposite team's base. There are a lot of things to empower titans, and seeing the massive struggle happen literally next to you is awe-inspiring and just plain awesome.
There is a pretty fun crafting system in place, allowing you to create or upgrade existing weapons, items and extras to be assigned to loadout slots. Weapons have a variety of effects and abilities so go wild and explore all that Minimum has to offer.
This game, is drop-dead gorgeous. It's like Minecraft or Trove, but without any of the crafting, and with highly detailed objects, environments and items. At maxed settings, the game's environments are sure to leave an impression on your mind, and yet the game is fairly well optimized to run on lower end pc's. The art style seems to be mostly futuristic and it really does this well.
The futuristic theme does not stop in the graphics department. In fact, the audio is even more so futuristic at times. Sounds in every part of the game are done very well, and combine with the already beautiful environments and interface for one pleasant package. Music is pretty entertaining, though there isn't much on the side of voice-overs; not that this game needs that necessarily.
There have been complaints about balancing items/weapons as well as the cash shop. This is one aspect of the game that I'm watching tentatively to see whether it will be addressed. At the moment, the game feels overall fun and fair in a deathmatch type-environment, but whether some items may be overpowered in a more confined, team-based setting is yet to be seen.
One thing is for sure, the current developers are actually working to get this game where it needs to be. Right now, I'm just happy to be able to experience the Titan mode once again, as well as the evolving crafting system. I believe Minimum is one of the first modern games to do this right.
A server browser has been added which is a breath of fresh air into the game, allowing people to actually join games on demand rather than wait for matchmaking.
I never thought this game would return, yet it did, and for what this game offers I'm glad it did. Minimum offers a fun, third-person shooter combined with a very unique upgrade system which makes each match just a little more different than the previous. It remains to be seen how much better this game can get, but the devs have already proven that they are willing to keep their promises, so for that I am willing to believe in Minimum again.
9/10 -

The servers were taken down for an indefinite time late 2015, due to reasons beyond the developer's control. The team has worked tirelessly to bring the game back into a playable state.
Before the game went down I spent a load of time on all 3 game modes. The combat is fluid and adaptable. Your character is responsive and agile. They are robust enough for new players to get into the game, but fragile enough that the element of suprise still plays a large factor in deciding who wins a 1 on 1 combat scenario.
One of the biggest criticisms of the game is that players using melee weapons are nearly invincible compared to other weapons. I've never had an instance where swords were decidedly unkillable, as mentioned in other reviews. Like any game, players need to adapt their playstyle to the weapon they use. Machine guns will not work well in cramped spaces. Likewise, swords are next to useless in wide spaces. Your weapon decides what lanes you take.
I have encountered two bugs, a texture error that does not affect gameplay whatsoever, and a leaderboard glitch that should be fixed with the new netcode the team is writing.
For me, the lack of gore is a huge bonus. I can play it with my young cousins without complaints from their parents.
When this game is playable again, I would recomend it to anyone looking for any type of non-military shooter.

This will be my third edit of my original review. I noticed the game had been updated and looked completely different so, I decided to give it another chance.
The original posting of Voxelized was a Minecraft clone where this new "version" is a medieval themed adventure. Here's my opinion of the new and "improved(?)" Voxelized:
I really like the look of the world. The lowpoly style is interesting and the world is quite beautiful. The animation of the knight is really pretty clean and the controls work fine.
These however are the only good things about this "game." Just like the previous version, there is NOTHING to do. You run around a very small walled in medieval city. There is multiplayer but there isn't anything to do with the other player. There is no way to fight. There are no goals to accomplish. You just run around with another player.
The game lists an achievement. It states all you need to do to earn it is play the game while it is in early access. I have played it quite a bit in early access and still have been unable to earn the achievement.
On another note, the name of the game is Voxelized. This made sense for the original idea. Now, the game doesn't in anyway make use of voxels so the name doesn't make sense. I don't know if this shows a lack of understanding of what voxels are from the dev or if they were just trying to get a new game onto Steam without going through the steps to get greenlit. It looks pretty shady to me.
If you look back at my entire review, you will see that this "game" has been in this completely unfinished state for over 2 years. This has been a major problem with this developer. Their games never reach a completed state. I haven't even seen one reach a playable state.
[First review revision] Pre August 2017
After noticing there was an update, I decided it would be good to re-evaluate the game. My original review can still be found at the bottom. Here are some things I saw after the update:
Improvements:
The textures look much better.
Blocks can be selected by scrolling the mouse will.
Selected block is shown in the lower left of the screen.
There are a few more block types.
Fly mode was added.
Things that could still be improved:
Flowers have collisions enabled so you can't walk through them.
Still no enemies to give the player a reason to do the things they are doing.
The player can only jump about 1 block high which makes it difficult to jump up a level.
All in all, this version of Voxelized is an improvement. However, I still can't recommend buying it.
[Original Review] - Pre November 2015
This should not be called an Alpha release. Even calling it a concept test at this stage is premature. The game is in such an early state, there is NOTHING to do. You can walk, jump and "POP" blocks (I say pop because of the sound it makes when you break anything) and that's it. The controls say you can place blocks by right clicking but nothing happens.
There is a grand total of 5 block types: all gray, all brown, half brown half green, all green and a white block with black lines on it representing what I suppose is a birch wood. When blocks are broken, they just disappear.
The truth is, I am really having a hard time calling this a game.
[Edit] - I figured out how to place blocks. The numbers 0 - 25 are in a column on the left of the screen. If you click one (other than the number 0) you will be able to place a block of the selected number. While a terrible design, I still think I should revise my review. There are actually 25 different blocks, not 5, that the player can build with. Does this in any way redeem the game? NO!

The game seems like it has potential, but it simply isn't even close to being there yet. Releasing it to the public in this state was a mistake. Everything feels extremely barebones, and I've encountered numerous bugs that forced me to start over (such as people getting stuck in an airlock). There's even a room type that does absolutely nothing (why even add it in yet?). I'm assuming said room will, in the future, function as a power plant for your station, but at the moment it's purely for decoration.
The character relationships aren't close to being where they should be, and it doesn't seem like there's any reason to build separate quarters for each character over one communal bedroom. I was looking forward to the inhabitants becoming friends, getting married, having kids, etc. At the moment it seems the only relationship types are "friend" and "enemy".
The random events seem limited to a debris pummeling your station, raiders arriving, and new recruits arriving. Debris is easily dealt with by installing a fire extinguisher in each room, raiders will leave if asked, and new recruits offer to stay no matter how poorly you're running your station.
I bought this game expecting to build my very own Babylon 5 or Deep Space 9, but it simply isn't anywhere close to being there yet. I'm very much looking forward to new features and improvements, but at the moment I cannot recommend this game. I do think that will change in the future if the game lives up to the potential of its concept.
Edit: Since I wrote this, Double Fine has announced that they're leaving this game an unfinished mess. Stay away. Far away. And boycott Double Fine.

Fingerbones is David Szymanski's first narrative horror game. While it is a bit rougher visually than his later games, it nails the sense of dread fueled discovery that made The Moon Sliver and The Music Machine so captivating. As the game lets you know from beginning, this is an experience meant to be completed in a single sitting. It's only thirty minutes long and there's no save system. The core of the experience – the narrative – is delivered through a series of notes scattered around a tiny building, a locked door cutting you off from the next set of revelations. There is little more to do here than read and open doors, but anything else would get in the way of a slow build towards the final, terrible truth.

This game is deceptively addicting.  The main goal is that you control the evolution of a pathogen (bacteria, virus, etc).  You choose where patient zero is (what country) and as more people are infected over time you earn DNS points that are spent to increase the infectibility of the pathogen.  Generally the goal is to infect much of the world without notice (avoiding the lethal symptoms) then develop more lethal symptoms (tumors, seizures, organ failure) to kill all the humans.  Once the pathogen is detected, humans will start researching a cure and the game becomes a race to kill off the humans before they can cure the pathogen.  In general the main pathogens (bacteria, virus, fungus, parasite, prion, biologic weapon) all play out similar to previous described.
The real fun are the 3 different pathogens (Neurax Worm, Necroa Virus, and Simian Flu).  Neurax Worm is an organism that inhabits the brain and takes control of the host.  You can force humans to take flights to infect other countries and eventually win by forcing the humans to worship the worm as a god instead of kill it.  Necroa Virus is a zombie plague and has some interesting events where humans try to band together to fight the zombies.  The Simian Flu was added recently for the Dawn of the Planet of the Apes.  In addition to the virus that infects the humans, you want to infect the apes to make them intelligent, form colonies, and ultimately fight against the humans.  In my opinion this is the best one and really shows the depth of the game.
There are also 10-15 specific scenarios that can be played and just over 100 achievements.  There are plenty of gene modifications to unlock in game increasing replayability.  All of this and the game is still Early Access!

The launcher fails to download required patches leaving you unable to play the game. It seems the solution to fix this issue is to disable every modern security measure on your computer or install a third party program and maybe, just maybe, one of these "solutions" might work. (Spoiler: They won't.)

Well,
I know the game itself is fun because I've played on PS4 previously.  That being said apparently the problems on PC start after the Square Enix FFXIV launcher start trying to download all the game files that aren't delivered via Steam.
It fails during the download process with "Unable to download patch files" and then it list three sets of numbers which I assume are error codes.  There is no helpful information about the issue from the FFXIV support site.  I've requested support on that site repeatedly and they don't even respond.
What I've found is that their are entire threads all over the web and places like Reddit devoted to this problem.  People have written about various arcane solutions that require all sorts of config changes to the PC in an attempt to get this luancher to successfully download files.
Anyways my point is I am running a very high end gaming PC, I don't have internet problems as the support forums on FFXIV site seem to suggest, and my computer is not the issue.  The fact that every single game I download from Steam downloads at an average of 16.9MBps and installs without problems says a lot about the quality of the product Square Enix has put forth on the PC.  The best speed I've seen that launcher downloading files (until it inevitably fails) is about 8MBps.
What's more is I work in IT professionally and when I am home and not working I'm not going to jump through a bunch of hoops like Square-Enix suggest to try to get their launcher working.  It should just work and if it doesn't they need to patch it.
That being said I can't recommend this game because like me you may buy it and find that you can't even get the launcher to download the rest of the game.  Oh, and the included 30 days of game time start counting once you log in to the launcher and enter the games keys.
You've been warned.

"Now! This is it! Now is the time to choose! Die and be free of pain, or live and fight your sorrow! Now is the time to shape your stories! Your fate is in your hands!" - Auron
MMOs have innovated greatly and has always been the staple of open world traditional fantasy gaming since their conception more than a dozen years ago. All MMOs suffer the catastrophic sympton of the level treadmill and Final Fantasy 14: A Realm Reborn is no exception. What separates a great MMO to a good one is a subjective one, and while FF14 doesn't bring anything new to the table, it does what it does extremely well.
While not the most impressive MMORPG I've ever played, it certainly does grant a plethora amount of content to do. At first, I was afraid that FF14 was simply riding on its brand loyalty and kept my expectations low in case it was just another lackluster and half-hearted mess, but what I found instead, to my surprise, is a high quality MMO with superb art direction and average narrative. You are not limited to a single class or a single craft and are able to freely change between them at your leisure. While you are not granted as much freedom as you are in WoW, FF14 is still a worthy contender that deserves your attention.
I have played dozens upon dozens of MMORPGs over the years, starting from EverQuest II, Maplestory and WoW, to Japanese and Korean MMOs which are not available on this side of the world. Most of them are plagued with toxicity in the community or unfaithful publishers and developers. Fortunately, FF14 seems to have kept these pitfalls to a minimum and for the most part, are quite pleasant. Of course, nobody can really control how the community evolves and it all depends on the server you chose to reside in.
One of the most glaring issues I have found in FF14 so far is the lack of character customization options, which I think is mostly due to the fact that this game is still being supported on old-gen consoles. Many MMORPGs, even pre-2013, are able to support more options and basic sliders. Hopefully this will be improved in the near future. Another issue which personally I don't mind, but some players might, is the lack of evident PvP options and activities. Final Fantasy was always about collaboration and PvE content so I was not too disappointed by this.
Overall, Final Fantasy 14: A Realm Reborn is a solid MMORPG with very little flaws and should be praised for its high production quality. There are no free or paid MMO which is similar in vein, and should you be an MMORPG fan, at least give it a try.

Update:
This is definitely a promising alpha, and many of the issues I'd mentioned in the previous version of my review have been fixed or improved.
- The technician AI is very much improved.
- I haven't run into issues with bartenders holding up people at the bar, except when I didn't have enough bartenders assigned, which seems reasonable
- Intruder defense seems more manageable now, though the actual mechanics don't seem to have changed.
- Haven't seen any more accidental depressurizations in a while
The only part that is still somewhat frustrating is the builder sequencing. While building walls and floors still seems to be prioritized above everything else, tear down or vaporizing unused areas is still prioritized above building other objects. I'd love to see a queue that I can prioritize, but failing that, at least making tear down/vaporizing last in the priority list would be an improvement. Even better than that would be only deprioritizing those tasks if they're part of unclaimed structures.
Some other issues I've noticed:
- Occasionally people will get stuck in airlocks and eventually suffocate
- There are sometimes odd placement issues with room objects randomly getting removed from the building queue, or sometimes not being able to place an object in a place that you should. I've had this happen with research consoles, beds, and rugs
--------------------------------------
Original Review
--------------------------------------
This looks promising, but in its current state, is not very fun to play. Most of the issues center around not-very-effective AI:
- In order to keep your base functioning, you need technicians to keep all the systems in repair. However, the technician AI is TERRIBLE, and there's no way to force a technician to repair a specific machine. The only way I've been able to play is to keep my base relatively small. Once a hostile docks with my station and as a result, adds more machines, it's an unrecoverable downhill slide to all machines eventually breaking down, no matter how many technicians I add. I've also seen my technicians attempting to repair broken machinery in areas I'm deconstructing, which is a huge waste of time.
- Your citizens need to eat. They also need to sleep. If they go to the bar to eat or drink, and the bartender isn't on duty, they'll wait until he is. Even if the bartender is, himself, waiting to eat or drink. The bartenders will not serve themselves, nor is there any sort of timer that allows them to give up and move on to do something else. There's also no way to force a bartender to go on duty. When your citizens get stuck waiting on food, it makes it very easy to start a downward spiral (especially for technicians) since they obviously aren't doing their jobs if they're waiting for food.
- Defending against intruders is incredibly unreliable. From what I can tell, you're supposed to assign citizens to security duty, and use a beacon to make them congregate in a specific area, either to explore or defend against intruders. In practice, they seem to take an "I'll get to it when I'll get to it" attitude, even when their comrades are getting gunned down around them.
- Sequencing building instructions is irritating - things seem to happen only in the order you enter them in - once you put in a request, there's no way to prioritize it against other requests, except to erase it and do it again, effectively putting it at the end of the queue. The exception seems to be building walls - those seem to get built before anything else.
- Citizens coming in and out of airlocks will occasionally kill their comrades by an ill-timed depressurization
Given this is an alpha, I'm guessing/hoping these issues will be smoothed out, but as it stands, it is more frustrating to play than enjoyable.

Hmmm, what to say about Fingerbones? Well, it's very short, and for horror games, short means you have to be creative with how you manage to scare the player.
Is it creative in that endeavor? I'd say yes, fairly so. Starting in a stark room with harsh light pouring through the window sets a very grim tone that definitely fits the eventual outcome of the story, and the way that the game progresses from there to progressively deeper and darker locations gives the game a good symbolic flow, but does it actually manage to scare the player?
Unfortunately, I'd say no. The game compensates for its short playtime by relying on the shock value of its horror, with the power of its reveals relying on the player being disturbed by the implications of the story. However, I feel that novelty is an important aspect of good horror, and while the final revelation this game provides is indeed terrifying, without having the time to build the necessary tension, it just comes off as cloying and cliche.
Also, the clarity of the clues given to help the player solve the few puzzles in the game, all of which involve entering various passwords into the same computer terminal, are a bit vague and when I finally figured them out, I felt more frustrated than clever for having done so. They also require the player to repeatedly backtrack to the starting room which sort of breaks up the tension that comes with descending into deeper and deeper darkness, which is otherwise the most powerful builder of fear the game has.
Still, it's not bad, not great, but it hits all the right marks for atmosphere, aesthetic, and tone. I feel like the creator absolutely has the potential for greater things, and for a free game that kills about a half hour, it's not bad, so ultimately I'd say give it a look.

The game is run by the ancient community of players who became so obsessed with the game that when the developer abandoned the IP  they rebuilt the game from scratch and kept going.
Sadly, the community is aging now, with the game being released in the 90's, many of the players have been playing for 20 or so years on and off. many of the game servers that still run have very small populations rarely seeing change and often running maps first made 20 years ago.  and the download times for these maps are horribad.
The only server that sees much in the way of population is Trench wars which you can always find a fight in. but I never found it all that interesting.
Servers in continuum have the ability to define and script thier own rules into the game, so you join and you are playing whatever thier rules are, there are two main active zones (servers)
Chaos:
which runs nearly stock subspace settings weighted towards faster upgrades and a more agressive pace of gameplay.
but these days rarely has any players hanging out in the public arena
Trench wars:
which runs ship balances that are task oriented, you have ships that carry other players into battle, and act as spawn points, you have long range heavy bombers, snipers and cloaked brawlers. you also die in one or two hits to just about anything.
this is the most populous server
In addition, unlike your standard game servers, each zone in subspace, actually has sub zones, called arena's  so, most new players won't realise that a server that looks empty might actually have players in it playing in a sub arena without anyone realising it. which doesnt help player numbers much.
With a steam realease, the game really needed some modernization and quality of life improvements but the original developers who once owned the IP of subspace long ago abandoned it and the people who programmed continuum, have probably moved on since then. and while, the older players all know the quirks and how to play the game, newer players will have a tough time adapting to use controls that are akward.
So, sadly, while I love the game and would reccomend people play it, I would also say. please. play it with a group of friends otherwise you will have a tough time finding a decent fight.
The game really needs a reworking or remake that captures the spirit of the original but opens the game up to younger players.
